Tuesday, 14th March, 1922.
LOCAL BILL (STANDING ORDERS
COMPLIED WITH).
Mr. Speaker laid upon the Table Report
from Examiner of Petitions for Local Bills,
that he has certified that the Standing
Orders have been complied with in the following case :-
Belfast Harbour.
The Second Session of the First Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to
meet 14th March, 1922, in the twelfth year
of the reign of King George V., was duly
opened.
The House met at Twelve of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker (the Right Hon. Robert William
Hugh O'Neill, D.L., M.P.) in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. D. H. Hackett, D.S.O.) was announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman
Usher said: I am commanded to inform this
Honourable House that the Speech of his
Excellency the Lord Lieutenant General and
General Governor of Ireland opening this
present Session of Parliament is to be communicated in the Senate forthwith, and,
further, I am commanded to invite this
Honourable House to attend in the Senate
in order to hear the said Speech.
Mr. Speaker, accompanied by the Prime
Minister and other Members, went to the
Senate.
On their return the Sitting was suspended
until a quarter after two of the clock, and
then resumed.
SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members who are returned for two or more places in any part of
Northern Ireland do make their Election for
which of the places they will serve, within
one week after it shall appear that there is
no question upon the Return for that place;
and if anything shall come in question
touching the Return or Election of any
Member, he is to withdraw during the time
the matter is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been elected or returned a Member of this House or endeavoured so to be,
by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices,
this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against all such persons as shall
have been wilfully concerned in such Bribery
or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been tampering with any
A
King's Speech.
King's Speech.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Witness, in respect of his evidence to be
given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from
appearing or giving evidence, the same is
declared to be a high crime or misdemeanour; and this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath given false evidence in any case
before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against such offender.
ROYAL IRISH CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of the
Royal Irish Constabulary do take care that,
during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets leading to this
House be kept free and open, and that no
obstruction be permitted to hinder the pas
sage of Members to and from this House,
and that no disorder be allowed in the precincts of or in the passages leading to this
House, during the Sitting of Parliament,
and that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at Arms
attending this House do communicate this
Order to the Commissioner of the Royal
Irish Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings, and
Records of this House be printed, being first
perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do
appoint the printing thereof; and that no
person but such as he shall appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges
be appointed.
OUTLAWRIES BILL.
Bill" for the more effectual preventing
Clandestine Outlawries" read the first time,
and ordered to be read a second time.
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to acquaint the
House that this House has this day attended
in the Senate to hear his Excellency's
Speech to both Houses of Parliament, in
pursuance of His Excellency's commande,
and of which for greater accuracy I have
obtained a copy. The Speech is as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commonsmoving the causes of delay and enabling
your Departments to cope with the difficult
administrative problems which necessarily
confront a new Government.
Your Parliament has been established for
some months, and the legal process of
transferring services to the control of the
Government of Northern Ireland has now
been completed. I regret that the transfer
of staff and the due allocation of property
and records to the Departments of Government have not proceeded as expeditiously
as might have been desired, and I trust
that means may shortly be devised for re-
I congratulate you on the manner in
which, in spite of these obstacles, the Departments of Government have been
brought so rapidly into smooth working
order.
I regret that Northern Ireland is still
faced with the serious problem of unemployment, but
am confident that the
Ministry of Labour is giving the matter
constant and sympathetic consideration.
The spirit of conciliation shown in Northern Ireland in the settlement of industrial disputes is tending towards a more
satisfactory state of affairs, and I trust
that spirit will continue to animate all
classes of the community.
I am glad to know that, acting in conformity with a decision arrived at by the
British Cabinet, the Cabinet of Northern
Ireland has decided to grant an additional
six weeks' benefit during the present
period of special distress.
Members of the House of Commons-
The estimates of expenditure on the
Services for the ensuing financial year will
be laid before you in due course, but owing
to the fact that your finance is largely
dependent upon that of the Imperial Parliament, it will only be possible to make
partial and tentative estimates until the
Imperial Budget for the coming year is
available. Every effort has been made by
'the Government to reduce expenditure to
the lowest possible limit consistent with
the security of the Province and the efficiency of its public services.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
It is hoped to lay before you measures
dealing with the following matters:-
The conferring of such additional powers
on the Government of Northern Ireland
as are necessary for the prevention of
crime, preservation of peace, and the
maintenance of order.
The continuance of the issue of Savings
Certificates.
The amalgamation of the General Nursing Council with the Central Midwives'
Board for Northern Ireland,
I
I
Debate on Address

Debate on Address
14 MARCH 1922.
The amendment of the Intermediate
Education (Ireland) Acts.
The Breeding of Cattle.
The Imperial Government is introducing
legislation for making permanent the
principle of Daylight Saving. It will be
for you to consider whether in this matter
you will remain in conformity with the
Mother Country.
It is hoped that the Committees dealing
with the improvement of Education, the
establishment of the Constabulary, the
system of Trade Boards and the Employment Exchanges in Northern Ireland will
shortly complete their labours. In that
event it may be found possible to introduce measures for giving effect to their
recommendations.
I pray that Almighty God may bestow
His abundant blessing upon your deliberations.
Mr. M'BRIDE: I beg to move-
"That an humble Address be presented to
His Excellency as followeth :
Your Excellency,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland,
in Parliament assembled, beg leave to offer
our humble thanks to your Excellency for
the Speech which your Excellency has
addressed to both Houses of Parliament of
Northern Ireland."
we
We are pleased to see that his Excellency
has recognised the great inconvenience which
has been caused by the delay of transfer
of records, etc., but we accept his Excellency's congratulations on the fact that,
notwithstanding the obstacles which have
been placed in our way, we have been enabled
to carry on so well our different departments.
I think a true note has been struck in his
Excellency's Speech when it mentions the
problem of unemployment with which
are faced at the present time; but we are
confident that, in the hands of the most
capable Minister of Labour and his reliable
staff, in the near future we shall be enabled
to grapple with that great problem. We also
appreciate his Excellency's recognition of the
conciliatory spirit shown by all classes in
the matter of trade disputes, which I would
venture to say is also largely due to the
confidence reposed in
Minister of
Labour by all sections of the community.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Coming to
the matter of unemployment benefit, we are
pleased to see that a decision has been
arrived at by the Cabinet which will enable
the Minister to extend the unemployment
benefits for another six weeks, which period,
we hope, will bring us to the end of the
great trade depression. Then we shall have
before us the Estimates, which we know will
be handled by our efficient Minister of
Finance. We are also pleased to know that
our
powers will be ere long conferred upon the
Government which will enable them to
grapple with the crime now so prevalent in
our midst, and which we are determined
shall cease at whatever cost, 60 that
everyone, no matter at what altar
he worships, shall not only obey the law, but
shall be protected by it. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Other Bills, such as Nursing,
Intermediate Education, and the Improvement of Cattle are, we believe, in the hands
of most capable Ministers. Upon other debatable Bills which will come before the
. House I will not touch, but before resuming
my seat I must thank the Government for
allowing me the privilege of moving this
Address. I do not look upon it as a personal favour, but as an honour to the many
thousands of loyal men and women in the
ranks of Labour I have the honour to represent in this House. I have now very great
pleasure in moving the Address. (Hon Members: Hear, hear.).
Mr. DUFF: I rise with some diffidence
to address you for the first time.
I am
aware that under such circumstances any
hon. Member is assured of the full sympathy
of the House. But I ask for their special
indulgence to-day, because the honour and
privilege of seconding the Address has been
placed on me. I take it as a compliment to
the great industrial constituency of East Belfast. In the King's Speech there are two
matters of vital and supreme importance to
the industrial progress of our Province; I
refer to unemployment and to the suppression of crime. This suppression of crime is
causing considerable trepidation amongst the
masses, and they are continually asking can
nothing be done to wipe this sordid
thing out of our midst. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.). We are particularly grateful
that His Majesty has seen fit to mention that
he will increase the powers of the Government to such an extent as to enable them
sufficiently to grapple with this terrible evil
and state of affairs.
Now, with regard to unemployment, this
matter presses very grievously on each of us,
and we admit that no Government, no political move, can cure unemployment. We are,
therefore, very grateful that the question of
the alleviation of unemployment is in such
capable hands as those of our present Minister of Labour. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). We feel hopeful that because
of the signal successes that he has
accomplished since he took over the
reins of office in settling the trouble in
Derry, the trouble in railways, and other
matters, these are an augury of hope
us that he will be able to
do something to alleviate the eorrows
and
the troubles that are consequent
on unemployment in our midst. We also
have to congratulate him that he is able
to guarantee to the workers in this great Province the utmost benefits that are secured by
anyone in Great Britain, and also that he
has been able to arrange the finances in
such a way that our members in East Belfast and in the other industrial constituencies will benefit by the six weeks' extension of the benefit.

There is one matter that I think is of vital
importance to us all, and that is the matter
of finance. We have
of what we have been taught and what
was practised during the past eight
years, and we are very happy to
see that the matter of private thrift, and
above all, the matter of public thrift,
receiving the closest attention of the finance
managers of this House. I would like just
at this moment to pay a small tribute of
praise to the tact, ability and timely as idu ty
of our Prime Minister in negotiating the
finances with the Imperial Government, so
that the Corporation, of which I have the
honour to be a member, was able to give considerable relief to the citizens during the past
month in the way of a reduction of rates.
We feel that under his supervision and his
helpful guidance we may look forward, if not
to a larger or even as large a reduction of
taxation, at least to some measure that will
put hope and courage into all our pioneers
of industry.
The necessity for the utmost supervision
over finance is of very great importance to
the whole Province; but I would like just to
remind the Members of this House and the

Michael Collins has told us frankly and

force us into bankruptcy. Mr. Speaker, forewarned is forearmed, and I think that he has
taken the wrong measure of the Province of
Ulster, and that all will give such support to

like to congratulate the Government on, and

Government are to be congratulated on their

The PRIME MINISTER: It is customary,
and it gives me very great pleasure to congratulate my hon. Friend, the Member for
Down, who has just moved the Address, and
my hon. Friend, the Member for East Belfast, who in such felicitous term has just
seconded the motion. I have listened to
similar speeches since the year 1906 in the
Imperial Parliament, and like the rest of us
here since last year in this Parliament,
and I can say sincerely that to meet the
occasion I have never heard words used so
fitting as those that have fallen from
my two hon. Friends. Before I proceed to
deal with some of the subjects that have
been mentioned by them, I would like to
tender my heartfelt congratulations and best
thanks to those who since we last met have
been in great danger and great difficulty. I
must, first of all, pay a fitting tribute to the
military, the Royal Irish Constabulary and
our Specials, not alone here in our midst,
but all along our borderland. The three
forces I have named are daily and nightly,
one might say hourly, carrying on under
great difficulty, and in many instances under
great danger. Our hearts beat with pride
when we consider what our Ulsterfolk are
doing in order to save the country from devastation, and in order that no reproach
may be cast on them, and that their determination to stick up for the old principles
has in no way diminished. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). I must also add to that how
much we all recognise the courage of the
people of Ulster as a whole who, faced by
provocation beyond measure, have shown
great fortitude, great patience, and have
upheld in the most worthy way the traditions which are attached to the name of
Ulster. Further, I think the House as a
whole, and certainly the country outside,
would desire that I should say a word or two
regarding those members of this House who
have also the distinction of representing
Ulster interests in the Imperial House of
Commons. We adjourned our House for a
considerable time in order that they might
take up the cudgels on Ulster's behalf at
Westminster, and those who have followed
the reports of the debates in both the House
of Commons and the House of Lords, will
have recognised the magnificent work that
our local members in the Imperial Parliament have performed. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
It is always very difficult on an occasion
like this to select any names for special mention, and if I say that all those who sit in
this House have put in their full weight,
and done their duty most manfully against
great odds, I will complete, I think, my
obligations here; but they themselves would
be the first to permit me to say a word or two
regarding the Leader of the Ulster Group in

For the convenience of myself-and I hope,

I would prefer to-day to ask-What

We have come through very anxious

to-day and to-morrow, I think it would be

that the Boundary Commission is still the predominant danger confronting the Loyalists of
Ulster. I can only say, with regard to the
question of the Boundaries, that it stands in
exactly the same position as it did when this
House rose; and I may be permitted to read,
for the convenience of those who may not

'We cannot consent to any alteration of
our Boundary except by mutual agreement,
failing which, in respect of any territory in
dispute, the Boundary to stand as defined
in the Government of Ireland Act of 1920."
By that we stand, and we intend to stand, no
matter what the consequences may be. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) It would interest the
House if I told them that I personally inspected the greater part of the Boundary
myself.
I was moved by what I saw in all that long
tour. I was struck, first of all, by the
moderation-the extraordinary moderationof those chiefly concerned in this vital question, and no more by their moderation than
by their determination-determination to
stand by every measure which is considered
necessary to protect our dear Borderland from
further incursion, or from being filched away
by Commissions or by anything else. It is
astonishing to find, when talking to people in
the Government, in the House of Commons,
and in society in London, the way in which
they will split hairs as to whether,
if So-and-so was Chief Commissioner, or the
number of Commissioners was five instead of
three, or if the question were narrowed down
to merely clipping the Boundary, would that
not satisfy us? My answer to them all is-
"Come across and talk to those on the Border,
and see for yourselves how any Commission
or any band of men can ask the Loyalists of
Ulster to go out from under the Empire and
the Union Jack, not necessarily into a
Free State, but very possibly into a Republic,"
because, if the tactics of our opponents can be
read by deduction, it looks to me as though
it were possible, at all events, that when the
Free Staters have got all they can from the
Government, the Republicans will say-
"Thank you very much; we will now take
charge of the machine." So it really is one
of the most serious problems that ever confronted a people, how to deal with the possibility-the bare possibility-of men, perhaps
more loyal than any of his Majesty's subjects
throughout the broad Empire-being requested, or possibly forced from their loyalty
to Great Britain and the Empire, and asked
to go into a Republic, or something which is
practically the same thing only under a
different name.
I can only say that this whole matter has,
from the start, given me more anxiety than
any other problem that has ever confronted
me with regard to Ulster. In London, on
several occasions, I have had very hard work
in getting the situation here properly under-

I turn to the second great difficulty that
confronts the people of Ulster, and that is the
unrest in our midst. The Speech which
has just been read has already indicated
that a Bill will be introduced giving power
to the civil authorities for dealing with a
situation which is a cause of grave anxiety
and alarm. The Bill proposes to give to
the civil authorities of the Government of
Northern Ireland power in respect of
matters within its own jurisdiction to take
all such steps as may be necessary for preserving the peace and maintaining order. The
civil authority, for the purposes of the Bill,
will be in general the Minister of Home
Affairs but he again will have power to delegate wide executive powers to officers of police
who are under his control. The powers, for
the exercise of which it is proposed in the
first instance to provide authority, are those
which have hitherto been exercised by the
Competent Military Authority under the
Restoration of Order in Ireland Act. Accordingly there will be scheduled to the Bill
in an adapted form such of those regulations
as in the opinion of the Government are
most useful for dealing with the present
state of disturbance. The Bill will also
give power to the Minister of Home Affairs
to amend the scheduled regulations or to
revoke or to add to them, and provision will
be made for regulations made by the
Minister being laid before both Houses of
Parliament. Offences against the regulations will be prosecuted under the authority
of the Attorney-General before the courts,
that is, the courts of summary jurisdiction,
consisting in each case of two Resident
Magistrates. There will be an appeal from
these courts to the county courts, consisting
of the County Court Judge sitting alone.
The court of summary jurisdiction will have
power to inflict severe sentences and heavy
fines. Special punishment will be authorised
by the Bill to be inflicted both by the
ordinary courts and the courts of summary
jurisdiction in the case of breaches of the
ordinary law, and offences against the regulations, where connected with the illegal
possession or use of firearms or ammunition.
The proposed penalty will be that authorised
by the Larceny Act, 1916 for robbery with

Before leaving London I settled down to
think out if ever there was a parallel in
the world to what is going on in the city
of Belfast, and had I discovered that in
America, Africa, India, or anywhere else,
similar conditions had ever prevailed, I
would have sent someone out charged with
the duty of discovering from the authorities

to the steps that should be taken here to
deal with this nefarious campaign. There
is no parallel. The nearest parallel is that
which is going on in the Rand at the present
moment, but that, of course, is one that has

Government troops pn the spot. I would
have the House bear in mind the smallness

one we have to deal with here. However,
not being able to lay my hands upon any
expert who could advise me on the subject
I took the step before leaving London of

(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and asking

I considered it only fair in asking so much

country has just paid him a tribute as

It is too early to thank him. He will know

Meanwhile I may take it that the House

May I take the opportunity of appealing on

authority, and to refrain from being provoked into illegal action of any kind, which
not only embarrasses the police and the
forces of the Crown, but also encourages

In dealing with this subject I have also
to announce that I tackled the Government
in London on the difficult subject of the
relations between the military forces and
the civil forces in our midst. I wish to
emphasise once more, in order that there
may no longer remain doubt in the minds
of the public outside, that the Imperial
House of Commons, and the Imperial House
of Commons only, through the Secretary of
State for War, can control the military
forces of this country. In other words, we
can only get on with the military here by
co-operation and friendly working together.
No one in this House, no Member of the
Government, has the power of ordering the
military to do anything. It is obvious that
the military forces, like the Naval forces of
the Crown, are Imperial forces paid from
Imperial sources and controlled from Westminster, and Westminster alone. One of
the difficulties in all these crises is that of
harmonising the working of the military
and civil authorities. I have to say that
the position in this respect has been greatly
improved. I have learned this morning
that my suggestions to His Majesty's Ministers have been adopted, that with the
incursion into our city of another battalion
to-morrow we will have six battalions upon
the spot, and those six battalions are to be
used in the permanent assistance of the civil
authorities, and not in a sporadic way as
has been the custom in the past. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I do hope that this
will be carried out in the spirit as well as
the letter of the agreement that we have
reached in London. Times are far too
serious to stand upon the letter of regulations regarding the Army or the principles
laid down for the co-operation of troops with
the civil authority. I believe that with the
gallant General Cameron, who has been sc
helpful to us, and who has only been
hindered by regulations from helping more,
we will get on better in this co-ordination

I have to congratulate my right hon.

That meant that as we had promised
to do, and as we were all most
willing to do, we

which voted down our hon. Friends in the
Imperial House of Commons carried the day,
our hon. Friends carried the argument to
the hearts of the people of the country and
of the Colonies, and it is really that which
matters so long as we steer the straight and
honourable course we are steering to-day.
There may be further unforeseen difficulties
which will come along-I cannot say-but
whatever they are my colleagues and I will
meet them with the same courage and the
same firmness with which we are prepared
to tackle the three problems to which I have
referred. Although I have gone through
these dangers and difficulties at some length
I do not want the House to break up without
appreciating the other side of the pictureand there is always another side to every
picture. The other side is, firstly, that we
are here in this free Parliament of our own,
not under a Dublin Parliament. We have
not been jockeyed into that position.
Secondly, we have our own Courts firmly
established, and I venture to say, with all
respect, that the conduct of these Courts,
the dignity, the justice, and the manner in
which they have carried out their work so
far reflects the greatest credit upon those
who are occupying distinguished positions
on the Bench. Thirdly, we have, perhaps,
the most magnificent force of Royal Irish
Constabulary and Special Constabulary
that was ever in Ireland during its
long history. They are those to whom
we
turn for assistance at all times.
We have also got the British people more
turned in our favour than
appears outwardly either in the Press or upon the
platform; and in spite of some of the gloomy
forebodings my right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance has steered the financial ship
through this year without having to come
to the House to ask for any Supplementary
Estimates, and without a penny extra
taxation on the people of Ulster, and I
think, and I trust, that he will have a small
balance at the end of the financial year. That
reflects great credit on his department. I
do not suppose that anyone expected when we
took up our duties here, with difficult
financial problems staring us in the face,
with grave anxiety across the water, that we
would be able to turn out in this first year
a satisfactory Budget, one that does not
show a deficit, and without extra taxation
upon the people. Not only that, but we
have not had to borrow a penny more than
the ordinary day to day requirements from
the bank. We have not had to issue a loan
or anything of that sort to raise money, and
consequently we start the new financial year
in a position at all events of economic
soundness. Moreover, owing to the British
Government having met us with regard to
compensation for malicious injuries the
taxation on many local authorities has
been considerably eased, and those who
are best able to judge of the situation tell
me that it may be possible for the rates in
future to come down still further. Not
only that, but in London there seems to be
a feeling that there will be a reduction in
taxation this coming year, in which,
and in all of which, of course, we in Ulster
here will benefit along with the rest of the
United Kingdom. Consequently, from that
point of view I think we have nothing to
complain about, and we may rest assured
that the same scrupulous care and economy
will be exercised by my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) in regard to the coming year,
with the single exception of the expenditure
of money on the protection of the lives and
property of our people. No man can put a
value on that, and therefore my pledge will
hold good that whatever is necessary will
be done to carry through that particularly
difficult task.
I think it would be unfitting for us to
pass over to-day without a word of commendation for the Civil Servants. I do
not suppose hon. Members themselves are
able to judge, but I can assure them, and
my right hon. Friends on both sides of me
can assure them, that, with a staff utterly
out of proportion to the amount of work
that had to be done, the few Civil Servants
here have worked in a manner which brings
the greatest credit to them and to their
departments. They have got us through
most difficult times, so that at the present
each department is practically in full working order. I understand that some of them
have suffered in health through the long
hours they had to work on account of their
fewness of number and the enormous tasks
which lay before the departments. My hon.
Friend has mentioned the question of unemployment. I can only say that we will
most carefully and most jealously look into

With regard to one point that was hardly
touched upon, namely, the question of
Summer Time, the position stands
follows: Owing to the desire that we all
felt that our Members should attend in the
Imperial House of Commons, we came very
near to the day on which we ourselves had
to meet, and with this very important measure to tackle as the very first thing when we
met-that is to say dealing with the disorders in our midst-I felt it would be very
necessary for us, in this our first year, to
harmonise with Great Britain with regard
to its time throughout the whole year, and
at the same time to prevent having a discussion in this House just at the very
moment when our time and energy should
be concentrated on a measure for the
restoration of law and order. I therefore,
arranged with the British Government that
they should embody Northern Ireland along
with the Channel Islands in the Bill dealing
with Summer Time; but-and this is an
important point-reserving the right of this
House to reverse the decision at any time if
it were so desired. That is to say, that the
Act which passes becomes a stereotyped and
permanent Act so far as Great Britain is
concerned, but so far as Northern Ireland
is concerned it is open to revision, at any
time the House feels so inclined. Since I
have returned here I have noticed in the
papers that Southern Ireland is adopting the
same time as Great Britain for this
particular year, and consequently I hope
that some of the difficulties which
anticipated will not arise. And now I have

I do not know whether he will think it

The PRIME MINISTER: As my hon.
Friend is aware I have had no further conference with any of the leaders of the Provisional Government since the time I met Mr.
Collins in Dublin. At that time I had great
hopes that the conference would lead to
peace and harmony in our midst. I went a
long way-a very long way-in meeting Mr.
Collins at all-(Hon Members: Hear,
hear")-but having met him, and having
entered into an agreement with him, as I
say, I was hopeful that the South would re-.
cognise that it could never get the North
except by winning her, by showing sound,
good government in the South, and that consequently the agreement would go through
from the first word to the last. The Press
has, I think, informed everyone quite accurately of what occurred. When I got into
the train to go to Dublin to meet Mr. Collins
to discuss further matters connected with
the Treaty, I took up a paper and for the
first time I recognised that he had a different view regarding the Boundary Commission to that which I held myself. That
was the first hint I ever had that there was
the slightest difference between us, and I
determined, even at the cost of jettisoning
all the other conditions of the agreement. to
have it out with him at once (Hon.
Members: "Hear, hear ")-because I felt
that if there were any difference between us
there was no agreement, and if there was
any difference the proper course was to
have it straight out and let the country
understand that something had taken place,
over which I had no control, which made it
impossible for us to agree. As the House
is aware, our hon. Friends have brought the
whole matter out in the Imperial Parliament, and have shown the great difference
there was in the matter of interpreting the
terms of the Treaty. That is a matter between Mr. Collins and the British Government, not between me and the other two.
I was prepared honourably to carry out the
agreement to the last letter, as far as I
could do, and I had taken long steps towards doing it as regards that part of the
agreement which applied to Northern Ireland. However, the difference arose, and it
was well it did arise, for we have been able
to make preparations which might have been
left lying in abeyance, and we might have
been living in a different atmosphere to what
we are to-day, an atmosphere of knowing
that a large section of Southern Ireland desires to coerce Ulster, to stir up strife, to
bomb her citizens, to snipe at them, and to
carry on their warfare to the very best of
their ability. We have discovered all that,
and it is far better that it should come out
now than when we were unprepared. I do
not think my hon. Friend (Mr. M'Guffin) will
expect me to say anything more on that today, but I can assure him that I have never

expressed any different view to that I expressed to this House on a former occasion
that Ireland wants peace (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear) and will never prosper, North

My concluding remarks will be addressed
not to those who are and have been in
danger on our borderland, but to those who
are on the borderland of this horrible campaign in Belfast. I do not know how to
speak unmoved about the anxiety of the
Loyalists living in certain quarters, with
wives and families on edge, unnerved by day
and by night by the awful happenings at
their very door, or at the end of their street.
I think I would like to couple the Government and this House in sending to them a
message of sympathy in all the sorrows that
have come upon them, and asking them to
trust us to do our very best to relieve the
situation and to help them in the terrible
times in which they are living. I know
many have the feeling that they are deserted
and not thought of. Such is not the case
at all. We are thinking of this problem
above all other problems, and we assure
them that everything that the weight of the
law can do to protect them will be done, and
that speedily. I do not suppose any people
in Ulster will welcome the news of the intervention at my request of Field-Marshal Sir
Henry Wilson more than those who are wondering when this murder campaign will
cease. If any man in the world is able to
devise something to meet these hordes of the
Irish Republican Army, these promoters of
rebellion, I would say that that man is that
gallant Ulsterman, Sir Henry Wilson. He
will bring comfort to these homes, and I only
hope the people will be able to bear themselves with the best fortitude they can until
we get his scheme into full working order.

Mr. LYNN: I would like to join with the
Prime Minister in congratulating the two
hon. Members who moved and seconded the
Address to the gracious Speech from the
Throne. There was no necessity for either of
them to apologise, because both showed how
very competent they were to take part in
debate, and I hope we will hear them both
very frequently in the discussions that take
place later on. I would like to join with
the Prime Minister in the tribute he has
paid to the Civil Service set up in such a
short time. I think myself the Civil Service is one of which this Parliament, as the
years go on, will feel prouder and prouder.
It is an excellent Civil Service, and it is
one, I am sure, that will not only do credit
to the great Imperial Service, but render
great service to Northern Ireland.
I was
glad to hear the Prime Minister say that
no extra taxation would have to be imposed
and that the Chancellor of the Exchequer
has managed the finances so well that he
will be able to make ends meet. May I be
permitted to congratulate the Chancellor of
the Exchequer on his recovery from illness?
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We all missed
him; we are all delighted to find him here,
and some of us hope that his grip on the
purse-strings will be even stronger than it
was before his illness.
Now, I come to the question of the Address. On reading the Address and listening
to the speeches of our two hon. Friends, one
would have imagined that they had never
heard of the City of Belfast recently. Does
this House realise that since the 1st January
83 persons have been done to death in this
city and 150 have been injured? Last year
110 deaths took place, and I forget the number of injured, but it was certainly
close on 2,000. For the ten weeks that have
elapsed we have had a murder at the rate
of more than one a day, yet the King's
Speech pays no attention to it. Hon. Members, glide over it, as if it did not exist.
Believe me, the citizens of Belfast are not
treating this subject in the same way. They
feel that they are up against anarchy, and
I am sorry to have to say it, they feel that
the Government is not doing what it should
do to throttle it. What is the Government
doing to stop this murder campaign? We
are told that new legislation is to be introduced, and I agree with the Prime Minister
that there is no necessity to introduce
martial law. People talk lightly of martial
law as if it were the panacea for every ill
of a criminal character. Martial law means
no law at all; it is simply the will of the
military commander. I agree with the
Prime Minister that it is most important
that civil authority should keep the grip in
Northern Ireland, and the civil authority
has got forces enough at its disposal to deal
with this menace-not only a menace to
peace but a menace to civilisation itself. We
expect the Government to do more than they
have. I am not going to go into details.
This is not the place, I think, for one to
suggest remedies, but there are many remedies that might be applied, and have not
been applied, and so far as the general public are concerned they are gravely dissatisfied, and I am sorry to say that there are
good grounds for the dissatisfaction at the
present moment.
It strikes me that this campaign of murder
has a twofold driving force behind it. Sinn
Fein-and I think there can be no doubt
about it has been stimulated and driven
on by the Provisional Government that has
entered into the Treaty with Great Britain
-the Treaty of Peace. And they are stimulating and carrying on this agitation for
the purpose of making the administration
of the Northern Government impossible, and
not only trying to make the administration
here impossible and make life intolerable for
law-abiding citizens, but working this campaign for the purpose of carrying on propaganda across the water. The Prime Minister
knows he has just come with others of us
from the other side-they are utilising what
is happening in Belfast and saying that
every arime committed was a crime committed by Protestants against Catholics. At
every corner we are met with the cry that
an attempt is being made to drive out the
whole Roman Catholic population, that we
in Northern Ireland are bigoted, intolerant,
and allow nobody to live except our
own. We know how untruthful that is. We
know, unfortunately, how many of the victims of murder are our own people
whether the murdered man or woman is a
Protestant or Catholic, is a matter that
does not concern me. I protest against murder in every shape and form. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Murder is a disgrace to
civilisation, and people are acting in this
city as if there was not a God in heaven and
as if there was no civil law to put them
down. To me the real seriousness of the
situation is that although 83 murders were
committed since the 1st January there has
been no one brought to justice. We are told
of reprisals. I have no doubt there have
been reprisals. Mr. Speaker, whenever you
read of reprisals in the country it is an admission that the Government is not promptly
dealing with the crime that has arisen and
that the people have got out of hands and
want to deal with it themselves.
I say,
I agree with the Prime Minister that it is
the business of every loyal man and woman
to rally round the Government and to help
the Government. I think every one of them
wants to do that; they want to help the
Government in every practical way, but they
do expect the Government to do something
itself, and something more than it has done
during the last ten weeks. I have told my
constituents often when they complained of
what
happening before the 21st
November to "wait until our own Parliament gets control." We have got control,
and I am sorry to have to say it, the position
is not better but worse than it was before.
It is time it should end. The Prime
Minister can make no demands on us that
we do not want to respond to; whether those
demands are made on the person or property,
we are prepared to respond most cordially to

General Smuts is dealing with the situation
there. It has only been going on for a few
days. Murder is going on there as
in our own city, but General Smuts
is
stamping it out with an effective
hand. I say it is the duty of the
Government to stamp out crime in this city
and make it possible for any man to walk
in the streets at any hour of the day and
night in safety, and until the supremacy of
the law is re-established you will not have
that. I do impress most seriously on the
Government as a friend of the Government
that a terrible feeling is growing up, and if
the Government does not stamp out crime,
then you will have a worse state of affairs
than exists to-day.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I rise this afternoon to try if I can say something in this
very interesting debate that may not have
been said by any other speakers up to the
present moment. That, I feel sure, will be a
somewhat difficult task, but there are a few
thoughts passing through my mind on various
matters that I would like to give expression
to, and that I would like an answer from the
Ministry upon. Since thie Parliament was
opened in May of last year we have passed as
a people through many difficulties and many
dangers. No new Government has ever had
so much to contend with, and I take leave
to say that, taking all the circumstances into
consideration, all the difficulties that our
Prime Minister and his Cabinet were up
against, have been met in the most
admirable way possible. I think, taken
as a whole, their actions have commended
themselves to this House, and they have
secured the confidence and the trust of the
people of the Six Counties as a whole,
No one could have anticipated in June last,
when his Gracious Majesty opened the Parliament, that in such a short time so many
serious questions would arise, questions driving at the very root of the Government that
his Majesty opened in person. What has
been the policy pursued by my right hon.
friend the Prime Minister and his colleagues
associated with him since the opening of that
Parliament? I think I am right in saying
that the one thing that they have consistently
pursued since that Parliament was opened
has been to try to secure peace in Northern
Ireland, and peace in all Ireland, if that was
possible to be secured. (Hon Members:
Hear, hear.) When I see in some quarters
to-day the criticisms-and very severe criticisms of the action of the Government of
Northern Ireland, I feel that the people forget exactly what the course we have pursued
from our establishment here as a Parliament
has been. Our Prime Minister at a very
early stage approached Mr. De Valera-perhaps I should not say approached, but met
Mr. de Valera. Some people thought that
was an unwise action. Other people thought
differently; but behind it, as I conceive his
action, there was shown not only great cou-

Then the next thing that occurs to me is
the history that followed that interview.
Immediately following that interview, the
British Government began to think of negotiating with Southern Ireland, and I shall
presently show what the result of their
action in that connection really was-what
the final result was. Although our Prime
Minister, as representing his people, offered
to meet the British Government and discuss
the whole question of the Government of Ireland, right up to the final Treaty, except by
informal meetings with Members of the Cabinet, the Government never considered their
attitude towards Northern Ireland, but negotiated with those of Southern Ireland as if
they represented the whole country, and they
arrived at a Treaty arrangement with them
in which we as a Parliament were never consulted, and they proceeded to insert a penal
clause in that Treaty-to give away territory
without our consent. What was the attitude
of our Government? Again a good deal of
criticism was made in regard to the interview
that the Prime Minister of Northern Ireland
had with the acknowledged head of the Provisional Government of Southern Ireland;
but I take leave to say that my conception
of the underlying thought in the Inae
Minister's mind in that connection was to
try again to secure peace, peace with honour,
to try to co-operate-if that co-operation was
possible-with Southern Ireland.
I do not think that any Member of this
House, or the inhabitants of Ulster as a
whole, desire in any way whatsoever to interfere with any Government established by our
friends in the South of Ireland. They desire
to see the South happy, prosperous, and contented, and we desire as far as we possibly
can to make the North a peaceful, happy,
law-abiding community. Now, the Prime
Minister in that interview tried to secure cooperation between the North and the South,
and I think I remember a speech of his when
he stated that the South would benefit by
the prosperity of the North, and the North
would benefit by the prosperity of the South,
and he has consistently pursued the policy of
trying to co-operate for that one great
supreme purpose. The foundation of any
State, its prosperity, its development, its
strength, its stability, begins upon the recognition of law and order. By respect for those
great principles you will be able to build up
a country; and in seeking to do all this the
Prime Minister, I take leave to say, was rendering splendid assistance to Ireland as a
whole, which we desire to see redeemed
from its present state of disorder and strife.
We desire to see the North and South both
prosperous, and co-operating together, if such
a thing were possible.
Now, what has followed since then? Those
who say we as a Parliament have any desire
to coerce the South, or have any aggressive
intention in regard to them, are mistaken.
What followed after that interview? A few
short weeks elapsed, and the territory of
Northern Ireland was invaded by men from
Southern Ireland, whether with the consent
of the Provisional Government or of the Republican party we cannot tell; but the result
was that some of our leading citizens were
captured and taken away. From the estabsum nt of te ister arment ia su o
last there has been no unkind act by this
Parliament, or the Cabinet of Northern Ireland. Any aggression, any opposition, any
bitterness or strife that has been shown, has
been shown by those in control of the affairs
of Southern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Now, that takes me up to another
point. Who is to blame for the present unfortunate state of affairs-I will not say in
Southern Ireland; I do not want to criticise
anything in regard to their actions-but who
is primarily responsible for the unfortunate
state of affairs that exists in Northern Ireland to-day?
If we have unfortunate bloodshed, if we
have bitterness, if we have disappointment,
if we have a community whose loyalty has
been tested in days gone by and whose loyalty
has been sorely tested during the past three
months, the British Government when they
proceeded to interfere with the Act of 1920
without the consent of the Northern Government and tried to break up the arrangement
that was solemnly arrived at, and promptly
proceeded to break the pledges they made to
Ulster-the blame of all this strife and bitterness that exist to-day must be put at the
doors of the British Government, and cannot
justly be placed at the doors of the Northern
Government, who have tried to carry on
under the most difficult circumstances that
any Government established for the first
time has ever had to contend with.
Now, I come to what is closely linked up
with the last point. The Prime Minister
informed us in that very interesting, very
able, and very comprehensive speech he
made yesterday that he is seeking special
powers in order to bring peace to this
distracted Province of ours, and to try to
get at the criminals who are disgracing the
land they belong to. He has told us he is
going to get the best advice possible-the
advice of a gallant Ulsterman, Field-
Marshal Sir Henry Wilson. Again I see
that our critics tell us that this is a provocative act, that we are going to proceed to
wage war upon the people of the country.
I think that all classes in the community,
whether they are Protestant whether
they are Catholic, no matter at which altar
they bow, should be delighted to know that
our Government is trying to get the best
advice and the best assistance they possibly
can to protect the community, to put down
crime, and to make the lives and property
and the privileges of the citizens not only
of Belfast, but of every other district of the

the Minister of Finance is here.

refer to. The question of unemployment has
been raised to-day by three separate speakers.
Now, the function of any Government is not,
after all, to find employment for the people.
It is to try to get the causes that create
unemployment removed. I am tired reading
about this dole that the majority of these
people are receiving. The more doles we give
out to the unemployed the more you
impoverishing your own State, so I say that

better it will be for the community and the

not going to get rid of the legacy and inheritance we have received from past British
government in this country, you are not going

Irish Constabulary no country ever boasted--
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear) and they have
received very shabby treatment. (Hon.

receiving orders from here, there, and

and they have done wonders under

in which they are placed, they have rendered

hope that we in this Parliament will do our

come into our ranks and serve the Ulster

the same degree of capacity and ability with

Members: Hear, hear.)
There are other matters which I leave to
some other speakers to deal with. The
gracious Address of his Excellency covers a
great many subjects which would afford
splendid themes for interesting debate. I
really regret the fact to a certain extent
that we have been deprived of a debate on
what is known as Summer Time. I am
afraid we would have more than summer
time in this House had that particular
subject been discussed here by those who
take an interest in it. If I understand the

after this year the right of this Parliament
to determine that question for itself. I
think that is so. I see the Channel Islands
are protesting against the action of the
Imperial Parliament in the matter, and I
take leave to say that questions of this and
a similar character which affect our people
as a whole must, in the future, be determined by our own Parliament, and not by
the British Government.
Taking a survey of the whole position, as [
can understand it to-day, I take leave to say
that although we may see dark clouds here
and there upon the horizon, although we feel
we are up against a very serious position,
although we may feel in our hearts a degree
of bitterness, to which expression cannot
possibly be given, against the British
Ministers who have tried to deceive us and
break their pledges to us-they do not, in my
judgment, represent the masses of the British
people at all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I believe that Ulster is right in the attitude
she has taken up, and I believe that the
principles for which we stand, and which we
seek to vindicate, will yet be vindicated by
the vast majority of our friends in England,
in Scotland, and in Wales. I have no doubt
at all that, if our people restrain themselves,
and if the leaders of the people do their very
best not to get the people into a despondent
mood, but will encourage them in every way
they possibly can not to outstep the law as
laid down, the difficulties we are up
against will in due course disappear. I have
been from the foundation of this Parliament
an optimist in regard to Ulster, and I am still
the same. I believe that, with the hearty
co-operation of all concerned, we will surmount our present trials and difficulties. If
our people throughout the Six Counties will
not only be true to themselves, and true to
all that their past stands for, but if they will
loyally co-operate and give all the assistance

scattered

known as the Free Staters and the Republicans, a distinction in my opinion without
a difference, for I firmly believe that ultimately they will all aim, if they are not at

There is a unanimity of ideas and of policy

North you have a population which is far

always to make it a menace to those
who govern in this area.
If you
take the entire nine counties I suppose they
are in the proportion of eight to six, that is
Protestants and Catholics, and if you take
the Six Counties comprising our present
area, they probably would be in the proportion of two to one. Those proportions
are formidable enough for those who are
going to contemplate the government of the

You have the border difficulties. You have
in the first instance the area in which we live
invested by those we call our enemies. We

Act of 1920 has been placed under the government of this Parliament. What did the
Prime Minister tell us yesterday? That it
was a most unreliable condition upon which
to operate. Those are not exactly his words.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Many of the speeches
made here to-day and yesterday have contained allegations against the Government
for its neglect to restore law and order in
this city. I am not here to apologise on
behalf of the Government, because I hold
that in no sense has this Government been
negligent, nor have we failed in our duty. I
ask hon. Members to consider the present
condition of affairs and to realise what has
led to the condition in which we are living
at the present time. One would think, to
listen to the speeches made here that up to
the time this Government took over control
Belfast was a happy and peaceful city and
had never heard the sound of a gun or the
explosion of a bomb, and that this condition
of affairs is solely due to the neglect of this
Government. What are the facts of the
case? In July, 1921, the Imperial Government entered into a Treaty with the Irish
Republican Army.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: A truce.
of
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS:
And under that truce, to which this Government was no party, all the operations of the
Imperial forces of the Crown against the
Irish Republican Army were suspended, prosecutions under the Restoration
Order in Ireland Act ceased, and
under the orders of the Imperial
Government recruiting for the Royal Irish
Constabulary and for the Special Constabulary ceased. The B" members of the
Special Constabulary were ordered not to
function, and from that time right down to
the time when this Government took over
control on the 22nd November-because up
to that time the service of law and order
was in the hands of the Imperial Government alone-the Irish Republican Army proceeded to re-arm, re-equip, and re-organise
their forces. Arms and ammunition were
imported into Belfast, drilling with arms was
carried on, rifle and revolver practice was
indulged in, and all in the presence of the
police, who under orders from the Imperial
Government were unable to interfere. În addition to that, Sinn Fein Courts were established, and the police were ordered not to
interfere.
This was the situation which confronted
us when this Government took over on 22nd
November, 1921. This Government had to
meet the re-organised and re-armed forces of
the I.R.A. with a depleted and unorganised
machinery. What were the forces that
we had to deal with? The forces which we
had available for this purpose were the
military, the entire control of which remained in the Imperial Parliament; the
R.I.C., which remained for discipline, pay
and promotion-a most important thing in
regard to the Constabulary force-under
the control of Dublin Castle, and the only
force over whom this Government had complete control was the Special Constabulary,
a force which since its inception in 1920
the authorities in Dublin Castle had done
their utmost to discredit and discourage.
The total number of men in the R.I.C. in the
area of the Six Counties when this Government took over were 2,324, while today that
force numbers only 2,279; the Special "A”
Constabulary numbered 3,515, and to-day
there are 4,346, and we are budgeting for 1,000
more and are recruiting. When we found
that condition of affairs on the 22nd November the first thing this Government did was
to throw open the ranks of the "A" Constabulary for recruiting purposes. They could
not do that in regard to the R.I.C., because
that was a force over which the Imperial
Government had control, and a force, which
as an encouragement to these men to serve,
they announced their intention to disband
at an early date.
But I tell hon Members here that it is
entirely a different thing from recruiting,
You cannot make a policeman in a day.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Therefore,
we are suffering for the period that lapsed
between the 7th July, 1921, when the Truce
was entered into, and the time we took over.
Now. I want to clear up a matter in regard
to the question of the use of the troops.
There seems to be a great deal of misunderstanding in regard to this matter. It
has long been the established custom in the
British Army, and under the regulations
providing for the use of troops in aid of the
civil power,
that troops are not to be
brought out to the aid of the civil power
until that power has broken down, and then
only with the approval of the officer commanding those troops, but that practice was
broken through by the Imperial Government at the time when they found it
necessary to introduce the Restoration of
Order in Ireland Act to deal with the situation created by the I.R.A., and accordingly
troops were used jointly with the police for
the purpose of restoring law and order.
In other words, troops were brought out for
what I may describe as preventive purposes
rather than being brought out. after the
mischief had been done for curative purposes.
After the truce the Imperial Government, no
doubt with the idea that war with the I.R.A.
was over, decided that the old custom should
be reverted to, and that in future troops
should not be brought out in aid of the
civil power until that power had
broken down. These regulations, I
suggest to this House, were framed for
conditions other than those with which we
are confronted here to-day, and I say here
that it is a disgrace to think that troops are
not to be brought out until the citizens of

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
our city are shot down by skilled members
of the I.R.A., and such a policy could only
emanate from the Government that made
the terms they have with the I.R.A.
Now, what was the attitude of this
Government towards the I.R.A. since we
took over on the 22nd November? The first
thing we did was to order our constabulary
to refuse to continue the liaison arrangements with the Irish Republican Army or to
recognise that force in any sense as a
legalised one.
Mr. COOTE: Do you mean the old Constabulary?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS:
I refer to both. We refused to admit the
principle that the members of the I.R.A.
should be allowed to stalk through the
country armed, even though they may
happen to be disguised as footballers.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I may also
add that we refused to allow Sinn Fein
Courts to operate, and I venture to say today that I do not know of a single Sinn
Fein Court that is operating. What was the
result of the policy which this Government adopted? On the night of the
1st December, the very night that we took
over the administration of the prisons,
two of our constables were brutally and
callously done to death in an attempt on the
part of the I.R.A. to rescue certain of our
political prisoners. Then followed organised
raids along the border under which many
law-abiding citizens living in our territory
were kidnapped. Then we were informed by
the Irish Free State that these men should be
held to ransom until this Government released the prisoners that were in their lawful custody. We refused that demand, but
what followed?
were
Our Special Constabulary going through
the territory in Southern Ireland, which the
British Government was still responsible
for,
attacked. Many of their
numbers were butchered, and some of them
are still in the custody of the Irish Free
State. Notwithstanding the representations
of the Imperial Government they still remain
there. After these raids took place this
Government at once despatched police out of
this city. We had to reduce an already insufficient police force in the city, because
this Government had to consider other places
outside Belfast. A new demand was now made
upon this Government for the release of
Sinn Fein prisoners, but we still declined to
release any of them. What happened? The
Irish Republican Army proceeded to put
into force in Belfast the same policy that
they had put into force in the South
of Ireland, and which to them had been so
successful; a policy directed towards making
Government impossible by a campaign of
murder against everyone who refuses to bow
the knee to Sinn Fein. In that policy they
attack every link in the machinery for enforcing law and order, whether it is the
public who are anxious to come forward to
give evidence, the police, or the prison
administration, and when they are brought
to justice they profess to ignore our courts.
I say here to-day that if this Government
had acceded to the demands of the Irish
Republican Army to release the prisoners
that were in our lawful custody this murder
campaign would have ceased. A Dublin paper
stated the other day that the only way to
put an end to strife in this city was for the
North and South to cement their political
differences. I suggest to this House that
there is more than a political difference at
stake. There are differences of principle, and
certainly this Government is not going to
buy peace at the sacrifice of principle. But
this murder campaign still goes on. I hold,
and I have always held, that under these
circumstances it is the duty of the Imperial
authorities to place the troops of His
Majesty at the disposal of this Government.
The primary duty of the police is to preserve
the peace and not to do the work of soldiers.
The Northern Government at the present
time is faced with the same situation here as
that which confronted the Imperial Government in the South of Ireland. As a Government we are precluded from raising an army
of our own, and as long as that is so I say we
are entitled to have the same unrestricted
right to use the troops as the Imperial
Government has. Suggestions have been
made that this Government were negligent
in making requests for the use of troops,
and that they did not realise the seriousness
of the situation. May I say that requests
were made again and again that troops
should be supplied. We asked that troops
should be placed at fixed points in anticipation of trouble and not after trouble had
broken out.
I would like to refer to the way in which
General Cameron, the officer commanding
the troops in Belfast has, so far as lay
within his power and so far as he could
carry out our wishes in accordance with the
views of his superior officers, come to our
assistance. But he was tied by his superior
officers, and 30 late as 20th February he laid
it down that troops will not be detailed to
provide protection for persons and
businesses, or for what they regarded as
police work, and later on, in reply to further
representations he stated that the battalions
in Ulster amounted to 13 and that he considered these were "sufficient to meet the
emergencies." The military authorities
were again warned as to the necessity for
providing troops for preventive purposes,
but the reply was that
"More troops can be supplied when
there is any military necessity for it; that
the General Officer Commanding did not
consider that any such necessity exists;
that he was not prepared to employ the
troops in the manner suggested by the
Divisional Commissioner nor to recommend
such employment, and could not imagine
that the Imperial Government would consent to a manner of employing troops so
inconsistent with the regulations laying
down the duties of troops in aid of civil
power."
We have passed the stage for regulations
for the use of troops. The Imperial
Government must recognise that we are at
war with the Irish Republican Army. The

result of this failure to supply troops has

to say a more effective one, and that is the
punishment that is inflicted upon the criminal. But before you can inflict punishment
you must, first of all, get a conviction, and
before you can get a conviction you must

time is that of obtaining evidence. I do
appeal to the law-abiding citizens for their

duty of bringing criminals to justice should
not rest entirely in the hands of the police.
There is another matter I would like to refer
to. When we do get criminals convicted I
find that in many cases petitions are sent in
to the Home Office signed by some of the
most representative citizens in this city praying that a criminal should get out. I venture
to say here that if many of the people who
sign those petitions would take the trouble
to investigate the true facts of the case they
would not have appended their signatures to
the document. It is a most embarrassing
position when one is trying to enforce the
law to find efforts being made to weaken our
administration in this direction.

But do not let us be under any delusion. We are not going to get peace in a
day.
The only way we are going to get
peace in this community is by breaking the
power of the Irish Republican Army in the
Six Counties and by insisting, so far as regards the administration of the law, that it
be vigorously carried out. Justice will be
fairly and impartially administered to all,
irrespective of creed or class, and the
distinction hitherto recognised by the Imperial Government shall cease the distinction between a political criminal and an
ordinary criminal. Let me say a word about
the police, both regular and special. These
men carry their lives in their hands, and
those citizens who are free from attack will
realise how much they owe to them. It is
easy to criticise. It is easy to say that these
men are not doing their work. The citizen
claims, and rightly claims, that he is entitled
to protection as a ratepayer, but do not forget that there is also an obligation imposed
on every citizen to come to the help of the
police, and in my opinion this obligation has
by no means been fulfilled. Stories are
circulated as to the neglect of their duties
by the police, but it is peculiar when it
comes to the point no one is available who
is an eye-witness.
Now with regard to the "B" Class Specials.
These men voluntarily carry out an onerous
and dangerous duty; but what has struck
me is that they are recruited mainly from
the industrial class. This is not what it
should be. I consider that those who are
better circumstanced in life and who have
more at stake, should join that force, and if
they cannot join the force they should at all
events interest themselves in its welfare.
A good deal has been said about Martial
Law. I think the Prime Minister cleared
that point up. What does Martial Law
mean? It means handing over the management of the city to one individual-the
General Officer commanding, who can make
whatever arrangements he wishes. From
his decision there is no appeal except to the
Secretary of State for War, who in turn is
responsible to the Imperial Parliament and
not to this Parliament. Where does this
lead to? Is it likely that the Imperial
Government, who have recognised and made
peace with the Irish Republican Army in
the South of Ireland, will take any other
course with regard to the handling of the
Irish Republican Army in the Six Counties?

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 16th March, 1922.
The House met at a Quarter after Two of
the Clock, Mr. Speaker in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
SUMMER TIME IN NORTHERN IRELAND
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Agriculture if, in the interests of the farming community, and in accord with the
expressed desire of the Farmers' Association, he will take steps to prevent the
application of Summer Time to Northern
Ireland?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): While in entire sympathy with
the whole agricultural community in their
antagonism to Summer Time I am afraid
that, it having been passed for the United
Kingdom and Northern Ireland, it is not
possible for us to prevent its application this
season, though it is in our power to prevent
its application to Northern Ireland next
season if desired by the House.
HOUSING OF EX-SERVICE MEN.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state whether any
representation has been made to the Imperial
Government, with a view to expedite the construction of houses in Northern Ireland,
under the Irish Land (Provision for Sailors
and Soldiers) Act, 1919?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS: Sir
Dawson Bates): The Government of Northern
Ireland have been fully alive to the urgent
necessity of pressing on the construction of
cottages for ex-Service men, and with this
object made representations some time ago to
the Imperial Government offering to carry out
the administration of the Act as an Agency
Service. Pressure is still being brought to
bear on that Government, and I am not without hope that schemes formulated and
contemplated will be expedited.
3. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state the number of
houses constructed or bought in Northern
Ireland under the Irish Land (Provision for
Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919?
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
seeing that the quota for Belfast and district
was 170 cottages, does my right hon. Friend
think that sufficient pressure has been
brought to bear on the Imperial Parliament
in regard to this important matter?
Sir DAWSON BATES: 68 cottages, have,
I understand, been actually erected under
the Act in Northern Ireland, and there are,
I believe, an additional 380 cottages in course
of erection.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I can assure the
hon. Gentleman that all the pressure possible
has been brought to bear on the Imperial
Government in the matter.
SHOOTING OF SPECIAL CONSTABLE
VOKES.
Mr. GRANT (by private notice) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is prepared to institute an inquiry into the
circumstances surrounding the death of
Special Constable C. B. Vokes, who was shot
on Sunday, the 12th day of March, 1922 ?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am taking this
matter into very careful consideration, and
I am in communication with the military
authorities in regard to it.
POLICE EVENTS IN COUNTY DERRY.
Dr. MORRISON (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs if he can give
the House any information with regard to
important police events which took place in
County Derry last night?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received the
following telegram from the County Inspector, Londonderry:
"Seven armed men with Crossley tender
captured at 12-40 inside the Northern
border by police patrol from Derry City.
Three rifles, two German automatic pistols
and quantity of ammunition seized."
This is the only information I have received up to the present.

CLASS II. No. 2.
LAW CHARGES AND CRIMINAL PRO-
SECUTIONS
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That a Supplementary sum not exceeding One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty Pounds be granted to His Majesty
for the services of the period ending 31st
March, 1922, to defray the expenses of Law
Charges and Criminal Prosecutions."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The sum originally provided under this sub-head was £500.
That sum was arrived at on the assumption
that the Ministry would only be responsible
for these charges as from 22nd November,
1921, which was the date on which the maintenance of law and order was entrusted to
the Northern Government. However, subsequent to the 22nd November, 1921,
the Treasury decided that the Northern
Government should pay in the first
instance all claims which came forward for payment subsequent to that date,
irrespective of whether the sums required had
been incurred before the 22nd November or
subsequent to the 23rd November, 1921. I do
not know whether hon. Members are aware of
the way in which these payments are madethat is for prosecutions, witnesses, and so on.
When a prosecution is undertaken the Crown
Solicitor gives a certificate that a certain
amount of money has been incurred, and the
Clerk of the Crown and Peace also gives
certificates. These certificates are presented
to the local authorities; that is, they are presented in the case of the County to the County
Council, and in the case of a County Borough
to the appropriate Borough Council and those
sums are paid to the persons who are entitled
to them by the local bodies. The County
Councils have their accounts audited halfyearly, and the County Boroughs have their
accounts audited yearly, and, accordingly, the
Ministry has been presented with demands for
the payment of expenses for a whole year, so
far as the County Boroughs are concerned, and
for half a year so far as the County Councils
are concerned. That means that so far as the
County Boroughs are concerned we are now
bound to pay for a full year instead of four
Ionths-from 21st November to 31st March.
In respect of the County Councils we are
bound to pay for a full half-year instead of
four months. The Imperial Government will,
of course, repay to us a large portion of the
charges that were incurred before 22nd November, 1921, so that although we are now
asking for a Supplementary Grant, a great
portion of what was incurred before 22nd
November, 1921, will be repaid to us.
Question put and agreed to.

The ASSISTANT PARLIAMENTARY

Dr. MORRISON: I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to an important resolution passed by the Shorthorn
Breeders' Association of England. A unanimous resolution was passed, I understand, by
them, calling upon the Agricultural Department in that country to prohibit the importation of store cattle from Ireland. It is a
curious fact that, while we have 600 members
of the Shorthorn Breeders' Association in
Ireland, so far as can be gathered, no consultation has been held with regard to this
matter. The farmers find themselves in a
very serious position just now, owing to the
depreciation in the prices of cattle, and if this
resolution is carried into effect it will increase
the depression and be a source of serious loss
to Ireland, both North and South. I should
like to hear a statement from the Minister of
Agriculture on the matter, and to ask if he
could suggest any effective means by which we
can prevent this unreasonable attitude being
carried into effect.

for the importation of Canadian and foreign
store cattle. He also proposed a similar resolution at the English Sheep and Pig Breeders'
Association, with the object of stopping the
imports of pigs and sheep. We have communicated with the leading agricultural societiesthe Royal Ulster and the Mid-Ulster Shorthorn Breeders' Associations-and I hope to
receive resolutions from them on the subject.
I am going to London to-night, and I shall
present them to the Minister of Agriculture,
and will take the strongest means possible to
induce the Government to prevent this libel
being put upon Irish cattle.

ALLEGATIONS AGAINST SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
1. Mr. M'GUFFIN asked the Minister for
Home Affairs if his attention has been called
to an article from the pen of Louis J. Walsh,
in the Freeman's Journal" of 9th March,
in which, amongst other things, it is suggested that members of the "B" Specials
when on duty are in the habit of spending
their time drinking in public houses;
whether it is not a fact that it is strictly
against the regulations to do any sucn
thing, and that the utmost care is taken
by officers to see that their men faithfully
carry out their orders and comply with
the regulations, and whether, seeing that
statements and insinuations of this kind
are clearly made for propaganda purposes
in England and elsewhere in order to discredit the Ulster Administration and to
cast a slur on a body of men of whom
loyalists are justly proud, any effective
steps have been taken by way of counterpropaganda to deny such charges; and
whether any official contradiction has been
given to the various statements and suggestions made in this article?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have seen the article
referred to. The hon. Member is quite
right in his statement that Police on duty
are not allowed to enter public houses for
the purpose of drinking, and I may add
that breaches of the regulations in regard
to this are rare. I agree that the report
referred to, and other equally unfounded
reports, are published to discredit a Police
Force of whom I can speak in the highest
terms, but the fact that this report is over
the name of Louis J. Walsh, and appeared
in the "Freeman's Journal," renders it
hardly necessary to contradict it, and it
is impossible for the Government to deal
with every malicious statement which appears in print. This Government have already publicly declared their intention to
stand by their Police, and the Police are well
aware of the Government's intention to
support them in their difficult duties.

LABOUR
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF
Andrews): I am in frequent communication

to undertake the task of governing North-

ern Ireland not light-heartedly, but on the

Such an agreement, apart from an Act of

Let me give you a brief sketch of our

The Government that would not give us

Within a month of the meeting of this
House that Government practically
pended law in Ireland. Parliament had

My hon. and learned Friend referred to
the Truce. Well, ever since July of last
year this Parliament has been severely
handicapped in that respect; and on the
Imperial Parliament-I have said it over

was going to happen, in view of the fact

which were very limited. But the same

to establish themselves. Any criticism I
