I feel very sorely what has taken place
and what is taking place in Belfast and
the Six Counties. What is the position of
the city at this moment? Business people
are handicapped. What happens when they
send men out with horses and carts? My
sympathy goes out to the carters and those
who have got to go round the city with
horses; numbers of them have been shot
in the execution of their duty. Take, for
instance, East Belfast. You go over the
Queen's Bridge with a horse. You go as
far as Memel Street and deliver your goods.
But you have got to come back. You go up
the Sand Quay, round the Albert Bridge,
down Templemore Avenue, and back to
Newtownards Road in order to continue
your business. I hope this Bill will do
something to give protection to these people,
so that no one, however great or small, can
hold up any avenue in our city. That is
the position of affairs at Bridge End,
because no man can pass that corner without taking his life in his hands. What
happened the other day? Almost a dozen
people were told to get out of their houses
or they would be bombed out. What protection are authorities going to give in
cases of this description? I was speaking
to a merchant the other day, and he told
mne he was compelled to take some of his
carts off the streets altogether. He said,

has to deliver goods in a Roman Catholic

of the Roman Catholics decamped with
£150, and sent the horse and cart home
with another man." All this means a
great loss to the business of the city. Then,
in the other case, what do you find? Take
the bread servers, who have to go round
the whole city. What protection are these
men going to get? I say under this ill
the Government will have to take nore
stringent measures in order that these men

The Hon. H. MULHOLLAND: I rise
because I feel it is necessary and right that
the Government should receive support from
every quarter of the House. May I congratulate my hon. and learned Friend who

To my mind he took up a far too apologetic

We require to make no apology for taking

learned Friend was far too mild. He talked

We do not want to give the Government
further powers in the future. We do not
want to give the Government powers by instalments. Let them take every power they
require to stamp out this ruthless campaign
and every member of this House will be
behind them. The hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. M'Guffin) mentioned that in
his opinion flogging was not sufficient. If
he carries his mind back to the time when
there was garrotting in Liverpool he will
remember that flogging then completely
stopped that criminal practice, and I may
say that if an artist is employed in flogging
these criminals there will not be much of
them left to go to prison. I would make
this suggestion to the Government. Of course
I am no lawyer, although I was trained
as a lawyer for two years, but I have such
a strong feeling for the truth that I was
compelled to abandon it and become a politician. I would make this suggestion to the
Government:-Give four days' notice to the
people of the Six Counties to the effect that
anybody found with arms or bombs upon
them, or in the performance of any illegal
practice will be brought to trial within 24
hours; that there will be no appeal from the
Tribunal they appoint; and that on conviction these criminals will be flogged within
24 hours of their conviction. We have seen
that in the South and West of Ireland the
British Government have fooled with their
regulations. We know quite well they passed
Martial Law in Co. Clare, and what happened? They found criminals with revolvers
in their possession and their trial was delayed for several weeks. Then there was an
appeal, and eventually they managed to go
out of the back door of the prison, with the
result that they never received any punishment at all. It is most important that if
these criminals are convicted they should

Mr. HANNA: I regret that on first rising
in this House I should take an altogether
different view to that of the promoters of
this Bill and the hon. Members who have
spoken in support of it. I think that a Bill

intended, as explained by the hon. Member

for preserving peace and maintaining order
in Northern Ireland." There is no peace
now to preserve, and there is no order to be
maintained.
What we want is to restore
order and you will not do it by sitting here
passing Bills. In my view there are two
ways to deal with the situation. One is to
confer with those who are in power in other
parts of Ireland. Have a conference, see
what can be done, and if it fails then you
must have recourse to the other method, and
the other method is force. But you will
not do it by passing a Bill. I do not know
if hon. Members have taken care to examine
this Bill and tried to find out what it really
is we are passing-what it is we are asked
to give a Second Reading to. If we pass
this Bill into law as it stands this Horse
will have nothing more to do with it The

to the Civil Authority, which later on in

But the Home Minister need not necessarily
deal with this Bill himself. He can delegate

officer of police, a man of whom he may
never have heard, and he has the full authority of this House after it has abandoned
its fundamental function of restoring order.
I hope it will not be said of me that because
I oppose this Bill I am favouring lawlessness,
as my hon. Friend (Mr. M'Guffin) indicated
would be said of those who opposed this Bill.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Perhaps the hon. Gentleman will permit me to say that in expressing
that opinion I had not present in my mind

who were opposing the Bill outside.
Mr. HANNA: I would like my hon. Friend
to know that it is because I do oppose lawlessness that I oppose this Bill. I think it

wants something more drastic than handing

is the whole Bill. We would have nothing

Dr. MORRISON: Before dealing with the
measure that we are considering to-day, I
would like to say a word or two with regard
to what has fallen from the Member for
Antrim (Mr. Hanna). I cannot for the life
of me understand what position he takes up
with regard to this Bill. It may be due to a
lack of intelligence on my part, but he seems
like a man hesitating between two opinions.
In the first place he made reference to a conference. There was a conference, and the
conference failed. I think it was a wise and
a reasonable thing for the Prime Minister
of this Northern Area to attempt to settle
this thing by a conference, but it failed, and
now the Member for Antrim (Mr. Hanna)
talks about a conference without proposing that we should lay aside this measure
and go into a conference. He is doubtful, he is hesitating, and he is hesitating also on the only alternative that
is before this House, namely, that of force.
He made some reference to backbone, and 1
must say that so far as I have been able to
see there is very little evidence of backbone
in his contribution to the debate or to the
serious state of affairs that exists in the six
County Area at the present time.
Dealing with the Minister's reference to
the Bill, I am-and I am sure the Members
of the House are with him when he regrets
that it should be necessary for us in the
Northern Area to introduce a measure like
this. There are three rather important questions, three broad questions, in connection
with it that I would like to refer to. The
first is in connection with the first section.
It states here clearly and distinctly that the
Civil Authority may do certain things, and
there are very wide powers being conferred
on the Civil Authority under this Bill. But
the next paragraph says:-
Provided that the ordinary course of law
and avocations of life and the enjoyment
of property shall be interfered with as
little as may be permitted by the exigencies
of the steps required to be taken under
this Act.
It appears to me that that is just evidence of
the vacillation that damaged all action by
past Imperial Governments. You had first
severity, and then you had conciliation.
There is no use in us passing a measure like
this-we have no option but to pass it—and
putting in a clause that the regulations are
to be carried out so that you are not to interfere with the enjoyment of liberty as far as
possible. I think the Ministry are only asking for trouble by putting in this clause.
There is an unctous rectitude about it that I
think should be eliminated, because, having
made up our minds to do a certain action
that we regret, but that we are forced to do,
I would get rid of all this sentiment and say,
"We cannot help ourselves. We are up
against a wall, and we must make a fight for
our lives"
Next I would like to say I listened with
very great pleasure to some of the Belfast
Members when they described the appalling
conditions that exist in this city. I do not
know anything about them, but I know the
conditions that prevail in the country districts. I see here in Clause 6 there is power
to-
Prohibit the holding of inquests by
Coroners on dead bodies in any area in
Northern Ireland specified in the Order,
either absolutely or except in such circumstances or on such conditions as may be
specified in the Order.
Then it goes on to prohibit the holding of
any particular inquest, and to provide for the
duties of a Coroner and a Coroner's jury as
the case may require. I think, if you will
allow me to say it, that it is a very unwise
thing to abolish Coroners' inquests.
Mr. MEGAW: We are not abolishing them.
Dr. MORRISON: You say "Prohibit the
holding of inquests."
Mr. MEGAW: It is only "may" prohibit.
Dr MORRISON: I am only making this
suggestion to the Home Office. I find that
publity is the best solvent for abuses. I
hope this Act will be administered in such a
way that, even if you have Coroners' inquests
no discredit will be done to the constituted
authorities of this House, that we can go
through any inquest and risk any sworn inquiry and come out of it with credit and with
honour. If these inquests are prohibited it
raises a suspicion that will enable the enemy
to blacken us further, as far as that may be

possible. I think on the whole it is a very

that if the police in carrying out their duties

There is just one other point to which I
would like to draw the Minister's attention,
because I think it is a very important one,
and that is with regard to the question of
treating. Earlier in the day reference was
made to wet canteens in the police barracks.
I think there is a very sufficient reason for
the police, if they think it wise, to have a
wet canteen. I do not see why a policeman
should not have a drink as well as ary of
the rest of us, and I would rather re would
have it in his canteen, where he is seen, than
run the risk of him taking it outside where
he is not seem. But irrespective of that
question altogether, I would want this House
to remember that we are not all total
abstainers, and that the majority of the
people in this Northern area are not total
abstainers.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: They could be with
advantage.
Dr. MORRISON: I quite agree with the
hon. Member for North Belfast. The consumption of drink is deplorable, and action
must be taken. The fact that in 1920 we
spent nine-and-a-half million pounds on
strong drink shows in my opinion that we
are going soon to become a race of mental
and physical degenerates if some change
is not affected. Coming to this question of
treating, it is an important thing. I, as a
coroner, have held three inquests in connection with the reign of terror that has
prevailed during recent years,
and my
opinion is this, that while our police, that
is the Royal Irish Constabulary and the
Special Constabulary, and soldiers are as upright and as courageous and as deserving of
public confidence as any class in the community. yet there may be times when under
special conditions some of these men may not
be wholly responsible for themselves. There
is no use of us blinking that fact. We are
not a community of angels, nor anything
approaching angels, and I venture to say
that if everything were known about the
Members of this House we are not angels
nor anything approaching angels. And when
you come down a little lower in the social
scale you may find even a worse condition
prevailing. But what I would like to say to
the Minister of Home Affairs is this: He is
prohibiting treating-of course he may
amend his regulations-in a vague way, and
I would like him to make it clear
and distinct. I would like him
to make the offering of drink
to a police constable or a police officer when
on duty, either by a licensed trader or by a

friend, a violation of the regulations.
would not make it subject to whipping, but
subject to two years' imprisonment and a
fine of £100. You will stop it in that way.
I assure this House and the Minister of
Home Affairs, from my experience as a
practical man, that this would be a wise
thing to introduce. I do not say that by
way of disparagement of the police or the
military, but I think it is a wise thing that
when a man goes out on duty with a rifle
or a revolver he should have a clear mind
to act with consideration and to know
exactly what he is doing according to the
intelligence that God has given him. If
this trouble is coming on us-and I think
it is-I want to use clean instruments in the
fight, so that we will not be ashamed of anything we do, even the indiscreet action of
some irresponsible member of the police
force. If we can make up our minds to go
into this thing with clean hands, and fight
our corner, I have no doubt that what has
happened in the past, from 1640 until now,
will occur again, and that, notwithstanding
dangers that almost overwhelm us, Ulster
will come out triumphant, respected, and
with clean hands.

CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): It has been
deemed advisable to introduce a short Bill
for the amendment of the Superannuation
Act of 1921. Hon. Members will be aware,
of course, of the conditions under the 1920

to them, and the service which they had

Doubts have arisen, however, in the case

officers." Those were officers who had not
hitherto been employed in the Irish service,
and consequently did not come to be transferred under the Act. They were especially
those gentlemen whom we considered to be
possessed of that special knowledge which

Departments, and we induced them to come

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 22nd March, 1922.
The House met at a Quarter after Two
of the Clock, Mr. Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
OUTRAGES IN COUNTY DERRY.
Mrs. CHICHESTER (by private notice):
asked the Minister of Home Affairs with
regard to the recent outrages in County
Derry, and particularly in the neighbourhood of Maghera, will he state what precautions, if any, were taken in the R.I.C.
barracks to guard against attack, and
how it is possible for large bodies of men
to have entered and held up the town of
Maghera and taken possession of the
barracks without any resistance by the
R.I.C.? Did the R.I.C. sergeant in charge
receive warning on the Sunday morning of
an impending attack, and if so, what steps
did he take to deal with the situation?
Will he also state what steps will be taken
and how soon to prevent the repetition of
such outrages in towns similarly situated,
and to protect the Loyalists in these areas?
Is any information to hand regarding
the fate of Sergeant M'Kenzie of Swateragh,
who has not been heard of since Sunday
night, March 19th?
•
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In answer to the first
question put by my hon. Friend, every
possible precaution is being taken to prevent
the repetition of such outrages and to pro
tect the Loyalists in these areas. Certain
measures are being taken which it is
inadvisable to announce publicly. I very
much regret that no trace has yet been
found of Sergeant M'Kenzie. In answer to
the second Question, the matter is at present
the subject of inquiry, and if the hon.
Member will put her Question on the paper
I will give the reply as soon as the necessary
particulars are available.
ELECTION OF SENATOR.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to announce to
the House that I have received a writ for
the election of a Senator in the place of
Sir Basil Brooke, Baronet, who has resigned
his seat in the Senate. In due course
notices with regard to the election and
nomination papers will be sent to each
Member of the House.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I should like to remind the Committee that in the December sittings of the
last Session of Parliament my hon. Friend,
the Parliamentary and Financial Secretary
(Mr. Barbour), presented Estimates and
Supplementary Estimates to provide for the
services of the State to the end of the
current financial year now rapidly approaching its close. If I may judge from the
official report, my hon. Friend performed his
task with a brilliance and lucidity which
justly earned him the commendation of the
House. (Hon. Members: "Hear, hear!")
The moneys which were then voted and the
moneys represented by the Supplementary
Estimates which the Committee considered
yesterday cannot be used legally for any
purpose whatsoever after the 31st day of
the present month. It therefore becomes
necessary in order to ensure continuity in
the supply of the services that Parliament
shall adopt one of two courses-either these
Estimates must be passed in their entirety,
or, alternately, Parliament must agree to
a Vote on Account. It would be opposed
to all Parliamentary procedure-indeed I
think it would be lacking in respect to the
Committee-to expect that the multifarious
details contained in this volume of the
Estimates could be examined, and analysed,
and, I suppose, criticised by hon. Members
in the six Parliamentary days which remain
of the present financial year. It is the
practice, as I understand it, in the Imperial
House to distribute the consideration of the
Estimates over a large part of the Session,
and I think we may follow that course with
propriety. It is a great advantage that
hon. Members should be in possession of the
information which is submitted in the
Budget of the revenue and expenditure of
the Province to enable them to judge the
proper relation that exists between the
expenditure embodied in the Estimates
and the revenue of the State. There
are, however, one or two small departmental Estimates, which, I think, may
conveniently be disposed of, and there are
also some minor Estimates in the larger
Departments which may be suitably con-
Supply.
-Vote on Account.
22 MARCH 1922.
sidered by the Committee and passed,
merely, as it were, to open up the Estimates,
while holding over the larger and more
important proposals till the Session is
further advanced.
In submitting the Motion that the Committee vote a sum on account of the necessary supplies for the coming year, I do not
propose to enter with any detail into our
prospective financial situation or requirements. Indeed, any statement I might
submit on the subject would be largely
speculative, and, therefore, it would be
misleading in the absence of the full details
of revenue, for which we are entirely dependent upon the Imperial authorities. The
House will remember that fully 90 per cent.
of our revenue and a not inconsiderable
portion of our expenditure is carried out in
connection with the reserved services, such
as the Inland Revenue, Customs and Excise
and the Post Office, all of which are reserved
to the Imperial Parliament. Information
on these heads cannot be obtained until the
Imperial Chancellor has finally settled his
Budget scheme. The Chancellor on the
first day of this month said that he could
scarcely imagine anything more imprudent
than for a Chancellor of the Exchequer to
announce before the end of the current
financial year, when he did not know results,
what taxes he proposed to impose in the
following year. Some apparently circumstantial reports have been circulated in the
Press that the Chancellor had in contemplation a reduction in the Income Tax by a
shilling in the pound, and possibly a reduction of the duties on beer. I think
too much reliance should not be placed on
a statement of that kind in the meantime.
Until the year has run its course the
Chancellor will not be in a position to know
what his reserves are, and it will, therefore,
be, impossible for him to determine his
policy, except such policy as will be determined by the political situation.
I need hardly remind the Committee that
the decision of the Chancellor is of very
serious moment to us. One shilling reduction in Income Tax would affect our revenue
to the extent of £700,000, and 3/- per barrel
on beer would mean another £100,000. We
are thus so dependent on the convenience
of the Imperial Government, the Committee
will appreciate the fact that it is impossible
for me to frame any complete Budget scheme
of our own State revenue for next year
and expenditure before the end of April
or early May, and when that period is
reached I hope to be able to review at
length the whole financial outlook of the
Province. At that time I will also be in
with
a position to report to the House
exactness the results of our four months'
experience from 1st December till 31st
March, and whatever deductions may
be drawn from this experience. But I can
say now that assuming the revenue returns
of Income Tax for the next eight days are
normal, we shall be able to finish this
broken period of a full year with a surplus
of £30,000 to £40,000.
The Committee will, therefore, understand
that the Estimates we now submit are
limited to the cost of services which we
control. These are calculated on the basis
of current rates except where commitments
which have already been made involve
increases. Teachers' Salaries, Housing, etc.,
are in the latter category. There are
also new charges, such as the additional grant to Intermediate Teachers,
and the setting UD and development
of Agricultural Stations. Of the latter
we expect to get a large refund from
the Imperial Government, as part of equipment expenses for which that Government
is liable. I should have liked, had it been
possible, to have given the Committee
comparative figures of the expenditure of the
present year to guide it in considering the
Estimates now submitted, but there are 60
many adjustments which have been made,
and changes in the methods of accountancy,
it would only have been misleading.
As an example of what I mean, there are
now provided in our Estimates charges
which were hitherto met from the Endowment Fund of the Department of Agriculture
or the Church Temporalities Fund. Moneys
from these Funds went directly to the
Department concerned, and did not appear
in the National Estimates. I propose that
the receipts, not only from these funds,
but from every other source shall come
direct into the Exchequer. This is a reform
which I regard as sound accountancy, and
very essential to the easy comprehension
of all sources of revenue on the one side
and the total expenditure of the Province
on the other. There is only one valid
method of comparison for us and that is
with the year 1920-21, upon whose Estimates
the financial clauses of the Act of 1920 were
based. I call this year for purposes of easy
description the basic year. In a few
moments I will present some interesting
comparisons of the figures of that year
compared with our present Estimates.
My hon. Friend in his admirable statement in December submitted comparative
figures of the Estimates for the past two
years as calculated by the British Treasury.
But I would remind the House that however
useful these figures may be for purposes
of approximating the financial position for
the periods in question, they are merely
Estimates and not ascertained results. When
we entered our protest in 1920 against the
unfairness of the demand for a contribution
of £18,000,000 from Ireland as a whole,
but more especially against the gross
injustice of the apportionment as between
Northern and Southern Ireland-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-we based that protest

On the other hand, the Treasury experts
estimated the expenditure for that year at
£23,539,000.
The actual expenditure (excluding the
Bread Subsidy, which was non-recurrent)
was £28,700,000.
By contrast with this blunder the expenditure calculated by our Committee and
scheduled to their report was after deducting
bread subsidy £28,000,000, which was almost
exactly correct, whereas the Treasury
Estimate turned out ludicrously short of
actuality by more than £5,000,000. To put
it clearly, the British Treasury Budgeted
for a surplus of £22,000,000 from Ireland in
that year.
As a fact, they only received
£15,000,000 so that had we been responsible
for the year's finance we should not only
have received no surplus, but we should
have been almost £1,000,000 in debt. The
acceptance of the Treasury Estimate by the
Government is at the root of our financial
worries to-day. I do not question the right
of the Minister, who was acting with Cabinet
authority, to prefer the calculations of his
own technical experts to those of a Committee of lay men, but I certainly urge that
when he discovered the egregious miscalculations of his officers he was bound by
every canon of honour and honesty to exert
himself to remove the difficulties that arose.
I was innocent enough in those days to
believe that the promise of a British Minister and English gentleman was sacred and
inviolable, and when we had the assurance
in conclave that Ulster would have a surplus
of £2,000,000 after all her services were provided for, and when that assurance
repeated in the Parliament of the nation
with all the force of Government authority,
and when Parliament passed the measure
with this assurance ringing in their ears,
I had no doubt the undertaking would be
implemented.
was
I have learned something, however, since
then. I know that the Minister in question
-now one of His Majesty's principal Secretaries of State-is a man of honour, and
I have not given up hope that when the
measure required to amend the present Act
is submitted to Parliament it will contain
such provisions to enlarge the power of the
Joint Exchequer Board as will enable that
tribunal to take full account of all our
circumstances.
I can now give some comparative figures,
which I think will interest the Committee.
The figures which appear in these Estimates
are, with a few exceptions, legacies from
the Imperial authority, and it was not competent for us to repudiate them, even had
we desired. I would remind the Committee
that material increases were made after the
passing of the Act, and before our Government assumed control. These increases
are reflected in some of the Votes which
will be considered by the Committee. The
Education Estimate is a type and there
are others to which I will presently refer.
As regards the cost of our Parliament
and our administrative services, no doubt
Members will recall how pessimists and
croakers-friendly and unfriendly-predicted
that by reason of the smallness of our area
the splitting of the administrative Departments centralised in Dublin would involve
us in heavy additional expense, which
would add to the burdens of our people.
I am glad to be able to report to-day that
all these doleful prognostications have been
falsified. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). By
the savings which we have been able to
effect in the costs of our administrative
Departments, not only are the expenses
of our Parliament and Government covered
but in addition a substantial margin of
saving has been accomplished.
My hon. Friend and colleague (Mr.
Barbour) has given of his best to this work.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). My own share
in it has been negligible, but neither he
nor I regard it as honest if we did not
admit that these satisfactory results have
been largely the work of a great and loyal
Servant of Ulster-Sir Ernest Clark. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear) His devotion to
this work has been unsparing, and I willingly bear tribute to it. I must also bear
testimony to the loyalty which the Heads
of the different Departments have shown
in the furtherance of the difficult task of
establishing our system of Government,
which has been above all praise, and I
think we may congratulate ourselves in the
possession of as competent and efficient
staff of Civil Servants as can be found
anywhere
.
The amount of our Parliamentary and
Cabinet expenses is £36,000. This is less
than per cent. of the cost of our transferred services and less than of 1 per
cent. of our revenue. I cannot think that
we can be accused of undue extravagance

22 MARCH 1922.
in conducting our Government. The savings
to which I have referred have been effected
in such Departments as Finance, Home
Affairs, Law and Prisons and Local Government, all of which by comparison with two
years ago when the administration
was
centred in Dublin-show a reduction of some
£150,000. But all these savings have been
outweighed—and tremendously outweighed—
by the increased cost of Education, Health
and Labour and the Special Constabulary.
The increased cost of Education is £600,000.
This is a legacy from the Imperial Government and imposes a heavy additional burden
on the State. I am not questioning the
propriety of the advance. I think money
invested in education probably yields a
better return than most other expenditure,
and I have always felt that the best way
to ensure efficient teaching is to make the
service worth the attention of the very
best class of men.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Might I ask the right hon.
Gentleman what is the amount of the concession that has been promised by the British
Government?
Health Insurance and Labour show an increase of £265,000. These are in the domain
of sociology. Reform in this Department has
been a prominent feature in Imperial policy
for some years, and we are bound to conform
to national schemes in the interest of our
working people. But the most serious feature
in the list is the Estimate of £2,562,000 for
Special Constabulary. I had some diffidence
about submitting this Vote to the Committee,
but my hesitancy disappeared when I listened
to the patriotic speeches of my hon. Friend
the Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr.
Coote) and also my hon. Friends from the
West Division (Mr. Lynn) and from Londonderry (Sir Robert Anderson), whose declarations no doubt reflected the views of the community. My hon. Friend from Tyrone said
truly that "No sacrifice can outweigh the
obligation to secure liberty in this province."
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That sentence
crystallises the whole of the Government's
policy. This Estimate for the Special Constabulary interprete the settled determination
of the Government of Northern Ireland so far
as money can interpret the policy. Our
people have been rightly clamouring for vigorous measures to cope with the camarilla of
outrage in our midst. This Vote is the
Government's response. The Imperial Government has undertaken to bear the expense of
the special force till 1st October, and I am in
hopes, if the circumstances should necessitate
its continued existence, that the Imperial
authority will realise its further responsibility. But even if it should disclaim responsibilty for further support, I greatly misjudge the temper of our fellow-countrymen if
they will grudge any sacrifice to ensure the
safety of their heritage and to rid the State
of these marauding gangs who would turn
our peace-loving and law-abiding province
into an inferno.

Mr. POLLOCK: Roughly, one
pounds. I turn now for a few minutes to an
Estimate which deserves special commentthat is the Housing Estimate. In 1919 the
Imperial Parliament passed an Act designed
to encourage the construction of houses,
primarily for the working classes. Grants
were offered to private builders of such houses
ranging from £230 to £260 per house in
respect of houses commenced prior to 25th
August, 1921, and completed by June of this
coming fiscal year. Our liability under this
head is estimated at £30,000, and is nonrecurrent. In the case of municipalities and
public bodies, however, a much more serious
liability was undertaken, of which we now
reap the unfortunate result. To assist the
public authorities in economic house building,
the Imperial Government agreed to contribute
259 for every £1 of rent collected, and the
Northern Government is bound to accept this
burden on all commitments entered into prior
to August, 1921, but not thereafter. I should
mention that the Treasury practically agreed
to increase this subsidy to 35s for every £1
of rent-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-but
the regulations had not been issued before the
appointed day, and have not been applied
even in Southern Ireland. Owing to our own
financial conditions the Government has
decided to adhere to the lower rate, and it is
expected that by careful and prudent management this subsidy will be adequate to insure
authorities against serious loss. Our liability
under this head for the coming year is estimated at £15,000, rising to £30,000, yearly
when the various schemes are completed.

to
If, unfortunately, unemployment should
continue to remain at its present high level,
it will be necessary to consider what action
shall be taken to re-establish the Fund on a
solvent basis: that is to say, whether to
increase contributions, or reduce benefits, or
increase the State grant-in-aid. This question is already receiving the attention of the
Imperial Parliament, whose decision in the
matter we shall probably be compelled to
follow, both to ensure that our burdens and
benefits in respect of the Fund correspond to
those attaching to similar trades in Great
Britain, and also to save the inextricable
confusion in administration which would
arise from varying rates of contribution or
benefits between this country and Great Britain.
I have thus far dealt with our advances to
the Unemployment Fund to the end of the
present year, amounting to £490,000. Owing

towards this end the House will be asked to
provide powers for the Exchequer to make
further advances to the Unemployment
Fund, until the new conditions of the Fund

1920, amended, as I can see that it will be,
by the Constitution following the Treaty
In regard to finance, it will be remembered that our Prime Minister, in his
correspondence with the British Cabinet,
pointed out a third alternative to the two
proposals of that body-namely, a fiscal
status for Ulster equal to that of Southern
Ireland. This was refused, and, therefore,
we continue-as I think most of our people
desire-in close fiscal relationship with
Britain.
If a frontier is to be created in Ireland
between North and South, it will be a
British frontier, under British protection;
but if wisdom and good sense guide the
leaders of Southern Ireland there is no
reason why, in the common interest, some
measure of accommodation cannot be devised. If they are wisely directed, the
Southern Government would adopt the
British standard of taxation for some
probationary years, so as to learn exactly
its effects on the material interests of the
country; but if they allow their judgment
to be disturbed by sentiment or prejudice,
and a system of tariffs against British goods
is instituted, the policy will be a constant
menace to the peace and prosperity of the
country. Probably such a policy would have
a much less injurious effect on our Province
than on Southern Ireland, because we are
more self-contained, and will continue to
have a free market with the forty millions
of people at our doors. Although the Council
of Ireland is non-existent, there is at least
hope that some other link of communication between North and South may he forged
which will help us to deal with the difficult
questions of our fiscal relationship with the
South.
Our position in regard to the British
Exchequer is clearly defined by the Act, and,
as I have already stated, the financial clauses
of that instrument have been so drawn that
they embarrass us not a little, for under it
there is no question of any adjustment for
two years. Meanwhile, we are called upon
to pay from a diminished revenue towards
an expense which has also been materially
reduced (namely, the expense of the Army,
Navy, and the National Debt). So unjust
is this that the British Government has
referred the matter to the Joint Exchequer
Board, who fortunately are still functioning,
and I am not without hope that some proper
basis of adjustment may be arrived at in the
near future Meanwhile, our contribution
for the four months of the current financial
year is calculated at one-third of the yearly
amount.

Sir CRAWFORD M'CULLAGH:
glad to find he has reached that stage. I
found it out long ago, and only yesterday I
was in London dealing with a promise given

Exchequer Board will be appointed to deal

to be scrapped, and something new put in

There is one point I wish to refer to in
connection with the erection of houses. My
hon. Friend, the Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn) said-and I quite agree with
him-that the building of houses should be
carried on by means of private enterprise.
Unfortunately we were at a point when
private enterprise would not build houses,
and indeed to-day private enterprise cannot
supply the needs of the community. The
trouble to a large extent was brought about
by Government restrictions. The Government, through the Local Government Board
in Dublin, insisted on a certain type of
houses being built, houses which were be
yond the requirements of the Belfast working
men, with the result that the average cost
of a house was something like £1,000. But
my complaint goes further than that. When
this Bill went through the House of
Commons we there again pointed out that
the finances were not correct. The inducement held out was that this scheme
so far as Ireland was concerned, would cost
the ratepayers. nothing. The subsidy of
25/- in the £ for every £ collected was an
ingenious arrangement. Of course, anyone
could see it was really intended to make
the different municipalities collect rents
and let the houses at fair rents, but at
that point the buildings had not reached
the high standard that they attained in
the following eighteen months. We found
out that owing to Government restrictions
the cheapest house that could be built
would cost roughly £1,000. We asked the
Government to modify their requirements
in regard to the standard, but they would
not do it. We pointed out that the rents
at which we would have to let the houses
would be prohibitive, and that consequently
at some point there was bound to be a
loss which would fall upon the ratepayers.
It was then that the Local Government
Board took up the matter, and the information was conveyed to us that the Government had decided to increase the subsidy
from 25/- to 35/- for every £ collected. I
want to point out that, although that may
seem an extraordinary proportion, you must
always bear this fact in mind, if you reduce
the rent the less in proportion the Government have to pay. That seems to be forgotten in all the discussions.
With some of my friends I saw the Chief
Secretary, Sir Hamar Greenwood, yesterday.
He did not deny that he wrote the letter
stating that he had made an arrangement
with the British Treasury to increase the
subsidy to 35/-. I myself heard him say
SO on a former occasion. Unfortunately
we were able to get nothing out of him.
The Government were responsible for making
the different councils build more costly
houses than were necessary, and having
done that, and having promised to increase
the subsidy to 35/- to meet those requirements, they are in honour bound to fulfil
their engagements and great pressure ought
to be brought to bear upon them to see
that they pay the 35/- subsidy. Otherwise
there is bound to be a great deficit, so
far as we are concerned.
I hold the view strongly that our Government to-day ought to cut their losses. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.). Subsidise the loss,
whatever it is, and sell the houses at the
earliest possible moment.

these services under one head and to save a
very considerable margin as compared with
the administration of these services when

CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY

Treasury. The amendment is added to this

of the United Kingdom, the aforesaid

ment of the United Kingdom, and any

That is legal phraseology, I suppose, and
I think hon. Members would like to know
what it means. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It simply means that in respect of
this guarantee that we constitute any loan
and any interest thereon absolutely a first
charge on our Exchequer. The involved
paragraph that I have just read out is intended to carry that into legal effect. I quite
agree with what has been said that it would
be very nice if we could meet these unusual
charges on our funds out of revenue. Still
if we were to raise our annual taxation to
the sum which would enable us to meet a
very heavy strain of a temporary character
on our finances I think we might be very
properly charged with overtaxing the taxpayer. There is no doubt that non-recurrent expenditure is very justifiably met by
means of a loan and a suitable sinking fund,
so as to enable the loan to be repaid in easy
stages. One purpose for which borrowing
would be necessary would be for loans to
local authorities. We never can tell what
loans we may be asked to make.

THE ENGINEERING DISPUTE.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: There is a matter that I
would like to bring before the House, and
particularly I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Labour to it. We are
all aware that a very serious crisis obtains
at the moment in respect of the engineering
industry. An attempt is being made to
bring the employers and the representatives
of the workers together in order, if possible,
to adjust the difficulty. We all hope that
good may attend that effort, but up to the
moment the British Parliament have not
felt themselves warranted in intervening in
the dispute. It is rather regrettable that
they should have taken that course, because
there at at least two alternatives that could
be adopted with respect to it. There are at
least two boards that could be called in to
intervene in the situation. What I want to
bring before the Minister of Labour is this.
While this difficulty is still pending, and
while arrangements are being suggested with
respect to bringing it to a solution, acrimonious criticism is being indulged in from
one quarter and another, and in particular
with regard to the attitude of the workers.
It has been suggested that they have been
provocative in the past, that they have
assailed from time to time the position of
the employers and challenged their rights
upon
the managerial principle. Well, I
want to say, as one associated with the
Union that is at the moment locked out,
that we deny those allegations-we absolutely deny in respect of that that the engineers
of this city have been in one instance guilty
at least for the last ten years. I think the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) will
admit, and perhaps the House will agree,
that during the war there could have been
no better record than that achieved by the
industrial forces of this city. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We did as efficiently, and
we achieved as much, as any other centre in
the three Kingdoms, and in some particulars
we excelled all other centres in our contribution to the winning of the war. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Under those circumstances, to be charged
with a provocative attitude, with aggravating the situation, and with bringing about
the present impasse is, I think, a most regrettable thing. I have had a communication, I may as well say to the
House, from the Amalgamated Engineering
Union (Belfast Committee), who have
invited me to put a question to the
House, and to ask the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) if he will concede
to us a Court of Inquiry, or let me say Committee of Inquiry, to look into the question
of these allegations. The communication
reads:-
"We here in Belfast have never had at
any time any trouble with the Belfast
Employers' Association."
I want the Minister of Labour to mark that.
That is a specific statement on the part of
the Union, and they disclaim any
responsibility.
"We here in Belfast have never had at
any time any trouble with the Belfast
Employers' Association on the question at
issue, and are assured if an inquiry were
held the same could be said of many other
centres, which would go to show that the
employers have no ground for their present
attitude."
Now, I want to support that attitude on
the part of the District Committee of the
Engineering Union. I want to take up that
attitude and support it with the testimony
of my own experience. I would only ask the
right hon. Gentleman to take this into consideration, though as perhaps he knows the
Imperial Parliament, particularly the
Minister of Labour, has declined to intervene at the moment or to set up a committee.
Well, in view of the fact that other alternatives were open but not adopted, it would
be only fair to the engineering union if he
constituted a committee that he will be
absolutely free to nominate, and whose
umpire or chairman he will be free to nominate, too. I think it is only fair that he
should take into consideration the suggestion

That being so, I really fail to see why we
should form Committee, or what the

this House would agree to take notice of
such statements. (Hon. Members: Hear,

local trouble, but is, as I have said, a
national trouble. Indeed, I was able to arrange with our employers here and the local
a
representatives of the Union referred to that
provided the local employers were able to
obtain the permission of their Federation in
the United Kingdom to allow them to withdraw the notices there would be no lock-out
in Belfast and district, subject to the condition that whatever settlement was agreed to
in Great Britain would be binding on both
parties here.
Unfortunately, and to my great disappointment, the local employers were unable to ob
tain the permission of the Federation in Great
Britain to adopt this course, and so the lockout notices were kept up. However, I see from
the Press that this matter is receiving considerable attention across the water, and I
hope that a settlement will be brought about
at no distant date. I feel that if we were to
set up a Committee now while ballots are
being taken across the water it would prolong the trouble here. I think I ought to
point out to the House that this dispute is
the result of the men refusing-of course
within their rights-refusing to accept the
advice of their own leaders in Great Britain.
A vote was taken, and I think I am right
in saying that only about 70,000 voted out of
a total membership of 400,000.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: 21 per cent.
Mr. ANDREWS: About 21 per cent. of the
whole. Of course if a large percentage had
voted we would have had a proper indication--
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Might I point out to my
right hon. Friend that the vote upon which
the conditions were established was only an
18 per cent. vote, so that we improved the
vote in respect of this matter.
Mr. ANDREWS: I think that bears out
my point and strengthens my argument that
so few voted that a poor indication was given
of the real feelings of the men themselves.
I am satisfied now, however, that conciliation
is at work in Great Britain, and I am very
hopeful that this trouble will be brought
to an end quickly. In the capacity of a
negotiator I would be pleased to do all I can
to bring about that very desirable result.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

or two generally on the question of the lockout. Having some previous experience with
regard to industrial matters as they concern

of the Belfast employers at this juncture.
It was always held that they were not members of the Federation. Indeed, for 20 years
or more the Belfast shipbuilding and engineering firms carried on while a national
strike took place on the other side. If there

Oral Answers.
23 MARCH 1922.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 23rd March, 1922.
The House met at a quarter after Two of
the Clock, Mr. Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
BELFAST PRISON DISCIPLINE.
1. Mr. WILLIAM GRANT asked the
Minister for Home Affairs whether there
have been complaints from residents in the
vicinity of Belfast Prison respecting undue
noises and disorder; whether strict discipline is being maintained in the Prison,
and whether the Regulations are being duly
enforced? What is the position of affairs
with respect to prisoners who have been
sentenced to hard labour for so-called political offences, and whether any distinction
is made between them and persons sentenced
to similar terms for ordinary offences?
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): No complaints have
been received for some time as the Prison
has been quiet. Strict discipline is being
maintained, and the Prison Regulations are
being duly enforced. Certain prisoners who
have been sentenced to hard labour have
refused to work and have been confined to
their cells. The only concession made in the
case of certain so-called political prisoners
was to allow them to receive two parcels
of food per week and to receive and write
a reasonable number of letters. This has
been continued only to that class of prisoner who were committed before we took over
the administration of the Prisons, but prisoners convicted by the ordinary Courts are
now subjected to the ordinary prison regulations irrespective of whether the offence is a
so-called political offence or not.
PROPOSALS OF GEDDES COMMITTEE.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has received any protests
against the proposals of the Geddes Commitee on National Expenditure to impose a
fee of 10s on each annual valuation return
sent to the Chief Registrar of Friendly
Societies; if so, whether he will state the
intention of the Government with regard to
this matter?
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The answer to the
first part of the question is in the negative.
The Northern Government have deferred
consideration of the question of the imposition of any such fee pending the decision of
the Imperial Government regarding the proposals of the Geddes Committee on

CIVIL AUTHORITIES OF NORTHERN
IRELAND (SPECIAL POWERS) BILL.
Considered in Committee.
[MR. MOLES in the Chair.]
Clause 1 (Powers for preserving peace and
maintaining order.)
Exchequer Borrowing and Local Loans Bill
"to empower the Ministry of Finance to raise
money for certain purposes and to issue sums
for local loans and for temporary investment"
presented accordingly and read the First
time; to be read Second time to-morrow, and
to be printed.
1.-(1) The civil authority shall have
power, in respect of persons, matters and
things within the jurisdiction of the Government of Northern Ireland, to take all such
steps and issue all such orders as may be
necessary for preserving the peace and
maintaining order, according to and in the
execution of this Act and the regulations
contained in the Schedule thereto, or such
regulations as may be made in accordance
with the provisions of this Act (which regulations, whether contained in the said
Schedule or made as aforesaid, are in this
Act referred to as "the regulations"):
Provided that the ordinary course of law
and avocations of life and the enjoyment of
property shall be interfered with as little
as may be permitted by the exigencies of the
steps required to be taken under this Act.
(2) For the purposes of this Act the civil
authority shall be the Minister of Home
Affairs for Northern Ireland, but that Minister may delegate, either unconditionally or
subject to such conditions as he thinks fit,
all or any of his powers under this Act to
any officer of police. and any such officer of
police shall, to the extent of such delegation,
be the civil authority as respects any part
of Northern Ireland specified in such
delegation.
(3) The Minister of Home Affairs shall have
power to make regulations-
(a) for making further provision for the
preservation of the peace and maintenance
of order, and
(b) for varying or revoking any provision
of the regulations;
and any regulations made as aforesaid shall,
subject to the provisions of this Act, have
effect and be enforced in like manner as regulations contained in the Schedule to this
Act.
(4) All regulations made as aforesaid shall
be laid before both Houses of Parliament as
soon as may be after they are made, and, if
an address is presented to the Lord Lieutenant
by either House within the next fourteen days
during the session of Parliament after any
such regulation is laid before it praying that
the regulation may be annulled, the Lord
Lieutenant may annul that regulation and it
shall thenceforth be void, without prejudice
to the validity of anything done thereunder,
or to the power of making a new regulation;
and regulations made as aforesaid shall not
be deemed to be statutory rules within the
meaning of Section 1 of the Rules Publication Act, 1893.

Where after trial by any court a person is

this section applies, the court may, in addition to any other punishment which may

of firearms, military arms, ammunition or

Larceny Act, 1916 (which relates to demanding with menaces, with intent to steal).

document relating or purporting to relate

emanating or purporting to emanate from
an officer of any such association, or addressed to the person as an officer or member of any such association, or indicating
that he is an officer or member of any such
association, that person shall be guilty of
an offence against these regulations unless
he proves that he did not know or had no
reason to suspect that the document was
of any such character as aforesaid, or that
he is not an officer or member of the association.
Where a person is charged with having
in his possession any such document, and
the document was found on premises in his
occupation, or under his control, or in
which he has resided, the document shall
be presumed to have been in his possession
unless the contrary is proved.

Mr. LAVERY: It has absolutely nothing

Mr. POLLOCK: I beg to move. The House
will remember that in my statement submitting the Vote on Account on Wednesday
last I entered with some elaboration of detail
into the capital requirements of the Government during the coming year. These were
particularly for the purpose of advancing
money to Local Authorities for their public
schemes, advances to the Unemployment Insurance Fund, and any possible deficiency of
revenue that might arise particularly in the
early part of the year, which is generally
described as the lean months of the yearthat is to say, when revenue does not
flow into the Exchequer in sufficient
amount to meet the liabilities. The
object of this Bill is to deal generally with
the subject matter that I have referred to,
and, specifically, first for borrowing for the
Exchequer Account, and secondly for issuing
from the Consolidated Fund all the loans to
which I have just made reference.
of revenue that may arise. This present Bill,

requirements which can be discussed later.

There are other respects in which one

There are non. Members able to criticise

seems in the first instance to be a degradation to the Minister to have it paid in the

I have is with regard to the matter of the
Prime Minister's Secretary in connection
with what is called the Secretariat of the
Cabinet. That was a question that was
under consideration and criticism in this
House. The House took strong objection
to the adoption of the principle of a Secretary to the Cabinet. I do not know
whether there is any precedent for that.
It does not obtain across the water. The
point of my objection is this: I think when
the Prime Minister came to reply he stated
that he wanted it provisionally adopted and
to that the House assented. I find the word
"permanent" is placed in front of it. I
think it is going to be a permanent institution in this House. My objection
is this: You have a person present in the
Cabinet listening to the most important
discussions, who is privy to everything that
takes place, and is not responsible to this
House. Cabinet secrets are always very
important matters. I understand there are
no minutes kept.
Under these circumstances we can see the very great importance of having no person present at the
Cabinet meetings who is not in some degree
responsible to the House so that we can
hold him answerable for any dereliction of
duty of which he may be guilty. Then
we have, as a necessary consequence, the
assistant secretary. This represents further
expense. I am not going to cavil over the
matter, but I would rather it were presented
in a different way. In so far as the appointment of the secretariat is concerned,
if we get the assurance that it is not going
to be a permanent secretary-a permanent
institution in connection with this Parliament-it will disarm much of the criticism
I have made. I know that at the outset
of the Parliament and with such a tremendous undertaking as the Prime Minister had
in hand something in the nature of that
office was almost necessary. But while that
would be a justification at the moment, if
it is going to be declared a continuous policy
then my objection holds good, in view of
the fact that it does not exist in the Imperial Parliament.

The PRIME MINISTER: With reference
to the first criticism of my hon. Friend (Mr.
M'Guffin) on the question of how the extra
£500 for Cabinet Ministers appears in the
Votes, I think perhaps I should call his mind
back to the fact that this was an arrangement
of the House itself, not of the Government.
The House set up its Own Committee to
deal with these matters, and it wa
a specific recommendation from the
Committee that Cabinet Ministers should
have the £500 in addition to their Ministerial
salaries. The Cabinet at that time were faced
with the alternative of either accepting the
report that was brought in by Members of
the House, or rejecting it, or amending it.
We decided, and I think rightly decided,
that, as we had asked Members of this House
to go into the whole matter, to go over to
London-to consult experts and authorities,
and to take all the difficulties and trouble on
their shoulders of dealing with the matter,
it would only be wise and reasonable on our
part to back up that Committee and to embody their findings in our Estimates. That
remains to-day as it did last year in exactly
the same position, but, of course, as all Votes
can, and properly can, be revised from year
to year, my hon. Friend can raise the point
from time to time. We still think it would
be wiser to adhere to the recommendations of
the Committee, for if we had deviated from
them in one respect we might have had to
deviate from them in other respects, which
would have caused considerable discontent
and trouble.
With regard to the second criticism, dealing with the Permanent Secretary of the
Cabinet, the hon. Member says there is no
precedent for the position, but he must know
there is not only one but many secretaries of
the British Cabinet-a Permanent Secretary
and a regular secretarial staff. Consequently we are not creating a precedent by

CONFERENCE WITH IMPERIAL
GOVERNMENT.
THE PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT.
Dr. MORRISON, by private notice, asked
the Prime Minister of he is in a position to
make a statement with regard to the Conference which is to be held in London tomorrow?
The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend
has asked me to make a statement with regard to the Conference that it is proposed
should be held to-morrow, and I will crave
the indulgence of the House if I have to
cover a considerable amount of ground. In
the first place, I would like the House to
understand that this is an invitation to meet
His Majesty's Government, and the policy
that we laid down very early in the controversy over the Free State Bill was that we
were always ready to present our case to the
British Government, that we had a good
case, and that we were not afraid of any
arguments that might be brought up against
the policy which we have pursued consistently from the beginning, which policy has
never been changed, and from which policy,
I personally never intend to deviate one inch.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
There may be critics who will say that it
is an error of judgment to go into any such
Conference, and there are other critics who
say we should lay down conditions before
going into such a Conference. That may be
So. I do not deny that the time might come,
as a time has come before when we refused
to go into such a Conference to discuss the
question of an All-Ireland Parliament in
which Ulster would be involved, and that
situation, or a similar situation, might
arise again. But, in the meantime, the
Government of which I am the head, have
carefully considered the whole matter, and
have come to the conclusion that in the best
interests of Ulster and of peace, which we
all desire, we should accept the invitation
extended by His Majesty's Government.
I would not to-day have made any statement on the subject at all had it not been
for the serious charge made against me yesterday by Mr. Collins, to overlook which
might cause dissatisfaction amongst my loyal
supporters in Ulster-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and might at the same time allow an
unfounded impression to get abroad that I
had not honourably stuck to my word, and
had not done my utmost to carry out the
Agreement that he and I entered into. I
notice various discrepancies in Mr. Collins'
statement. May I, first of all, bring the
House back to the Agreement that we entered into mutually on the 21st January
last? The Agreement is well known to everyone, but, before I read the Agreement, may
I read Mr. Collins' comments upon my attitude? He said:
"Unfortunately Sir James Craig has not
been so meticulous in his attitude towards
us. He has neither kept his undertakings
with us nor done anything to meet us on
the several points of controversy."
No. 1 paragraph of our Agreement reads:
"The Boundary Commission as outlined
in the Treaty to be altered. The Governments of the Free State and of Northern
Ireland to appoint one representative each
to report to Mr. Collins and Sir James
Craig, who will mutually agree on behalf
of the respective Governments on the
future boundaries between the two."
I am prepared to stand by that Agreement
to-day, and there has been no breach on my
part of the undertaking that he and I made
in the Colonial Office on the 21st January,
and to which we both added our signatures.
Mr. Collins at that meeting kept me
entirely in the dark regarding-and I am
going to use his own wordsthe agreement with Mr. Lloyd George
that large territories were involved in the
Commission, and not merely a boundary
line.
I quote these words from the subsequent

There has been no going back so far as I am

I do hope and pray that there will be no

Now, my third reason for such a

I am not dismayed. We know ourselves
the righteousness of our cause, and we know
that traducing outside will neither injure a

Members: Hear, hear.). Mr. Churchill yesterday in the House of Commons cast the

Roman Catholic districts."
Our Special Constabulary are open to all

open to them. We have officers and men

up in their thousands and take charge of
their own districts, to see that the hooligansthe Bolsheviks, the bomb-throwers and criminals of every class and creed-are kept in
their proper place and brought to justice.

The "far worse state of things" will not
prevail for very long. My right honourable
Friend the Home Secretary (Sir Dawson

and brought to justice, and under the new
Act, which we propose to pass as quickly as

Therefore Mr. Churchill need not any further
cast reflections upon the city, which was

created against any sort of authority what-
Those were the conditions under which

intricacies of the police force, as well as

stood the strain, never ending day or night,
of all the reports brought in, and taking a

the Ulster people take a matter of this kind

the Imperial authorities themselves. Now,
let me just say this-there are charges flung
about that we do not, in our speeches, sufficiently sympathise with the victims of these
outrages, or sufficiently condemn the outrages
which take place in our midst. That is
another wanton statement which it pleases the
Opposition Press to make, and most of the
Press is, unfortunately, in opposition to
Ulster. We cry inwardly to ourselves when
we hear of the widows created and the young
families left fatherless after these foul assassinations take place. And it would be a count
against us of insincerity if we were to repeat
that from day to day. Our condemnation of the
outrages has been made on frequent occasions
by different bodies and persons. Our clergy
have, as usual, entered into the spiritual side,
and done their utmost in these difficult
times, but our energy must be spent in
overtaking the difficulties and troubles in our
midst. We have had a pause. I believe there
was nothing to stain the name of our city
last night or this morning. Murder is a
terrible thing, and it is almost impossible to
place any variation on one type of murder
more than another. I say, standing at this
Table, that there can be no more foul murder
or assassination than the next one that takes
place in Belfast. The next murder will be
one of the foulest crimes that any citizen
could perpetrate, and let the person who
dreams of such a thing search his heart. It
may not be one man who may be murdered,
but hundreds, and perhaps thousands. On
the man who starts this thing, either by
speech, pen, or word, will rest the guilt and
sin. I earnestly pray that this slight pause
that has taken place will continue, and that
a better day will dawn for the citizens
of the city generally. But I &m
going to have no charge laid upon the Protestant population as a population. In no city
in the world will you find a finer picture of
better self-control and self-restraint than has
been exhibited in Ulster. It is very easy for
editors in London offices and others to sit
down and write glibly about the Protestants
of this great city of ours. The long and the
short of it is that I will always say the Protestants are not to blame.

The PRIME MINISTER: They are too
loyal to the Crown and Constitution, and too
loyal to their Protestantism, ever to allow
themselves to lose their self-restraint. I
know of no other body which has stood what
they have stood under provocation unparalleled in the history of the whole world. If
people only knew of that provocation, if they
thought for a moment what it means to have
two of our gallant men, while doing their best
to preserve the peace of the city, shot dead by
assassins who steal up behind them in broad
daylight and pull the trigger that leaves them
both lying on the ground- The least said
about these things the better. The only way
to stop these outrages is for the South and
West to keep themselves in hand, for the
British Government to give them all the aid
they can to set their own house in order, and
not be constantly irritating and inflaming
passions amongst the Protestant community
of the North.

Now might 1 counsel moderation on the
part of public speakers. Let no man have it
laid upon him that by any unreasonable word
spoken on a public platform, he once more
started this sordid business. It is a time for
public men to practice self-restraint, coupled
with energy and effort to help the Government. At one time there was no Government.
Now there is a Government, firmly constituted with proper authority, with Police and
Specials who will be produced in
numbers. Therefore, may I appeal to the
people for confidence, courage, and selfrestraint. Mr. Collins I presume, by his
speech, intended to create an atmosphere
before he went across to London. That is
what it is called in modern times; trying to
create an atmosphere before a meeting takes
place. I am going to create an atmosphere by
my concluding words, and that is to express
an earnest desire even at the eleventh houreven if I may say so on the stroke of twelvethat vindictiveness and hatred in Ireland
should give way to reasonableness and a sense
of proportion leading to peace. I want to
create an atmosphere of a helpful nature,
and not of an obstructive nature. God knows,
the difficulties and troubles through which
we are passing are heavy to a degree. Losing
one's head or heart will not solve the difficulty. What will solve it is what has solved
Ulster's difficulties before-that is the rallying of the people and of the spirit of the
people round their leaders in these trying
times and even placing greater restraint on
their private conversations. Let them stop
the criticising of little things which may take
place from day to day; let them take a grand
conception of their duty and help in the
great struggle between those not alone in our
midst but in the South and West of Ireland.
Let us daily and hourly pray that peace may
descend upon our land, peace for those at the
I believe that there is a possibility of
speedily wiping out the worst characters in
our midst. It may be more difficult to get
rid of the extremists and worst characters in
the South and West, but let us be no party to
backing up the extremists in these great and
dangerous times. Let us where we can see an
opportunity, even half a chance or no chance
at all, still talk to one another to endeavour
to save life and bring peace to our country.
That is the atmosphere which I hope will
surround us in London, the atmosphere which
I hope the British Government will welcome,
an atmosphere that we should allow all
that has passed to remain behind us-
I will not say to be forgotten, for it
is hard to forget some of the dreadful
things that have been done but I would
say let us start by thinking less of the
wrongs of the past and more of the great
possibilities that lie in the future. This is
a time above all others for men to do their
utmost to grapple with a serious situation,
to speak for peace, to work for peace, and,
if 1 may say so in all solemnity, to pray
for peace to pray for peace in the Churches
and in the home, so that God may hear us
when we ask Him to send His blessing upon
our land.

LOCAL BILLS, STANDING
(JOINT COMMITTEE).
ORDERS
Resolved: That a Select Committee be
appointed, with such Members as may be
appointed thereto by the Senate, to consider
how far the Standing Orders of Parliament
relating to Local Bills have been complied
with on such Bills, and to report to the
House.
That Sir Crawford M'Cullagh, Mrs.
M'Mordie, Mr. Thompson Donald, and Mr.
Lavery be Members of the said Select Committee.
That all Petitions relating to the compliance with the Standing Orders on Local
Bills which shall be presented during the
present Session, be referred to the Committee
unless otherwise ordered.-(Captain Dixon.)

Mr. M'GUFFIN: I do not think I would
have intervened at this stage but for the
fact that we are committed to a very large
expenditure in regard to the Special Constabulary, and the House as a whole has
pledged itself to the utmost possible
economy with respect to expenditure, not
only in that Department, but in every
Department of the Government. I am
satisfied that it is the intention of the
House to effect all the economies it can, but
I am afraid I cannot agree that the Departments are proceeding upon the principle
that has been adopted in this House and has
been frequently suggested by hon. Members
who have spoken on the various financial
measures. The point I want to bring before
the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Home Affairs, and perhaps
directly before the Minister of Finance, is
whether at the moment the Special Constabulary is being constituted upon an
economic basis, and in asking that question
I would also like to ask the Minister of
Home Affairs if it is a fact that at the
moment there are being transferred to the
Northern area six police inspectors-either
County or District Inspectors--who in few
days will be subject to disbandment, and
that in the event of them being disbanded
in this area their pensions will be a charge
upon the Northern area and become a fixed
charge from that date. The House does not
resist an appeal from the Prime Minister
when he asks for financial support. We
willingly and cordially agree to the sums
asked for, but in this particular case, if it
is decided forthwith that these men are to
be transferred to this area and disbanded
here it is not a matter of expense at the
moment but of a fixed charge that must
remain upon this House, and which, I presume, would amount to between £2,500 and
£3,000 a year. If that is the case I think it
is a matter with which this House should
concern itself. I do not know whether the
question relates to the Minister of Finance
or the Minister of Home Affairs, but whichever is concerned in the matter it is a
subject upon which the House is entitled to
be enlightened and to know what procedure
the Minister concerned means to adopt.

Mr. COOTE: I should like to have some
information, if I may, on the question of the
officials connected with the Departments of
this Government. There is very consider.
able unrest, and to some extent a
feeling of irritation, at the way in
which the Departments are being
filled by people other than Ulster men aud
women. I should like to know, for instance,
from the various Departments, how many of
the present officials have been transferred
from the service in Dublin, and how many
have been transferred from other places; and
with regard to those transferred from outside Dublin, for instance from across the
water, what were their salaries before they
were transferred, and what are their
salaries now? I have heard that a great
number of these are in the Finance Depart
ment, and there is very considerable dissatisfaction in the City and in the Province that
many eligible men and women who had
hoped that they might receive employment
in their own Government offices are debarred, and others are brought in under a
claim that they are from the transferred
services in Dublin, who never were in
Dublin at all. This is a matter which i
consider ought to be cleared up, and if it is

to some of the Departments, so that we shall
have an answer at a later period.
I am probably accused of being as loose in
my statements as other people, but I want
to say here that, since the Provisional Government was set up, and since matters took
any definite shape, I do not think anybody
can point to where I made a speech in any
way provocative, or denunciatory of the organisation that ought to, and we hope may,
come into power in Southern Ireland. I want
to say at once we are in sympathy with any
power that will grip the situation, control
and govern the people of the South, and bring
them into ways of industry and peace. We
are with any such Government heart and
soul, and we are not here to taunt them, to
pick holes, or by word or act to say or do
anything provocative that might in any way
make wider the unfortunate breach that
exists between the two peoples.
May I also draw attention to another fact
-at least it is alleged it is a fact-that there
is considerable waste of officers and men in
the Constabulary Depot at Newtownards. I
am informed, on very good authority, that
there is one gentleman there who is a
retired District-Inspector. He was intended
as paymaster for County Donegal some nine
months ago, but was never sent there, and
he is employed at the very noble work of
teaching policemen how to fill up their own
pay-sheets, a matter of instruction that
ought to be given by a gentleman who is in
charge of the general instruction, and who
probably is not employed at this work for
more than three hours a day. Then there
are other matters, such as motors, petrol, and
such tremendous use or abuse of privileges
there as amount to waste. I hope the
Minister in charge will say whether or not
there is anything in these allegations. They
were brought to my notice by a gentleman
whose word I have to accept until I find
there is proof to the contrary. Might I re
vert to a few facts on which I should have
liked to have made a statement immediately
after the speech of the Prime Minister, but
which, owing to the manner in which it was
taken up, precluded any general discussion
by the Members of this House. I share with
the Prime Minister the feeling that this is a
time when we ought to bridle our tongues,
But there have been some statements made
which give us a perfect right to intervene in
defence of our own people. Statements have
been made, for instance, that the loyal people
of this city or the people of the Protestant
denomination are committing murder for the
love of murder, and I think it is time we
refuted these statements, if we can. From
reading the speech which Mr. Collins delivered on Sunday, and which was reported in
yesterday's papers, one would be led to think
that the Protestant people are entirely to
blame for all that is happening in the city
of Belfast, but he forgets that the methods
adopted by the Provisional Government are
something like this. Some time ago a communique was issued by the Provisional Government finding fault with a certain officer
of a regiment stationed in the city, and just a
few days after attention was drawn to this
man he was done to death. A few days later
the police were mentioned in another communique, and following their mention by the
Provisional Government five policemen were
shot in the city. Three of them were Roman
Catholics who were shot down in Roman
Catholic districts, entirely removed from
Protestant influence.
Then in connection with the troubles
on the Border, surely it is unfortun
ate that the loyal people of Tyrone and
Fermanagh should be blamed for a condition of things brought about entirely
by Southern Ireland. It was not the local
people who did the kidnapping.
There was
absolute peace on that Border. The Border of
South Tyrone was one of the most peaceful
districts in Ireland. It was so peaceful that
in connection with all the party demonstra
tions held in the old days, either on the 17th
March or the 12th July, it was not necessary
to draft in an extra policeman. There never
was any party bitterness of such a nature as
to lead to a breach of the peace. But, suddenly, without any notice, twenty-two peaco
able citizens were taken from their homes
