HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Coote]
carried away, and kept for days in Southern
Ireland. Since the time of the invasion, for
miles along the border, and for about two
miles inward, the farmers cannot attend to
their farms; they have had to cease ploughing, and they have to steal out in the nigh;
time to leave food for their cattle Only the
day before yesterday a very peaceable citizen.
a Mr. Robert Scott, died of wounds that he
received while he was attending to his cattle
along the Border. Commandant O'Connor
the other day charged Commandant O'Dufiv
with making all the trouble on the Border
Commandant O'Connor is a Republican,
charging O'Duffy, the Free State Commandant, with making the trouble on the Border,
and O'Duffy says it may be true, or it may
not be true. He does not deny it. So far as
the Loyalists are concerned, their hands are
clean. They did not give any provocation
along the Border, and they are in no way
responsible for the terrible troubles that
stare the community in the face now.
We would like, if we could, to impress upor
our own Prime Minister the necessity of
taking stronger measures for the protection
of the Border. When peaceable citizens are
done to death while attending to their cattle,
the time has come when the force of
authority should be so strengthened as to
give the necessary protection to people of this
kind. We believe that if the British Government, who are still responsible for the
government of the Free State, would put a
line of military inside the Free State, ind
declare a radius of two miles on the Southern side out of bounds, so that the Sinn Fein
snipers from that side could not send their
bullets across to Northern territory, it would
probably have the desired effect, or would
at least mitigate very much of the trouble.
Meantime we look with very great suspicion on this Conference in London. We fervently hope it will do good, but we believe
that it is a herring being drawn across the
trail, and that when the British Government
find themselves in a difficulty they will
always try to get Ulster to intervene to take
them out of the abominable position in
which they find themselves. We believe the
British Government are humiliated before
every British citizen, and we hope and we
believe that our Prime Minister, and those
associated with him in his mission to-night,
will be exceedingly wary of the gentlemen
with whom they have to deal, not only on
the side of Southern Ireland, but more particularly on the side of Great Britain itself.
We have no faith whatever in the British
Government. The only hope we have is that
they will soon be relieved of office, and that
they may never hold the reins again. Our
position is to try to enlighten the British
people the British people are all right-as
to the condition of things in this country, in
the hope that we may get a Government with
some backbone, with some desire to maintain
law and order, and to preserve some form of
civilisation in the North and the South of
Ireland.
We believe, further, that this may be
another move on the part of the Southern
Government to weaken our own authority
here in the North. We believe that the
Government of Northern Ireland are now
gripping the situation; that, although things
look black to-day in the city and Province,
it is the beginning of the end of the Bolshevist and the gunman, and that in a very
short time, if our Government go on firmly
and steadily, supported by the great mass
of the people, Ulster will yet be a fit place
for decent people to live in and go about
their business. But we are afraid of anything that will in any way arrest
the hand of authority in tracking
down the murderer, be the murderer
Protestant or Catholic. That is our position. We want to assure the Government
that we are behind them in all their efforts
honestly and squarely to maintain law and
order, but we do view with very great suspicion this Conference in London. We hope
it will lead to no weakening of the means
taken here to protect the loyal citizens of
this Province, no matter what is their religious persuasion. We must be pardoned
when we say we have no faith in the British
Government or in any of their attempts to
restore order in Ireland, because they, and
they only, are responsible for the disorder
and for the terrible inheritance they have
handed on to the people of Northern Ireland. They only are responsible for it, and
we believe they have neither the backbone
nor the inclination to put down murder
North or South. They simply are drifting,
and they are now anxious to have us brought
in that we may to some extent take the responsibility off their shoulders and bear it
for them, a responsibility which will go
down in history as theirs, for the maladministration of things in Ireland.

No; we have been playing with crime too

Who to-day in our Empire is looked upon as
the strongest man? General Smuts' Why?
Because he gripped the Bolshevists in South
Africa, who were trying to destroy the very
foundations of civilisation, and to pass their
principles on to other colonies and other parts
of the Empire. He gripped the situation, and
thus did much to shorten the sum total of
destruction of human life. He ended in a
few days that which might have gone on for
years and put South Africa on a par with
Russia. Heaven only knows where it would
have led to. Contrast South Africa with
Russia. In Russia men came in and, there
being no strong man to resist them, they
taught methods of revolution, and used them.
So we have Russia to-day committing
cannibalism. We do not know the horrors.
If we do not do our duty with Ireland we

how

AGRICULTURAL GRANTS.
1. Mr. DONALD (for Mr. CRAWFORD)
asked the Minister of Agriculture if,
when the services of the Department
were transferred, (1) there was a balance
of the yearly grant to the credit of
each County, (2) and if so, will he state the
amount lying to the credit of each County in
the Northern Area, (3) and whether these
balances will be available and each placed to.
the credit of its own County?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
M'KEOWN): I have been asked by my right
honourable Friend the Minister of Agriculture
to deal with this question.
When the powers and duties of the Department of Agriculture and Technical Instruction in so far as they related to Agricultural
Services in Northern Ireland were transferred
to this Ministry, accumulated balances of
annual grants to County Committees of Agriculture stood in the books of the Department
to the credit of each of the Six Counties.
So far as this Ministry has been able to
ascertain, the amounts of these accumulated
unexpended balances are as follows:---

County Tyrone

As to the third part of the hon. Member's

the question of the transfer of these balances.
The Ministry has asked that these balances

ATTEMPTED MURDER AT JOY STREET.
2. Mr. DONALD (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs what information he can give regarding the attempted
murder of a workman, named Lyle, at the
corner of Joy Street and Ormeau Avenue in
the city this morning; and in view of the fact
that Lieutenant Bruce was recently murdered
convenient to the spot on which this murder
was attempted, will he state whether special
precautions can be taken to preserve life in
this neighbourhood?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): At 9.10 a.m. to-day,
James Lyle, Protestant, and native of Dromore, Co. Down, was fired at by several men
with revolvers at corner of Ormeau Avenue
and Joy Street, Belfast, while going to his
work at Messrs. M'Kinney & Co.
He was
seriously wounded, and taken to the Royal
Victoria Hospital. I am glad to say that I
understand he is progressing favourably. This
is one of the localities which is causing the
authorities considerable trouble, and honourable Members may rest assured that all possible steps are being taken, with the resources
available, to preserve life.
HOLD-UP OF A TRAIN AT ADAVOYLE.
3. Mr. DUFF (by private notice) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he has
received a report regarding the holding up
of the train at Adavoyle on the night of the
28th-29th instant, and can ho give particulars
for the information of this House?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yesterday morning
about one o'clock the goods and mail train
proceeding from Belfast to Dublin was held
up at a place known as Cloghogue, 2 miles
North of Adavoyle Station. A red light was
exhibited to the driver by about 100 armed
men. The driver did not, however, observe
the danger signal, owing to the fact that the
goods train from Dublin was passing the
place at the same time. The raiding party,
who had evidently well prepared plans, had
removed a rail, with the result that the
engine, sorting carriage, passenger guard's
van, and two goods wagons were derailed,
fortunately without injury to the staff of the
company or Post Office. Seven of the wagons
were set on fire and destroyed, and in addition
a large number of consignments were thrown
out of other wagons on the permanent way,
and afterwards burned.
The police, who were in the neighbourhood,
proceeded to the spot, when they found that
the train was not proceeding on its normal
course, but the raiders had decamped.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask my right hon. Friend if any arrests
have been made in connection with this
dastardly occurrence?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Not yet.
Mr. DONALD: There have been no arrests?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
CAPTURE OF BELCOO BARRACKS
4. Mr. M'GUFFIN (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs what information he can convey to the House regarding
the capture of Belcoo Barracks, . County
Fermanagh, and whether any of the police
who have been kidnapped have been released?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received a
report from the police stating that a few
minutes before ten o'clock on the night of
the 28th instant the police in Belcoo Barracks
were surprised by the entry of about twenty
armed raiders. The raiders rushed into the
dayroom from the front door shouting
"Hands up," and captured two sergeants and
eleven constables. Four constables who were
in the kitchen escaped into the yard, and
were not noticed by the raiders.
All revolvers, rifles, equipment, ammunition, and contents of the men's boxes were
stolen. The raiders stayed about two hours,
and then drove off in three cars to Blacklion,
bringing the captured police with them.
While the raid was in progress the village
was surrounded by sentries. One constable
returning from a walk was halted, but
escaped.
Two Special Constables were also halted
and taken to Sergeant Flannery's house,
where the sergeant was on sick leave, and the
three of them were then taken to Blacklion.
Sergeant Flannery was subsequently released
on account of illness. It is thought that the
raiders came into Belcoo on foot, and that
the cars came later when the barrack was
captured. The raiders were not disguised.
Apart from Sergeant Flannery, none of the
men who were taken have yet been released.
The total strength of the barracks was three
sergeants and nineteen constables. Sixteen
of these were captured, of whom one, Sergeant
Flannery, was, as stated, released; the others
escaped.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask the right hon. Gentleman if he
thinks that where an attack of this sort can
be carried out with such deliberation, skill,
and expedition, sufficient vigilance i being
observed by those who are in control of the
barracks?
Mr. DONALD: Before my right hon.
Friend answers, may I ask him if it is his
view that these happenings are in the nature
of reprisals for what has occurred in the City
of Belfast; and, if so, what steps the
Government are going to take in view of the
speech that was made in the Imperial House
the other night?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure my hon.
Friend, the Member for North Belfast (Mr.
M'Guffin) will understand that, having regard
to the fact that the men are in the custody
of these raiders, it is impossible for the
Government to get information in order that
fuiler inquiry may be made as to the cause
of the raid, and as to whether or not there
was any negligence on the part of the police.
I am sure the House will not expect me to
give an answer to a question of that sort at
the present time.
MURDER AND WOUNDING OF POLICE
AT CROSSMAGLEN. -
5. Major SHILLINGTON (by private
notice) asked the Minister of Home Affairs can
he state the circumstances in connection with
the murder and wounding of police at Crossmaglen, and whether he has any information
which shows who is responsible for this
dastardly outrage?
Sir DAWSON BATES: A patrol of Police
left Crossmaglen about 10-0 o'clock yesterday
morning. At about 11-30 a.m. they were ambushed at Culloville within our area. The
.patrol consisted of Sergt. Patrick J. Early,
R.I.C., and six Special Constables.
Sergt. Early was shot dead.
Special Constable Harpur, shot dead.
Special Constable Samuel Dougall, wounded
in left elbow.
Rest of party uninjured.
Ambushers numbered about fifty, with two
machine guns, one on each side of the road.
Survivors returned the fire and believe they
wounded several of the ambushers.
Arms and ammunition taken from the dead
policemen.
This is part of the attacks being made by
the I.R.A.
Mr. DONALD : I would suggest to my right
hon. Friend that these questions be submitted
by telegram to the Prime Minister at the Imperial House.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I will undertak.
have that done.

Mr. M'GUFFIN: There is a matter which
would interest the entire membership
of the House, but for some reason there has
been some hesitancy in bringing it before
your notice. I think it is a matter upon
which, with very great respect, we are entitled to invite your opinion, and perhaps
your decision. When this Parliament was instituted I understood that there was to be a
daily issue of the Official Reports of the
Debates, but I find that by some means, or
by some authority, there is now only one
issue per week. The importance of the
Official Reports of Debates, as far as hon.
Members are concerned, is really for reference. If a debate is taking place to-day, and
is to be continued to-morrow, the value of the
Report lies in the fact that it serves as a
handy reference; but if it is to be used simply
as a memorial of the proceedings of the
House then I submit that it is a question for
the House whether it is worth while continuing the Hansard under such circumstances.
When this matter was debated incidentally
at the beginning of the last Session it was
suggested by some hon. Member-I think it
was the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Lynn) that, as far as he was concerned, he
would prefer to do without the Hansard at
all. I do not take up that position, but if
it is going to be issued I think it should be
issued under the usual conditions, that is
as a daily report, which would enable hon.
Members to consult it from time to time.
Moreover, the price was threepence formerly,
but now any person who wishes to secure
a copy of Hansard must pay a shilling. One
might not hesitate to pay threepence in order
to consult Hansard on a particular subject—
I mean ordinary members of the community
outside the House-but now if they are to
have an opportunity of referring to a particular subject they must pay a shilling. I
am not at all sure whether this is a matter
upon which you, as custodian of the privileges of this House, might give a decision,
but I would like to know by what authority
the change was made.

The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS
(Mr. Moles): I hope the House will indulge
me for a moment while I make my maiden
speech to this Assembly. It is difficult, I
can quite conceive, for the average man, who
cannot be expected to be acquainted with the
difficulty of producing Hansard, to understand the reasons for this departure. If the
House will allow me, I will try to explain
them. Firstly, as to the shorthand writers;
whether you produce your Hansard daily or
weekly you must have the same shorthand
writing staff. They have their professional
Adjournment.
Official Reports.
30 MARCH 1922.
regulations just as other colleagues of theirs,
and you cannot lay upon an insufficient staff
more duty than it is capable of discharging.
If you do you will have a mutiny in the
ranks of the shorthand writers. Therefore,
let us dismiss them out of our calculations
for the moment. The other difficulty is the
real difficulty. You must realise that the
Labour market in respect of the printing
trade in Belfast is entirely different from
the Labour market in the same trade in
London. In London there is always a floating
population which can be called upon at once
to case or linotype to meet any emergency.
More, and this is by far the greatest difficulty, his Majesty has a Stationery Office,
which includes a printing department of its
own, and that makes all the difference in
the world. In Belfast there are not, in fact,
in the ordinary course of newspaper production enough linotype operators to go round.
Trade union regulations forbid more than a
given period of overtime in the entire week.
If you are going to produce your Hansard
at night so that it can be perused by Members
in the morning, it can only be done by violating Trade Union rules in respect of overtime,
so that precludes that being done. What is
the alternative? You can import from other
centres linotype operators, but if you do this
follows: no firm will import linotype operators to keep them idle for six months of the
year in order to employ them for six months
to produce your Hansard. If they do, they
must include the cost of keeping those men
the other six months in the charges they impose in respect of the production. Therefore
as a simple matter of business work and de.
tail you have to come down to hard facts, and
that involves that you must produce under
day labour and not under night labour, because the latter is not possible; but if you
produce under day labour you cannot deliver
the Report between the interval of the sitting
which concludes at six o'clock at night and
its resumption on the following morning.
Therefore it becomes a practical difficulty. It
was imperative from the point of view of
the printers to consider whether, as you
were producing a Hansard under these
changed conditions, you should not produce
two or three or four days together at very
much reduced cost, and as there has been
such a great cry for economy-I do not say
that it came altogether from that particular
quarter of the House, and I am not suggesting I do not sympathise with you--but
since that is the position, the Minister responsible for making the arrangement was
up against these facts and has dealt with
them in what I think is a business-like way.
With regard to the point as to the utility
of Hansard, both professionally and personally for the last three or four years I have
had some experience as to the value of
Hansard, and I give my opinion for what it
is worth that the value of Hansard is not
in its issue the next day. I cannot recollect
a single instance where an appeal was made
to Hansard on the day of its issue. Its
value is proved next week, next month, next
year, when Ministers, fluctuating as they do,
variable in their attitude towards public
questions-that is the time Hansard becomes
of value, when you can drag it from its
shelf, the dust lying upon it, and convict
a'Minister of insincerity and untruthfulness.
Mr. ANDREWS: And hon. Members.
Mr. MOLES: That is the value of Hansard.
Therefore, I suggest that you have got to
make up your mind
on two thingseither a Hansard is worth producing,
or it is not. The opinion of every
Parliament in every country in the
world is that it is worth producing.
There remains for us this question: Is this
the best method, in the light of the facts
that surround us, for producing Hansard?
With all respect to the House I beg to
suggest it is.

Let me point out, first of all, one or two
essential features. Before putting one's

There is good in those few words. Article

Now, before I close, may I refer to the very
important meeting which was held yesterday
in the city, when leading business men, representative or all parts of our land, met

Whether those resolutions were passed or

thousand responsible citizens of Ulster were

"Have full faith in the Government not to
let you down." I ask each and all of you to

back to our country. That is a hard task.
It is no easy thing to carry with you all the

live, where you have passions roused for

will be playing a great part once more for
Ulster and for the Empire if you tackle
this serious problem in the spirit in which 1
tackled it, and that was to bring peace to
our country, and to bring that peace with
honour to all concerned.

We might divide it into what we give in the

Let us look for a moment or two at what we
are giving in the interests of peace In the
first place you have got under Clause 3 the

police force in Belfast, and which are to apply
to the whole Six Counties. I would like hon.
Members to note that fact afterwards. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Clause II., subsection (1) reads
'Special police in mixed districts to be
composed half of Catholics and half of
Protestants. Special arrangements to be
made where Catholics or Protestants are
living in other districts. All Specials not
required for this force to be withdrawn to
their homes, and their arms and ammunition handed in."
I for one object, and object strongly, to a
sectarian police force. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I want to know a policeman as
a policeman, neither as a Protestant nor a
Catholic. I have had many opportunities,
night and day, of watching the old R.I.C. for
the last thirty-five years, and I have never
found a body of men who did their work
more faithfully. I have known many of them
for years, and I have not the slightest idea
whether they are Catholics or Protestants,
and I have never stopped to ask whether
they are or not. The only thing that appeals
to me is that they are wearing the King's
uniform, and doing their duty faithfully and
well. I think it was a mistake in this
Agreement to lay down any specific figures
with regard to the number of police or of
the denominations of the police in any paiticular district. I do not want to labour the
point, but I do think it was a mistake and a
mistake that will probably only result in
accentuating the difficulties of which we want
to get rid. There is also the fact that if
a raid for arms is to be made in a district
half the men engaged in that raid must be
Catholics and the other half Protestants.
Could any arrangement be more absurd than
that? Imagine the police officer having to

go and ask his men-probably it is necessary

Now I come to another and more important
point. I would like to direct the attention
of the Prime Minister to this because I do
not know what the feelings of other Members
may be, but I hold very strong views with
regard to the trial of prisoners, which is
dealt with in Clause IV. In this Clause you
are going to abolish trial by jury. One of
the fundamental principles of the Great
Charter was that a British subject was
always to be tried by his peers.
One of the real reasons why Britain
has become great, why the freedom of
Great Britain is unequalled in any other
country in the world, is that Clause of the
Great Charter. Yet at the dictation-well,
probably dictation is too strong a word, let
us say at the suggestion of Mr. Colline and
Mr. Griffiths we are going to abrogate Magna
Charta and insult the jurors of Ulster. I
would like the Prime Minister, or any other
Member of this House, to tell me if they
ever knew of an Ulster jury refusing to do ite
duty, no matter how difficult the circumstances might be. I have had a long experience of our jurors in the Courts, and have
watched them with great care for many years,
and I have never yet known a jury in Ulster
to give a verdict otherwise than what they
believed to be just and what their conociences
dictated. I think it is a mistake that this
thing should be done. It may seem to some
people a small thing, but after all it is a
very big thing. The things which are eo
common to us, and which come to us so
easily, we are apt to treat lightly, but this
infringement of the British Constitution, an
infringement of the Constitution which has
existed for century after century, is not
to be lightly passed over, and I hope that
when some Member of the Government replies
he will be able to tell us that this is merely
a temporary arrangement.

Mr. LYNN--There are two persons to this.
The person who is being tried may think he

Can anyone tell me that there ever has been

incursion of the murder gang, whose business

are being penalised under this Agreement as
if they were the aggressors, instead of the
people imported into our midst who are

of the Northern Parliament. It is an unfortunate Pact. It savours very much of the
practice of the Government of the United
Kingdom-when they come to the solution of
a problem, when they are within reasonable
distance of enforcing the law, some rearguard
attack is made on the institutions of law
and order, everything is scrapped or set
aside, and the powere of dieorder prevail.
That to my mind seems to be what is happening in Northern Ireland. We sat here for
days while the Minister of Home Affairs and
the Attorney-General piloted the Special
Powers Bill through this House, with the
whole-hearted assent of the Members, and
after that is done the signature of His
Majesty is given to the document. Then
our Prime Minister goes over to London with
his Cabinet and they agree to things that set
aside the most important provisions of the
Act, that require alterations in it, and that
practically break it up. Trial by jury is
abolished under certain conditions. Speaking
for this House of Commons, I say that we
object to be made the tool of intriguing parties over in London. We are being used in
this matter simply to further the intereste of
the British Government in their policy of
surrender and of scuttling out of Ireland,
while by implication they make grave charges
against the honourable acts of our Special
Constabulary and against the Constabulary in
general. While they practically allow it to
be said that our people are breaking the law,
and are out for disorganisation and riot, there
is not one word said about Southern Ireland,
and the fact that the loyal population there
are being driven from their homes, their
farme, and their businesses. The private
letters of those people to us-I wish we could
only read them out before the public and give
their names are pathetic beyond measure,
and yet there is not one sentence in this
Agreement pleading for better conditions for
our friends in the South and West.
I hope the Prime Minister is not serious in
expecting us to pass the Pact in this House.
There is not a motion before the House
to-day, but if there was, I am afraid there
would be very great trouble in getting a
unanimous vote, if he got a vote at all. The
feeling in the city and in the country is such
that he would be a very bold man who would
give assent to this Pact in its present form.
I want to refer to the words of the Prime
Minister at the great meeting of business
men held in Belfast yesterday. There was no
Pact publicly-I believe there was privatelyin the air when that meeting of businese men
was called. That meeting was called for a
different, a bigger, and a greater purpose, and
I protest against making it subservient to
this issue, making it a tool of Lloyd George
and his surrender pack-I cannot call
them by a more respectable name
the men who have surrendered everything and have humiliated not only
Ireland but Great Britain before the
world. I object very strongly to the use that
the Prime Minister made of that meeting, and
I say that that use will recoil upon his own
head, if he persists in it. I am very sorry to

engineered a committee of Peace with Honour,
when the gallant men who are out night
after night patrolling our city and the
country at the risk of their lives, free,
gratis, and for nothing, are being scrapped,

in and help to bring about peace, because

humiliated, as they have, in fact, been

in this Agreement, which I think is a very
serious matter, although apparently very
small. I refer to the fact that the Constabulary are to be numbered, or, in other
words, they are to be a real, proper, visible
target for the gunmen who come here from
other parts of the country. Say a gunman
comes here from the South to look for
Brown, or White, or Black. He does not
know Brown, or White, or Black. He knows
there is such a name, but he cannot connect
the name with the personality. With the
use of numbers all he has to do is to take
up a certain beat, and No. 1, No. 4, or No.
6 is the man he wants. It is quite easy
for the gunman to find out the number,
and then use his revolver. He has not
to identify the personality. Is not it a
fact that the numbers on the uniform of
the old Constabulary had to be taken off
for that very reason? Here the Members
of the Northern Government have included
in the Pact the provision of a real, visible
target, so that the gunman can identify
his man by the number, instead of having
to identify the personality. I think that it
is a very serious mistake, and that it is
fatal to the efficiency of the force. It is
not fair to the men who are risking their
lives for the peace of the city that the
representatives of Southern Ireland should
suggest to our Government what we are to
do with our police, and how they are to
be marked. Why, the thing is ludicrous.
If we had sent so many children away to
London they could not have behaved in a
more puerile fashion. They simply allow
themselves to be played upon every time
by these men who cannot deliver the goods.
My hon. Friend, the Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Lynn), has dealt with the
question of trial by jury. I agree with
every word he said, and I will not take
up the time of the House by mere repetition, but we do hold very strongly that men
charged with crime involving capital
punishment, or with other serious offences,
should be tried by a jury of their fellowcountrymen.
In regard to the activities on the Border,
the signatories to this Pact, just by a stroke
of the pen, have settled them all, and we
hear that for the last twelve hours or so
the Border is at peace. I hope so. I want
to ask the Prime Minister and the other
Northern signatories to this Agreement if
Mr. Michael Collins and the other Southern
signatories are speaking the truth in other
places? What can they do to relieve the
situation on the Border? They say the
I.R.A. operating on the Border does not
belong to them. They have a wonderfully
convenient way in the South of Ireland, when
they do an illegal thing or commit an overt
act of illegality, of having somebody else to
blame, and so they deceive us all the time.
I submit that if the Members of this House
were living on the Border in constant fear
and dread, and realised that their only help
was the "A" and "B" Specials especially
the "B" Specials, the countrymen who are
doing their work in the fields by day and
going out and tramping the roads at night
in order to protect the people they would
be slow to make any changes on the Border
until the I.R.A. is taken away, root and
branch. There is another way of settling
the Border problem. The British Government could easily settle it by putting
garrisons in four or five of the towns on
the Southern side of the Border, and the

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 5th April, 1922.
The House met at a quarter after Two of
the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
BILL PRESENTED.
Criminal Procedure.-Bill to make special
provision for the trial of persons charged
with serious crimes in Northern Ireland,
and for purposes connected therewith.
Presented by the Minister of Home Affairs
(Sir Dawson Bates), supported by the
Attorney-General (Mr. Best)
Ordered to be read a Second time tomorrow, and to be printed. (Bill No. 7.)
MESSAGE FROM THE SENATE.
That they have agreed to:-
Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Bill,
with Amendments, to which they desire
the concurrence of the Commons.
BELFAST HARBOUR BILL.
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND
MEANS (Mr. Moles) reported from the Joint
Committee on the Belfast Harbour Bill as
followeth :-
"That they had considered the said Bill
and examined the allegations thereof,
which were found to be true, and that the
Committee had gone through the Bill and
made Amendments thereto."
Ordered: "That the said Report do lie
upon the Table."
The Orders of the Day were read and deferred.
Report of Police Committee,
MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn." (Mr. Burn).
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In accordance with the
undertaking I gave to this House at the
time the Report of the Police Committee was
laid on the Table I think this would be a
suitable opportunity to enable hon. Members
to discuss the terms of that Report. Before
referring to the Report itself, I would like
to take this opportunity of expressing the
thanks of the Government to the Committee,
and in this connection may I especially refer
to the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Lloyd Campbell) the Chairman of the Committee for undertaking a task which was
both arduous and difficult. No one except
one who was on the Committee, or who was
in close touch with it, could possibly realise
the enormous amount of work involved, and
the extent of the investigations which had
to be undertaken by the Committee. The
object of referring this matter to a Committee
was in order that the Government might get
the combined views of representative men in
Ulster, so that, based on their Report, a Bill
might be brought in setting up a new Police
Force which would be a credit to Ulster, and
which would, above all, enjoy the confidence
of the community. I believe that in this
Report we have these essentials.
The Report is in the hands of hon. Members, but I would like to take them very
briefly through the main recommendations.
The first point to which I desire to refer is
the question of pay. In 1920 a Committee
was set up by the Imperial House of Commons
under the chairmanship of Lord Desborough
for the purpose of inquiring into the various
police forces in England, Scotland, and Wales,
and making certain recommendations. The
result of their Report was that certain standards of pay were set up for the police forces
in England, Scotland, and Wales, and these
standards were subsequently adopted by the
Royal Irish Constabulary. I think any hon.
Members who have had any connection with
the Royal Irish Constabulary will realise
that up till that time the terms of pay of
that force were entirely inadequate. In the
Report which is now before the House it will
be seen that the Committee recommend that
in the new force about to be set up, and
which is limited to a total of three thousand
men, the pay should be the same as that now
paid to the Royal Irish Constabulary, and I
suggest to this House that this is a
reasonable and adequate amount. A policeman has to display many qualifications. He
has, unfortunately, more especially in this
country, frequently to carry his life in his
hands. He has to have-and this is a point
which I think the public do not quite realise
-a good knowledge of criminal law, and,
above all, know how to apply it. His occupation imposes upon him many restrictions
which do not exist in the case of ordinary
employment. He is liable to be called upon
for duty at any time. He is restricted not
alone in his mode of living but in where he
lives. Therefore, having regard to the nature
of his work, the pay should be sufficiently
good to attract to the Force men possessing
these qualifications.
There is another reason why I suggest that
this standard of pay should be adopted. It
will be found that the Committee recommend
that two-thirds of the Force should be
recruited from the members of the Royal
Adjournment
5 APRIL 1922. -Police Committee's Report.

to introduce a Bill setting up the new Force
prior to that date.
Irish Constabulary, and one-third from the
Special Constabulary. I think hon. members
will agree that it is essential at the outset of
our new Police Force that a large proportion
of its members should be fully trained policemen. In order to attract a sufficient number
of the men of the Royal Irish Constabulary
it is suggested that they should receive an
allowance of one-sixth of the pension to which
such members will be entitled on disbandment as members of the Royal Irish Constabulary. Members of the Royal Irish Constabulary will also retain their existing ranks
when they join the new Force. In regard to
the Special Constabulary-and may I say
that no body of men has done more to earn
the gratitude of the people of Ulster than the
Special Constabulary-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear) it is recommended that one-third of
the recruits for the new Force should be
taken from their ranks. Members of that
Force will all enter as constables, but any
member of the Force who has served as an
officer, or who has served for a period of six
months от more in the rank of headconstable, will be granted for the purposes
of pay, and pension, and seniority six years'
service, and any member who has served six
months in the rank of sergeant will be
deemed to have served four years. In addition, members of the Special Constabulary
joining the new force will be entitled to have
the benefit of their service in the Special
Constabulary. In regard to the age limit it
is proposed that for members of the Special
Constabulary the age limit should be 32, and
in the case of those who have served in any
other of the forces of his Majesty it should
be extended to 35. In the case of ordinary
candidates the age limit should be 27 years.
With regard to the scale of pay of officers
it is also proposed to follow the rates of pay
now in force in the R.I.C. After the senior
officers of the Force have been selected a
Selection Board will be set up consisting of
the senior officers of the Force, who will thereupon select the head constables, ergeants,
and constables of the new force. In regard
to the general question of pay it is proposed
that after the first 3,000 men are recruited a
lower rate of pay may be introduced for new
recruits, but that will be a matter for future
consideration. It is further recommended
that one-third of the new Police Force should
be recruited from the Roman Catholic members of the R.I.C. and Special Constabulary,
and the balance of one-third (1,000) from
Protestant R.I.C., and the remaining onethird (1,000) from the Special Constabulary.
Under the arrangement which this Government has entered into with the Imperial
Government the R.I.C., as regards the members of that Force serving in Northern Ireland, will be disbanded at a date not later
than the 31st May. The Government proposes
Before I conclude may I say that it is hoped
that His Majesty will consent to allow the new
Force to be styled "The Royal Ulster Constabulary," and while I regret it has been
found necessary to disband the old R.I.C.
with its traditions of loyalty and work well
done, I can express no greater hope for our
new Royal Ulster Constabulary than that
they may continue to carry out those traditions. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Before
sitting down I should invite criticisms from
all parts of the House, and I can assure hon.
Members that they will receive very careful
consideration at the hands of the Government.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I would like first
of all, on behalf of the Committee and myself
personally, to thank the Minister of Home
Affairs for the kind words he used towards us,
and I can assure him and the other Members
that if we have accomplished any good we
have done it with a will and a half. Now, I
would like to pray the indulgence of the
House for a few moments to read, if I may, a
few extracts from what was called the Desborough Report. The Desborough Report is
the report of a Committee which was set up
in England, Scotland, and Wales, presided
over by Lord Desborough, to inquire into the
whole question of the police system there, and
I think the few lines that I wish to quote
bear very much indeed on the point that we
are discussing here this evening:-
"The primary function of the police is
the maintenance of law and order and the
preservation of the peace. . . We consider it important also to bear in mind that
the constable, even in the execution of his
duty for the preservation of peace, acts not
as an agent of the Government, exercising
powers derived from that fact, but as a citizen, representing the rest of the community,
and exercising powers which, at any rate in
their elements, are possessed by all citizens
alike. The citizen is still bound, at the
direction of a magistrate or on the appeal of
a constable, to take his part in the preservation of the peace and suppression of disorder, and, in this country, the whole power
of the constable rests on the support, both
moral and physical, of his fellow-citizens.
We desire to emphasise this point as, in our
opinion, it has an important bearing on the

-as to the consideration to which the police

even mainly, the rates of pay in force before

proper in all the circumstances, and likely

view of the evidence which we have heard

his calling and distinguish him from other
public servants and municipal employes,
and we consider the police entitled thereby
to special consideration in regard to their
rate of pay and pensions.
"A candidate for the police must not only
reach certain standards of height and physical development, but must have a constitution which is sound in every way. The
duties the police have to perform are varied
and exacting; they are increasing, and will
probably still increase in variety and complexity, and a man cannot make a good
policeman unless his general intelligence,
memory, and powers of observation are distinctly above the average. His character
should be unblemished: he should be
humane and courteous, and generally, he
should possess a combination of moral,
mental, and physical qualities not ordinarily
required in other employments. Further,
when he becomes a constable, he is entrusted
with powers which may gravely affect the
liberty of the subject, and he must at all
times, be ready to act with tact and discretion, and on his own initiative and responsibility, in all sorts of contingencies. The
burden of individual discretion and
responsibility placed upon a constable is
much greater than that of any other public
servant of subordinate rank."
I am sure the House will forgive me if I
continue this. I consider it is very important
from our point of view:
"The police also stand in a special relationship to the community. Each constable
on appointment becomes one of the duly
constituted guardians of law and order for
and on behalf of the citizens as a whole, and,
as we have pointed out, he makes a declaration of service to the Crown as such. He
undertakes special responsibilities in regard
to the prevention and detection of crime,
and while he does not relieve the citizen
from all responsibility for the protection of
his own property and for bringing offenders
to justice, he claims to be and is the principal agent in the prevention and detection
of crime of all kinds, and generally holds a
position of trust which it is important he
should be able to maintain. We consider it
essential that the sense of obligation to
the public should be preserved in the police,
and the reason we dwell on these considerations at some length is that they are fundamental to the views we have formed as to
the status of the police and the pay they
should receive."

Some people seem to think that a policeman

something crops up in the job which he does

Take the case of the ordinary policeman out

must know the law. I do not mean to say

of law so far as police duties are concerned.
Another point is that he is always on duty.
He cannot go to an evening party; he may
be called away in the middle of it. He may

Now, I would like to try and explain what
is certainly a rather complicated mathematical problem, and that is the question of
pension. But let me say at the outset that I
have not yet seen-I do not know whether the
Prime Minister has seen more-any binding
document produced by the British Government with regard to the R.I.C. on this question. We have heard a lot of things, but no
Act of Parliament has been passed by the
Imperial Parliament yet as far as I know.
However, we have reason to believe that
certain things are going to take place. As
far as I can understand the way the financial
question of the R.I.C. was settled for a certain
number of years was as follows: In the
Imperial House there was on the estimates
a Police Vote for the police of Ireland. The
amount of that Police Vote included pay,
upkeep, and all that sort of thing,
and, in addition, it also included the
actual amount of money which would be
expended during that year in paying pensions. In other words, as far as pensions
were concerned they were simply working out,
with the result that at the end of the financial year across the water they, in conjunction
with our finance people, drew up the financial
arrangements for the 1920 Act. They said:
"The police force in Ireland is costing so
much, which includes the pensions paid
every year; you people in Ireland will be
credited with that amount, and you will have
to pay the pensions yearly out of that
amount."
We
Now, the question then arose as to how we
were to arrive at the amount which the
Northern area would be liable for for pensions under the disbandment scheme of the
Imperial Parliament, and under which they
give a man 12 years' additional service.
could not possibily begin and select out each

we took was that, roughly speaking, the
whole of the R.I.C. in Ireland numbered
8,000. The proportion in the Northern area
would be the quarter of the whole R.I.C.
Therefore, we would in round figures be
responsible for the pensions of 2,000 R.I.C.
men. The only way, therefore, we could get
at the figure was to take what I think
is a fair assumption, namely, the
line of averages. We decided that it was
necessary to take 2,000 R.I.C., so as not to
have the pension of any R.I.C. man
who was disbanded charged against the
Northern Government. On an average the
man who serves three years up to 30 years
would be entitled to a pension of £97 a year,
for which we would be liable. Now, if we are
going to add that man's pension on to the pay

going to cost a further considerable sum of
money. The way we fixed the 2,000 was by
first of all fixing that a fair number for the
whole area would be 3,000, and the way we
arrived at that figure was in 1921 the authorised strength for the Six Counties and Belfast was 2,817 of all ranks.
But that number did not include the
Headquarters in Dublin or the Depot, where
there were three hundred or four hundred
men who could be drafted to any part of
Ireland as required. In fixing that figure
of three thousand we considered it was a

it was necessary at the present time. We do,

I can see the discussion on this Report can be
confined to two points, namely the question of
pay and the composition of the Force. On the
question of pay I admit there were very conflicting opinions in the Committee, and some
of us, especially the Members of Parliament
who have to face the taxpayer, realised what a
serious situation this was, and what a serious
undertaking it was to pay the Force on such
substantial lines. I hope the House will bear
with me if I try to visualise the situation.
We have a Royal Irish Constabulary who are
to-day enjoying certain pay and emoluments,
and they are about to be disbanded. It is of infinite importance that we should have as many
of them in our new Force as we require,
and I hope we shall get all we require, and to
offer them less pay than they have up to now
been receiving would, I think, be an excellent
way of defeating the ends we had in view.
Assuming that we are going to get a certain
number of R.I.C. men, we then come to the
question of linking up the Special Constabulary. Realising that they have very handsome
pay, although it is only temporary, and realising also that they have been two years in our
service, taking very serious risks, and risks
which most of us would rather not run, the
question occurred to our minds, and I hope to
our consciences, "can we ask these men to
come into the new Force for less pay than the
flat rate of the R.I.C.?" We felt that we
could not. To have the R.I.C. with one rate
of pay and the "A" Specials with another
rate of pay-two classes of men walking the
street on different scales of pay-would be very
anomalous and unworkable, and no business
man would recommend anything of the kind.
Therefore, taking into consideration the wider
and bigger interests of the community, we had
to take our courage in our hands and suggest
a unified rate of pay for both sections of the
force. But you may say there is an extra inducement offered to members of the R.I.C.
For the first six years' service there will be a
year added to their pension, and for the next

confess there was a difficulty in the minds of

enjoy reasonable pay, and, in fact, to have
pay better than that given to other ranks of
the same type of men outside, but if we go

and right that fifty per cent. of the Special
Constabulary should be asked to join the
new Force. We think it is only fair to them,
and I am sure that when this matter comes
up for discussion on the Bill, which the
Minister for Home Affairs will bring forward,
there will be very, very strong opposition to
the proposal of the majority of the Committee. I submit that this should also apply to
the junior officers of the new Force-the men
who soldiered in France, the men who stood
before the guns-that fifty per cent. of the
officers of the new Force should be taken from
the officers of the "A" Special Force as it
exists to-day. Surely we are not asking too
much. We realise that you must keep a due
sense of proportion, that you must have as
many of the old Constabulary and the old
officers as will run the new machine, and run
it effectively and properly, but surely fifty
per cent. is enough and more than enough.
If we keep a proper balance the result will
be a very effective Force, because in the "A"
Force you are getting the young men, the
ambitious men, the men with their futures
to make, men who are as keen as mustard,
and who are trying to do the best they can
for their country. These will be the men
who wish to get on, and will not be waiting
merely till their time is up to enjoy
their pensions. They will not be simply
putting in the remainder of their days, but
will have their careers before them, and I
hold that they should not be left out in the
reckoning of the proportions of the composition of the new Force.
The other point I wish to make is in regard
to the Selection Board. If you look at Clause
17, it says that the Minister in charge is to
gather some of the officers of the old Force,
the existing Force-that is, the Royal Irish
Constabulary. I do not wish in any way to
misrepresent the Committee, Clause 17
says:
"That in the formation of the New Force
the Minister of Home Affaire should appoint the Officers after consultation with
such Senior Members of the existing Police
Forces in Ireland as he may consider
advisable."

I think it should be clearly understood that

make one unified force, and that we should

That is all the comment I wish to make on
the Report at present. I confess that the
salary is a good salary for the Constabulary,
but let us remember the conditions which
prevail in our country round us. It is up to
this House to see to it that under every
reasonable circumstance they will have
Police Force to cope with any disorder that
may face us and which is facing us every day.
It is not suggested that this is a salary laid
down for all time. I do not agree with the
Chairman (Mr. Lloyd Campbell) when he says
that these 3,000 men must have this salary
guaranteed to them for the rest of their days.
I hold that it should be subject to the fluctuations of the cost of living as is provided in
the Desborough Report, and if it is not in
the Report of this Committee it ought to we
put in. It would be a very anomalous condition that any class of men should be supported by the State, high and dry, above all
the laws of the fluctuation of prices and the
cost of living, and enjoy a salary that was
fixed in war time, when the cost of living was
at its height, and that that salary could never
be brought down. Apply the rule to the
Civil Service and you will land yourselves I
know not where. I hope the Minister of
Home Affairs will not make it an iron rule
that we are never to reconsider the salaries
of these 3,000 men. They must take their
chance just like any other people in the community, and if the Desborough standard is
lowered in England, Scotland and Wales, then
-and I know the police are quite agreeablethe scale must be revised here. We must not
by anything we do have the police charge us
with not playing the game. Let us speak our
minds at once, and let it be understood that
they must come in under the same scale as
all other Civil Servants. I hope the House
will also understand that the salary suggested
here only affects the first 3,000 men, and the
Committee have yet to consider what should
be the salary of the men coming after. We
suggest that it should be very much lower.
There is no dissentient voice in the. Committee on this point. Some of us think it
should be very considerably lower, and 1
suggest to this House that we ought to be
very careful in fixing that salary in view of
the outlook in the trade and industry of this
country. I am afraid we are coming to such
a state of finance and business procedure in
this country as will bring the cost of living
and prices generally very much down, and
you will be offering very much lower salaries
to these men than your minds lead you to
think of at the present time. Let us remember that the salary of a policeman before the
war was only something like £85 a year. His
salary now is over £200 a year. Do you think
that this will go on? Do you think that we
will be able to pay £700,000 or £800,000 to our
Police Force? These are suggestions I am
making, but the Committee feel as keenly as
any Member of this House that the permanent
salary, the future salary, of all outside these
first 3,000 men ought to be well and
seriously considered when the Report comes
finally before this House. There is nothing
further I wish to discuss in this Report. The
Committee gave every attention to all the
ramifications of the whole situation, but no
gave anything like the amount of
research and infinite industry and pains in
the whole undertaking that our Chairman
devoted to the task. (Hon. Members: Hear,

I asked the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Lloyd

the pay given a policeman and the wages

Thursday, 6th April, 1922.
The House met at a Quarter after Two of

Oral Answers to Questions.
UNEMPLOYED MEN IN BALLYMENA.
1. Mr. M'MULLAN (for Mr. CRAWFORD)
asked the Minister of Labour if he will state
the number of unemployed men in Ballymena, according to last returns; if a portion of the £500,000 granted for relief works
in Belfast and neighbourhood will be available for Ballymena, and if so, what steps
would be necessary for the Ballymena Coun
cil to take in order to participate in the
grant?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
ANDREWS): I regret to have to inform the
honourable Member that on April 3rd there
were in Ballymena 655 men totally unemployed and 249 men on systematic short time.
In reply to the second part of the Question, the honourable Member is probably
aware that the £500,000 grant for relief
works in Belfast and neighbourhood was obtained from the Imperial Government in
consideration of the very exceptional position
in Belfast. This grant is not available, therefore, for the country districts.

answer, I would like to ask the right hon.

their own, by reason of the present stress in

Orders of the Day.
Criminal Procedure Bill.
STATEMENT BY THE ATTORNEY-
GENERAL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed, "That
the Bill be now read a Second Time."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
It will be within the recollection of Members
of the House that the Prime Minister made
a very important statement on Tuesday
dealing with an Agreement that had been
entered into between the Northern Government and the Provisional Government, and
countersigned by representatives of the Imperial Government. The Bill, of which I
have the honour to move the Second Reading,
is concerned really with one particular clause
of that Agreement, Clause No. IV. Might I
say, in answer to my hon. and learned
Friend, the Member for the University (Mr.
Robb), who spoke just a moment ago, that
we have been frightfully pressed in connection with the preparation of this Bill. I
myself am personally aware that the
draftsman has been working at very high
pressure indeed. This is a Bill of a novel
character, one for which there is practically
no precedent to be found. I say practically
no precedent, because there is one precedent
at least. The greatest care had to be taken
to make provision, as well as could be done,
for carrying out the words contained in this
Bill. I know that SO far as the
draftsman is concerned the draft left his
hands yesterday afternoon, and it was sent
to the printers. I do not know whether they
were asked to do overtime-we heard a lot
about overtime the other day-but I understood the Bill was to be ready by 12 o'clock
to-day However, I myself, who am
cerned with moving the Second Reading of
the Bill, have only had the Bill in my
hands for about ten minutes. Therefore if
hon. Members are at a disadvantage they
will remember that I am to a very large
extent at the same disadvantage. May I
read Clause IV. of the Agreement that was
entered into? It is as follows:-
con-
"A Court to be constituted for the trial,
without jury, of persons charged with
serious crime, the Court to consist of the
Lord Chief Justice and one of the Lords'
Justices of Appeal of Northern Ireland.
Any person committed for trial for a
serious crime to be tried by that Court:
(a) If he so requests, or
(b) If the Attorney-General for Northern
Ireland so directs.
Serious crime should be taken to mean
any offence punishable with death, penal
servitude, or imprisonment for a term
exceeding six months. The Government of
Northern Ireland will take steps for
passing the legislation necessary to give
effect to this Article."
Now, that is the article which has given
rise to the present Bill, and as far as I have
had the opportunity of considering the matter, and, of course, I have been in consultation with the draftsman, who gave me every
assistance that he could, I think the Bill
which is before the House, and which will
385 Criminal Procedure Bill
1922.
6 APRIL
-Second Reading.
now, I hope, be read the Second Time, carries
out the agreement contained in Article 4.
The Bill consists of five clauses. The first one
in the words of this very Clause 4 of the
Agreement provides-
"Where any person charged with a
serious crime is committed for trial, he
shall
(a) If he so requests, or
(b) If the Attorney-General for Northerr
Ireland so directs
be tried by the Court established under
this Act."
Now, if as a lawyer I had been asked, shall
I say, to give my blessing to a clause of this
description, I might have had great difficulty indeed.
(Hon. Members; Hear, hear.)
But it is in the Agreement, and I take it
that this House is prepared to carry out the
Agreement. Up to the present, whatever
may be said against the Government of
Northern Ireland, it cannot be said that any
promise which has been made by us has been
unfulfilled, and I hope that so long as we do
carry on this Government that same observation will apply Once we have passed our
word, that word will be as good as our bond,
and in the very letter and in the very spirit
we shall proceed to carry out our engagements. If he so requests, a prisoner when
committed for trial may require that he shall
be tried by this special Court which is to be
set up, instead of being tried by a jury of his
peers. I listened with great interest to my
hon. Friend the Member for West Belfast
when speaking on the motion for adjournment on Tuesday, and he complained-and in
certain circumstances the complaint would
have great weight in it-that this was to a
large extent doing away with a provision of
Magna Charta, and that it was depriving
Irishmen, shall we say, of that sure shield
which has always protected them-trial by
jury.
a
Is there any ground for complaint if
prisoner himself, the person who is committed
for trial, does not wish to be tried by a jury?
If he thinks that is a tribunal which may
be dispensed with to his own advantage, then
there may be an objection undoubtedly from
the point of view of those who have to carry
out the law and administer the law, but there
can be no objection put into the mouth of
that man such as was put by my hon. Friend,
namely, that he is being deprived of trial by
jury, because, although I have no definite
information on the subject, I am perfectly
certain, as anyone must he certain, that this
provision was never put in at the instance
of the Northern Government. (Hon.
Members: "Hear, hear!") The Northern

Government have nothing to fear from the
way in which juries have done their work.
They have done it magnificently, and I
believe that in the future they will do it
magnificently, too. Therefore, so far as
the objection arising from the deprivation of trial by jury is concerned, there can
be no objection if the person charged so
requests.
I admit that there may be something to be
said against Clause B, which I have just read,
"if the Attorney-General for Northern Ire
land so directs." Well, I do not know what
is thought of the present Attorney-General
for Northern Ireland, whether he is a reasonable man or not, but speaking for myself,
and, of course, without giving any binding
pledge or anything of that kind, I would like
to indicate what my attitude would be in
reference to cases that may come before me
to be dealt with under this Clause.
I am
perfectly satisfied up to the present with
the way in which juries have discharged their
duty. They have discharged their duty
without fear, favour, or affection. (Hon.
Members: "Hear, hear!") If they continue
to do that, then I think I might go so far
as to pledge myself, as far as I am concerned
personally, while I hold the reins of office
of Attorney-General I shall be quite satisfied
to allow that state of affairs to continue, and
to deprive no man of his right to trial by
jury, unless it should happen that jurors
through fear, through intimidation, through
cowardice, through partisanship, or for any
other reason, should fail to do their duty; and
if they fail to do their duty ought there not
to be a remedy?
If such a serious departure has been made
in Clause A as to allow a person to select his
own tribunal, surely it is not a very great
thing to say that the Attorney-General of the
day, the Officer responsible for the administration of law, more responsible than anyone
else for the administration of law and order,
should be allowed to say in particular cases,
This is a case that could not fairly be tried
by jury, this is a case in which trial by jury
must be withdrawn." I take it that hon.
Members will give the Attorney-General of the
day credit for trying to do his duty to the
utmost of his ability. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The Crown never seeks, and it is no
part of the Crown to seek, for victims. They
want to see that the law is administered, and
administered fairly and impartially, and as
long as the ordinary tribunals are prepared
to carry out their duty then the Crown
ought to be, and will be, satisfied with that
duty so carried out. So much, then, for the
request which may be made by the prisoner,
or for the direction which may be given by
the Attorney-General as to the withdrawal of
the trial from the jury and the sending of it
to the Special Court to be set up.

In 1882, when the jurors of the South of Ireland were terrorised, and failed to do their
duty, Parliament was forced to bring in a
Bill setting up a Commission of three
Judges, and, as the learned Attorney-General
very fairly admitted, the whole thing proved
a dead letter. Therefore, because this precedent proved a dead letter, it is one which
is going to be adopted by the Government of
Northern Ireland. I should say that this
precedent is not one which ought to
be followed, or which is in any way useful.
The Attorney-General was also fair enough
to admit that if he had been asked as a lawyer
to defend this Bill he would find it very difficult to do so. I can well believe it. He says
Magna Charta is not impinged upon because
a prisoner has the right of saying whether he
shall or shall not be tried by this Special
Court. I never knew of a criminal who
had any desire to be tried by any Court,
special or otherwise, and I did not know
that it was the duty of Parliament to
consult merely the wishes of the criminals
concerned. If we are to make this change
-and it is a serious change, though only for
twelve months- in the criminal procedure of
the country surely some substantial reason
should be given why we should make it.
I could understand the learned Attorney-
General coming to this House and saying
that the jurors of Ulster had failed in their
duty through fear, or through partisanship,
or for any cause like this, that the jurors
had failed to carry out their oath to give
a verdict according to the evidence-I could
understand the learned Attorney-General
coming to the House then, and asking us to
set up a special Commission under those
circumstances. But he has not given us
a single case where a jury in Ulster has
failed to do its duty. Not only so, but I
challenge him now to give us a single
instance even in these terrible times in
which we are living-where an Ulster jury
has failed in its duty. If he were able to
do that there would be some justification
for asking us to pass this Bill, but I submit
that under the circumstances, and the juries
having done their duty, there is no case
whatever for departing from the ordinary
procedure.
I agree with the learned Attorney-General
that crime is crime, and that it is an absurdity for us to start to classify crimes as
political crimes. Whether a man shoots
another man because of his political opinion,
because he has got some personal spite
against him, or because he wants to rob him,
surely that is murder, and I do not know
why we should go into different classes of
murder. To me there is only one class of
murder, and all murders are equally black
and equally detestable. Further, I do not
see why, because a man calls himself a
political murderer, some special provision
should be made in his case that is not made
in the case of an ordinary citizen. I would
like the learned Attorney-General to tell us
what is going to happen in case the two
judges disagree.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. LYNN: There must be two judges,
one of whom must be the Lord Chief Justice
of Northern Ireland. Suppose they disagree
what is going to happen? Why, one of
the two judges will always come back
on the case. You are not going to get
a fresh tribunal. I would like whoever
replies on behalf of the Government
to tell us what they are going to do in a

popular thing nowadays. You may murder,

I do not want to waste the time of the
House by traversing ground which has been
gone over already. I object to this Bill on
two very simple but very important grounds.
The first is that it interferes with the great
Charter under which our nation has grown
up, under which freedom has developed as
it has developed in no other country in the
world. The second is that under present
conditions this Bill is an insult to the jurors
of Ulster who in all circumstances and under
all conditions have faithfully discharged
their duties. What are we going to get
in return for abrogating Magna Charta even
for twelve months, or for casting a slur---
although I am sure it is the last thing the

of Ulster, because inferentially there is a

the run. To-day, Mr. Collins and Mr.
Griffith have got no influence whatever in
the South of Ireland. They are unable to
defend themselves or their friends, but yet
we are making this grave change in the
constitution of the law in order to please
two politicians who, as I say, are on the
run and who are unable to carry out the
pledges they have signed and agreed to. I
do not want to hamper the Government in
any way, I do not even want to force this
matter to a division. I have my own im-

After Clause 8 insert as a new Clause-
"The provisions of section fourteen of the
Petty Sessions (Ireland) Act, 1851, in relation to the readings of depositions as
evidence upon the trial of a person
charged with an indictable crime
offence, shall extend so as to authorize the

Mr. BEST: I beg to move, "That this
House doth agree with the Senate in the
said Amendment."
This is a very important Amendment, and
perhaps the full significance of it does not
appear from the words that are upon the
Paper. My hon. and learned Friends will
appreciate the full significance of it.
Section 14 of the Petty Sessions (Ireland)
Act, 1851, provides that where a deposition
has been taken and a person has been re
turned for trial, and where the person who
has made the deposition dies before the trial
is carried through, then on proof of certain
formalities that deposition may be used
upon the trial. Of course the person who
made the deposition cannot be there; he is
dead and gone. What is proposed in this
new clause is that that provision should be
extended so as to include depositions taken
before a magistrate, and that we should be
authorised to read those depositions as
evidence where it is proved that a witness
is so ill as to be unable to travel, or where
the attendance of the witness cannot be procured owing to the prevalence of a state of
disorder or otherwise. It is a curious
matter, but it is a fact, that the first of the
new provisions is already used in English
statutes. In other words, in England, where
a witness has made a deposition, that deposition can be used upon the trial either
in the case of the death of the witness or in
the case where the witness is so ill as to be
unable to travel. But that latter provision
has never applied in Ireland. We want it
to apply now, and further, we want this
Amendment, namely, where a witness has
been kept back from a trial, where threats
have been resorted to and intimidation has
been used against him, we wish to have the
power of using the deposition made by that
witness, so that the effect and value of his
evidence shall not be lost. It has been
found most effectual where depositions have
courtsbeen taken, particularly before
martial, and where a warning has been
given. Now if anything happens to this
witness, if this witness is kept out of the
way, still his sworn statement can be used.
When that becomes known it will mean
there is no good trying to intimidate a wit-
Less because his deposition can still be used,
and the accused will not have the advantage,
if it be an advantage, of having the witness
there for cross-exmination.
Question put, and agreed to.

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE BILL.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That notwithstanding any Standing Order
or custom of the House, the Criminal Procedure Bill be passed through all its remaining stages at this day's sitting."—(Mr.
Burn.)
Mr. LYNN: In view of the state of the
country at the present time, and in view of
the fact that this Bill has been brought in
for the purpose of carrying out the Agreement made between the Northern Government and Mr. Griffith and Mr. Collins, and
also in view of the fact that these gentlemen
may disappear from public life inside a few
weeks, or even a few days, I would ask the
Government would they not consider the advisability of postponing further consideration of this Bill for some time?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): It is the view of the Government
that under the circumstances it is better that
this measure should be proceeded with. I
would point out to my hon. Friend (Mr.
Lynn) that, unless the Bill is expedited and
taken in all its stages, it will be impossible to complete it before the adjournment,
which we contemplate on Thursday-and I
am quite sure I interpret the views of hon.
Members when I suggest that Thursday
would be a suitable day for the adjournment
over the Easter holidays-so that we should
not impinge upon the holiday season.
In
regard to the point that has been raised by
my hon. Friend as to whether the Bill
should or should not proceed, I think under
the circumstances we at least should be expected to do our duty in this matter irrespective of what may happen in regard to
the position in Southern Ireland.

crime or offence was committed or in
which the accused person was returned for
trial or elsewhere, have the same powers,
authorities and jurisdiction as if sitting in
the county in which the offence was committed, or in which the accused person was
returned for trial.

THE SCHEDULE.
CRIMES AND OFFENCES TO WHICH
THIS ACT APPLIES.
(1) Treason or Treason Felony.
(2) Murder or Manslaughter.
(3) Assault which either causes actual
bodily harm or grievous bodily harm or is
committed with intent to cause grievous
bodily harm.
(4) Arson whether by common Law or by
Statute.
(5) Any crime or offence cognisable by law
involving (a) the breaking into, firing at or
otherwise attacking or injuring a dwellinghouse; (b) larceny or robbery with threats
or violence; (c) malicious injury or damage
to or destruction of any property whatsoever,
including any crime or offence under the
Malicious Damage Act, 1861.
(6) Any crime or offence against the Explosive Substances Act, 1883, or the Firearms Act, 1920.
(7) Any attempt or conspiracy to commit
any of the said crimes or offences or being
accessory to or aiding or abetting in the
commission thereof.

We simply ask that treason and treason
felony which should be tried by the ordinary
Courts, should now be tried by the Special
Tribunal. We are not altering in the
slightest degree the law as to what constitutes treason or treason felony. I think my
hon. and learned Friend would not suggest
for a moment that if under present circumstances a man were charged with having been
guilty of treasonable practices or having
committed treason felony our Courts are
powerless to try that man. Our Courts as
constituted at the moment can try that man,
and what we propose in the Bill is that a
man charged with one of these offences
should have the choice of being tried in the
ordinary Courts or the Special Tribunal now
being set up.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I beg to move that the Bill be
now read a Second time. If I had been told
a year or so ago that I would to-day in a
Northern Parliament, as Minister of Labour,
be responsible for moving the Second Reading of an Emergency Unemployment Insurance Bill, affecting, approximately, a
quarter of a million insured persons, about
one fourth of whom at the present time are
unfortunately unemployed, I would have
said that such a chain of circumstances was
almost impossible, and that my friend was
a false prophet. However, as we get older--
and in this respect at any rate I am making
progress-I think we feel that our lives are
in large a measure portioned out for us.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) In the first
place, I should tell the House that (except
in two of its clauses to which I will refer
later) this Bill is drafted on parallel lines
to the Bill which has just passed the Imperial House of Commons. This is in comformity with the decision of the Cabinet of
Northern Ireland, of which I am sure Hon.
Members will all approve, namely, that our
unemployed persons should be dealt with
similarly to those who are unemployed in
Great Britain.
This Bill amalgamates the Unemployment
Benefit authorised by the Unemployment Insurance Acts of 1920 and 1921 with the Grants
authorised by the Dependants Act of last
year.

The present unemployment situation will

The House can be assured that this money

have almost completed the appointment of

me in connection with this all important
matter. The names of this Committee I hope
to announce in the Press to-morrow or the
next day. I will be much disappointed if
some of these relief works are not started
within a week from to-day.
