Mr. M'GUFFIN: I would like to join the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn)
in offering congratulations to the Minister of
Labour for the very efficient, very clear, and
adequate way in which he has presented this
Bill to the House. It is most important that
this Bill should pass as quickly as possible.
There is very little criticism that can be
offered, because the Bill runs on parallel lines
to that passed in the Imperial House. There
are a great many lapsed claims in connection
with our system of insurance, and it is very
desirable that as soon as possible, by means
of a Bill of this kind, claims for the resumption of payment should be provided for. I
was in company one evening which was discussing the question of which is the most experimental of the sciences. Some said that it
was biology, others said it was chemistry, but
a more intelligent individual than the rest
suggested it was law. In connection with
this question we have had eleven Bills in the
course of as many years, all tending to
improve the conditions of insurance and the
position of the worker. I was very pleased,
in reading the discussion that took place in
the Imperial House the other night, to see that
the Minister of Labour took occasion to clear
away a very false impression that existed in
the House to the effect that unemployment
insurance constituted a dole. I want to protest against that. I think I have even heard
it suggested in this House. It is by no means
a dole; and, in view of the fact that the
system is contributory, I fail to understand
how any person can regard it as a dole.
From November, 1920, until the present time
£80,000,000 will have been expended by the
Imperial Parliament on insurance benefits,
and of that £80,000,000 the Government will
have contributed £16,000,000. That is to say,
the Government have contributed about
one-fifth, and, therefore, the workers and the
employers are entitled to the credit of having
contributed four-fifths of the entire amount.
To talk of that system as conducted on the
basis of a dole is, to my mind, preposterous.
I quite agree with my hon. Friend (Mr. Lynn)
that there are many respects in which the Bill
might be criticised, but, considering that it
has got through the Imperial House, where it
was subjected to very few criticisms, and in
view of its urgency, we will accept the Bill,
and put it through the House as quickly as
possible. We are glad to know that it is
only a temporary measure, and that the right
honourable Gentleman has in contemplation,
through the assistance and advice of the Committee which he set up, an even better Bill.
However, this Bill has to run for fifteen
months from now, and it will be the end of
June, next year, before that period will have
elapsed. I am quite sure that during that
time the Minister of Labour will focus his
attention on this matter, and give it every
possible consideration, and that he will then
introduce to this House a Bill that will be
worthy of our position as a new Government.
There is one particular in which an improvement might reasonably he effected, and that
is the amalgamation of Health and Labour
Insurance. If that were done, valuable
economy could be achieved, and that is very
desirable, because, at the moment, our financial status is very uncertain, and the amount
of our income is even more problematical.
In view of that fact, I think it is very necessary that the Minister of Labour should see
that the system of Unemployment Insurance
in the Northern area is carried out with the
greatest possible economy.
There is another respect in which the Bill
might very usefully have been amended, and
am sorry that the Imperial Parliament did
not see its way to adopt the amendment that
was proposed, and thus in all probability
have secured the advantage to us. I refer to
the disqualification that takes place through
strike exigencies. Take the case of a man
who is employed in one section of a firm.
The workers in another section of that firm
go out on strike, and, because the first section
I mentioned is dependent on the second section for the supply of the necessary material
to carry on their work, they are thrown out
of employment. Those who are thrown out of
employment in that way are deprived of their
work through no fault of their own, but,

under the present Bill, they are not entitled

Take the case of a man who is married.
He
is entitled to £1 a week, but if he has a wife
and two children he only gets 22s. That is to

The Government would have been well

in respect of the wife, and allowed more to
the children, because I am of the opinion that
the greatest hardship exists where children
have to be provided for. When you work it
out, it means 1d. per day to provide meals
for a child. That is absolutely inadequate,
and it is a pity the Bill could not have been
improved in this respect. The amount
allowed to children during the war was something like 6s, and 3s. per week, and as my
hon Friend (Mr. Lynn) has said, it requires
as much to support a child now as it did
during the war. Yet you are making the
miserable provision of 1s. a week for him,
whereas during the war you paid him 6s. and
3s. We are all glad to know that prices are
falling, but they are not falling to a degree
that enables us to say that we are better off
now than we were prior to the war. On the
whole, we are worse off.
The Imperial Government contemplate
paying £60,000,000 in respect of insurance
benefit within the next fifteen months. That
represents a great volume of relief, and
under present circumstances the question
that suggests itself is: how did we manage
prior to 1910 or 1911 when these measures
were first introduced? When a worker was
suddenly displaced he had no resources unless
he had made a little provision out of the
rather inadequate pay with which he was remunerated at that time. Now we find that
provision is made, and I regard it as the
duty of the State to provide for the workers
just as they do for soldiers. After all, our
workers are the backbone and the basis of
the riches and prosperity of our nation.
Where would we be without them? When a
serious strike occurs and certain utilities are
cut off, we know immediately how the mass
of the workers stand in relation to us. If
soldiers are useful in protecting us during a
period of war, the industrial worker, whom
I may call in the circumstances the industrial soldier, is just as important for our
maintenance during the years of peace. The
need of the moment is to get the Bill through
this House as expeditiously as possible. We
trust the House will deal with it in the
spirit of the appeal made by the right hon.
Gentleman who moved the Second Reading
(Mr. Andrews). We all feel the greatest
sympathy with those who, through no fault
of their own, find themselves unemployed.
We were glad to hear from the Minister of
Labour that things are a little more hopeful
particularly in the North of Ireland, and
we hope the time is not far distant when
normal conditions will return, though at the
moment I am very sceptical as to what may
happen within the next two or three years.
However, a Bill of this description, when it
becomes law, is certainly of great advantage
to the industrial classes. They recognise that
fact, but they do not like the benefit to be
given to them as charity or a dole, and if you
are administering an Act for the benefit of
the workers you are not to detract from its
advantages by associating it with an insult.
Workers have independent minds just like
other people, and they are entitled to anything towards which they contribute. Under
the circumstances I think we would be well
advised to push this Bill through as speedily
as possible.

Trade
and unemployment is widespread.

437 Unemployment Insurance Bill

suffering. Many persons are passing through
a time of great distress and privation. We
are faced at the moment with a period of
exceptional unemployment which I have
reason to believe may be increased to some
extent unless something is done to end the
crisis that is in the air at the moment.
I am one of those who believe that employment cannot be created by Acts of Parliament. I recognise that Acts of Parliament
cannot change the economic situation of the
country, and as we return to a healthful
condition of industry in that proportion
will prosperity come back to the country.
This is a most exceptional time of unexampled unemployment-it is the ebb and flow
of trade, and consequently I ask the Members
of this House to give this Bill its Second
Reading unanimously.
Mr. MARK: After listening to the Debate
that has taken place here I only wish to
add a few words of comment. I did not
want to intervene at an earlier stage, but
I would like to congratulate the Minister
of Labour, who has done his best to maintain industrial peace in the Six Counties.
The part of this Debate that struck me
more than any other was the reference
made by the hon. Member for Tyrone and
Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) to the administration of these funds. Nowhere in the Six
Counties is the state of affairs he referred
to better illustrated than in the city of
Derry. What is there to prevent any man
coming in from Donegal, and after a few
weeks asking for unemployment benefit? I
have known instances where men have had
the cheek to come into Derry to ask an employer to sign their cards although there
have been weeks in which they had never
crossed the threshold. That is done in
Derry city. Recently in Derry city two
local people, one an ex-soldier minus a leg,
were turned out of the labour exchange, and
two others, one of whom was not a Six
County man, were appointed in their place.
These things naturally create friction in
the district, and I think that in drafting
a Bill such as this something should be inserted which would prevent an imposition
of this sort taking place.
It has been stated that an inspector of the
Ministry of Labour could not find a single
case of an I.R.A. man having received unemployment benefit. I am afraid the inspector could not find out who the I.R.A.
men were, but notwithstanding what the
inspector reported I am strongly of opinion
that in all the Counties there are I.R.A. men
receiving benefit from the Six County funds.
It was a matter of comment at the recent
Revision Sessions in Derry that twelve or
fourteen young unmarried men who were
not born in the city but had come in during
the last few years were getting votes in respect of two rooms. Surely there is something wrong when these men can come in
and hold up the street corners while at the
same time drawing unemployment benefit
from us. There are men employed in agriculture who are receiving benefit and they
never contributed anything towards it. Take
the case of the men employed on the new
Basin in Derry. These men are all farmers'
sons who are engaged daily looking after
their blackfaced sheep on the hills, and they
come into Derry once a fortnight or once a
month, and because they have been working
a few weeks on the new Derry Basin they
can get benefit, although they have been
working on their fathers' farms. Some limit
should be put on the drawing of this benefit,
and I think we should not have followed exactly in the footsteps of the Imperial Parliament. We should have gone back on the
old system of 10s a week for a married man
and doubled the allowance for the children.

to rule the hon. Member's amendment out

well established rule that nobody may move
an amendment the object of which is to
impose an extra charge upon the people or
the taxpayers except the Government of the
day. It is one of the elementary rules of
constitutional financial procedure that no private Member may move an amendment the
effect of which will be to impose or increase
the charges upon the people.

for the man, five shillings for the wife, and

that you get nothing. Our object in bringing

allowance for the child. It is not a very
big sum for the area under the jurisdiction
of our Parliament compared with what the
cost would be for the whole country. We were
going to table the Amendment to see if my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) could not
meet us. The wife who has children is not
in the same position as the wife who has
no children. The latter is able to give her
attention to some work, but where there are
two or three children the woman must give
her whole attention to them. Our reason
for bringing this important matter before
the House was to see if two shillings could
not be paid instead of one in respect of each

Had this been a permanent measure for a

and everything is improving, and I am quite
sure my right hon. Friend will have our

not want to rule out Clause 1 at all.
I am merely taking up the time of the

ing it is only a shilling for the child. After

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 13th April, 1922.
The House met at a quarter after Two of
the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
FIREARMS
FOR "B" AND "C" CLASS
SPECIALS.
1. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister for
Home Affairs if he will state whether "B"
and "C" Class Specials are entitled to keep
firearms for their protection at home?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I would refer the hon.
Member to the Notice which has appeared
in the Public Press. The applications for
permits for this purpose should be addressed
to the County Commandant concerned.
FLAX PRODUCTION.
2. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Minister of
Agriculture if he can state the number of
tons of Flax produced in Ireland in the years
1920-21; if he can also state the number of
tons likely to be produced in the present year.
Also whether the Ministry has taken any
action to encourage the farmers to put in
more, in view of the certainty of a great
shortage?
The ASSISTANT PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Burn): I have been asked
to reply to this question on behalf of my
right hon. Friend. The number of tons of
flax produced in Ireland in 1920 was 17,020
and in 1921, 4,788 tons. It is not practicable
at this stage, when the seed has not yet been
sown, to estimate what weight of flax fibre
is likely to be produced from this year's crop.
There is no reason to anticipate that the
area under flax in the 1922 season will vary
to any great extent as compared with the
area in 1921. The Minister has had the
matter under consideration, but the question
of extending the area under flax depends
almost entirely on the factor of price, viz. :—
whether the farmer is satisfied that it will
be more remunerative for him to grow flax
instead of some other farm crop.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of that
question, might I ask the hon. Gentleman
if representations on this matter have been
made by the North of Ireland Spinners'
Association with respect to a great shortage
of raw material, and if he can say if they
anticipate a larger import from Russia than
has been the case for the past four or five
years?
Mr. BURN: I am unable to answer the
supplementary question put by my hon.
Friend (Mr. McGuffin) but I will have it
brought before the Minister of Agriculture.
ADJOURNMENT OF THE HOUSE
(EASTER).

the railways in Ireland; whether any communication has passed between him and the
representatives of the Provisional Government with respect to this matter, and what
action he proposes to take in respect of this
effort to ignore the authority of the Northern Parliament?
Southern Ireland Commission has any authority to deal with Railway matters in Northern Ireland. My right hon. Friend, the

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James
Craig): The answer to the first part of the
question is in the affirmative. Notwithstanding that my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour, and Mr. M'Grath,
Minister of Labour in the Provisional Government, were for some time in complete

with the Joint Railway Commission, the
Provisional Government have refused to
honour the agreement arrived at last February between the two Ministers of Labour
and the representatives of the Railway Companies and the Trade Unions. As regards
the alleged reason for breaking this agreement, this Government has carried out the
London Pact, but I should point out that
the terms of that Pact have no connection
whatever with the agreement to set up a
Joint Railway Commission. The Chairman
of the Commission for Southern Ireland is
in complete error when he states that the
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Arising out of that

the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford)
I do not say it in any offensive way.

is happening all over Ulster, and it is this:
You have consumption produced by a
microbe, and no man is attacking the microbe

Empire Day.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 17th May, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker in the chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
EXTENSION OF CURFEW.
1. Mr. GRANT (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
inform the House why Curfew has been
altered to 10 p.m. over the entire City, whilst
disturbances are confined to small areas?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The disturbed state of the
City demands that during non-Curfew hours
the number of police on duty shall be greatly
in excess of normal. It is, therefore, necessary
to restrict free movement of the populace
earlier to enable the police to obtain adequate
rest. At present strength the police are
working at an average of twelve hours per
day.
Owing to disbandment of the R.I.C.,
which is now taking place, the number of
trained police in Belfast is being, and will
still further be, materially reduced.
Mr. GRANT:-Arising out of that answer,
I would like to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs if he considers that men who are
engaged at their work during the day, and
have agreed to the Summer-time Act for the
benefit of the extra hour of light, and are
devoting that hour to working in their plots
in different parts of the City and suburbs,
should be punished by this particular Order,
which is unfair to those who are law-abiding
citizens?
Mr. DONALD: The Minister of Home
Affairs says that the Royal Irish Constabulary
are overworked. May I ask my right hon.
Friend if he will take into consideration the
advisability of enrolling "B" Specials, who
will be delighted to give their services free
for this particular work?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Unfortunately, as
I explained in my answer to the hon. Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Grant), the "B"
men are not trained men in the sense that
the Royal Irish Constabulary are.
these outrages which have been committed
have been perpetrated during the daytime?

workmen on Saturday morning from the
tower of the Roman Catholic Chapel at the
head of the Falls Road-

being made with the local authorities for a

State-provided schools in Northern Ireland.
and the hoisting of the Union Jack on all

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Prime Minister
has asked me to reply to this question. The
attention of local authorities is being drawn
by circular to the question of the observance
of Empire Day, and it is hoped they may be
able to give the matter every consideration.
As regards schools, I understand that the
Minister of Education has only power to enforce a holiday upon those schools directly
under the management of the Ministry,
namely, the Model Schools. He can only
proceed in regard to other schools by request
that a holiday be observed and by giving his
sanction that the holiday taken shall not be
included in the normal school vacation which
is limited to 40 school days. In this connection a notification is being inserted in the
Press by the Ministry of Education to-day.
The Union Jack will be hoisted
on all
Government buildings on Empire Day.

CLASS II. No. 4.
I. PRISONS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding Fifty-five
thousand six hundred and sixty-two
pounds be granted to His Majesty for the
service of the period ending 31st March,
1923, to defray the expenses of Prisons."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This is an estimate
for the cost of the prisons in Northern Ireland, of which there are only three-Belfast,
Londonderry and Armagh, the last-named
being used for female prisoners only. These
prisons were handed over to the Northern
Government in a very poor condition.
Belfast and Derry, as you are aware, had
suffered severely from the damage done by
Sinn Feiners, while none of the three
prisons are at all up to modern requirements
The Imperial Government, which spent
large sums on bringing the Scotch prisons
up-to-date, spent nothing on the Irish
prisons, most of which, according to the
Royal Commission of 1884, were of an antiquated type devised for an obsolete system of
discipline. This affects all Irish prisons, but
a point which affects us particularly is the
fact that the stocks of requisites in these
prisons, such as clothing, bedding, etc., had
fallen to a very low level, so that this
Government has to incur extra expenses in
bringing the stocks up again to their proper
level. As regards the staff of the prisons, we
were placed in a difficult position owing to
the serious illness of the Governors of both
Belfast and Derry Prisons. Their duties
have been discharged by two officers of the
Special Constabulary with marked efficiency,
and I must express my gratitude to these
officers for the admirable way in which they
have carried out the task imposed on them.
The staff generally have had a heavy task,
but I trust the decision to revert to ordinary
prison discipline will remove many of the
difficulties which have thrown an increased
burden on the staff. I may say that this
decision applies to all prisoners committed
after the 31st March, without distinction of
creed or class.
II
Supply-
Prisons.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
As will be seen, nearly half the estimated
cost of the prisons goes in pay and allowances. The rates of pay were fixed before we
took over control and were assimilated in
1920 to those of the English prison service.
The staff cannot be considered excessive, as
the number of prisoners in custody has
increased considerably, owing to the activity
of the police. Since the 1st December, over
1,900 prisoners have been committed to
Belfast Prison alone. As regards victualling,
the average cost at Belfast and Derry is £18
per head, practically 1s. a day, which, I
think, is very moderate, having regard to the
dietary allowed. The provision for clothing,
etc., is increased to some extent by the
renewals rendered necessary by the malicious
destruction of property by Sinn Fein prisoners.
The sub-head dealing with repairs and new
buildings, etc., are also increased by the
amounts necessary to repair damage done by
Sinn Fein prisoners. I am referring to the
time prior to the period we took over.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Is the Imperial Parliament responsible for any portion of that?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would like to consult the Minister of Finance in regard to
that matter. I certainly hope we will get
something from them. One wing in the
Beifast jail, which was completely wrecked,
has been completely restored, and I think at
an extremely moderate cost. It was done
by prison labour under the supervision of
artisan warders. Owing to the fact that
there is no convict prison in Northern Ireland, and no Borstal Institute, it has become
necessary to arrange to send a certain number of convicts and Borstal inmates to
Scotland and England respectively, and this
accounts for part of the amount shown
under the head of escort and conveyance and
for the cost of maintenance of prisoners in
other countries. Although the conveyance of
these prisoners throws a small extra cost
on this Government, the arrangement is on
the whole economical, and has given us time
to consider what can be done to provide a
convict prison and Borstal Institution. As a
matter of fact, the maintenance of a convict
in the Scotch Convict Prisons is very much
less than the cost of a convict in the South
of Ireland prisons. I think the cost in
Scotland is something like one-half the cost
of the maintenance of a convict in Southern
Ireland.
I would like to add that officials of this
Department have visited England and Scotland, and discussed the question of prison
accommodation with the English and Scottish
Prison Commissioners, to whom I am much
indebted for the help which they have already
given us, and for the assistance promised.
We have to consider the provision of a Convict Prison, a Borstal Institution, a place of
Preventive Detention, an Inebriate Reformatory, and a Central Criminal Lunatic
Asylum. At the present time criminal
lunatics have to be sent to Dundrum, in
County Dublin; but these questions are being
very carefully gone into. I referred before
to the fact that our prisons are very much
out of date, and I would like to see them
more up to date.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: More comfortable?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
may disagree with me, but I am most anxious
that while imprisonment should be a
deterrent to the wrongdoer, the importance
of its reformative side should not be lost
sight of. Since this Government took over
the jails we tried to restore prison discipline,
with, I may say, a great deal of success. I
am glad to say that practically all the
prisoners in the jails are now working. I
would like to point out that, from the
prisoners' point of view, I think it is most
necessary that they should be engaged in
carrying on useful work in the jail-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)—instead of being left
in their cells in complete idleness. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I beg to move.
Mr. LYNN: I cannot claim any intimate
knowledge of the internal arrangements of
any of the jails and I will not cross swords
with my right hon. Friend as to what a
proper or comfortable jail ought to be, but
there are just two points I would seek information about. Under the head "B" I
notice, for example, that in Belfast and
Londonderry the cost is £18 per head,
whereas in Armagh it only costs £15. I
wonder can the right hon. Gentleman tell
us why the cost is £3 per head less in
Armagh to feed 75 prisoners, whereas, with
the larger number of 275 in Belfast it costs
£18 per head. I am sure he knows what
the answer is. I would also like him to
tell us whether he does not think this £145
per head under the head O for 50 prisoners
who are accommodated outside Northern
Ireland is rather high? (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) There may be a suitable
reply to it, but it does seem at first sight
that to pay £145 for keeping a convict in
any prison is pretty high. I would like
the right hon. Gentleman to say what it
does cost in English prisons and see whether
we are being charged more than we ought
to be.

hon. Gentleman has commented pretty
strongly on the fact that only 1s. a day is
spent for food. I have tried this afternoon
to see what it really costs, and I find the

Coming now to the sub-heads under the
vote, I desire to draw the special attention
of hon. Members to the vote for training
colleges. In all Ireland there are 7 training
colleges. Only one of these-St. Mary's,
Belfast-is in Northern Ireland. The total
estimated grant for the whole of Ireland is
£104,000, and if this is shared between
Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland in
proportion to the number of teachers in
each, £32,600 would be our share, and that
is inserted in the Estimate. I regret, however, to have to inform the Committee that
when we approached the Provisional Government so that we might co-operate with them
in the Easter examination for monitors,
pupil teachers, and candidates for admission
to these training colleges our representations
were more or less ignored. Moreover, in
regard to the course of training at the
colleges, the Provisional Government, without
any reference to the Government of Northern
Ireland, decided to alter existing arrangements, and to hold the students' examinations
at the colleges a month earlier than usual,
so that the pupils could have the last month
of the session to devote to the study of the
Irish language, literature and literary history. Hon. Members will readily realise
that we could not fall in with such a proceeding as that. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We thought such action was unfair,
and I am sure that in the public estimation
it will be considered unfair. We, therefore,
had no alternative but to make independent
plans. I would like just now to remind hon.
Members that although in the Estimates
before the House there is a provision for
the post of Organiser of Irish Language in
Northern Ireland, that post is now vacant,
and it is not the intention of the Ministry
to fill it at present. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We hope to be able to get the
necessary work done by one of our inspectors.

I now come to the question of the salaries of
national school teachers, which absorb such a
very large sum. Hon. Members are aware
that in November, 1920, an agreement was
come to between the Treasury officials, the
Commissioners of National Education, and
the teachers, whereby improved scales of
salaries and capitation grants were fixed.
The last instalment under the arrangement
came into force on 1st April of this year, and
it means an advance of the salaries of the
teachers of £170,000 over the preceding year.
It is interesting, and hon. Members should
know that the average income of teachers
from State sources in Northern Ireland now
stands as follows:
For men teachers, £354;
Women teachers, including principals,
£266;
Junior assistant mistresses. £134.
It is difficult to compare these salaries with
the salaries of teachers in England and Scotland, but I think it may be assumed that the
salaries paid here are not inferior to those
paid in England and Scotland. One thing
which it is necessary to point out is that the
salaries here are subject to deduction for
superannuation, which is not the case, as
hon. Members know, in England and in
Scotland.
Mr. McGUFFIN: It was very nearly being
the case.
Mr. McKEOWN: We heard something of
that last night. The whole question of the
salaries of teachers in Northern Ireland will,
at some time, receive the earnest consideration of the House, as also the desirability of
maintaining them at their present level, and
increasing the standard of efficiency of the
teachers. We also hope to save money in our
administration at the same time through the
amalgamation of schools and in other ways.
I come now to the question of intermediate
education, and I would touch upon it shortly.

system of Curfew for the whole city, which

I can assure this House that if the Government think it necessary to do so they will
not hesitate to do so. With regard to the

Marshal Sir Henry Wilson and General Solly
Flood they decided to restrict the issue of
permits to hold or keep firearms to members
of the Special Constabulary. There are two
reasons why this arrangement was arrived
at. First, to ensure that no one who was not
a loyal citizen in the Province should have
firearms. Secondly, we felt that it was not
too much to ask any citizen to come forward
and enrol himself in some branch of the
Special Constabulary, no matter in what
category that might be. To meet the cases
which, I think, were referred to by my hon.

to provide for old men and invalids.

18 MAY 1922.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 18th May, 1922.
The House met at Three of the clock, Mr.
Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
INTERIM GRANT TO SECONDARY
TEACHERS.
1. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Education if the Interim Grant to Secondary
Teachers has been paid; and, if not, whether
he will explain why this very urgent matter
has been delayed.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
M'Keown): This grant has not yet been paid
and cannot be paid in full before the end of
the current school session. It has hitherto
been paid in one sum at the end of the school
year; but now that the Ministry's Estimates
for the current year have been considered by
the House in Committee a first instalment
amounting to £6,000, being the amount due
for the six months ended 31st January last,
will be paid very shortly.
MALICIOUS INJURIES TO PROPERTIES.
2. Dr. MORRISON askel the Minister for
Home Affairs if his attention has been drawn
to a resolution of the Coleraine Rural
Council protesting against widespread malicious injuries to property, with consequent
increase of local taxation, and proposing
certain remedies; and what action the
Minister proposes to take to deal with this
very serious matter.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I have received a copy of
the Resolution referred to, which, I think,
calls attention to a very important point.
I am giving the matter serious consideration,
and i shall be glad to discuss with the hon.
Member the steps which have been and which
can be taken to limit these outrages and protect the ratepayers.
THE PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): My right hon. Friend the Minister of Labour has laid upon the Table of the
House a copy of the Interim Report of the
Advisory Committee on the Administration
of the Employment Exchanges and Unemployment Insurance System in Northern Ireland. The appointment of Local Employment
Committees in connection with the Exchanges
is unanimously recommended in this Report,
and my right hon. Friend is making arrangements to set up these bodies, as he fully
shares the opinion of the Advisory Committee
that their establishment is urgently required
and should effect substantial economies.
COMMITTEE ON LABOUR EXCHANGES.
3. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is in a position to lay upon
the Table of the House a copy of the Report
of the Committee on Labour Exchanges, also
a copy of any regulations, instructions, or
recommendations issued for the guidance of
the Local Employment Committees in connection with the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1922.
My right hon. Friend has also laid on the
Table of the House a copy of the instructions
which have been issued in connection with
the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1922.
Pending the establishment of Local Employment Committees, these instructions have
been issued to Courts of Referees.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: May I ask the hon. Gentleman if these Committees are to be established prior to the introduction of the new
Bill? Are these Advisory Committees to be
set up immediately?
Mr. GORDON: I do not think it is the intention of the Minister to establish these
Committees until such time as the Report of
the Committee on Employment Exchanges
and Unemployment Insurance is submitted
to this House. On the recommendation of
this Committee these Employment Committees will undoubtedly be set up.
WIRELESS TELEPHONES.
4. Mr. DONALD asked the Prime Minister
whether any representation has been made
to the Postmaster-General with regard to the
installation of wireless telephones in
Northern Ireland; if so, with what result.
Whether it is a fact that licences will not
be issued until a Broadcasting Station has
been erected in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTTR OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): I have been asked to reply. The
answer to the first part of the question is in
the affirmative. The Ministry of Commerce
have obtained from the General Post Office
a verbal assurance that Northern Ireland
will participate in any facilities devoted to
the development of wireless telegraphy or
telephony, and that the fact that licences
cannot at present be issued in Northern
Ireland will not prejudice the future grant
of this assistance. The Postmaster-General
has been asked to confirm this assurance.
With regard to the second part of the
question, it has been necessary to request
the Postmaster-General to withold licences
for private wireless installations in
Northern Ireland for the time being.
Oral Answers.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that question, is it the intention of the Northern
Government to issue licences later on and to
install a Broadcasting Station in Northern
Ireland?
Mr. ARCHDALE: The whole question is
under consideration, and I am sure my hon.
Friend knows the reason why we cannot at
present instal a Broadcasting Station in
Northern Ireland.
Mr. M'GUFFIN-May I ask if it is true

The PRIME MINISTER: There is no truth

normal, as we hope it will in a short time,
will the Prime Minister take steps to place
Northern Ireland in the same position as
Great Britain?
The PRIME MINISTER: Certainly. We
hope to keep parallel with Great Britain in
every advance.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Ahead of her,
if possible.
PUBLIC ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS.
5. Mr. DONALD asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Minister of Education if he
will state the total number of public elementary school places in Northern Ireland;
whether all these public elementary schools
are carrying out the instructions of the
Government; and whether Roman Catholic
teachers have refused to accept their salaries
from the Northern Government.
Mr. M'KEOWN: There are about 2,100
public elementary schools (National Schools)
in Northern Ireland, and the average daily
attendance of pupils at these schools at the
date when the last available return was prepared was 144,160.
There are about 740 of the National Schools
in Northern Ireland under the charge of
Roman Catholic managers and teachers. In
some 270 of these schools the teachers are not
now receiving payment from the Northern
Government. In such cases the monthly
school returns and salary claims have not
been furnished to the Ministry, but from the
information available it is not practicable to
state in how many cases respectively responsibility for this action rests with school managers and with teachers. In the case of a
small number of these National Schools it
has come under notice that the instructions
of the Ministry have not been acted upon in
some other respects, but the Ministry is not
without hope that matters may be satisfactorily adjusted.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask where these teachers are receiving
their salaries from, seeing that they have not
recognised the Northern Government?
Mr. M'KEOWN: It is very difficult to find
out exactly where the money is coming from,
but we do know it is coming from some source
in Dublin.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask what steps the
Government propose to take to have that
matter put right?

as compared with the cost of living at the date
of A. 83 (July, 1920), including all items which

SINN FEIN ATTACKS ON CROWN
FORCES.
Mr. LYNN (by private notice) asked the
Minister for Home Affairs whether he can
give the House any information regarding
the attack which was made on the Crown
Forces by the Sinn Feiners in the Marrowbone area last night; and, further, whether
he can give any details of the Sinn Fein
attack on Musgrave Street Barracks this
morning.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received a
report from the police stating that at about
8-45 p.m.
on 17th inst. intense rifle and
revolver firing took place in Flax Street and
Havana Street, both of which are in the
Roman Catholic area. The firing extended
from Ardoyne to the "Marrowbone" area.
This
Special Police were posted at Fearon's
spirit grocery on the Oldpark Road.
post was fired on from the above area, and
the police returned the fire.
No casualties have been reported.
The firing lasted until about 9-30 p.m..
when Crown Forces on duty in the area got
the gunmen under control.
During the firing the public-house of Owen
Taggart, Roman Catholic, 289 Crumlin Road
(mixed area), and the pawnshop of Edward
Mitchell, Protestant, 24 Ardilea Street (a
Sinn Fein area), were found to be on fire.
The Fire Brigade was called out, and subdued
the flames.
The attack on Musgrave Street started at
3-40 a.m. this morning.

Bills Presented.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, certainly not.
The raiders were beaten off owing to the
courage of the constables on duty.
Seven men dressed in police uniform and
caps knocked at the front gate, and said they
were "police on duty." The barrack
orderlies, Constable Collins and Special-
Constable M'Keown, after due scrutiny,
appeared to have been satisfied that the men
were police, and admitted them. As soon as
they got in they rushed the two constables
and ordered "Hands up." Constable Collins
was shot down. Special-Constable M'Keown
ran for help, and raised the alarm. He was
shot in the leg as he ran away.
The action of this constable, as well as
Sergeant Toomey, who fired on the raiders
from an upstairs room, upset their plans
completely, and they retired at once.
All available police were summoned, and
an extensive search carried out during the
morning.
Up to the present six revolvers, three rifles,
and about 500 rounds of ammunition have
been found.
I should like to pay a tribute to the gallant
manner in which Constable Collins and
the
Special-Constable
M'Keown resisted
attack of these armed men.
I regret to say that Constable Collins, who
was of exemplary character, and was due for
disbandment in a few days, has since died.
Special-Constable M'Keown's injuries are
not, I am glad to say, serious.
Mr. LYNN: Arising out of that raply, will
my right hon. Friend, who has paid a tribute
to the two Constables injured, see that they
are rewarded for discharging their duties in
such an exemplary manner?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Constable M'Keown
has already been recommended.

present.

AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £29,671 be
granted to His Majesty for the service of
the period ending 31st March, 1923, to defray
the expenses of the Minister of Agriculture
in respect of agricultural institutions, improvement of live stock, agricultural research, developments, including summary
grants in aid."
Mr. ARCHDALE: This Estimate, which I
am sorry to say is only one of my agricultural estimates, is No. 2 on the list, and
it covers all our agricultural activities. It
does not include, however, the cost of the
buildings at Greenmount and the North-
West Institute, Strabane, which are down
on the Public Works Estimate.
I hope
that the cost of such buildings will come
out of the Imperial Exchequer later on.
Agricultural research, which is one of the
principal subjects of this Estimate, is one
of the most important we have to deal with.
There are
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
five sub-sections in it :-
Seed Testing and Plant Diseases Division.
Agricultural Chemical Divison.
Animal Diseases Division.
Plant Breeding Division.
Poultry Division.
I think the Committee must know that
during the last twenty years there has been
a very marked increase in the general average yield of crops in Ireland due to ex-
Take one
perimental and research work.
example potatoes - which is one of the
most important crops in our country, during
the last ten years the increase in the potato
crop has been 1.6 tons per acre more than in
the ten years previous to that. This gives
a total gain in yield each year during the
-
last ten years (1911-1920) of 978,691 tons, which
if multiplied by an average price of £3 per
ton would give an increase of £2,936,073 per
annum, or a total of £29,360,730 in the ten
years ending 1920, the last year which we
have statistics for.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Is that improvement
through seed potatoes?
Mr. ARCHDALE: That is owing to a better
way of planting, a better way of manuring,
sprout seeds, and things of that sort, which
have been experimented upon in the various
stations.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: I see.
Mr. ARCHDALE: We intend to continue
that work also in our Six Counties. Rye
grass seeds are raised so extensively, and in
such quantities within the Northern Area,
that Belfast merchants practically control
the trade in this seed for the whole world. A
seed-testing station is, therefore, probably of
more importance to the North of Ireland than
to any other part of the British Isles. We,
therefore, have put down a small sum, as you
will see here, to establish a seed-testing
station in one of our institutions. The annual
value of grass seeds exported is £475,000. As
the result of this research and investigation
into plant diseases we have been enabled to
cope with such diseases as potato blight,
smut, and bunt, and various other diseases
which are common to all plants. We have
every hope of getting one of the best men in
Great Britain at the head of our Research
Department. Turning to the Animal Diseases
Division, we find that the value of the
animals exported from Ireland in 1920 was
£42,360,000. That was for cattle, horses,
sheep, and pigs. Of that total amount a
sum of £35,600,000 was for cattle. You will
see what an important industry that is to
this country.
Owing to the Diseases of Animals Act not
being under our control at the present moment, and owing to the Provisional Government having taken control, when they should
not have taken control, and not answering
letters of hon. Members who are trying to
import animals to improve the breed in this
country, I have been over to London this
last week, and I have every confidence that
we will now get the principal Veterinary Surgeon over, and have control of our own work
under the Chief Secretary and acting as agent
for him, instead of letting the Provisional
Government take control and appointing
men in our area, as they have been doing in
the district of my right hon. Friend for Derry
without any reference at all to the Veterinary Department or branch which they preside over. Therefore we are continuing those
investigations. Diseases such as abortion and
redwater in cattle, braxy and louping ill in

brought in.
As regards the Plant Breeding Division,
we intend to carry on our plant breeding and
cross fertilisation by all means in our power.
By using experiments and cross fertilisation
you can make one plant produce what two
used to do in the old times. That Department will carry on its own work. We have
been trying to get a man as head of our
Plant Breeding Association. He is an Irishman, and has so improved barley by cross
fertilisation and selecting the best plants
that he now produces double as much as
before, and every brewer in the country has
been trying to get that barley. Whether
prohibition will have any effect, as some of
my hon. Friends hope, on the growth of
barley I do not know, but it is certainly
good for cattle feeding as well as for other
purposes. In Southern Ireland there are two
research stations, and none at present in
Northern Ireland. I think we are certainly
entitled to have one in our Northern area.
We have put down £700 in the estimate for
a Research Station.
I turn to the Poultry Division. I do not
know whether the poultry part belongs to
the ladies or gentlemen of Northern Ireland,
but it is the second highest export in value
from Ireland. The amount is something
enormous. In 1920, the last year we can get
figures for, Ireland exported almost
£17,000,000 of poultry products, and of this
Northern Ireland exported £6,312,000. The
Department in Dublin has conducted an
egg-laying competition in Cork for the last
twenty years. The records of eggs laid per
annum per bird show an increase of 69 eggs
during the last eight years. We are getting
here the head of that institute in Cork to
have charge of our egg-laying competition,
which we hope to have in a field at Stormount. We have begun to prepare for it.
If we had that improvement of 69 eggs per
bird, which they had at Cork, all over the
Northern area it would mean a sum of two
million pounds in the pockets of the ladies
of the Six Counties. In 1920, as showing the
interest that our Northern people took in
that, 40 per cent, of the entries in the egg
competitions were from the Northern counties. I think no one will complain of the
little sum of money spent on the egg-laying
competitions.
about. The Cookstown School is doing most
extraordinarily good work. The Strabane
School was started originally-I think I can
say nothing better-to make good wives out
of girls. They were taught dairy work,
poultry work, laundry work, and cooking and
sewing. Their course is about eight weeks.
The school only holds 29 at a time. They
come for eight weeks from the counties of
Tyrone, Derry, Fermanagh, and Donegal. The
Donegal people are being kept on for the
present. A settlement will have to be come
to, but they are being kept on this year. The
county councils give scholarships in these
schools. The average attendance for the past
eight or nine years was 61 pupils per annum.
They are wonderfully well taught, and the
schools are most interesting places. The
students from the North-West school at
Strabane, after a bit, are drafted to Cookstown, where they go in for a more advanced
course. There are four terms of three months
cach. They get a very thorough education
there. They become cookery instructresses,
poultry instructresses, dairy instructresses,
and things of that sort. They learn laundry
work and sewing. At Strabane we want to put
up houses for poultry work in connection with
the poultry scheme. We want more outdoor
work. We have no outdoor houses at all.
We want to spend money on houses outside
and labourers' cottages, instead of bringing
in casual labour, which has been found very
expensive. We also want it for experimental
and demonstration plots. The land is most
suitable for demonstration plots. Greenmount in County Antrim was bought by the
old Department and turned over to the
Antrim County Council to work it under its
control, with the Department paying a certain
sum of money every year. It is for farmers'
sons in the Northern counties. It is the only
one we have in Northern Ireland. There are
six similar ones in Southern Ireland. We
want to make this one as good as the Albert
Agricultural College and have the full science
and research work there. Therefore we propose to spend a suitable sum of money which
we hope we will get back from the United
Kingdom. We also want to establish a Horticultural School there. There is a splendid
walled garden. We want to put up houses
for horticulture and apple culture, and
things of that sort. There are no real
scientific schools for young farmers to go to
who want to come back to their farms,
except this one at Greenmount. We hope to
make it worthy of the Six Counties. It was
well supported by Antrim and Down prior to
the war, but during the war the students
could not come to it; they were away at the
war. Since the war it has been used for
training ex-soldiers in horticulture. Now we
hope to get it back to its proper work, where
young men shall learn scientific farming. We
ask £1,000 for that, fer upkeep and so on.

The next sub-head (E) is Grants to County
Committees. That is only the usual contribution to the six County Committees of
Agriculture in respect of their agricultural
schemes on a basis similar to that adopted
by the Department.
Of the remaining sub-heads, the largest
items are those in respect of the potato industry and the flax-growing industry.
Everyone knows the importance of the industry in Northern Ireland. If we no not
grow enough flax we cannot keep the mills
going. If it is to be grown it must be
encouraged. We have to try to find flax
that will have a better fibre and better produce with that flax. Farmers have got to
contend with every mortal thing. I used
to hear people over in the United Kingdom
saying that the farmers were millionaires,
that they were the ones that were coining
money. No one else was making a penny.
They forgot about the seasons. You cannot
have seasons to order. I would like to bring
some of these people down to the stiff bad
lands and let them have a week's work. It
would change their tune altogether. Unless
we can instruct people or help them to have
a better means of retting flax, a better time
for pulling it, and unless we can get the
clerk of the weather to give weather suitable
for flax you cannot get good fibre. You
cannot get good fibre unless you have proper
weather for drying flax.

n and

think our agricultural industry can be fostered, and ought to be fostered in every way,

What I rose to speak about more particularly was the flax industry. I have been all
my life associated with the textile business,
and the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Archdale)
may remember that in April I put a question
in respect to the flax crop that we might
expect this year. In 1920 it appears there
were 17,020 tons of flax grown in this country,
and the quantity dropped in the following
year to the miserable amount of 4,788 tons.
What it will be this year the Department
were not able to say, but they did give us an
assurance that they had no reason to doubt
that an equal acreage would be under flax,
and that, given propitious weather, the crop
would result favourably so far as produce
was concerned. This is a most important
matter so far as Northern Ireland is concerned, and particularly the Metropolis of
Belfast. Everywhere there are spinning
works, and in the past they have been depending upon the importation of flax from Russia.
I suppose more than half the flax used was
Russian flax, but now we have no longer the
advantage of drawing upon Russian resources.
It is, therefore, most important that the
resources in Ireland should be developed to
the utmost. The right hon. Gentleman did
not take pains to say what he had
done with respect to that matter, but
I am quite convinced that he is
as anxious in this connection as any
Member of the House can be. He knows
as well as any hon. Member present, and
perhaps even better, that it is necessary that
flax should be raised here. I am speaking
in the presence of an expert in the spinning
industry. I do not know whether he intends
to contribute to the debate this afternoon,
but I should like him to state something with
respect to what representations have been
made to the Spinners' Association and to the
Board of Agriculture. I put that as part
of the question but I did not receive any
answer to it.
The Farmers' Union are most anxious to
develop the industry and increase production
but they get no encouragement. I do not
know to what extent the right hon. Gentleman has had communication with the Association or what encouragement he has
given them in that matter, but if the flax
acreage is less this year than it has been
for the last few years the blame will have
to be allocated in some direction. I do not
know whether it will be to his Department.
Perhaps the right hon. Gentleman will tell
us what has taken place with respect to
this matter, what prospects there are, and
whether we can hope for an improvement.
The general anticipations at the moment are
in favour of an improvement, not exactly
a boom, in trade. It would be a great pity,

I hope the right hon. Gentleman will not lose

interests of this community very much.
Dr. MORRISON: I would like to say a
word or two with regard to some of the
matters mentioned by the Minister of Agriculture. In the first place, I would like to
refer to the fact that two or three years ago
£40,000 was granted by the Imperial Parliament to the Agricultural Department in
Dublin with the object of establishing and
promoting research. I would like him to
inform the Committee if the unexpended
portion of this grant which should come to
Ulster will be available for research in the
Six County area. I, for one, am glad to
be free from the Agricultural Department in
Dublin. I had a long experience of it, and
a very unhappy experience, because I found
one peculiarity about a man when he got
established in the Dublin office. I think
even a decent man when he went there acquired habits that were very disconcerting
to the average man. It is not the fact

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Agriculture
[Dr. Morrison]
that he disagrees with the conclusions you
have arrived at, but he actually refuses to
discuss the question. It is hopeless to do
anything with a Department that constitutes itself the final tribunal that can settle
all questions without discussion, that is a
sort of Athanasius contra mundum that
knows everything, while everybody else
knows nothing. We are in a new atmosphere
here and we are in what I hope will be a
democratic atmosphere, and I think that
with the present Minister it will be that.
I hope we have got rid finally of red tape,
and that whoever presides over the Department of Agriculture in the North of Ireland
will be like the present Minister, available
to any man who wants to see him. I have
been several times in his Department and
received nothing but courtesy. The officials
think I may know something that they do
not know-that never presented itself to the
Dublin men-and they recognise that they
do not know everything and are there to
receive suggestions from practical men like
myself.
The Minister of Agriculture has mentioned
that two of the things proposed are the
establishment of a Veterinary Department
and a Research Department. When you
consider the losses which agriculturists
suffer from deaths in cattle you will see that
it is a very serious thing. There are certain
diseases that I have come in contact with
when moving freely among farmers, and,
knowing something about disease myself,
I know that there are two outstanding
diseases which the Department has practically been unable to do anything for up till
now, and which even now are causing very
serious loss to the agricultural community.
The first is milk fever. You would naturally think that if there is a disease that is
causing great loss there should be some
attempt to keep statistics so that the Government would be able to tell the extent of
the losses. So far as I know no statistics are
kept with regard to the loss of cattle from
milk fever. And again I am perfectly satisfied that milk fever is a bacteriological
disease. We know the remedy, but we
should know how the disease is caused, and
how to prevent it. The Department in
Dublin has hitherto failed to do this. I
make this suggestion to the Minister of
Agriculture that he will devote his attention
to this question, and that if the Department
under his auspices is not able to do this
he will give a special fee to some pathological
research man in the medical profession. He
could take up the question of milk fever,
and find out what is the origin of this
disease. Then you will go about the business
on something like a scientific basis. It is
an extraordinary thing that in this scientific
age we are still blundering with the old
methods of mediævalism.
There are operations being performed upon
cattle, and horses, and colts all over Ulster
without ordinary antiseptic precautions, not
altogether antiseptic precautions, but precautions that would protect them from lockjaw. Lockjaw is a disease very frequently to
be seen in horses. Before performing the
operation you can produce immunity in a
horse by using half-a-crown's worth of antitetanic serum. I think the Department
should in the first place have statistics by
which the number of cattle that die from
lockjaw can be known. They should insist
on every veterinary surgeon giving a dose
of serum, because scientific knowledge bas
now established beyond question that this
disease is preventible, and it should be
compulsory for a veterinary surgeon to administer the serum before he uses the knife.
And in the same way people should know
that if a horse gets a wound in the leg,
or shoulder, or anywhere else, all that is
wanted is to walk him down to the veterinary surgeon for a dose of serum. He is
then proof against this serious disease.
There are a number of other diseases, and
there is a very wide field open for a Veterinary Department if it is equipped with
a properly qualified man. I think that if
he has difficulties in this matter-and there
are very difficult problems that he will have
to unravel-the Department should call in
the assistance, if necessary, of the skilled
men who are engaged in similar research
work in connection with the University in
Belfast. Unitedly they may be able to
solve some of these problems that have
hitherto baffled the veterinary branch alone.
I do not see why we should not give an
example to the world of scientific research
and discovery in these very important and
serious matters.
Poultry have been referred to, but no reference has been made to what I think is one
of the most fatal diseases in poultry, tuat
is gapes in chickens. Any man going about
the country and going into labourers' houses
or farmers' houses as I have been, can see
chickens with wings spread and mouths
open gasping for breath. That is due to
a worm developing in the throat. This is
capable of prevention, it is capable of treatment, and yet thousands die every year. One,
I think, of the chief causes of death is inbreeding. In-breeding reduces the vitality
of any living species, and if you reduce the
vitality you reduce the resisting power of
the system, with a consequence that you are
open to attacks of enemies that otherwise
you would be free from.
The Minister of Agriculture mentioned
schools for educating the people-I hare a
good deal of knowledge of this system-and

Mr. ARCHDALE: I have brought in a Bill

Dr. MORRISON: I am glad to know that.

With regard to cow testing, that is also a

that the milk production of our cows is very
much below the average. There is this difficulty, that it is very hard to get the farmers
to adopt cow testing. I have had experience of

he outlined the possibility of a large expenditure in connection with them. Now, there
are two sides to this question. I have no
doubt in my mind that the Department in
Dublin wasted a very large amount of public
money by unwise expenditure and unwise
experiments in connection with many questions of agriculture. I had practical experience of it in connection with a creamery
with which I had a good deal to do, and of
which I am still president. Money was
wasted because doctrinaires sat up in armchairs and theorised about matters that they
had no practical knowledge of, and they
experimented in the main at the expense

done practically without any guidance from
these men that were sent down from the
Department in Dublin. If you propose to
train people and you put them through a
little course of training in some of these
schools that the Minister has referred to
it perhaps is a wise thing, but my experience
of it is that you can molly-coddle people
too much. I think the farmers of Ulster
know as much as practical men. I can take
you through the district in which I live
and there is not a point in the growing of
potatoes, or in the breeding of cattle or
horses, heavy or light, or in the production
of milk upon which they could not give
points to many a man who sits in
Dublin and dogmatises on these questions.
I know of one man who got a start in life
through going to one of these schools, but
only one. He may become a distinguished
man-possibly he will-and his case would
justify a good deal of expenditure, but the
majority would not. Take a young girl or a
woman there for the purpose of teaching her
to make butter. I tell you this, if a woman
is born a trollop she will continue to be a
trollop all her life; it is born with her. 1
know; I have had long experience. A woman
who insists on using pins instead of buttons
is a trollop. You may put her in a straight
jacket and compel her to sew on buttons, but
as soon as she is free from restraint she goes
back to the use of pins. and it is dangerous
for any man to put his arm around her
waist.
With regard to live stock, sire animals,
stallions and bulls, the Minister of Agriculture knows that it is very necessary to breed
from pure stock, and my hon. Friend, the
Member for County Down (Captain Mulholland), has emphasised that point. But we are
allowing, as he knows, waste both in stallions
and in bulls, and producing a stock that is
now being scattered all over Ulster. I think
the Department should grapple with that
matter seriously, and make it compulsory
that any animal that is kept for public
service should be sanctioned by the Department.
•
We had in the old Department dreadful
opposition to the Friesian. Anybody who
knows anything about the milking qualities
of cattle knows that the Friesian will produce
1,500 or perhaps 2,000 gallons of milk, whereas
in recent years the average cow only gives
about 300 gallons. Yet the Department in
Dublin obstructed the introduction of Friesians. There is no reason why the Friesian
should be excluded because we want to benefit
the shorthorn. The shorthorn should be
allowed to stand on its own legs and be judged
by the results. The introduction of shorthorns
produced a very fine type of beef animal here,
but it has seriously injured the milking
quality of our cows. I hope the Department
will have an open mind, and will facilitate
the farmers with regard to this matter of
introducing a big, broad, well-grown cow like
the Friesian which will give something like
1,500 or 2,000 gallons of milk in the year.
I think it is the duty of the State to do,
and to do only, what the people cannot do for
themselves. If the people can do it for
themselves they should do it or do without
it. If they cannot do it, it is the duty of the
State, if the State is able to do it, to help the
people in that respect. No single individual
is able to bring in a very valuable sire animal
at a very big price without serious loss, and
I think the Department should undertake
these matters for us.
There is just one other point that I want
to refer to, and that is the flax industry.
The Member for North Belfast (Mr.
McGuffin) has talked a great deal about
flax, but he does not understand why
the flax crop is diminishing. The reason is
a very simple one: because there is no money
in it. It does not pay the farmer now to
buy flaxseed at a huge price, and to pay the
Supply-
Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Dr. Morrison]
very heavy wages. He cannot grow it practically except at a loss, and unless it is profitable the Ulster farmer will not grow it;
he cannot be expected to grow it. Further,
there are very serious difficulties in connection with the growth of flax, and I think
if they were approached in the proper spirit
they might be removed. In the first place,
you all know that the flax, after it is pulled,
is steeped in a dam. These dams are filled
with water perhaps three feet deep. There
is a law that you cannot pollute a stream
and there is undoubtedly the fact that if
flax water goes into a stream it pollutes it
and may kill the fish. The consequence is
that farmers' labourers have to go into the
dams and work in water up to their waist
in order to throw out the flax. Another
result is that the flax water poisons the
whole atmosphere. There is not a man in
this House who, if motoring along the road
at the proper season, has not smelt the flax
water, and who does not know the abominable nuisance it is to passers-by. And how
much more injurious it is to the man who
lives near by. Flax water undoubtedly injures the fish.
Conservators, the men who
own salmon fisheries, and people who have
an interest in fly-fishing, have ideas that I
think are old and wrong, that the salmon
fry are in the river when the flax water is
let off. My experience and belief is, and
I have good reason for that belief, that the
salmon disappear to the sea long before the
autumn, and that there is no damage done
to the salmon by the flax water. I do not
ask the Minister of Agriculture to take that
from me, but I do not see why, with his
powers, he could not isolate a certain stretch
of river to watch the fish, and see if he
could get one salmon fry in the river between
the months of May and October, when the
flax goes into the water. That would determine the question. There is another
matter. The same thing happens in the
South of Ireland as in the North. There
is the diminution of fish in the river where
they have no flax water at all. I believe
we have quite as many fish in the Northern
waters as they have in the South where there
is no flax water. I do not know that I
have anything more to say; I am sorry I
have spoken so long.
The hon. Member for County Down (Capt.
Mulholland) has spoken about goats. There
is a great deal of truth in what he says.
It is recognised that the goat is immune to
the poison of tuberculosis. That is, it cannot
contract tuberculosis, and consequently there
is some anti-toxine in its system that is valuable. That is why the milk of the goat is
supposed to be valuable for persons who are
suffering from tuberculosis. I think from
that standpoint there is something to be said
for the goat, but I have always looked upon
goats as dangerous things and as useless
things.
Captain MULHOLLAND: Why?
Dr. MORRISON: Because they are tethered
along the road and are a danger to any
person who happens to be riding, and they
destroy the bushes. I could not be bothered
with them. Another reason why I object
to goats is-

Mr. ARCHDALE: In presenting the
estimates for the Ministry of Commerce it
might be as well to bring under the notice
of the House the additional responsibilities
placed upon the Ministry since the
estimates for the period from the appointed
day (1st January, 1922,) to 31st March, 1922,
were before the House. Since that time this
Ministry has taken over the collection of
Trade Statistics, the administration of
weights and measures, and-and this will
interest the hon. and gallant Member for
Co. Down (Captain Mulholland)-the control
of the Royal Harbours at Donaghadee and
Ardglass. These I believe are the only two
Royal Harbours in Northern Ireland. We
have also taken on important administrative
duties in connection with the registration of
Companies, Friendly Societies, etc., Electricity and Gas undertakings, Harbours,
Docks and Piers, and the inspection of
Mines and Quarries. These have all been

of Ireland. We have been developing new

markets in every way we can and we have

Board of Trade, the Post Office, and the

Great Britain, but into foreign countries.
That is the right thing, and we hope they
will go on stretching further and prosper.
My point is in regard to the £50,000,000. I
would like to ask the right hon. Gentleman
will he in the near future approach the
Advisory Committee set up by the Imperial
Government as to the building of better
harbour ferries with a view to stimulating
employment amongst the Belfast workmen ?
Deputation after deputation has approached
the local authorities with regard to this important matter. Our ferries are to-day
licensed to carry 150 people, but the truth of
the matter is that there are far nearer 250
people being carried. I want my right hon.
Friend to see could we not get a grant of this
money so as to afford employment for the
building of larger and more up-to date ferries.
When we have so many men unemployed at
the present time they could, if this grant
were secured, build these ferries. It would
help to stimulate employment. We could then
have these additional and larger and more
up-to-date ferries. I am not casting any
reflection on our local authority-the Harbour
Commissioners-in any way, but they themselves have this matter under consideration,
and I am quite sure if my right hon. Friend
approaches them something will be done in
the very near future. This is a very important matter. It is easy to put it off and
say that we will put on extra boats. One has
only to go down and see the state of things
when thousands of men are all rushing to
get on to the ferry boats at the same time.
It is impossible for the officers in charge to
keep these men from overloading the boats.
The point is that the boats are too small and
not up-to-date enough for the traffic. My
reason for bringing this matter forward is
that at this particular time it would not only
give employment, but these boats could be
built and ready when normal times come
again, and we would have an additional
service at the disposal of the working people.
We cannot wait until some day one of these
ferry boats goes down with hundreds of
people. Then perhaps we can get something
done. We are perfectly well aware that
proper facilities will have to be given to the
public, and I rise to put this important
matter before my right hon. Friend. I know
he will give attention to it.
I thank you, sir, for allowing me to put

say. I congratulate my right hon. Friend

the disposal of our representative Government. We believe that people on the spot
can deal far more effectively with these
questions of export and import trade than
people at a distance can do. That is all
I wish to say. I thank my right hon. Friend
for the very able way in which he has put
these Estimates to-day.

BALLYMENA PENSIONS APPEALS.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state reasons for the
delay in deciding appeals from decisions of
the Ballymena Pensions Committee, nearly
six months having elapsed in cases of Thos.
M'Cullough and James M'Kay, both having
been appealed by Pension Officer early in
December, 1921; to state whether steps will
be taken to have appeals decided within reasonable time, so that poor people may not
be kept so long in a state of suspense; to
state if in cases where documentary proof of
age cannot be had, instructions will be
issued to accept without question affidavits
made by two persons, known to and considered reliable by the Local Pensions Committee?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): As regards the first part of
the question, it is regretted that there has
been necessarily some little delay in dealing
with these papers owing to-
(a) the fact that at the date of the transfer there were a considerable number of
arrear claims handed over by the Local
Government Board,
(b) the dislocation consequent on transfer of powers, and
(c) shortage of staff and necessity for
training new officials in the work.
In this connection it may be stated that,
since taking over the powers and duties on
the 1st December, nearly 1,000 claims have
come before the Ministry for decision, and
each one of these requires careful consideration, and in many cases involves considerable correspondence.
staff of the Ministry is complete and fully
trained all arrears will be brought up to
date.
However, the arrears are rapidly being
overhauled, and it is hoped that when the
As regards the two cases mentioned by the
hon. Member, Thomas M'Cullough's claim
was disallowed some weeks ago on the
grounds that his means exceeded the statutory limit. James M'Kay's case is at present being investigated, and all the papers
in connection with it have been sent back to
the Pension Officer for further report.
As regards the second part of the question,
as indicated above, every effort will be made
to deal with appeals expeditiously.
As regards the third part of the question,
every appeal must be decided on its merits,
and every factor in connection with it taken
into consideration, and it would, therefore,
neither be possible nor expedient to deal
with these age cases on the stereotyped
method suggested by the hon. Member. Affidavits in themselves could not be regarded as
sufficient evidence, but are often of great
value in corroborating other information or
evidence supplied by claimants for pension.
PROGRESS OF HOUSING SCHEMES.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister for
Home Affairs if he will state the number of
houses now completed and occupied under the
various Housing Schemes, the number in
course of construction, and what is the policy
of the Government with regard to Housing
in the future?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Under the Housing
Acts of 1919 and 1921, 244 houses have been
completed by local authorities, of which 232
are occupied: 210 houses are still under construction.
Under the arrangements made for subsidies
to private builders in pursuance of the
Housing (Additional Powers) Acts, 1919, and
1921, 400 houses have been notified as completed, and of these, subsidies have been paid
in respect of 386.
As already pointed out in this House, the
policy of the Government of Northern Ireland is governed by financial considerations
which apply to Northern Ireland in the same
manner as to Great Britain. The Imperial
Government have limited their subsidies to
the case of houses in respect of which local
authorities had actually entered into contractual commitments last July, and as the
Government of Northern Ireland is in no
better financial position than the Imperial
Government, it is the present intention of
this Government to follow a similar policy in
regard to local authorities.
As regards subsidy to private builders. This
is limited to houses which had actually been

MURDER OF MR. TWADDELL.
VOTE OF CONDOLENCE.
The PRIME MINISTER: By leave of the
House and with your permission, Sir, I beg
to move:
That this House places on record its
detestation of the cowardly assassination of
our esteemed colleague, the late hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Twaddell),
and tenders deepest sympathy to his widow
in the sorrow that has befallen her; and
that this resolution be entered upon the
Journals."

This Parliament has been in existence for a
very short time, and we have passed through
times of grave anxiety and of peril. We
have had to undertake tasks of great magnitude involving the whole of the citizens of
the Six Counties. Awful attacks have been
made upon our community, and they have
593 Murder of Mr. Twaddell-

23 MAY 1922.
Vote of Condolence.
culminated in the foul assassination of one
of our most esteemed and revered Members.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Words fail
any man to convey, first of all, the horror
that is in our hearts at such a thing having
occurred, or to convey to his widow the
feelings that are deepseated in the hearts of
all of us that she should have been left at
this period without her husband, young, in
the flower of his life, and destined in my
opinion to hold an even higher position in
the affection and esteem of his colleagues
here and of the people of Ulster as a whole.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) He has been
stricken down. I am not sure that his death
has not rendered to Ulster a great service,
and I am certain that all those who are engaged in the heavy task that lies before us
will ever treasure his memory as the first
man in this Assembly to lay down his life
for no other reason whatever-there is no
private stain upon him that could have
called for such a dastardly outrage-than the
fact that he was true to the faith, true to the
honourable traditions of an Ulsterman, true
to the Empire, true to all those instincts
that go to make a simple and straightforward honourable man.
It is not
customary on these occasions to say much,
nor can much be said, but if those
who committed this dastardly outrage
thought it would for a moment weaken the
functions of this Parliament or the steadfast
courage of the people of Ulster they never
made a greater error (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) If those who were instrumental in
ordering his death, which was a more important matter than carrying it out, if they
thought by these means or any other means
they could weaken the unflinching courage
of the people to go straight forward upon
the path mapped out for them they have
miscalculated Ulster and the Ulster people.
In asking the House to pass this short,
simple resolution I feel sure that all concerned will put into the passing of it their
whole-hearted detestation of what occurred
and their deepest sympathy with Mrs.
Twaddell in her bereavement. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. LYNN: It is with feelings of horror
at the crime and of sympathy for the
widow that I rise to second this resolution which has been SO eloquently
proposed to the House by the Prime
Minister. It seems sad to think that
a colleague with whom we met a few days ago
is now lying dead as a result of cowardly

runner-up. Sometimes on an occasion like
I
that a man's bitter feelings show, but it was

As the Prime Minister said, he has been

should say that he had an idea that he would
