HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 25th May, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION ACT.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour whether it is the intention of the
Government to introduce a Bill this Session
to amend the Workmen's Compensation Act,
seeing that the War Addition Acts expire at
the end of this year?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I am aware of the necessity for
amendment of the Workmen's Compensation
Act in view of the impending expiration of
the War Addition Acts. No doubt my hon.
Friend will have observed a statement by
the Imperial Home Secretary in the Imperial
House of Commons recently to the effect that
he hoped it would be possible to prepare an
amending measure before the end of the
present Session, which would be acceptable to
all parties. I am anxious for obvious reasons
that as far as possible the law relating to
Workmen's Compensation should be the same
in Northern Ireland as in Great Britain,
and I am in communication with the Im
perial Home Secretary on the matter. Some
weeks ago I stated publicly on behalf of the
Government that the workers of Northern
Ireland would not be placed in a less advantageous position in this connection than
their fellow-workers in Great Britain.

is a fact that a wet canteen has been established, which is quite contrary to the principles and regulations of the Y.M.C.A.?
alternative premises. If this Parliament
agrees to the abolition of wet canteens for

Adjourned Debate. 658
The Budget-
25 MAY 1922.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand that
this problem is being considered in Great
Britain, and in the event of fresh legislation
being undertaken in that country, the
question of assimilating the law in this
country will be carefully considered. While
the matter does not strictly come within the
scope of the Roads Advisory Committee, any
recommendations made by that Committee
will receive careful attention.

Mr. LYNN: I do not intend to delay the
House for any length of time in going into
the very exhaustive and very interesting
statement that was made by the Finance
Minister yesterday. It may be a fact that
under other circumstances I should have
been inclined to enter into some detailed
criticism on the Budget statement, but I
realise that we are living under conditions
which make criticism, even the most friendly
criticism, rather out of place, and certainly
not in keeping with either my own feelings
or, I am sure, the feelings of the majority of
the Members of the House, because Ulster is
being attacked. Ulster, as I pointed out two
days ago, is in very serious danger at the
present moment, and whatever differences
we may have in regard to the financial
ability or otherwise of the Government, this
is not the time for dealing with these matters. Our business is to strengthen the
hands of the Government, to let it go out to
the public that we stand not even with the
shadow of a shade of difference, but that we
stand as a united House and as a united
Province. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It
is in this spirit I rise to-day. I was referred
to by the Minister of Finance as one who
assumed to have some knowledge. I am
quite sure from what I know of my right
hon. Friend he did not intend it as a sneer,
but I would say that possibly, like himself,
I have spent a great many weary days and
weary nights going through Finance Bills.

I just want to clear up one point. There
may be an impression in the House that the
Government cannot possibly go in for
extravagance, because seven-eighths of the
taxes are levied by the Imperial Parliament.
If my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)
will refer to the Act of 1920 he will find,
as he knows very well, and his highlyqualified understudy (Mr. Barbour) knows
also, that you cannot increase any of the taxes
levied by the Imperial Parliament, but you
can do what is much more important-you can
reduce any tax imposed by the Imperial
Parliament. But that is not the whole
matter. This House can, if it so desires, levy
extra taxes, and I put it to my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) that if his Budget
statement did not balance, and if he had not
been in the satisfactory position of having a
surplus of at least £69,000, if instead of a
surplus he had a deficit of £69,000, I presume,
then, the House would have had to levy fresh
taxation. We are very fortunate, and we are
very thankful to the Finance Minister for
the fact that under very difficult conditions
he has made his Budget to balance, and has
a small surplus. I congratulate him
heartily as anyone in this House on that fact.
I know the enormous amount of work he and
my hon. Friend opposite (Mr. Barbour) have
done. The general public have no idea how
heavy a burden has been placed on them, and

Perhaps

the salaries of the Government Ministers are

could not possibly have gone on, and our

to join in that chorus of congratulations.
But at the same time I feel it my duty, and
I take the earliest opportunity of getting up,
to criticise a few remarks which my hon.
Friend the Member for South Belfast (Sir
Crawford M'Cullagh) made-I am sorry he is
out of the House at the moment-with reference to economy. He said that in his
opinion not only could we not economise, but
that there was no possibility of economising
in next year's Estimates, and that there was
no possibility of economising in officials. In
fact, to my mind, such remarks as he made
were calculated to flatter the Ministry of
Finance and to divert them from their proper
and necessary duty of examining every item
of expenditure which comes before them.
Although we agree that the Ministry of
Finance have done their duty well during the
time they have been in control of our
financial affairs, I take leave to say that there
is always an opportunity for further economy
--(Hon. Members: Hear, hear) and I would
implore my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Finance not to relax his efforts one single
moment in keeping our expenditure down to
the lowest possible limits. The only way that
this country can come round to normal
conditions is, first of all, reduction in
expenditure; and, secondly, production; and
if my right hon. Friend will look after the
reduction of expenditure, the other Departments of our Government will look after the
question of production.
I am very much obliged to my right hon.
Friend for the clear manner in which he has
explained his Budget statement. To such of
us as have a very poor knowledge of financial
affairs it is extremely pleasant to have it put
in a manner which is intelligible to the
ordinary individual, because, after all, people,
like myself, who have not been engaged in
large businesses only have experience of the
domestic circle; and, although we try to get
our better halves to economise, and, although
we have some knowledge of the difficulty of
making both ends meet, yet we have not got
the experience of my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance. I congratulate him most
heartily on his statement, and assure him of
every support on my part.
Dr. MORRISON: I would like to say a

dissipation. (Hon. Members-No, no.) That
may be. I confess myself that in my desire
for economy I went a good deal further than
I should have done, and in due time I came

Coming down from these little side issues,

We can
raise it I know in Committee of Supply, but

Supply, and we will insist on having

But we began with a credit balance of, I
think, £49,000 or £50,000, so I do not think
we have added very much to our balance this
year. The one point I wish to speak about
is that of Old-Age Pensions. It is one of
those items in the Budget costing over
£1,000,000. I have already had communication with the Finance Minister, and I am
informed that he has seriously considered the
liabilities the scheme involves us in, and also
the fact that there are abuses in connection
with it.
Any man who knows the working of the
Old-Age Pension Scheme will admit that
there never was a more admirable law passed
than that for giving a pension to keep old
people out of the Workhouse. Everybody
approves of it. It was a thing that was far
too long delayed, but in the country there
are large numbers of people who own portions
of land worth, perhaps, £200 or £300 who are
drawing that pension. Nobody grudges
giving it to working people, but the people
to whom I refer are diverting to their own
use funds that should go to deserving working people. These people who own this land
die, and probably leave property worth £200,
£300, or £400, which goes to their friends.
Not only that, but in many cases people who
own land assign it to their friends so as to
qualify for the pension. I am not saying a
single word against the scheme, because I
thoroughly approve of it. It is the first and
primary duty of the State to provide for its
infirm workers, and I was glad to hear the
Finance Minister say that he had improved
and economised on the administration of the
fund, which I think is just as costly as any
other form of administration in connection
with this House. I hope the Finance
Minister will look closely into this question.
I have one other point to raise in connection with the Constabulary. I hope I am not
violating your ruling, Mr. Speaker, but I
took the opinion of a very wise man in this
House before I mentioned these points. He
may have led me astray, but he said one
could raise almost any subject on this debate.
However, I bow to your superior knowledge
and I would not question your ruling. The
subject I wish to speak upon is that of wet
canteens. The question of stimulants to be
supplied to the Constabulary is an important
one.

duty, having taken hold of this Government,
to set to work and try to carry it through
on the lines laid down for us and to try to
make a success of our Northern Parliament.
But we realise that in each step we take we
are necessarily following along the line of
dissolving those financial ties, whether they
are personal, commercial, or even national,
which unite this country with the sister
countries of England and Scotland, and with
whom, it seems to me, our destinies, whether
financial or political, are so indissolubly
united. Be this as it may, we have to carry
out the duties that have been entrusted to
They are complicated to a degree, and
we are very far from having seen the end of

us.
I quite agree with what the Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) has said, that in
our Budget, where our power to raise revenue
is restricted, our attention must in the first
instance, and always in a greater degree, be
directed to reducing our expenditure, the
great item in which stands out as £7,920,000,
which I regard as being only provisionally
fixed as the amount of our contribution
towards the debt service, and the Army,
Navy, and Air Forces of the Empire. Abuse
of British institutions does not come with
any facility to my lips. I have always had
the very warmest regard for England and
Englishmen, and although we may feel
strongly at times the way our interests here
have been treated, still, however they may
appear publicly and no matter how apathetic
they may be to what we consider the
very serious issues in our affairs over
here, I think there are many occasions
on which we have to regard their attitude towards us and their treatment
of us financially as generous and very
friendly indeed. As a matter of fact they
have already departed to some extent from
the strict letter of the law as laid down in
the Government of Ireland Act. Hon.
Members who have touched on this matter of
our contribution and the manner in which
it should be arrived at have been in a large
measure correct, but the provisions as laid
down in the Act have since been modified,
generally speaking in our favour. They have
agreed that it will not be necessary for us
to wait for two years before we begin to feel
the benefit of any reductions which the Joint
Exchequer Board may consider we are
entitled to. In the meantime they are
only deducting from our revenue as it is
collected one-sixteenth of that sum instead of
one-twelfth, and we are encouraged by that
move on their part to hope that our
contribution of £7,920,000 may be reduced by 25 per cent. Even then
we shall not accept that readily.
We shall, as my hon. Friend the Member for
South Belfast has stated, continue to watch
every point and study it closely to see that
our contribution is fixed at a fair and
equitable figure. I do not know whether we
should adopt any fixed sum unless we were
sure that it would be favourable to us and
that we were making no mistake, but with
the variations that recessarily take place in
taxation or reduction of debt or even in
reduction of armaments, naturally policy
changes from time to time so that we must
resort to some sort of sliding scale to fix the
contribution from the Northern area to the
United Kingdom.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Do I understand the
hon. Gentleman to say that he hopes the

Mr. BARBOUR: I am sorry I did not make
myself quite clear. I said the Imperial
Government were only deducting one-sixteenth of £7,920,000 each month from our
revenue as collected, instead of one-twelfth.
The reduction from one-twelfth to onesixteenth is 25 per cent., but there again I

Although the matter of our contribution falls

appreciation of the very great personal acti-

There are one or two questions which have

The £500,000 and £42,000 come entirely from

Supplementary Estimates. This £50,000, as

Parliament to show their desire to try to do
something to alleviate the feeling of unrest

great deal of this discontent and outrage

with in the last few months in Belfast.

It was a free gift on the part of the
Imperial Parliament, and they were able to
dictate the terms upon which that gift should
be made. My right hon. Friend the Minister
of Labour is administering that fund on the
lines laid down to you, but it was stipulated
at the time the gift was made that that fund
should only be made available for Belfast
and the immediately contiguous neighbourhood. The Cabinet of Northern Ireland have
realised that these difficulties which exist in
Belfast exist, though possibly not in
acute a form, in other portions of the Six
Counties, and they decided it would be right
from their own funds to grant a sum of
£50,000 to be administered in as nearly as
possible the same manner as the £500,000
given by the Imperial Parliament, but that
this sum from the loan fund should be
available throughout the Six Counties in
Northern Ireland. As regards some items
that were criticised I think the criticism of
these details falls or should fall more conveniently to such debate as may take place
on the different Estimates, and it would not
be right to go into matters of minor detail
at the present time.

675 Referees and Arbitrators Bill. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. BARBOUR: The object of this Bill,
the Referees and Arbitrators (Procedure)
Bill, is two-fold. Sections 33 and 34 of the
Finance (1909-10) Act, 1909, provide for the
hearing of appeals in regard to Mineral
Rights Duty and Estate Duty by Referees
taken from a panel of persons appointed by
a Reference Committee. Article 9 of the
Government of Ireland (Adaptation of Taxing
Acts) Order provides that there shall be a
separate Reference Committee and a separate
panel of Referees for Northern Ireland. The
Reference Committee for Northern Ireland
shall consist of the Lord Chief Justice and
the President of the Surveyors' Institution,
or some member of the Council of the Institution nominated by the President, having
special knowledge of valuation in Northern
Ireland. The Referees appointed need only be
part-time officers and are paid by fees.
Difficulties have arisen in regard to one of
the qualifications of the representative of the
Surveyors' Institution, viz., that he should be
a member of the Council of the Surveyors'
Institution; and Section 1 (2) of the Bill
makes provision that the person appointed
need not necessarily be a member of the
Council. As steps have already been taken
by the Lord Chief Justice to appoint a panel
of Referees, the Bill makes provision so as to
give covering authority for these appointments without going to the inconvenience of
reappointment.
a
a
Section 1 of the Acquisition of Land
(Assessment of Compensation) Act, 1919,
provides for the appointment of official
Arbitrators, to be taken from a panel of
persons appointed by a Reference Committee.
These arbitrators arbitrate on questions in
regard to compensation for land taken over
by Public Departments. As in the case of
the arrangements under the Finance Act,
and
separate Reference Committee
separate panel of arbitrators, similarly
constituted and with the same qualifications,
are set up for Northern Ireland. The arbitrators under the Acquisition of Land Act
must be whole-time officers, but in Northern
Ireland there is insufficient work to occupy
the time of one official, either under this
Act or combined with the duties under the
Finance Act. The Bill, therefore, proposes
to remove the qualifications in regard to the
whole-time, and provides for remuneration by
way of fees instead of salaries. Moreover,
the distinction which exists in the original
Acts and which has been maintained in the
Adaptation Orders under the Government of
Ireland Act between these two Reference
Committees and their subsidiary arbitrators
or referees is now abolished, one committee
and one set of referees being made to do
duty for both. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): The subject of this Bill
has been before the country for a very long
time. When the Government started the
Department of Agriculture and spent a lot
of money in the country it was found that
the full results of all their expenditure
could not be obtained. Sires were allowed
to produce stock that could not be sold in
any fair or market in the country, and as
long ago as 1906 the matter was brought
forward by the Council of Agriculture. The
resolution of the Council of Agriculture was
very much on the lines of this Bill. In
1907 and in 1909 it was again brought
forward, but they found the only chance
they had of securing the object in view was
bringing in a Bill for stallions only.
They tried that, but the difficulty of getting
time for Irish business in the House of
Commons in London was so great that it
was unavailing. They continued to press
for it. In 1918, owing to England, Scotland
and Ireland joining together they brought
in the Horse Breeding Act, and they tried
to get the Bill which the Ministry is bringing in to-day at the same time, but it was
not possible. They pressed again in 1919,
and it was thought then that the war being
over there was a chance of getting it passed,
but they found there was too much business.
In 1921 they pressed again. It has been
six times pressed by all the Boards of Agriculture. They tried to get the three other
Boards to co-operate, and there was a good
deal of progress made in the year 1921, but
it was again found that the difficulty of
getting an Irish Act pure and simple through
the House of Commons was too much. In
1922 we found the opinion of this country,
when we had a Government of our own,
was so strong that the Ministry, although
they had a great amount of other work on
hands, were forced to consult all the various
Committees in the country. We consulted
every kind of Committee, the Royal Ulster
Agricultural Society, the Ballymena Agricultural Society, the North-West Agricultural Society in Derry, and the Ulster
Farmers' Union. They every one of them
pressed us to bring in this Bill on the lines
suggested by them. It was then put before
the Cattle Advisory Committee which has
been set up by the Ministry, and also the
Consultative Committee on general agricultural subjects, and they made Some
suggestions. It was then put before a full
meeting of the Executive of the Ulster
Farmers' Union, and I am glad to say they
went through it section by section, and my
hon. Friend, one of the Members for Derry

(Mr. Mark) made some exceedingly useful
suggestions which we were able to incorporate in our Bill.
Of course, it entrenches a little bit, some
people may say, on the liberty of the subject,
but we have the Horse Breeding Act to work
upon, and we have no intention of putting
it in force severely or to do any harm to
any man. On the Continent it has been
in force in Switzerland for many years, and
there is never any trouble about it. There
is no trouble about the Harse Breeding Act
at the present time, and I am certain when
this Act is worked in a sympathetic manner
by the Ministry, which they intend to do,
and with the full assistance of the various
agricultural societies and the various County
Committees that no one will be injured at
all in any shape or form. It is not meant
to hit any man who is trying to benefit
the country; but what we do want to stop
is the indifferent farmer using a bull which
is really more like a goat than a bull or
anything else of that sort.
alter a licence or forge one you are subject

I believe this Bill will improve the price
of our store cattle enormously, and give
springing heifers that can be bought. I
know men about the country who when
they get a lot of heifers send them to
England or sell them to their neighbours
and have no calves for their own rearing.
They do not care twopence what sort of bull
it is that runs with those heifers, and the
produce is not at all to the benefit of Ireland
or to the benefit of the purchaser of these
cattle. This is a very well-known fact,
and we are determined if possible to stop
that work. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The restrictions we are putting on are very
moderate. A person who owns or has control of a bull is subject to a fine not exceeding £20 unless the bull is licensed or he has
a permit. The licence can be obtained at
a fee, and a copy can be given to a man
at a fee not exceeding 5/-. The fee will be
about 2/6 an animal. Surely no one can
complain about that. Anyone who wishes
to fatten a bull and only keeps it for that
purpose can get a permit for a fee not exceeding 2/-. We do not intend to charge
more than, I suppose, 1/-, but there
must be some small fee for a bull kept for
that purpose. Anyone who is in control of
a bull must produce a licence if he is
required to do so, or he is subject to a
penalty not exceeding £5. Anyone who has
got a bull and does not submit it to inspection or does not produce the licence and show
it to the person going to him and asking
for it, is also subject to a fine not exceeding
£5. That is under Section 6.
If you
obstruct a man entering your premises to
see if the bull is registered-we have an
official told off to do such a thing-you are
subject on summary conviction by Section
7 to a fine not exceeding £20, and if you
The Ministry does not propose that this
should be enforced until the 1st January,
which is the appointed day for having these
licences. That gives time enough for farmers
round the country in backward districts to
acquire the knowledge that they must have
licences for their bulls, or if they have a
bull of a sort to get rid of it, or act as
required in the Bill.
Mr. MARK: I would like at the outset to
congratulate the Ministry on the pluck they
displayed in bringing this Bill before the
House. I know it has been long in expectation in various parts of the United
Kingdom, but for Northern Ireland to be
the first to have such a Bill says a great
Ideal in favour of the Ministry we have here.
Undoubtedly the Bill is a crying necessity
at the present time. Only last week the
need was glaringly brought before my notice.
A neighbour of mine who has the best herd
of shorthorn cattle in the three Kingdoms,
at least in Ireland, with bulls costing up to
£1,000, saw the other morning that his
neighbouring farmer had let the grazing of
his farm to a cattle dealer, who had put in
a lot of blue, and grey, and black bulls
beside his heifers. If that sort of thing
can go on I do not know what damage will
not take place in the future. However,
we have now got a Bill which will brand
such a man as a criminal, and we can get
him fined at a court of summary jurisdiction.
The Minister of Agriculture rightly states
he has the support of the farming community
all over the Six Counties. The matter has
been brought before the various breeding
societies, agricultural societies, and show
committees in Ulster, and has been
thoroughly approved by the Ulster Farmers'
Union. I have spent, as he says, a whole
day going over this Bill in company with
some other farmers. We suggested some
improvements which we thought might be
put into the Bill, and the Ministry at once
agreed and have done everything in their
power to do what is fair and reasonable.
Some people may think it is not quite
drastic enough. Some may think it interferes
too much with the liberty of the person,
but I think, properly administered, it will
be an excellent Act. I hope the Ministry
will see it is lived up to and is not more
honoured in the breach than in the observance. There are some things in it not
quite complete, but I see powers have been
reserved for the making of regulations for
the carrying out of the Bill. One thing I
notice is that the Bill does not say when
a calf becomes a bull and when a man
becomes responsible for having a bull.
Probably the Regulations will set all those
matters right. The Ministry will have power
to make those Regulations, and I am sure

In moving this amendment I do so, as I

with the object of making this Bill as simple

put down this amendment. It is a draft

Minister. I have listened to many debates

objectionable in including this amendment
in the clause, and I hope my hon. and
learned Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary

regulations. I contend that this House
should be responsible for the legislation that
passes through it dealing with this Police
Force, and that while we are held responsible
for financing the Force, we should also be
responsible for its administration. We have
been told time and again that this House
should legislate in line with the Imperial
Government, and I may say that that is why

Force should be in an equally good position
with those in England and Scotland, and that
our Act governing that Force should be on
similar lines to the Act covering the Forces
in England and Scotland. I beg to move the
amendment.

something to say about it. There is just one
other point, and I do not want to make any
apology, but in this case here I would ask
the county Members to watch it carefully.
In Section 3 there is a distinction made between the prescribed rate and methods that
will be applied to County Councils and to
County Boroughs. If you come across a thing
like that in the Bill you know it is there for
some purpose, and we would like to know why
it is that there is to be a difference between
the differential rates and method of calculation for County Boroughs? You see we have
two County Boroughs and six counties, and
naturally we are just a trifle suspicious. On
the general Bill I want to make-
The CHAIRMAN: Not on the general Bill,
but the Clause.
Mr. DUFF: On this point of Clause 4,
Sub-section 4 says,
"According as the Minister may direct,"
We feel that in all the Clauses there is an inordinate power given to the Minister. The
only essential difference in this Bill is the
power given to the Minister. We feel if that
is merely a matter of form all is well-a
matter of form in this sense that previously
the Chief Secretary was the man responsible,
and now it is the Minister who is responsible.
There are some men who have had considerable experience of law equal to that of any
member of the profession in this room, and
they have stated after careful consideration that the powers given to the Minister in
this Bill are extraordinary, so that I am
not giving it as my own opinion, I am
merely expressing the opinion of some one
more capable than myself of judging such a
thing.
26 MAY 1922.
Constabulary Bill-

Committee.
The hon. Member (Mr. Duff) asked another
question, where the additional force would
come from as distinct from the quota? The
additional force, as I understand it, will
first of all be drawn from the reserve force,
and then from the various counties. If
there is a quota in a county which is not
necessary, part of it may be drawn away and
may be used as an additional force if
another part of the country requires its
services, but I should say that it would only
be on occasions when there was a very considerable need for the force arising from
difficult circumstances in the area that
wanted the force for the time being.
The following amendment stood on the
Paper in the name of Mr. Megaw:
Mr. MEGAW: I do not know that I have
ever heard a speech which is so full of
suspicion as that which I have just
listened to. Apparently the Ministry here
has been guilty of trying to cover up its
meaning by innocent words, and have been
laying plots against someone in a way that
is certainly of a very startling character. I
had no idea that there were so many pitfalls
in this Measure as I have come to the conclusion there must be from the time I heard
the hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr. Duff)
make his last speech, and I am rather suspicious that we have not been taking suffi
cient precautions to guard against some of
those gentlemen who, he says, have been instructing him, because apparently it has
been scrutinised line by line in a very careful way, and an endeavour has been made
to get some statement made by the Ministry
here that will bind our hands in the future.
The Bill stands there for scrutiny, and it
has been open to my hon. Friend to see the
particular clause. All that he has done from
beginning to end is to ask questions us to
my construction of it. I can give no more
than my own construction. We have not
been investigating it in that particular way;
we have got the words here before us. One
thing, I think, may relieve his mind somewhat. If he thinks that there is a plot made
against the City of Belfast, which he seems
to be representing, I would remind him that
there are 16 Members in this House from the
City of Belfast, and that if there is likely
to be any ill-treatment of that body we should
hear about it.
Mr. DUFF: It might be too late.
Mr. MEGAW: It is a matter of administration. This is a Constabulary Vote which
takes place from year to year, and if there
is any injustice wrought it can be raised on
the floor of this House from time to time.
It has been suggested that there is some
difference made between the county boroughs
and the various county councils. I cannot
say whether that is so or not, because I
can very well understand how the prescribed rules would somewhat
vary in
a county district and in a city district.
One thing occurs to me which should
have been taken into consideration. The
city police have to work day and night; the
country police have only to work practically
by day. I do not say that the city force would
have to be almost double, but it would have
to be something near it. However, it is a
matter entirely for the administration, and
in the framing of these rules these bodies
will get an opportunity of making any observations and putting forward any views
that they wish. I cannot really investigate
all these matters meticulously. I only say
I am not aware that there is any such desire
to hide our meaning in the language that
has been embodied in the Bill.

NEW CLAUSE (IMPROPER USE OF
UNIFORM.)
"If any person, not being a member of
the Police Force, wears, without the permission of the Police Authorities, the uniform
of the Police Force, or any dress having the
appearance or bearing any of the distinctive marks of that uniform, he shall, on
summary conviction, be liable to the fine
not exceeding Ten Pounds; provided that
this section shall not prevent persons from
wearing police uniform dress in the
course of a stage play or music hall or
circus performance."-(Mr. Donald.)
or

CAUSING DISAFFECTION, ETC.
"If any person causes or attempts to
cause or does any act calculated to cause
disaffection amongst the members of the
Police Forca or induces or attempts to induce or does any act calculated to induce

Caune be read a Second time. My reason for

stage, and if we think there is any real

that ten County Inspectors would not be

As to
required for a Force of 3,000 men
District Inspectors there are four at Headquarters, six at the Depot, and two
in the Reserve Force, and there is
power to appoint thirty-eight through the
counties. That would make a total of fifty
District Inspectors. With a Force of 3,000
that means one for every sixty men. I think
it is absurd. Then as to Head Constables,
there are to be one at Headquarters, two at
the Depot, and two on reserve. There is
power to appoint sixty-four more. That is
a total of sixty-nine, or one to every fortyfour men. It may be said that these men
will not be appointed, but I think it is a bad
thing to have the power to appoint so many.
There are always temptations to get certain
people appointments, and if the Government
have power to do it the possibility is that
some person in authority will so manipulate
things that these people will be appointed. I
think the Bill is far too heavily weighted
with officers. I would like to know how
many were in the old Force in proportion to
this number. I would like also to ask where
will the Headquarters of these men be. It
seems to me unreasonable that a County
Inspector should live in the extreme end of
the county and have heavy bills for travelling
expenses. County Inspectors should live in
the centre of the county and District
Inspectors in the centre of their districts, and
not live where they please, and charge
travelling expenses for travelling through the
country. I think that should be in the
cognisance of this House. No man should
have power to allow a person to live in the
extreme end of a county and charge travelling
expenses on the public road. He should live
in the centre of the county. I think it would
be well if we could understand something of
where the Depot would be also.

HEALTH AND UNEMPLOYMENT
INSURANCE.
(1) Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Labour :-
(1) What are the amounts contributed by
employers and employees, and also by County
Councils, during the past year ending 28th
February for each of the Six Counties in
Northern Ireland-
(a) For Health Insurance?
(b) For Unemployment?
(2) What amounts have been expended under
each head?
(3) What amounts have workers received?
(4) What amounts have been spent on
salaries and administration?
(5) What balances are in hands of Approved
Societies?
been compiled for the different counties, but
figures associated with each Employment
Exchange could be given if desired.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I regret that I am not in a position
to give figures for the year ending February
28th, 1922, since my Department was not
responsible for the administration of the
funds during that period, and no separate
figures were compiled for Northern Ireland.
I propose however to circulate in the official
report of to-day's debate a statement of the
estimated expenditure for an average year,
but I should say that our experience of these
funds is short, and our first estimates may not
be as accurate as they would be with longer
experience. No separate figures have ever
It is not possible at present to state the
amount of the reserves of Approved Societies
until the valuation of the Societies has been
completed.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Arising out of that,
has there not been a valuation since these
things came into force? Can the right hon.
Gentleman say where these balances are
invested, and what is the rate of interest?
Mr. ANDREWS: I believe the last
valuation available is 1918. That audit, I
understand, was only completed a few days
ago, and has not been circulated yet. I
regret to say that these audits, which are
conducted by the Imperial Ministry, are very
slow, so far as the publication of the returns
is concerned. As regards the rate of interest,
that has varied recently, according to the rise
and fall of interest, but a large proportion of
the funds of those Approved Societies are
invested in War Loan.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that, may
I ask the right hon. Gentleman if a Bill will
be introduced in this House shortly on the
question of Unemployment Insurance, when
he will have an opportunity of giving us facts
and figures?
Mr. ANDREWS:-I do not quite understand the hon. Members' question. As regards
Unemployment Insurance-
Mr. DONALD: Health Insurance.
Mr. ANDREWS: We propose to proceed
on parallel lines with Great Britain for the
present, and if a Bill is introduced in the
Imperial House dealing with Health Insurance we will introduce a somewhat similar
Bill here. There is a Bill being considered
in the Imperial House dealing with the
transfer of medical certificates. The liability
at the present time is attached to the taxpayers, and the Approved Societies in Great
Britain have taken that obligation on
themselves. I am pleased to be able to say
that the Approved Societies here have agreed
with me to take upon themselves a similar
obligation. That will mean a saving to
Northern Ireland of £28,000 a year; but until
the matter has been further dealt with in the
Imperial House I do not propose to take
action here.

INCREASE OF RENTS ACT.
3. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of Home
Affairs if the Government is considering the
introduction of legislation to modify the Increase of Rents Act, in view of the considerable reduction which has already been
affected in the wages of the artisan classes.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The question of introducing
legislation restricting rents or modifying existing Acts has been carefully considered by
the Government of Northern Ireland.
The Government have had strong representations made to them from various sources
and interests, from which it would appear
that any legislation, if introduced, would be
of a most controversial character. The
Government also feel that any further legislation on this question might act as a check
to private enterprise, and they feel that it
is only by free and unrestricted building
operations that rents will ultimately be
lowered.
The Government of Northern Ireland have
kept in close touch with the Imperial Government on this important subject, and understand that that Government have decided
after careful consideration not to introduce
any further legislation on the subject of rent
restriction.
It appears to the Government of Northern
Ireland that, in the present condition of
trade and industry, any differential legislation in Northern Ireland and Great Britain
on matters of this sort might be prejudicial
to the best financial interests of Northern
Ireland.
In all the circumstances, therefore, it has
been decided that it would be inadvisable to
introduce any legislation on this subject.
Mr. DONALD: Is my right hon. Friend
aware that it would have been a very good
job if there had never been any legislation on
this question, and then the matter could have
righted itself in a proper way? That is where
the Government failed at the beginning.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Motor Vehicle Races [S] Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read the Second time." (Sir
Dawson Bates.)
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of the
present Bill is to confer upon local authorities powers to enable them to close roads in
their particular areas for the purpose of holding Motor Races for a period not exceeding
three days in one year. It will be within the
recollection of hon. Members of this House
that in 1913 the famous Gordon Bennett Race
was held in the South of Ireland. To enable
races to be held on that occasion a special
Act had to be passed, but that only remained
in force for one year. With regard to the Bill
itself, the public are safeguarded, inasmuch
as that, under Clause 1 sub-Section (2), any
Order made by a County Council must contain
the necessary provisions approved by the
Ministry of Home Affairs for the purpose of
protecting the public, and no Order can be
made without the consent of the Ministry. I
would suggest that this Bill should meet with
the approval of the House, because it does not
impose any additional burden either upon the
taxpayers or the ratepayers. Any expense will
have to be borne by the promoters of the particular enterprise.
I am sure that hon. Members will agree
that as a Government we should do everything
possible to help to develop tourist traffic in
the Six Counties, and not only will races of
this kind help the tourist traffic generally,
but, by doing so, will help hotel keepers, farmers, and others, and will generally bring
money into the country. It is estimated that
something like £200,000 was spent annually in
the Isle of Man in connection with the races
held there. I am sorry it will not be practicable to hold these races in the immediate
future, but I hope, before long, when more
lawful conditions are resumed within our
area, we will have them. I can only say that
so far as this Government is concerned we
intend to support everything of this kind
which will bring money into the country. I
beg to move.
709 Motor Vehicles Races Bill.
Mr. DONALD: I only wish to say a few
words with regard to this Bill, and, as a lover
of sport, I congratulate my right hon. Friend
(Sir Dawson Bates) on its introduction. But
I think our country is not in a proper state
at the moment for the holding of such races,
and, although it may be necessary to pass a
Bill of this description, I hope my right hon.
Friend (Sir Dawson Bates) will see that, under
sub-Section (5) of Clause 1, the powers of the
County Councils shall not be exercised except
with the consent of the Ministry, I hope
that until things become more settled, my
right hon. Friend will not give his sanction to such racing, and, may I also express
the hope that it will not be very long till we
get a reduction in the taxation of motor
vehicles. This is really a non-controversial
measure, and I do not want to offer any opposition, but I think my right hon. Friend
(Sir Dawson Bates) should use his discretion
as to when he gives permission for these races.
I think it should not be given in the near
future, at any rate, until the country becomes
a lttle more settled. I am very pleased to see
a Bill of this description being introduced
in order that Northern Ireland may benefit
by such competitions. We are all lovers of
sport, and this is the right way to foster it.

JOINT NURSING AND MIDWIVES
COUNCIL [8] BILL.
Order for Second reading read
Motion made and Question proposed,

Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to amalgamate the Joint Nursing
Council for Northern Ireland and the Central
Midwives Board for Northern Ireland. The
Midwives Act of 1918 established a Board for
the whole of Ireland, and in 1919 an Act was
passed establishing a Joint Nursing Council
for Ireland. These Councils correspond generally to the General Medical Council and the
recently established Dental Board. These
Boards are not in any sense Government
departments. They are entirely selfsupporting, and the expenses are defrayed
out of the fees of applicants who seek to be
registered under the Act. Following on the
passing of the Home Rule Act, and the
necessary transfers being made, two separate
Boards had to be set up for the Northern
Having regard to the limited means
which these bodies possess, it has been felt
that there should be an amalgamation of
both bodies and thereby save a great deal
of unnecessary expense caused by the duplication of the various offices.
After very
careful consultation with the various
interests affected the constitution of the new
body has been worked out, and I think it
will be found that it allows for very fair
and adequate representation of the interests
concerned.
area.

It is a
corporate body and will have a seal, Subsection (2) of Clause 1 sets out the constitution. This only applies to the first three
years, that is the constitution on its formation. Four persons shall be appointed by
the Ministry, of whom one shall be a medical
officer of the Ministry, one a person appointed
by the Ministry after consultation with the
County Councils and County Boroughs, and
two registered medical practitioners, who
shall be appointed after consultation with the
various medical organisations. The remaining six shall be appointed by the
Ministry, and they shall all be nurses, but
two of them must have special qualifications
in regard to midwifery. These will all be
appointed after consultation with the various
nurses' organisations. The first Council

he called for a report from the D.I. in charge

Mr. M'GUFFIN: I want to offer a few observations with regard to this measure. I am
not going to criticise its principles or its
details. With that I have got nothing to do,
but I do want to say that it is rather surprising that in the grave condition of affairs
which exists at the moment this House should
be content to discuss a Bill which merely
makes provision for pleasure and enjoyment.
It seems as if we were oblivious to the real
situation in which we are living. I do not
mean to say it is true of the Prime Minister,
but it is true of us as a House if we discuss
things of this kind in the midst of so many
urgent difficulties. I cannot see what urgency
there can be in a matter of this sort, and I
do say that when a Bill such as this is about
to be introduced in the House, the House
is entitled to have the Bill circulated. I have
brought this matter before the House on another occasion, and I have shown that in a
particular instance it was intended to read a
Bill a Second time before it was printed.
With regard to the Constabulary Bill I
pointed out that we were entitled to receive
a copy of it and it was agreed that it would
be circulated. I am not sure whether my hon.
Friend, the Junior Whip, gave me that prɔmise, but until this moment I have not eceived a copy of it. The same applies to the
Bills we are discussing here to-day. We have
not had an opportunity of looking into them
to see what principle is involved. So far as
the details are concerned it may be that we
will be able to agree with them, but the
main and important point is the Second
Reading. It is at that stage that the principle of the Bill is examined and it is upon
the principle of the Bill that it is frequently
defeated, and it gives us absolutely no chance
when we are asked to pass a Bill like the
Constabulary Bill without having it in our
hands. From the remarks made by the hon.
Member for North Belfast I understood that
certain suggestions would be incorporated in
the draft of the Bill, but apparently
notice was taken of them and we have not
had an opportunity of seeing how far the
recommendations contained in the Police
Committee's report were adopted or recognised. I invite the Prime Minister, if he is

urgency it will be circulated sufficiently early
to give us an opportunity of examining its
principles and seeing how far we can subscribe to or support them. I think this is
a very important matter.
It is the usage
which is observed on the other side. There

Librarian has not got instructions. It is
only a question of giving instructions that
all Bills should be circulated immediately
they come into his hands. That is the
custom in another place, and not only Bills
but regulations are circulated. I would
suggest that all matter which comes into the
Vote Office should be circulated to hon.
Members at the earliest opportunity.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James
Craig): May I deal with the last point which
has been raised by both my hon. Friends
(Mr. M'Guffin and Mr. Donald) first? The
Bill in question, as I suppose they are both
aware, followed exactly the same course as
was followed in the Imperial Parliament.
In other words, it was introduced in the
Senate, and as soon
as the Senate was
finished with the Bill it came to this House.
It is quite true that the period between the
Bill being dealt with by the Senate and its
coming to this House was very short; but we
thought that, on the whole, as the Bill was
non-contentious, and also as it was fulfilling
a pledge given by my right hon. Friend (Sir
Dawson Bates) to the motor industry-if I
may use that broad expression-it would be
to the advantage of the House to go straight
on with the Bill fresh from the Senate,
where it was discussed, or, at all events, an
opportunity was given of discussing it, and
it was then re-printed and in the hands of
hon. Members yesterday, when it was taken
through its Second Reading. Therefore, as
there seemed to be a general acquiescence
throughout the House that the Bill should
go on, we naturally took the Committee
stage and the Third Reading to-day. I can
assure hon. Members that there is no desire
to rush the Bill through, or that they should
not be in possession of printed copies of it;
but as it was introduced in the Senate, and
not in this House, they will be aware of the
procedure which had to be followed. The
next point I want to make is that my hon.
Friend (Mr. M'Guffin) laid some emphasis
on our pushing this Bill through at a time
when

our country is so disturbed.
Government are fully aware of the criticism

as a point of honour that once having set our

I may just say with regard to the Bill as
a whole that I myself felt very strongly, in
the first instance at all events, that we owed
a great deal to the motor industry. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) When I looked back
upon the way in which motor car proprietors
and motor car owners during the last year,
and, indeed, during this year, have responded
to the appeals of the Government to pay their
full licences, although everyone knows that
the full use of their vehicles was not assured
to them, and when I bore in mind the
extremely honourable and frank manner in
which the whole industry in Ulster met us
during trying times I thought it was only
due to them that we should do everything in
our power to show that they had the hearty
sympathy of the Government and this House
in promoting the industry, which is becoming
so important in all parts of the world. I
may also point out to my hon. Friend (Mr.
M'Guffin) that, as he knows, the motor car
industry is really in its infancy, and we hope
that this Ulster community of ours will not
be behindhand in competing in the manufacture of all those mechanical devices which
go to make a good car, and that we will
continue to keep in the front ranks along
with other parts of the country. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Another very important point is the
enormous amount of employment assured by
the industry, not only by the manufacture of
car engines, but by body-building and upholstery and so on. In fact there are very
few of us who are not wrapt up in this motor
car industry, and therefore we felt quite
justified in doing all we possibly could to
help the industry in their competitions.
The last remark I have to make is with regard to what was a suggestion rather than a
reasoned argument, which was made
yesterday on the Second Reading, that it

think the hon. Member (Mr. Crawford) did

to a great extent motor-car competitions, one

"That a sum not exceeding £735,864 be
granted to His Majesty to defray the charge
which will come in course of payment
during the year ending 31st March, 1923, for
the salaries and expenses of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary."
Sir DAWSON BATES: In presnting this
Estimate for the expenses of the Royal Contabulary for the remainder of the financial
year, I would like, before proceeding to make
a summary of the various items in the Estimate, to express the great regret which I,
and I am sure every Member of this House,
and indeed every Irishman, feels at the
passing of that great and historic
Force the Royal Irish Canstabulary,
for close on
which
Force,
cause of law
century has upheld the
and justice impartially and fearlessly. While
we all have that feeling of regret, at the
same time this event has given to Ulster an
a
opportunity of having her own Police Force,
and I feel certain that that Force will carry
on with the same efficiency the work of the
Royal Irish Constabulary, and that the great
traditions of the Royal Irish Constabulary,
from which the new Force will largely spring,
will be safe in the keeping of our new Force.
Hon. Members are aware that His Gracious
Majesty has been pleased to bestow upon our
new Constabulary Force the title " The
That Force
Royal Ulster Constabulary."
will never disgrace its name, and, composed
as it will be of all that is best of the Royal
Irish Constabulary and our own Special
Constabulary it will, I venture to say, make
a Force that any country might be proud of.
It only rests with the people of this province
to give the new Constabulary their support
and goodwill. Without this, no matter how
excellent a Police Force may be, it must
suffer and its efficiency be impaired. I think
I can promise for the people of Ulster and
for this Government that our new Police
Force will never be subjected to the treatment which the Royal Irish Constabulary
received. (Hon Members: Hear, hear ").

With regard to the Estimate it is, to a
large extent, self-explanatory. As hon.
Members are aware, we are simply continuing, at any rate for the moment, the existing
Royal Irish Constabulary Estimate. To take
any other action for the present would be
impossible. Better adhere to the old tried
machinery than make hasty, and perhaps
disastrous changes. Any modifications
which we may require later on, and which
may be found desirable, can be made gradually from time to time.
Provision has been made to meet the
various recommendations of the Police Committee. It will be observed that in the
Headquarters and Depot Staff we have a
number of redundant officers. These are for
the purpose of meeting the very heavy additional work which must necessarily be accomplished in setting up and training a new
Force, and to meet the emergencies of the
present grave situation in Ulster.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Have the redundant officers been engaged on the understanding that
their positions are only temporary?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly not. I
will deal with that question afterwards.
While the R.I.C. who join the Royal Ulster
Constabulary will be, of course, trained, it
will be remembered that at least one-third
of the new Police Force, which is drawn
from our Special Constabulary, will require
a period of training in technical police
duty. Once the Police Force is running en
normal lines, and the condition of the
country becomes more normal, I hope it will
be possible to dispense with the services of
certain of these officers indicated for this
special purpose, and they will be absorbed
in the Police Force with a consequent reduction in the numbers.
Royal Ulster Constabulary. 726
Supply-
30 MAY 1922.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman in what way they will be
absorbed. I cannot understand it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
will understand that we are taking over a
certain number of the old R.I.C. officers who,
in course of time will go out on pension,
some sooner and some later.
I might point out that we have decided a
City Commissioner should be appointed for
the City of Derry. We feel that the importance of Derry, lying on the North-West of
our Province, warrants that such an appointment should be made.
It is impossible in this year's Estimate to
forecast with precision the amount payable
in respect of pay. This depends very largely
upon the number of Royal Irish Constabulary who join the Force and the period of
service which they carry into the new Force.
The amount has been taken, however, on an
average basis. It should be pointed out that
the existing scale of pay only applies to the
first 3,000 men. In many cases the figureshaving regard to the fact that we had no
previous Estimate to go by-have been taken
from an Estimate furnished to us by the
Royal Irish Constabulary authorities with a
proportional increase in respect of the increase in strength. The strength of the
Royal Irish Constabulary in Ulster was something like 2,700; that of the new Force will be
3,000.
The Estimate under the head of Clothing is
taken on a lower basis than that furnished
by the Royal Irish Constabulary, as it is
believed that owing to falling prices
there will be a reduction in this head.
With regard to arms, in the ordinary
course a comparatively small amount is
necessary to cover this cost, but in the
present position of the new Force it is necessary to provide for the complete equipment
of a proportion of the Force.
Under the head of Rent, it will be observed
that a nominal provision has been made for
the establishment of a Depot. It is essential,
in order to ensure that the training of
recruits is carried on under proper conditions, that a suitable Depot should be provided for, and we hope that a Depot will be
established this year. Meanwhile, the work
is being carried on at Newtownards Camp.
Regarding damages to property, provision
has to be made for the damage done by
members of the Force by accident.
Provision will have to be made for the
repairs to barracks. A great deal of neces
sary maintenance work seems to have been
postponed by the Imperial Government pending the disbandment of the Police Force, and
nothing has impressed me more-and I think
our Prime Minister referred to it himselfwhen going round the country than to see the
condition of the barracks in many of the districts. The Government feel that it must be
one of its first duties to see that the members
of their Force and their families are housed
in a reasonable degree of comfort.
Special Advances.-In the case of members
of the Force being injured and claiming from
the county, it has been found necessary to
advance, either to the constables or to the
dependants, moneys pending the payment of
the claim to which they may become entitled
under the Malicious Injury Acts.
With regard to the Appropriations in Aid,
this is the amount estimated by the Royal
Irish Constabulary authorities and consists
of payment for ex-police.
With regard to the payment to ex-police,
in accordance with the undertaking given by
my hon. Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary, the Local Authorities will be consulted
before the free quota is fixed.
I have dealt very briefly with the various
items, but I cannot close my remarks without adding a tribute to those already given
to the members of the Police Committee,
whose assistance in this important and
difficult problem-the establishment of a new
Police Force-has been invaluable. I feel I
owe a personal debt of gratitude to them all
for the time and labour which they bestowed
upon this question.

With regard to these particular blankets,
I may say that, roughly, the tender accepted
is half-a-crown cheaper than the tenders of
the firms, who, it is alleged, should have
got the contract. If you are going to confine
tenders to Ulster let it be so, and let that
be understood, but in the first instance you
have got to pass an Act of Parliament, and
it also means that you have got to abolish
the post of Comptroller and Auditor-General,
because when the official of the Ministry
responsible comes to have his accounts
examined he has got to show to the Comptroller and Auditor-General some reason for
accepting a tender for a larger sum when he
could get the article for a smaller. I think
in a democratic House like this it is a right
good principle that a man has got to give
for taking a thing at a larger
figure when he could have got it at a smaller
figure. If the responsible official in the
Ministry of Home Affairs had taken one of
these tenders at half-a-crown dearer than
what he actually got them for, when ne
came to have his accounts audited he would
have found himself surcharged and personally responsible for the amount of the
difference. Let there be no mistake about
that. I quite sympathise with those who
say, "By all means if possible keep your
contracts among your own people," but if
the difference in price is so great it is
clearly impossible to do so, and it is also
clear that you have got to introduce a very
different system of Parliamentary Government. You have got to abolish the functions
of that officer to whom I have already
alluded.

organisation at present, and I would be very
slow to make too serious suggestions to the

1. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Finance if he is satisfied that the directions
of the Registrar-General as to the cause of
death in inquest cases are of such a nature as
to enable the Government and the public to
determine accurately the direct and indirect
cause of many of the cases, and, if not, will
he issue new instructions to Coroners regarding this very important matter.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): My right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) regrets
that he is engaged on a Committee at the
moment, and he has asked me to reply to this

The instruction referred to by the hon.
Member was apparently inserted in the

The Minister will be glad to consider any

Dr. MORRISON: I beg to give notice that

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
BENEFIT.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour if he will state the conditions of
benefits under Section 3 of the Unemployment
Insurance Act relative to single men and
women, seeing that some misunderstanding
exists regarding young persons maintained
wholly or mainly by their relatives, and
whether he is aware of the great hardship
caused to many families by this decision.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The special conditions applicable
to claims to Unemployment Benefit, irrespective of stamp contributions, by single persons,
whether juvenile or adult, who are residing
with parents or other relatives, are proof,
firstly, that when in employment they support
themselves; and, secondly, that when unemployed they cannot reasonably look to their
parents for support.
The first condition is satisfied when a
claimant establishes that when he is employed
he supports himself, although he lives with
his parents or relatives. The second condition
is fulfilled when a claimant proves that his
parents or other relatives are unemployed, or
if employed are not in a financial position to
support him.
The misunderstanding to which my hon.
Friend refers would not arise if the distinction were borne in mind between benefit
payable. irrespective of stamp contributions,
and that which is payable on the basis of the
contributions standing to the claimant's
credit. In the latter case the conditions
above mentioned do not apply, and a claimant
would receive the amount of benefit to which
his credit of contributions would entitle him.
I am not aware that hardship has been
caused by applying these conditions, which
seem to me to be eminently reasonable when
a single person without any dependants
claims Unemployment Benefit and he has no
stamp contributions to his credit. Parallel
conditions are in force in Great Britain.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
does my hon. Friend not think there is a
very great hardship, say, where there is a
family of a father and three sons, and the
three sons are unemployed, and
are not
entitled to a halfpenny of benefit? With
regard to the other question might I ask my
hon. Friend if he will be good enough to see
that when these deserving cases come before
the Minister of Labour they will receive
special consideration when the parents are
not in a position to support the family?
Mr. GORDON: In reply to my hon. Friend,
I have already stated in my answer to his
question that if a claimant can prove that
members of his family are unemployed he is
entitled to benefit and accordingly benefit is
granted to him.

The PRIME MINISTER: I think this
would be an opportune moment for me to
make a statement regarding the grave affairs
that have once more agitated our area. The
House knows that not only has an incursion
been made into our territory on this occasion,
but that those forces from the South have
had the audacity to seize and hold on to that
territory-an offence the gravity of which no
words of mine are needed to emphasise. If a
happening of this sort were to take place in
any other part of our wide Empire, it would
be classified without hesitation by the Government and the people as
out-and-out

which has redounded to its credit, and

We have gone along the most peaceful lines
with the earnest and heartfelt hope that by

We have done all that, month after month,
and many a time against my own inclination
and my own feelings, but all the time in
the true interests of the Ulster people. I
have done what I could to preserve the peace
and secure better feeling throughout the
length and breadth of our country. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Unfortunately a
Minister is not always in a position to put
the whole of his cards on the table. Sometimes Ministers are blamed and have to
take the blame for this and that, when an
explanation in the House and in the country
would clear away the mystery which seems
to surround some of our deeds and what are
classed as our misdeeds, but nothing of the
kind ever influences me in the slightest. I can
only repeat what I said a few days ago in
this House that, taking a wide view of
this Ulster question, the people are perfectly
safe. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

An incursion, a nipping off of a place here
or a place there is an operation against
which we will take special precautions in the
future, but which, owing to one cause and
another, it was extremely difficult to prevent in the case which has just occurred. I
am not going to say what I think regarding
the actual loss of the territory; but I am
going to assure the House and assure the
people in that locality that they will be
restored to their homes. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) There is no question whatever about
that, and they will be restored to their homes
intact as far as this Government can do
it. I hope that no one in this House will
press me as to how that is to be done.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I assure them
of it; but, in case there should be a feeling
of uneasiness outside, may I in that connection take a letter an anonymous letterwhich appears in the "Belfast News-

of the feeling of certain persons
throughout the Six Counties. It is
true that letter is signed by a Radical, and
I presume he and some of his friends were
instrumental, in the first instance, in
getting us into the position in which we are
"
I have felt all along it was much more to the
interests of the Ulster people to bring the
British Government along with us in the
hard task that lies before us, rather than
constantly to irritate them by saying it is
part of its duty. It is no small thing for the
Imperial Government so far to have trusted
the Loyalists of Ulster as to have undertaken
on the one hand to supply as many troops as
are necessary to deal with whatever situation arises, to have sent the "Dauntless"
to guard our shores, to have sent the "Warwick up to the Foyle, and also to have sent
other vessels to Carlingford Lough and
above the bridge on the Foyle, which my
hon. Friend (Mr. Mark) knows was done
immediately it was asked for. It is no small
matter for them to say to us: "We look upon
your territory as British territory, and any
incursion into it is an incursion into Great
Britain." (Hon. Members: Hear hear.) And
although, of course, there is and always will
be the difficulty of getting one Government
to see eye to eye with another, still I bear
testimony here in this House to-day that,
in response to every reasonable request that
we made for assistance in the hour of
our trouble and difficulty, the Imperial
Government has come forward and helped
us. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I admit, of course, and admit frankly,
that in order to secure that consummation
it required a good deal of argument and, I
may say, skill on the part of myself and my
colleagues who were with me; but believe
me, reading as I have just read the speech of
the Secretary of State for the Colonies in the
Imperial House this morning-believe me
when I say that running all through that
speech there is not a single word that would
cause the slightest misconception or misunderstanding in Ulster. There seems
to be running all through it the
right tone of dealing with those who would
in any way attempt to overthrow the honourable undertaking that was arrived at under
the Treaty. I have received from the Government a telegram asking that I should cross
over to London to have a talk with them, not
on this immediate situation so much as upon
the future which will develop of course when
action is taken in connection with recovery of
our territory. My reply to the Government
is that Lord Londonderry, who so ably, as my
colleagues are willing to admit, backed me up
in the most delicate negotiations with the
Government, and myself, would cross over tonight-I quote from the telegram-
Prime Minister's Statement.
Motion for Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
"On the distinct understanding that we
are not asked to meet the delegates from
Southern Ireland."
(Hon. Member: Hear, hear.).
I make that statement public, because I see
no chance whatever of having negotiations,
either directly or indirectly, with a body of
persons so composed of Republicans, who in
my opinion are out to bring about the fall of
Ulster. I can put no stronger words upon it
than that. Therefore we have accepted this
invitation, which the House will quite readily
understand we could not refuse. It would be
ungracious on the one part, unncessary on the
other, and be repugnant indeed to my own
feelings that where a Government-the great
British Government-has held out every
assistance to us in our hour of trouble, we
should refuse to go across to consult with
them as to the best way they can help and to
clear up misunderstandings which are sure to
have arisen after their being closeted for a
week with Mr. Collins and his colleagues.
Therefore, the House and the country may
rest assured that neither the Noble Lord nor
I would leave our place here for one moment
if we did not think that we could do better
service to the cause of Ulster talking to the
Ministers of the Crown, who are helping us,
than being here. The only other comment I
have to make on this dangerous situation is
this: We shall easily win through. I have
not the slightest doubt about that. Remember that the situation as regards Sinn Fein in
Ulster is very different from the situation in
the South and West of Ireland. In the South
and West the British troops were up against
not only those who were actively engaged with
bomb and pistol, but up against a hostile community. Throughout the whole length and
breadth of that part of the country there was
a hostile community against the troops and
police. In Ulster, as everyone is aware, it is
exactly the opposite. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.). The troops, the police, and Specials
are welcome in the castle and cottage, and
every assistance that can be given to bring
about the old state of peace is being given by
the local inhabitants. In the South and West
it was dangerous for a Loyalist to possess arms
to defend his house and home. In Ulster,
owing to our system of A, B, and C Constabulary, there is no reason why every Loyalist
should not have arms to his hand, legally
agreed to by the Government. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.).
The consequence is that, instead of having
to take away arms from those holding them
for the protection of their life and property,
we are able to say to them:
"All of you come along, all join in order
to have some sort of record and some control over affairs; all come along, and you
can be armed in defence of your own country."
That is a great difference. Another thing
from the psychological point of view is the
grit of the people against whom the Sinn
Feiners are up. They are up against Ulster.
Nobody has ever been against Ulster without
finding that they were knocking in vain in
this way against the people's will, and I can
only repeat what my predecessor (Lord Carson) in the leadership of the Ulster people
repeated on many a platform:
"Time will reveal that the Ulster people
can never be coerced-they can only
won."
be
How long it will take the South and West
to learn that lesson I do not know;
but
whether we are in for a short, sharp campaign
in order to bring them to a realisation of that
fact-whether it is long or whether it is
short, the Ulster people, I am perfectly certain, will wear them down. As far as I am
concerned and as far as my colleagues are
concerned we are quite unruffled by any of
these foul attacks which have been made on
our liberty, and we are only nerved to
go on and on in
our preparations to
meet whatever eventualities may come.
They are trying every dodge, they are trying
every nefarious scheme, not for the benefit of
Ireland-not a bit of it, that is the last thing
these men seem to think about-what they
are aiming at is, as I said before, the fall of
Ulster, so that Ulster may be brought to the
same welter that exists in the South and
West. Ulster will put up such a stern resistance that these persons will be sorry they
ever attempted it.
My last word is to ask the people of Ulster
once more for absolute confidence, for courage
to stand up to anything that may come along
on the one hand, and on the other
to rest assured that, whether it be in
Belleek, or whether it be on the
coast of Antrim, in Down, or in the
heart of the City of Belfast, the Government
are absolutely determined that the law of the
land shall run, and that there shall be in
future that stabilised Government to which
the people of Ulster are entitled. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

but I agree with the Prime Minister that we
have to take long views, and if we can get the

Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn."-(Mr. Burn).
Dr. MORRISON: I want to say a word or
two in connection with a reply which was
given to me with regard to Registrars of
Deaths in inquest cases. I have got to sit as
a Coroner, and as a man having practical
experience of the statistics available in connection with these inquests, I can say they
are wholly misleading. This is a very serious
statement to make with regard to any public
statistics. We have, and I have attempted to
have the practice extended, to get statistics
of the deaths of our cattle. That is a very
necessary thing, because no remedy can be
devised for certain diseases if you do not
know the actual extent of the problem with
which you are dealing. I think every Meinber of this House will admit the first consideration of Parliament should be the health
of the people. In order accurately to determine that you must have a correct record of
the death rate and the causes that produce it.
In the Registrar-General's Returns you will
find very accurate descriptions of nearly all
diseases. You will find tuberculosis classified
under three or four heads, infant mortality
analyzed, and all the other information you
wish to secure except this very important
question of deaths investigated at inquests.
Parliament, as I have said, must have a
knowledge of these facts before they are able
to provide a remedy.
With regard to the question of inquests, it
is an unfortunate thing that one of the
amenities of this House under present conditions is that some of us may die a violent
death, and it will explain the position if I
tell you what is going to happen if this rather
awkward contingency should arise. In the
first place we are asked by the Registrar-
General to state the primary cause of death
and then the secondary cause of death. Now,
the primary cause of death in an ordinary
case of wounding is shock and hemorrhage,
and to this you will probably add heart
failure. That defines exactly where you are,
but it gives no information to the public as
to how this death arose. The Registrar-
General in his instructions says you should
put down the primary cause of death and the
secondary cause of death, and then you
classify them under three heads-suicidal,
homicidal, or accidental. I maintain that
under these headings the public are entirely
at sea as to what in many cases is the direct
cause of death in inquest cases. It misleads
the public, it misleads this House, and it
prevents a remedy from being found for the
deplorable condition which I say exists in
these statistics. Let me give you one or two
concrete cases. I held an inquest on the
bodies of three persons who, according to the
evidence which came before me, went down
the street in one of our towns under the
influence of drink, got into a boat and
capsised it before they had gone a mile. The
result of the inquest was that asphyxia was
the primary cause of death. It was classified
"Drowning; asphyxia; accidental." I think
is is fairly obvious to any man that any
person reading these three case of accidental
drowning from the Registrar-General's Returns will be absolutely incapable of
diagnosing or telling what really was the
cause of death. In another case a man who,
according to the evidence, was so drunk
in a public-house that he was unable to put
a glass of whisky to his mouth, walked out
of the house and stumbled and fell on the
tramway. A tram went over him nd
smashed his legs, and he died some time
afterwards. I had to hold an inquest, and
the primary cause of death was put down as
"fracture of the legs," and the secondary
Registrar-General's Returns. 770
