cause of death "heart failure; accidental."
Is the saddle on the right horse in
a case like that? The third case in
which I was called upon to hold
an inquest was that of a man who, when
pulling down a window while under the influence of drink, cut his radial artery. It was
a very small cut. As people will do under
the influence of drink, he wandered round the
room keeping the door closed until all the
blood was drained from his body. I held an
inquest. His friends were so much under une
influence of drink that I could not examine
any of them the following day. The result of
that inquest is classified "Hemorrhage;
accidental." I need not multiply these details; I could go on indefinitely. I have had
to hold inquests in something like 236 cases,
probably nearly 250 cases, and I would think
that in 50 of those 250 cases these misleading
returns occur.
thing uniform, something that would apply
to the whole community, and not to a section
and not to a class. I have had a conversation
with my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance. He tells me he has also acted at
one time, when he was a smaller man than he
is now, in the influential position of
Coroner, and he is willing to meet with me
and help me to devise some plan by which
the public may learn who is responsible for
these calamaties that take place in our midst.
I shall gladly avail myself of his assistance,
and I should like this House to hear what he
has to say in regard to this matter.
I think that in public statistics which are
drawn up with the object of enabling Parliament and our people to put their fingers on
certain sores, there should in cases of death
be accuracy. I maintain under this system
it is wholly inaccurate, and the people are
blinded and cannot possibly do anything for
themselves. No man goes so far as the man
who does not know where he is going. I do
not want to indulge in sentiment in regard
to this matter, but I want it put on a
scientific basis, exactly in the same position
as tuberculosis and infantile mortality. As
Thomas Carlyle said. "The British Empire
consists of thirty millions of people, mostly
fools." I am inclined to believe there is a
very large amount of truth in that statement,
although it is not altogether true.
Mr. ANDREWS: There are exceptions.
Dr. MORRISON: Fools usually blind their
eyes to the thing that will ultimately destroy
them. There is the drug habit. If we had
people in this country and this great city
who had developed the habit of using
cocaine, and if there was an inquest following
a death from it, there would be a great uproar in the Press. If we had two or three or
half-a-dozen deaths from it there would be a
public demand for measures by this House to
deal with it. We have nothing of that demand in regard to the cases that are happening in our midst. Not only have we no legislation for dealing with it. but we have a
cloak put over it which hides it from the
public gaze.
I have heard a good deal of
discussion lately with regard to temperance,
and if I mistake not some of the licensed
traders have put forward a claim that they
are really in a manner public philanthropists.
I am not going to discuss that matter, but I
want every herring to hang by its own tail,
and to let the truth be known. What I
would like to see done in this matter is some-
Mr. POLLOCK: My hon. Friend from the
University (Dr. Morrison) has drawn me into
a somewhat technical discussion. He can
certainly claim a knowledge and experience
in this matter which is denied to the majority
of the Members at any rate. In my position
as magistrate I have had an opportunity of
meeting coroners' juries, and I know that it
is not always easy for the coroner to force the
jury to any particular form of verdict. Now,
what is in my hon. Friend's mind is
obviously to secure that the coroner's certificate of the finding of the jury shall disclose
not only the actual and immediate cause of
death, but also the contributory circunstances that may have been associated with
that death. The certificate given by the
coroner, I find, is of a very wide nature indeed. comprised under the heads which my
hon. Friend has read, that is to say, whetner
the death was accidental, suicidal, or homicidal. These three words cover a very wide
area indeed, and I am afraid that any amplification of the circumstances-the primary
circumstances perhaps from which the death
resulted would entail a very considerable
amount of work by my hon. Friend,
the Coroner (Dr. Morrison). However,
be that as it may, the coroner is
simply returning to the Registrar-
General a certificate of the finding of the
jury, and as I have before remarked, he must
be confined to some extent to the
ipsissima verba of that finding. However,
I should say this that if the hon. Member
(Dr. Morrison) can discover any formula that
he thinks would be valuable for statistical
purposes, as that is apparently in his mind,
or affording further and more detailed information to the public in specific cases, and will
submit to the Department any suggestions in
regard to the formula. I can give an undertaking that every consideration will be given
to his suggestions. That is really all I can
say in the matter. It is not a subject that
lends itself to general discussion.

by the Civil Service Committee of individual
claims a work which is still incomplete.

being administered under the same system

will spend it. I move that this Vote be

ESTIMATES. 1922-1923.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
CLASS II, No. 1.
MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £38,599 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1923, for the
Salaries and Expenses of the Ministry of
Home Affairs." (Voted on Account £12,500).
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In introducing this Vote
I feel that it is unnecessary to amplify to
any great degree the explanation which I
gave in December last in regard to the internal organisation of the Ministry of Home
Affairs. I then pointed out that there are
two main divisions in the office; one which
deals with the services formerly administered
by the Chief Secretary's office in Dublin,
and the other dealing with those services
formerly carried out by the Local Government Board and the Ministry of Transport.
The Estimate which is before the Committee
provides for a staff of 100 officials, and I
can assure the Committee that when this
was drawn up it was hoped that this would
be sufficient. It is only right, however, to
say that since the Estimate was prepared we
have been obliged to increase the numbers
of some of the minor classes of officials. On
the crime side especially our activities have
been greatly increased, and the work has
developed far beyond our anticipations. It
will be appreciated that the criminal activities which are going on in our midst must
necessarily impose a very heavy additional
burden upon the Home Affairs Branch of the
office, and we have been obliged to augment
the staff accordingly. I would like, however,
to point out that these extra officials only
hold their appointments temporarily, and I
hope, when we get back to normal times and
normal conditions, that we will be able to
dispense with their services.
In
I would like to remind the Committee that
my Department is faced with exactly the
same difficult problems as confronted the
Chief Secretary's Department in Dublin
during the last three or four years. These
problems are precisely of the same magnitude,
and officials who have been transferred to my
Department from the Chief Secretary's office
have told me that the number of papers
coming daily into the Home Affairs Registry,
relating to Home Office affairs, far exceeds
that which had to be dealt with in the Chief
Secretary's Department in Dublin. In regard
to that, I might point out that the Chief
Secretary's office in Dublin was provded with
two Under Secretaries, and a total staff of
over 200. We have only one Secretary and
a total staff of 56, dealing solely with Home
Affairs, other than Local Government.
connection with Local Government work, in
addition to the intern staff, we have only
one General Inspector for our Local Government work as compared with 13 in Dublin;
2 Medical Inspectors as compared with 9 in
Dublin; 3 Auditors as compared with 20; and
one Engineering Inspector as compared with
9 Engineers and Architects. The services
we have to attend to are, I may say, the
oldest of all the Irish services. The roots
of the Chief Secretary's Department were
deep down in Dublin, and I can assure you
it was no easy task to pluck up these roots
and to transplant them here. Many difficulties were placed in our way, and one of
the greatest difficulties lay in securing the
to us.
transfer of properly trained men
However, I am glad to say that we have
overcome those difficulties, and I venture to
say that we have now got some of the best
officials in any branch of the Civil Service.
In addition to setting up a fresh office
organisation, we have had to establish our
new Police Force, and I can assure the
Members of this Committee that that was
by no means an easy task. Again, we found
our prison administration in a hopeless condition when we took it over, and I think I
may claim the credit for a substantial
strengthening of this branch of our administration. Might I also remind the House
that since we took over, Parliament has
imposed on us many difficult and troublesome
duties. The Civil Authorities Act, with its
wide powers, has imposed upon us a great
many duties which we had not anticipated.
The Act empowering us to dissolve local
bodies imposes very troublesome duties.
am glad to say that that Act has been a
most successful one, and from all parts of
the Province I get communications to show
that the Commissioners whom we have appointed are doing their work well and
economically, and many of the ratepayers
I
Supply-
Home Affairs.
21 JUNE 1922
would be sorry to revert to the old condition
of affairs. In addition to that, we have
got the new Nursing Act, and now the new
Local Government (Northern Ireland) Bill,
which I hope to introduce to the House
next week, will impose further additional
duties upon our Department.
I am also glad to be able to announce that
we have almost completed arrangements with
the Imperial Government for taking over,
as an agency service, the administration of
the Irish Land for Sailors and Soldiers Act
in Northern Ireland. We have been continually pressing the Imperial authorities
to hand over to us the administration of this
Act as an agency service, and our efforts
have at last been successful. I think I may
confidently say that we will in a very short
time be in a position to carry out the administration of that Act. Out of a total of 3,500
cottages which has been allotted for the
whole of Ireland, we in Northern Ireland
are to have 1,000. We are not satisfied with
this proportion, and are pressing the Imperial
authorities further to see that that proportion is increased more in comparison with
the number of men we sent out from Ulster.
Additional staff will be required for this
work, but the cost will not fall
on the
Government of Northern Ireland. The Imperial Government have promised to place
at our disposal a sum not exceeding £250,000
for the purpose of carrying on this agency
service for the present year. I think the Members of this Committee will readily understand that all this involved a very heavy
addition to our work. The staff we have can
certainly not be described as excessive, and
I may safely say that there is no one in the
whole office who is not pulling his whole
weight. Many of them, and especially the
higher administrative officers, work early and
late, Sunday and Saturday, and the strain
upon them is very considerable. I would like
to testify my appreciation of the work
which my staff is doing. I would like particularly to refer to the new recruits from
Ulster who have joined our staff. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I think it is very
promising to find that in the recruits I have
got from Ulster in my Department we have
as good men for our Civil Service as could
be obtained anywhere. I beg to move.
Dr. MORRISON: In the absence of any
other person to speak on this matter I desire
to make a few remarks. In the first place
I think an extraordinary amount of work
has been placed on the Minister of Home
Affairs. In addition to looking after justice
and prisons and the other multifarious duties
he has to do he has the whole of the
Local Government Board work to attend
to, and I cannot really perceive how it is
possible for one man to do so unless he has
specially equipped and capable, efficient servants to carry out the work imposed on him.
I think the Minister has met that difficulty
by getting men who are specially qualified.
There are men behind him who are capable
of running the Local Government Board, and
running it more efficiently, in my opinion,
and more cheaply than it was run in Dublin.
There are, as far as I can judge, three or
four departments under him. He has a very
serious responsibility, the most responsible
position I think of any Minister in the
Cabinet. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do
not think if he were not provided with the
capable business men he has behind him it
would be possible for him to carry on the
work as efficiently as he has done. I have
been in and out of his office and have been
brought into contact with him and I gladly
bear testimony to this fact.
With regard to the Minister of Home
Affairs himself, the fact that he stands in
the front rank at this crisis in our history,
that practically his office is responsible for
dealing with all the criminals in the community-and God knows they are very
numerous and very active-brings naturally
on him criticism-criticism that is very often
ill-considered, and, in my opinion, very unjust. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) My
opinion may not carry much weight, because
as I told the House on an earlier occasion
the public do not always take you at your
own estimate. I have laboured under that
disability all my life, but I venture to give
this opinion, and at least I hope that the
public do not consider I am altogether a
fool, that in this matter of the way our
Home Minister is looking after the serious
affairs that come before him he has displayed
grit and determination. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Any man in Ulster, especially
in Unionist circles, who thinks that he is
weak or timid or hesitating is making a very
huge mistake. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I venture to make this prophecy, that if he
is supported as I think he will be by this
Committee he will be able to put down crime
and restore normal conditions in the Six
Counties. I have no doubt whatever about
that being the result.
There is another matter, and I am a little
bit timid about beginning it. In this report
which he has submitted he has made reference to work done under the Local Government Act, and he has made reference to
inspectors. I take it I am in order in offering
some criticism with regard to this matter.
I take the two medical inspectors who repre
sent the Local Government. What amazes
me in connection with the figures I see here
is that those two medical inspectors start
at the modest salary of £500 a year. Now
in the medical profession it has always been
admitted that the man who became a Local

Government Board inspector became a special
dignitary, and the whole medical profession
looked up to him as a man who had gone

not only great emolument but of great

now ask for the very best men that the
medical profession can produce, to do very
important and very serious work, that has
been increased since the Northern Government was been established, by putting
additional duties upon them in connection
with the Prison Board, men who will be
responsible for the administration of the
whole poor-law system of the Six Counties,
men who will have to visit the workhouses,
make long elaborate reports, and occupy
their time in looking after the prisons and
nursing schemes, in looking after the
health and welfare of the people, and all
the other multifarious activities you are
involved in, and you start them at the
modest salary of £500 a year.

I venture to tell the Home Minister that
there is no decent well-qualified young doctor
going to start out on his profession would
think £500 a sufficient salary, and I press
upon him the necessity of reconsidering this
thing, and pay these men something like a
decent salary for the very responsible work
they have to do. You have these two men
with the senior medical inspector doing the
whole work that used to be carried out by
the full staff of the Local Government Board.
They are brought down from Dublin and
placed in the Northern Parliament where
there is practically no promotion, the offices
being SO few, and they are paid
wholly inadequate salary. If the matter is
looked into the Minister of Finance will
surely assist the Minister of Home Affairs,
and some means may be devised to remedy
this matter, which I think, and which the
whole medical profession of Ulster consider,
is a very serious and very grave injustice
and slur on their profession. You have
chaplains here paid £50 a year, and you
start your Local Government Board inspectors at £500. Why, no dispensary doctor
would look up to these men or pay any
attention to them when they find that they
themselves are in a much superior position
as regards salary.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In answer to my
Friend the hon. Member for the University
(Dr. Morrison) I undertake to go into the

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews): The total of this Vote which the
Committee are now called upon to consider
is £552,000 for works for the relief of unemployment in Northern Ireland. It is
made up of three sums. First, £42,000 from
the Lord St. David's grants for relief works in
Northern Ireland approved by the Unemployment Grants Committee in London. Of
this sum £14,000 still remains to be applied
to schemes under the altered conditions to
be approved by the Minister of Labour
in Northern Ireland. The second sum is
the very substantial one of £500,000 which
was obtained under the London agreement,
and the third is £50,000 which you are
asked to grant on behalf of the Northern
Government, making a total of £592,000 in
all. Of this amount £40,000 was voted by
this Committee on the 22nd March last, so
that the total sum which the Committee are
asked to vote is, as I have already said,
£552,000.

I observe that Mr. Devlin in the Imperial

I welcome Mr. Tallents, and I court his

now obtain employment will be very quickly
As regards the £50,000 referred to, I would
like to explain that the Government of
Northern Ireland felt that while so much was

in Belfast and neighbourhood, it would
be unfair to the unemployed throughout the Six Counties that something
should not be done for them. I may
say on behalf of the Government that we
never forget that we are a Government for
the Six Counties and not a Government only
for the City of Belfast. The £50,000, therefore,
which you are asked to vote is for schemes

Personally, I think that the importance of

cannot be over-rated. A great many people
object to National Insurance against unemployment, a great many people carp at what
they call the dole, and have always said,
"Give the people work."

CHURCH TEMPORALITIES FUND
(MONEY).
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to authorise the
Ministry of Finance to dispose of that
portion of the Irish Church Temporalities
Fund, and of the income arising therefrom
belonging to the Government of Northern
Ireland, in such manner with respect to
investment of capital moneys and the ap
propriation of income to the Exchequer as
may be determined by an Act of the present
Session."
I think on this resolution it is only
necessary to give a very short outline
of what is contemplated by the Measure.
Under Section 31 of the Government
of Ireland Act it was provided that
the Irish Church Temporalities Fund should
belong to, and be apportioned as between
Northern and Southern Ireland, that its
apportionment should be carried out by the
Joint Exchequer Board, and that the Church
portion of the fund should be managed,
administered and disposed of by the two
Parliaments of the Northern and Southern
areas. As a result of this Section the Joint
Exchequer Board have already considered the
question and they have decided on a provisional apportionment of the money as
between the North and South, and in order
to enable our Government to appropriate the
proceeds of this Fund it will be necessary
that legislation should ensue to that end.
Therefore, the Bill which I have mentioned
will be introduced. The income from this
Fund, I may say shortly, is derivable from
accumulation in the past as well as from
the original capital, and also from redemption of some of these charges.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE: I propose
to circulate to-morrow a Bill to be known
as the Church Temporalities Fund Bill. As
this measure will be concerned solely with
the disposition of moneys it is necessary
that as a prelude there should be the necessary money resolutions, which have now
reached the Committee stage. I propose on
the Second reading of the Bill which it is
intended to introduce, to go into, with
fulness, the incidence and history
of the Church Temporalities Fund, but
some
This money is almost all derived from land,
and this land was the property of the then
Established Church which disappeared, I
believe, in 1869. So far as charges on
the Fund are concerned I do not desire to
go into them in detail because they will be
produced when the Bill relating to the matter
is submitted, but I may mention that
£10,000 which the Queen's University receives is earmarked upon that Fund. A large
proportion of the National Teachers' Pension
Fund is also derivable from it, and the
Department of Agriculture receives a terminable grant from that Fund. Therefore, it
is necessary that the Northern Government,
which is now the custodian and in effect the
owner of this Fund should by legislation be
placed in a position to administer it in the
same way that it was administered before
by the Commissioners. This means that all
moneys, no matter from what source they
are derived, must find their way into the
central Exchequer, and that all outgoings
therefore must necessarily come under the
control of this Parliament. The great
advantage of that position is this-that no
possible payment of any kind can be made
without the knowledge of this House. I think
that short explanation is all that is necessary
on this stage of the resolution. I beg to
move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolved: "That it is expedient to authorise a charge upon moneys provided by
Parliament of all such sums as may be required in respect of any existing charges on
the Irish Church Temporalities Fund."-
(Mr. Pollock.)

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
Naturally the House will understand that
I have had no private notice that this matter
would be raised, but I fully realise the great

in the position. I wish to weigh well any

One reason why I refrained yesterday from
making a statement, as it is generally called,
at the beginning of the sitting of the House

upon what is taking place at the moment
in the South. I felt, and Ministers of the

that with fuller information-to put it

In dealing with this serious railway situation, I may say that what I hope will be a
satisfactory arrangement is being come to
with regard to what is known as the Belleek
salient, and, if the experiment which we are
endeavouring to apply to the Belleek salient
proves successful, it may be possible to try
the same scheme with regard to that portion
of the county to which my two hon. Friends
have referred. But, there is one answer that
I may make emphatically, and that is, that
if any attempt is made to interfere in such
a way as was suggested by my hon. Friend,
the Member for Derry (Mr. Mark), with the
transferring of goods inside our own area,
exactly the same prompt measures will be
taken as were taken when the Free Staters
or Republicans invaded Ulster territory.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There can be
no doubt whatever about that. Wherever
there is a direct challenge of that kind to
the authorities of Northern Ireland, then
Northern Ireland will reply at once. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I hope at the same
time that saner counsels may prevail. The
result of the elections in the South and West
at all events indicates one thing, and that
is, that the general body of the people want
peace. Whatever other lessons may be learned
from the elections, they mean that the general
body of opinion in the South and West, like
that of the North, wants peace, and if the
leaders therefore are desirous of properly
interpreting the voice of the people of the
South, it may lead to peace. At that result,
of course, we here in the North will rejoice
with everybody else throughout the country,
and if peace does come then some of the
problems will be solved for us without our
taking any action whatever. That type of
solution of the problems of course will be
much more agreeable to our Government
than any other solution. But, at the same
time, do not let there be any mistake. The
determination of this Government is to deal,
as they have done before, with the problems
as they crop up. I give this message of

UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF GRANTS, AD-
MINISTRATION.
1. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of

Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) to

£500,000 Relief Grant, and whether he will

of this grant?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have read the official report of
the question put to the Secretary of State
for the Colonies by the hon. Member for
West Belfast, who, I regret to say, was
quite misinformed as to the facts. I would
refer the hon. Member to the statement which
I made yesterday when moving the estimate
for this grant.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
is my right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) aware
that these people are placed in a very high
and unique position in view of the fact that
the amount of this £500,000 allocated to them
places them in exactly the same position as
ex-Service men? I see no reason for complaint by the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) but on the contrary.
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not know to whom
the hon. Member (Mr. Donald) refers as
"these people."
Mr. DONALD: The question arises out of

Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member must

CONDITIONS GOVERNING GRANTS.
2. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of Labour
if any applications have been received from
the various County Councils for a portion
of the £50,000 granted by the Northern
Government to relieve unemployment through.
out the Six Counties, and if he will explain
the conditions of the grant?
Mr. ANDREWS: The grant of £50,000 for
the relief of unemployment in Northern Ire
land outside Belfast and neighbourhood has
been provisionally allocated to the six County
Councils in Northern Ireland, to the Borough
of Londonderry and to certain Urban
Councils, due regard being paid to those areas
which are bearing the heaviest burden of
unemployment. I am glad to inform the
hon. Member that almost all of the local
authorities are co-operating in a publicspirited manner. The toal cost of the Relief
Schemes which have been sanctioned under
the grant is about £33,000 up to date. The
total amount to be spent on wages is about
£16,000, and the total subsidy from the grant
is about £9,000.
With regard to the second part of the hon.
Member's question, the conditions governing
this grant are in the main the same as those
governing the £500,000 grant, namely, schemes
are subsidised to the extent of 50 per cent.
of the wages of unemployed men who are
engaged on revenue-producing works, and
60 per cent. in the case of non-revenue producing works; all labour must be engaged
through the local Employment Exchange in
order to ensure that preference is given to
ex-Service men and expelled workers, with
priority to those who have been longest unemployed and who have the largest families.
The wages to be paid to all men employed
on unskilled work will be the local authority's
rate for such work, and skilled workers will
be paid the current Trade Union rate of
the district.
FLAX AND HEMP TRADE BOARD.
3. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of Labour
if he has decided to abolish the Trade
Board in the flax and hemp trade?
Mr. ANDREWS: On June 12th I published
in the Press an announcement of my intention
to make a Special Order withdrawing the
flax and hemp trade in Northern Ireland
from the operation of the Trade Boards Acts.
Objections to this course may be lodged
during the period of 40 days from June 12th
and any such objections will be considered in
the manner prescribed by statute. I took this
step in consequence of an agreement reached
between representatives of the Flax Spinners'
Association and the Trade Unions concerned.
The agreement provides for the recognition
of the principal of collective negotiations
and for the constitution of a joint body to
deal with general questions affecting wages
and working conditions in the trade. It also
contains an agreement as to a reduction of
wages and stabilises the reduced wages until

the end of this year. Further, it contains
some valuable provisions relating to the
future settlement of industrial conditions in
the trade.
The request for the withdrawal is very
properly accompanied by a statement that
it is without prejudice to the policy of the
Government as a result of whatever report
may be made by the Advisory Committee
on Trade Boards which is at present sitting
and which, I hope, will very shortly report.

December, 1918. It should be stated, however,
that all Societies which were certified by the
valuers as having disposable surpluses at
that date have adopted schemes for the distribution of those surpluses in additional
benefits to their members. The Northern
Ireland Societies, like Societies in Great
Britain, have also undertaken to relieve the
Exchequer of financial responsibility for the
cost of medical certification until the end
of 1923, and I propose to introduce a Bill
this Session to give effect to this arrangement.
I am prepared to give every consideration
to any representations such as that of the
Portadown Chamber of Commerce with regard to the finances and administration of
the National Health Insurance Scheme, and
I will not overlook the holding, at the proper
time, of any investigation which may be
necessary. But it should be recognised that
the initial years of the National Health
Insurance scheme were abnormal owing to
the conditions created by the war, and until
the financial results are dislosed at the next
valuation, which will begin next year, it
is not possible to speak with any degree of
confidence of the experience of the Societies
under normal conditions.
Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of that reply,
I would like to ask the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Andrews) if he recognises that that is
root and branch condemnation of an Act
which is costing us £500,000 a year, and
which has been in force for practically
twelve years?
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not at all admit that
is is condemnation of the Act in question.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) On the contrary, as I think I have pointed out, owing
to the abnormal conditions through which
we have been passing we have not a sound
basis to go on to say whether things are
right or whether they are wrong. As far
as we know they are right, but I would like
to point out that I think a great deal of
the criticism directed against this Act is due
to misunderstanding. Only a portion of these
surplus assets are available for additional
benefits, and the Societies acting in Northern
Ireland are all paying additional benefits at
the present time. I have interviewed on
several occasions representatives of these
Societies, and I think their spirit is satisfactory and they are anxious to do what is
right and fair in connection with the matter.
TUBERCULOSIS SECTION, ADMINIS-
TRATION.
5. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Labour how much of the £50,000 granted
yearly to County Committees who administer
the Tuberculosis Section of the National
Insurance Act in Northern Ireland is spent
with the object of preventing infection from
Tuberculosis, or of enabling the people to
protect themselves and their children from
this disease.
Mr. ANDREWS: The sum which is available out of the National Health Insurance
Fund for County and County Borough Insurance Committees in Northern Ireland to
enable them to carry out their powers and
duties in connection with Tuberculosis is
about £18,000 a year. The main use which
is made of this money is the provision of
treatment in Sanatoria and in other suitable
ways for insured persons suffering from this
terrible disease, and this treatment in itself
tends to protect the public from infection.
In addition, Committees have discretionary
powers to spend money on the education of
the public by measures designed to prevent
the spread of the disease, and I am glad to
say that, thanks, I believe, to my hon.
Friend's influence, the Londonderry County
Committee has done useful work in this
direction. I may say that the whole question
is engaging my attention at the present time.
Dr. MORRISON: I beg to give the Minister
of Labour notice that I will raise this question
on the motion for adjournment.

ESTIMATES, 1922-1923.
The PRIME MINISTER: I have asked my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance
to be kind enough to allow me as the head
of the Government to move this motion in
the Committee to-day as a special tribute
to the memory of our late colleague, Mr.
Twaddell. I should say that immediately the
sad news reached my ears that this foul
assassination had taken place I communicated
with the bereaved widow, expressing
the deep regret and sorrow of all Members
of the Government, and at the same time
I said to her that there was no way in which
the Prime Minister, the Cabinet, or the
Government could express their sympathy
except by offering to her what is tantamount
to a State funeral. Broken with grief she
and the other members of our late colleague's
family acknowledged at once the right, I may
say, as well as the privilege of his old colleagues, to pay him this last respect, and
they were kind enough in the midst of their
grief to acquiesce in the proposal.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
CLASS I, No. II.
PUBLIC FUNERAL OF MR. TWADDELL.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £130 be
granted to His Majesty to defray the
expense of the public funeral of the late
Mr. W. J. Twaddell, a Member of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland."
This is one of those instances where the
Government cannot at once ask for permission.
but I felt at the time I would be voicing the
sentiments of all the Members if I took on
myself the responsibility of incurring this
small charge, not only on behalf of the
Government but on behalf of the whole of
Ulster. It is not necessary to make a long
speech to the Committee. It is true that the
first horror of this dastardly outrage may
have passed way, but the memories of Ulster
people are long, and I am sure there is not
a Member of this first House of Parliament
of Ulster who will ever forget the tragic end
that met our dear friend who has departed.
I do not think any further words are necessary in moving that this sum be granted
as a tribute to the memory of our old colleague. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
OBJECTS OF ESTIMATES.
STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I think it would be convenient if
I made a short explanatory statement upon
the general character of the Estimates and
Supplementary Estimates, which I understand are in circulation and probably in
the hands of all hon. Members. These Estimates are very largely of a formal character,
and they are directed to attain several
objects. The first object in view, although not
necessarily the most important, is to regularise the whole accountancy system or arrange-
Supply-
Criminal Injuries.
22 JUNE 1922
ments between the Imperial authority and
ourselves. The second object, and also one
of some importance, is to distribute the
different liabilities from the Ministry of
Finance to their appropriate departments;
and the third, which I am sure hon. Members
will agree is not less important than any
other object to be attained, is to enable hon.
Members to be fully seized of the various
financial transactions and activities of the
Province.
As regards the first, that is to say, the
harmonising of the accountancy system of
the Imperial Treasury and our own, I think
I can recall that in my Budget statement I
dwelt at some length on the extreme perplexity of the financial movements that took
place as between the Imperial Treasury and
ourselves. The Imperial authority makes
payments direct and on its own, but they
ultimately reach us by way of deduction
from the revenue which that authority collects,
matters such as customs, excise, income tax,
etc. Then again they have to arrange with
our Ministry of Finance to act as agents
in regard to expenditure on buildings and
their maintenance for which they are liable.
Again, they ask us to meet expenditure for
which we are liable, but for which initially
under the Act they are primarily responsible.
An example of this is the case of certain County
Court Officers. Then again we have to undertake our own expenditure direct, which is the
simplest operation of all. But all these
things taken together will convey to hon.
Members' minds the great difficulty and complexity of the arrangements necessary to
harmonise all these matters and to bring
them before Parliament, so that all hon.
Members will be in a position to grasp fully
the nature of every financial transaction-no
matter of what character-how large it may
be, or how infinitesimal it may be. Everything must appear here before Parliament,
and hon. Members are brought into direct
relation to them.
supervision which naturally will develop

with stationery requisites without charge. In
our case it distributes its material over the
whole of the various departments of the Government, but charges each department with the
cost of the stationery it requires, and these

differ in our arrangements from the methods
adopted by the Imperial Parliament in respect of this department, and

one, however, that I think it is convenient

for ex-Servicemen. The position of that
matter is this. A sum of £600,000 was
provided by the Imperial Parliament to cover
their liability in regard to these houses for
soldiers and sailors for the whole of Ireland.
But a difficulty has arisen in regard to the
apportionment of this amount as between
Northern and Southern Ireland. Our claim
is that the apportionment should be made
in proportion to the number of ex-Servicemen
who joined up from Northern Ireland-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear) and not upon the
basis of population. The ratio of population
is 28 per cent. for Northern Ireland, and the
Chief Secretary, who has purview of this
matter, proposes to allocate that £600,000 in
the proportion of 28 per cent. and 71 per
cent. We resent that apportionment, and
although we are proposing, through the
machinery of the Home Office, to carry out
this arrangement with the Imperial authority
and prosecute the scheme for the erection
of houses for ex-Servicemen, the whole matter
is still sub judice and under discussion, and
I can assure the House it will not be for
want of any effort on our part if we do not
succeed in securing a larger proportion for
Northern Ireland.
There are other agency matters of a somewhat complicated nature which I think can
be better explained when we reach the Estimate involved matters relating to Clerks of
the Crown and Peace, County Court Officers,
Resident Magistrates, and such like, but I
think I have indicated sufficiently the general
nature of these Estimates which I propose to
submit without detaining the House any

will, therefore, when you call upon me, deal

The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps it will
be for the convenience of the House if I
took charge of this particular Vote as I
probably know more about how we came to
arrange this than any other Member of the
Government. My right hon. Friend and
were faced with the fact that very large
sums of money were being demanded in our
Six-County area in connection with the
criminal loss that was sustained in all
quarters by the murders and burnings that
had been going on. An arrangement was
come to by the Imperial Government with
the Provisional Government in Southern
Ireland to set up a Commission to inquire
into all the cases which had arisen there
where compensation might be claimed, and
the suggestion was thrown out that we here
in Northern Ireland should also have a
Commission to sit and inquire into all the
claims that had been made with a view to
the same amelioration being got out of the
Imperial Exchequer. I pointed out at once
to the Government that the difference between
Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland was
this: that our Courts were running; that
claims for malicious injury were all being
tried by the County Court Judges throughout
the length and breadth of our area, and
that these claims, therefore, had already been
the subject of the most meticulous inquiry
before a decree was given, and consequently
we were in a position to know exactly where
we stood for the period for which this particular grant was made. I argued also with
the Chancellor of the Exchequer in Great
Britain that the horrors that filled pages of
our daily papers were quite sufficient without
having a re-hash of all these sordid happenings which had taken place during the
period to which these Votes refer, and to
have a Commission sitting, and going back.
for instance, to the terrible murder of
Inspector Swanzy at Lisburn, recalling in
one's mind the horrible details, and all being
served up for the relatives and friends, and
also for those in whose midst these terrible
crimes were committed, was not, in my
opinion, a very suitable arrangement to make
when the passions of the people were sufficiently high. Therefore, after very close
consultation with my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance, we both came to the
conclusion that it would be better to take
a hard and fast sum from the Imperial
Government something approximating to
two-thirds of the whole of the claims-than
to have a Commission sitting and inquiring
into them and in the end perhaps not dealing
so generously with us as we have been dealt
with under this grant. At all events, two
moieties of £750,000 are to be paid. One
moiety has already been lodged to my right
hon. Friend's credit which he is now prepared to dispense with in accordance with
the claims put in by the Local Authorities,

823 Assassination of Sir H. Wilson. HoUSE OF COMMONS. Statement by Prime Minister 824
Assassination of Sir Henry Wilson.
STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to move
that the House do now adjourn. I have
to break sad news to the House. Field-
Marshal Sir Henry Wilson has been
murdered. (Hon. Members: Shame, shame.)
I am sure this young
Parliament of
ours is getting many a sad task to
perform. Sir Henry Wilson has laid down his
life for Ulster. Of that we have no doubt
whatever. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) A
short time ago, as is in the memory of the
House, I had occasion to ask his assistance in
our hour of trial, and trouble, and difficulty,
and his answer was very characteristic-no hesitation,
He said,
no thought necessary.
"You need hardly have asked me. Now that
you have, all that I can do for you shall be
done for the cause of my country." (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I believe the acceptance of that request has cost him his life, and
I am sure he would not have it otherwise.
A more gallant or a finer soldier never stepped.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). To his widow,
we as a House tender our profound and
deeply-felt sympathy. The news has only just
come through. I have barely heard it myself.
There are no details. There is no doubt Sir
Henry has been murdered and assassinated.
He has laid down his life just when he was
emerging after a long term of service to the
Empire and to the country that he loved, looking forward as many men would have looked
forward after escaping an honourable death
upon the battlefield-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear)--to some relaxation, some quiet, some
peace, after all the arduous work he had performed. That has been denied him. He has
been called away. I suppose he was one of our
greatest men. It has often been said that
Ulster has produced men who have lived in
her very midst who were an honour to their
country, to their Empire, and yet their greatness was not recognised by the people among
whom they lived. And that may be true to
some extent, or may have been true, with
regard to the gallant Field-Marshal up to a
short time ago. I do not believe that the people
of Ulster appreciated what a great man he was
till he retired from the Army-I should not
say retired, for a Field-Marshal never retires
from the Army, but from active service with
the Military Forces of the Crown. His name
is really a monument amongst the whole of
the countries of Europe. They recognised in
him a great man, and they knew that towards
the winning of the War no single person lent
so much as our late comrade and friend,
Field-Marshal Sir Henry Wilson.
I have counted him a close personal friend
He was most lovable
for many years.
a
character, and the people of Belfast had a
deep reverence for him. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Strange to say, one of the last
letters that passed between him and myself
was with regard to the seat rendered vacant
by the death of Mr. Twaddell. The Committee, through our Chief Whip, asked me to
communicate with him to say how honoured
they would be if he would allow his name
to go forward as the standard-bearer of the
Loyalists in that division. He was unable to
do so. He felt that his work lay more in giving advice to us on military matters, and ad-
Imvice to the Government in London on
perial matters. I mention the incident to
show that here in this great city of Belfast
his marked qualities were appreciated by the
He is one more
people. They loved him.
stalwart fallen in this desperate battle which
we are fighting. But it will make no differ-
(Hon.
ence to any man in this Assembly.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. DONALD: We will carry on.
The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend
the Member for the East Division says we
will carry on. We will carry on more vigorously. We have now the death of Mr.
Twaddell and the death of the Field-Marshal
always before us. Guiding lights they will
always be to us-the one in a humble capacity, lovable, the other in a higher position,
equally lovable. They have been carried
away. I am sure everyone in this House will
think it would be ill-fitting for me to say any
more on the subject. I have hardly recovered
from the terrible shock, and I am sure the
House will not like to proceed with any further business. Even had we had the news
earlier in the day, I would have proposed an
adjournment, but it has come in at the end
of the day's work. It is all very sad. I feared
when I spoke last of the loss of our late
Member (Mr. Twaddell) that he would not be
the last to be taken away from us. The realisation of that fear has come sooner than I
expected. I know that my colleagues feel with
me, that the situation has become additionally
grave, and it should now be clear even to
those men who through prejudice have had
blinded eyes with regard to our position, or
through ignorance have failed to understand
it, that this foul murder which has taken
place in London proves beyond all further
argument that there is a wide conspiracy
against those who are fighting the battle of
Ulster.
I do hope and trust that there will be no
further doubt in the mind of any man that
what Ulster is engaged in is a battle not for
Ulster alone, but for the Empire, and if any
thing is needed to steel the nerves and hearts
of Ulster people it is the fact that they are
battling not for a selfish cause but for one
825 Assassination of Sir H. Wilson.
22 JUNE 1922
which affects the whole of the people of the
great Empire to which they are proud to belong.
I have just had the following further particulars handed to me:-
"Field-Marshal Sir Henry Wilson was
returning from unveiling a Memorial to
War heroes at the Great Eastern Railway
Depot, where he wound up a moving speech
by quoting from Kipling's "Recessional,"
and he was approaching his house in Eaton
Place when two men approached and fired
three shots, all taking effect. The crowd
rushed at the attackers, who fired again,
Statement by Prime Minister. 826
two policemen being wounded. One of the
assailants, seeing he could not escape,
turned the weapon on himself and was taken
to hospital badly wounded. His accomplice
was captured."
I have nothing further to say, except once
more on behalf of this House to tender to the
widow, whom I personally count as a friend,
the deepest sympathy of the Parliament of
Northern Ireland.

MAILS FOR BELLEEK-PETTIGO DIS-
TRICT.
1. Mr. MARK (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Minister of Commerce if he is aware that the
people residing in the Belleek-Pettigo district
have received no mails for at least a fortnight; whether these mails are accumulating
at Omagh, and by whose orders the mails are
held there, and if he will have an inquiry
instituted into the matter?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
M'Keown): I am aware that there was a sus
pension of deliveries of letters from the
Belleek, Letter and Pettigo Post Offices for
about a fortnight from the 1st of June owing
to the stoppage of trains from Omagh and the
The
military operations in the district.
mails were necessarily held by the Postal
Authorities at Omagh until arrangements
could be made for their delivery.
The control of the Postal Services in Northern Ireland remains in the hands of the
Imperial Government. On the matter being
brought to the notice of my Department,
however, representations were made immediately to the Postal Authorities, and I am informed by those authorities that instructions
were given to the Postmaster, Omagh, to
make immediate arrangements for correspondence addressed to places within the Northern Ireland area, and hitherto delivered
from Pettigo Post Office, to be delivered from
an adjacent office within the Northern area
pending the re-opening of the Pettigo office,
and that arrangements were also made for
the delivery of correspondence addressed to
Belleek and Letter. I now understand that
the Pettigo office has been re-opened within
the past few days.
REGISTRATION OF GOVERNMENT
MOTOR CARS.
2. Mr. MARK (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether the Government has recently purchased a large fleet
of motor cars, which are being used without
registered numbers, and without paying taxes
in the counties in which they are being used,

of affairs remedied?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Government has recently
received a large number of motor cars which

3. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of

what is his remuneration, and does he supersede the Coroners? Also, in view of the fact
that there are already efficient Coroners for

of public money?
or
a
Sir DAWSON BATES: There has not been
made any permanent appointment as Officer
to hold inquiries in lieu of Coroners' inquests.
A Solicitor
Barrister has been
appointed to hold inquiries in a few cases in
which the circumstances were such as to
render it undesirable to ask either juries or
the local Coroner to act.
For instance, in the cases of the recent
murders near Newry, it was considered it
would not be right in the turmoil of local
feeling to ask either the local Coroner or a
Jury to act.
The professional gentleman appointed will
be paid £10 10s for each inquiry, but his fee
is limited to this sum where the inquiry is
into more than one death at the same time
and place.
When the nature of the duty, and the
circumstances in which it is performed are
considered, as well as the fact that there are
frequently adjournments, and that more
than one day's work is necessary, it will be
seen that the fee is not excessive.
It is essential to secure the services of a
gentleman whose qualifications are beyond
dispute.
Each case is carefully considered in all its
aspects. including that of economy, and it
is only in exceptional cases that the Special
Inquiry is ordered. In all other cases the
ordinary inquests are held. The Coroners
have not been superseded.
The policy of holding these Special
Inquiries was adopted by Parliament a
couple of months ago, and it is this policy
which is being carried out.
It must be remembered that before the
passing of the Civil Authorities Act, Military
Inquiries were generally held in similar

Order for Second reading read.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw): My right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs, who has so many
pressing duties to attend to, has asked me
to take charge of this measure, and I consider in the circumstances it is a pleasure
as well as a duty to relieve him of any of
the heavy burdens that are on his shoulders
at the present moment. The primary object
of the Bill is to abolish Proportional Representation so far as it affects Local Government. Till a short time ago only a few
who might be styled political philosophers
knew anything of what was meant by Pro-
Second Reading.


portional Representation. Yet the principle
is not a present-day invention. In his work
on Representative Government," John
Stuart Mill, whose life was spent in trying
to reduce mental and political problems to
hard and fast laws, discussed the theory which
had been promulgated some time before
by a gentleman called Mr. Haire. The conclusion of John Stuart Mill with regard to
Proportional Representation was that in no
other way which it seems possible to suggest
would Parliament be so certain of containing
the elite of the country. Of course
he was there speaking of the Parliamentary
representation, and I think that hon. Members should appreciate the compliment that
they are chosen after the best fashion on
which political science could form a theory.
Notwithstanding the great authority of Mill,
the system of Proportional Representation
remained a theory till modern democracy
came into contact with the constituency of
Sligo Sligo has a very unique political
history. It has proved something of a
stumbling-block to those who believe in the
infallibility of the collective wisdom of the
people. Long ago it was disfranchised in
the Imperial Parliament for corruption and
bribery. Afterwards, when the Household
Franchise was introduced in Local Government, Sligo remained true to its traditions,
and held the palm for wasteful and inefficient administration, giving a lead that
was followed later by Poplar. The result
of this was that bankruptcy stared the
Council of Sligo in the face, and something
had to be done. The Government in power
shirked any course that would suggest a
doubt on the theory that all Irishmen were
fit for self-government. Something had to
be done, and someone suggested Proportional
Representation. The suggestion was adopted
and we had a typical instance of the old
maxim:
Fiat experimentum in corpore vili."
It was said that the result was good, and
that some respectable men got elected, whereas, it could not well have been worse than
it was before, and under any system of
government the probability is that a better
Council would have been returned for Sligo.
The doctrinaires who had been promulgating
this theory regarded it as a panacea for
all the evils of the State, and they proceeded
to fresh achievements. The new franchise
had just been introduced by the Imperial
Parliament which would apply to Local
Government, and even the most firm believer
in majorities was somewhat afraid of what
might happen in Ireland. The proposal
was made to apply the system of
Proportional Representation that had turned
out, as they said, well in Sligo to all Irish
self-government, and the Local Government
Act of 1919 was accordingly passed. It was
intended to give an opportunity to moderate
men to take part in the business of Local

results of the 1920 election reduced the
Dublin Corporation to something worse than
it ever was before, and it had the same
effect in the constituencies in Southern
Ireland. At the previous election the local
authorities had been bad, but those which
were elected under Proportional Representation were worse. You may remember that
after these various new bodies were elected
all through Southern Ireland, they defied
the law. The Local Government Board,
as it had practiced before, tried again to
reduce them to something like order, but
it did not press the matter to anything like
a serious head, and the result was that local
government broke down all through Southern Ireland-and that was with the local
bodies which had been elected under this
system of Proportional Representation.
In the North we did not fare so badly,
but I think anyone who has had experience
of it will say that most of the electors
and candidates-successful and unsuccessfuldisliked the system, which by its complication lent itself to manipulations by clever
electioneering agents. It was not generally
understood, and the House will remember
that lectures had to be given all through
the country by those who were qualified to
instruct the various officials as to how its
administration should be managed.
As a
result, the percentage of voters who went
to the polls, except in the counties of Tyrone,
Fermanagh and Derry, was very small
indeed. The areas were so unwieldy that the
candidate was frequently not known in the
parts distant from his residence. The
theories about the electors welcoming the
best known public men were falsified very
largely in practice as the candidate who
provided the largest number of motor cars
and had the most pressing canvass got the
Number 1 preference. Comparisons are
invidious, but I think there are few who
will contend that even in the North the
local bodies elected under Proportional Representation were an improvement on their
predecessors. You will remember that a
few of them in some parts of the Northern
area defied the law and have been suspended
by our own Government. There can be no
doubt as to the experience of the last
Parliamentary election. Hardly anyone
wants the system to be continued. All of
us who have gone through the mill-and
we all have successfully-know how deeprooted the aversion to Proportional Representation is. The English Lord Chancellor
after the late Southern elections has been
very loud in his encomiums of the system,
but his observations have been from a
distance. I hope he will have cause to
retain his complacent admiration when he
has had experience of the mental and moral
equipment of the Members of the Southern
Parliament who are chosen under the system
which has been regarded as the panacea for
all the ills of the Commonwealth. It has
been found more costly both to the candidates and the ratepayers. I am informed
on good authority that the elections under
Proportional Representation have cost two
or three times as much as under the old
system. The elections themselves are cumbersome, and they often lend themselves to
freakish incidents and results.

There are three points that were very ably
and eloquently made by my hon. Friend the
Chairman of Ways and Means in the Imperial House, and the first was, if I recollect aright, there was no mandate for
this change, the second was that several

from the Parliamentary point of view it
gives us much too large a constituency. I
agree with my hon. and learned Friend that
it is essential in order to get work well done
the representative, whether he be in Parliament, in the Corporation, the Board of
Guardians, or any public body, should really
know his constituency well and that his
constituency should know him if that were
possible. When there are four members or
more for a constituency, the question is,
how are the constituents to visit the sins
on any member, or how are they to appraise
or give him credit? You get hopelessly
mixed up. You do away with the control
that the constituents have over the members,
and in that way you weaken public life.
For that reason I am glad that in this
Bill we are going back to the old principle.
I think the old principle worked very well.
I know theorists can work out all sorts of

Mr. DONALD: My object in rising to say
a few words on this Bill is that I do not
wish to give a silent vote on this important
matter. I have a strong objection to the
bringing in of this Bill. It has been rather
rushed. Since I was elected in 1918 the
boundaries were altered. I have a strong
objection to Clause 2. Now, here we are in
the course of two or three years beginning
again to cut and carve up our boundaries
and to set up a Commission which will
necessarily involve expense. This is not the
time to incur expense in our city or the
Six Counties. This is a majority Bill. That
majority is fully represented in this House.
Where do the minority come in? There is
no minority represented in this House. I
am not a convert to proportional representation. It is a very cumbersome measure, but
I do contend that it gives minority representation. I think it would have been quite
time enough to bring in a Bill of this
description say in two years from now,
seeing that we all agreed when before the
electors twelve months ago that we would
repeal the Proportional Representation Act
in the course of three years. But here is a
Bill presented now to alter our boundaries.
Then in the course of two years a further
Bill will be brought in, causing unnecessary
expense, to take up again this very question.
We have a group in this House, and I think
in all fairness the minority should have
representation.

Local Government Bill. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Supply.
[Mr. Megaw]
It gives power to the Home Ministry, when
it is required, to fix boundaries. There is
no suggestion that Belfast is going to be
divided straightway into wards different
from those that exist at present. All that
the Bill provides is that the Ministry of
Home Affairs may from time to time make
orders dividing a borough, urban district or
town into wards. That does not mean that
everything is in the melting pot,
and that there will be a new division
of Belfast now. There will necessarily
ble divisions of places that have
been fixed under the Act of 1919, where
very large areas were fixed for the purposes
of Proportional Representation, but that will
not affect the question of existing wards. No
doubt one or two wards that were put together for the purposes of Proportional
Representation will be interfered with. The
hon. Member also suggested that this measure was being introduced in some way as
against the Labour party.
Mr. DONALD: No.
Mr. MEGAW: He is entirely mistaken-
Mr. DONALD: I did not put it that way.
I said that it was certainly against the
minority getting representation. I had in
my mind that hon. Members (when they
were supporting this Bill, were afraid of that
minority, the Labour Party. I said that I
was like Lord Carson-I was not afraid of
the Labour party.
Mr. MEGAW: This Bill has nothing to
do with the Labour party. As a matter of
fact the Labour party through its Central
Council at the quarterly meeting in Portadown, having delegates from Larne, Lurgan,
Comber, Newtownards, Londonderry and
Belfast, passed a resolution calling for this
measure that is introduced here to-day, so
that it cannot be suggested that this is in
any way antagonistic to the Labour party.
As to the statement that it will mean
additional expenditure, how would it cause
expense? I rather think my opening statement cannot be controverted that elections
under Proportional Representation cost two
or three times as much as they would under
the ordinary system with which we are all
familiar.
So far as the hon. Member for Down (Mr.
Lavery) is concerned, I think the points

will be taken into consideration, and if there
is any general desire for it, we can see if
the thing can be done in Committee. At any
rate we are open to consider the question.

(1) The Ministry of Agriculture for

being made in the prescribed manner, at
the prescribed time, and on compliance
with the prescribed conditions as to inspection and examination, grant to the

form in respect of the bull and also, if so
requested, a certified copy thereof on payment of such fee (not exceeding five
shillings) as may be prescribed:
Provided that the Ministry may refuse
to grant a licence or may suspend or revoke
a licence in respect of a bull if it appears
to the Ministry that the bull-
(a) is calculated to beget defective or
inferior progeny.
(b) is affected with any contagious or
infectious disease;
(c) is affected with any other disease or
defect prescribed as a disease or defect rendering the bull unsuitable for
breeding purposes;
(d) has proved to be inadequately prolific; or
(e) is of a breed or type unsuitable for
the district in which it is kept, and
is not a pure-bred bull belonging exclusively to a single individual and
kept for the service of cows belonging
exclusively to him.

fee (not exceed two shillings and sixpence)
as may be prescribed, and in compliance

owner of a bull intended to be fattened
off for slaughter a permit authorising the
keeping of the bull for such period and
subject to such conditions as may be specified in the permit, but the permit shall not
be transferable from one person to another.

Clause 3 (Transfer and Production
Licence or Permit).
(1) If a bull in respect of which a
licence is in force is sold, leased or hired
out for a period exceeding one month, or
if the ownership of the bull is otherwise
changed, the licence may, on application
to the Ministry, be transferred to the new
owner by endorsement of the licence or
otherwise, but unless so transferred a
licence shall cease to be in force at the
expiration of one month after the change
of ownership.
(2) A licence granted under this Act or
certified copy thereof shall be produced at
the time of or before the service of a cow
by the bull, if so required by the owner
or person in charge of the cow.
A licence or certified copy thereof or permit granted under this Act shall be
produced at any time, if so required by
an officer of the Ministry or a police officer
or any person authorised by the Ministry
under this Act.
If the person for the time being in
charge of or having control of the bull
fails to produce the licence, certified copy,
or permit when so required, he, or the
owner of the bull if the failure is due to
the default of the owner, shall be liable

exceeding five pounds.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 27th June, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
DISEASES OF ANIMALS ACT.
Mr. MILLER (by private notice) asked the
Minister of Agriculture who is the authority
at ports in Northern Ireland under the
Diseases of Animals Act to grant licences for
the export and import of live stock?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): By Order in Council of the 1st
of April last the powers of the Department
of Agriculture, Dublin, which would have
gone to the Council of Ireland became
exerciseable in Northern Ireland by the Chief
Secretary or his agent. At the request of
the Chief Secretary I agreed that my Department should act as agent for him under
Section 63 of the Government of Ireland
Act, and he had the following telegram sent
to each of the Veterinary Officers whom he
placed at my disposal:-
"Chief Secretary desires me to inform
you that he has appointed Ministry of
Agriculture for Northern Ireland as his
agent for purposes of administration of
Diseases of Animals in Northern Ireland,
and you should, therefore, comply with all
instructions received from the Ministry of
Agriculture for Northern Ireland relative
to the administration of those Acts in
Northern Ireland."
All officers so notified have been retained
by me and no officers except those employed
by the Ministry of Agriculture have authority to issue licences for Northern Ireland.

MINISTRY OF LABOUR.
Motion made and Question proposed:

as
we
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I feel that it will hardly be
necessary for me to occupy the time of
the Committee for more than a very few
minutes in explaining these Supplementary
Estimates 1 and 3, which I have the honour
to bring before the Committee this afternoon. As the two Estimates are very closely
interlaced, with the permission of the Committee, I would prefer that my explanatory
statement should cover both Estimates. The
effect of the new Unemployment Insurance
(Northern Ireland) Act, 1922, which was
passed by this House a few weeks ago
following legislation of a similar kind in
the Imperial House, made the dependants
grants scheme for the time a part of the
unemployment scheme. The Dependants'
Grant scheme would have ended on the 7th
of May last, but I have said
extended it by introducing certain clauses in
the last Unemployment Insurance Act to
enable it to be continued, and I am sure
that hon. Members will agree that we took
the proper course in doing so as it made
the benefits payable more closely approximate to the needs of the unemployed
beneficiaries than heretofore. The State
contribution for this scheme for the period
to the 7th May was included in the original
Estimate. The additional amount of £98,050
now asked for covers the remainder of the
present financial year. Opportunity was
also taken in our Bill, as in the Imperial
Bill, to raise the contribution from the
Unemployment Insurance Fund to the State
towards administrative expenses from onetenth of the income of the Fund as heretofore
to one-eighth. The estimated additional
amount to be paid over under this head for
1922-23 is £45,930.
1922-23.
The net financial effect of the Supplementary Estimates for both Votes is that Ulster
is asked to spend £2,000 on the Exchanges
and to contribute an additional sum of
£98,050 towards the Unemployment Fund.
The total of these two items is £100,050.
After the appropriation in aid of administration, amounting to £45,930, is paid
over there will be left a net additional
charge to the State of £54,120. I would
like to Say in reference to Class 3,
No. 1, that we found most of the
Exchanges in Northern Ireland in a
very disgraceful state. They were unkept,
unfurnished, and one of them in particular
was a veritable deathtrap in the case of
fire. It was absolutely necessary that we
should start immediately to put these Exchanges into a condition which will allow
the work to be carried on efficiently, economically and safely, and we think that when
we have spent this £2,000 upon the Exchanges
we will not have spent a larger sum than
was absolutely necessary. You will see that
it is really under this head, £10, that the

Mr. DONALD: Are we to have no explanation with regard to these Votes?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I thought that perhaps hon. Members would
understand that this was an extremely unfavourable moment to raise the question of
the expenses of the Special Constabulary.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) After all, the
Special Constabulary is to a very large
extent, if not wholly, paid by the British
Government, and unless an hon. Member
has some very specific question to raise regarding the Special Constabulary I think it
would be more fitting if this House allowed
the Vote to go through without discussion.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There is more
than one reason for that line of conduct at
the moment. I am sure the House desires
to help the Government in every possible
in these anxious times, and I am perway
fectly certain that in the autumn when this
whole matter is taken under review an
opportunity will be given to hon. Members
to discuss it. It would be more feasible to
do it then than to-day.
Mr. DONALD: Does that apply to the
Secret Service?
The PRIME MINISTER: It applies equally
to the Secret Service.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 28th June, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions
UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour if a person who is in receipt of unemployment benefit, and who is arrested and
remanded for seven weeks and eventually discharged, is deprived of unemployment benefit
for the period above mentioned?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Unemployment Insurance Acts
provide that benefit is not payable to anyone
whilst he is an inmate of a public institution,
such as a prison, and is maintained at the
public expense.
I assume that the case which my hon.
Friend has in mind is that of a person who is
detained in custody during remand If this
is not so, or my hon. Friend is aware of any
other particulars relating to the case in question which appear to take it outside the statutory conditions, by which, of course, I am
bound, I will give it the most careful consideration on his sending me all the facts, and
will submit it to the Umpire if it is a case
requiring his decision.
PAYMENT OF MEMBERS.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Prime Minister
whether the Government will now consider the
question of payment of Members of Parliament?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I presume that the House, as a whole, is in
favour of the principle of the payment of
Members. (Hon. Members: "No, no," and
"Hear, hear."). In the circumstances, then,
I think the best procedure for the Government is to put down a Resolution dealing with
the subject for some day convenient next
week, when the question can be thoroughly
discussed in all its bearings, and if the House
comes to a decision that the principle of the
payment of Members should be established in
this House we can set up a Committee to deal
with the whole matter.

(Mr. Megaw): I beg to move:

I think it will be perhaps for the convenience of this Committee if in moving this
amendment I make a general statement
with regard to the Government's policy
affecting the various amendments which
have been tabled to this Bill. As I stated, in
moving the Second reading, the Government
are anxious to have the assistance of the
House in making the Bill as full and complete as possible, and in rendering it
consonant with the wishes of the various
local bodies. There were certain amendments suggested during the debate on the
Second reading, and the Government have
taken these into consideration. I stated
myself when I was replying to criticisms on
the Second reading that there were certain
of these amendments which the Government
were prepared to accept. Hon. Members
have tabled quite a number of amendments,
and it was felt that perhaps it might be
convenient if some of the Members of the
Government met and discussed as far as
possible these amendments before coming to
this Committee, and try to see that they were
put in the best form possible, and find how
we could accommodate as far as possible our
own proposals to those put forward by hon.
Members. The general effect of what has
been done is this: Some criticisms were
offered with regard to the position of the
Water Commissioners of Belfast, and the
Government was prepared to embody this in
the present Bill. An amendment has been
tabled by an hon. Member (Mr. Lynn) in
regard to this, but the Government has also
an amendment which, I think, will suit all
the requirements of the case, and will meet
the undoubted grievance the Belfast Water
Commissioners would have had if there had
not been some such provision made in this
Bill.
Then, on behalf of the Belfast Corporation,
it was put forward that the old system of
electing councillors and aldermen was preferable to the new, and it appeared to be
generally accepted that a triennial election
was disadvantageous in a good many ways,
and so far as the borough of Belfast itself
was concerned it was quite clear that they
wished to have an annual election in respect
of one-third of the whole number of councillors retiring each year. This has also
been provided for as we have brought
forward an amendment which will put in
force the Belfast Local Act, and leave the
position exactly the same as it was before
the 1919 Act was brought into force. The
same has been done with regard to the
election of aldermen, and I may say here
that, so far as
the urban districts are

We think that would meet the circumstances
of the case instead of the form which has
been set out in the Schedule. I do not
think there is very much more to which
I need refer except a new clause which has
been introduced with regard to the consent
of candidates to serve as members when they
are nominated. Under the orders in force
under the 1919 Act, I understand it was pussible for some very grave malpractices to
occur in the case of nomination of members,
by which any member may be baulked of
standing for the constituency in a rural
district for which he desires to be nominated.
All that is necessary is that some enemy
may put in a nomination paper for him,
and, according to the present rule, he is
bound to stand for the constituency for
which he has been nominated first; so that
all that is really necessary to prevent a man
being chosen for any particular board is to
have him nominated for a place in which
he has no earthly chance of being elected,
and then he is disqualified from standing
for any other constituency in the district.
This Bill provides a remedy for that.
provides that a candidate on being nominated shall consent to his nomination, and
he cannot be nominated without his consent.
I rather think there has been a failure to
deal with one aspect of the case. I think
It
that not only the member but his agent
should have the power to consent to the
nomination, because it may happen that a
man is away for the time being and he
may have an agent, and that agent should
be able to give consent on his behalf. However, that is a matter of detail. The other
point introduced is to save the expense of
useless elections, and to prevent candidates
who have no earthly chance from coming
forward. The same system has been adopted
as in the Parliamentary elections, by which
candidates on being nominated will be
called upon to pay a deposit to the Returning
Officer. The deposit fixed is not large, but
it will prevent a man from standing for a
multiplicity of constituencies. The amount
provided in the amendment of which I have
given notice is a sum of five pounds for
rural and urban district councils, and ten
pounds for county and borough councils.
I am not sure whether that is large enough.
An amendment has been tabled by an hon.
Member by which ten pounds and twentyfive pounds respectively
suggested,
but when the matter comes forward we
will be better able to deal with it.
I think that this covers the general scope
of the amendments. I have mentioned the
amendments that the Government are prepared to accept and the way in which they
are prepared to accept them. I beg to move.

New Clause (Declaration of Allegiance of
Members and Officers of Local Authorities)—
(1) A person elected as a member of a
Local Authority shall be deemed not to
have accepted office, and his office shall
be deemed to be vacant, unless he has,
within the time required by law for
making and subscribing a declaration of
acceptance of office, also made and subscribed the Declaration of Allegiance prescribed in Part III of the Schedule to
this Act.
