profit under or in the gift of the council
of a county, borough, urban or rural
district, Board of Guardians, or Commissioners of a town, shall make and
subscribe the said declaration of Allegiance-
(a) in the case of an officer holding
office at the date of the passing of this
Act, within one month after that
date; or
(b) in the case of an officer appointed
after the passing of this Act, within one
month after his appointment.
No such officer shall enter upon the duties
of his office until he has made and subscribed the said Declaration of Allegiance,
and if an officer fails to make and subscribe the Declaration within the said
month, his appointment shall be void and
of no effect.

The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.

Oral Answers to Questions.
PORT MUCK PIER.
1. Dr. MORRISON (for Mr. Crawford)
asked the Minister of Labour whether he is
aware that Port Muck Pier, Islandmagee, is
in such a bad state of repair that very great
inconvenience is caused to the fishermen, and
whether he will consider the advisability of
granting a portion of the £50,000 under the
Unemployment Scheme for the purpose of
having this Pier repaired.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
GORDON) (for the Minister of Labour): If
the authority responsible for the maintenance
of the Pier at Port Muck will make representations to me on the subject I will give
the matter my sympathetic consideration.
Mr. DONALD: I am very pleased to hear
the reply of my hon. Friend, and I hope that
my hon. Friend who put the question will
see that this matter is carried through. It
is very necessary indeed.
IRISH LAND (PROVISION FOR SAILORS
AND SOLDIERS) ACT.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister for
Home Affairs if he will state whether the
services have yet been transferred from
Dublin for the Irish Land (Provision for
Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919; if so, who
will have charge of the administration of
this Act in Northern Ireland, and whether
every step will be taken to expedite the
building of these houses for ex-Service men.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The administration of the
Irish Land (Provision for Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919, being an Imperial Service,
has been vested in the Irish Office, but
arrangements are being made whereby, so
far as Northern Ireland is concerned, the
Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of
Home Affairs will undertake the administration as an agency service. The Ministry
of Home Affairs will be responsible for
selecting sites, allocation of applicants to
cottages, collection of rents, and other incidental services, while the Ministry of
Finance, acting through their Technical
Officers, will undertake the erection of cottages and work ancillary thereto. Every
possible effort will be made to expedite the
erection of the cottages.

the present Session to make further provision

spect of the amount of the charge to be borne

Mr. BARBOUR: I beg to move the motion
standing on the Paper for to-day's business.
It will be seen that this rather lengthy notice
in the first five lines consists of a mere recitation of the National Health Insurance
Bill which will come up for Second Reading
in the course of a few minutes. The latter
part, reading from "it is expedient" down
to the end is in order to give effect to the
provisions contained in lines Nos. 11, 12 and
13 on page 2 of the National Health Insurance Act. It is briefly an arrangement of
mutual advantage between the Minister ot
Labour and the Approved Societies, whereby
the Ministry of Labour will have the use of
certain funds which are in their own hands
for some time, and in order that when these
sums become eventually repayable to the
Approved Societies the societies may
be
credited with the interest on such sums as
have been utilised by the Ministry of Labour
so that the Approved Societies may be at no
disadvantage in respect of these funds. They
are put exactly in the same position as if
the sum utilised had remained in the fund
and had drawn interest for the whole time.
It has been considered that the amount of
interest to be paid away constitutes an extra
burden on the Exchequer, but on the other
hand it must not be forgotten that the Ministry of Labour has had the use of this money
during that time. What we pay back in
interest only recognises the use of this money
when it was found necessary to take advantage of it.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): The objects and aims of the Church
Temporalities Fund Bill are outlined in the
preface to the measure which I take it is
in the hands of the hon. Members, but I
think it would be of interest, perhaps, if
I sketched in short outline something of
the incidence of the history and of the disposition of this fund. Prior to the year 1869
the incomes of the established Church
of Ireland were derived from lands that had
been originally granted to them by the
British Government. In many cases prior
to or about the year 1820 many of the emoluments of the incumbents were really procured
in kind, that is in the produce of the land,
but after 1820 or so these were all merged
into money equivalents, and from that time
forward the incomes of the incumbents of
the Established Irish Church were derivable
from the rentals on land. When the Church
was disestablished in 1869 the amount of
these rentals was calculated at about
£600,000 a year, and in order to bring into
effect the operation of the measure it was
necessary that the incumbents of the Church
should be bought out.
On an actuarial calculation it was found
that this required a capital sum of about
nine million pounds, and having paid that
sum to the Church authorities, the Government then became the owners of this £600,000
a year which formerly was devoted to the
emoluments of the clergymen. The Government as would ordinarily have been the case
instead of devoting or merging this £600,000
a year into the general funds of the country,
decided to maintain it as an Irish fund applicable to Irish purposes, but during the
period following the disestablishment of the
Church until quite recently the whole character of the fund
became transformed,
because many of the tenants elected to buy
their farms under the Irish Land Acts and
their rentals were therefore turned into
terminable annuities. Others redeemed
their rentals by the payment of capital sums,
and these capital sums were invested by the
Commissioners in Government securities.
The moneys derived from this fund were
mainly contributed to the provision of grants
for agricultural purposes and for education,
and to provision for teachers' pensions,
and perhaps mainly for the relief of distress
which, as hon. Members will recall, was
unfortunately prevalent in different parts
of Southern Ireland. The income from the
Church funds to-day arises from three
different sources, that is the original tithe
charges, the terminable annuities which I
have mentioned, and also yields from investments. So much has the fund been depleted,
however, from the extensive use that was
made of it for the purposes which I have
indicated that not only was the income
entirely used but the capital itself was considerably eaten into, so that at the beginning
of this year when an estimate was made of
the position of the Church Temporalities
Fund it
was found that the total revenue accruing from the Fund was only
£180,000 as distinct from £600,000 at the
time when the incomes of the clergy were
purchased with capital money. But the
charges which are levied or appropriated to
this income amount to about £184,000. So
that in handing it over as provided for by
the Act Irish Governments got something
of a barren legacy. The charges at the beginning of this year were-£39,000 for contributions to teachers' pensions, the Congested Districts Board absorbed £41,000, the
Queen's University Grant, our own University, £10,000; the National University,
£10,000; agriculture, which is a grant
terminating in 1930, I presume, concurrently with many of the annuities, amounted
to £70,000; management expenses, £11,000,
purchase of small life annuities, £3,000-making a total of £184,000 charged against the
Fund. The Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
transferred this Fund to the two Irish Governments. The form of the transfer is embodied in the 31st Section of the Act, which
reads as follows:-
The Irish Church Temporalities Fund
shall belong to and be apportioned between
the Governments of Southern Ireland and
Northern Ireland in such manner as may
be determined by the Joint Exchequer
Board, and the parts apportioned to the
several Governments shall be managed,
administered, and disposed of as directed
by Act of the appropriate Parliament:
"Provided that all existing charges on
that Fund shall, if and so far as not paid,
be paid out of the Exchequer of the United
Kingdom, and be made good by means of
deductions from the Irish residuary share
of reserved taxes in accordance with regulations made by the Treasury."
It will thus be seen that this revenue of
£180,000 will be apportioned by the Joint
Exchequer Board in such sums as they in
their judgment consider each area is entitled
to. Provisional apportionment has already
been made with a view to meeting the
charges that are assessed against it, and as
you will see from the wording of the clause
which I have just read, that unless we, the
Government of Northern Ireland, pay the
portion of charges which are levied against
Northern Ireland, it will be competent for

Second Reading.
National Health Insurance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): When the National Health Insurance Act was first brought into operation
in 1911 it was proposed that the Government
grants should assist the cost of benefits and
administration. It was not then the intention of the Government further to subsidise
the Funds to any greater extent out of the
public moneys. After the scheme had been
working for some time it was found that
there were further expenses which would
have to be incurred and which were not
originally contemplated.
In Ireland, as you are aware, there are
no medical benefits by way of medical attendance, but the Government decided to bear
the cost of medical evidence of incapacity
in connection with claims for sickness benefit, which meant that an insured person
could obtain a certificate free of charge
which entitled him to sickness benefit from
his Approved Society. This meant a burden
on the Northern Exchequer to the extent
of £28,000 per annum.
But the axe is now being laid at the root
of the spending Departments, and in the
interests of economy in the public service
it has been necessary for the State to reconsider its attitude towards this supplementary grant. We are anxious to achieve
economies without inflicting undue hardship
on either the Approved Society or the contributor. The question naturally arises-
How are these economies to be effected?
There are only three methods of doing this:
I. By reducing benefits-which would not,
for a moment, be considered.
II. By increasing contributions, as suggested by the Geddes Committee. This would
meet with such a storm of opposition, both
from the employer and employee, that we
are not anxious to carry that recommendation into effect.
III. By using, for a temporary period to
meet the difficulty, some of the very large
surplus funds the Societies have been able
to accumulate during the years of the war.
And it is this third method that we have
decided to adopt and which we have embodied
in the Bill that we have presented for
Second reading. The Approved Societies in
England were opposed to increasing the contributions by placing a further impost on
both sections of contributors, and suggested
voluntarily that out of their reserve funds
they were prepared to shoulder this responsibility for a limited period.
When we saw the generous attitude of
the Consultative Committee of the Approved
Societies in England, my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Labour for Northern Ireland,
took counsel with the Consultative Committee
in the North and frankly stated the position
-that we were desirous of promoting a
similar Bill in the Northern House of Commons, and what support might we expect to
receive from the Approved Societies. I am
glad to say they met us in the same magnanimous and generous manner with which
the English Societies met the Minister in the
Imperial Parliament, and their action was
subsequently endorsed by the North of Ireland Association of Approved Societies which
operate in Northern Ireland. When this
Bill was going through Committee stages
in the Imperial Parliament it met with some
opposition from Members representing the
interests of Approved Societies.
As a result of negotiations a compromise
was effected, whereby one-third of the funds
required is to be drawn from the Central
Fund and two-thirds from the funds of the
Societies. The Central Fund is a pool fund
made up of deductions from the weekly contributions of Employers and Insured persons
and reinforced by a yearly contribution from
the State. This contribution ceased as from
January, 1921, when the fund then stood at
£2,000,000. So that this colossal fund is well
able to bear the demand made upon it for
a temporary period. It was brought into
being and under the control of the Joint
Committee to assist any Approved Society
showing a deficiency not due to mal-administration.
The result of the arrangement is that
the cost of certification will be met as
follows:-two-ninths will be undertaken by
the State-but taken from the funds I have
referred to and the remaining seven-ninths
will be borne as follows:--two-thirds from
the funds of the societies and one-third from
the Central Fund. I should here explain,
lest there may be some misapprehension
on the part of those of the societies connected with and having their head offices in
the North of Ireland, that the two-ninths
which we purpose taking from the two funds
as the State's proportion will be returned
after the next valuation and interest will
be paid on the sums borrowed and the State
Grant will be allowed on such interest. The
last valuation of Approved Societies which
was carried out and ended on 31st December,
1918, revealed the fact that they were carrying
forward huge surpluses, due largely
the war.
to

I know there is an upward tendency in
sickness. There is a lower condition of
physical efficiency due to prolonged unemployment. And I know that these reserves
which the societies have built up for benefits
will be required to meet the ever-increasing
claims as a result of the present abnormal
conditions.
Clause II of this Bill arises out of the
present severe conditions of unemployment.
When an insured contributor is unemployed
for a considerable period-and I regret to say
many are suffering from this disability-he
gets into arrears under National Health
Insurance. Ordinarily an insured contributor who had less than 17 contributions
to his credit was not entitled to any benefits
during the succeeding benefit year. A large
number of persons are in that position
and as a consequence would not be entitled
to draw from the Benefit Fund of their
society. This constitutes a very serious
hardship we desire to avoid. Last year,
societies regarded all members who were
unemployed for prolonged periods owing to
trade depression as having 26 contributions
to their credit and paid them benefits accordingly. This liability was met out of
the funds of the society, and they are again
faced with this serious position, which we
are, and I think properly so, dealing with.
Having undertaken voluntarily one financial burden, we desire to relieve them of the
burden of added expense which would confront them if they again undertook to credit
contributions to their unemployed members.
The Act of 1918 deals with the question of
unclaimed contributions, which is a constantly growing fund, and we desire to take
power by Clause II to place at our disposal
these unclaimed contributions and to make
payments to Approved Societies which will
enable them to pay benefits to those not
entitled through unemployment. This fund
represents the difference between receipts
from the sale of stamps and the contributions represented by cards surrendered by
insured persons.
I think there could be no better purpose
for which this money could be used than by
devoting it to keep the unemployed man and
woman within the Act and I have every
reason to believe you will assist us in passing
this extremely useful Act of Parliament. I
beg to move.

Health Insurance Bill-
Second Reading.
29 JUNE 1922
The Act means to the Northern area an
expenditure of £550,000 a year. It is a tax
on capital, it is a tax on labour, and it is a
tax on the overburdened ratepayers of this
community. Look at the huge sums of money
which they have in their reserves. The
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Labour (Mr. Gordon) has applied the term
"huge reserves," and he proposes to take
out of these huge reserves a certain sum to
qualify our workers so that they will not be
shut out from the benefits of the Act by
unemployment. When the Act was passed
the State ordered that no unemployed should
pay contribtions under the Act, and I think
the Insurance Societies-as they took any
advantage which accrued to them under the
Act-should take responsibility for any liability, especially when they have huge sums
which they have extracted from the people,
unnecessary sums which were lying to their
credit in Government funds. When the Act
was passed the contribution was 4d, and even
under that huge sums accumulated, as the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Labour has said. For some mysterious reason
the contribution has increased to 8d. I never
could understand why, if these accumulations
existed, it was necessary to double the contributions from the employer and the insured.
Then you come to the administration of
these huge sums. Each of these friendly
societies is managed by a committee. That
committee disposes of these large surpluses
as they think wise. I state here, and I
defy contradiction, that ninety per cent., or
possibly ninety-five per cent., of the members
of these insurance societies are not consulted
and know nothing about how these vast
surpluses are disposed of. You have a little
group of men representing the different
societies who meet, and, without let or
hindrance from anybody, except the nominal
interference of the Commissioners, or my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews), they dispose of these profits.
It is a little oligarchy who take advantage
of this Act and who disburse these huge
profits in whatever way meets with their
approval. I admit they have to secure the
approval of the Minister of Labour, but does
any man think that, if the members of any
insurance society had an opportunity of expressing their minds on this question, they
would allow fancy schemes, such as convalescent homes and other white elephants to
be developed by these societies? Would they
allow them to spend money, which has been
contributed out of their hardly-won earnings,
on schemes like that instead of it going
directly to the benefit of the insured? I
would like the Minister of Labour to take
this matter in hand. He has a large business
experience and he radiates geniality, and he
is always armed with a disarming smile, but
if he is coming to deal with this oligarchy
I beg of him-

Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: That
the Bill be now read a Second Time. (Mr.
Barbour.)
Mr. BARBOUR: As this is, I think, only the
second measure of its kind that this House
has been asked to pass, I might refer in a
word or two to the Parliamentary procedure
by which the expenditure and the finances of
Northern Ireland are controlled. Hon. Members, will, of course, be aware that the first
introduction of expenditure to them consists
in the presentation of the Estimates of the
costs of the services for the following year.
These are presented to the House, and then
are considered generally in matters of principle and policy which the Government wishes
to put into force. They then go to the Committee of Supply, where the nature of the
services is carefully considered and also the
cost of providing those services. They then
pass to the Committee of Ways and Means,
which, in its turn, recommends that the
amount of money required to provide these
services should be placed at the disposal of
the Ministry of Finance, and then in order to
give statutory effect to the recommendations
of Committee of Supply and Ways and
Means it is necessary to pass an Act of Parlia
ment enabling the necessary drafts to be
made on the Exchequer of Northern Ireland
in order to provide for these services. And
that is the effect of the Act of which I now
beg to move Second Reading. It will be
known that the amounts referred to in this
Act have already been before this House and
been sanctioned by the Committe of Ways and
Means, and the first paragraph is what might
be called the Consolidated Fund portion of
the measure. It authorises the Ministry of
Finance to issue from the Consolidated Fund
the sum of £7,321,211. If hon. Members will
refer for the moment to the third page of the
Act they will see that the total expenditure
for the year amounts to £9,346,629. Consolidated Fund Acts have already been passed in
respect of the first two items, and consequently
all that you are asked to authorise in the
present Act is the remaining sum which I
have just mentioned. Then there is a further
clause, Clause 2, authorises the Ministry of
Finance to borrow on the credit of this sum
any sum not exceeding £4,000,000. I hope
hon. Members will not take alarm at this in
any way. They must realise that the flow of
revenue into the Exchequer does not necessarily keep pace with the flow of money out
of the Exchequer, and that while the expenditure for the year may balance the income, it
may mean that that income may come in later
than this expenditure, and until it overtakes
the expenditure it may be necessary to borrow
certain sums of money. In England, I understand, it is usual to take powers in the Consolidated Fund Act to borrow up to the entire
income for the year, but we have not thought
it necessary to take powers for more than the
sums stated. In fact I think it is very unlikely that we shall utilise that power to any
great extent. Further sections of this clause
of the Act provide for the repayment of these
sums of money should it be necessary to borrow. And then the third Clause is what is
called the Appropriation Act. Although you
may vote this in one sum it does not mean
that you place all this money in bulk at the
disposal of the Ministry of Finance. What
you are doing is to vote specifically to each
service the amount of money set opposite that
service in Schedule B, Part 2. It means that
the Ministry of Finance is entitled to expend
a sum not exceeding the amount set opposite
each service as given in that Schedule. And
so the total sum which you are asked to vote
is appropriated to each particular service.
As these matters have already been before the
House so frequently in different stages, I
think it is unnecessary for me to say any more
on the present occasion. I beg to move.

It is necessary to move this slight amendment, which is a purely technical one, and
which, of course, does not involve any extra
demands on the funds of the Northern
Parliament. It appears that the Parliamentary interpretation of the term "receipts
appropriated in aid" implies sums received
from outside sources. I can illustrate that
from the Stationery Department, where sums
are received from the sale of the "Belfast
Gazette," or in the case of the Home
Office where certain sums are realised
by the sale of work done in prisons.
This amendment is now necessary in
order to make the working of this clause
conform to the practice and form of accounts
which has been followed in framing the
Estimates. It will be necessary to extend
the meaning of this term so as to include
also under the heading Receipts Appropriated in Aid" the inter-departmental
credits which are gained by those branches
rendering services to other departments. It
is to extend the meaning of this phrase
that I move this addition to the clause.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT (NORTHERN

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."
(Captain Dixcn.)
Mr. DONALD: I want at this juncture to
draw attention to one or two matters of
urgent importance. The House rises to-day
till Tuesday, October 10. That is a very
long period, and we will not have another
opportunity of bringing these matters before
the House. I want, in the first place, to
protest most strongly against the Bill which
has just been passed, the Local Government
Bill. It certainly did not meet with the
approval of all the hon. Members of this
House, and it certainly does not meet with
the approval of the democracy of the Six
Counties. An amendment was tabled in the
Senate to Clause 2 in regard to the raising
of the deposit from ten pounds to twenty-five
pounds. There is a very strong feeling on
this subject. I was at a meeting on Saturday, and that meeting was unanimously
against not only this clause but all the other
clauses of this Bill. Although hon. Members
may congratulate themselves on the passing
of this Bill, I may tell them straight that
they will not congratulate themselves after
the elections take place. I consider that this
Bill has been rushed through this House just
too quickly, and not with the will of the
people. I have an idea that it is to meet certain demands. It certainly does not meet with
my approval, and I take very strong exception to the Bill, which will be known in the
future as the "Coercion Act." That is all
I wish to say with regard to that matter. I
am simply voicing the opinion of the working
classes when I bring the matter forward.
The next point to which I want to draw
the attention of the Prime Minister is the
administration of this relief money, this
£500,000. There is a very strong feeling with
regard to its administration. My right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) says that some 700 odd
people have been employed. Now I want to
tell him that not a solitary worker who was
in a munition works during the war is
getting a job under this relief scheme. Being
in a similar position to these men myself
I consider that we were serving our country
during the war equally with a great many
who joined up. They come to me time and
again to protest. The shipyard workers have
been worst hit during this trying period, and
I do not see any prospect of betterment in
the shipbuilding for some twelve months to
come. I consider it is a very great hardship. No doubt we all agree that ex-Service
men should get the preference-married men
-but I say they have no right to turn away
men who served their country as munition
workers during the war. Only the other
day one of those men came to me and told
me that he had been out of work for eleven
months. He served his country during the
war in what is called the Merchant Service
-in a dummy ship. He showed me an eviction notice, which he had received because
he is not able to pay the ten pounds of his
rent which is owing. I considered that that
man should get some temporary relief, or
should get employment. I sent him to the
Labour Exchange, and the manager there said
he did not come under the category of ex-Service men. We are adjourning now for a long
period, and I want my right hon. Friend
(Sir James Craig) to note that I am not
taking up any hostile attitude, but am acting
really for the benefit of the people. We
have a very large sum of money. I think
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) said he
already had opened up something like 27
schemes. I made the suggestion here that
there are other schemes which could be
opened up, and which would give these very
men employment. I was in conversation
with a gentleman the other day, and he drew
my attention to a very serious matter, namely
the Belfast ferries. These ferries are not
capable of carrying the people who crcss
even in normal times. I think it is the duty
of the Government to get into touch with
the local authorities, and let us get better
ferries for the convenience of the people.
Now is the time to build them so as to give
these men employment. I merely throw out
the suggestion to my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews). He has got quite a lot of money,
and I think this would be a very productive
scheme. He could pay, say, fifty per cent.
towards wages for the building of more upto-date ferries. It may be said that this
matter is not acute. I was speaking to a
shipbuilder only the other day, and he said
he got a fright, for the simple reason that
the people rushed into these little boats and
before they got to the other side they were
in six inches of water. I know exactly the
reserve buoyancy of these little boats, and
are we going to wait until two or three hundred people are drowned before we take the
matter up? I think it is a very necessary
question, and now is the time to bring it
forward so as to secure a more up-to-date
method of conveying people across the river.

[Mr. Donald]
When His Gracious Majesty opened this
Parliament he said it would be the duty of
this Parliament to furnish such an example
of wise and just government as would inspire
the confidence of the people throughout the
country, and ensure a brighter future for the
great masses of the industrial workers. Certainly, some of the sloppy legislation which
is passing through here is not for the benefit
of the people. I want to protest most
strongly against this kind of legislation.
Even the Health Insurance Bill is not
through the Imperial House yet, and we were
told we were going to get better conditions
for our people. The other House gave the
thing serious consideration with regard to
the question of medical benefits, and how we
would stand with regard to contributions,
and so forth. The Bill has only been amended and put to the Third reading this week
in the Imperial House. I contend that we
would have fared far better with regard to
the Six Counties in the Imperial House than
we are doing here under this measure,
because I know we would have had the
unanimous support of two-thirds of the
representatives in the Imperial House to put
us on a similar basis, a matter in which
we have been in arrears for many years
now. This is another matter on which the
workers feel most strongly, and yet here
we are with a Government of our own and
they are not trying to bring us up to the
limit. This is not a democratic House,
remember. My right hon. Friend told me
on Thursday, when I withdrew my motion
with regard to the payment of Members,
that he was indebted to me for facilitating
the business. We sat on Friday for something like two minutes, and now we are
adjourning till October. I have no doubt
we require the rest.

THE PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT.
The PRIME MINISTER: I would like to
answer point by point the matters to which
my hon. Friend has referred, and of which,
I am sorry to say, he has not given us
any notice.
I think, considering the work
of the House during this past Session, it
was somewhat ungracious of my hon. Friend
to talk about "sloppy legislation”—(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-because I can only
say from my own point of view, and from
that of those who have been busily engaged
in the preparation of these Bills, that the
greatest care was exercised in their draughtsmanship, and the House gave to each of them
the deliberation which they deserved. At
all events, my hon. Friend (Mr. Donald) is
somewhat at fault when he uses so strong an
expression considering that there never has
been any limit placed by the Government on
the period which this House might sit. The
business has gone through the normal course,
and everybody has had an opportunity of
discussing the various measures from time
to time. May I make-if it is necessary
for me to do so-two points against my hon.
Mr. DONALD: I said I opposed the Bill.
I oppose it still. No doubt when the amendment was put down and moved here the
Government would have been very pleased
if I had taken exception, because there was
a very strong feeling after the House rose
about accepting that amendment even by
the Government.
The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend
(Mr Donald) will have to bear in mind that
when Proportional Representation was first
threshed out in the Imperial House of Commons he, along with all our colleagues there,
was very much opposed to it, and it seems to
me a very strange thing that, after all the
attempts which have been made in the Imperial House to protect our interests by
doing away with Proportional Representation, my hon. Friend (Mr. Donald) should
come here and take an entirely different tone.
I cannot think what has changed his mind
considering that the Government was pressed
by no less than fifty-nine local authorities
in the Six Counties to bring forward this
Bill as quickly as possible. It was in order
to meet what we might consider the unanimous desire of the democracy of the Six
Counties that this Bill was brought forward.
Mr. DONALD: Not at all.
The PRIME MINISTER: I may say that
when the Act of 1920 was going through the
Imperial House of Commons this question
of Proportional Representation gave us a
great deal of anxiety-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and I can safely say that every Ulster
Member there was determined that on the
very first opportunity that could be given,
the principle of Proportional Representation
should be swept out of the Bill and that we
should revert to the old-fashioned method
of each candidate having a seat to fight on
a clean issue without going through the expense and tortuous methods of Proportional
Representation. That was the unanimous
desire and unanimous expression of every
Member of the Imperial House, and I think
anyone who looks back on the debates will
discover that we took this attitude from the
beginning to the end, convinced so far as the
South and West were concerned that Proportional Representation would secure no
benefits for loyalists there, and so far as we
are concerned in the North, we would be
prejudiced by having Proportional Representation as part of our electoral system
whether for the Parliament here or for local
Government. So far as I am concerned,
for many years in the past I have been
strongly opposed to the system. I gave
evidence, I think in 1908, at any rate, it was
Local Government Bill. 922

Frederick Cavendish as the chairman, and
from then until now I have been absolutely
convinced that the old-fashioned system is
the better system so far as we are concerned.
Nothing has changed my mind on the subject.
Well, then, my hon. Friend (Mr. Donald)
drew attention to the limit with regard to
the deposit to be made by candidates, and
more or less blamed the Government in some
way for having fixed the limit, whereas it

I feel that I would have preferred my right

I intended to raise this question of National
Health Insurance, and I am not going to
find fault with any legislation passed by
this House. I approach it from a wholly
different standpoint to that of my hon.
Friend (Mr. Donald), who condemned this
House. I approach this question from the
standpoint of a sensible Northern Irishman
who objects to the sloppy legislation forced
on Ulster by the British House of Commons,
and I think I am justified in appealing to
this House for some relief from the injustices
under which we suffer in regard to it. On
two previous occasions I raised this question,
but something intervened to prevent me
discussing it fully. It is a very serious
matter and I am glad to see so many Members
present because it involves a sum of £550,000
and it is very important to see that that
money is economically administered.
On the last occasion on which I addressed
the House on this matter I made two or
three points. The first was that a very important body of business men, the Portadown
Chamber of Commerce, had condemned this
Act. The second point was that £550,000 is
spent in Ulster on this Act, and the third
point was that when we were paying 4d
of a contribution the societies were accumulating huge reserves, and now when we are
contributing 8d the benefits have not risen
in proportion to the increased contribution.
A fourth point was that these huge reserves,
contributed by the workpeople and the employers, were spent by five or six men who
claim to represent the whole body of insured
persons, but who in reality represent nobody
but themselves. A Labour Member in this
House said that the only people who had
profited by this Act, Fo far as he knew,
were the doctors. When the Act was passed
the statutory fee for a certificate under the
registration of Births and Deaths Act was
3/6. This Act compelled dispensary doctors
in Ireland to give certificates once a week
for 2d instead of 3/6. We have 2/- a year
for certification for the insured. That means
that you might have to go six miles, or
twelve miles altogether, and might have to
write 50 certificates in a year and do all the
details of this examination for 2/- a year. If
that is an El Dorado for the doctors a man
is very easily satisfied. But you have here
a Labour Member who says the only persons
he knew of who benefited by this Act are
the doctors. Therefore, I take it he knows

nothing about the benefits Labour receives

large proportion of that £180,000 is paid by

maintain is that the Government has no
control over these societies. Our Labour
Minister may give advice to them to deal
with a particular case as he thinks best, but
he has no power to compel them to adopt
that course. He may supersede them altogether, but that is only done in exceptional
cases. I do not think it ever has been done.
What happens is this, and I would like hon.
Members to take particular notice of it. A
sick person comes to me as a doctor, and I
write a certificate which lasts for a fortnight
or three weeks. Then the society objects,
and they may send a doctor or they may not.
But there is a dispute between the insured
person and the society. How is that settled?
The great bulk of the workers in rural
Ireland know nothing about appeals or the
bye-laws of the society. They do not know
to whom they should go, and I state here
without the slightest scruple or hesitation,
the result is that in 95 per cent. of the cases
the people have no remedy if the decision is
unjust, and they have to submit to the decision of the secretary or doctor of the
society. You may lodge an appeal, and in
that case there is a Court of Arbitration
fixed.
A large number of these appeals are in
connection with small sums of something
like £1 or 30s., and if he lodges an appeal a
poor person has to take his witnesses to
Belfast or some other centre. I think it is
the society who fix the centre, and you spend
probably £5 when at the best you can only
recover something like £1. I could mention
cases showing the result of this procedure,
and that, I think, shows that I have not
been neglectful of the claims of labour
although I am not a labour representative.
I knew a woman in my district who in order
to get her benefit had to make three journeys
to Coleraine, a distance of 60 miles. I wrote
to the National Insurance Commissioners
about it, and said that such a thing would
not be possible in any country outside
Russia. I knew a man who was insured, and
he had a defective eye. I think, perhaps,
he was born with a defective eye. Some
years after he received an injury to the
other eye, and I had him sent to a specialist.
He reported that, the man would never be
able to see sufficiently to enable him to do
his work. Naturally one would have thought
the Insurance Society would have paid disability benefit, but they wrote to the manand I saw the letter-stating that he had
joined under false pretences, that he had
misled them as to the state of his health,
and they asked this blind man to appear in
Derry, 30 miles away, to show reason why
he should not be expelled from the society.
As a matter of fact the man did not go before the society, and he was expelled. I
saw the letter stating that he was expelled,
but so far as I know the society held on to
the money they had got from him. Quite
recently a man who had been insured in one
of these societies came to me. He had paid
into the society for four years, and at the most
he had got four weeks' benefit.
He got ill again, and on an anonymous
letter being sent to the society they, on the
information contained in that anonymous
letter, wrote to this working man asking
how many people he employed. They raised
the point that he was not entitled to be
insured at all. They had got as much as
four years' contributions from him, and
when his wife wrote asking that if he were
not allowed to be insured would they be
kind enough to sent back the money he had
contributed, they sent an explanation that
they were willing enough to pay. I have
in my own employment a maid who came to
my district from Belfast, who was insured
in one of these societies. She came to my
district and she was three months under my
care for gastric ulcer. She got a certificate
from me every week, but she never got a
penny. At the end of three months I wrote
to the Commissioners to see why she did
not get paid her benefit, and then the society
sent down a doctor who found her carrying
an empty tin can and reported her fit for
work. They never paid her a single penny
for all that time. I maintain that these
people have no protection. You may say
what you like and you may raise and produce
excuses, but I maintain that in the country
where these people are illiterate they have
no protection, and I maintain also they are
victimised, and not victimised in any in
dividual case but wholesale. Yesterday a

Coleraine; my abdomen was opened; two
tubes put in and kept in for five weeks;
after eight weeks I came home. I have

of the cases it is impossible to cure it. The
only way in which you can deal with it is by

that is the proper way to educate the people,
and especially the young people who will by
and by be the governing community here,

the considered and unanimous opinion of

maintain we are wasting money in treating
victims while the tubercle bacillus is allowed
a free hand to act as a recruiting sergeant
and to walk unchallenged through our streets
and houses and through our homes with no
attempt being made to prevent it.
Here is a sample of what happened in my
own personal experience. A man suffering
from tuberculosis came from County Down
and went into a cottage and died in that
cottage. A family in my district went into
it. There were seven or eight children and
the parents were healthy on both sides.
They were not more than six weeks in that
house till one of them developed hip-joint
disease, which is one of the forms of tuberculosis. As soon as I heard it I had him
sent to the Cottage Hospital and I told them
to leave the house. They did leave it, but
two of the other children, bright little girls
of eight and nine, took pulmonary consumption and they both died. Then, ultimately,
the father died. That was solely due to
ignorance, culpable ignorance, that should
not exist in any community. Yet it is said
we have Public Health Acts. It is a fact
that we have Public Health Acts, and I am
the Public Health Officer in my own district.
We have no notification of the disease, and
these things are cumbersome. What I beg
is that you do not spend your money in this
reckless, improvident fashion, and that you
should take some particular means of instilling into the young the elementary knowledge that will enable them to protect
themselves and, when they are grown up,
their children. The Minister of Labour is
a very able man, but he has a very stiff
proposition before him and if he cleanses
this Augean stable of the National Health
Insurance Societies and builds up a system
of prevention to wipe out this white scourge
he will enable us to refer to his name with
pride, and coming generations will applaud
it. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The ASSISTANT PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Burn): We have frequently
heard in this House that the Government of
Northern Ireland intend to advance step by
step with the British Government. I. for
one, am indeed very glad to know that such
is the case, especially by this House passing
the Local Government Act. On three occasions in the British House of Commons a
Bill to conduct future elections under the
system of Proportional Representation was
defeated, each time with an increasing
majority. Therefore, by this measure,
which will now do away with elections
under Proportional Representation, we
are coming into line with our friends
on the other side of the channel.
Hon. Members of this House who
are also Members of the Imperial
Parliament will recollect the very
stiff fight that was put up by the Ulster
Party on the Committee stage of the measure
introducing Proportional Representation.
That was due to the fact that in Ireland
no public authority whatever had asked to
have its elections conducted under Proportional Representation. (Hon Members:
Hear, hear.) The claim by those who espouse the cause of Proportional Representation, that it secures the representation of
minorities, is not proved by facts. I take
the City of Belfast as an instance. In Belfast
approximately one-fourth of the population
are Nationalists, and under Proportional
Representation they have only one-sixteenth
of the representation in this House. That
shows at once that Proportional Representation defeats the very end that it is supposed
to attain. I will take one of the divisions of
Belfast as an instance. My hon. Friend who
represents East Belfast in this House (Mr.
Donald) is the Member for the Victoria
Division in the Imperial Parliament. At the
General Election of 1918 my good Friend and
colleague was returned for that division by
an overwhelming majority. I have no doubt
that he believes the result of that election was a true reflex of the opinion of the
people of that constituency. I myself do.
But what happened in the Municipal Elections of 1920, some twelve or eighteen months
later? In the same division a Nationalist
was returned at the head of the poll to serve
in Belfast Corporation. I put it to my hon.
Friend, which of these two elections showed
the true reflex of opinion? My hon. Friend
seems to forget--I am speaking from memory
and am open to correction; I have no desire
to do him any injustice-that in the election
campaign of last year, when he and his three
colleagues were returned to this House, he
assured the electors at every meeting which
he addressed that one of the first things that
would be done would be the introduction of
measure to do away with Proportional
Representation. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

The PRIME MINISTER: I think that all
Members of the House will agree with me
that we meet to-day under more satisfactory
conditions than on any occasion since we
undertook the responsibilities of self-government. Although it is quite impossible to
probe far into the future, and there are so
many unstable elements prevalent in the
country, we do know that since the rising
of the House in the summer there has been
a slow but steady progress towards that end
for which we have been striving, and striving
under the most inauspicious circumstances.
We find ourselves to-day more cheerful at
heart, perhaps, than at any time I can recollect since His Majesty entrusted us with
the government of our own affairs.
The people throughout the Six Counties
have to be, first of all, thanked most
heartily for their co-operation, their steadfastness, and loyalty to the Government of
the day, and I personally must take this
early opportunity of tendering my appreciation of the cordial manner in which each
and every Member of this House has carried
on and assisted and encouraged the people
and shown them their duty through trying
times.
I think it would be advisable for me
to-day, not only for the convenience of Members of this House, but for the convenience
of the public outside, to cast my mind over
the various Departments of State, endeavour
to make some explanation of those matters
which appear still to be misunderstood, if I
may say so, regarding the Government, and
to clear up some of the mis-statements that
have appeared from time to time,
Prime Minister's Statement. 940

Trade depression still continues, as it continues not only here but across the water,
and practically in every country in the

still in a chaotic state. I can only say that,
perhaps, on the whole, if we take the past
few months as some indication of what we
are all hoping and praying for, Ulster, after
all, is not the worst place in the world to
live in at the moment. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

hear).

towus and with the exception of an odd case

I now turn to the general situation, and
although, as I have said in my opening
sentence, we have passed through times of
great anxiety that have taxed the courage
and energy of our own people, the splendid
spirit which animates all sections of the
community has carried us through to the
present position in which we find ourselves.
A word of warning is somewhat necessary
at this stage. Just as the passengers and
the crew on board an Atlantic liner look to
the captain and to his officers in storm and
stress to see them through, not one of them
venturing to interfere with the management
of the ship, so Ulster looks to her leader
and his colleagues in the storm and stress,
whenever it may be, to guide them wisely
With regard to finance, may I turn to my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance
(Mr. Pollock)? Little rumours, little stray
words have reached me about the burden
of debt, about the fear of increased taxation,
even about bankruptcy. There is not one
word of truth in it. There is no debt upon
Ulster whatever, and I see no prospect of
creating any debt. There is no taxation in
Ulster above the taxation of our brothers
in Great Britain. We are all in the same
boat as far as that is concerned, and there
is no intention or suggestion on the part of
the Government to put one penny of extra
taxation upon the people of Northern Ireland, nor is there any necessity for it.
Further than that, last year with all the
heavy expense that fell upon our shoulders
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) not only
balanced his budget but had a small balance
on the right side, and I am as confident
as I was last year that my right hon. Friend
will perform exactly the same miracle
this
year. In other words, in spite

There are very few countries in the world

Therefore, I do hope that some of the criticism with regard to finances in that direction

duties.
With regard to some of the charges that

As to agriculture and commerce, I have
already stated that my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Archdale) is fairly optimistic about

I touch upon commerce I hope I will not
weary the House, but I look upon our
position with regard to trade and commerce
as of far-reaching interest to every man,
woman and child within our borders, and
I cannot too strongly emphasise the importance of conveying to Great Britain, and
especially to her commercial centres and
those of Scotland, that trading with Ulster
is just as safe as trading with Norfolk or
Suffolk or Essex or Kent-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear) or may I say with Glasgow,
Birmingham, Manchester, or with Leeds?
I cannot emphasise too often that we are

Britain, and we might as well talk of Great

may understand that in carrying out contracts with us here in the North they may
rely upon the same commercial integrity and
stability as in the past. And I may say

and the Ulster Association in convincing the
British public that there can be and must
be no

The number of persons registered for employment at the Labour Exchanges and the
branch offices attached on the 10th January
last was 58,410; on the 25th September,
47,596, an improvement of 10,814.

The PRIME MINISTER: For the whole
Six Counties. The number of persons
working systematic short time on 10th January, 1922, was 17,495; on 25th September,

With regard to industrial relations, the
number of disputes since the Appointed
Day has been remarkably small, and those
which have occurred have been quickly
settled. I would like to make comment on
that that I hope all industrial disputes can
be as readily settled, and if my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) were in the position
in some other parts of the United Kingdom
which he occupies here I believe there would
be less industrial troubles in the country.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The railway
position, he tells me, has been giving him

shipyards in Great Britain, work was carried

importance to this industrial centre. The
services of the Department in the conciliation of industrial disputes have been
extended to Londonderry, Coleraine, Ballymena, Lisburn, Newry, and other centres.

the Fund has resulted in the promotion of
schemes to the total value of £104,267. In
addition to this unemployment work, the
House is aware that His Majesty's Office of
Works and the Treasury have given their
sanction to proceed immediately with the
building of our new Parliament House. Of
course, it may be that hon. Members may
think that there has been undue delay. I
can only say that the delay that has taken
place is owing to no shortcomings on our
part. The delay was occasioned by most
cautious investigations in the interests of
the case, the necessity of deciding as to the
foundations, drawing up plans and specifications, and, I presume, taking out
quantities. However, I am glad to say that
this matter has been settled, and the first sod
will shortly be cut, and with all the power
that we command the work shall be in full
swing before the winter fully sets in-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)--in order that every
avenue possible may be made open to pick
up those persons who are in dire distress
owing to unemployment.
My right hon. Friend intimates that the
administration of the Health Insurance
which was taken over on 1st March, 1922,
has been continued on similar lines to those
previously followed in the United Kingdom.
A consultative committee of approved
societies has been set up to advise the
Ministry in close relationship between the
Ministry and the societies in Northern
Ireland. As the schemes of Health and
Unemployment Insurance have been brought
together under one Ministry, it has been
found possible to effect many economies by
the combination of duties of officers, records,
etc. There are about 300,000 insured persons
in Northern Ireland. In a normal year,
under present conditions the contributions
by employers would be about £197,000 and
by employees £180,000, the State paying, in
addition, two-ninths of the cost of the benefits paid out by the societies.
With regard to Advisory Committees, in
order to ensure as far as possible that in
matters of general policy he was acting with
the approval of the community, my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) established Advisory Committees on certain matters. He
had a committee called the Trade Boards
Committee, presided over by Lord Dufferin.
This committee has presented a unanimous
report, and legislative proposals based on
that report will be submitted to you in due
course. The Employment Exchanges and
Unemployment Insurance Committee, presided over by my hon. and gallant Friend,
the Member for Armagh (Major Shillington)
has already presented an interim report recommending the establishment of Local
Employment Committees. It has reached
an advanced stage in its deliberations, and
its final report is expected shortly. The
Advisory Committee on Health Insurance
Approved Societies is a standing committee
under the chairmanship of my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) himself, and it advises him from time to time on matters
affecting the approved societies. The Cost
of Living Committee, under the chairmanship of my hon. and learned Friend, the
Member for the University (Mr. Robb), was
set up to explore the vexed question of the
cost of living in Northern Ireland, and it
has recently, as is well known, begun its
labours. The Belfast Relief Grants Advisory Committee, the constitution of which
is well known to us all, has advised the
Minister in respect of all the schemes to
which I have just referred. The Railway
Commission is under the chairmanship of
the right hon. Mr. Justice Brown, and it is
hoped it will shortly present its report.
Then the Local Employment Committees, to
which I have just referred, are getting under
way, and we will be able to give further

I am glad to be able to say in regard to
this Ministry that, in spite of the vast
amount of work which it has to do, there has
been a considerable economy in administrative expenses. The Ministry is saving
actually on staff as compared with the staff
employed by the Imperial Ministry itself.
The headquarters work is done by a substantially less staff in proportion as a result
of the grouping of several of the services
under one head. The total Employment
Exchange staff when the Ministry of Labour
assumed control on the 1st January was 532.
On the 2nd inst. the figure had dropped to
412, a reduction of 120 in numbers and an
economy in money of approximately £19,000
a year. This reduction is, of course, in
part due to the fall in unemployment, but
the bulk of it is accounted for by the increased amount done by the staff itself, and
by the speeding up and perfection of the
Department. The cost of the Courts of
Referees in the month of January was £886,
giving a yearly rate of £10,632. By the
improvements which have been introduced,
the cost for the month of July fell to £418,
which works out at a yearly rate of £5,016,
a considerable saving in that direction, and
the introduction of the Local Employment
Committees, it is hoped, will obviate the
whole of the charges altogether.
With regard to Health Insurance, an Act
passed last July relieved the State of the
cost of the certification of sickness, saving
some £30,000 per annum, while the Health
Insurance Commission, and a special medical
and legal staff which have hitherto been
considered necessary in Ireland, have been
dispensed with altogether, and this means
a saving to the Department of, roughly,
£10,000 a year. I mention these matters in
some detail in order to show the public
outside that the loose charge of extravagance
in the Departments is unfounded and that
the Departments themselves are slowly but
surely making improvements which save a
considerable sum to the country in various
directions.

was commenced by the Ministry. The wide

Such a measure must involve every other
Ministry, and there must necessarily be an
interval for Cabinet and inter-departmental
discussion before a Bill of this importance
can be brought before Parliament. It is intended, therefore, to introduce the measure
at the earliest possible moment of the next
Session of the New Year. Those who are
clamouring for immediate legislation during
the present Session must be reminded that,
while piecemeal legislation might be possible, only a comprehensive measure
satisfy our educational requirements.
I would like to add also that the Committee
has yet to report further, and that, of
course, it is impossible for the Government
to undertake the task of laying before this
House a Bill of such importance until they
themselves are thoroughly satisfied as far as
human foresight can provide that all the intricate matters are successfully and properly
dealt with, in order that the needs long overdue of education in this part of the country
should be properly undertaken. Therefore, I
trust there will be no undue pressure from
outside, because it would be utterly impossible to tackle the Bill this Session, but we
intend to give it preference and very careful
consideration next Session.

The Home Office have in their purview the
whole administration of the law as far as the
preservation of the peace is concerned. I
would like to take the opportunity of dealing
with our new R.U.C. and Specials. First of
all, may I say that after the most serious
consideration and negotiations with the
British Cabinet
have been able to
carry on our Special Constabulary to the
present time without placing any extra cost
upon the people of Ulster-no small benefit
conferred by the Imperial Authorities upon
us. (Hon. Members, Hear, hear.) Towards
the middle of this year, when the situation
began to show signs of improvement, naturally the Government there and our own
Government here considered whether it would
be possible to effect economy with regard to
the Special Constabulary. We took the whole
matter into our careful consideration, and
consulted the Authorities at Westminster,
and the Cabinet came to the conclusion that
on the whole the present system of Special
Constabulary met the peculiar needs of
Ulster better than any plan that could be
devised at the moment. We have always to
bear in mind the peculiarities of the situation, that our Special Forces are absolutely
necessary for maintaining within our borders
that law and order which is necessary to the
good reputation of our country, and, on the
other hand, we have to remember that these
same forces, in case of any future
aggression firom
the border or
any uprising of our opponents within
the border, are to be ready to
meet every emergency. They are not necessary to meet the smaller emergencies, but it
is necessary that they should meet every and
all the great emergencies. Does anyone
wonder, with the weight of responsibilities
upon my shoulders, that I consulted the late
Field Marshal with regard to the proper way
to work the forces in such channels as to
secure on the one hand a very efficient police
force to my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson
Bates), and on the other hand a very strong,
well organised, striking force to be under the
authority of whoever had to combat an attack
from outside our borders? His advice has
been followed up to the present.

only wish that the future held out hopes to

may be years before we are really settled

to say there is no further use for any organisation to meet an enemy from either without
or within. In securing that Staff I took the
fullest responsibility for saying to those
officers: "We want you. If you come and
help us we cannot ask you to leave your home
and leave your particular profession and to
come on the off chance that we can
keep you for a fortnight or three weeks or
months, and then give you a return ticket
and say, "Thank you very much,' and allow
you to go." No, Sir. The terms I arranged
personally, and for which I take full responsibility, is that that Staff of able advisers
should be employed for the term of one year
to the end of this financial year. At the end
of the financial year our plans, of course, are
modified, and we go ahead in perhaps an
easier manner than we have been able to do
during this distressful year.

I feel it in my bones that in every part

be unnecessary to make any drastic changes

of our military force. One has to keep an

and one has to watch most carefully that
the balance of our power here in Ulster
is not in any way interfered with if
further depletion of the troops takes place.
That is where the power, if I may say so,
of the C1's would immediately come in, and
it is proposed by the Government as far as
possible to go ahead with perfecting the
machinery of the C1 class and bringing it

discipline.
Another point in that connection is this:
It is not good for us to talk too much in
public as to what our plans are, or what is
the size of our Force or organisation. If I
could tell all the story it might be considered
provocative. Provocation does no good at
the present moment when we are endeavouring to secure better relations; it all comes
down to trusting those who have the heavy
burden to carry on their shoulders; and I
venture to say that Ulster will some time recognise what a debt of gratitude she owes to
those officers and gentlemen who at her call
came over here to take in charge what was a
very delicate and difficult duty. They have
performed that duty well; they have tided us
over the most difficult period in our history,
and our thanks are due to them. We may
all rest assured they will meet the requirements of Ulster in a proper way, not only in
the immediate but in the long future. Now,
in announcing that there is no change to be

With regard to one or two other matters,
they may in consequence of time be left to
a later date. In conclusion, I would like to
deal with the situation in the Six Counties
as far as that political element is concerned
which goes to make this House and this
Government serve the people properly. Unless the Loyalists of the Six Counties have
every confidence in the Government and in
their representatives here the same effect
may arise as though we had been beaten by
our enemies. Let there be no mistake about
that. Whilst we welcome all criticism-fair
criticism we always welcome as I have said
at this table-still there must be a pulling
together of all society that wishes well to
this community, so that it may speak with
one united voice in the backing up of the
Ulster Government at the present time, because although we have gone through several
stormy periods does anyone for a moment
think we are over our difficulties? We have
an anxious time before us, and it will require
steady nerve to enable us to surmount those
difficulties as we have overcome difficulties
in the past.
There is a good deal of loose talk about
a want of policy. Has any Government ever
had a more settled policy than the Ulster
Government? That policy is to retain a
Parliament of our own, and not to come
under a Dublin Parliament. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) We have done all that human
ingenuity and courage could do in order to
reach the position in which we stand. That
is our policy to-day, and that will be our
policy so long as I have the honour to stand
at this table. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
There is no Dublin Parliament for us.
Members: Hear, hear.) What man in his
senses would suggest that there should be
anything but the voting out of the Free
State, when that time comes in the near
future? (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That
is the policy of this Government, and it
will be the policy to the end. (Hear, hear.)

Then there is loose talk sometimes about

I can understand how annoying it must be
to the Prime Minister and to his colleagues
to suffer from what might be called backstair criticism. Personally I have never indulged in it. (An hon. Member: Hear, hear.)
When I have had any thing that was nasty

that it is annoying, and that it is not very

Cabinet, that I do think that they are largely
responsible for it themselves, and I will tell
them why. They submit probably too much
to pressure from Members in this House and
from influential people outside, and they
make appointments, and they hope that by

these unnecessary appointments that you
make, for every friend you gain, you are
creating forty enemies. But when these positions fall vacant if you want to retain
friends you will never fill them up at all.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Really I think
the Prime Minister knows that a good deal
of the dissatisfaction is due to people who
wanted something and did not get it. Let
us in this House realise that we are not here
for the purpose of satisfying ourselves or our
own selfish ambition or of putting friends and
relatives into jobs. We are here for the purpose of doing all we can for the good of
Ulster, and if we do that there will be less
of this whispering and grumbling that is
going on. And therefore I suggest to the
Government in order to have an easy lifetime, the best thing they can do is to practise what I advised them to practise at the
beginning economy in the truest sense of
the term.
I am sure everyone will join heartily in the
protest-the dignified protest--that the
Prime Minister made against some of the
happenings in this City during the last few
weeks. We are out to denounce murder, no
matter who the murderer may be. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We are out to say to
the Prime Minister that we expect him and
the Members of his Government, and those
that are under him, to see to it that murder
is stamped out, no matter what the colour of
the murderer may be. We have got to see
to it that this Province of ours is made a
place fit for deceat people to live in. I
would also join with the Prime Minister in
appealing to the general public, who are apt
enough to criticise but are not so ready to
give the help that they ought to give, to
follow the example of those citizens in London and see that the murderers are tracked
down and brought to justice. Until we
arouse the people to a sense of moral responsibility we cannot hope for settled peace in
this City or in this Province. I hope that
the Prime Minister's words will go to the
hearts of all right-thinking men and women
in the Province of Ulster to-day, and that
they will join with the Members of the Government in stamping out what is not only a
pest but a disgrace to this Province. We
want all men of good-will to live in peace,
and we want them to feel that the law is no
respecter of persons. We want men who are
pursuing their ordinary duties, giving offence
to none, to feel that they can hold whatever
religious and political views they like, and
that no one will dare to make them afraid.
The situation is much better, and we congratulate the Government. Whatever
smaller grumblings we have had, and I suppose we shall always have grumblings of
some sort, we do congratulate the Governmont on the success that has attended their
efforts in bringing about peace. I am sure,
so far as this House is concerned, it will
back the Government up in any action it
may take in order to suppress disorder and
to bring peace to this Province.

That represents all I have got to say at
present, though there are quite a lot of
things about which I would desire some further information. One point which struck
me while the Prime Minister was speaking
was that he seemed to be aggrieved at the
idea that anything done by the Cabinet
should be adversely criticised. We would be
a very trusting House indeed if we accepted
all their doings and regarded them as infallible. I cannot adopt that position, and I
do not intend to do so. I shall always claim
the right while I am a Member of this House
to express my dissent from anything with
which I cannot agree, and I will always
adopt that course in this House. I am sorry
I had not the opportunity of saying what I
have said in the presence of the Prime
Minister, who has gone out. I should not
like to be regarded as saying behind his back
what I would not say to his face. Had he
been present I might have said more than I
have said, and uttered it in a more censorious
vein.
Prime Minister alluded to the question of
education, and the hopes of the Government
that early in next Session they would be able
to introduce a measure to deal with it. I am
rather surprised to hear that the Government are in such haste that they are actually
proceeding to incorporate the recommendations of that Committee in a Bill to be introduced to this House at such an early date.
I would have thought that they might have
extended to the House the ordinary courtesy
of allowing hon. Members an opportunity of
discussing the opinions and suggestions contained in the Report. I do not know whether
the Government is prepared to allot a day for
that purpose. I think perhaps it might lead
to the enlightenment of the Government to
some extent in regard to the manner in
which the recommendations of the Lynn
Committee are regarded. In the first place I
want to say that the Report has not earned
the confidence of the people in respect of the
recommendations set forth, because the Committee as constituted is of a very partial
character. I have not a copy of the Interim
Report at hand, but if I had and looked
down it I would find that the Committee contained Ministers, Graduates of the University, business men, and one representative of
Labour in the person of the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant). I have now got a
copy of the Report, but I do not want to
weary the House by reading the names of the
members of the Committee. We have the
Rev. Dr. Bingham, and so forth. I can
find hardly a business man on it. They are
all Graduates and acknowledged literary men
-men in all probability capable of expressing opinions and giving advice upon the
higher reaches of education, but, so far as
I know, they are no more competent to express opinions on Primary Education than
the representatives of Labour, who have been
excluded from the Committee. The Committee is dealing with the interests of the
people in Primary Education. It is their
children who will be going to the Primary
schools, and the expenses in connection with
the contemplated reform will be contributed
to by the taxation of these people. Yet not
a solitary representative of Labour was nominated, with the exception of the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant). I wonder
was he elected in the interests of Labour?
He is a good Labour man, I quite agree-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear) and has performed an
honourable and a noble part in connection
with the Labour movement; but if I am
forced to acknowledge that the hon. Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Grant) is a representative of Labour, I am bound to conclude
that the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Lynn) is there to represent the newspapers.
Mr. GRANT: I would like to take this opportunity of congratulating the Prime
Minister on the speech which he has delivered
to the House this afternoon. To my mind it
is one of the finest and most comprehensive
he has ever delivered, and the manner in
which he referred to the various departments
and went into details should satisfy the most
severe critic. With regard to the question of
temperance I must say I am rather disappointed. I am not an official member of any
temperance party and am unbiassed on this
subject, but I am of opinion that the temperance people were entitled to more kindly
consideration at the hands of the Government. On the question of education I am
rather sorry that I do not agree with my
colleague for North Belfast (Mr. M'Guffin)
in his criticism of the Londonderry Commission. The one reason I can give for my
election on that Committee is that amongst
the Labour representatives I have the

I am disappointed to a certain extent that

I should call him in this House-the hon.

to call him Mr Devlin. Mr. Devlin, to my

constipation, because he has not spoken in
public for a considerable time. The readers
of the Irish News," however, have no
reason to complain, because for years they
have been befogged with columns of the hon.
Gentleman's bombast and nonsense, and they
were very thankful for a little relief. Now,
at this time, when everyone is doing his

ours, it is disappointing that gentlemen like
Mr. Devlin should be going about doing
their best to create trouble. I only hope
that we on our side will not follow their
example, but that we will do our best in
the interests of peace and prosperity.
Dr. MORRISON: I should like to say a
word or two with regard to the speech
of the Prime Minister. Before I refer to
any question he has raised may I express my
dissent from the views put forward by the
hon. Member for Derry (Sir Robert Anderson) and the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn) with regard to the holding up
of the Local Government Act. I think if
you look at this question you will see that
there are two sides to it. It dealt with what
I think is a most mportant matter in connection with this country-the treatment of
minorities. While I approve of the Act-1
voted for it-nevertheless I think it was the
duty of the Imperial Government to hetate, and to weigh the whole question before they sanctioned the repeal of the Act,
which was specially introduced by them with
the object of protecting minorities, both in
the South and in the North. When we consider the fact that any outbreak of disorder
here or in the South is to be met, and the
expense is to be paid for, in large measure
by the Imperial Government, I think it is a
right and proper thing for them to look well
before they sanction an Act which, in their
opinion, might bring about results that are
not to be desired. I do not like this constant
carping at and denunciation of the Coalition Government and of the Prime Minister
of England, and I dissociate myself from it.
With regard to the questions raised by the
Prime Minister, I think the record of the
Government on the whole is good. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) People begin, when
they refer to the Government, in an apologetic strain and explanation, that in spite of
this, that, and the other thing the Government has done very well. I think there is
no need for any qualified apology. I think
the Government from the Prime Minister
down has done remarkably well. There is
one exception, one Department to which I
would like to refer, which perhaps prevents
me from making that statement general. He
referred to the different Departments. There

Bill. That question was in charge of the

the next Session.

should keep its pledges-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and not refer the matter to a Commission, a step which will have the effect of
shelving it. Leave the question to the good
judgment of this House, and I will be satisfied. We are here as the representatives of the
people, and I see no reason for setting up a
Commission of this description. This House
is quite capable of dealing with the problem.
By setting up a Commission the matter will
be deferred till next year. Then you want a
contented people. These people got a promise from the Noble Lord who was the leader
of Ulster previous to my right hon. Friend.
The Noble Lord said this was one of the first
questions he would deal with. I know my
right hon. Friend (the Prime Minister) would
be as anxious to keep that pledge as the
Noble Lord would himself. I see no reason
why Temperance Reform cannot be openly
introduced into this House and dealt with
early next year. That is one of the things
that is causing unrest in the minds of the
people.
I now come to the question of Education.
I cannot understand why the question of
Agriculture being taught in the Primary
Schools has been omitted from the Interim
Report. The Prime Minister himself said

a
that agriculture was one of the greatest industries of the country. I quite agree, but,
if that is so, why are these people not represented on the Education Council, and why is

important Bills passed by the Imperial
House quite recently was a measure known as
the Allotments Bill. We could not have a
finer thing for teaching our people agriculture. Let them have a piece of ground of
their own, let these people go out and learn
to cultivate something to help to keep themselves, instead of depending upon exports
and imports. I think that their time will be
well spent, and that we should follow the
example of the Imperial House by passing an
Allotments Bill.
I take it, it will be well on next year before
we have the Education Bill, which will be a
very comprehensive measure. I agree that it
is necessary, but would my hon. Friend, the
Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministry of
Education, tell me what is to become of the
pensioned teachers, 60 of whom have only
something like £40 a year and under. Twenty
of these people have only £13 a year. They

Bill was brought in. I want my hon. Friend
(Mr. McKeown) to give these poor people some

of living is so high and they have only a mere
pittance to live on.

what is being done by our gallant Special
