men. The men who have already been disbanded have only added to the number of
unemployed. Had this House taken my advice, and the advice of others, when the
Committee presented their report, and reduced the salaries, they could have afforded
to have kept on larger numbers without involving the country in any greater expense.
You were paying them far too much, 70/- per
week, in comparison with the skilled worker
in the workshop.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps my hon.

we took over

Mr. DONALD: I quite appreciate the statement made by the Prime Minister, but this

When I was younger and more energetic

Mr. LAVERY: 1 rise to say a very few

We were all delighted to hear the Prime
Minister say that he is not quite satisfied yet that we are out of the wood.
I was delighted to hear that. I do not think
that we are by any means out of the wood.
The quietness and peace that we are now enjoying is simply because of certain eventualities that are taking place elsewhere. I trust
I may be wrong and entirely a false prophet,
but I am strongly of the opinion that we will
be in this trouble again sooner or later. I
quite agree with the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Donald) with regard to the demobilising of the "A" Specials. I was one
of those who offered an opinion-and I was
afraid perhaps I was wrong then, because I
did not get much support. Eventualities
have proved that I was right-that we were
paying more money to these men than we
could possibly continue to pay, and that if
we had paid less and retained them longer in
our service it would have been very much
better, particularly in times of unemployment
that were threatening twelve months ago. I
was very sorry indeed for many of these men.
They have nothing now to turn their hands to,
no employment, many of them with wives and
families, and the winter coming on. I do not
know whether anything can be done to alleviate the distress of these men who served us
in the past. I hope that if the Minister of
Home Affairs can see his way to do anything
in that direction he will do so, and we will
be very glad.
With regard to another matter, I should
say, I, like the hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Grant) was disappointed that the Prime
Minister made no reference to the wild utterances by Mr. Devlin, which are bound to do
Northern Ireland harm. Probably the Prime
Minister thought it better to pass them by in
contempt. I think some reference should have
been made to them. We allow these things
to pass by. They go to the public all over the
world, and it is impossible to overtake them,
no matter how fast we go, and here we are
not going fast. With all due respect to the
Prime Minister, I think it is a mistake. I
think some reference should be made.
I could scarcely believe my ears to-day when
I heard the Prime Minister say that this
matter of temperance, after all that had been
said and done, was to be relegated to a Royal
Commission. I have had some experience in
my municipal career of what is done by Royal
Commissions. I have no faith in them, absolutely none. It is simply the shelving of this
matter, a matter which should have been
dealt with by the House. We all know the
trouble that the drink traffic is giving. Alas!
whether people have money or not, they
find money for this pernicious evil, and we
are here to legislate and to endeavour to keep
that evil from them, by the three items we
have mentioned, Sunday closing, the spirit
grocery business, and the bona-fide humbug, I
call it. These three items we should deal
with and we should deal with them
ourselves, and not by a Royal Commission. I am not an extremist by any means,
but, at the same time, I am here to see that
justice is done so far as I personally can help,
and I would strongly advise my temperance
friends that if this Royal Commission is appointed we should take some other steps, if
it is at all possible.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 11th October, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
BILLS PRESENTED.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE (AMEND-
MENT) BILL,
"to amend Section Four of the Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern Ireland),
1922," presented by the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews); supported by the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Labour
(Mr. Gordon); to be read a Second time on
Tuesday next, and to be printed.
SOLICITORS BILL,
"to provide for the carrying into execution
of certain enactments of the Solicitors (Ireland) Act, 1898, by the Incorporated Law
Society of Northern Ireland, and to amend
the said Act in its application to Northern
Ireland," presented by the Minister of Home
Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates); supported by the
Attorney-General (Mr. Best), and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Home
Affairs (Mr. Megaw); to be read a Second
time to-morrow, and to be printed.
UNIFORMITY OF LAWS BILL,
"to apply to Northern Ireland certain
Acts passed by the Parliament of the United
Kingdom in the present Session thereof,"
presented by Sir Dawson Bates; supported by
Mr. Best and Mr. Megaw; to be read a Second
time to-morrow, and to be printed.
LOCAL AUTHORITIES (ELECTIONS AND
CONSTITUTION) BILL.
"to postpone Elections of County and Rural
District Councils and Guardians in Northern
Ireland, and to remove difficulties with
respect to the constitution of certain Local
Authorities," presented by Sir Dawson Bates;
supported by Mr. Best and Mr. Megaw; to
be read a Second time to-morrow, and to
be printed.

WAYS AND MEANS.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
ENTERTAINMENTS DUTY.
"That the duty charged on payments
for admission to entertainments shall extend to-
(a) Payments for admission to an entertainment made to a person other than
the proprietor of the entertainment;
and
(b) payments of rent made in respect
of an interest in any premises which
is primarily acquired for the purpose
of securing admission to an entertainment.
The
PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): It is now
nearly two years since there was transferred
to the Parliament of Northern Ireland that
portion of the revenue which came under
our own immediate jurisdiction. We have
the duty to levy and collect that reserved
revenue, to make our own arrangements for
the collection of it, and the proceeds go
directly into our own Exchequer. But during
the interval that has elapsed it has been
found necessary in the Imperial Parliament
to make certain modifications in the laws
and regulations under which those taxes were
collected in order that the administration
of the law should carry out more fully the
intentions of the drafters of those regulations. The particular Clauses which I now
rise to move have to do with the Entertainments Tax, but I say that, in addition to
dealing with this feature of the revenue at
the present time, it is intended to deal with
other matters with which it has been found
necessary to deal in the Imperial Parliament
at Westminister. I should like to assure
hon. Members right away that it is not considered that these new regulations will in
any way add to the taxation. They will
clarify the regulations and remove dubiety,
which has existed, I think, owing to certain
conditions not having been kept well in mind
at the time this tax was originally produced,
which was as far back as 1916. The Entertainments Tax, so far as we are concerned,
brings in a revenue of about £80,000 a year,
and the conditions which have required the
passing of this resolution at Westminister
obtain almost entirely on the other side of
the Channel. I do not know whether we
will be greatly affected by their adoption,
but, as in all other things, we consider it
wise to follow the lines of Westminster,
and so, although there may not be any immediate necessity for the adoption of these
Clauses at the present time, it is always
well to benefit by their experience and be
ready for such conditions should they arise.
The first Clause will read:
"payments for admission to an entertainment made to a person other than the
proprietor of the entertainment;"
11 OCTOBER 1922
In Committee-

Entertainments Tax.
Then, we are anxious to tighten up the
collection of the revenue in one way by
restricting the exemptions from the Entertainments Tax to the following undertakings,
namely, that
where the whole of the takings are devoted
to philanthropic or charitable purposes
without any charge on the takings for
any expenses of the entertainment;
where the entertainment is of a wholly
educational character;
It was clearly the intention when this Act
was passed that all admissions to entertainments should bear this tax, but it has been
found, owing to the wording adopted, that
it has been possible for people to derive
enjoyment from an entertainment without
actually having paid for admission to the
proprietor or promoter of that entertainment.
It may be difficult to see how this could
arise, but I could illustrate it by taking
the case of a certain society or club which
was promoting a regatta on a river, which
occupies a large space. The promoters of
the regatta might have their own enclosure,
for admission to which they would charge,
and of course that would bear the tax; but
there might be someone with a lawn or premises convenient thereto, who had nothing
whatever to do with the promotion of the
regatta, and yet might be able to erect a
stand and charge for admission to that
stand. Under the old regulation there was
dubiety as to whether the tax was leviable
on that stand so erected.
Similarly the second Clause reads:
"payments of rent made in respect of an
interest in any premises which is primarily
acquired for the purpose of securing admission to an entertainment."
I think this also has to do with customs on
the other side of the Channel. I believe on
some very large racecourses there are boxes
in the stands which can be rented, and the
person who rented those boxes might entertain his friends there, and yet that rent
would not be subject to taxation under the
Entertainments Tax, whereas it was clearly
intended that all admissions, whether by
means of rent for part of the premises or by
the purchase of an individual ticket, should
be subject to this tax. Another matter which
requires clearing up is that of exemption
from taxation, or the repayment of the tax
charged on admission. Under the present
law every ticket for admission to such an
entertainment should bear clearly imprinted
upon it the price of the ticket, and whether
or not that price includes the Entertainments
Tax. In many cases it is the custom to sell
tickets of admission in advance of the date
of the entertainment itself, and if by any
chance the purchaser of those tickets did not
make use of them, and did not present them
at the barrier for admission, it meant that
the promoter of the entertainment derived
the benefit of the tax instead of the State,
so that is the necessity for making this read:
"payment for admission to an entertainment."
instead of, as the Act read formerly,
"each person admitted for payment."
You will see we wish to make all tickets,
whether the person is actually admitted or
not, subject to this Entertainments Tax.
where the entertainment is intended for
the amusement of children, and that the
charge is not more than one penny for

Also,
that the entertainment is provided for
partly educational or partly scientific purposes by a society, institution, or committee
not conducted or established for profit.
It is proposed that exemption from taxation shall be restricted absolutely to those
classes of entertainment to which I have
referred.
Then we have to safeguard ourselves in the
matter of refund of entertainment tax where
in the first case that entertainment tax has
been collected. Under the law as it has stood
hitherto entertainment tax is only refunded
in cases where the expense of the entertainment did not exceed 20 per cent., and all the
balance goes to the charitable or philanthropic object in aid of which the entertainment has been promoted. It has been found
in actual experience that this limit of 20
per cent. is rather too narrow a margin on
which to work, and therefore it is proposed
in future that this shall read 30 per cent.
That will be introduced in the Finance Bill
which will be duly brought before this House.
Then we wish to make clear that in the reklemption of the tax the tax so refunded must
go towards the charitable object for which
the entertainment was promoted. As the
law stands at present, the refund of the tax
is made to the proprietor of the entertainment, whereas it was intended that the
charity alone should benefit. In the majority of cases the tax so refunded has been
handed over to the charity, but where this
has been a matter of goodwill in the past
we wish to ensure in the future that it shall
reach its proper destination. There are some
matters in connection with the collection of
motor taxation which require to be dealt
with. Where the tax has been paid on a
motor, and during the lifetime of that license
that motor is so transformed that it is
rendered liable to a higher rate of duty,
as soon as that motor is so transformed, it
shall immediately become subject to the
higher rate of duty. Then it is intended to
extend the privilege which is at present

Oral Answers to Questions
THE ULSTER MONTH.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Prime Minister
whether he will state the actual position, so
far as it can be surveyed, regarding the ratification of the Treaty with the Irish Free
State, and when does the month begin to
run during which Ulster may exercise her
option of contracting herself out
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
The Treaty providing for the setting up of
the Irish Free State was signed on behalf of
the British and Irish Delegations on the 6th
December, 1921. The Articles of the Treaty
were given the force of law as from the 31st
March, 1922, being the date of the passing
by the Parliament of the United Kingdom
of the Irish Free State (Agreement) Act,
1922.
Articles 11 and 12 of the Treaty stipulated
that if before "the expiration of one month
from the passing of the Act of Parliament
for the ratification of this instrument" an
Address were presented to His Majesty by
both Houses of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland, Northern Ireland should continue
under the Government of Ireland Act and be
outside the Free State. The question was
raised in the House of Commons at Westminster whether the Irish Free State (Agreement) Act was the Act of Parliament for the
ratification of the Treaty. No satisfactory
assurances were forthcoming in Debate, and
eventually the question was set at rest by
insertion in the Act itself (Section 1 (5)) of
the following words:-
passing whereof the month mentioned in
Article 11 of the said Articles is to run."
"This Act shall not be deemed to be the
Act of Parliament for the ratification of the
said Articles of Agreement as from the
Accordingly, the month runs from the
passing of some future Act, and it does not
seem to be open to doubt that it will run
from the date of the Act of the United Kingdom Parliament, which will, in effect, finally
ratify the Treaty by confirming the Constitution of the Irish Free State. This Constitution is at present under consideration in
the form of a Bill which is proceeding
through the Provisional House of Parliament
in Dublin. When that Bill receives the
effect of an Act of the Provisional Parliament it will be submitted as part of a Bill
to be introduced at Westminster when Parliament reassembles next month.
The Westminster Bill must receive the
Royal Assent early in December in view of
the Agreement expressed in the last Article
of the Draft Constitution of the Irish Free
State, which is as follows:-

The passing and adoption of this Constitution by the Constituent Assembly and the
British Parliament shall be announced as
soon as may be, and not later than the 6th
day of December, 1922, by Proclamation of
His Majesty, and this Constitution shall
come into operation on the issue of such
Proclamation."
Accordingly, as far as can be foreseen, the
"Ulster" month will begin to run from a
date subsequent to the reassembly of Parliament at Westminster, but in any event not
later than the 6th of December next.

RENTS RESTRICTION ACT.
3. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister for
Home Affairs whether it is the intention
of the Government to appoint a Committee
of Inquiry to deal with the questions arising
out of the Rents Restriction Act, and to
advise what steps should be taken regarding
the Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question of
legislation amending the Rents Restriction
Acts has been engaging the serious attention
of the Government of Northern Ireland and
the Imperial Government for some time past.
The latter Government have set up a Committee of Inquiry to deal with the matter,
and it is hoped that that Committee will
present a report during the next few weeks.
This Government feels that any differential
legislation in Northern Ireland on matters
of this sort will be highly prejudicial to
Northern Ireland, and the Government of
Northern Ireland are therefore awaiting the
report of the Imperial Committee.
The hon. Member may rest assured that
a close watch is being kept on this important
matter and that legislation will be undertaken in this House before the present Act
lapses in the event of the Committee not
having reported in time.
Mr. LYNN: May I ask my right hon.

Sir DAWSON BATES: That is a matter

12 OCTOBER 1922
Address to the Lord Lieutenant.
PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That an Humble Address be presented to
His Excellency the Lord Lieutenant,
followeth :-
as
Your Excellency, we, His Majesty's most
dutiful and loyal subjects the Commons of
Northern Ireland in Parliament assembled,
towards raising the necessary supplies to
defray His Majesty's expenses in Northern
Ireland, do, as from the appointed day for
the purposes of the financial provisions of
the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, freely
and voluntarily give and grant unto His
Majesty the several duties and taxes existing at the said appointed day, and
available for raising the said supplies by
virtue of grants made to His Majesty from
time to time by the Parliament of the
United Kingdom, being duties and taxes in
respect of the imposing, charging, levying
and collection whereof the Parliament of
Northern Ireland has, as from that day,
power to make laws.”
The PRIME MINISTER: In case there
should be any misapprehension as to what
is the exact meaning of this rather legal
formula, I think it right to explain to the
House that I myself had some little difficulty
in probing into it when it was first put before
me. However, there is no precedent for it.
It is the advice of the legal side of our
Ministry of Finance that this should be done
in order to maintain the rights and privileges of this House in exactly the same way
as the rights and privileges of the House of
Commons of Great Britain is exercised over
purely financial matters. It is following
constitutional practice declared by the Bill
of Rights in the year 1688. It has been the
custom, when a new tax was imposed, for the
Commons of the United Kingdom Parliament
to grant freely and voluntarily the proceeds
of that tax to His Majesty. Thus, immediately prior to the establishment of the Parliament of Northern Ireland, all existing
taxes, including those which are now known
to us as transferred taxes, were, at the time
they were imposed, granted to the Crown.
The setting up of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland introduced a new element, inasmuch
as the power to impose, levy and collect,
Sittings of the House.
certain taxes, namely, the Entertainments,
Stamps and others, was transferred to us
in pursuance of Section 21 of the Government of Ireland Act, These transferred
taxes must be regarded in the light of new
taxes as between the Parliament of Northern
Ireland and the Crown. It is, therefore,
necessary for the Commons of Northern Ireland itself to grant the taxes to the Crown
in order to regularise the constitutional position and preserve the authority of the
House of Commons of Northern Ireland over
transferred taxation. The formal resolution
now before the House is intended to achieve
this object. I merely give that concise explanation in order that there should be no
misapprehension outside that there is any
other motive behind the motion except to put
us in exactly the same position as the Imperial House as regards taxation. I beg
to move.

SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE.
ARRANGEMENT OF BUSINESS.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House, at its rising this day, do adjourn
until Tuesday next." (Mr. Burn.)
Dr. MORRISON: I understood that it was
definitely arranged that the House would sit
on Fridays. I got a notice from the Chief
Whip this morning, and there is no mention
that the House is going to adjourn to-day,
which, I think, is a violation of the understanding to which we came. Some of the
hon. Members were talking about a day for
the discussion of the Interim Report of the
Education Committee, and here is a Friday
free, and yet it is not utilised. Country
Members are brought up here at very serious
inconvenience, and when they are here they
like to transact whatever business has to be
done. There was an understanding that we
should sit from Tuesday through the week,
including Friday, and it should not be violated without some reason and without notice
being given to the House. I would like to
register a protest against the way this House
is being managed in that respect by the
Whips' Office, and I think this position could
be obviated if they arranged their business
with ordinary intelligence.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am sorry that
the Chief Whip (Captain Dixon), who is a
man of extraordinary intelligence, does not
happen to be here to-day owing to a slight
illness. I can assure my hon. Friend (Dr
Morrison) that in this motion we were merely
1007 Sittings of the House.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Sittings of the House.
[The Prime Minister.]
consulting what we thought to be the wishes
of the House by not sitting on Fridays and
Mondays. As far as we are concerned, it
is all the same to sit on Fridays and Mondays
and even Saturdays, but this is the beginning
of a new portion of the Session, and there
are several Bills, which will soon be in the
hands of hon. Members, and which we
thought it would be wise if they had some
little time to thoroughly examine before they
come up for Second reading next week. It
was entirely to meet the convenience of hon.
Members that we suggested adjourning till
Tuesday. With regard to the subject of
giving a day for the discussion of the report
upon education, I would only say that we
would most willingly allocate to-morrow for
that purpose, but, there again, we thought it
was rather short notice for those who had to
make up their case and for the Government
who have got to reply to that case. Perhaps
to-morrow week would suit hon. Members
for that discussion, and if so the Government
will be only too delighted to fall in with their
wishes.
Mr. LYNN: Would the Prime Minister
take into consideration the advisability of
giving us more work to do when we come
here for a day? I do not mind whether you
sit two, three or four days a week, but really
it seems to me that we spend more time
coming here and getting back again than we
spend in this House, and it strikes me as
not being a very business-like arrangement.
Looking over the sittings of the House, I
find that the average is less than two hours
a day for every day we have sat. I think that
ought to be improved upon, and I would ask
the Prime Minister to give some consideration
to hon. Members' time. I do not mind coming
here and spending a whole afternoon, but I
do hate to come here and stay for ten, fiftden
or twenty minutes and then go away again.
It is not good for the House, and I am sure
it is not good for the Government. I suggest
that we should sit on fewer days and do more
on the days on which we do sit.
The PRIME MINISTER: I quite agree
with what my hon. Friend (Mr. Lynn) says,
but he must not take it that our procedure in
the past year has been any criterion of how
we hope to carry on in the future. Really
we have been working under exceptional conditions during the past year, and sometimes
it was awkward for hon, Members even to
get to the House. The Government were
most anxious to meet an extraordinary occasion by extraordinary means, but the question of when we meet and how long we sit
depends to a certain extent upon the hon.
Members themselves. If we get through the
business rapidly we do not, I am sure, desire
to create business for the purpose of prolonging the sitting. On the other hand, the
Government, at the start of this new part of
the Session is not anxious to rush any
measure, and so we decided that we would
not take the Bills on the Order Paper for a
few days, in order to give everybody in the
House a fair chance of being able to study
the various measures. In future we will endeavour to put on the Order Paper sufficient
business to occupy the House when it meets,
so that there will not be any complaint, as
the hon. Member (Mr. Lynn) says, of Members spending more time in coming here and
getting away again than they spend in the
House itself.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I am delighted
to hear the announcement of the Prime
Minister in regard to the business for the
future. As the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) has told you, the average
duration of our sittings has been something
like two hours I am quite certain the Prime
Minister and the Government recognise the
extreme difficulty which Members coming
from a distance experience in serving in this
House. Very often we come up here early
in the morning and have to wait till three
o'clock for the proceedings of Parliament, and
then we sit only for an hour and a half.
Some of us, I am afraid, would be in danger
of getting into serious temptation if such a
practice were to continue. I foresee that
there are certain Bills coming on which may
occupy quite a considerable time, but if
there is going to be any change in the arrangement of the business, I should like to
get notice. I quite recognise that it will
be very difficult for the Government to always
have a full programme. I acknowledge that
at once, but I do think that, now we are
getting settled down, if they could arrange a
full afternoon's work it would be very desirable, and if we can carry on the deliberations of Parliament in two days or three
days, it would be to the advantage, I think,
of all parties concerned. It is going to be
extremely difficult to get men from a distance
to stay here for four days in the week if we
only have an hour and a half's work in the
day. I am glad the Prime Minister has held
out the hope that this state of affairs will be
remedied as soon as possible, and I sincerely

a larger programme. I know if all the hon.

sits next to me do not like to occupy the
time of the House.
The PRIME MINISTER: I only just wish

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
SUPPLY.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In asking this Committee to pass this supplementary Vote it will
at first sight appear somewhat unusual that
the amount asked for should so greatly exceed the original Estimate, but I hope to
satisfy hon. Members that I am justified
in coming before the Committee and in asking
them to pass it. When the original Estimate
was framed we had nothing to go upon
except the existing conditions, and we accordingly adopted as an average 470 prisoners
as the population for the jails. Owing, however to the better enforcement of the law
and the offences created under the Civil
Authorities Act the number of ordinary
prisoners, as distinct from those to which
I will refer, increased from 470 to 830. That
is an addition of 360 ordinary, convicted
prisoners, and this Estimate makes provision
for that addition in respect of ordinary
prisoners. But apart from these ordinary
prisoners we have something like 500 prisoners who are interned under the Civil
Authorities Act, SO that as against the
original Estimate of 470 prisoners we are
now budgeting for an additional 860. With
the exception of one item, which I will refer
to later, the amount that I come to this
Committee for is entirely due to this increased prison population.
SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES, 1922-1923.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
Class II. No. 4.
PRISONS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£83,865 be granted to His Majesty to defray
the charge which may come in course of payment during the year ending 31st March,
1923, for the expenses of prisons."
As hon. Members know we have only threa
prisons-ordinary prisons-in the North of
Ireland, and at one time, if I may use the
expression, We were dangerously near
breaking point, but when the Civil Authorities Act came into operation we had to look
round for further accommodation. After
very careful consideration in regard to this
extremely difficult subject we came to the
conclusion that the most efficient way to
deal with the case was to put these prisoners
on to a ship, and accordingly the Government
purchased a vessel known as the "Argenta,"
together with its tender. The Press, hon.
Members know, was full of propaganda
against the scheme. Horrible tales were told
of the atrocities perpetrated against the
prisoners and their awful sufferings, but
imitation is, I suggest, the most sincere
form of flattery, and we find that the Provisional Government who were perhaps our
most hostile critics have now adopted the
same method as we adopted to deal with
the situation in the South of Ireland. So
far as I can see, and having regard to the
health of the prisoners, and from economical
grounds in addition, it has proved an unqualified success.
The "Argenta "
.. was at first moored in
Belfast Lough, and that was done for reasons
of safety. You all realise the conditions
QQq
Supplementary Estimates. 1012
Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
prevailing at the time that vessel was brought
into commission. But on the ground of
economy, and also because it has been considered that a vessel of this size cannot very
well remain in the fairway of Belfast Lough
during the winter it has been decided to
remove the vessel to Larne, and as a result
we have been able to effect a great many
economies in the meantime a reduction of
the crew and in other respects. Unfortunately, the accommodation in the "Argenta
was not sufficient for the purpose, and we
had to turn our attention to another method
of dealing with the situation, and the Larne
Workhouse being vacant and it being the
property of the Ministry we decided to convert that into an auxiliary prison working
in conjunction with the Argenta." Hon.
Members will see that in the Estimates the
cost of converting this workhouse hospital
into a prison amounts to £5,000. Hon.
Members will realise that converting any
building into another purpose is an expensive
thing, but more particularly converting a
hospital into a prison. Now, as a result of
these two prisons, the " Argenta" and the
Larne Workhouse prison, we have accommodation for 500 internees, and I do hope
and pray that may be sufficient for the
purpose of the Government, but if it is not
sufficient the Government will have no hesitation in coming to this House to ask for
further accommodation.
Now with regard to the different items,
we have had to find a complete staff for
the "Argenta" and Larne prison, and in
addition we have had to increase slightly
the ordinary staff in the two male prisons,
Belfast and Londonderry. The items for
provisioning, clothing, and fuel and light
speak for themselves. We have endeavoured
to effect as many economies as possible, but
dealing with certain classes of prisoners such
as we have got to deal with there is more
destruction in prison clothing than otherwise
would be the case.
Coming down to sub-Head O, which is for
the maintenance of prisoners in prisons outside Northern Ireland, I would like to remind
Members of this Committee that we have
not got a convict prison. Therefore, we
have entered into arrangements from time
to time with the English and Scotch authorities for housing our convicts. In the
original Estimates we provided for 50 convicts. Now we come and ask for an addition
of 20, and that increase is also due to the
fact that at the time this Government took
over the administration of the prisons there
were a number of prisoners in Scotch and
English jails who had been sent there for
reasons best known to the Imperial Government, and, therefore, they were not in our
custody at the time we took over administration.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Has it been added to
since?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, I am budgeting for a further 20. With regard to these
old prisoners sent over prior to us taking
over administration, the Imperial Government have now suggested that we should
pay for their maintenance at the present
time. I am not prepared to admit the equity
of their claim, and negotiations are going
on in regard to it. This Committee may
rest assured that this Government will do
its utmost to prevent itself having to pay
for the maintenance of these prisoners. At
the same time if we fail it is necessary
to make provision for that amount.
With regard to the original Estimate,
which was presented, that works out at a
cost for 470 prisoners of something like £127
per head per annum, and that figure is lower
than is charged or what it costs in Scotland;
but in the present Estimate which is now
before the Committee, that is in respect of
the 860 additional prisoners, if one deducts
from the total Estimate of £83,865 first of
all the capital cost of the " Argenta" of
£19,000, the cost of fitting up the workhouse
of £5,000, and the amount for the prisoners
maintained in England, £17,000, a total of
£41,920, we find that the actual cost of the
maintenance of these 860 prisoners, which we
are budgeting for to-day, works out at something like £47 for nine months or £63 per
head per annum. I do suggest that those
figures speak for themselves. I think they
illustrate in a practical way that we have
endeavoured to provide as economically as
possible for our unwilling guests.
When this Government took over the
administration in December last the condition
of our jails was deplorable, but I am glad
to say that has been completely altered. I
think the most satisfactory change is the
complete restoration of prison discipline.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We have had
an extremely uphill task, but our Governors,
some of whom were new men and inexperienced, and our warders, many of whom were
new and inexperienced, have risen to the
task, and I would like to bear tribute to
the way in which they have restored prison
discipline. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The old familiar hunger strike which disgraced Irish administration is now entirely
a thing of the past. I do not think we are
likely to have a recurrence of it. I have
not touched on the absence or the necessity
of providing a convict prison. Sooner or
later that will have to be dealt with, but
Supply-

we should first of all get back to normal
conditions, and see exactly what we have
provided for before we bring that matter

will also have to be taken into consideration.
Meanwhile we have to pay the rates demanded by the other side by the Scotch
authorities--for the maintenance of the convict prisoners, and this works out at £133
per head. I ask the Members to agree to
this Vote.

Regarding the staff of the Home Office, in
the original estimate we asked for 100, which
has now been increased by 35. I should like,
however, to make it clear that a large proportion of our staff is temporary, and in fact
at the moment, out of a total of 135, 56 are
employed purely on a temporary basis. We
have not therefore, committed ourselves to
any large permanent expenditure. When it
is remembered that half the total expenditure
in Northern Ireland is accounted for by the
Ministry of Home Affairs no one, I think,
can reasonably suggest that the staff of the
supervising department can be described as
excessive.

to 35s. f.o.b. at port in Great Britain, according to the district from which the coal

DRIVING OF CROSSLEY CARS.
3. Mr. COOPER asked the Ministry of
Home Affairs if he is aware that a number
of accidents have occurred in Northern Ireland through the negligent driving of Crossley cars, and that many people of moderate
means have suffered considerable losses, and
have been unable to obtain either compensation or inquiry into their cases. Whether
any remedy exists against the Government
other than by Petition of Right, and, if not,
whether he is prepared to introduce some
remedy, having regard to the fact that such
proceedings are a luxury which cannot be
borne by the pocket of the ordinary citizen?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): It is true that a number of
accidents have occurred, though it must not
be assumed that most of these accidents are
due to negligent driving. Close inquiry is
made in all such accidents, and where negligence can be established the person responsible is either prosecuted at Petty Sessions,
or if the offending person is a member of the
Police Forces, disciplinary action is taken
against him. Instructions have been issued
that every precaution shall be taken to prevent reckless driving, and the Police authorities will, to their utmost ability, carry
these instructions into effect.
In regard to the latter part of the question, no legal remedy exists against the Government, but the Government is always willing to consider an application for compensation where legal liability would attach if
the car were the property of a private owner.
Of course, proceedings can always be taken
against the driver if he has been guilty of
negligence.

LAND PURCHASE.
6. Mr. COOPER asked the Minister of
Finance whether he is aware that an owner
of land purchased under the Irish Land Act,
1903, cannot charge his holding for more
than ten times the amount of the annuity
without the consent of the Ministry of Finance, although a holding with a small
annuity is very often more valuable than
one with a large annuity, and that this
restriction is regarded with disfavour by
owners, bankers, solicitors, auctioneers and
all other persons acquainted with the transferring and sale of lands, more especially as
requests for liberty to exceed the statutory
charging powers are dealt with by persons
sitting in an office in Belfast who know
nothing whatever either about the land, the
buildings thereon, or the market value; and
whether he is prepared to abolish or assist
in abolishing this restriction.
Mr. POLLOCK: Under Section 54 (3) of
the Irish Land Act, 1903, as adapted by the
Government of Ireland Act and the Orders
in Council thereunder, the consent of the
Ministry of Finance is a necessary condition
for the creation of a charge on a purchased
holding of more than ten times the annuity
payable.
Each application for the creation of a
charge exceeding the statutory limit is dealt
with on its own merits and after investigation by officers of the Ministry who have
a long acquaintance not only with the
principles adopted in the past by the Land
Commission, but also with questions of house
and land values in Northern Ireland. The
restriction is directed towards securing that
the tenant does not burden himself with
charges which might by hindering or preventing the payment of the annuities, lead
to loss to the Exchequer of Northern Ireland
or result in the Ministry being forced to sell
the lands to recover arrears. Where the sum
applied for is to be utilised towards improving the holding, e.g., building and
drainage, or for liquidating family charges
and so forth, applications have been and will
be freely entertained. There is no evidence
that the present policy is the subject of
complaint from the general body of persons
referred to by the hon. Member, and in fact
1 am sure that tenant purchasers themselves
welcome the restriction as affording them
protection against undue pressure during
periods of agricultural depression. It is
not proposed to abolish the restriction seeing
that there is ample power under the existing statute to remove it in cases where
such a course appears desirable, and having
regard to the fact that dealings of this kind
in Northern Ireland are usually of a prudent
character, it may be possible in future to
take a wider view than the Land Commission
allowed themselves in their dealings with
the whole of Ireland.
In conclusion, I feel that the hon. Member
would, on re-consideration, desire to withdraw the imputation contained in the closing
lines of his question.
Dr. MORRISON: I should like to ask a
further question with regard to that answer.
Is it not a fact that this limitation on the
amount that can be borrowed on a holding has
deterred in many cases an insolvent or semiinsolvent tenant from bidding up the place
against solvent men and shutting out solvent
men and substituting himself when he is unable to tackle the job?
Mr. COOPER: Arising out of the reply, I
would like an answer from the Minister as
to whether the official ever sees the land on
which he expresses an opinion and gives a
value.
Mr. POLLOCK: With regard to the latter
question by my hon. Friend from Tyrone and
Fermanagh (Mr. Cooper) I think it is highly
improbable that a person who is understood
to value land and to arrive for purposes of
the application that has been made at its
value would fail to examine it and inspect
it. I have no personal knowledge that they
have departed from that practice.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: They might do it by
deputy.
Mr. POLLOCK: They might possibly, but
I am not in a position to state that now.
I am always very careful about making a
reply to a question of fact. With regard to
the question by my hon. Friend from the University (Dr. Morrison), I do not quite follow
him. Assuming that the holding is embarrassed to the extent of ten times the value of
the annuity-I am bound to say I do not
quite follow his argument.
Dr. MORRISON: If a man proposes to buy
a holding-
Mr. SPEAKER: These arguments cannot be

Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of the answer,
I should like to ask has it not frequently
occurred that a farmer who wants to enlarge
his holding and who has not the capital may
undertake to acquire another holding if he
has power to borrow to the fullest extent

and also shuts out, by bidding a far higher

Mr. POLLOCK: I think it is rather an
involved case which my hon. Friend has
given. The general principle of the Measure
is this, that a farmer must be protected
against liabilities that would exceed ten times
the amount of the annuity for several reasons.
One main reason, speaking from the point of
view of the Administration is that it would
materially weaken the security of the Government in regard to the payment of the
annuity if it were admitted that the tenant
of a holding or the owner of a holding could
mortgage his property to an unlimited extent.
I do not think it desirable that transactions
of the kind indicated by my hon. Friend
(Dr. Morrison) should be encouraged.
MOTOR TAXATION.
7. Mr. DONALD asked the Prime Minister
whether it is the intention of the Government to introduce a Bill this Session dealing
with Motor Taxation.
I meant this question to be put to the
Minister for Home Affairs, therefore I ask
him to answer it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am asked by
the Prime Minister to reply. The whole
system of Motor Taxation is being inquired
into in Great Britain, and is being followed
carefully by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
The Departmental Committee which is investigating this matter will, it is expected,
present its report in the course of the
next couple of months, and pending its
receipt it is premature to make any statement as to the intentions of this Government.
SEA AND INLAND FISHERIES.
8. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he proposes taking over
Sea and Inland Fisheries and Lighthouses.
Mr. ARCHDALE: By Order in Council,
dated 1st April, administrative powers and
duties in connection with Sea and Inland
Fisheries, so far as Northern Ireland is concerned, are vested temporarily in the Chief
Secretary. The present situation is most
unsatisfactory, but the question of delegation or transfer of those powers and duties
to the Ministry of Agriculture is one for
decision by the Imperial Government.
As regards the second part of the question,
Section 4 (i) (11) of the Government of
Ireland Act, 1920, declares lighthouses,
buoys, or beacons (except so far as they can
consistently with any general Act of the
Parliament of the United Kingdom be constructed or maintained by a local harbour
authority) to be a reserved service.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Archdale) if he is aware of the
great inconvenience that some of the people
on lighthouses have been experiencing recently? Some of them have not received
wages, for some months, owing to the most
unsatisfactory arrangements made by the
Chief Secretary.
Mr. ARCHDALE: In answer to that, I am
not aware of it, but we will call the attention
of the Chief Secretary to the fact.

further cottages are in course of preparation,

Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill, the
Second reading of which I have the honour
to move, is one for adapting with the necessary modifications the provisions of the
Solicitors (Ireland) Act of 1898. The
Solicitors Act, 1898, applied to the whole of
Ireland, and provided for, amongst other
things, the keeping of a roll by the Incorporated Law Society, in which were entered
the names of all persons entitled to practise
as solicitors. It also gave authority to the
Incorporated Law Society of Ireland to make
regulations with respect to persons seeking
to be admitted to the profession, and provided
for the holding of preliminary examinations
and the general legal training, and the holding of the final examinations prior to these
candidates being admitted to the roll of
solicitors, which enabled them to practise as
such in Ireland. The Act also provided for
the oversight of solicitors by the Incorporated
Law Society, and for investigating charges of
misconduct, if that ever took place, and in
suitable cases bringing them before the Lord
Chancellor with a view to having such
solicitors punished by being suspended or
struck off the roll, as the case might be.
There were certain other subsidiary divisions
incidental to the regulations with which I
think it is unnecessary to trouble this House.
As a result of the passing of the Government
of Ireland Act of 1920, and the setting up of
a separate judiciary in Northern Ireland, the
Northern Law Society applied for, and

With regard to Clause 1, Sub-sections A,

Act, it was necessary for the Incorporated

recognised at once that the task was beyond
us, and that some other course would have
to be taken with regard to the elections
that were coming next year.
A study of the question showed certain
alternative courses, and the ones that presented themselves to our minds were these-
First of all, to let the elections proceed
with the electoral divisions as they were
in existence before the P.R. Act. The second
would have been to ask the House to pass
a Bill suspending the operation of P.R. for
a year. The third was to ask the House
to postpone the elections until redistribution
can be effected. As regards reverting to the
old electoral divisions, we felt that in the
face of the inequalities disclosed we could
not justify the course. We would make it
more difficult to re-arrange the divisions
afterwards if we had proceeded to have elections in these divisions as they had been
before the Act of 1919, and indeed the House
had assumed that there would be redistribution. It had laid down cardinal principles

drawn from rural district areas. If a county
area was to comply with the conditions of
the Act in regard to equality of population
you had to see that the rural areas of
which it was composed had also been dealt
with in the same way. After our experience
of the mind of the House as to proportional
representation we felt that it would be im-

the elections there is one other matter of
very considerable importance that forms the
subject matter of this Bill. I am asking
the House to postpone the rural elections
for a year. As I have said the urban elections will be held in the normal course in
the old constituencies. The elections for
urban districts among other things will be
held to elect members of those councils that
have been dissolved by virtue of the operations of the Emergency Powers Act. The
constituencies will elect the members of
those councils that defied this Government
and declined to administer the law and were
consequently dissolved. The administration
of the functions of those councils has been
admirably carried on by the men appointed
by the Ministry. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We have heard no complaints at all
as regards their work; very much the
opposite. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
However, it was never intended to resort
to this system except to meet a temporary
emergency, and we hope when the elections
take place in all the urban districts we shall
find that councillors are elected who will
obey the law and discharge their duties properly in accordance with the declaration that
they now must sign before taking office.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
As regards rural councils, however, if this
Bill is passed there will be no elections
until May or June of 1924, and it may be
that a little reflection on the advantages
of good and firm administration may have
changed the hearts of some of the councillors
who have been superseded. The Ministry
would like to have the power of putting
rural councils on the same level as the urban
councils, and if it is convinced that the old
council or some of the members of it are
ready to discharge the duties according to
law we should like to have the power of
reinstating them.

Unemployment Insurance (Amendment) Bill.
proposed:
Order for Second reading read.

"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): This Unemployment Insurance
Bill, No. 2, which I have the honour to bring
before the House to-day for Second reading,
is a very simple measure, notwithstanding the
far-reaching importance of the great social
problem with which it deals. Hon. Members
will remember that, when this House rose on
the 5th July last, the Imperial Government
had not made up its mind as to what it proposed to do in regard to the third and fourth
special periods in the Unemployment Insurance Act which was passed at the beginning
of the present year. It was felt by hon.
Members generally that the matter might become urgent during the time that this House
was not sitting, and, therefore, in an informal
way, they gave me power to follow on parallel
lines with whatever was done at Westminster.
Acting upon that expressed wish of this
House, I arranged to follow exactly on the
lines adopted by the Imperial Parliament,
with the result that I increased the fifteen
weeks' benefit period so payable to twentytwo weeks, and reduced the gap period from
eight weeks to one week. This Bill, in the
first instance, gives statutory authority to the
action which I took at that time in connection
with this matter.
Hon. Members will also probably be aware
of the fact that a few weeks ago it was
brought before my notice by several very important deputations that a very great hardship would be inflicted upon certain covenanted persons owing to the fact that for them
there would be a gap period of seven weeks
at the end of their twenty-two weeks' continuous benefit. I was able to arrange, on
behalf of the Government, that four weeks
would be transferred from the fourth special
period to the third spacial period, and that
arrangement, I think, eased the situation to

I would like to refer to another aspect
of this case. Our Government are not
content to deal with this subject alone
by paying benefits to unemployed persons.
What as far as possible we want to obtain
for our people is work-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and that is, I think I am right in saying, beyond the shadow of a doubt what the
vast majority of our people desire. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) But the difficulty
which we find here is really an international
difficulty at the present time, and that is
to find work to keep our people going. Very
often I am asked in the streets and elsewhere
"Why not wind up this unemployment benefit
business altogether?" Well, my answer invariably has been this: Let us find employment
for our people, and unemployment benefit will
automatically end. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) In this connection, as I have said,
our Government are doing all they can. The
Ministry of Commerce has taken a very deep
and a very keen interest in the revival of
trade, and I am sure our whole community
greatly appreciates the efforts they have made
in connection with the United States Tariff
Bill, which has created such a serious position
for our linen trade in the North of Ireland
during the last few months. Personally
speaking I am very hopeful that the worst
of our industrial crisis is past. I remember
the figures-I do not think I will ever forget
them-when I was appointed Minister of
Labour, now more than a year ago. At that
time there were totally unemployed in Northern Ireland about 78,000 persons. On the 1st
January, when we took over, the figure had
fallen to about 58,000 persons totally unployed, and to-day, I am glad to say, it is
rather below 47,000. Of course 47,000 totally
unemployed is a huge total for an area such

"On all hands I found an appearance of

found them to be clean and well fed."

I regret to say that in this city of ours we
have children practically in starvation. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I regret to say in
this House that in my own constituency if
we had not taken steps to get some voluntary
help these people, decent pecple, would be
starving. We do not go outside to see their

to find the troubles. Really, children are
starving in Belfast to-day. He goes on to

"I found also that building was active.
Apparently throughout the country new

of existing factories, and this was to be

taxation has been very low in Germany.
Workmen's wages all were very low, but
subsidies were paid by the Government."
There is a solution. I have quoted millions
and millions of money being paid out for
producing nothing. I think our Government
should take steps in this matter. For the
millions that have been paid out we could
have every man employed. I am satisfied if
it applies to Germany it should apply to this
country if we are paying out millions to get
nothing in return. Surely there is another
way out of the difficulty for the Government.
Give it by way of subsidy and take these
people off the streets. He said also:-
I found five new railways with stations
being constructed. Hundreds of men were
employed on these electric railways.
Then he goes on to say that the merchant

tons is being restored again, and that all
the berths in Hamburg were filled, shipbuilding activity, was speeding up, and apparently there were nothing but signs of
prosperity in the country.
We went to war. What did we go to war
for? Was it that after the war our country
was to become destitute, that millions of
people should go about unemployed, and that
those against whom we went to war are to
go on prospering, as it were, at our expense.
I think there is something seriously wrong
with this whole problem of unemployment.
My right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) said it
was work that our people wanted. I agree that
it is work they want. Able-bodied men are
walking the streets. What is the reason of
our prisons being full to-day? Young men
are going about with empty stomachs. They
are liable to get into trouble. I heard a
very decent man stating at a public meeting
that rather than let his wife and children
starve he would loot. He is breaking the
law if he does that. We are spending, I
think, something like £80,000 to keep up our
prisons to-day. We have to keep those men
who are locked up in the prisons. They have
got to be fed there.
Like my hon. Friend (Mr. M'Guffin) I went
before the Guardians. I am satisfied so far

our Belfast Board of Guardians have plenary
powers under the Act of Parliament to give
assistance in some degree with regard to this
vexed question of unemployment. I said I
did not favour this question of paying out
money and increasing the rates for nothing.
I understand the Guardians are now meeting the City Council with a view to seeing
if they can come to a solution that will
develop something that will give employment. Those are the right lines, but if they
cannot do that there is no alternative but
to pay this money out. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Take a small place like
Whitehaven. The rates are 13s 6d in the £,
and they have paid out over £50,000. That
is, they give people who are in bad circumstances £1 a week, 5s for the first child,
and 4s for the next child, but there is a
maximum stated. I quoted at that meeting
different centres in England and Scotland
some of which are paying £100,000, but if
they do that the rates have gone up to 18s
3d and 18s 6d in the £. Take the case of

is in hard cash. I do not agree with that.
I say there is a solution if the Government
make up their minds. Our shipbuilders today cannot quote in the open market owing
to the high prices of everything, and owing
to Germany which is paying low wages and
giving a subsidy in order to get its people into
employment.
I am speaking of facts. I say that our
shipbuilders are confronted with this very
problem, and that if £100,000 were guaranteed to one of our yards it would give employment for some five thousand people.
They are confronted with this very question.
They cannot quote in the market. Norway
and Sweden are subsidising shipbuilding.
This is a question for the larger Government.
My right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) sked

Dr. MORRISON: I would like to make a
remark or two on this question, and I think
that on the Second Reading you are allowed
a certain amount of latitude. The last

I think that up till now from certain clearly

large burden is borne by other sections of
the community that have not been stressed.
I listened to the painful stories about
starvation of children in Belfast, and
I confess I have very great difficulty
in believing or swallowing statements
like that. I have looked
up, since
I first got in the way of these things,
to that modern institution, the Belfast Board
of Guardians. I think the Belfast Board of

it struck me, that they granted 25/- a week

can get relief, and for a man to stand up

This unemployment benefit, which the
Minister for Labour has been explaining to

when employment is plentiful and when

I venture to dissent from that. I state
here and I know that I am incurring a
certain amount of responsibility and criticism-I state here that in my opinion this
unemployment insurance and in the opinion
of a great many men amongst whom I have
included myself-has created a new class who
will live on the unemployment doles. I am
not making any charge against decent working men; I am making a charge against a
class that is being created by these unemployment doles, and who do not want to work
and are perfectly satisfied to live on these
doles We have reached this stage in the
humanitarian provision for the necessities of
the poor that we have passed certain fundament laws that govern our attitude; and
one of these laws is that the producer of
wealth, the creator of the State, should be
the first charge on that State. Everybody
admits that that is so. We act on it in
diffe nt Parliaments and different laws that
deal with economic questions. The second
fund mental law is that the State should
do for the people only what the people cannot do for themselves and to stop there.
Now I should like to ask what has occurred
in this country. The old beggar we used
to see wandering about is gone, but his or
her place is being taken in the country
towns and in the country districts by men
who live on unemployment benefit, by men
who claim from the National Insurance Act
benefit that they are not entitled to receive,
by men who have been in the Army and
have got real or imaginary diseases that
would not prevent them from working if
they chose, but who make a special system
of this and are able to get a living out of
it without working, by people who defraud
the Old Age Pensions Act and have property
while they are getting the pension-property
amounting perhaps to £500 or £1,000, and
they draw the pension. These things are bad;
I
they are injurious to any community.
think it is necessary that somebody should
protest against it. This course is injurious
to the deserving working man and to the
deserving poor personally. They are a charge
on trade, a charge on industry. Take for
instance what happens in my own district.
I have this from respectable working men
who can testify to the facts. A man in that
district is able by special employment to earn
£9 a week, and on Monday morning when

They told me of a man who went to receive

He may

to have a cargo discharged
All this proves that strict administration
is necessary. But you must set a limit to
this expenditure if possible. The hon. Member for Derry told us here, and I could
hardly credit it, that Irregulars who were

through independent sources that he was

like that are going on over the whole country.
It is injuring the ratepayer, injuring industry, injuring the working classes themselves. I for one in the interests of the
taxpaying community who belong neither to
Capital nor to Labour, hope that the administration of this Act will be done so
carefully that these frauds will be limited
and finally eliminated.

19 OCTOBER 1922
SUPPLY.
SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES, 1922-1923.
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
CLASS 2. No. 7.
SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a
sum not exceeding £313,348 be
granted to his Majesty to complete the
sum necessary for the services of the period
ending on the 31st of March, 1923, to defray
the expenses of the Special Constabulary."
The PRIME MINISTER: It will be within
the recollection of the House that when the
Estimates were introduced in the early
part of the year I asked hon. Members to be
kind enough to defer criticism until the
autumn for many weighty reasons.
The Vote itself ought, strictly speaking,
of course, to be introduced by my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Home
Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), but when I tell
the House that the sum of money involved
here, amounting to £2,875,000 odd, is borne
entirely by the British Exchequer, and that
the cost of the whole of our Constabulary for
this year does not fall upon Ulster money or
Ulster funds in any respect, it will be realised
that, as I was instrumental in persuading the
British Treasury to grant us this sum of
money, it is more fitting that I should explain to the House exactly how matters
stand. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It does
not do to be ungracious in matters involving
such large principles and such a vast sum
of money as we are dealing with in these
Estimates, and I would like to pay tribute
to Mr. Winston Churchill especially for the
manner in which he has helped me and
helped Ulster in those matters which
materially affected our welfare. (Hon. Members: Hear hear.) I am only too sorry to
see that he has been laid aside by serious
illness just at a very critical moment in the
affairs of Great Britain. His judgment, his
tact, his patience during very long and try
ing conferences, at which I and some of my
colleagues were present, won the admiration
of all of us. I can only say that from my
heart, and give honour where I think honour
is due. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Some
may take exception to those words, but I will
say that I got more assistance from Mr.
Churchill than from some of our Own
Unionist colleagues-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and that, strange as it may seem, he
against whom Ulster bore so heavy a grudge
at one time, has reverted to the real heart
within the man, the heart of his father-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and I have told
him that after all there is some little benefit
in heredity. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
This sum of money, therefore, which we
discuss to-day is a sum of money which is
not only promised to us, but a sum of money
which has already been voted by the British
House of Commons, and which is to all intents
and purposes in the Treasury of my right hon.
Friend beside me (Mr. Pollock); so that there
can be no doubt, no question as to its availability for this particular purpose without
costing the Ulster people one single shilling
above what appears here on the Estimates.
I would like to clear away some of those
misapprehensions which still exist regarding
a portion of this Vote. May I ask hon.
Members not to pay very much attention
to Page 2, which classifies the Vote in a
different manner to the way in which it is
laid out on the subsequent pages and summarised more readily for us to be able to
discuss it. With regard to the first item-the
Military Adviser's staff, consisting to a large
extent of persons who came over here, and
not of what are called pure Ulstermen-I
would like to make only a very short comment.
There should be no antipathy towards those
gentlemen and officers-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear)-none, because they came over here
at my invitation. They did not thrust themselves upon us, but they came at my invitation
specially to assist Ulster during one of her
gravest crises, and it was only natural that
the people of Ulster at that time were in a
better position to judge of the value of their
services than perhaps to-day when, the crisis
having passed, we have drifted into more
quiet, peaceful times, But is anyone prepared
to tell me that the risk is all over? Will
anyone say to me that you can scrap your
machinery, that you can take the mainspring
out of your watch and it will still go on?
That is a risk which I as Prime Minister
and Leader of the people of Ulster will not
take at the present time. There are still
looming before us several very difficult and
complicated matters. There are still looming
before us the questions of the boundary and
of the relations between the North and South
as regards the Council of Ireland; and besides
all that there is a considerable amount of
what I may call inflammable matter in our
midst, to which if any ill-advised person set
a match at any moment no one could foresee
how far-reaching might be the consequences.
I like to be prudent. I like to be very pru-
'dent where there is any danger on the
horizon. Therefore, I am asking the Committee to-day to pass these Estimates on the
broad grounds that they are the very mini-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Supply-
Special Constabulary. 1088
[The Prime Minister]
mum on which we could work this year,
and also that they did afford to Ulster in
my opinion the system of Constabulary which
was most fitted to her peculiar needs, and
to bear in mind that while I am asking for
this Vote in the ordinary way in order that
the House may have full cognisance of what
is going on, I have also to cast my eyes to the
financial year 1923-24, for we are living still
in a state of uncertainty. The attitude I take
to the British Government is this: You have
handed us over an imperfect machine; you
handed us over a country which was seething,
and which was in such a turbulent condition
that your own military forces were unable
to control it, and, therefore, it is really your
duty to supply Ulster with some substitute
for those forces by allowing her to raise her
Special Constabulary to protect the lives and
property of the people inside our area. I
have always held that that is the proper
way to approach the British Government,
and I still tell the British Government that we
do not consider that we are fully out of the
wood, and it is on those grounds I can
approach them with respect to meeting us in
some way as regards the cost of the Special
Constabulary for next year. I have, then,
dealt with the first item, namely the Military
Adviser's staff, except as regards the point
that the Military Adviser and those officers
were instrumental in securing for the benefit
of Ulster equipment to the value of at least
£850,000, which does not appear on these
Estimates at all. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It may be that some people will say
"Why have twenty or thirty thousand pounds
spent upon a headquarters staff?" It is a
mere fraction of the stores and equipment
which came into Ulster here, and besides
which it is a mere fraction in connection
with the grave responsibility they had to
share with me in making such plans as would
ensure the safety of the people.
I pass over the Criminal Investigation
Department altogether. It is being reorganised, and in the coming financial year I hope
my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
will be able to give an account of that reorganisation, and how the Department stands
in relation to his office. I come, then, to the
three classes of Constabulary on which we
rely for our safety and security over and
above the splendid new force the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. The Royal Ulster Constabulary
as a Force is not involved in these Votes
to-day, but the four classes of Special Constabulary-A, B, C and C1-are involved.
May I take Class "A," and may I try to
meet some of the criticism that reaches me
from various quarters throughout the Six
Counties? You are all aware that about
the middle of the financial year the British
Government rationed us-I think that is
perhaps as good a word as I can use with
regard to the amount of money they would
allow us to spend on these particular Services
-they rationed us by first of all voting
£850,000 and then £2,000,000. They wrote to
our Government, they wrote to me, and they
finally decided that we must arrange our
forces in such a way that the cost would
not fall beyond £2,850,000. I had then, of
course, to face a very great difficulty, and
whatever may be said with regard to the arrangements that are shown in this paper
here the critics must criticise me and my
Cabinet, and must not think that orders
are given by either the Military Adviser or
the Inspector-General, or County Commandants or anyone else prejudicing the position
of those Specials who are within their area.
I take the full responsibility on my own
shoulders for the arrangements that are
made here, and when I take that responsibility I take it for this reason, that I was
the originator of the Special Constabulary
myself. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I had
nursed that Force and tried to protect that
Force, and to see fair play granted to each
of the categories "A" and "B" and "C."
Further than that, I have fought like a
tiger on the other side of the water to get
all this for the Special Constabulary and to
build it up into the splendid Force it is
to-day. Oh, how I fought and fought for
those men who are protecting our homes
and who are acting as Ulstermen in the
very best sense of the term! I fought for
them, and fought successfully, and I ask
any of the critics throughout the Six
Counties not to criticise those who really
had nothing to do with the scheme, to let
them criticise me, and let them send me
any possible modifications or improvements
in the scheme which, after consultation with
those very highly efficient officers, we had
been able to devise. Let me take a few
of those criticisms that have come to my
ears. One is that we should never have
reduced the pay-you will observe it on
Page 4 at the bottom-from 70/- to 49/- a
week. Well, to meet that criticism, let me
put it this way: I was faced first of all with
the problem confronting all of us of serious
unemployment in the Six Counties. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I was faced with the
problem that we had to have men, armed
men, trained men, those who were prepared
to take on the work of protecting where other
people were unable to do it. If we had
continued at the full rate of pay to the end
of this financial year, it is obvious that I
would have been forced into the awkward
Special Constabulary.
Supply-

19 OCTOBER 1922
predicament of having to cut off another
20 per cent. at least of our "A" Special
Constabulary. Was it better to take this
wage of 49/- per week, plus the allowance
to which I will refer presently, in many
cases, in nearly all cases-was it better to
take that as a standard pay for this Force
and allow us to keep as many of them as
possible employed in the Force? (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. DONALD: That is right.
The
a
manner.
The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friends
throughout the House, I think, agree with
me it is far better than to have a smaller
and better paid Force. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). I am glad to receive the
approval, and I think it is the unanimous
approval, of all the hon. Members of this
House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
second criticism directed against us was that
we might have done what is customary in
trades unions across the water, and I believe
here, that we might have had a more gradual
sliding scale, that is to say, instead of ruthlessly cutting down from 10/- a day to 7/- a
day we might have gone in stages covering
a few weeks or even a few months in order
that the reduced amount would have
been arrived at more gradually and not
in
such precipitous
Their
argument there again was one that
was threshed out by my colleagues and myself
till we came to the conclusion that if we
were to take that step once more we would
have to discharge men in order to make up
for the pay that would be paid in that period,
and it struck us that on the whole it was
fairer to make this cut which was necessary
to keep us within the £2,850,000, to make the
cut at once, to face the consequence, and at
all events be able to say, "We have got
the most of you employed, we have got most
of the benefits for all of you," rather than
having to cut down still further a Force
which we are all most anxious to maintain
both in efficiency and numbers. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That is the answer to
those who say we might have done something
to ease the situation instead of precipitously
cutting off the full number of men in one
fell blow. Then another criticism is directed
against us because they say, "Your 'A'
Special Constabulary are performing the
same work in many instances as the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, which is still at the
Desborough rates of pay." Well, first of all,
there is really this distinction, the Royal
Ulster Constabulary is to be a permanent
Force, and it is desired to attract into that
Force the very best men from any other
occupation they may be in in Ulster at the
present moment. We want the very best
men who are fit to be police constables in
the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and we do
not hesitate for a moment to take a man
who is fit for the post, even if he is one of
the best men in the yards, because we know
it is a permanent position for him for which
he is suitable, and serving in the Force he is
serving the best interests of Ulster without
doing any harm to the yards because he
makes a vacancy which can be filled by someone who possibly is not of the standard
necessary for the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
But with regard to the "A" Specials, it is
an entirely different pair of shoes.
If you
have the wage with the allowances, to which
I am going to refer later, up to such a high
standard you may take men from permanent
positions in trade into the "A" Specials,
which is a blind alley-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear) and which causes such disappointment to them later on when they may
have lost their job in the yard and may have
lost their job as a Special. Therefore, it is
the height of wisdom to differentiate in that
way in order to hold up some little warning
to men who are short-sighted, and because of
the pay and conditions of the Specials they
would be wise not to give up a permanency
in order to get into the Force, which we all
know is bound sooner or later gradually to
disappear, and, I hope, to disappear with the
same honour and glory with which it has
covered itself up to the present day. This is
another very important reason why the
differentiation has been found necessary.
Again, I say that those who clamour for
bringing the pay up to the same level as the
Royal Ulster Constabulary are only doing a
disservice to some of their colleagues by
having them cut off and turned out into the
world at the present moment. Then I would
ask those critics to bear in mind that with
regard to the "A" Special Constabulary you
will observe an item of £1,052,103. If hon.
Members will turn to page 6 they will see
there the allowances that are also granted to
the "A" class. I do not desire to go through
item by item, it is very plair for anyone to
read; so that when one talks avut the wages
or pay of the men being 49s a week it will
readily be seen that that is supplemented in
very many instances by those various items
here. Motor transport drivers get 2s 6d per
day up to 30th September and then 2s; motor
transport fitters, 5s per day extra, after 30th
September 4s per day; wireless operators,
2s 6d per day to 30th September, 2s from that
date onward. There are rent allowances
to the constables coming to £32,000; medical
allowances, £8,066; boot allowances, £25,252;
and there are subsistence allowances which
will be found on page 7 under a special
heading, the allowances for officers and men
