HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
amounting to £80,000. The rents of barracks
and compensation in respect of commandeered premises come to very nearly
£100,000; barrack furniture, £12,000; fuel,
light and water, £7,000, and so on. I do not
say for a moment that in all instances these
men have had a bed of roses, but I do say
that we have, after anxious thought and
consideration, done our very best for this
splendid Force, and I hope the critics will
take into consideration all I have said, and
they will find there are very few cases where
emergency has raised a Force of the kind
where it has been possible for a Government
to deal with them so well.
Another point I would like to make is
this: In persuading Great Britain, through
its House of Commons, where the Votes have
to be passed and Ministers sit round the
Cabinet table as we do here-in persuading
them of the necessity and justice of this
Force I have always been able to point out
the marvellous accomplishments. I do not
believe there is any part of our Empire
where you could suddenly transform such a
vast percentage of the people into armed
men, and at the end of eighteen months or
two years have such a magnificent record as
we have in the case of our Special Constabulary. Therefore, in fighting their
battles, as I shall do before the Cabinet for
the coming year, I trust I shall be able to
approach them with the same clean record
that I have been able to do on every previous
occasion, and I have no fear on the subject.
I now come to Class B. Everybody knows
the B's. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Everybody praises the B's. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I have not heard in our broad
acres a complaint against the B's since they
were first formed. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). They have been simply magnificent,
and everyone knows how well they have
adapted themselves to a very peculiar
situation. They are the holders of our outposts. They are always on the spot. They
know everything that is going on in their
locality. They are ready at a moment's
notice to take up any duty which they are
called upon to do in order to protect what,
after all, is the heart of Ulster, and that is
the boundaries of Ulster. No praise is too
high for them, and therefore when one looks
at the Estimate that is here, a modest Estimate-it has to be looked for on
two pages, on page 5 and on page 6-the
item that is really worth considering is the
£220,000 for the year's Service.
actually got for the sum of £220,000 the men
upon the borderland and in our interior who
are best fitted to deal with a certain class of
disturbance in our midst. They have performed their duty at what I call the minimum compensation, and I believe I am right
in saying here that with that spirit that
animates them, if they were asked to do the
same duty for nothing at all they would only
be too delighted to do it for the honour of
Ulster. I believe in my heart if there were
no money forthcoming they would be delighted to do the work they have done without any compensation or reward. I trust,
however, that the same remarks regarding the
A's are applicable to the B's, and that I will
be able to convince His Majesty's Government of the wisdom, not altogether for the
sake of Ulster but for the sake of the Empire,
that there should be no more stirring up of
trouble which only spreads elsewhere, which
only causes a conflict in other parts of
the Empire and in other parts of the world,
that there is really no protection against that
except having a firm, strong, well-disciplined
force such as comprised in these three catagories.
Page 5 is for those who are fully mobilised
and become members of the R.U.C., with
full responsibility for the time, but we have
With regard to Class C, I need not touch
upon that Class, which is well known to
everyone as merely the old men, if I may
say, of the Force, or the specially circumstanced men who require protection and are
not physically or otherwise able to go out
to assist in the common danger. I come to
Class C1. Now, C1 is, in my opinion, very
necessary to complete the picture. You have
your mobile A's, the A's who are 60
staunchly helping their brothers of the
R.U.C., to maintain our barracks at full
strength, and you have our B's always on
duty and engaged in civil work. The C's
have a more-shall I call it-military formation, although under the same jurisdiction
as the rest of the Constabulary, and under
my right hon. Friend the Minister of Home
Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates).
The C's have been conceived because there
is always a feeling in my mind that perhaps
our military would be taken away, and that
having no military we have no military
formation to take their place; and the C's
are ready and willing, most of them ex-
Service men, to undergo the fortnight's
training and the drills which take place from
time to time in order to perfect themselves
in case there is a withdrawal of troops from
our area. Just picture the anxiety quite recently with regard to the Near East. You
can imagine the Commander-in-Chief in that
theatre of war calling out urgently for more
troops and more troops if it had been necessary to have gone to war? The people of
Supply-
Special Constabulary.
19 OCTOBER 1922
Ulster, knowing them as I do, would have
said, Well, we will look after ourselves on
behalf of the Empire, and if the British Government requires the troops here they shall
have them." Then we were bound to picture
the gap that would be left by the depletion
from our shores of those fine regiments that
have done so much for us during the past
18 months.

The C's fit into that picture most accurately. They are, of course, more readily got
together and controlled in the largest
centres than in the scattered country areas,
but wherever they have been organised I can
only say that the same good name and reputation have followed them as the other catagories of the Specials, and I am most hopeful
that this scheme, which up to the present
has been so fitting for our needs, may be perpetuated sufficiently long to see us over every
danger. I will, as long as I am needed, not
allow any man to say when that danger is
over except myself. I am the only judge.
I am splendidly advised by my right hon.
Friends here, but, as you know, the final
decision with regard to a matter of such
supreme importance must rest upon the
Prime Minister for the time being.
Until I am perfectly satisfied that the South
of Ireland means business, besides all the
talk that is going on, and proposes to deal
with the miscreants in the way we have dealt
with them here, and brings them before the
bar of justice; until it has secured stable
conditions so that we are able to talk to them
on the same plane as we are happy to find
ourselves here to-day; until they have settled
those crucial points that affect not only
Southern Ireland but Northern Ireland;
until they have thoroughly satisfied the
British Government that they mean to remain loyal and true inside the ambit of the
Empire; and until we can really see all these
things, not only spoken about and hoped for,
but actually accomplished, I certainly will
never say that Ulster is in a sufficiently
satisfactory position to do away with the
magnificent Force which I ask this Committee to support by passing the Estimates
to-day. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. DONALD: Dealing with this Vote,
may I take my mind back to this sum of
money when it was before the House in
another place, due to a request that the right
hon. Gentleman the Prime Minister made
to the Imperial Government. When I take
my mind back to that Supplementary Vote
in the Imperial House, and think of the

whole situation I have come to this conclusion, that even if it was an experiment it was,
in my judgment, a very cheap experiment,
when we take into consideration the state of
the country outside the Six Counties. The
plan adopted by the Prime Minister and our
Government has turned out to be very economical. What is the state on the other side
of the Six Counties? Why, I read the other
day that the Criminal Injury Bill is going
to be 25 or 30 millions.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: It is far more.
Mr. DONALD: I am putting it very
moderately. I have an idea of what it will be
when it comes to the Imperial House for
their sanction, and what will be said. What
I want to make out is this, that if our
Government, for the sake of a few millions,
have, by this method of setting up a voluntary
Force, put the Six Counties into such a position that people can go about their daily
avocations, then I say they have done a great
service not only to the Six Counties but to
the Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
May I say that I think this sum is not
enough, and for this reason? My right hon.
Friend should have kept on all the "A"
Specials, and made the Imperial Parliament
pay for it, in view of the fact that here in
our midst we have law and order. I hope
he will put that argument up to them again.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps my hon.
Friend will not object to me intervening at
this stage. After all I am not a Member of
the Imperial Parliament. My hon. Friend
(Mr. Donald) and several other hon. Members
of this House are Members of the Imperial
Parliament. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I have got £2,850,000 single-handed out of the
Government. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I would ask my hon Friend just to put on
the Table of the House of Commons in Westminster an application for what he thinks
will cover any more of these Special Constabulary, before he does what I think is
very injudicious, holding out hopes to men

the danger of saying all should be kept on.
Would to God I could employ every man in
Ulster. I would do it to-morrow, but as to
the suggestion he makes, is it not holding

have done our utmost here to minimize the

other way that we can spread it over these
men, let him come forward. He and his

but I know, as Prime Minister, a little
Supply-
Special Constabulary.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
courtesy will be extended to me. Let me

I could criticize some of these salaries but
the Prime Minister has stated clearly that
the money is coming from the Imperial
Government, although I must point out that
it is coming from the taxpayers both in
Great Britain and the Six Counties. They
have all got to pay into the same till. However, in view of the condition of things I
am prepared to give my vote in favour of
these Estimates, and I do not wish further
to criticise anything they contain. It is an
economical proposition that if we are able to
keep our country in a peaceful condition by
the expenditure of this sum we should not
hesitate to sanction it, but when it comes to
the question of asking for four or five times
this amount I shall probably vote against it.
Mr. DONALD: If I was not able to get
these millions the Prime Minister referred
to at any rate I have drawn from him a
very important statement. I do not wish in
any way to cause any alarm or misconception.
I will proceed further to develop my argument by asking the Prime Minister if he
could not strike a further reduction in the
pay of the Special Constabulary and thus
retain more men in the Force. That was
the suggestion I was going to make to the
Prime Minister. The Prime Minister said
before that the pay was reduced from 70/-
to 49/- a week. The right hon. Gentleman
knows that from the very beginning I have
always said that the pay was too high. I
maintain still that these men should never
have had 70/- a week. The reply of the
Government was that it was laid down for
them and they did not fix the figure. We
have now arrived at the time when we can
fix the figure. Even 49- will practically be
the wages of a skilled worker in the near
future, and I do not think the Special
Constabulary would have any grievance if
you struck another reduction and thus tried
to keep a few more men on for a further
period. That is my suggestion. They now
have 49- a week, plus an allowance, which
is a considerable amount. A skilled worker
has no "plus" on his 49/-. I say quite
frankly that the Government is justified in
asking for this sum. I know the Prime
Minister is a very good beggar, and if he
will go back again and ask for a further
sum I hope to be in my place to help to
fight for the money he asks for. I know
quite well what is at the back of the Prime
Minister's mind. It is also at the back of
my mind, and that is that we have not yet
passed through the danger zone. I know
that perfectly well. This country, as well
as Great Britain, is passing through a very
trying period. We do not know what the
composition of the next Government is going
to be, and we should hold on until we see
what it is going to be and not make any
reduction in our forces in the meantime. I
do not think there is any room for criticism.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I do not rise for the
purpose of offering any criticism, because
I do not think I am in a position to criticize
the admirable statement made by the Prime
Minister. I think it was a compliment to
the House, and one that the House appreciates, that the Minister of Home Affairs
saw fit to ask the Prime Minister to present
this Vote. It is a very formidable Estimate,
and it is not possible for us to criticize it
in detail. We can only rely on the wisdom
of the Cabinet when they say they endorse
it because it is indispensable and necessary
for the establishment of peace and of law
and order in our midst. We are quite entitled to criticize the Vote if we feel inclined
to do so, and we are not justified in refraining from offering observations upon it on
the ground that we have not got to meet
the bill. I am very much afraid lest it may
become necessary to establish such a system
as this for the permanent protection of our
own area. I would not like it to have to
be done on so large a scalle, but if it is
necessary the House has already subscribed
to the statement of the Prime Minister that
he would vote to the very last penny in
order to organize a force that will enforce
law and order in our midst. We are glad
to know that the Vote will be modified in
future both as regards staff and expenditure.
We are not going to look upon this as a
permanent Vote that will require to be renewed every year. We are very glad to
recognise that peace and order have been
established, and we hope that will be permanent, but if fresh measures are necessary I
think you may rely on this House to vote
any expenditure that is necessary. There
is nothing so important to us as the maintenance of peace, and if peace and order
are restored and maintained in our midst it
is a consequence, almost a corollary, that
we will have industrial prosperity in our
City. That is a very important consideration.

19 OCTOBER 1922
I do not think this Government is in any
way responsible for the condition of affairs
that makes this Vote necessary. It is a
legacy that has been handed down to us and
a burden that has been imposed on the
Government by the condition of affairs that
existed when the Government came into
power. For that we have no responsibility
whatever. I am very much of the opinion
that what is put down to religious, and even
political differences is not after all attributable to that cause. I think we are still
suffering in a moral sense from the aftermath
of the War, and I think the prodigality that
took place during the War has been imitated
on a smaller scale in other places throughout
the world, and even in our own country. I
have the idea that if those who are in spiritual
authority would administer an admonition to
those who are under their care and raise
them to a higher ideal of moral duty something could be accomplished which even the
power of the law or military force would
never be able to effect. Scientists tell us we
have been evolved from a lower to a higher
existence. I suppose it is true in the moral
sense, and I am afraid that the sad spectacle
of murder and outrage that we are looking
on to-day is, as it were, a reversion to type.
I hope it is not so, but very much depends
on those people who are in a position of
most influence to see that such wrong ideas
as obtain at the moment in society shall
quickly disappear. I do not think there
is anything in connection with this Vote
that we are in a position to criticize, and
I can only say that it is with the greatest
possible pleasure that I accord my assent to
the Vote on the ground that the object for
which it was created has been abundantly
realized.

RELIEF OF UNEMPLOYMENT.
Mr. DONALD: It occurred to me that 1
should not allow this opportunity to pass
without making my position clear in regard
to some observations that I made in the
House yesterday. I made them in all
sincerity as a representative of the working
people on the subject of unemployment,
which is causing me as well as the Government grave anxiety. I tried as far as
possible as a Labour representative to centre
my thoughts on how I could assist the
Government in every possible way to bring
about a solution of this great problem. I
offered a solution yesterday, and in consequence of a reply in a sneering way by one
of my Belfast colleagues some misunderstanding got afloat this morning. I want
to be clear about the statement I made. I
congratulated the Government on what they
had done up to the present, and I can see
a possible solution of the problem by means
of a very much larger scheme if the Government will only adopt my suggestion,
which is that they should come to the aid
of the shipbuilders in Belfast at this moment.
The Government may say in reply,
66 That
is a big scheme. That would require legislation." It will not require legislation. Our
Government have it in their power-and they
have the money-as a temporary measure, as
a purely temporary arrangement, to vote
some of this money. Let them meet the
shipbuilders and discuss this thing, and they
will find that what I said yesterday will be
confirmed by the shipbuilders in Belfast,
namely, that if you are prepared to give

taken off the streets of Belfast. I made it
my business since yesterday to confirm the
statement I made here, and I have been
asked to state in this House that, if the
Government will accept this suggestion, or
set up a Departmental Committee if you like,
or meet the representatives of the shipbuilding employers, along with some of the
Members of this House, and take this question
up, in a few weeks you will have ships
started on the slips which are now empty.
That is a bold statement to make, but as a
representative of the workers I am here to
try to do my level best on behalf of the ablebodied men who have been walking the
streets of Belfast for the past twelve or
eighteen months. This would not be the only
Government to adopt such a method. What
is Norway doing to-day? Norway is subsidising the shipbuilding industry, and that industry only, in order to take her people off
the streets and to give employment. What
happened in our country? Only three
months ago there was a ship to be put into

R.I.C. AND R.U.C.
1. Mr. GRANT (for Mr. M'Guffin) asked the
Minister for Home Affairs if he can state
the number of men of the late R.I.C. who,
having refused transfer to the R.U.C., have
since their disbandment been admitted to
the latter Force, also the reason of their
admission?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): 28 Members of the
R.I.C. who withdrew their applications for
the R.U.C. have since their disbandment
been admitted to the latter Force. Each
application was thoroughly investigated, and
in no case was any applicant accepted unless
some special and exceptional grounds for his
withdrawal were disclosed, and that his
former Officers recommended his readmission.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Uniformity of Laws Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed, "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
This Bill, as its title shows, is intended to
apply to Northern Ireland certain Acts already passed by the Parliament of the United
Kingdom. I am sure that so far as general
legislation is concerned we desire to keep
abreast, as it were, with the Imperial Parliament, and accordingly we thought it was
proper that where certain Acts had passed
which but for the separation of Ireland from
Great Britain and the separation of North
from South would probably have been made
applicable to Ireland, these Acts, or some of
them at least, should be applied to Northern
Ireland. Accordingly the Bill before this
House provides that certain Acts which appear in the Schedule, and which are already the law of the land so far as Great
Britain is concerned, should be applied to
Northern Ireland. I do not suggest for a
moment that we should slavishly follow
Great Britain in everything in the way of
legislation, but at the same time where we
find an Act which probably would have been
applied to this country had it not been for
the changes consequent on the Government of
Ireland Act, I think we should as far as
possible try to adopt that legislation, and the
Bill before the House is intended to carry
out that object in so far as it goes.
I know that there are other Acts which hon.
Members perhaps think ought to have been
included in this Bill. We have considered a
XXX
1107 Uniformity of Laws Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Best]
great many of them, and we think those
other Acts will in some respects need modification when applied to Northern Ireland.
Therefore, we came to the conclusion that
instead of putting an Act of that description
in the Schedule and perhaps having to cut it
up more or less it would be better to introduce an Act on the same lines in our own
Parliament and pass it through. One of the
Acts I have in mind is the Criminal Evidence
Act, 1898. That Act would have been passed
for the whole of the United Kingdom in 1898
had it not been for the opposition in the
Imperial Parliament of the Nationalist
Members of Parliament. It was not applied
to Ireland, but we in the North regard it as a
very good Act and I think I may say that we
have come to the conclusion that it ought
to be applied. At the same time, the Act
has been in operation in England for twentyfour years, and certain defects have been
discovered and those can be remedied when
the Bill is introduced here as a new Bill in
our own Parliament. I think it is advisable
that the matter should be dealt with in that
way instead of putting it in the Schedule
and having to cut it into pieces. There are
other Acts we have not included but I hope
hon. Members will be satisfied with the small
but important instalment we are putting
before them this afternoon.
The Act provides that certain Acts passed
by the Parliament of the United Kingdom
which are set out in the several Schedules to
this Act are enacted with the modifications
appropriate to Northern Ireland and set out
in the scheduled Acts, and the scheduled
Acts shall have effect as Acts passed by the
Parliament of Northern Ireland as from the
respective dates specified therein, or if no
date be so specified, from the commencement
of this Act. The first Schedule deals with a
matter connected with the prosecution of
women who had unlawfully caused the death

of their newly-born children.
woman who perhaps in the throes of her
agony and before she had fully recovered
from the pains had destroyed her illegitimate
child, was indicted for murder. The sense
of the community revolted against that, and
juries practically never found a person guilty

Now we want to do away with that as

The Second Schedule deals with the Gaming
Act of 1885. It would be a very difficult
thing to explain to a non-legal audience the
various bearings of the legislation on gaming
transactions, but I think I may sum up
the matter in this way; that under the Act
of 1835 and under certain decisions which
have been given by the Courts, it was possible for a person to be paid a bet by cheque,
and after the cheque had been paid out of
the person's banking account it would be
possible for him under certain circumstances
to recover the money he had paid on
foot of that cheque. Litigation has been
going on over the matter, and there was a
very famous case decided in the Court of
Appeal, Day against Mayo, and another case
was decided this year in the House of Lords,
Sutter against Lewis. It was held that if
I, a person who had made a bet and lost,
paid a cheque over to a bookmaker, and
even though the cheque may have passed
through the Banks and through a number
of hands, still if it can be proved that the
bookmaker ultimately got the money placed
to his credit I should be allowed to turn
round and sue the bookmaker to get back the
money I had paid him. Now all that is going
to be put an end to. Once the money passes,
whether it is money or whether it passes by
way of cheque, it is no longer recoverable; in
other words, you may agree with the thing
in principle or you may disagree, but when
a man has paid money for betting transac
tions he must stand or fall by them. Consequential upon that, suppose, in a case 1
put, I had not been a thrifty young man and
I was, shall I say, scattering my patrimony,
and that I had trustees who were looking
after my estate and all that sort of thing,
the trustees would have been bound to have
sued the bookmaker or the person who got
the money, and if they failed to take that
action they would have been guilty of a
breach of trust. The Act passed in Great
Britain abolishes that state of affairs, and,
therefore, relieves trustees from the perilous
position in which they were placed as the
result of previous legislation and previous
decisions.

1838 it was unlawful to use for

household and every baker's shop. Under

to wipe away that anomaly. The practice
has been in existence for a number of years,

reality is not treated as being illegal, and

remove this illegality. At the same time it
safeguards the public against adulteration,
because it empowers the Ministry of Home

public. Similarly, powers were vested by the

The next Schedule is "An Act to provide
for the better protection of the public in
relation to the sale of tea." I do not think
this requires very many observations.
Select Committee sat in Great Britain in
the year 1914, and this Sale of Tea Act was
carried in the Imperial Parliament as an
agreed Measure. Tea used to be sold in very
heavy paper packets, the net weight of the
tea being less than what was paid for. It
was held in numerous places where attempts
were made to convict the seller of the toa
for obtaining money by false pretences that
the only remedy open to the buyer was by
civil action. That was a very unsatisfactory
state of affairs, because it was not worth
any particular person's while to bring an
action to recover, say, the value of onesixteenth or one-quarter of an ounce of tea.
Accordingly the Tea Act, which was passed
as an agreed Measure, deals with this state
of affairs and makes certain consequential
regulations which, I believe, will be of great
benefit to the public.
The next one is the Fifth Schedule. This
is "An Act to make better provision for
the prevention of fire in premises where raw
celluloid or cinematograph film is stored or
used." The object of this Act was to give
effect to the recommendations of a Special
Committee which sat in the year 1913 regarding the question of the public safety
in shops and other places in which celluloid
films were used or kept. The effect of that
Act passed in Great Britain was to apply
permanently certain Regulations which were
made under the Defence of the Realm Act
for securing safety in connection with celluloid. The Act which is now before the House
is identical with the Imperial Act, subject,
of course, to the necessary modifications to
make it applicable to Northern Ireland. It
provides for the registration of premises in
which raw celluloid or cinematograph films
are stored and for the inspection of those
premises by the Local Authorities. It empowers the Local Authorities to require
reasonable means of escape in case of fire
from such premises, and also prescribes certain conditions of construction and situation
so as to obviate the danger of fire to adjoining premises. The Act also prescribes certain
precautions which must be observed in the
workrooms and store-places. The Bill does
not relate to cinemas. The reason of that is
that they are already dealt with under the
Act of 1909. The expenses of the Local
Authorities are provided for by the payment
of fees. Those are to be prescribed by the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and they are to
be payable by the occupiers of the premises
involved. These fees have already been fixed
in England and Scotland at two guineas a
year by Order of the Ministry of Health
and of the Secretary for Scotland.
Now, I hope I have not detained the House

1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of

arrangement of offices in connection with the

been stated, will be at the disposal of the
Minister of Agriculture in Belfast, what
portion of the technical and administrative
staff of the Ministry will have permanent
offices in the City? Having regard to the
fact that the Minister of Agriculture and
Commerce will have his entire staff in connection with the Ministry of Commerce in
the City, is it not most desirable that his
entire staff in connection with the Ministry
of Agriculture should also be located in the
City?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): It is the decision of the Government that the Administrative Headquarters
of all the Ministries with the exception of
that of the Ministry of Commerce shall be
located at Stormont. In order that the convenience of the public might be met as far
as possible, it was provided that, subject to
the general decision, each Ministry was free
to establish a branch othee in the city. I
went into this aspect of the matter very
carefully and arrived at the conclusion that
in practice, a small branch office of the
Ministry of Agriculture would prove to be
merely a local telephone exchange, and that,
consequently, so far as it was intended to
meet the needs of Members of the farming
community having business to transact with
the Ministry, such an office would be of no
real convenience.
I next considered the question of having a
city office which would be fairly representative of the various departments of the
Ministry's activities, and I now give you the
factors which determined me to have no accommodation in the city other than a Conference or Committee rooms.

Regarding the question which the hon. Member (Mr. Grant) has raised on Section 1, subsection 4, I do not know whether he was

to the House on the Second reading of this
Bill, but I intimated that it would be absolutely impossible for us in a Bill of this

Britain, to accept any Amendment. If in
practice it is found that provision of this
kind creates hardship then we can introduce
subsequent legislation of our own, but the
very frame of this Bill is that we wish to
adopt in Northern Ireland specific Acts which
have been passed in the Parliament of Great
Britain. Accordingly, it would be altogether
foreign to our ideas that we should first start

I think the hon. Member (Mr. Grant) may

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO

Megaw): In moving the Second Reading of
1119 Expiring Laws Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading
[Mr. Megaw.]
this Bill, which has already passed through
all its stages in the Senate, I wish to give a
few words of explanation to the House as to
the necessity of a Measure of this kind. It is
a procedure that is quite familiar to the
British Legislature, and an Expiring Laws
Continuance Bill passes there every year
without comment of any kind. Last year
we had no such Measure here, because we
were not functioning at the time when an
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill would
naturally need to be brought forward, but
the British Parliament, by arrangement
with this Government, passed a Bill that
applied their Expiring Laws Continuance
Bill to Irish measures. The practice of
having an Expiring Laws Continuance Bill
arises in this way: The Legislature, for
various reasons, comes to the conclusion that
it is unwise to give the Government full control, perhaps, over some matter of policy,
and wishes to retain that control from year
to year in its own hands; or it often is not
quite satisfied with regard to the wisdom of
any particular measure, and thinks it would
be as well to pass it through an experimental
stage before putting it upon the Statute
Book. For that reason legislation is often
passed for one year, even in the case of
measures that are intended to have a permanent character. Very often this arises by
way of compromise, but, at any rate, it is
quite a familiar method of legislation to have
certain measures passed for one year. Perhaps the best example of annual legislation
arises in respect of the Army Act in England.
The people of England, for some reason, have
a great distrust of giving the Government
permanent power over the Army, and the
result of that is that the Executive is not
entrusted with the management of the Army
for more than one year at a time. However,
the Army Act does not come within the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill, because it is
usual each year that there should be some
modification of the Act that has been passed
the year before; but in the case of a great
many of the other measures, even where the
working of the Acts has proved quite
efficient, it has been the custom to put a
number of these measures together and to
pass them without change in the form of the
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill. A great
number of those Bills arise in regard to
emergency measures. There are times when
the necessity arises for special legislation
which it is not convenient or proper to make
permanent. A good example of that is to
be found in the legislation during the war,
when so many emergency measures were
passed. Some of these still exist, and, indeed,
some of them are included in the Bill of
which I am now moving the Second reading.
To come to the provisions of this Bill, and
to examine them seriatim, the first Clause
refers to certain measures that have already
been passed for a year, some of them of the
nature I have already mentioned as being
originally intended to be permanent, but
where the Legislature was not quite satisfied
as to the wisdom of the measure, and so they
passed them as expiring laws year by year.
The first Clause is intended here to make a
few of those measures permanent, including
the Employers Liability Act, which was
passed as far back as 1880, and which has
been included in the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill from 1880, till the present
day. Another one is the Motor Car Act,
which enables Local Authorities generally to
control the registration of motor cars and
to make regulations with regard to it. It is
now proposed by Clause 1 to make those Acts
permanent so far as Northern Ireland is
concerned.
Clause 2 provides that certain Acts
mentioned in the Second and Fourth
Schedules are to be repealed altogether so
far as Northern Ireland is concerned. The
Second Schedule contains one Act-or rather
a section of an Act-namely, the National
Insurance Act of 1911, Section 78, by which
certain powers were given to the Insurance
Commissioners, a body which does not exist
in Northern Ireland, and for which no necessity has been found by our Administration
here. The Fourth Schedule contains a
measure which was passed about six months
ago by this Parliament itself. It was one of
a purely emergency character, of which my
right hon. and learned Friend the Attorney-
General (Mr. Best) himself was not particularly enamoured, but which enabled us to
have trials in certain cases without juries.
Since that Act was passed no one has taken
advantage of it. It is alien entirely to our
constitution and to our principles of administering our laws, and we propose in this
Bill to have it repealed altogether.
Clause 3 mentions certain Acts that are to
be continued for one year. Some of these
measures, no doubt, might be made permanent measures, but a good many of them re
quire amendment if the Government had only
time to devote attention to the proper
amendments that are necessary. They include such measures as the Jurors Qualification Act, the Licensing (Ireland) Act of 1902,
and the Workmen's Compensation (War
Addition) Act of 1917, and quite a number of
Acts that are set out in these Schedules, and
it is merely proposed by this Bill now beford
the House to continue these measures in
operation till the 31st December, 1923. Subsection 2 of Clause 3 refers to Acts that are
mentioned in Parts 3 and 4 of the Third
Schedule. These Acts have to do with the
increases in charges on railways and tram-

ways, which were permitted during the war,
and the time has not yet come for any modification of those Acts. The third sub-section
refers also to legislation that was passed for
war purposes, and, though the whole Acts in
these cases are not extended for a year, there
are certain Clauses of them which it has
been found necessary still to include.
The only other Schedule to which I need
refer is the Fifth Schedule. That again refers
to legislation of our own Parliament, part
of it in December of last year, and part
in March of the present year. I refer to the
Local Government Emergency Powers Act by
which Councils, that is County Councils and
Local Authorities, if they did not discharge
the duties imposed upon them by the Statutes
under which they were formed, were dissolvea
by the authority of the Government here.
Well, I do not think the time has yet come
-if one can judge by the feeling of the House
when the proposal was made a short time
ago that the Ministry would have power to
re-constitute them-when the powers that
were given by that Act can be entirely done
away with, and accordingly it is proposed
that the Local Government Emergency Powers
Act shall be continued to April of 1924. The
same reason applies to the Civil Authorities
Special Powers Act. Though the state of the
country is now very much better than it was
when this Act was passed we feel that is
largely due to the powers given to the Government by that Act. We think it would be unwise to take away those powers from Parliament, and that they should be continued for
a year from the time they were originally
given.

Mr. CRAWFORD: I would like to assure
the House that in attempting this afternoon
to voice the feelings of about three quarters
of a million of people who I believe are
suffering under an injustice I am not endeavouring in any way to embarrass the Ministry
in their attempt to make such arrangements
as they think fit for carrying out the business
of this portion of the Empire. I would like
to remind the House that the farming industry is the greatest industry in Northern
Ireland. Without in any way attempting to
minimise the importance of such a thing as
the great shipbuilding concerns that reflect
so much credit on Northern Ireland, I would
like to point out that poultry and eggs alone.
which would be a very small proportion of
what is produced by the farming industry,
amount to more money than the great shipbuilding industry of the City of Belfast. 1
would like to remind hon. Members away deep
down at the very heart of things we have
inspired authority for saying that the King
is served by the people, and it was with
great astonishment that the farming people
throughout the whole of the North read on
the 5th ult. in the public Press that for the
convenience of the public a portion of the
staffs of the Ministers of Finance, Home
Affairs, Education, Labour, and the whole of
the staff of the Ministry of Commerce would
be in the centre of the City. Notwithstanding
the fact that the farming population constituted three-quarters of the whole population of Northern Ireland there was
absolutely no mention of any convenience
being made for agriculture.
On the 6th ult., the day after that appeared.
it was intimated that the Ministry of Agriculture would have a large room in the City
for the purpose of holding conferences. Such
a thing exists already in the City, and if
the Minister of Agriculture had been trying
to manage things in as economical a way as
possible he would have known that in the
future as in the past a room occupied by the
farmers a large room for the purpose-would
be placed free and without expense at his
disposal. If they were only wanting to have
a conference room where they could meet
deputations of farmers that room could have
been had easily and without any expense at
all. It is really of great advantage to farmers
to have a room of this description. The
inference in the answer given by the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Archdale) is that it is
convenient that all papers and statistics, and
the whole of the staff, should be at Stormont.
Just think of the inconvenience that means.
The head office of the Farmers' Union is in
the City of Belfast. Any important branch
of business that they want to bring forward
before the Minister of Agriculture can only
be discussed in a conference room with the
Minister, but they would have to go to Stormont to get any information or statistics or

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Crawford.]
anything of that description.
Bad as that
would be for representatives of the Farmers'
Union it would be a great deal worse for any
farmer coming into the City. We must remember that the work of the Ministry of
Agriculture is not only an administrative
work but an educational work as well, and
farmers coming into the City require not only
to get a leaflet put into their hands but to
get much more valuable information in the
matter of conversation.
Supposing a farmer wants to import an
animal from Scotland for the purpose of improving the breed of his cattle it is necessary
under the present Orders to get a permit to
do it. Is the farmer to be expected to come
into Belfast, and, having transacted his ordinary business, find his way out to Stormont?
It would take more than half an hour in a
taxi to get to Stormont. Is it fair to the
farmer who is introducing an animal to
improve his breed to be compelled to go from
the centre of the City to Stormont to get that
permit? It may be right, but I say it is not
fair to put him to this inconvenience. Supposing he wants to get information as
to the value of manures, a most important thing, or he wants to get information as to the value of seeds, is it
right that he should have to go to Stormont to get the information there from clerks
in that place? Supposing a farmer has got
an idea-and farmers are not destitute of
ideas and are reading rather more now than
in times past-into his head that it would
pay him to produce some other crop than
he was in the habit of producing, and he
wanted to get the statistics of prices as to
how much was paid to produce it in other
places, and wanted to get first hand advice,
is he to go to Stormont? Surely it would be
advisable to get it inside the City.
I am not making any complaint on behalf
of farmers as to the facilities given to other
branches. It is quite right to have the Ministry of Finance in the city. There is no
question in the world about that. In the
matter of income tax we would have no complaint if they removed that a great deal
further away than Stormont. The Home
Affairs are perfectly right. Finance
is largely administrative and attractive and
the Home Office is punitive. Education is
right to have some office in the city, and the
people most interested in it are the trained
teachers who are able to fight their own case
and the result is they have an office in the
city. Commerce is quite right. It is right
that commercial men should have an office in
the city where they can get information
quickly that would help them in their business. None of us complain of that. With
regard to these things we say to the Government what ought to be done ought not to be
left undone, and why agriculture should be
the only one left out is a thing I cannot
understand. Farmers have few people to advocate their claims. Labour is well organised
and can make its voice heard and is always
listened to. No one complains of that. Business men can make their voice heard through
their Chambers of Commerce, but the farmers
are scattered through the country-225,000 of
them, and of that number 115,000 are farmers
under 50 acres. They have not the time to
organise and cannot make their voice felt the
same as other people. The matter is an exceedingly important one, and my mission this
afternoon is to ask the Cabinet of Northern
Ireland to make things easy for these people.
It is said by a great man that the person who
can make two blades of grass grow where only
one blade grew is a public benefactor. Help
these men; help them to produce as much as
it is possible, and make it as easy for them to
help themselves as it is possible to do.
I know that the Ministries can divide their
departments into watertight compartments.
It is comparatively easy to sectionalise these
things, and have one office here and another
there. The Ministry of Agriculture is a
comparatively small department. I would
remind the House that the Minster of Agriculture and the Minister of Commerce are
one and the same person, and much as the
right hon. Gentleman is esteemed throughout
the country-he is a great favourite with the
people, who are on better terms with the
Ministry of Agriculture than at any time in
my memory-clever as the right hon. Gentleman is, he has not any of the qualities
associated with Sir Boyle Roche's bird-he
cannot be in two places at once.
In mercy to the right hon. Gentleman I
ask you to see that the Ministry of Commerce
is in the same place in the city as the
Ministry of Agriculture, and make it easier
for the right hon. Gentleman to continue on
a greater scale in the future the noble work
he has been doing in the past. You may say
it will cost something, and that I have not
advocated anything in the nature of expenditure. It will cost less if the Cabinet make
the place for the Ministry of Commerce a
little larger, and put the Ministry of Agriculture there, and make the system a little
smaller. You will gain in the roundabouts
what you lose in the swings, and the result
will be that the farming population throughout Northern Ireland will be pleased and
gratified. I believe you will be doing a
great work for the country and a great work
for the Government of Northern Ireland. 1
hope the Government will see its way to includa the Ministry of Agriculture along with
the office of the Ministry of Commerce in
the centre of the city.

I cannot sit down without saying how useful and attentive the Central Committee of
the Farmers' Union has been to my Ministry. They have done everything they could
to help. They have put their committee
rooms at our disposal on various occasions.
We have had many committee meetings
there, and everything they could do to help
has been done. They have not attempted in
any way to embarrass us or to cause us discomfort. I have to express my gratitude to
them for all the assistance that they have
given. I hope that my hon. Friend who
started this debate (Mr. Crawford) will be
satisfied with what I have said, and I will
do all I can to give the farmers satisfaction.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I think that my right hon. Friend
who has spoken so energetically in this matter is labouring somewhat under a misapprehension, and as I in my position have had,
perhaps, closer contact with the whole subject than my right hon. Friend who has just
addressed the House, I think, perhaps, hon.
Members will bear with me for a few mo
ments if I explain something of the history
of this transaction as a whole, apart altogether from any question of the accommodation that will be available for the Ministry
of Agriculture. I do not for one moment
wish to derogate from the importance of
agriculture, notwithstanding the suggestion
of my hon. Friend, the Member for the University (Dr. Morrison), that my travels have
not extended sufficiently far to make it possible for me to become acquainted with the
farming interests. I may, perhaps, inform
him that I am a farmer myself, and a very
considerable farmer, as I have had unfortunate reason to know during this period of
depression, and I admit with him that agriculture is the most important industry in
Ulster. I think, therefore, whatever consideration may be shown to other Ministries
should certainly not be lacking in the matter
of agriculture. That is by the way of preliminary.
The history of this whole arrangement can
be summarised in a few words, and let me
suggest that the discussion and the protests
that have emanated from my hon. Friends
are somewhat belated, if I may say so. It
is more than a year since the Prime
Minister called a large representation of the
Province of Ulster, and submitted the proposals for the construction of the Parliament
House and the administrative buildings on
the Stormont Estate. After the matter had
been discussed at considerable length it was
decided unanimously that that was a suitable programme to adopt. Following that,
Adjournment-
24 OCTOBER 1922 Facilities for Farmers.
this programme which I have mentioned was
submitted to this House, and also to the
other House, and it was agreed unanimously
that the Stormont scheme should be proceeded with. No protests of any kind
reached the Government from that periodnow fifteen months ago I am speaking
purely impromptu-until recently to the
effect that there was any objection to the
erection of the administrative offices in the
Stormont Estate. A short time ago the Chamber of Commerce and other public bodies did
give evidence of a desire that there should
be from their point of view a closer connection between the various interests in the
city and in the country, and the Government
by the provision of a central building in Belfast. I was commissioned to discover if
some modus vivendi could not be reached in
this matter, because this fact cannot be
overlooked that during the intervening
period, to which I have referred, the
Imperial Office of Works in London was
concerned with the planning and with the
carrying out of all this vast work. They
have been progressing with the plans and
with the arrangements necessary for the construction not only of the Parliament Buildings, but also the administrative offices.
Therefore, this protest coming at this period
places the Government, and especially that
section of the Government concerned with
this matter, in a position of great embarrassment in their relations with the First Commissioner of Works, Lord Crawford, and the
authorities under him. As I say I went into
this matter with the representatives of the
Chamber of Commerce and others, and out
of all this discussion arose a suggestion,
which, I think, will satisfy even my hon.
Friends who have taken such an interest in
this matter now, and that is that a large
central building should be erected in the city
of Belfast in a convenient position, and that
there should be housed representatives of all
the offices-my own included, notwithstanding that my hon. Friend, the Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison), if I understood him rightly, rather suggested that the
offices under the control of the Ministry of
Finance were not of sufficient importance
to deserve central consideration. I suggested
that the Ministry of Commerce, which
numerically is the least important Ministry
in our Province, and which requires a very
small amount of accommodation as compared
with the other Ministries, should be
accommodated in a central building, and
that, in addition, the various departments
of the Ministry of Finance-the Stamp Office,
the Office of Works, and a number of others
--should also be located there, and that there
should be responsible officers of the various
departments located in the building, so that
not only those coming from the country
concerned with agriculture, but those having
business to transact with other departments,
should be able to get whatever information
was desired when they reached the city,
and would be under no necessity of going to
Stormont in order to reach the point they
had in view. By general consent these suggestions were regarded as acceptable by all
those who were interested in the discussion,
and I do not think that agriculture was left
out of consideration by any means. Therefore I say to the hon. Gentlemen who are
now interested in agriculture that I do not
think they need be concerned or afraid that
there is anything approaching a tendency
to cause inconvenience, or that there
will actually be any inconvenience, in
regard to the method that will be adopted
for the conduct of business concerned with
agriculture by the arrangement which I have
outlined.

POLICE RAID IN FALLS AREA.
1. Mr. DONALD : I thank you, Mr.
Speaker. I beg to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs a question of which I have given
private notice: Whether he is in a position
to give any information regarding a police
raid which is stated to have taken place in
the Falls Road area this morning.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): A party of police this
morning raided a house, No. 14 Dunmore
Street, in the Falls Road area, and discovered, concealed under the floor of the
house and buried in the yard, the following:
37 Rifles.
40 Bayonets.
30 Bombs (most of them detonated).
4 18-lb. Shells.
5,000 rounds mixed rifle ammunition.
1,000 rounds of small arm ammunition.
1 Aerial torpedo.
3 Verey pistols.
10 Revolvers and pistols.
Bag of bomb parts.
1st. Gelignite.
Large bag of detonators.
3 doz. Fuses for land mines.
5 Thompson machine gun drums.
Various parts of machine guns.
13 Bandoliers.
6 Water bottles.
9 Revolver holsters.
Large quantity of mixed shot.
Various parts of small arms.
1 Electric battery.
1 Electric torch.
Three men were found on the premises and
were arrested.
CENSORING OF LETTERS.
2. Mr. DONALD (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether it is
by instructions of the Northern Government
that letters are being censored in Northern
Ireland, and if so, for what reasons.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Letters have been
censored for some time back in Northern
Ireland on the instructions of the Northern
Government in order to assist them in dealing
with the exceptional situation.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
while I agree that it is necessary to take these
steps, may I ask my right hon. Friend if he
is aware that only this week grave anxiety
has been caused to Loyalists through their
letters having been censored, and will he in
future be more careful in censoring the letters
of loyal subjects?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I shall be very glad
indeed if the hon. Member will bring to my
notice any particular case of this kind, but
he may be perfectly satisfied that the Censor
takes great care in carrying out his duties.

Message from Lord Lieutenant.
The PRIME MINISTER, at the Bar,
reported the following Message from His
Excellency the Lieutenant-General and General Governor of Ireland :—
"I cannot leave Northern Ireland without
saying how thoroughly I have enjoyed my
visit and how deeply grateful I am for the
welcome that has been given to myself and
Lady FitzAlan. Both of us have been
greatly struck by the efficient arrangements
made for our visit throughout the Six
Counties, by the authorities both Civil and
Military.
I was honoured on the occasion of my
visit, for I was proud to be invited to
unveil at Enniskillen a Memorial to the
Fermanagh men who fell in the late war;
and I have received during these last three
days a vivid impression of the loyalty and
the active determination, which have meant
so much in the history of the Six Counties.
I have been profoundly encouraged by all
that I have heard and seen of the work
which the Government and Parliament of
Northern Ireland have done for the happiness and welfare of their people, and I see
in the peace and order now prevailing a
notable contribution towards that general
return of prosperity to all Ireland for which
I earnestly pray, and to which I confidently
look."

LICENCES FOR WIRELESS APPARATUS.
Mr. ROBB asked the Minister of Commerce
whether the issue of Licences to use apparatus in Northern Ireland for the reception
and transmission of wireless signals has now
been sanctioned by the General Post Office,
and, if so, what arrangements he has made
with the General Post Office in regard to the
procedure to be adopted, and what steps he
has taken to ensure that the wireless interests
of Northern Ireland are safeguarded.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): I am glad to be able to inform
the House in reply to the honourable Member's question that while the Ministry of
Commerce has no statutory or other powers
in connection with wireless matters it has
come to a satisfactory arrangement with the
Postmaster-General, under which an undertaking has been obtained that Northern Ireland will participate to the same extent as
any other part of Great Britain in all facilities granted by the Postmaster-General.

[Mr. Archdale]
Moreover the Ministry of Home Affairs is
now able, in approved cases, to agree to the
granting of licences, for the reception of
wireless signals, by the Postmaster-General
to persons interested in wireless telegraphy
from the scientific standpoint and possessing
some practical knowledge of the use of wireless apparatus. Applicants for such licences
should apply to the Ministry of Commerce.
In regard to broadcasting no arrangements
have yet been made either here or in the
rest of Great Britain for the issuing of
licences for broadcasting receiving sets,
which are used merely for purposes of
entertainment. The Ministry of Commerce
is, however, making arrangements with the
Postmaster-General in connection with this
matter, in order that as soon as the machinery for the issue of these licences is set up
in Great Britain, similar facilities, adapted
to special local conditions, may be made
available simultaneously in. Northern Ireland.

27 OCTOBER 1922
Adjournment of the House.
Statement by the Prime Minister.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn."-(Capt. Dixon.)
The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend
opposite (Mr. M'Guffin) anticipated me in
suggesting that something might be said
before we adjourn. I had intended to refer
to one or two matters which I consider of
such importance that it would be a pity if
we broke up as a House without my being
able to say a word or two in explanation.
In the first instance I think the House will
consider it only courteous on my part to
refer with the deepest sense of gratitude to
His Excellency the Lord Lieutenant for
having honoured us with a visit-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and not confined himself
alone to the unveiling of the War Memorial
at Enniskillen, but for having visited other
parts of our Province and laid himself out
to get to know as many of the citizens as it
was possible in the time at his disposal. 1
feel sure that all of us are deeply grateful
for the manner in which he made himself
acquainted with our local needs and requirements, and also associated himself with all
those with whom he came in contact. I have
had a wire from His Excellency this morning
announcing his safe return to London, and
I can inform the House that he left here with
the best wishes of all classes and denominations. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I think I may also crave the indulgence of
the House to pay a tribute to Lord Londonderry for the loyal manner in which he has
stuck to us during these trying times. This
is the first time the House has met since he
came to a decision of no ordinary importance
in the life of a man who has devoted himself
to politics, and the House is well aware that
there is no higher ambition that can be felt
by a politician than a seat in the British Government. It was offered to him freely, and
he would have filled with distinction the post
that was allocated to his talents. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We who are in
closest touch with him know of the intense
interest he has taken in the Flying Service,
which, I have no doubt, will become more
and more important as time goes on. His
ideas have been far-reaching and very broad
regarding that branch of the Service for the
defence of our country, and, therefore, it is
something at all events to know that he has
been able of his own initiative to refuse that
high honour on the ground simply and solely
that he felt his duty lay in Ulster and that
Ulster required him and wanted him. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) In interpreting the
feelings of the people he certainly interpreted
my desire, my earnest wish. Therefore, we
as a House tender to him our heart-felt gratitude for having taken the decision that he
did at this time, and we only trust he will
live to remember that in our defence he
thought of us first and himself afterwards.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The next point that I desire to touch upon
is one that I would not have brought into
the House had it not reflected upon the
honour of my colleagues in the Cabinet and
practically upon every Member of this House.
There was a meeting against Prohibition yesterday where the chairman "charged the
Government "-I quote from the paperwith a complete breach of faith and with
weakness in going back on their first idea
of a Royal Commission on the subject at the
clamour of teetotallers." I only wish to
make this remark that there is only one thing,
practically only one thing, that I resent and
deeply resent, and that is the charge of a
breach of faith-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-and I felt so deeply my colleagues and I
were involved in this that I take the earliest
possible opportunity to refute such a charge.
I have in my hand my own election address,
and embodied in it is a manifesto that I issued
to the people of Ulster just before the last
paragraph?
<<
"The first Parliament will be faced with
problems gravely affecting the future. The
best way to extend our resources, expand
trade, stabilise agriculture and other industries, re-model education, amend the
Licensing Laws-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and to ensure a brighter future for
the great masses of workers in our midst
is to begin by concentrating on the supreme
issue of securing a strong working majority.
without which government could not be
carried on, and without which society must
inevitably fail."
I stand on these words at the election. It
was forecasted there quite clearly that the
first Parliament would be faced with the problem of amending the Licensing Laws, and I
repudiate in the strongest language that there
has been any breach of faith by the Government; and I would also like to say that from
that date to this the Temperance Party,
either inside this House or outside this House,
have never approached me on one single
occasion to fulfil that pledge in our election
address-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-because I believe the people of Ulster trusted
that what we put into that was sincerely
meant by those of us who signed it. And,
therefore, I must pay a tribute to those who
so keenly feel on this subject that they have
never by word or sign indicated that they
thought the time had come to deal with this.
When as a Cabinet some short time ago we
reviewed the situation and when we, I think
quite rightly, diagnosed the fact that we had
reached somewhat calmer waters and that
there was no risk of the disturbances which
we had in the past, we thought we ought
Prime Minister's Statement. 1144
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Prime Minister]
loyally to carry out what each of us subscribed to in our election address, and we
intend to do it. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I am only sorry that the words I used when
I first mentioned this in the House have not
carried more weight. It is our desire, and
I am sure it is the desire of all hon. Members
of this House, to be fair and just in the
matter, to be moderate to a degree, in order
that there should not be started throughout
Ulster any division of opinion amongst those
Loyalists who have carried us so far on the
path of peace and prosperity. Even at the
eleventh hour I appeal to all to be moderate
in their language, to study these questions
purely from the point of view of advantage
to the people as a whole, and not allow to
creep in any acrimony such as was apparent
in the report of the meeting that was held
yesterday.
I now come to the fourth point I would
like to touch upon, that is with regard to the
calling of the House together again. The
House is fully acquainted with the situation
across the Channel, and hon. Members acquiesce in the view that this House should rise
as early as possible in order to release hon.
Members of this House who have to seek reelection, and who otherwise have to take part
in a campaign which may have a very vital
effect upon the future of our province.
Therefore, in deciding to adjourn with the
power of calling the House together again, it
will be within the recollection of everyone
that when the 6th of December is passed the
month begins in which we will have to make
the choice either to vote out dr remain
within the Free State. There has never been
any doubt in the mind of any hon. Member
of this House on that point. At the same
time we have to go through the formula of
doing it, and, therefore, we are very anxious
to sit as soon as possible in the early stages
of that month in order that it may not go
forth to the world that we had the slightest
hesitation about the act we propose to take.
If there was any delay people would wonder,
whereas if we take the first moment available
for us to call the House together and to lay
before it a motion which the Government will
propose, then I think there can be no misunderstanding in any part of the globe about
our continued anxiety to remain with Great
Britain in the closest possible alliance, and
at the moment, at all events, to stay quite
clear of a Dublin Parliament. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
That will be the important business, but by
then it may be possible to consider any other
matters that have arisen in the meantime. I
hope and trust that the anxious questions
which will be engaging my attention between
now and that date will eventuate with success
to our province. I need hardly emphasise to
the House the gravity of the questions that
still remain outstanding-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-but I know that in my absence,
as I must be a great deal in London in
connection with this ticklish business, not
only will Members of this House but the
people of the whole Six Counties will stand
firm and true together, so as to get over
what I sincerely trust will be the last fence
leading to the land of promise, peace and
happiness to our people. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. M'GUFFIN: I do not purpose to
occupy the time of the House in following
the right hon. Gentleman in the statement
he has made, but I would like to express,
-and I think I am warranted in doing it-on
behalf of the Labour Members, our recognition of the very magnanimous action of the
Minister of Education in retaining his portfolio in this Government rather than taking
what, under the circumstances, would have
been undoubtedly a more conspicuous
position in the Imperial Parliament. We
believe Lord Londonderry is qualified for
either position, but particularly for the one
he occupies here. He has done good service
in the Department that he adorns at the
moment, and we are quite convinced that his
work will still be of great advantage to us
as a Government and lead to successful reform in our education system in the North
of Ireland.
The particular point I had in view in
rising was to support the Prime Minister in
repudiating the suggestion made by the
Distillers' and Brewers' Association with respect to the attitude of this House
temperance question. If it were represented
to me that I was coming into the House
setting aside my convictions with regard to
the temperance question and with no right
of prerogative to express them in this House,
1 would not have been a candidate at the
last election, nor would I have been a Member of this House to-day. I had given a
specific pledge, not a promise. I was aware
of the pledge given by the Prime Minister—
if you call it a pledge, when he said he would
favour temperance reform. I do not think
that in any sense we have broken our pledge.
We are not out to sacrifice the interests of
the trade. We are not out for confiscation.
I am pledged to that extent-I am not out
for that. I am out for reform, and that is
what is demanded by the Prime Minister
himself-nothing more than reform, such reform as will be beneficial to the community,
and such reform as the Temperance Party
will insist on having.
I am glad to know
that the Prime Minister is fully alive to the
dangers and difficulties of the situation, and
the House is prepared to support him in any
action he may take to have the rights and
privileges of our House established by such
a measure as may be necessary. That is all
I wish to say with respect to the matter. I
Adjournment.
Adjournment.

I had not expressed my attitude with regard
to the temperance question I would not have
done my duty.

Adjournment of House.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House, at its rising this day, do adjourn
till Tuesday next." (Captain Dixon.)
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
As far as I know we ought only to occupy
two or three days when we meet to close up
the business for this year. I may say that we
called the House together for a special purpose to-day, and we did not like to continue
the business because there are steps that have
to be taken between now and next week.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Before we assent to that
Resolution I would like to know how long the
House is likely to sit next week, and if we
are to expect any more important business
than that already announced. I see the Imperial Parliament is rising about Thursday,
and I would like to know if the sittings of
this House will continue beyond that date.
Question: "That this House, at its rising
this day, do adjourn till Tuesday next," put,
and agreed to.

Constitution Act-
7 DECEMBER 1922.
The PRIME MINISTER: I think it will be
for the convenience of the House if I read the
terms of the humble Address to his Majesty
in the first instance, make a few remarks on
the subject afterwards, and that, unless some
very important point arises that hon. Members would care to discuss, we should allow
this very important and serious Address to
go through without unnecessary discussion.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There are
several reasons for such a course. We desire
that it should get to the Senate at the earliest
possible moment in order that they may likewise take their part in opting out of the Free
State, and that there should be no risk run
of the Addresses not both crossing over to be
in the hands of His Majesty to-morrow. My
suggestion, therefore, is that, as there are
other matters on which I myself would like
to make a few comments, we should confine
ourselves really to debate when the Motion
for Adjournment is put, when we can cover
all the ground and express our opinions quite
freely as to matters that have recently happened. The Address which I beg to move is
as follows:
MOST GRACIOUS SOVEREIGN,
We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland
in Parliament assembled, having learnt of
the passing of the Irish Free State Constitution Act, 1922, being the Act of Parliament
for the ratification of the Articles of Agreement for a Treaty between Great Britain
and Ireland, do, by this humble Address,
pray your Majesty that the powers of the
Parliament and Government of the Irish
Free State shall no longer extend to
Northern Ireland.
In moving this humble Address I desire
first of all to say that no one could take exception to the fact that we assemble at the
earliest possible moment in order to make
perfectly clear not only to Southern Ireland
but to the world that, so far as we in Ulster
are concerned, we have no desire to do more
than co-operate with our separate institutions here for the prosperity and peace of the
whole of Ireland. No one in this Assembly,
and certainly none of the Loyalists in Ulster
have expected any other action on our part
for a very long time past, and I am sure hon.
Members will acquit me of any ambiguity on
this subject since I have had the honour to
lead them in this House. The Provisional
Government in their debates yesterday
touched upon the question of Ulster at some
time, either sooner or later, desiring to join
up with them in some form, or other in order
to secure what they call the co-operation and
unity of Ireland. I have to say with regard
to that that the only possible way of securing
co-operation and happiness is for the South to
settle its own affairs, and for the North to
carry on as it is at present under its own
Parliament, its own Executive, and its own
other authorities. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) There is no use our holding out at the
moment any hopes whatever of a desire on the
part of the Ulster people to go in under a
Dublin Parliament. To reiterate this over
and over again becomes necessary, because
some people seem to take fright at an action
here or an action there which ought not in
any way to cause alarm. I would like to
point out that so long as I stand at this Table
there is no thought in my mind, and certainly never any desire in my heart, to do
other than carry on the Northern Government with its own Parliament and its own
affairs, so that there is at all events a very
good barometer for the people to judge by in
finding me still at this Table. The moment
there is any question of going under
Dublin Parliament I refuse to stand here.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I cannot conceive that it is for the good of the people
or for the good of Ireland as a whole to
attempt anything of the kind, and therefore
we may go ahead in our own way for the
betterment and well-being of our own people
here, trusting that the South may settle its
affairs and get settled down to good government.
a
There may be in the minds of some people
an idea that it is a sign of weakness
because I. and my colleagues have
endeavoured strenuously to secure peace
in the Six Counties and have asked our
fellow-citizens, the minority in our midst,
to come along and to work with us, because
I have urged as far as possible we should
forget the past and take up the future together, working together for our common
interest, which is the prosperity of the people
as a whole. It is a sign of strength.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is only
when one is in a powerful position that one
can afford to make these appeals to the people
and, because I myself am of a pacific disposition though very stubborn, I would not for
a moment have people misunderstand any
action which I may take from time to time
and which I think is for the good of our
people in the Six Counties. Having made
our position perfectly plain and a position
which indicates no change in our hearts or
in our minds, we do not desire to take any
provocative action to-day. We are simply
fulfilling our old decision, our old determination, to vote out and to remain an
entity ourselves. I cannot add anything to
what has been said on former occasions regarding this very important matter, but I
would just like to quote Mr. Cosgrave's own
words, with the substitution of "Great
Britain and the Empire" in one line of it,
as what I think is a very fitting conclusion
to the remarks I make to-day on this subject

The Prime Minister]
as they were the concluding remarks of his
on a similar subject yesterday. He said:
"In so far as the Government and myself
are concerned, we shall say nothing or do

common
I think that if we take those words as relating to ourselves and Great Britain and the
Empire we have said all that can be said on
a matter of this kind. The South have decided that they can do better separated from
the great Mother of the Empire, that they
can do better isolating themselves and becoming what they call a Free State. We,
on the other hand, say, No. We can do
better for ourselves and for the Empire by
maintaining the closest connection between
Great Britain and ourselves-a connection
which has served us in the past and has also
served our colonies in the past, that has
served the whole of the vast Dominions over
which His Majesty rules; and there is no
question whatever that the old standard of
Great Britain throughout the world is a
standard which many countries would desire
to copy.
We, however, feel safe and sure
whilst we remain under the Imperial Parliament. We have hon. Members who represent us there, we have our right there,
we have our say there on those affairs which
affect the country and the Empire as a whole,
and we have our own institution here with
our Senate and our Commons, and I pray
God as long as I have anything to do with
it we shall remain steadfast in the true
faith. I beg to move. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. M'GUFFIN: On a point of order. I
did not know you were going to conclude so

some persons who will say they occupied a
