ADJOURNMENT OF THE HOUSE.
Statement by the Prime Minister.
The Boundary Question.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn." (Captain
Dixon.)
The PRIME MINISTER: I wish to thank
the House for the very cordial way in which
they have supported me in the suggestion that
we should discuss any matters of importance
when we are out of the Free State instead of
when we are in it, although that is a mere
technicality. I observed with astonishment
some remarks made yesterday in the Southern
House, and it is because I fear that certain
persons may take alarm at the views expressed
regarding the Boundary Commission that I
desire to say something of serious importance
to this House to-day. We are all aware of the
various criticisms made from time to time
regarding the Boundary Commission, and the
House has still in recollection my statement
on behalf of the Government that we would
take no part in that Commission. (Hon Members: Hear, hear.) The House still bears that
statement well in mind. I had the pleasure
7 DECEMBER 1922,
Adjournment--
The Boundary Question. 1152
when in the Maiden City of Londonderry a
few nights ago to explain with the Press present that as time went on the conviction of
the Government and myself is becoming
stronger and stronger in that direction. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) May I make one more
remark with regard to the whole Border?
This bargain was entered into by the wrong
people. We feel no responsibility for
assisting to carry out a bargain which
was arranged behind our backs, and
must have been arranged with the full
knowledge of the signatories to the Treaty
that it was a breach, and a most serious
breach, of a distinct pledge of the Prime
Minister to me personally. Therefore, I sweep
away altogether the idea that by implication
or in any other way we can be dragged into
this Commission. When the outrageous attack was made, the incursion across our boundaries, the British Government said, "We
will help, but you must take steps to protect
yourselves. We will support you and give
you money to pay for your Special Constabulary, but you must ask the people to rise and
protect themselves." And right nobly did
they respond to that appeal. (Iion. Members:
Hear, hear.) But just as they rose to that
appeal, just as they, made such sacrifices, just
as they came forward and, some of them, laid
down their lives in this matter-and many of
them suffered and their blood is still upon
the heather, it is still almost at the cottage
door on the borderland where these men were
defending it from outside aggression-just as
they responded, so does it become more and
more utterly impossible to impose a Commission upon such people. Some persons, including Mr. Austen Chamberlain himself, talked
about this Commission merely bringing into
the North those dissatisfied persons who are
over the border and putting out of the North
those persons who are dissatisfied and want to
get into the Free State. Behind all that is
the practical question: Who is going to do it?
May I just illustrate this very clearly, because there is no use, now that the Free State
Bill has been consummated, in my holding
my hand any longer in these matters? Yesterday, by implication Mr. Cosgrave was still
throwing out the suggestion that because of
the recent election, Tyrone and Fermanagh
might possibly be voted by this Commission
into the Free State. Now, just picture
Tyrone and Fermanagh, and picture Mr. Cosgrave or his representative and myself or my
representative sitting at a table with a third
party-and I cast no reflections upon the third
party; we do not know who he is; he may be
a distinguished judge or he may be anyoneno matter how distinguished or powerful he
may be, or what great capabilities he may
have for the position makes no difference to
my argument. The whole thing is that if
Mr. Cosgrave or his representative claims the
whole of Fermanagh and Tyrone, and if I
say I am not going to give away one inch of
the soil of Fermanagh and Tyrone, does it not
immediately mean that the destinies of these
two counties rest in one hand-in the hand of
one man? Was there ever such a preposterous
suggestion? If I cannot give way on the question of Tyrone and Fermanagh, and the other
man will not by any sort or manner of means
reduce his demand for the two counties, is
there not a complete deadlock without a
chance of success, and is not any Chairman,
whoever he may be, in the position of having
to decide the fate of these two places, and of
Derry City?
I once had a most interesting conversation
with Mr. Lloyd George on this subject, and
I remember very well saying to him in regard to this Commission: "You may have
set a match not only to a magazine of grave
difficulties in our own country, but you may
have aroused a religious war in our
colonies." I said to Mr. Lloyd George: "Do
you know that there is not an Orange
standard throughout the whole world which
has not got inscribed upon it Derry, Enniskillen and the Boyne?" I said it was unthinkable that the fixing of the boundary
should rest in the hands of one man-one
man who probably did not understand Ireland or
Irish history, one who might by
a stroke of the pen hand over the
houses. the homes, the cottages of those
gallant men who had spilled their blood for
the safety of their own country, and one who
might also sacrifice those historic emblems
which every Protestant banner bore throughout Canada, Australia, and America as well
as here at home. Our hon. Friend (Mr.
Coote) whom we are so delighted to see back
with us again after his very long and very
useful travels across the ocean, will be able
to confirm me in saying that the feeling
abroad is as strong as the feeling on the very
walls of. Derry. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). Therefore, it ill becomes any man to
suggest that it would be possible for me or
anyone in the Goverment, on behalf of whom
I am speaking here, to lay our hands to such
dirty work. It will not be done. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I am not quite sure
whether the House is aware that whilst the
Free State Constitution was being got
through the House in Dublin as well as the
Imperial Parliament there was almost a
chorus that the Treaty was sacred.
It was
the Treaty, nothing but the Treaty, and every
word of the Treaty. Sentiment did not
count for anything. The interpretation was
another matter. What they had to do in
Dublin and the Imperial House of Commons

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
and the House of Lords was to stick to that
Treaty word for word and line for line.
To tell the truth I was rather glad that
was the attitude taken by those in Dublin
who were so anxious to get the Treaty, and
for this reason: I held from the very beginning that the portion of the Treaty which
deals with the Commission is ultra vires.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I have held
that opinion straight through without any
hesitation whatever. I believe it is common
law that if an arbitration is suggested, and
one party to that arbitration refuses to function, the arbitration cannot take place. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). It is my deliberate
opinion, and I am fortified by the opinion
of counsel of the highest eminence, which I
have in my pocket at the moment, that if
the two who entered into this bargain behind
our backs agree together and say that there
is to be a Boundary Commission, they will
find that it is impossible for them to have
such a Commission. And they dare not
bring an Amending Bill through the House
of Commons-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear) ---
because, thanks to the indefatigable energies
of our delegation recently in going through
the whole of the constituencies, we have
secured a majority for Ulster in the British
House of Commons that would not pass a
Bill which would impose on us some persoa
to act for us as a member of that Commission.
Therefore I feel perfectly clear in my mind
that if one party to the arbitration is
sufficiently stubborn-and I have already
said that I am very stubborn in a matter of
this kind-then the Commission cannot get to
work, and therefore the drafters, those who
put their heads together and drafted the
Constitution of the Free State have made a
drafting error, and the consequences can rest
upon them, and them alone. I was never consulted, and this House and the country were
no party to it. The House may suggest that,
therefore, a deadlock has been reached. May
I read the words of one of the signatories to
the Treaty only a few days ago? Sir Laming
Worthington-Evans on the 6th November
said:
I do not believe for one moment that such
a body would ever come into existence. I
feel certain the sound common sense of Sir
James Craig and Mr. Cosgrave would assert
itself in a satisfactory settlement on the
lines of mutual consent.
That is the statement of one of the signatories to the Treaty. I have already quoted
Mr. Austen Chamberlain, who said it was
merely a boundary business, a clipping, and
so on. He is another signatory to the Treaty.
The Prime Minister said- I am quoting Mr.
Lloyd George-
Six Counties but a readjustment of the
boundaries of the North of Ireland.
What we propose, I think, is wise for
Ulster, namely, that she should have a readjustment of the boundaries not for the
A readjustment of the boundaries of the North
of Ireland means, of course, that there would
be give as well as take. There is no other
meaning.
Then we may take the statement which was
made by Mr. Bonar Law, the present Prime
Minister, who spoke so feelingly on this subject on the 15th December last. He said:
I am going to deal now with the only
aspect of this Treaty which is open to
serious objection. That is as to the Boundaries Commission. If ever the Ulster
people considered that anything was settled.
and settled for ever, it was the boundaries.
I think it is hardly worth while elaborating, but I may point out that in the letter
written to me by the Prime Minister just
before the last election he specified that in
dealing with Ireland anything which interferes not with Ulster but with the Six
Counties is impossible. That was not accidental. We know, everybody knows, how
bitter the controversy was over it during
the passage of the Home Rule Bill. My
right hon. Friend the Member for Paisley
knows, I think, that it would have been
settled but for that difficulty. That latter
was worded in that way to settle that question so that as far as this Government and
Parliament were concerned it could not rise
again. Then, of course, there was the passing of the Act of 1920, and there was the
King opening the Parliament of Northern
Ireland. Nothing, one would have thought,
could have been more binding than all these
things, but I want to say something else.
In substance, I do not think that that is so
important. In the secret negotiations
which were carried on by my right hon.
Friend, the Member for Paisley, with the
view of settling this question, we who spoke
as representing Ulster were prepared to
have an adjustment of the boundaries. If
we had agreed to some clearly defined modification of the boundaries I am inclined to
think they would have accepted it. The
great mistake which has been made is that
the Government should have put this provision in, signed, scaled and ratified, without consulting Ulster.
Now, there is our case placed as plainly as it
could be by the present Prime Minister, and
I say standing here at this box, on behalf of
my colleagues and myself, that there can be
no adjustment of the Ulster boundaries without the free consent of both North and South
--(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and that so
far as I and my colleagues are concerned we
will not give our assent to anything in the
nature of a boundary adjustment unless the
specific border counties are satisfied themselves. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is
not for us to take any supreme authority in

Mr. COOTE: I wish very briefly to thank

The PRIME MINISTER: The hon. Gentleman is quite wrong. From yesterday Dublin
Castle ceases to exist, and my right hon.
Friends here, the Minister of Agriculture and
the Minister of Labour, have nothing whatever to do directly or indirectly with Dublin
Castle. Everything is carried on by Great
Britain. In other words, they carry on the
Post Office and other services, and the only
difference is that until a period has arisen
when we can come to some arrangement with
the South they carry out the duties allocated
to the Joint Council of Ireland, as far as the
Northern portion is concerned, and Dublin
has nothing to do with a single inch of Ulster
soil.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Do they deal with records?
The PRIME MINISTER: No.
Mr. COOTE: I brought this matter forward
so that I could get an answer in the House.
I want to ask the Prime Minister what office
is to take the place of Dublin Castle?
The PRIME MINISTER: The ordinary
method of communication between this Government and the British Government will in
future, I believe, be through the Home Office,
as we were never a Colony. At the same

Government have to say which is the most

indicated that it would be more proper and
more in accordance with the feelings of the
people of this Province if they communicated
through the Home Office.
Mr. COOTE: I do not think the Ulster
people care one straw what office takes up

indirectly with Dublin Castle, because there

Mr. Cope, and we do not wish to have any

Office to administer it as the Local Government Board would if they had been responsible? Instead of this they set up a Committee consisting, I think, of three representatives of the British Government, a representative from Northern Ireland, and one
from Southern Ireland. But suppose, again,
that in this three-cornered compact Southern
Ireland does not act, then is our scheme for
the erection of cottages for ex-Servicemen to
fall to the ground, and are we to be debarred

The PRIME MINISTER: No. I have taken
Counsel's opinion on that point. As long as
we pass the necessary legislation we can go
abead even if the South declines to move.
Mr. COOTE: These replies of the Prime

that we in Ulster are in a different position

These two peoples are in exactly the same

in London, but we in Ulster are in a different

we have a right to have free access to England, Scotland, and Wales, just as they have
a right to have free access to our ports. 1
think it is putting us in a very invidious and

have
any control over the Diseases of
Animals in Southern Ireland, but Great

rade here to-day, but they would not agree

I think that deals with that point. The next

I am sure my hon. Friend opposite (Mr.

to make is that it was not our Prime Minister

The third point made by my hon. Friend

fullest confidence in the Prime Minister and

If we have not got control of those reserved

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: There are just
one or two observations that I wish to make
on the various points that have been mentioned here during the last few minutes.
First of all. I think this House will be impressed with one thing, and that is the wis
dom of the course that this Parliament and
the people of Ulster adopted in having their
representatives in the Imperial Parliament.
We see that questions vitally affecting Ulster
as a whole will be dealt with there from time

forceful and effective way that the representatives from Ulster in the Imperial Parliament have dealt not only with this question
of the restriction upon cattle, but with other
matters that are vital to the prosperity and

A good many things have happened since we

one question that everybody in Ulster is interested in-that is the question of the boundaries and after that speech I do not think

whole. The only observation that I would
make in regard to the question of the boundaries is this: this House, I believe, has the
I think the question of the ex-Servicemen's

made when we have secured a Governor-

Hear, hear.) The hon. Member for Fermanagh
and Tyrone has told us that we have had to

not to go to Dublin Castle now on any matter, and Ulster's position as a separate governing entity has been emphasised by the fact
that we are going to have a Governor-General
for Ulster itself. That is a very big advance
on anything that existed previously.
There is another matter in which a considerable improvement has been made by this
Consequential Bill. The hon. Member for
Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr. Coote) elicited
the fact that the probability is that we might
in future not be dealing with the Colonial
Office, but that we might be dealing with the
Home Office. Of course, that may be an improvement or it may not. I believe there is
at the Home Office at the moment an Ander.
son who was formerly at Dublin Castle, but
there may be others there to deal with matters affecting Ireland. If I read the Consequential Bill aright. I think we have secured
some very valuable improvements. On the
financial question I think we have made progress. The arrangements that have been
arrived at are, I think, very much more
elastic than what existed in the 1920 Act. The.
question of the just contribution that Ulster
should make towards the Imperial Services is
going to be adjusted without any undue
delay. Various facts have to be taken into
consideration, and I hope the Minister of
Finance will agree with me that a very considerable improvement has been effected
there, and that the matter has been considerably simplified by the arrangements that
have been arrived at. Those are the various

I think this House and country will endorse
the Prime Minister's attitude in regard to
the boundaries, and they will have the fullest
confidence in him and his Ministers in regard
to any future action that they may take. I
think we have a right to congratulate ourselves upon the successful efforts made by
the Government in effecting various and considerable improvements by the Consequential
Bill. I sincerely hope that we are now settled
as a Government upon strong and firm foundations, that this House and the people as a
whole will work loyally together, and that
they will co-operate in the efforts of this
Government in all that they may do to establish law and order and to have a peaceful
community. I believe, notwithstanding all
the difficulties that we have passed through,
that there never has been a period in our
history as a Government here in Ulster that
is so full of promise as it is to-day. I believe
all the difficulties will be surmounted, and
that through the goodwill of the people and
through the energy and ability of the Government as a whole, in the coming days we will
see an Ulster not only loyal to the British
connection, but anxious to do everything
that they can to help Great Britain and to
help the Empire, and in that way they will
be true to their best traditions. I hope further that in our efforts in the coming days
we will be able so to legislate that we will
help our people as a whole, and thus make
Ulster a happier and a more prosperous place

I think we should do nothing at the moment

people? The people are living amicably to-

gether, and will be living as amicably in the

suggested that something might be done by

later. Let us abide by the Act as it is. Mr.

an adjustment of what I may call the perimeter of the area, something where there is
one portion that can be beneficially transferred to another, and vice versa, but that
would be a dangerous policy, especially when

area that it might involve the taking of large

pin our faith to the expression of opinion

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

With regard to the Council of Ireland I

land? It was put in specifically, I believe,

that the object which we are going to facilitate? I hope it is not. I would say with

should stick rigidly to what has been guaranteed under the 1920 Act, not swerve one

throughout Great Britain that we are going
to recognise only the 1929 Act, that we are
not going to permit any tampering with our
interests in this matter, but that we are going
to insist upon that 1920 Act in all its particulars. If we do that, we will be doing something to spread abroad a specific policy on
the part of the Government, and we will be
giving to people of the North what they will
recognise as an assurance of security.

NEWTOWNSTEWART POSTAL
SERVICES.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of Commerce if he is aware that farmers and others
living within a mile of Newtownstewart are
handicapped by the fact that their letters
and newspapers, which are received in the
Newtownstewart Post Office about eleven
o'clock a.m., are kept over until the next
morning, and whether, in the interest of the
trade of the district, he will use his influence
with the Post Office authorities to revert to
the arrangement of some months ago, when
the departure of the postmen was delayed
until the day's mail came in?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): This matter was taken up by
the Ministry of Commerce with the Postal
Authorities in October last. The system of
delaying the departure of the postmen to
which the hon. Member refers and which
was in operation during the summer months
not only dislocated the system of collection
for the evening outward mail, but frequently
kept the postmen on duty till a very late
hour, and accordingly the Postal Authorities
cancelled this temporary arrangement.

SUSPENDED URBAN DISTRICT
COUNCILS.
2. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs if he will give the
number of Urban District Councils in the
Northern area which were suspended owing
to their refusal to recognise the Northern
Government; and if he will state what is the
policy of the Government in regard to these
Councils?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): Four Urban District Councils
were dissolved by Order of the Ministry, and
the Commissioners appointed to discharge the
duties of these Councils will remain in office
until the 16th January, 1923, when the new
Councils to be elected at the forthcoming
municipal elections come into office.
As the hon. Member is aware, all newly
elected members of local authorities must
make a declaration of allegiance before they
can act as such.

Loans Guarantee Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This small Measure known as the
Loans Guarantee Bill, of which it is now
my duty to move the Second Reading, is an
adaptation of a much more pretentious
measure called the Trade Facilities Act.
which has been passed recently by the Im-
1179 Loans Guarantee Bill-

Second Reading.
perial House. The British measure consists
of three separate sections devoted to three
separate and distinct subjects. This measure
of ours, on the other hand, concerns itself
with only one single matter, and is designed
to achieve only one single object, and that
is to assist industry and at the same time
to create employment in our own area. As
the House will observe it contains practically
only one Clause with six sub-sections, and it
is so comparatively simple in its character
that its import will be readily grasped by
bon. Members. As its name implies it is a
guaranteeing measure, that is to say it is a
measure intended to authorise the Government to guarantee loans to public bodies, to
Corporations, and to other persons, provided
that there is sufficient security behind the
borrowers to warrant the Government in
undertaking the liability of guaranteeing the
lenders against any possible loss. It is a
fact, of course, that there is a clear differentiation between lending and guaranteeing.
The duty of the Government under this Bill
is simply to guarantee and not to lend.
Towards the end of the year 1921, it will be
remembered, a Bill of a similar character,
authorising the Government to guarantee
manufacturers and others, passed the Imperial Parliament with a maximum of
£25,000,000. This was largely taken advantage
of on all hands, and the results from the
point of view of the employment of labour
were of such a satisfactory character that
the Government considered it wise to pass a
similar measure the one to which I have
referred earlier guaranteeing a maximum of
a second £25,000,000 for exactly similar pur
our case it is proposed
to follow the precedent of the Imperial
Government in respect of the procedure
under this Bill, that is to say we propose to
establish a small Advisory Committee composed of three persons of financial experience, intelligence and independence, whose
duty it will be to determine on the evidence
which is submitted to them whether the
conditions or circumstances of the applicants
conform to the intentions of this Act. The
two primary considerations involved are,
first, that the security offered is sufficient
to warrant the Government in undertaking
the liability, and, second, that the amount
of employment provided under the scheme is
commensurate with the Government guarantee. These two important considerations
will be determined by the Investigating
Committee to which I have just referred.
This Committee will have the assistance of
experienced technical persons, such as trained accountants of knowledge and experience,
to advise them on this matter, while the veto
of the Ministry of Finance is, of course,
constantly maintained.

:
The principal advantage of this measure
arising from a Government guarantee to
individual firms is that a low rate of interest
can possibly be secured by having the Government guarantee behind the transaction.
This guarantee will be offered to banks,
large insurance companies, and institutions
of that class which are in the habit of advancing money under certain measures of
security, while at the same time it will,
I am sure, be agreed that it will enable
individual firms to use their own capital to
a larger extent in developing industrial
works in fact, the facilities which will be
offered them in this measure will assist in
providing them with liquid capital with
which to carry on their own undertakings
with greater energy than perhaps they
would otherwise do. Again, the main concern of our Government, naturally, in prosecuting this Bill is that work may be
provided for the unemployed, and I can
hardly think that any sacrifice we would
make, or could make, would be too great to
accomplish such a desirable result. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Unlike Great
Britain, our industries are not sufficiently
distributed or widespread, and we are peculiarly unfortunate in this respect, that
our two staple industries here-shipbuilding
and linen-are just the two industries which
have been most severely stricken by the
unexampled depression of trade with which
we are all familiar.
use our
The author of the Excess Profits Tax, the
present British Prime Minister, has, I
believe, admitted that the extraction of such
vast sums of money from industry has had
its repercussion in the present conditions of
trade, whilst I think it is generally agreed
that the heavy burden both on national and
local taxation is probably the greatest of the
contributory causes of the deplorable conditions of unemployment at the present time.
It is useless, I suggest, to moralise upon the
causes unless by an analysis of the causes
we could discover and administer some
remedy, but I am sure of this, that we
cannot make any mistake if we
utmost endeavours to provide facilities for
encouraging those of our people who can
and who are willing to prosecute schemes
for encouraging the employment of labour
which would, I have no doubt, ameliorate
the conditions under which we are unfortunately labouring at the present time. The
employment of men is in one sense more
important than that of women, because it
is obvious that the man, who is generally
the head of the house, makes provision for
an average of from four to five in his household. Therefore, if any additional employment in our shipbuilding yards can be
secured it will undoubtedly be very helpful
to us in the present conditions. We know,
as a matter of fact, that there are a number

type of men, men who, for a very considerable time, as we know, have been walking
unemployed, and to whom it is a great
humiliation indeed to have to accept what
is known as the unemployment dole from the
Bureau. These men are generally selfrespecting men-I am speaking now of the
high-class artisans employed in the shipbuilding works-and to afford them an opportunity of getting work will, I am sure,
commend itself to this House as it does to
the Government. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I think if we can tide over the next
twelve months so far as our shipbuilding
trade is concerned-I am referring to that
now-that we shall see a revival of conditions in the trade, and for this reason,
that so many of the older ships are now becoming obsolete and, as it is fully appreciated by shipowners that steamers equipped
with modern types of engines are so much
more economical than those already in existence, there will be a great temptation to
shipowners to undertake new work and to
provide themselves with fresh tonnage of the
improved type if the necessary capital is
forthcoming to enable them to undertake
investments. Of that I am satisfied, but
I believe it will take some time before these

The First Sub-section of the Measure empowers the Government, as will be seen,
through the Ministry of Finance, to guarantee certain loans, the limit of such guarantee being £2,000,000. The Second Subsection limits the operation of this Measure
to twelve months. We think this is desirable under the circumstances, as it is unwise
to allow measures of this kind, where Government pledges may be given, to remain
unlimited. Sub-sections 3 and 4, as will be
seen, are purely formal and are not likely to
become operative. Sub-section 5 makes provision for the submission to Parliament
every three months of the transactions which
have been undertaken by the Ministry, and
at the expiration of the year a full statement
will be laid before Parliament of the operations of the Measure as it has been carried
out. I think with these explanations the

Standing Orders (Local Bilis).
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS
(Mr. Moles): I beg to move the first of the
Amendments to the Standing Orders relative
to Local Bills which appears on the Paper
in my name. A year's experience of the
Standing Orders, which we drew up with so
much care and attention, has suggested to
us little more than verbal changes and some
little detail which make at once for public
utility, the convenience of the House, and
the cheapening of expense. The first amendment on the Order Paper, which I now beg
to move, is to leave out No. 38, in order to
insert the following:---
On or
before the twenty-first day of
December a printed copy shall be deposited--
(1) Of every Local Bill at the Ministries
of Finance, Home Affairs, Labour, Education, Agriculture, and Commerce in Belfast.
(2) Of every Local Bill at the Office of
His Majesty's Treasury, at the General
Post Office, at the Irish Office, and at the
Office of Woods in London.
(3) Of every Local Bill affecting any dock,
harbour navigation, pier or port, at the
Board of Trade in London.
If hon. Members will look at the original
Standing Order they will find that the Ministries of Finance, Home Affairs, Labour, and
Agriculture were included. It is proposed
now to add to that Standing Order the additional Ministries of Education and Commerce
in Belfast which have been set up. The purport of that is so obvious that I need not
explain it. It is simply to keep in conformity
with the original Order that all Ministries
should be kept in touch with the provisions
of these Private Bills. The second has been
arranged in consultation with the authorities
upon the other side, at Westminster, and
there again the object is, of course, to safeguard and protect the public interests that
may be involved. The third is so palpable
that I do not propose to take up time in
explaining it. I beg to move.
Question proposed, That Standing Order
38 be repealed."
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
My hon. Friend, the Chairman of Ways and
Means, has explained this matter very carefully, but I would like to call attention to
the question of the abolition of the Irish
Office. I have been in consultation-I think
it is only four days ago-with the Colonial
Office and the Home Office regarding the
future arrangements between ourselves and
the British Government. It has been decided
that Southern Ireland-the Free State-shall
use the Colonial Office as its general channel
of communicating with the British Government, and that on the other hand the Home
Office will be the natural channel for the
Government of Northern Ireland to communicate with the British Government. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I understand that
the Irish Office has already been, or is in
process of being, practically obliterated. Consequently, if my hon. Friend (Mr. Moles) does
not object in any way I would suggest to him
that he should add after the General Post
Office"
the words "the Home Office," as that
would be our channel of communicating with
the British Government in future. I do not
suggest that he should omit the Irish Office
from his list, but the adoption of my sugges
tion would prevent him having to come to
this House later on to insert the Home Office
in the Standing Order.


The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS:
There can be no possible objection to the proposal submitted by my right hon. Friend.
The technical difficulty was that there was,
and is for the moment, an Irish Office in
being, though in actual practice what occurs
is that the duties that would ordinarily be
discharged by the Chief Secretary have been
in the hands of the ex-Colonial Secretary and
of the Colonial Office. It is not desirable that
we should have to make even a textual amendment at some later stage, and I have pleasure
in complying with the suggestion of the
Prime Minister.

Land Purchase.
Land Purchase.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
LAND PURCHASE.
2. Mr. COOTE asked the Prime Minister
whether he is able to give any information
with regard to the steps to be taken by the
British Government in fulfilment of their
pledge to transfer the remaining property
of the owners of lands in Northern Ireland
subject to the Land Acts to the occupiers
on terms fair to both parties, and on the
basis agreed to by the Land Committee of
the Irish Convention of 1917-1918.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): As the administration of land
purchase is a matter which is reserved to
the Imperial Government under the Government of Ireland Act, the question cannot
be answered with authority in this House.
Assurances have from time to time been
given by Imperial Ministers that legislation
would be forthcoming for the purpose of
completing land purchase in Ireland, and I
have no reason to believe that these promises
will not be carried out so far as Northern
Ireland is concerned at an early date. I
have no information as to the provisions
which will be contained in any such legislation, but possibly it may follow the lines
of the abortive Irish Land Bill presented
to the Imperial House of Commons on 11th
November, 1920.
Mr. COOTE: Arising out of that answer
may I ask the right hon. Gentleman whether
his Government is taking any steps, or has
taken any steps, to press upon the British
Government the necessity of performing the
obligations which they solemnly entered into
in respect to many questions put to them
principally by the Speaker of the present
House. Has anything been done to fulfil
the specific promises entered into that they
would bring in simultaneously with the Act
of 1920 an Act for the liberation of landlord
and tenant in Ireland?
Mr. POLLOCK: No formal pressure has
been brought by this Government on the
Imperial Government to implement their
promises in regard to land purchase, but I
may remind my hon. Friend (Mr. Coote) that
Mr. Ormsby Gore, the Minister concerned
with this matter, stated in the House on the
27th November last, that a Conference of
Irish Ministers would be held in Dublin
to arrive at a scheme of land purchase, and
he anticipated they would then consult the
United Kingdom. The conditions, of course,
were materially changed by the rebellion in
Southern Ireland, and by the new Constitution that was agreed to with Southern
Ireland, so that I apprehend whatever delay
has taken place is largely the result of the
political conditions rather than a disinclination of the Imperial Government to
implement their promises.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that reply,
will our Government be represented at that
Conference?
Mr. POLLOCK: In Dublin?
Mr. DONALD: Yes.
Mr. POLLOCK: This is the matter that
Mr. Ormsby Gore referred to touching upon
the relations of the British authority with
the Free State in regard to whatever
obligations exist between Britain and
the Free State in respect of land purchase.
The position of the British Government in
Northern Ireland is, of course, very different,
because I understand that so far as any
financial obligations are concerned the
British Government has repudiated them in
respect of Southern Ireland. Of course,
such repudiation would not apply to Northern
Ireland, and, therefore, it may be that the
Imperial Government is anxious to settle or
to define an arrangement for the whole of
Ireland before undertaking their legislation.
Mr. COOTE: May I intervene for a moment.
Our point is that the Government of Northern
Ireland is taking no steps in regard to land
purchase to impress upon the British
Government the necessity of carrying out
their pledges. Would the Government not
be better employed on this matter than on
some of the smaller things which are engaging
their attention? Is this not a matter that
has to do with the settlement of the country
generally?
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I might
be allowed to reply to that. The question
of land purchase is one which is always
before my colleagues and myself. My hon.
Friend (Mr. Coote) is in a great hurry in
regard to this matter, but until we voted
ourselves out of the Free State it was impossible for the British Government to
decide a matter of the kind. Now that we
have done so I am just as anxious as my
hon. Friend to see the whole of the land
purchase scheme carried out for Northern
Ireland, and he can rest assured that I will
prosecute the matter with the same vigour
as I have always done.

in the Schedule to the Irish Free State

the Irish Free State Constitution Act, 1922,

Irish Free State Government to be so informed.

I would insist that the right hon. Gentleman (the Prime Minister) in connection with

causes of these depressions. After all,
political economists will tell you that it
depends upon the supply and demand, but
we are getting away from that theory. We
find that supply and demand sometimes do
not control the situation, and we will have
to get at something else. I think it was
John Ruskin who made a direct improvement
upon the political economy of his day. Не
woke the nation to the fact that you must
deal with men not as hands but as souls.

the chief element which underlay our

and if I am right I can see in the very near

When our industries are revived one of

especially as the Government, although

Mr. POLLOCK: I do not apprehend that

with large companies who have ships partially paid for, or partially constructed, is
that the necessary money is provided to

which I am now outlining. This schememay I say?-is not limited to shipbuilders.
I only mentioned shipbuilders yesterday because the shipbuilding industry is so visible,
if I may say so, is before us so much, and
because it is one of the great staple industries whose workers are unemployed. It was

be undertaken in Northern Ireland, and in
which advantage might be taken of credit
of this kind, and in which the saving of
interest might be a great inducement to

think, by hon. Members who will take some

In regard to road grants and such like
improvements as my hon. Friend (Mr. Coote)
touched upon, it is not conceivable, I think,
in the interests of the taxpayers of Northern
Ireland, that grants of any kind, or even
guarantees of any kind, should be made to
county councils in such circumstances, in
view of the fact that they are getting very
substantial amounts indeed from the taxation
that accrues from mechanically propelled
vehicles. I judge that that will not exactly
come under the purview of this measure.
Agriculture also must be ruled out, because
there is no substantial asset there in the
form of security, and one of the very first
things that must be required by this Government and by the Committee is that the
character of the security behind any guarantee must be of such a substantial character
that the taxpayers of the country will not
be subjected to any risk. I think I have
made the matter sufficiently clear that my
hon. Friends will understand that this is
a matter of vital interest in regard to the
question of unemployment.

FORTHCOMING VISIT OF LORD DERBY.
Then I would like to make another
statement to the House that may be of interest, and that is, that when I was last in
London I asked Lord Derby, the Secretary
of State for War, if he would be kind enough
to pay us a visit here, in order to inspect
our great Force of Special Constabulary as
well as our Royal Ulster Constabulary.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am glad to
say that, with his usual geniality and kindness, he acquiesced in my suggestion, and
has promised to come over here to witness
a review, or if necessary to go round the
country to inspect the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the Special Constabulary at
their work. I can only say that I welcomed
his consent on behalf of Ulster, and on behalf of this House, and I said I knew that
when he came he would meet with a right
royal welcome, and would see a Force which
he, as Secretary of State for War, would feel
proud existed inside the United Kingdom,
because that Force is one which he knows,
and we all know, is for the purpose of resisting the King's enemies and preserving
peace, law and order in our midst. Therefore, I thought I would take the opportunity
to-day of letting it be known throughout all
ranks of the Force that, when the Secretary
of State does come here, I will look to them
to have a brave show, if I may say so, in
order that he may be deeply impressed with
the steps that we have taken here to safeguard our interests and to preserve law and
order.

Mr. COOTE: Pursuant to the notice which
I gave, I wish to develop my argument in
connection with the reply of the Minister
of Home Affairs to Question No. 1 upon the
Paper. I do not approach this question in
any captious mood whatever. With hundreds of thousands of others I was deeply
pained when I saw by reports in the Press
that on two occasions official Government
inspections were held of members of the "B"
Force before they entered upon their Church
parade. I should not have taken up the
time of the House to develop my argument
on this question were it not for the reply
that the Minister himself gave on the floor
of this House. To my mind it was petty and
captious, and it was unworthy of any Minister to stand up there under the protection
of a reply which could not be the subject of
comment, and to answer with a sneer and an
innuendo which were entirely, I think, out
of place. If I may say so, it was very small
indeed.
He said, I think, that it would be a sorry day,
or something to that effect, when loyal men
could not take part in a Church parade. This
question does not condemn ordinary Church
parades by military forces. We have all
taken part in these. We have nothing
to prick our consciences with on that. What
we object to is that prior to or after the
Church parade there is an inspection-a
military inspection to which the Government
lends its aid, to which the head of the force
goes down and gives his official sanction.
This is very aggravating, and is causing very
great pain to the people of Ulster. We know
also that prior to these parades there were
people going through many sections of
Ulster trying to institute parades on Sunday.
I suppose the idea is that it is an ideal day,
and because the people are not doing manual
work on Sundays they will go to these
parades. The man who gives such a reply
does not deserve the name of Ulsterman. He
does not understand the spirit of Ulster. He
does not realise the deep convictions which
are held on this matter. Remember, a man
will not rob God in order to save himself.
That is not the way in which Ulster has been
built up and held. That is not the way it is
going to be held. In breaking the Decalogue,
and in working for material considerations,
you are not going to have the blessing of

Oral Answers to Questions.
MINUTES OF INSPECTORS' AND
TEACHERS' MERIT MARKS.
1. Mr. M'BRIDE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Minister of Education if it
is a fact that copies of Minutes of Inspectors'
EEee
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. M'Bride].
and Teachers' Merit Marks in National
Schools have been forwarded to Larne Urban
Council, and, if so, why it has been done; if
these Reports are sent out to all Councils for
Schools in their area; how long this Rule
has been in force; and whether these Reports are not confidential and for the information of Manager, Teachers, and
Ministry's officers.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In the absence of my hon. Friend,
the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry
of Education, I have been deputed to reply
to the question of the hon. Member.
The Larne Urban Council, as successors to
the Town Commissioners, are the Trustees of
the Kirkpatrick Endowments under Endowment Scheme No. 204, framed under the
Educational Endowments (Ireland) Act, 1885.
Under the terms of that Act and the Endowment Scheme framed thereunder the Trustees
or Governors of the chemes are entitled to
receive the Inspector's Report on the schools
included in their respective Schemes.
The Reports so furnished to the Secretaries
of the Schemes include the Inspector's
Minute on the General Inspection and a copy
of the Table showing the efficiency of instruction by each teacher in each subject
taught by him.
These documents are confidential and are
for the information of the Managers,
Teachers, Ministry's officers, and Governors
or Trustees of the Endowment, and are not
sent to any Councils not entitled to them.
ESTATE DUTY.
Mr. MARK (by Private Notice) asked the
Minister of Finance whether in case of a
person dying domiciled in Northern Ireland
leaving assets in England and Scotland as
well as in Northern Ireland, Estate Duty on
the assets in England and Scotland as well as
on those in Northern Ireland has to be paid
before any Grant of representation will be
issued; whether before such assets in England and Scotland can be dealt with Estate
Duty in England and Scotland respectively
has to be again paid; whether in order to
relieve such hardship and loss by such double
payment and unnecessary realisation of
capital to pay such duties some arrangement
cannot be male to get over the expense of
obtaining a refund of such double duty.
Mr. POLLOCK: The points raised by the
hon. Member have already been under consideration and were very fully discussed between officials of my Ministry and members
of the Northern Law Society shortly after the
date when the powers of assessing and collecting Estate Duty were transferred to the
Northern Government. The position is that
in the case of a person dying domiciled in
Northern Ireland, Estate Duty must be paid
in Northern Ireland on all his movable
assets wherever situate, but under Section 28
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, the
Ministry of Finance, on being satisfied that
Estate Duty is payable in Great Britain in
respect of any property situate in Great
Britain and passing on such death, shall
allow a sum equal to the amount of that Duty
to be deducted from the Estate Duty payable
in Northern Ireland in respect of that property. Before the grant issued in Northern
Ireland can be resealed in Great Britain,
Estate Duty must be paid in Great Britain
on the personal estate situate there. It follows, therefore, that if the accountable
parties elect to obtain the grant in Northern
Ireland before they have passed in Great
Britain the Schedules relating to the assets
situate in England or Scotland, a double payment of Estate Duty must be made in respect
of the assets in Great Britain.
Now, as to the remedy. This difficulty can,
however, be avoided by paying the Duty in
respect of assets situate in Great Britain
first, and thereafter having the grant of such
Duty deducted from the assessment of Estate
Duty made in Northern Ireland. This is the
course which has been recommended to the
Northern Law Society, and which, in most
cases, is in practice adopted. It will be observed that the adoption of this course
obviates the necessity for the payment of any
of the Duty twice.

"

PAYMENT OF MALICIOUS INJURY
CLAIMS.
Mr. M'GUFFIN (by private notice) asked
the Prime Minister whether in a statement
recently made by him he mentioned the fact
that £750,000 had been obtained in alleviation
of rates in Beifast, and if this sum is restricted to Belfast, or does it include other
local bodies?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I am glad to have the opportunity of correcting an error, which I rather imagine was
occasioned by the fact that my voice was not
very well heard at the reporters' table at the
meeting at which I made the statement.
What I intended to say, at all events, was
that Belfast would receive its proportion of
the £750,000 in alleviation of rates. I did not
intend at that time to make a full statement
with regard to the matter, but the £750,000
is the second moiety of the £1,500,000 that has
been granted by the British Government to
this Government to disburse to the authorities where the cases have been approved for
meeting charges for malicious injuries, and,
of course, the counties as well as the city of
Belfast come into that arrangement, just in
exactly the same position as they came under
the arrangement whereby £750,000 was paid
in June of the current year to meet the half
of the damage done up to the 14th of January
of this year. I am very glad to have this
opportunity of fully explaining the matter.
I intended to use the words "
their proportion of the £750,000."
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Im very much obliged.
Mr. DONALD: I want to be clear on that
answer. Do I understand that the Prime
Minister made it perfectly clear that this
£750,000 is the second sum, or half of the
£1,500,000 that was granted to the local authorities to meet fifty per cent, of the cost of
malicious injuries?
The PRIME MINISTER: I thought I had
made myself perfectly clear. The £1,500,000
was promised by the Government.
Mr. DONALD: In two instalments?
The PRIME MINISTER: It was promised
in two instalments, but my hon. Friend (Mr.
Donald), who is acquainted with the proce
dure in the Parliament at Westminster, will
recognise that only £750,000, or the first
moiety of that amount, was granted in this
year's Estimates, and therefore this £750,000
had to be confirmed by the present Government to be voted for next year. That has
been done, and I have received an assurance
from the Government that that will be met
as an honourable obligation, and the £750,000
will be paid on the 1st June of the coming
year, and applications will be received on
the 1st July of the coming year for the disbursement of the money.
Standing Orders (Local Bills.)
Standing Order 97.-(Time for Presenting
Petitions against Bills.)
No petition praying to be heard upon the
merits against any Local Bill or Provisional Order Confirmation Bill shall be received unless the same is presented by being
deposited in the Office of the Clerk of the
Parliaments before three o'clock in the
afternoon, in the case of Local Bills on or
before the twelfth day of February, and in
the case of Provisional Order Confirmation
Bills or of Local Bills not presented within
the required time on or before the tenth
day after the day on which such Bill has
been read a first time in the House of Commons.
Amendment proposed:
Leave out" in the case of Local Bills on or
before the twelfth day of February, and in
the case of Provisional Order Confirmation
Bills or of Local Bills not presented within
the required time, on or before the tenth,"
and insert on or before the seventh."
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS
(Mr. Moles): I beg to move the amendment
standing in my name. The object of the
amendment is to correct what was clearly a
disadvantage. Suppose Parliament should
meet in January, and all the parties to a Bill
be ready to go on, and desirous of going on,
as the Standing Order now reads they cannot
proceed until the day mentioned in the
Standing Order. It is obvious that that prejudices their position, and it is desirable to
remove that obstacle out of their way. That
is the object of the amendment. I beg to
move.
Amendment agreed to.
Standing Order 98.-(Extension of Time for
Petitions in case of adjournment of H.C.).
When the time allowed for presenting
Petitions under the preceding Standing
Order other than Petitions required to be
presented on or before the twelfth day of
February, expires during any adjournment
of the House of Commons, the time shall
be extended to the first day on which the
House of Commons shall sit after the adjournment.

Prorogation-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Leave out "other than Petitions required
to be presented on or before the twelfth day
of February."
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS:
This amendment is purely consequential upon
the amendment just now adopted. I beg to
move.
Amendment agreed to.
Ordered: That the Standing Orders relative
to Local Bills, as amended, be printed.
Mr. SPEAKER: I propose now to suspend
the sitting till half-past three to await the
Royal Assent to certain Bills, and at that
time. I understand, a Message will be received from the Senate in connection with
the prorogation of Parliament.
Sitting suspended at Twenty minutes
after Three of the Clock.
Mr. SPEAKER resumed the Chair at
half after Three of the Clock.
ROYAL ASSENT.
The PRIME MINISTER (at the Bar) reported to the House that his Grace the
Governor, in the name and on behalf of His
Majesty the King, had been pleased to give
his assent to the following Acts agreed upon
by both Houses:-
1. Appropriation No. 2 Act, 1922.
2. Loans Guarantee Act, 1922.
3. Londonderry Bridge Act, 1922.
PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A Message was delivered by the Gentleman
Usher of the Black Rod, as followeth :-
:-
I am commanded by the Senate to inform this Honourable House that the
Speech of His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland, proroguing this present Parliament, is to be communicated
in the Senate forthwith, and, further, 1
am commanded to invite this Honourable House to attend in the Senate in
order to hear the said Speech.
The House went, and having returned,
where the Speaker of the Senate communicated His Grace's Speech to both Houses of
Parliament, as follows:-
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the Clark's
place at the Table): I have to inform the
House that the House has been to the Senate,
HIS GRACE'S SPEECH.
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons:
The Second Session of your Parliament,
which closes to-day, will be memorable in
the history of Northern Ireland; for during
that Session you have exercised, in accordance with the powers conferred upon you
by the Imperial Parliament, the right to
remain outside the Irish Free State.
By taking this step you have retained
the representation of Northern Ireland in
the Imperial Parliament, which, therefore,
remains responsible for safeguarding your
interests in regard to all Imperial questions.
Consequent upon the severance of the
Irish Free State from the United Kingdom
the office of Lord Lieutenant for Ireland
has ceased to exist, and a separate
Governor has had to be appointed for Northern Ireland. His Majesty has conferred
upon me the honour of being your first
Governor, a position which I highly appreciate as an Ulsterman and as one who has
been closely associated with you all my life.
I am gratified that the measures adopted
for restoring law and order in the Province
have been crowned with success, in achieving which both the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the Special Constabulary have to
be congratulated; they have won the confidence of all classes of the community.
I am pleased to learn that unemployment
in Northern Ireland, although still serious,
is gradually becoming somewhat less acute.
Its full effects have been mitigated by the
legislation which you have passed, in common with the Imperial Parliament, enabling you to provide, in co-operation with
public bodies in Belfast and Northern Ireland, relief schemes for a considerable
number of ex-servicemen as well as others.
Further, the Government, by providing
credit facilities, hope to encourage com-
His Grace's Speech.
Prorogation.
14 DECEMBER 1922.
mercial undertakings with a view to
unemployed persons being absorbed in
industries as quickly as possible.
Happily there are indications of a steady
though slow improvement in trade which,
beginning in the shipyards, is extending to
other staple industries. Not only have
active steps been taken by the Government
to assist this revival in trade, but it is
satisfactory to observe that many misconceptions in Great Britain and abroad regarding the high commercial standing of
Northern Ireland have been removed.
I trust that the great operations in
connection with the provision of the Parliamentary and other buildings for the
Province, which have just been started,
will make rapid progress.
Northern Ireland has been faced with
exceptional difficulties in regard to the
agricultural industry, difficulties which
affect a very large proportion of the community. The Act which has been passed
to endeavour to preserve a high standard
in cattle-breeding will, I have no doubt,
prove beneficial to your farmers by maintaining the prestige which Ulster has
acquired in Great Britain by the excellence
of her live stock, and of her other agricultural produce.
During the past Session you have passed
24 Acts of Parliament, some designed to
bring your laws into conformity with those
prevailing in Great Britain, from which
they formerly differed, and all of importance in making effective the administration of Government in Northern Ireland.
Members of the House of Commons:
I thank you for the provision of supplies
for the public services, and I congratulate
you on the fact that your financial position
is so sound, in spite of many adverse
factors.
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons:
education and licensing reform are now so
far advanced that it is hoped it may be
possible to introduce legislation on these
subjects during the next Session.
I am glad to learn that the necessary
preliminary investigations in regard to
I desire to express the earnest hope that
the time may not be far distant when the
Executive of the Irish Free State and the
Executive of Northern Ireland may meet
to settle in amicable conference those outstanding questions which affect the welfare
of both areas.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty God
may rest upon your labours.
After which the Proclamation for the
Proroguing of Parliament was read as followeth :-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
Proroguing the present Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided in effect by the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, as modified
by and in pursuance of the Irish Free State
(Consequential Provisions) Act, 1922, as from
the date of the presentation of such Address
as is referred to in the last-mentioned Act,
that the Governor of Northern Ireland shall
in His Majesty's name summon, prorogue,
and dissolve the Parliament of Northern
Ireland:
And whereas it is desirable that this present
Parliament of Northern Ireland should be
prorogued to the Twenty-seventh day of
February, One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty-three:
Now I, James Albert Edward, Duke of
Abercorn, Governor of Northern Ireland, by
this Proclamation do publish and declare His
Majesty's pleasure that the said Parliament
be, as from the reading of this Proclamation
in the Parliament of Northern Ireland,
prorogued to Tuesday, the Twenty-seventh
day
of February, One Thousand Nine
Hundred and Twenty-three.
And I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal will and pleasure to be that
the said Parliament shall, on the said
Twenty-seventh day of February, One
Thousand Nine Hundred and Twenty-three,
assemble and be holden for the despatch of
divers urgent and important matters, and the
Senators and Members of the House of
End of Session.
Prorogation.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Commons of Northern Ireland are hereby
required to give their attendance accordingly.
Given at Belfast this Twelfth day of
December, 1922.
(Signed),
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
[End of the Second Session (opened

Tuesday, 14th March, 1922) of the First
Parliament of Northern Ireland, in the
thirteenth year of the Reign of His Majesty King George the Fifth.]

Tuesday, 14th March, 1922.
LOCAL BILL (STANDING ORDERS
COMPLIED WITH).
Mr. Speaker laid upon the Table Report
from Examiner of Petitions for Local Bilis,
that he has certified that the Standing
Orders have been complied with in the following case:-
Belfast Harbour.
The Second Session of the First Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to
meet 14th March, 1922, in the twelfth year
of the reign of King George V., was duly
opened.
The House met at Twelve of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker (the Right Hon. Robert William
Hugh O'Neill, D.L., M.P.) in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. D. H. Hackett, D.S.O.) was announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman
Usher said: I am commanded to inform this
Honourable House that the Speech of his
Excellency the Lord Lieutenant General and
General Governor of Ireland opening this
present Session of Parliament is to be communicated in the Senate forthwith, and,
further, I am commanded to invite this
Honourable House to attend in the Senate
in order to hear the said Speech.
Mr. Speaker, accompanied by the Prime
Minister and other Members, went to the
Senate.
On their return the Sitting was suspended
until a quarter after two of the clock, and
then resumed.
SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members who are returned for two or more places in any part of
Northern Ireland do make their Election for
which of the places they will serve, within
one week after it shall appear that there is
no question upon the Return for that place;
and if anything shall come in question
touching the Return or Election of any
Member, he is to withdraw during the time
the matter is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been elected or returned a Member of this House or endeavoured co to be,
by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices,
this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against all such persons as shall
have been wilfully concerned in such Bribery
or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been tampering with any
A
King's Speech.
King's Speech.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Witness, in respect of his evidence to be
given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from
appearing or giving evidence, the same is
declared to be a high crime or misdemeanour; and this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath given false evidence in any case
before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against such offender.
ROYAL IRISH CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of the
Royal Irish Constabulary do take care that,
during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets leading to this
House be kept free and open, and that no
obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members to and from this House,
and that no disorder be allowed in the precincts of or in the passages leading to this
House, during the Sitting of Parliament,
and that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at Arms
attending this House do communicate this
Order to the Commissioner of the Royal
Irish Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings, and
Records of this House be printed, being first
perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do
appoint the printing thereof; and that no
person but such as he shall appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges
be appointed.
OUTLAWRIES BILL.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to acquaint the
House that this House has this day attended
in the Senate to hear his Excellency's
Speech to both Houses of Parliament, in
pursuance of His Excellency's commande,
and of which for greater accuracy I have
obtained a copy.
The Speech is as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons-
Your Parliament has been established for
some months, and the legal process of
transferring services to the control of the
Government of Northern Ireland has now
been completed. I regret that the transfer
of staff and the due allocation of property
and records to the Departments of Government have not proceeded as expeditiously
as might have been desired, and I trust
that means may shortly be devised for removing the causes of delay and enabling
your Departments to cope with the difficult
administrative problems which necessarily
confront a new Government.
I congratulate you on the manner in
which, in spite of these obstacles, the Departments of Government have been
brought so rapidly into smooth working
order.
I regret that Northern Ireland is still
faced with the serious problem of unemployment, but am confident that the
Ministry of Labour is giving the matter
constant and sympathetic consideration.
The spirit of conciliation shown in Northern Ireland in the settlement of industrial disputes is tending towards a more
satisfactory state of affairs, and I trust
that spirit will continue to animate all
classes of the community.
I am glad to know that, acting in conformity with a decision arrived at by the
British Cabinet, the Cabinet of Northern
Ireland has decided to grant an additional
six weeks' benefit during the present
period of special distress.
Members of the House of Commons-
The estimates of expenditure on the
Services for the ensuing financial year will
be laid before you in due course, but owing
to the fact that your finance is largely
dependent upon that of the Imperial Parliament, it will only be possible to make
partial and tentative estimates until the
Imperial Budget for the coming year is
available. Every effort has been made by
the Government to reduce expenditure to
the lowest possible limit consistent with
the security of the Province and the efficiency of its public services.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
It is hoped to lay before you measures
dealing with the following matters:-
The conferring of such additional powers
on the Government of Northern Ireland
as are necessary for the prevention of
crime, preservation of
peace, and the
maintenance of order.
The continuance of the issue of Savings
Certificates.
The amalgamation of the General Nursing Council with the Central Midwives'
Board for Northern Ireland.
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
14 MARCH 1922.
The amendment of the Intermediate
Education (Ireland) Acts.
The Breeding of Cattle.
The Imperial Government is introducing
legislation for making permanent the
principle of Daylight Saving. It will be
for you to consider whether in this matter
you will remain in conformity with the
Mother Country.
It is hoped that the Committees dealing
with the improvement of Education, the
establishment of the Constabulary, the
system of Trade Boards and the Employment Exchanges in Northern Ireland will
shortly complete their labours. In that
event it may be found possible to introduce measures for giving effect to their
recommendations.
I pray that Almighty God may bestow
His abundant blessing upon your deliberations.
Mr. M'BRIDE: I beg to move-
"That an humble Address be presented to
His Excellency as followeth :
Your Excellency,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland,
in Parliament assembled, beg leave to offer
our humble thanks to your Excellency for
the Speech which your Excellency has
addressed to both Houses of Parliament of
Northern Ireland."
We are pleased to see that his Excellency
has recognised the great inconvenience which
has been caused by the delay of transfer
of records, etc., but we accept his Excellency's congratulations on the fact that,
notwithstanding the obstacles which have
been placed in our way, we have been enabled
to carry on so well our different departments.
I think a true note has been struck in his
Excellency's Speech when it mentions the
problem of unemployment with which we
are faced at the present time; but we are
confident that, in the hands of the most
capable Minister of Labour and his reliable
staff, in the near future we shall be enabled
to grapple with that great problem. We also
appreciate his Excellency's recognition of the
conciliatory spirit shown by all classes in
the matter of trade disputes, which I would
venture to say is also largely due to the
confidence reposed in
Minister
Labour by all sections of the community.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Coming to
the matter of unemployment benefit, we are
pleased to see that a decision has been
arrived at by the Cabinet which will enable
the Minister to extend the unemployment
benefits for another six weeks, which period,
we hope, will bring us to the end of the
great trade depression. Then we shall have
before us the Estimates, which we know will
be handled by our efficient Minister of
Finance. We are also pleased to know that
our
of
powers will be ere long conferred upon the
Government which will enable them to
grapple with the crime now so prevalent in
our midst, and which we are determined
shall cease at whatever cost, 60 that
everyone, no matter at what altar
he worships, shall not only obey the law, but
shall be protected by it. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Other Bills, such as Nursing,
Intermediate Education, and the Improvement of Cattle are, we believe, in the hands
of most capable Ministers. Upon other debatable Bills which will come before the
House I will not touch, but before resuming
my seat I must thank the Government for
allowing me the privilege of moving this
Address. I do not look upon it as a personal favour, but as an honour to the many
thousands of loyal men and women in the
ranks of Labour I have the honour to represent in this House. I have now very great
pleasure in moving the Address. (Hon Members: Hear, hear.).
Mr. DUFF: I rise with some diffidence
to address you for the first time. I am
aware that under such circumstances any
hon. Member is assured of the full sympathy
of the House. But I ask for their special
indulgence to-day, because the honour and
privilege of seconding the Address has been
placed on me. I take it as a compliment to
the great industrial constituency of East Belfast. In the King's Speech there are two
matters of vital and supreme importance to
the industrial progress of our Province; I
refer to unemployment and to the suppression of crime. This suppression of crime is
causing considerable trepidation amongst the
masses, and they are continually asking can
nothing be done to wipe this sordid
thing out of our midst. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.). We are particularly grateful
that His Majesty has seen fit to mention that
he will increase the powers of the Government to such an extent as to enable them
sufficiently to grapple with this terrible evil
and state of affairs.
Now, with regard to unemployment, this
matter presses very grievously on each of us,
and we admit that no Government, no political move, can cure unemployment. We are,
therefore, very grateful that the question of
the alleviation of unemployment is in such
capable hands as those of our present Minister of Labour. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). We feel hopeful that
to
because
of the signal successes that he has
accomplished since he took over the
reins of office in settling the trouble in
Derry, the trouble in railways, and other
matters, these are an augury of hope
us that he will be able ta
do something to alleviate the Forrows
and the troubles that are consequent
on unemployment in our midst. We also
have to congratulate him that he is able
to guarantee to the workers in this great Province the utmost benefits that are secured by
anyone in Great Britain, and also that he
has been able to arrange the finances in
such a way that our members in East Belfast and in the other industrial constituencies will benefit by the six weeks' extension of the benefit.

The PRIME MINISTER: It is customary,
and it gives me very great pleasure to congratulate my hon. Friend, the Member for
Down, who has just moved the Address, and
my hon. Friend, the Member for East Belfast, who in such felicitous term has just
seconded the motion. I have listened to
similar speeches since the year 1906 in the
Imperial Parliament, and like the rest of us
here since last year in this Parliament,
and I can say sincerely that to meet the
occasion I have never heard words used so
from
fitting as
have fallen
my two hon. Friends. Before I proceed to
deal with some of the subjects that have
been mentioned by them, I would like to
tender my heartfelt congratulations and best
thanks to those who since we last met have
been in great danger and great difficulty. I
must, first of all, pay a fitting tribute to the
military, the Royal Irish Constabulary and
our Specials, not alone here in our midst,
The three
but all along our borderland.
forces I have named are daily and nightly,
one might say hourly, carrying on under
great difficulty, and in many instances under
great danger. Our hearts beat with pride
when we consider what our Ulsterfolk
doing in order to save the country from dereproach
vastation, and in order that no
may be cast on them, and that their determination to stick up for the old principles
(Hon. Members:
has in no way diminished.
Hear, hear). I must also add to that how
much we all recognise the courage of the
people of Ulster as a whole who, faced by
provocation beyond measure, have shown
great fortitude, great patience, and have
upheld in the most worthy way the traditions which are attached to the name of
Ulster. Further, I think the House as a
whole, and certainly the country outside,
would desire that I should say a word or two
regarding those members of this House who
have also the distinction of representing
Ulster interests in the Imperial House of
Commons. We adjourned our House for a
considerable time in order that they might
take up the cudgels on Ulster's behalf at
Westminster, and those who have followed
the reports of the debates in both the House
of Commons and the House of Lords, will
have recognised the magnificent work that
our local members in the Imperial Parliament have performed. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
It is always very difficult on an occasion
like this to select any names for special mention, and if I say that all those who sit in
this House have put in their full weight,
and done their duty most manfully against
great odds, I will complete, I think, my
obligations here; but they themselves would
be the first to permit me to say a word or two
regarding the Leader of the Ulster Group in

on
Parliament-my own brother, Captain
Charles Craig-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-who I have heard on all sides, has acquitted
himself in a difficult situation with credit to
the Party to which he belongs. And may
I couple with his name our old Friend Mr.
Ronald M'Neill-(hon. Members: hear, hear)
-who has delivered many eloquent speeches
the
our behalf, his last speech in
Imperial House of Commons being considered one of the masterpieces even in
that assembly. The Secretary of the
Party, Mr. D. D. Reid, a Member for my
own old constituency of East Down, has done
invaluable work in the interests of the
people here at home. We owe them all deep
and lasting gratitude for this manful stand
they have taken in the Imperial House, and
we can only say we hope they will long represent us there to fight the fight as they
have fought it in the past. It would be
impossible for me not to refer to our old
Leader, Lord Carson-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear)-who, in the House of Lords, has come
forward and spoken on our behalf in a way
which has impressed the House which he
adorns, and which has given comfort to
many a heart in Ulster. Lord Londonderry
and Lord Dufferin, in the House of Lords,
have equally with Lord Carson supported
everything which they considered was for the
benefit of this part of the Empire. It is also
a gratification to us all that some of the Press
across the Channel have supported us, and
I feel we owe unfathomable thanks to Lady
Bathurst, the owner of the "Morning Post,
who has given our old friend, Mr. Gwynne,
a free hand in supporting our cause, and in
confounding our enemies. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). I cannot pass over Lord Rothermere, who has placed his great organisation
in the Press practically at the disposal of the
Loyalist cause so long as we are prepared to
stand by Britain and the British flag, and
also, Sir Wm. Madge, the owner of
People," who has fought so gallantly for us
in his own way. I have hopes that other
great Kings in the world of the Press will
come more and more to see the justice of the
cause of Ulster, and that in the future days
we will find that our friends in the Press are
not so few as we have experienced 'during the
past few weeks.

I would prefer to-day to ask-What

We have come through very
anxious
times. We
never seem, indeed, to be
