Loyalists of this Province. We may take it
that the Boundary Commission is still the predominant danger confronting the Loyalists of
Ulster. I can only say, with regard to the
question of the Boundaries, that it stands in
exactly the same position as it did when this
House rose; and I may be permitted to read,
for the convenience of those who may not
recollect the exact terms of the letter that we
addressed to His Majesty's Government, defining our situation. I wrote on the 16th February :-
"We cannot consent to any alteration of
our Boundary except by mutual agreement,
failing which, in respect of any territory in
dispute, the Boundary to stand as defined
in the Government of Ireland Act of 1920."
By that we stand, and we intend to stand, no
matter what the consequences may be. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) It would interest the
House if I told them that I personally inspected the greater part of the Boundary
myself.
I was moved by what I saw in all that long
tour. I was struck, first of all, by the
moderation-the extraordinary moderationof those chiefly concerned in this vital question, and no more by their moderation than
by their determination-determination to
stand by every measure which is considered
necessary to protect our dear Borderland from
further incursion, or from being filched away
by Commissions or by anything else. It is
astonishing to find, when talking to people in
the Government, in the House of Commons,
and in society in London, the way in which
they will split hairs as to whether,
if So-and-so was Chief Commissioner, or the
number of Commissioners was five instead of
three, or if the question were narrowed down
to merely clipping the Boundary, would that
not satisfy us? My answer to them all is-
"Come across and talk to those on the Border,
and see for yourselves how any Commission
or any band of men can ask the Loyalists of
Ulster to go out from under the Empire and
the Union Jack, not necessarily into a
Free State, but very possibly into a Republic,"
because, if the tactics of our opponents can be
read by deduction, it looks to me as though
it were possible, at all events, that when the
Free Staters have got all they can from the
Government, the Republicans will say-
"Thank you very much; we will now take
charge of the machine." So it really is one
of the most serious problems that ever confronted a people, how to deal with the possibility-the bare possibility-of men, perhaps
more loyal than any of his Majesty's subjects
throughout the broad Empire-being requested, or possibly forced from their loyalty
to Great Britain and the Empire, and asked
to go into a Republic, or something which is
practically the same thing only under a
different name.
I can only say that this whole matter has,
from the start, given me more anxiety than
any other problem that has ever confronted
me with regard to Ulster. In London, on
several occasions, I have had very hard work
in getting the situation here properly under-

I turn to the second great difficulty that
confronts the people of Ulster, and that is the
unrest in our midst. The Speech which
has just been read has already indicated
that a Bill will be introduced giving power
to the civil authorities for dealing with a
situation which is a cause of grave anxiety
and alarm. The Bill proposes to give to
the civil authorities of the Government of
Northern Ireland power in respect of
matters within its own jurisdiction to take
all such steps as may be necessary for preserving the peace and maintaining order. The
civil authority, for the purposes of the Bill,
will be in general the Minister of Home
Affairs but he again will have power to delegate wide executive powers to officers of police
who are under his control. The powers, for
the exercise of which it is proposed in the
first instance to provide authority, are those
which have hitherto been exercised by the
Competent Military Authority under the
Restoration of Order in Ireland Act. Accordingly there will be scheduled to the Bill
in an adapted form such of those regulations
as in the opinion of the Government are
most useful for dealing with the present
state of disturbance. The Bill will also
give power to the Minister of Home Affairs
to amend the scheduled regulations or to
revoke or to add to them, and provision will
be made for regulations made by the
Minister being laid before both Houses of
Parliament. Offences against the regulations will be prosecuted under the authority
of the Attorney-General before the courts,
that is, the courts of summary jurisdiction,
consisting in each case of two Resident
Magistrates. There will be an appeal from
these courts to the county courts, consisting
of the County Court Judge sitting alone.
The court of summary jurisdiction will have
power to inflict severe sentences and heavy
fines. Special punishment will be authorised
by the Bill to be inflicted both by the
ordinary courts and the courts of summary
jurisdiction in the case of breaches of the
ordinary law, and offences against the regulations, where connected with the illegal
possession or use of firearms or ammunition.
The proposed penalty will be that authorised
by the Larceny Act, 1916 for robbery with

terribly exercised by the harrowing details
of murder in our midst. Hon. Members

Not only have I got to take responsibility for

am not dismayed by the problem. The
problem will be solved. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Before leaving London I settled down to
think out if ever there was a parallel in
the world to what is going on in the city
of Belfast, and had I discovered that in
America, Africa, India, or anywhere else,
similar conditions had ever prevailed, I
would have sent someone out charged with
the duty of discovering from the authorities
how they dealt with it, and to bring back
to me some report that would guide me as
to the steps that should be taken here to
deal with this nefarious campaign. There
is no parallel. The nearest parallel is that
which is going on in the Rand at the present
moment, but that, of course, is one that has
been dealt with rapidly and severely by the
Government troops on the spot. I would
have the House bear in mind the smallness
of that problem compared with the enormous
one we have to deal with here. However,
not being able to lay my hands upon any
expert who could advise me on the subject
I took the step before leaving London of
writing to Field-Marshal Sir Henry Wilson-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and asking
him whether in view of the serious condition
of affairs he would consent to come over at
an early date and advise our Government
as to the best method of safeguarding our
borders and restoring order within
boundaries. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I considered it only fair in asking so much
of so distinguished a soldier to pledge my
word that whatever scheme he recommended
would be carried out to the full, regardless
of cost and consequences. My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
welcomes the assistance it will afford him
in his difficult task, and the Cabinet has
unanimously endorsed the undertaking I
have given. I am now in a position to
inform the House that the gallant Field-
Marshal has willingly consented. Immediately on his return from France, which
country has just paid him a tribute as
unusual as it is well-merited, he wired "Yes."
Cur
It is too early to thank him. He will know
that we will do that at the right time.
Meanwhile I may take it that the House
approves of this undertaking that I have
entered into with him, and will see us both
through the difficult task that lies before us.
May I take the opportunity of appealing on
his behalf as well as my own to every
Ulster loyalist to render assistance to lawful
authority, and to refrain from being provoked into illegal action of any kind, which
not only embarrasses the police and the
forces of the Crown, but also encourages
the worst elements in our midst.
In dealing with this subject I have also
to announce that I tackled the Government
in London on the difficult subject of the
relations between the military forces and
the civil forces in our midst. I wish to
emphasise once more, in order that there
may no longer remain doubt in the minds
of the public outside, that the Imperial
House of Commons, and the Imperial House
of Commons only, through the Secretary of
State for War, can control the military
forces of this country. In other words, we
can only get on with the military here by
co-operation and friendly working together.
No one in this House, no Member of the
Government, has the power of ordering the
military to do anything. It is obvious that
the military forces, like the Naval forces of
the Crown, are Imperial forces paid from
Imperial sources and controlled from Westminster, and Westminster alone. One of
the difficulties in all these crises is that of
harmonising the working of the military
and civil authorities. I have to say that
the position in this respect has been greatly
improved. I have learned this morning
that my suggestions to His Majesty's Ministers have been adopted, that with the
incursion into our city of another battalion
to-morrow we will have six battalions upon
the spot, and those six battalions are to be
used in the permanent assistance of the civil
authorities, and not in a sporadic way as
has been the custom in the past. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I do hope that this
will be carried out in the spirit as well as
the letter of the agreement that we have
reached in London. Times are far too
serious to stand upon the letter of regulations regarding the Army or the principles
laid down for the co-operation of troons with
the civil authority. I believe that with the
gallant General Cameron, who has been so
helpful to us, and who has only been
hindered by regulations from helping more,
we will get on better in this co-ordination
in the future than we have done in the past.
I have to congratulate my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs and
the Constabulary authorities throughout the
whole Six Counties, including Belfast, on
the magnificent way in which they have
dealt with a most difficult problem. There
has been overlooked, I think, the fact that
when the incursion of the Sinn Feiners into
Ulster took place we had to denude the
heart of the Province here of some two
thousand armed Special Constabulary.
That meant that as we had promised
to do, and as we were all most
willing to do, we had to fly to the

imported gunmen and their schemes

am dead against any suggestion of martial

from Westminster, we would get back to

we were before. I feel that if we have

suffer immediately and intensely.
would say that one side was as bad as the

which carries great weight with me, is the
fact that the present state of the British
Empire is such that we never could count
upon the day or the moment when the battalions might be withdrawn, and if our own
Ulstermen were not in a position and well

find that the battalions now in our area
had been withdrawn to England either to
cope with some industrial unrest there or
to be brought up to a high standard of

the Expeditionary Force, facilities for which
do not exist in our midst. Or we might
have a change of Government and the new
authorities would say that it was no work
for British troops and that they should come
out of Ulster at once. The danger for me
has always been that if we relied upon the
They
Imperial forces only then it would be most
difficult for us to get our people together
and properly organised to meet what might
be a more serious condition of affairs than

all grounds I think it would be safer to

than someone sent over from Great Britain

may be fulfilled, and that not one penny
will be denied if he thinks it necessary to
guard our borders and guard our homes.
We are going through with this, and we
are not going to be intimidated by any party.
We are going through with this till, as I
said before, the citizens can walk through
every street of Belfast feeling that they are
safe, as they should be safe, from the
assassins. No matter how long it takes,
that will be an accomplished thing before
I lay down the seals of office. It is a negation of Government that any portion of
this great city belonging to the ratepayers
should not be open to the citizens for the
purpose of carrying on the fifth greatest
trading centre in the country, that they
should be only able to dodge round certain
parts of their town, and have to keep clear
of other portions. That has got to stop in
the long run, and if I get the backing I am
sure I will, we will be able to meet it,
no matter what difficulty we are up against.

seems almost intolerable that one difficulty

Now I pass from those three points to a
general survey of the situation. The attitude,
if not the policy, of His Majesty's Government up to the moment has resulted in the
utmost chaos and confusion in India, in
Egypt, and in Southern Ireland.

There may be further unforeseen difficulties
which will come along-I cannot say-but
whatever they are my colleagues and I will
meet them with the same courage and the
same firmness with which we are prepared
to tackle the three problems to which I have
referred. Although I have gone through
these dangers and difficulties at some length
I do not want the House to break up without
appreciating the other side of the picture
and there is always another side to every
picture. The other side is, firstly, that we
are here in this free Parliament of our own,
not under a Dublin Parliament. We have
not been jockeyed into that position.
Secondly, we have our own Courts firmly
established, and I venture to say, with all
respect, that the conduct of these Courts,
the dignity, the justice, and the manner in
which they have carried out their work so
far reflects the greatest credit upon those
who are occupying distinguished positions
on the Bench. Thirdly, we have, perhaps,
the most magnificent force of Royal Irish
Constabulary and Special Constabulary
that was ever in Ireland during its
long history. They are those to whom
outwe turn for assistance at all times.
We have also got the British people more
turned in our favour than
appears
wardly either in the Press or upon the
platform; and in spite of some of the gloomy
forebodings my right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance has steered the financial ship
through this year without having to come
to the House to ask for any Supplementary
Estimates, and without a penny extra
taxation on the people of Ulster, and I
think, and I trust, that he will have a small
balance at the end of the financial year. That
reflects great credit on his department. I
do not suppose that anyone expected when we
took up our duties here, with difficult
financial problems staring us in the face,
with grave anxiety across the water, that we
would be able to turn out in this first year
a satisfactory Budget, one that does not
show a deficit, and without extra taxation
upon the people. Not only that, but we
have not had to borrow a penny more than
the ordinary day to day requirements from
the bank. We have not had to issue a loan
or anything of that sort to raise money, and
consequently we start the new financial year
in a position at all events of economic
soundness. Moreover, owing to the British
Government having met us with regard to
compensation for malicious injuries the
taxation on many local authorities has
been considerably eased, and those who
are best able to judge of the situation tell
me that it may be possible for the rates in
future to come down still further. Not
only that, but in London there seems to be
a feeling that there will be a reduction in
taxation this coming year, in which,
and in all of which, of course, we in Ulster
here will benefit along with the rest of the
United Kingdom. Consequently, from that
point of view I think we have nothing to
complain about, and we may rest assured
that the same scrupulous care and economy
will be exercised by my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) in regard to the coming year,
with the single exception of the expenditure
of money on the protection of the lives and
property of our people. No man can put a
value on that, and therefore my pledge will
hold good that whatever is necessary will
be done to carry through that particularly
difficult task.

part of some of the hon. Members with regard to a pronouncement upon it. I refer
to the conference which took place between
the representatives of the Southern Government and the right hon. Gentleman himself.
I do not know whether he will think it
worth while to enlarge upon it and inform
the House what took place on that occasion.

The PRIME MINISTER: As my hon.
Friend is aware I have had no further conference with any of the leaders of the Provisional Government since the time I met Mr.
Collins in Dublin. At that time I had great
would
hopes that the conference
lead to
peace and harmony in our midst. I went a
long way-a very long way-in meeting Mr.
Collins at all-(Hon Members: Hear,
hear "--but having met him, and having
entered into an agreement with him, as I
say, I was hopeful that the South would recognise that it could never get the North
except by winning her, by showing sound,
good government in the South, and that consequently the agreement would go through
from the first word to the last. The Press
has, I think, informed everyone quite accurately of what occurred. When I got into
the train to go to Dublin to meet Mr. Collins
to discuss further matters connected with
the Treaty. I took up a paper and for the
first time I recognised that he had a different view regarding the Boundary Com-
That
mission to that which I held myself.
was the first hint I ever had that there was

out
have it
with him at once (Hon.
Members: 'Hear, hear ")-because I felt

there was no agreement, and if there was
any difference the proper course was to
have it straight out and let the country

over which I had no control, which made it

is aware, our hon. Friends have brought the
whole matter out in the Imperial Parliament, and have shown the great difference
there was in the matter of interpreting the
terms of the Treaty. That is a matter between Mr. Collins and the British Government, not between me and the other two.
I was prepared honourably to carry out the
agreement to the last letter, as far as I
could do, and I had taken long steps towards doing it as regards that part of the
agreement which applied to Northern Ireland. However, the difference arose, and it
was well it did arise, for we have been able
to make preparations which might have been
left lying in abeyance, and we might have
been living in a different atmosphere to what
we are to-day, an atmosphere of knowing
that a large section of Southern Ireland desires to coerce Ulster, to stir up strife, to
bomb her citizens, to snipe at them, and to
carry on their warfare to the very best of
their ability. We have discovered all that,
and it is far better that it should come out
now than when we were unprepared. I do
not think my hon. Friend (Mr. M'Guffin) will
expect me to say anything more on that today, but I can assure him that I have never
21 Debate on Address

14 MARCH 1922.
Debate on Address
expressed any different view to that I expressed to this House on a former occasion
that Ireland wants peace-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-and will never prosper, North
or South, while these terrible happenings
take place from day to day, and that all good
citizens should bend their minds on how to
secure peace, to help the authorities, not to
go against the authorities, but to help them
all they can to steady the people and prevent them doing anything in the way of an
unlawful action.
My concluding remarks will be addressed
not to those who are and have been in
danger on our borderland, but to those who
are on the borderland of this horrible campaign in Belfast. I do not know how to
speak unmoved about the anxiety of the
Loyalists living in certain quarters, with
wives and families on edge, unnerved by day
and by night by the awful happenings at
their very door, or at the end of their street.
I think I would like to couple the Government and this House in sending to them a
message of sympathy in all the sorrows that
have come upon them, and asking them to
trust us to do our very best to relieve the
situation and to help them in the terrible
times in which they are living. I know
many have the feeling that they are deserted
and not thought of. Such is not the case
at all. We are thinking of this problem
above all other problems, and we assure
them that everything that the weight of the
law can do to protect them will be done, and
that speedily. I do not suppose any people
in Ulster will welcome the news of the intervention at my request of Field-Marshal Sir
Henry Wilson more than those who are wondering when
this murder campaign will
cease. If any man in the world is able to
devise something to meet these hordes of the
Irish Republican Army, these promoters of
rebellion, I would say that that man is that
gallant Ulsterman, Sir Henry Wilson. He
will bring comfort to these homes, and I only
hope the people will be able to bear themselves with the best fortitude they can until
we get his scheme into full working order.
Mr. DONALD: Before the Prime Minister
proceeds further I would just like to ask
him a question which is causing very grave
anxiety at the present moment, and one
which he himself said he would take
in hand, with regard to the liberation of the
loyal prisoners in keeping with the action
of the Imperial Government when they
liberated Sinn Fein prisoners? What
attitude has the Government taken with regard to the release of loyal prisoners in keeping with the action of the Imperial Government in liberating Sinn Fein prisoners?
The PRIME MINISTER: The position with
regard to that is this-I refused to leave
London the last time until every prisoner
who had been kidnapped had been returned
to his home. They have all been returned.
The last two, I think, came from Kerry, on
Wednesday last. It was, if I remember
aright. either Wednesday or Thursday. I
came back on Friday. The only persons in
the hands of the Provisional Government
are five special constables, who were taken
at Clones. I could get them out to-morrow,
but I could get them out tomorrow on such
humiliating terms that I would not listen
to them, and I am perfectly certain not one
of the five men would walk out of jail if
they were asked to give such terms.
Consequently, I have succeeded in securing
the release
of all those kidnapped
from across our border, and the only ones
who are now detained are the five special
constables who I am hoping against hope will
be released when their captors come to their
senses. I am sure that this House would
not expect me or any other Minister to give
in to admitting that if these men were returned we were to release those who were
found guilty and committed to jail for
offences against our laws. If we once gave
in on that great principle, in my opinion,
we would be going back again across the line
I have drawn. and stultifying ourselves in
the eyes of the world as not determined to
uphold the ordinary law and justice. Therefore, I have put up a sufficient case with
regard to these five men in demanding their
release to the case I put forward in the case
of those taken from across the border. I do
not think it would serve any useful purpose
at the moment to say more with regard to
those particular constables, because it may
be if the Commission is held that they may
release them in order to give evidence on our
behalf.
Mr. DONALD:: I think the Prime Minister
misunderstands my question. I do not refer
to the late events at all. I am referring to
what happened last year-the political prisoners who were in prison for cases of robbery, violence, and trouble, and in possession
of arms.
They were put into prison at the
same time when the Sinn Feiners were put
into prison, yet the Sinn Feiners are liberated and our boys are still in prison. That
is my point.
The PRIME MINISTER: I apologise to
my hon. Friend. He was referring to pretruce prisoners.
Mr. DONALD: That is right.
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, to the pretruce prisoners. They were outside our
jurisdiction. We had nothing whatever to
do with them, and have not released a single
prisoner except the men from Derry and the
footballers. Those are the only ones we have
released. The others were released by the
Imperial authority, because they were
taken prisoners prior to our taking over the
subject of justice and law and order. Therefore, so far as those particular prisoners are
concerned, he would have to make inquiry
of the Imperial Government, and not of us.
In fact, so strongly did we feel about releasing these prisoners that my right hon.
Friend insisted on those from this district
being taken to Dublin and released there.
We felt so strongly that they should not be
released that we would have nothing to do
with them, and simply handed them over to
the authorities who demanded them, and
they were taken to Dublin and released
there. I do not know that there is any other
point that I have to touch upon to-day. I
resume with thanking the House for the
patience they have shown after what is a
lengthy and exhaustive explanation on my
part. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. LYNN: I would like to join with the
Prime Minister in congratulating the two
hon. Members who moved and seconded the
Address to the gracious Speech from the
Throne. There was no necessity for either of
them to apologise, because both showed how
very competent they were to take part in
debate, and I hope we will hear them both
very frequently in the discussions that take
place later on. I would like to join with
the Prime Minister in the tribute he has
paid to the Civil Service set up in such a
short time. I think myself the Civil Service is one of which this Parliament, as the
years go on, will feel prouder and prouder.
It is an excellent Civil Service, and it is
one, I am sure, that will not only do credit
to the great Imperial Service, but render
great service to Northern Ireland. I was
glad to hear the Prime Minister say that
no extra taxation would have to be imposed
and that the Chancellor of the Exchequer
has managed the finances so well that he
will be able to make ends meet. May I be
permitted to congratulate the Chancellor of
the Exchequer on his recovery from illness?
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We all missed
him; we are all delighted to find him here,
and some of us hope that his grip on the
purse-strings will be even stronger than it
was before his illness.
Now, I come to the question of the Address. On reading the Address and listening
to the speeches of our two hon. Friends, one
would have imagined that they had never
heard of the City of Belfast recently. Does
this House realise that since the 1st January
83 persons have been done to death in this
city and 150 have been injured? Last year
110 deaths took place, and I forget the number of injured, but it was certainly
close on 2,000. For the ten weeks that have
elapsed we have had a murder at the rate
of more than one a day, yet the King's
Speech pays no attention to it. Hon. Members glide over it, as if it did not exist.
Believe me, the citizens of Belfast are not
treating this subject in the same way. They
feel that they are up against anarchy, and
I am sorry to have to say it, they feel that
the Government is not doing what it should
do to throttle it. What is the Government
doing to stop this murder campaign? We
are told that new legislation is to be introduced, and I agree with the Prime Minister
that there is no necessity to introduce
martial law. People talk lightly of martial
law as if it were the panacea for every ill
of a criminal character. Martial law means
no law at all; it is simply the will of the
military commander. I agree with the
Prime Minister that it is most important
that civil authority should keep the grip in
Northern Ireland, and the civil authority
has got forces enough at its disposal to deal
with this menace-not only a menace to
peace but a menace to civilisation itself. We
expect the Government to do more than they
have.
I am not going to go into details.
This is not the place, I think, for one to
suggest remedies, but there are many remedies that might be applied, and have not
been applied, and so far as the general public are concerned they are gravely dissatisfied, and I am sorry to say that there are
good grounds for the dissatisfaction at the
present moment.
It strikes me that this campaign of murder
has a twofold driving force behind it. Sinn
Fein-and I think there can be no doubt
about it has been stimulated and driven
on by the Provisional Government that has
entered into the Treaty with Great Britain
-the Treaty of Peace. And they are stimulating and carrying on this agitation for
the purpose of making the administration
of the Northern Government impossible, and
not only trying to make the administration
here impossible and make life intolerable for
law-abiding citizens, but working this campaign for the purpose of carrying on propaganda across the water. The Prime Minister
knows he has just come with others of us
from the other side-they are utilising what
is happening in Belfast and saying that
every crime committed was a crime committed by Protestants against Catholics. At
every corner we are met with the cry that
an attempt is being made to drive out the
whole Roman Catholic population, that we
in Northern Ireland are bigoted, intolerant,
and allow nobody to live except our
own. We know how untruthful that is. We
know, unfortunately, how many of the victims of murder are our own people I say,
whether the murdered man or woman is a
Protestant or Catholic, is a matter that
does not concern me. I protest against murder in every shape and form. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Murder is a disgrace to
civilisation, and people are acting in this
city as if there was not a God in heaven and
as if there was no civil law to put them
down. To me the real seriousness of the
situation is that although 83 murders were
committed since the 1st January there has
been no one brought to justice. We are told
of reprisals. I have no doubt there have
been reprisals. Mr. Speaker, whenever you
read of reprisals in the country it is an admission that the Government is not promptly
dealing with the crime that has arisen and
that the people have got out of hands and
want to deal with it themselves.
I agree with the Prime Minister that it is
the business of every loyal man and woman
to rally round the Government and to help
the Government. I think every one of them
wants to do that; they want to help the
Government in every practical way, but they
do expect the Government to do something
itself, and something more than it has done
during the last ten weeks. I have told my
constituents often when they complained of
what was bappening before the 21st
November to "wait until our own Parliament gets control." We have got control,
and I am sorry to have to say it, the position
is not better but worse than it was before.
It is time it should end. The Prime
Minister can make no demands on us that
we do not want to respond to; whether those
demands are made on the person or property,
we are prepared to respond most cordially to

him and to rally round and help him to
stamp out this crime, but are you going to
stamp out crime unless you make it clear
to the criminal that crimes do not pay?
You have a case in Derry, and it is a very
important case, and I want to direct the
attention of the Home Secretary especially to
it. There is a case in Derry where three
men were charged with the brutal murder
of two policemen. They were brought to the
assizes, and convicted on evidence of the
clearest character, and yet they were reprieved. I want to know was that done with
the consent and with the approval of the
Northern Government?
The PRIME MINISTER: I can answer
that at once. It was not. Moreover, I
would have resigned on the constitutional
question only I think that it would have
suited the British Government and brought
this place into chaos. I have told them that
if anything of the kind occurs again I will
resign at once. Unless we have full power
to be able to say what is in the interests of
the community as a whole, it would be
utterly impossible for any government to
carry on. Consequently, my hon. Friend
may rest assured that the recommendation
in this case came from other sources and not
from the Government.
Mr. LYNN: I 'had the greatest fears that
such was the case, and that raises a very important constitutional question, and a constitutional question that this House has got
to face and deal with, unless it is going to
make itself ridiculous in the eyes of the
world. Since the days of Stuart Government
it has been a recognised principle that the
Sovereign can only act on the advice of his
recognised Minister or Ministers. If the
officer who represents the Sovereign acted
otherwise than on the advice of His Majesty's
Ministers for Northern Ireland it is, in my
judgment, a gross outrage not only against
constitutional law but against this House
itself, and I hope later on before the Session
ends that the House will take proper
methods of recording its protest against this
gross outrage--and gross outrage it isagainst constitutional law and constitutional
practice.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps my hon.
Friend will allow me to reassure the public
to a certain extent at this particular point,
As he knows the Government have
acquiesced in the proposal that there should
be a different Lord Lieutenant for Northern
Ireland to the person who holds the position
of Governor-General for Southern Ireland.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Consequently,
having, after a very strong representation
to them, gained that point, I hope in the
Letters Patent creating the Lord Lieutenant
of Ulster a creation will be made that will
prevent such a constitutional crisis occurring in the future.
Mr. LYNN: After all the Lord Lieutenant can have no greater authority than
the Sovereign who sends him here. If the
new Patent were laid out to give the Lord
Lieutenant, or the Sovereign who sends him
here, the power to release prisoners without
the advice of Ministers, it would reduce the
whole Ministry to an absurdity. I may say
the same thing happened to the so-called
footballers, the gentlemen who were arrested
in Tyrone with arms and ammunition-very
pleasing things to go to a football match
with-and bombs and all the other paraphernalia generally associated with Gaelic football. They were also let out, and I would
like to know in that case did the Lord Lieutenant get the approval of the Northern
Government?
The PRIME MINISTER: Well, it is
rather unusual to turn the Motion to the
Address into the cross-questioning of
Ministers. But still this is important, and I think it will probably
clear the air once and for all as to
the exact position as regards these
football players. On the occasion when I
met Mr. Collins in London, I had no idea
when I went into the room that there would
be any chance of coming to an agreement on
any points at all, but as we reached an
agreement regarding four or five points, he
immediately introduced the question of an
amnesty. I said to him that the question
of an amnesty was one which must wait until
a future date, until I consulted my legal
adviser. He said, "I have gone a long way
to meet you, to have conciliation and
peace, and it would greatly help peace if
the ten men who are now convicted, or who
have been charged in connection with some
offence, and who are really football players
were released." I said, "I have not any
knowledge of the case from the legal point
of view, but when I return home I will see
whether some special preference can be given
to dealing with these cases at once." I feltand I think the House will remember-the
spirit in the air at the time was more
friendly and a disposition to let bygones
be bygones. On my returning home-I was
two days later than he was getting back to
Belfast-I had a letter from him from Dublin
reminding me in regard to these ten men.
I wrote to him, and said if the men would
apply for bail, which was recognising our
courts, and that is really the point more
than any other, I would see, after consulting
my right hon. Friend the Attorney-General,
that a nolle prosequi was entered against
them. He agreed with me on the whole in
the interests of peace, and relying on the
new agreement that it would be more peaceable to take that action. Having given my
word that there would be no prosescution
against these men in spite of all that
occurred, I was determined that my word was
as good as my bond, and no one should say
the agreement had gone by the board. I felt
it was my word and letter to say that this
would be done, and that it was better to
carry that through rather than go back on
my word and letter.
Mr. LYNN: I raise no objection whatever
to any action that the Prime Minister may
take on the question of policy. The Prime
Minister says it was a politic thing to re-

Then we are glad to see in the Address

this

to be absolutely fair if I can.
deal with this matter from the point of view

I want to bring this matter home to the

With crime of any sort there is no Member
of this House has the least sympathy. We
hate bloodshed, we detest attacking a man in
the dark, and striking him in the back. It is
not plant which grows in Ulster. It is a
dishonourable thing; it is a mean thing; it is
a contemptible thing. It is foreign to the

want to assist the authorities to put down

hand. That being so, and the state of the

been done? They know that there are parts
of the city which have been in this state for
four months. Why did they not last session
of Parliament ask for these powers? Why
did they not get the power instead of listening to the Prime Minister of Great Britain's
talk of a truce, the simulacrum of a truce
which was not a truce, but the mere shadow
of a thing that did not exist at all? We say to
the Government that they should have done
these things four months ago. They ought
to have got busy four months ago. If they
had I venture to think that our city would
not have been disgraced to the same extent.
There would not have been the same number
of lives taken, the same number of widows
and orphans in our city or the same record
of blood and outrage right over the whole
country. These kidnappings on the border
would never have happened. No, we fanned
ourselves to sleep. The Government, I believe, fanned themselves to sleep, lulled themselves with the dope of the British Government, and did not take the reins of office into
their hands and exercise the authority they
ought to have exercised. This is our complaint to-day. Let us look at the facts as we
find them. We see Sir Henry Wilson invited
to come over here and establish peace for us.
There is no man in the British Empire we
reverence and admire more than Sir Henry
Wilson. We admire him probably most of all
for the fact that he is the greatest soldier
probably in the British Empire. He is willing
to come over here to this little Ulster of ours
to do the work of a policeman. A man who
is willing to humble himself to do such things
because of his love for Ulster, his patriotism
for Ulster, is a man whom we must if possible
admire more intensely than ever. I suggest
that there was no necessity for all this.
And when you get the services of Sir Henry
Wilson you will still require strong administration; you will still require policemen to
do the work. You will still require these
forces in every part of Ulster in order to seek
out and run down crime, and bring it home
to the proper quarter that justice may be
done. You will want the backing up of the
Government behind these policemen, and it
you have that, you will have a clean administration and put down outrage and murder
in a very few months.
We have drifted under the dope of the
British Government. I do not altogether
blame our own Government. They have
divided interests; they have divided authority. Let us view the facts. They could not
order the military out; they were simply
hamstrung by Dublin Castle. They had only
restricted powers. These things have all disappeared now. Dublin Castle does not exist.
We have nothing to say to them or to anybody outside of it in the rest of
Ireland. I hope that I am correct
in saying that we Owe no allegiance
to any authority outside Ulster unless the
British authority. So far as police authority
is concerned, when the new force is in working order it will be entirely in the hands of
the Home Secretary. And as regards the

Let there be no mincing of this matter.
This Government is on its trial at the present time. Better let us understand the facts
as we go on. We cannot have this orgy of
blood continuing interminably. It must be
put down or the people will rise and put it
down, and there will be a greater orgy of

of the police in the city. There is
sniping going on. An officer is sent out to

not the method of the dope administration
from Westminster. He has got to report to the
Commissioner of Police, and then the report
must go to the military authorities before
that house can be searched by the military.
Under that system-of course, there are
friends in the office; there are always
friends somewhere-word is sent to the
fellows doing the sniping. By the time the
military arrive on the scene of course there
is no sniper. It is a beautiful game. I do
hope the Minister of Home Affairs will end
all this, and that he will bring in such a
system as will give the policeman his proper
place, let him do his work, and do it freely,
in an unfettered manner, without fear or
favour, for the peace of the city and the
country. If the Minister for Home Affairs
does that he will have this House and the
whole country behind him.
I should like to deal with another matter.
It is not mentioned directly in the Speech,
but I hope that indirectly it is included in
the request which is made for larger powers
to deal with lawlessness. I refer to boycotting within the Six Counties. Boycotting
in the wider area, the rest of Ireland, is a
different matter. Our Northern people have
been cruelly boycotted for the last eighteen
months. We have all suffered by this boycott-we were content to suffer-but the
Southern people have probably suffered as
much or more than we have suffered, and
they are sick of the boycott. It is only being
re-enacted for political purposes. We do not
claim that this Government can do anything
to minimise the operations of the boycott out.
side the Six Counties, but we do claim that
it is up to our Government to see that there
is no flagrant case of boycotting within our
own borders. If you go to most of the towns
a market
and villages in the Six Counties on
day you will find one two hooligans

We should have powers to deal in a drastic

real
If you want to secure
comfort and peace for our people, delive
them from this wicked thing-boycotting and
reprisals of boycotting. It is an abominable

ment to see that it is stamped out. as far as

Then I wonder do the House and the
country realise how necessary it is for us

and will allow no man to interfere with
another. We are on our trial as a litt'e
community. If we fail now we fail in everything. If we succeed now we shall succeed
in spite of all the powers that may be ar
rayed against us. Speaking on the question

Counties for distribution in this country
They will inevitably be hit, but we cannot

give more employment to our people, and

as will be more and more self-sustaining as

Lastly, I want to say how much I appreciated the reaffirmation of the Prime Minister
in his quotation from the letter which he
addressed to the British Government on the
Boundaries question. May I also say to the
Prime Minister that he did a very excellent
two or three days' work when he visited the
border lines of these counties? Here are
counties lying on the Borderland, with the
people, outside the "A" and "B" Forces,
unarmed, and wondering if they will get the
protection which any and every Government
ought to give its people. They are looking in
the first instance entirely to this Northern
Government to see that they will be protected.
Since the raid they are being splendidly protected, and there is excellent organisation.
There will be a hot time on the Border if
there is another attempted raid. I do not say
a hot time with the people-it will never
come to that because the organisation on the
Border is such that they will be able to take
care of the people of these counties. These
people look for continued protection. There
is a fear that there will not be laid down
such definite lines as will preserve those
Borders for the time to come. I am afraid,
looking at the mentality of Southern Ireland
to-day-I turn to it, I hope, with the most
charitable mind, but we must realise the
facts we must come to the conclusion that
for some time to come there does not seem
to be any hope of any neighbourly rapprochement between the two peoples. If our people,
innocently living their lives, some of them
old men of 78 years of age, are to be seized by
those who were once their neighboure, and
who live probably one, two, or three miles
away, are to be dragged away to motor-cars
before they are properly clothed, before breakfast, and are to be taken heaven knows where,
away to the centre of Ireland, in midwinter-if that is the attitude of Southern
Ireland to Northern Ireland, I think there is
reasonable ground for me to say that there
does not seem to be any immediate hope of
that neighbourly rapprochement between the
two peoples that we so willingly and ardently
desire in order to make Ireland as a whole
a contented and happy place for both peoples
to live in. If these people were really
desirous of having us in agreement with
them, and of realising their dreams of an
All-Ireland Parliament, surely there should
never have been a Boundaries question. If
they simply had treated us in the neighbourly
way that people of one county should treat
another, as one self-respecting unit should
treat another, we might have grown up to
know each other, to be so inter-mixed in trade
and business and in friendly relations, that
when we saw Southern Ireland discharging
all the obligations of citizenship and trying to
hold an even scale for all the people within
their borders, we might away in the distance
have come to some understandable method of
working together.
But all that is wiped out by such tragedies
as have happened over the border. They
have put back civilisation; they have put
back anything like co-ordination of effort between the two peoples for a long time. I am
sure there will be much said in the House of
Lords to-night and to-morrow night on the
boundaries question. There will be decisions
taken which apparently look serious, but
really it is only play-acting. It is keeping
the letter of the Treaty. The question of putting the powers asked for in that Treaty into
effect is another matter altogether, and I venture to suggest that when the time comes for
the Boundary Commission to be set up, this
House, this Parliament, will have something
to say as to the right whereby the British
Ministry in the Imperial Parliament, behind
the backs of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
of this House and of this Government, comes
to an agreement with Sinn Fein, doling out
part of our boundaries to other territory.
This House will have something to say to so
flagrant an act of injustice and wrong as
that, an act that they dare not try in the
Colonies, an act similar to which they did
try once in the American Colonies and which
led to terrible results, and an act which must
be reprobated and condemned by people who
have any pride or self-respect. Those people
throw back in the face of the men who dare
to interfere with their territory the insult
that is levelled against them. If we ever
come-I hope we shall never come-to set up
the Boundary Commission, I hope and I am
sure this House will pause before it has anything to do with any interference with our
boundaries-boundaries given to us by the
British people, by an Act of Parliament of
the British House of Commons, and every
inch of which is possessed and controlled by
our Government at the present time.
I am sorry that those other matters which
I mentioned at the beginning of my speech
are not included in the Speech. Most important, I think, is the question of the franchise in relation to the elections which are
inevitable next year. You cannot shelve
responsibility. You must accept the present
situation if you do not take up the matter.
This is a thing that cannot be deflected.
You must face the issue one way or the other.
If the Prime Minister would take off the
Whip, and would not make it a Government
matter as to whether we shall have Proportional Representation continued in our municipal and rural elections or not, I think the
result would certainly enlighten the Government, and it would be the best way out of the
difficulty, which ought to be solved by the
House as a whole.
I am also sorry-I see there is an Amendment down to call attention to it-that the
Government did not think fit to make any

reference to Temperance legislation. I had
thought-

Mr. COOTE: I apologise. I can speak on

I take this opportunity of acknowledging our indebtedness to
the Prime Minister for his very resourceful
activities in connection with the later developments that have arisen. I am one of those
people who believe that if there is any sin
mixed up with the Prime Minister, it is the
sin of over-confidence in the good intentions
of Mr. Lloyd George and the British Government. I do not find fault with him for that.
He was a member of that Government himself. He lived and worked with them as his
colleagues. He believed in them. He told us
so. Most of us do not believe in most of
them, and I venture to think that even the
Prime Minister himself is disillusioned. I
am very glad to see that he has risen to the
occasion, and that according to the depth of
the infamy which he has found in the ramifications of the Government at Westminster
he is determined to stand fast by the principles which govern our Parliament.
We
believe this, and I believe it.
We recognise that the Prime Minister is getting, I
may say without any disrespect, a true idea
of the Constitution as regards the British
Government. After all, I do not know that
there are many people in this world believe
in the British Government. I am afraid few
of us do. I am afraid they themselves will
find that on this rock of Ulster they will
perish. On this Boundary question they are
bound to come to ruin in the end, and if we
as a people stand firm there is no cause for
pessimism. There is no cause, I say, for
pessimism on the part of the Ulster people.
I know there is none. They are grieved, they
are outraged at the bloodthirstiness abroad,
and they want to have it stopped, and they
are determined to have it stopped, but under
no circumstances will they fall out of the
ranks or show the slightest weakness in conserving to themselves and their children
this area which God has given them, and
which the Government has given to us, this
area which we hope to keep from the destruction enveloping us in Ireland. I am afraid
that it is destruction. I am afraid
the day is coming when it will not be a fight
over the Border. It will be a fight for bread,
it will be a fight for living; the youth and
manhood of the South of Ireland are running
into the Irish Republican Army.
They are leaving the plough, and the shop
and the animal, and some of them are going
to be Brigadier-Generals right away from the
anvil. Probably it pays better; but remember the Army pays no rates or taxes. It is,
however, eating up a lot of them, and there
will be a revulsion of feeling two or three
years from now when Southern Ireland comes
to her senses and realises the aftermath of
all this evil. In the meantime it is for us,
the Ulster people as a whole, to keep a stout
heart, and to support the Government in
every possible way, so that they may bring
us in a time of peace and of real tranquillity,
and give us real settled government that will
attract the best of industries and provide the
best of employment. Thus we will show
to the world that in the midst of the troubles
by which we are surrounded we can always
keep our heads and hold this outpost of the
Empire as loyally in the days to come as ever
we held it in the past.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I rise this afternoon to try if I can say something in this
very interesting debate that may not have
been said by any other speakers up to the
present moment. That, I feel sure, will be a
somewhat difficult task, but there are a few
thoughts passing through my mind on various
matters that I would like to give expression
to, and that I would like an answer from the
Ministry upon. Since thie Parliament was
opened in May of last year we have passed as
a people through many difficulties and many
dangers. No new Government has ever had
so much to contend with, and I take leave
to say that, taking all the circumstances into
consideration, all the difficulties that our
Prime Minister and his Cabinet were up
against, have been met in the most
admirable way possible. I think, taken
as a whole, their actions have commended
themselves to this House, and they have
secured the confidence and the trust of the
people of the Six Counties as a whole.
No one could have anticipated in June last,
when his Gracious Majesty opened the Parliament, that in such a short time so many
serious questions would arise, questions driving at the very root of the Government that
his Majesty opened in person. What has
been the policy pursued by my right hon.
friend the Prime Minister and his colleagues
associated with him since the opening of that
Parliament? I think I am right in saying
that the one thing that they have consistently
pursued since that Parliament was opened
has been to try to secure peace in Northern
Ireland, and peace in all Ireland, if that was
possible to be secured. (Hon Members:
Hear, hear.) When I see in some quarters
to-day the criticisms and very severe criticisms of the action of the Government of
Northern Ireland, I feel that the people forget exactly what the course we have pursued
from our establishment here as a Parliament
has been. Our Prime Minister at a very
early stage approached Mr. De Valera-perhaps I should not say approached, but met
Mr. de Valera. Some people thought that
was an unwise action. Other people thought
differently; but behind it, as I conceive his
action, there was shown not only great cou-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Robert Anderson]
rage on his part under the existing conditions that prevailed then in Southern Ireland,
but, I think, a great act of statesmanship as
well, the underlying desire being, as I understand it, to try to secure peace and contentment in Northern Ireland, and to try to bring
the stress and bitterness and murder that
existed in Ireland to an end; in any event,
to try and stop the conditions that existed in
the North and South. (Hon Members: Hear,
hear.).
Then the next thing that occurs to me is
the history that followed that interview.
Immediately following that interview, the
British Government began to think of negotiating with Southern Ireland, and I shall
presently show what the result of their
action in that connection really was-what
the final result was. Although our Prime
Minister, as representing his people, offered
to meet the British Government and discuss
the whole question of the Government of Ireland, right up to the final Treaty, except by
informal meetings with Members of the Cabinet, the Government never considered their
attitude towards Northern Ireland, but negotiated with those of Southern Ireland as if
they represented the whole country, and they
arrived at a Treaty arrangement with them
in which we as a Parliament were never consulted, and they proceeded to insert a penal
clause in that Treaty-to give away territory
without our consent. What was the attitude
of our Government? Again a good deal of
criticism was made in regard to the interview
that the Prime Minister of Northern Ireland
had with the acknowledged head of the Provisional Government of Southern Ireland;
but I take leave to say that my conception
of the underlying thought :n the
Minister's mind in that connection was to
try again to secure peace, peace with honour,
to try to co-operate-if that co-operation was
possible-with Southern Ireland.
I do not think that any Member of this
House, or the inhabitants of Ulster as a
whole, desire in any way whatsoever to interfere with any Government established by our
friends in the South of Ireland. They desire
to see the South happy, prosperous, and contented, and we desire as far as we possibly
can to make the North a peaceful, happy,
law-abiding community. Now, the Prime
Minister in that interview tried to secure cooperation between the North and the South.
and I think I remember a speech of his when
he stated that the South would benefit by
the prosperity of the North, and the North
would benefit by the prosperity of the South.
and he has consistently pursued the policy of
trying to co-operate for that one great
supreme purpose. The foundation of any
State, its prosperity, its development, its
strength, its stability, begins upon the recognition of law and order. By respect for those
great principles you will be able to build up
a country; and in seeking to do all this the
Prime Minister, I take leave to say, was rendering splendid assistance to Ireland as a
whole, which we desire to sce redeemed
from its present state of disorder and strife.
We desire to see the North and South both
prosperous, and co-operating together, if such
a thing were possible.
.
Now, what has followed since then? Those
who say we as a Parliament have any desire
to coerce the South, or have any aggressive
intention in regard to them, are mistaken.
What followed after that interview? A few
short weeks elapsed, and the territory of
Northern Ireland was invaded by men from
Southern Ireland, whether with the consent
of the Provisional Government or of the Republican party we cannot tell; but the result
was that some of our leading citizens were
captured and taken away. From the establishment of the Ulster Parlament in June
last there has been no unkind act by this
Parliament, or the Cabinet of Northern Ireland. Any aggression, any opposition, any
bitterness or strife that has been shown, has
been shown by those in control of the affairs
of Southern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Now, that takes me up to another
point. Who is to blame for the present unfortunate state of affairs-I will not say in
Southern Ireland; I do not want to criticise
anything in regard to their actions--but who
is primarily responsible for the unfortunate
state of affairs that exists in Northern Ireland to-day?
If we have unfortunate bloodshed, if we
have bitterness, if we have disappointment,
if we have a community whose loyalty has
been tested in days gone by and whose loyalty
has been sorely tested during the past three
months, the British Government when they
proceeded to interfere with the Act of 1920
without the consent of the Northern Government and tried to break up the arrangement
that was solemnly arrived at, and promptly
proceeded to break the pledges they made to
Ulster-the blame of all this strife and bitterness that exist to-day must be put at the
doors of the British Government, and cannot
justly be placed at the doors of the Northern
Government, who have tried to carry on
under the most difficult circumstances that
any Government established for the first
time has ever had to contend with.
Now, I come to what is closely linked up
with the last point. The Prime Minister
informed us in that very interesting, very
able, and very comprehensive speech he
made yesterday that he is seeking special
powers in order to bring peace to this
distracted Province of ours, and to try to
get at the criminals who are disgracing the
land they belong to. He has told us he is
going to get the best advice possible-the
advice of a gallant Ulsterman, Field-
Marshal Sir Henry Wilson. Again I see
that our critics tell us that this is a provocative act, that we are going to proceed to
wage war upon the people of the country.
I think that all classes in the community,
whether they are Protestant or whether
they are Catholic, no matter at which altar
they bow, should be delighted to know that
our Government is trying to get the best
advice and the best assistance they possibly
can to protect the community, to put down
crime, and to make the lives and property
and the privileges of the citizens not only
of Belfast, but of every other district of the
Debate on Address.
Debate on Address.
15 MARCH 1922.
Six Counties safe and secure. And I take
leave to say that the Prime Minister and
those associated with him, supported as
they are in this House, have no other
intention, and have no other desire, than
to do what is just and fair and right and
equitable to all classes in the community--
to punish every criminal, no matter what
name he goes by, and to establish in this
city and elsewhere respect, for law and
respect for the sacredness of human life,
without which no State can be secure in
itself, and, may I be permitted to say,
without which no State can expect to receive
the blessing of the Almighty upon its
labours. I believe that I am interpreting
the mind of the Government and the mind
of this House when I say that behind all
these measures that may be put down as
coercive, and as being vindictive, there is
only one desire, and that is to secure the
liberties and rights of the citizens of this
community, and make it possible for every
inhabitant in the territory of the Northern
area to feel that he can go into his house
and walk the streets of the city knowing
that his rights are secured and his property
respected, and that his interests are in safe
keeping under the law and jurisdiction of a
Parliament that knows no distinction in
these matters between one religion and
another. These are the only matters on the
political side I would like to deal with.

very pleasing yesterday to hear from my

interesting when the Finance Minister tells
us what exactly are the contributions we have
received from the British Exchequer, and
on what basis these contributions were
given. Will the Finance Minister tell us if
the present financial year is being wound up
on the basis of the finances of the Act of
1920, or what other system has been adopted?
Then I want to know-and this I want to
impress very strongly upon the Ministerwhat is going to be our future financial
relationship with the Imperial Exchequer?
I desire to say--and I am sure my right hon.
Friend will agree with me-that
the
financial arrangement of the Act of 1920 is
dead. There can be no Joint Exchequer
Board now. There can be no percentage arrangement between Northern and
Southern Ireland as a contribution to the
Imperial Exchequer. That disappears
automatically, I presume, and, therefore, a
new position has arisen. Why, the Finance
Act of 1920 was not six months in existence
until the facts on which it was founded
disappeared. The whole relationship has
got to be overhauled in regard to our
position from the Imperial standpoint. I
have noticed that this question has been
discussed in the Imperial Parliament; but
I hope my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Finance will tell us what the future
position is going to be, and what steps the
Government are going to take in order to
put it upon a firm and secure foundation.
That is one part of the Act of 1920 that
must be scrapped, and the Imperial Government have got to substitute something else
in its place. What are they going to substitute? What steps are the Government
taking to-day in order to assure us, because
the foundation of this whole Parliament
rests upon the financial position and the
relationship in which we stand to the
Imperial Government. The whole system
of taxation is going to be the same for the
Imperial taxpayer and the taxpayer in
Ulster; but let us know now where we
stand on this point, and what the future
attitude of the Government is going to be. I
trust we shall have some information upon
that point.
There is one other subject I would like to
refer to. The question of unemployment has
been raised to-day by three separate speakers,
Now, the function of any Government is not,
after all, to find employment for the people.
It is to try to get the causes that create
unemployment removed. I am tired reading
about this dole that the majority of these
people are receiving. The more doles we give
out to the unemployed the more you are
impoverishing your own State, so I say that
while these things that have been outlined by
my hon. Friend the Member for Tyrone and
Fermanagh, such as the building of our new
Parliament House and offices, the relaying of
the tramlines in Belfast. and the improvement of the country roads, are most admirable to relieve the present distress, I am
delighted to know that my right hon. Friend
the Minister for Labour is trying to do something far better. That is to secure a better
understanding between the employer and the
employee. He is trying as far as he possibly
can to make their relationship as agreeable as
possible, and I think that in these coming
days the more capital and labour can get
together and explain their differences the
better it will be for both interests, and the
better it will be for the community and the
Debate on Address.
Debate on Address.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Robert Anderson]
State as a whole. I think, if I may be permitted to say so, we are extremely fortunate
in having at the head of the Ministry of
Labour in our Parliament one who has such
large human sentiments, one who is able not
only to look at the employers' side and state
it candidly to the worker, but one who also
can take his place and understand the sentiments and feelings of the workers and try to
bring about an arrangement that will be
satisfactory to both parties. Every country
to-day is passing through a time of difficulty
and strain on the question of unemployment,
and I sincerely hope that as far as
we in
Ulster are concerned signs of an improvement
may soon come and work will be found that
will make the lives of the people that labour
from day to day happier and brighter and
more contented. I do not like to venture
upon the other subject of the police. I am
serving on a Committee that will in due
course present a report to this House, and
then I think I will have freedom to express
my mind upon that particular question. But
I feel that I should say-I think I am rightthat it is only since the end of November
that we as a Government have had handed
over to us the power to deal with law and
order. Now, we are not going to bring about
the Millennium in three months. You are
not going to get rid of the legacy and inheritance we have received from past British
government in this country, you are not going
to get rid of them in three, or in six, or in
even twelve months. I think sometimes we
are rather inclined to be a little bit unjust
to those who, under peculiar and difficult
circumstances, are trying to establish law and
order in our midst. The police force themselves are passing through a transition period.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I take leave
to say that a finer force than the old Royal
Irish Constabulary no country ever boasted-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear) and they have
received very shabby treatment. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Do you expect that a
discontented force, smarting under what they
believe to be wrongs that have been inflicted
upon them, and conscious that in one month's
time, or two months' time, they are going
to be disbanded and leave the force with
which they have been connected for a lifetime, and furthermore, at the moment
receiving orders from here, there, and
everywhere; they are only human,
and they have done wonders under
the circumstances in which they have been
placed-do you expect those men, leaving the
force in a month or six weeks, to risk their
lives more than they are doing at the present
moment to detect ariminals and bring them
to justice? I think, under the circumstances
in which they are placed, they have rendered
splendid services to the State, and I sincerely
hope that we in this Parliament will do our
very best to give these men who are willing
to serve us every possible encouragement to
come into our ranks and serve the Ulster
Parliament with the same faithfulness and
the same degree of capacity and ability with
which the vast majority of them have served
the British Government hitherto. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
There are other matters which I leave to
some other speakers to deal with. The
gracious Address of his Excellency covers a
great many subjects which would afford
splendid themes for interesting debate. I
really regret the fact to a certain extent
that we have been deprived of a debate on
what is known as Summer Time.
I am
afraid we would have more than summer
time in this House had that particular
subject been discussed here by those who
take an interest in it. If I understand the
Prime Minister rightly, he has .reserved
after this year the right of this Parliament
to determine that question for itself. I
think that is so. I see the Channel Islands
are protesting against the action of the
Imperial Parliament in the matter, and I
take leave to say that questions of this and
a similar character which affect our people
as a whole must, in the future, be determined by our own Parliament, and not by
the British Government.
Taking a survey of the whole position, as [
can understand it to-day, I take leave to say
that although we may see dark clouds here
and there upon the horizon, although we feel
we are up against a very serious position,
although we may feel in our hearts a degree
of bitterness, to which expression cannot
possibly be given, against the British
Ministers who have tried to deceive us and
break their pledges to us-they do not, in my
judgment, represent the masses of the British
people at all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I believe that Ulster is right in the attitude
she has taken up, and I believe that the
principles for which we stand, and which we
seek to vindicate, will yet be vindicated by
the vast majority of our friends in England,
in Scotland, and in Wales. I have no doubt
at all that, if our people restrain themselves,
and if the leaders of the people do their very
best not to get the people into a despondent
mood, but will encourage them in every way
they possibly can not to outstep the law as
laid down, the difficulties we are up
against will in due course disappear. I have
been from the foundation of this Parliament
an optimist in regard to Ulster, and I am still
the same. I believe that, with the hearty
co-operation of all concerned, we will surmount our present trials and difficulties. If
our people throughout the Six Counties will
not only be true to themselves, and true to
all that their past stands for, but if they will
loyally co-operate and give all the assistance

15 MARCH 1922.
they possibly can, both in the areas that are
not disturbed and in the areas that are disturbed and turbulent, if they will COoperate and assist, and give every information
they possibly can to the authorities, I still
believe that the troubles and difficulties and
murders that stain our land to-day eventually
will be overcome. We are all anxious that
goodwill should be cultivated- and I believe
that in the city of Belfast, all that is
best in the community is anxious and
willing to bring this terrible murder
campaign to an end. My opinion is
that there is no sympathy for it from any
right-thinking person, either on one side or
the other, except from these men who are
imported from other places, and who ought
to be told that they are not to come into our
jurisdiction, that they ought to go to the
jurisdiction of those to whom they belong-
I sincerely hope that, even as we are to-day,
and having reviewed the position as a whole,
we will take heart and courage to ourselves,
and that we will go forward striving to do our
very best for our people, working to establish
this Government on a sure and firm foundation, and thus contribute to the happiness,
contentment, and prosperity of this Province
of which we are all so proud to be citizens.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Yesterday the Prime
Minister delivered a very exhaustive speech
upon the present policy of the Government,
and spoke also a good deal in respect of its
future policy. In the course of his speech
there were very many encouraging statements which we who are not exactly
optimists with respect to the future of this
Parliament were very glad to hear. I am at
least as loyal with respect to this Parliament
as any hon. Member could possibly be. I am
as earnest as any Member can be that peace
and order may be restored as soon as possible,
not only in Belfast, but throughout the
Northern area and throughout our beloved
country as a whole. But I do not feel that
with what has transpired up to the moment
I can feel as optimstic as some of the hon.
Members who have spoken yesterday and
to-day. The Prime Minister dealt withand very efficiently, too-the difficulties with
which he and the Parliament are at the
moment confronted-difficulties that
known to us all; but there are other difficulties, which, perhaps, are only known to
the Prime Minister and the members of his
Cabinet, that have not been introduced or
emphasised in the course of this debate. We
have heard a great deal with respect to the
determination of the Government to restore
law and order. That is a pronouncement that
the Government has made repeatedly since
the inception of this Parliament. This
Parliament was itself inaugurated in the
midst of disorder and upheaval, and everything that has been said in this House has
are
had more or less respect to that condition.
But there are difficulties that must be present
in the Prime Minister's mind, and which, in
my opinion, frequently have operated to
produce a certain modification of policy of
which the vast majority of people are not
aware. There must be present, for instance,
in the mind of the Prime Minister the fact
that the Southern area is constituted of a
population which is strictly speaking homogeneous-homogeneous with regard to race
and religion-with the exception of the 400,000
Protestant Unionists who are scattered
abroad throughout the area, and who, so
far as the majority are concerned, are negligible with regard to power and opinion.
There are, of course, two defined political
sections at the moment in Southern Ireland,
known as the Free Staters and the Republicans, a distinction in my opinion without
a difference, for I firmly believe that ultimately they will all aim, if they are not at
the moment doing it, at the same idea, that
is the establishment of a republic in this
country. It will be a very easy matter,
therefore, for the Southern area to be governed and controlled under those conditions.
There is a unanimity of ideas and of policy
that does not exist in the North, and to my
mind never can exist in the North. In the
North you have a population which is far
from homogeneous which is divided,
and divided in such a proportion as
always to make it a menace to those
who govern in this area.
If you
take the entire nine counties I suppose they
are in the proportion of eight to six, that is
Protestants and Catholics, and if you take
the Six Counties comprising our present
area, they probably would be in the proportion of two to one. Those proportions
are formidable enough for those who are
going to contemplate the government of the
country. What I fail to see is how we can
be sure except under most extraordinary
pressure by the Government of anything like
a safe and satisfactory peace. Something
must be done. I am not here to suggest what
it will be. Something must be done if we
are to obtain the peace that I have heard
pleaded for so frequently here. The conditions are permanent. We cannot alter
them. We have been trying to control law
and order. Up to the moment we have
failed, and I do not know whether the policy
that is in prospect by the Prime Minister is
going to produce the necessary desirable
results.
You have the border difficulties. You have
in the first instance the area in which we live
invested by those we call our enemies. We
have the entire border encircled by those
who are hostile to us. The problem at the
moment to me is how is this to be dealt with.
How is this to be tackled? It is not for me
to suggest what the policy should be. But the
border difficulties are there, and we are
hoping for the assistance of the military to
keep intact the area that according to the
Act of 1920 has been placed under the government of this Parliament. What did the
Prime Minister tell us yesterday? That it
was a most unreliable condition upon which
to operate. Those are not exactly his words.
