HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. M'Guffin]
He simply told us that we cannot rely on the
military. We had not power to control them.
We had no power to order them into any
district.
The PRIME MINISTER: My honourable
friend must have misunderstood me. We
have power to requisition the military in any
exceptional difficulty. We have no power to
compel them, but hitherto they have never
refused. The difficulty we have been confronted with is this: Our desire-the Government's desire-was that the police should
take all the action that was necessary from
the police point of view, and that the military should occupy certain prominent posts
in order to relieve the police for police duty.
The military, up to yesterday at all events,
were restricted in their operations to coming
only when summoned by the civil authority.
I hope now that in future-it is settled between us--the military will occupy permanently posts of danger throughout the city,
and therefore the police will be quite free in
future to do police duty.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: 1 am very much obliged
to the Prime Minister for this modification of
his statement. It very largely alters the
position to know that in case of grave difficulty it is possible for the Prime Minister at
any moment to summon the military.
But the Prime Minister must have been
aware, too, of other difficulties. For instance
the opposition of the Imperial Parliament
itself. No Member of this House would, for
a moment, suggest that we have had anything indicative of sympathy, so far as the
Imperial Parliament is concerned, in establishing our Parliament in Northern Ireland;
and no one can suggest that they showed
the slightest sympathy. They have delayed the transfer of the necessary powers
for setting up the Government, and purposely
delayed them. I was always suspicious of
the Imperial Parliament. I have not done
much in the way of speaking, of intervening
in its debates, but I have been fairly studious
and critical of the attitude of the Government. I have come to realise that the politicians as understood in the Imperial Parliament are nothing but the merest opportunists, waiting for the occasion to further some
party interest apart entirely from the claim
of those looking to them for help and support.
An instance of that was easily seen when last
week in the Imperial House the Treaty Bill
was being discussed. Well, I took an opposite, a very different, view from my colleagues
with respect to what should be done. I put
forward my own view that under the circumstances we should not attempt to introduce
amendments, but that we should take occasion
to enter our solemn protest against the tyrannical attitude of the Government in introducing a Bill that there was no power on our
part to alter or amend, while at the same
time it cut across the interests of the
Northern Parliament. I thought when we
had done that, when we had made that declaration and withdrawn from Parliament,
we would have made the best demonstration
of our rights and claims in the House of
Parliament. A different attitude was taken
up and a different course was pursued.
Amendments were introduced and debated
with excellent effect, so far as our Ulster
Members of the Imperial Parliament are concerned. I have heard speeches delivered, and
without being invidious, I would refer particularly to the speech delivered by the
honourable Member for Ormeau, as he is
known there, a speech that in my opinion
covered the situation so forcibly as absolutely
to mystify the Prime Minister, who is acknowledged on all hands to be one of the
wiliest politicians that have been produced
in modern times. He was brought absolutely
to a standstill. The amazing thing is this,
that the sentiments were cheered throughout
the House, but the Members trooped into the
opposition lobby. They showed their sympathy, but gave us none of it. And this is
the Parliament that we are asked to regard as
friendly to us. The hon. Member for Derry
here referred to the fact that the Prime
Minister would some day see what trust was
to be put in British Ministers. I took up
that attitude some months ago. I expressed
the hope that the Prime Minister was not
wrong in the trust he put in his former colleagues. I am not going to say that the
Prime Minister has been disillusioned. The
Prime Minister can see as far as any Member of the British Cabinet. I never trusted
the Prime Minister of the British Parliament, and those of us who traced his history
farthest back trusted him least.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think the hon. Member
must be careful. It is rather difficult in view
of the new creation of this Parliament, but
the hon. Member must be careful not to
attack individual Members of the British
Government when they are not here to defend themselves.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: I suppose on a point of
order it is the proper course to pursue, but
I hope the time will never arrive when this
House will not have the right to criticise.
However, I bow to your ruling, and will not
further refer to the subject. The difficulties
with which we as a Parliament are faced by
reason of the British Government's desertion
of the conditions laid down in the 1920 Act
have been very fully, and I would say, forcibly set forth in the speech by Lord Carson
in the House of Lords last week. He demonstrated, if demonstration were necessary,
that under the circumstances it would be impossible for this Government to conduct
affairs. We are looking forward in the near
future to the introduction of a Bill to modify
the 1920 Act upon which this Parliament is
constituted. What the modification will
inean we do not know. I know what one
Member of our Cabinet must feel in regard
to it. I refer to the right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Finance. It will make all
the difference to him whether it is to be six
counties or three. And if the Commission
accomplishes its work in the direction it is
intended to do, there will be difficulties in
this direction which will require all the care
and judgment of this Parliament to obviate.
Well we have not, I am sorry to say, very
much assurance as to the restoration of peace
and order in our city. The last week has
been perhaps one of the most fatal in the
course of the history of these murderous pro-

That is a very considerable increase upon the

to change it in some way or other, then I

to a fair and reasonable statement put up
here in the House.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Many of the speeches
made here to-day and yesterday have contained allegations against the Government
for its neglect to restore law and order in
this city. I am not here to apologise on
behalf of the Government, because I hold
that in no sense has this Government been
negligent, nor have we failed in our duty. I
ask hon. Members to consider the present
condition of affairs and to realise what has
led to the condition in which we are living
at the present time. One would think, to
listen to the speeches made here that up to
the time this Government took over control
Belfast was a happy and peaceful city and
had never heard the sound of a gun or the
explosion of a bomb, and that this condition
of affairs is solely due to the neglect of this
Government. What are the facts of the
case? In July, 1921, the Imperial Government entered into a Treaty with the Irish
Republican Army.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: A truce.
of
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS:
And under that truce, to which this Government was no party, all the operations of the
Imperial forces of the Crown against the
Irish Republican Army were suspended, prosecutions under the Restoration
Order in Ireland Act ceased, and
under the orders of the Imperial
Government recruiting for the Royal Irish
Constabulary and for the Special Constabulary ceased. The "B" members. of the
Special Constabulary were ordered not to
function, and from that time right down to
the time when this Government took over
control on the 22nd November-because up
to that time the service of law and order
was in the hands of the Imperial Government alone-the Irish Republican Army proceeded to re-arm, re-equip, and re-organise
their forces. Arms and ammunition were
imported into Belfast, drilling with arms was
carried on, rifle and revolver practice was
indulged in, and all in the presence of the
police, who under orders from the Imperial
Government were unable to interfere. În addition to that, Sinn Fein Courts were established, and the police were ordered not to
interfere.
This was the situation which confronted
us when this Government took over on 22nd
November, 1921. This Government had to
meet the re-organised and re-armed forces of
the I.R.A. with a depleted and unorganised
machinery. What were the forces that
we had to deal with? The forces which we
had available for this purpose were the
military, the entire control of which remained in the Imperial Parliament; the
R.I.C., which remained for discipline, pay
and promotion-a most important thing in
regard to the Constabulary force-under
the control of Dublin Castle, and the only
force over whom this Government had complete control was the Special Constabulary,
a force which since its inception in 1920
the authorities in Dublin Castle had done
their utmost to discredit and discourage.
The total number of men in the R.I.C. in the
area of the Six Counties when this Government took over were 2,324, while today that
force numbers only 2,279; the Special "A"
Constabulary numbered 3,515, and to-day
there are 4,346, and we are budgeting for 1,000
more and are recruiting. When we found
that condition of affairs on the 22nd November the first thing this Government did was
to throw open the ranks of the "A" Constabulary for recruiting purposes. They could
not do that in regard to the R.I.C., because
that was a force over which the Imperial
Government had control, and a force, which
as an encouragement to these men to serve,
they announced their intention to disband
at an early date.
But I tell hon Members here that it is
entirely a different thing from recruiting,
You cannot make a policeman in a day.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Therefore,
we are suffering for the period that lapsed
between the 7th July, 1921, when the Truce
was entered into, and the time we took over.
Now. I want to clear up a matter in regard
to the question of the use of the troops.
There seems to be a great deal of misunderstanding in regard to this matter. It
has long been the established custom in the
British Army, and under the regulations
providing for the use of troops in aid of the
civil power, that troops are not to be
brought out to the aid of the civil power
until that power has broken down, and then
only with the approval of the officer commanding those troops, but that practice was
broken through by the Imperial Government at the time when they found it
necessary to introduce the Restoration of
Order in Ireland Act to deal with the situation created by the I.R.A., and accordingly
troops were used jointly with the police for
the purpose of restoring law and order.
In other words, troops were brought out for
what I may describe as preventive purposes
rather than being brought out. after the
mischief had been done for curative purposes.
After the truce the Imperial Government, no
doubt with the idea that war with the I.R.A.
was over, decided that the old custom should
be reverted to, and that in future troops
should not be brought out in aid of the
broken down. These regulations, I
suggest to this House, were framed for
conditions other than those with which we
are confronted here to-day, and I say here
that it is a disgrace to think that troops are
not to be brought out until the citizens of
civil power until that power had

raids along the border under which many
law-abiding citizens living in our territory
were kidnapped. Then we were informed by
the Irish Free State that these men should be
held to ransom until this Government released the prisoners that were in their lawful custody. We refused that demand, but
what followed?

attack every link in the machinery for enforcing law and order, whether it is the
public who are anxious to come forward to
the prison

I say here to-day that if this Government
had acceded to the demands of the Irish
Republican Army to release the prisoners
that were in our lawful custody this murder
campaign would have ceased. A Dublin paper
stated the other day that the only way to
put an end to strife in this city was for the
North and South to cement their political
differences. I suggest to this House that
there is more than a political difference at
stake. There are differences of principle, and
certainly this Government is not going to
buy peace at the sacrifice of principle. But
this murder campaign still goes on. I hold,
and I have always held, that under these
circumstances it is the duty of the Imperial
authorities to place the troops of His
Majesty at the disposal of this Government.
The primary duty of the police is to preserve
the peace and not to do the work of soldiers.
The Northern Government at the present
time is faced with the same situation here as
that which confronted the Imperial Government in the South of Ireland. As a Government we are precluded from raising an army
of our own, and as long as that is so I say we
are entitled to have the same unrestricted
right to use the troops as the Imperial
Government has. Suggestions have been
made that this Government were negligent
in making requests for the use of troops,
and that they did not realise the seriousness
of the situation. May I say that requests
were made again and again that troops
should be supplied. We asked that troops
should be placed at fixed points in anticipation of trouble and not after trouble had
broken out.

officers, and 30 late as 20th February he laid
it down that troops will not be detailed to

There is another matter I would like to refer

to say here that if many of the people who

to investigate the true facts of the case they

position when one is trying to enforce the

With regard to the future, the Imperial

and most or these powers are

when this Bill is brought before the House

Now with regard to the "B" Class Specials.
These men voluntarily carry out an onerous
and dangerous duty; but what has struck
me is that they are recruited mainly from

should be. I consider that those who are

A good deal has been said about Martial
Law. I think the Prime Minister cleared
that point up. What does Martial Law
mean? It means handing over the management of the city to one individual-the
General Officer commanding, who can make
whatever arrangements he wishes. From
his decision there is no appeal except to the
Secretary of State for War, who in turn is
responsible to the Imperial Parliament and
not to this Parliament. Where does this
lead to? Is it likely that the Imperial
Government, who have recognised and made
peace with the Irish Republican Army in
the South of Ireland, will take any other
course with regard to the handling of the
Irish Republican Army in the Six Counties?

Mr. CRAWFORD: I rise with feelings of
trepidation to move as an amendment to the
Address the addition of the words:-
"But regret that no mention is made in
your Excellency's Speech of any intention
to introduce much-needed Temperance
legislation."
I move this amendment in no antagonistic
spirit or with any desire to embarrass the
Government in the difficult task that lies before them. I stand behind the Prime
Minister in his efforts to establish law and
order. I have always done so, and will continue to do so in time to come. I am one of
those who believe that temperance legislation is one of the things that will enable
those responsible for the Government of
Northern Ireland to establish law and order
on a sounder basis than could possibly be
done without it. I have glanced at some of
the measures proposed to be put before us,
and I am strongly convinced that such
things as the breeding of cattle and arrangements about nurses and midwives would not
be nearly as helpful for the maintenance of
law and order as bringing in good temperance legislation. I view all these measures
as quite worthy of support, but why should
the Government do all these things and
leave the question of temperance untouched? I know temperance advocates have
been accused of fanaticism. Hon Members
will probably say that I am a dreamer, and
persons like myself have been described as
faddists, cranks, and visionaries, but I do
not believe that any determined opponent of
temperance reform at the present time can
say that the advocates of temperance reform
have been unreasonable.
If the House will pardon me I will read
a short extract from a sermon preached by
one who is highly respected in Northern Ireland, namely, the Lord Primate of All Ireland. He said recently in the Belfast
Cathedral, and I see the Prime Minister on
that occasion occupied a seat near the
chancel:-
"Now here in Ulster the forces that
make for very thorough-going temperance
reform are very powerful and very determined. Naturally, they look to the new
order of things as giving them the means
of carrying out their programme. The
moment it appeared that Ulster was to
have her own Parliament the temperance
reformers took the field. They put their
case with great power. They could easily
have formed a very powerful party and
contested every constituency with candidates of their own. But mark, as time
went on, and as the general situation became clear, they saw that this would have
meant a division of interests. They saw
that it would have imperilled the unity of
Ulster. And so, with splendid magnanimity and public spirit they made up
their minds that they would do nothing
which would weaken the position of their
province."

of

soon as possible. I do not know whether
the right hon. Gentleman has taken any
action up to the moment; but, if he has not,
I regard it as his bounden duty to do so.
Mr. ANDREWS: I did not know that this
was to be brought forward, but at the same
time I am very pleased my hon. Friend
(Mr. M'Guffin) has mentioned it, because it
gives me an opportunity of telling the Hous
first what I have done in connection with
the matter. When I saw a lock-out of this
kind was imminent I felt it to be my
duty to do what I could to prevent it
in Northern Ireland. I, therefore, got into
touch with the representatives of Labour and
the representatives of employers in Northern
Ireland, and I was able to arrange with
them a settlement of the dispute so far as
this area was concerned, provided the employers were able to get the permission of
their Federation in London to the agreement.
Unfortunately, the employers were not able
to get that permission, and, therefore, the
lock-out notices, which I had hoped would
be withdrawn, were not withdrawn. The
settlement which was arranged was thisthat so far as Northern Ireland was concerned, the notices would be withdrawn, on
condition that the National settlement later
on would be recognised, and agreed to be
put into operation both by employers and
employes. It was a great disappointment to
me personally that the employers were not
able to get the permission they had hoped
to get from their Federation. I do
not think there is any fault to be
found with our employers for not being
able to get the permission required.
They did all they could. The hon.
Member knows that when Labour is in
a Federation with Labour it is very difficult
for the representatives of Labour to break
away in any particular area, and as the
employers here were federated with the employers in Great Britain on the matter, and
in connection with engineering generally,
they could not honourably break away without getting the permission of their Executive.
It was put up in the plainest possible way to
the Federation in England that the state of
the city here was SO unfortunate
that it was a very bad time for
labour trouble to take place.
That argument was pressed home very
strongly, but it was not effective. I may say
I am in continual touch with Dr. Macnamara,
and he knows quite well I am as willing to
help him as he is always willing to help me.
We are working together in the most friendly
way, and I think the spirit of co-operation
that exists between us is good, not only for
the Northern Area, but for Great Britain as
well. I need not say anything further except
that if I can do anything to bring this dispute
to an end it will be my duty to do it, and, in
addition, it will be a great pleasure.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 16th March, 1922.
The House met at a Quarter after Two of
the Clock, Mr. Speaker in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
SUMMER TIME IN NORTHERN IRELAND
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Agriculture if, in the interests of the farming community, and in accord with the
expressed desire of the Farmers' Association, he will take steps to prevent the
application of Summer Time to Northern
Ireland?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): While in entire sympathy with
the whole agricultural community in their
antagonism to Summer Time I am afraid
that, it having been passed for the United
Kingdom and Northern Ireland, it is not
possible for us to prevent its application this
season, though it is in our power to prevent
its application to Northern Ireland next
season if desired by the House.
HOUSING OF EX-SERVICE MEN.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state whether any
representation has been made to the Imperial
Government, with a view to expedite the construction of houses in Northern Ireland,
under the Irish Land (Provision for Sailors
and Soldiers) Act, 1919?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS: (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Government of Northern
Ireland have been fully alive to the urgent
necessity of pressing on the construction of
cottages for ex-Service men, and with this
object made representations some time ago to
the Imperial Government offering to carry out
the administration of the Act as an Agency
Service. Pressure is still being brought to
bear on that Government,and I am not without hope that schemes formulated and
contemplated will be expedited.
3. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state the number of
houses constructed or bought in Northern
Ireland under the Irish Land (Provision for
Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919?
Sir DAWSON BATES: 68 cottages, have,
I understand, been actually erected under
the Act in Northern Ireland, and there are,
I believe, an additional 380 cottages in course
of erection.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
seeing that the quota for Belfast and district
was 170 cottages, does my right hon. Friend
think that sufficient pressure has been
brought to bear on the Imperial Parliament
in regard to this important matter?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I can assure the
hon. Gentleman that all the pressure possible
has been brought to bear on the Imperial
Government in the matter.
SHOOTING OF SPECIAL CONSTABLE
VOKES.
Mr. GRANT (by private notice) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is prepared to institute an inquiry into the
circumstances surrounding the death of
Special Constable C. B. Vokes, who was shot
on Sunday, the 12th day of March, 1922 ?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am taking this
matter into very careful consideration, and
I am in communication with the military
authorities in regard to it.
POLICE EVENTS IN COUNTY DERRY.
Dr. MORRISON (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs if he can give
the House any information with regard to
important police events which took place in
County Derry last night?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received the
following telegram from the County Inspector, Londonderry:
Seven armed men with Crossley tender
captured at 12-40 inside the Northern
border by police patrol from Derry City.
Three rifles, two German automatic pistols
and quantity of ammunition seized."
This is the only information I have received up to the present.

expenses of
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINANCIAL
SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): In introducing
these Supplementary Estimates I should like
first of all to draw the attention of the Committee to the comparatively small amount
of money that is now required to be voted,
and it possibly will be for the convenience
of the Committee if I explain just how it is
we come to ask for these additional sums.
My right hon. Friends the Ministers for
Home Affairs and Commerce will, I am sure,
be glad to give detailed information as to
the Class II. and Class VI. items which
immediately concern their departments. It
falls to my province to explain particularly
these items under Class I, namely Public
Works and Buildings. I think hon. Members
will quite understand that, at the time, in
December last, when the Estimates were presented, the process of transferring the
different services to our Northern Departmente was then in progress. The sum of
money for which we now ask is a natural
development of the gradual transfer of those
services. There were certain items which we
were unable to estimate accurately at the
time, and you will see that, although the
actual expenditure amounts to £18,400, there
are, I am glad to say, savings in the departmente concerned which more than enable
them to meet the extra expenses to which
we have since become liable, and so the only
additional sum for which we ask you at the
present time is that of £1,000 which may
be taken as for the supply of stores which
were considered necessary to meet the daily
requirements of the several departments.
In the case of the Special Constabulary
also there are more than sufficient savings
under other sub-heads in that fund to
enable them to meet the extra sum for
which we now ask you, but as this sum is
mainly required for the equipment of a new
force, namely, C" Constabulary, we have
put it in these estimates in order to bring
the nature of this expenditure before Parliament. The same remarks apply to the
payment of £480 under Class 6 for the
Ministry of Commerce. That is also an
expenditure of a different character to what
we had before us at the time our estimates
were submitted in December last. Hon.
Members will be aware, of course, that in
the framing of our estimates we have followed a slightly different procedure-although it is one that has been recommended
-to that existing at Westminster. It is
recognised here that where one department
renders service to other departments it is
right that the department served should be
charged its proportionate share of the services rendered, and although these items,
such as rates and rents, fall under the heading of Public Works and Buildings, each
of the other sub-heads or departments are
charged with their proportionate share.
That is how, owing to savings being made in
those other accounts, there are funds available to ease this extra expenditure, and we
only have to ask you for a sum of £1,000.
The only extra expenditure which is in-
Icluded this time is £504 in respect of rates
in connection with a building which has in
the meantime been provided for us by the
Imperial authorities. If there is any further
information desired in connection with
these accounts I shall be happy to reply to
any question which any hon. Member may
address to me.

CLASS II. No. 2.
LAW CHARGES AND CRIMINAL PRO-
SECUTIONS
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That a Supplementary sum not exceeding One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty Pounds be granted to His Majesty
for the services of the period ending 31st
March, 1922, to defray the expenses of Law
Charges and Criminal Prosecutions."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The sum originally provided under this sub-head was £500.
That sum was arrived at on the assumption
that the Ministry would only be responsible
for these charges as from 22nd November,
1921, which was the date on which the maintenance of law and order was entrusted to
the Northern Government. However, subsequent to the 22nd November, 1921,
the Treasury decided that the Northern
Government should
pay in the first
instance all claims which came forward for payment subsequent to that date,
irrespective of whether the sums required had
been incurred before the 22nd November or
subsequent to the 23rd November, 1921. I do
not know whether hon. Members are aware of
the way in which these payments are madethat is for prosecutions, witnesses, and so on.
When a prosecution is undertaken the Crown
Solicitor gives a certificate that a certain
amount of money has been incurred, and the
Clerk of the Crown and Peace also gives
certificates. These certificates are presented
to the local authorities; that is, they are presented in the case of the County to the County
Council, and in the case of a County Borough
to the appropriate Borough Council and those
sums are paid to the persons who are entitled
to them by the local bodies. The County
Councils have their accounts audited halfyearly, and the County Boroughs have their
accounts audited yearly, and, accordingly, the
Ministry has been presented with demands for
the payment of expenses for a whole year, so
far as the County Boroughs are concerned, and
for half a year so far as the County Councils
are concerned. That means that so far as the
County Boroughs are concerned we are now
bound to pay for a full year instead of four
months-from 21st November to 31st March.
In respect of the County Councils we are
bound to pay for a full half-year instead of
four months. The Imperial Government will,
of course, repay to us a large portion of the
charges that were incurred before 22nd November, 1921, so that although we are now
asking for a Supplementary Grant, a great
portion of what was incurred before 22nd
November, 1921, will be repaid to us.
Question put and agreed to.

Dr. MORRISON: I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to an important resolution passed by the Shorthorn
Breeders' Association of England. A unanimous resolution was passed, I understand, by
them, calling upon the Agricultural Department in that country to prohibit the importation of store cattle from Ireland.
It is a
curious fact that, while we have 600 members

matter. The farmers find themselves in a

to Ireland, both North and South. I should
like to hear a statement from the Minister of
Agriculture on the matter, and to ask if he
could suggest any effective means by which we
can prevent this unreasonable attitude being
carried into effect.

Mr. ARCHDALE: The attention of the
Ministry has been called to this matter only

We have got no information from the Shorthorn Breeders' Society, and we consider it a

I am going to London to-night, and I shall

and will take the strongest means possible to

being put upon Irish cattle.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 21st March, 1922.
The House met at a Quarter after Two of
the Clock, Mr. Speaker in the Chair.
ALLEGATIONS AGAINST SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
1. Mr. M'GUFFIN asked the Minister for
Home Affairs if his attention has been called
to an article from the pen of Louis J. Walsh,
in the Freeman's Journal " of 9th March,
in which, amongst other things, it is suggested that members of the "B" Specials
when on duty are in the habit of spending
their time drinking in public houses;
whether it is not a fact that it is strictly
against the regulations to do any Suen
thing, and that the utmost care is taken
by officers to see that their men faithfully
carry out their orders and comply with
the regulations, and whether, seeing that
statements and insinuations of this kind
are clearly made for propaganda purposes
in England and elsewhere in order to discredit the Ulster Administration and to
cast a slur on a body of men of whom
loyalists are justly proud, any effective
steps have been taken by way of counterpropaganda to deny such charges; and
whether any official contradiction has been
given to the various statements and suggestions made in this article?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have seen the article
referred to. The hon. Member is quite
right in his statement that Police on duty
are not allowed to enter public houses for
the purpose of drinking, and I may add
that breaches of the regulations in regard
to this are rare. I agree that the report
referred to, and other equally unfounded
reports, are published to discredit a Police
Force of whom I can speak in the highest
terms, but the fact that this report is over
the name of Louis J. Walsh, and appeared
in the "Freeman's Journal," renders it
hardly necessary to contradict it, and it
is impossible for the Government to deal
with every malicious statement which appears in print. This Government have already publicly declared their intention to
stand by their Police, and the Police are well
aware of the Government's intention to
support them in their difficult duties.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Arising out of that
answer, might I ask the right hon. Gentleman if he considers that the granting of
certificates for the establishment of wet
canteens in connection with the barracks
for the Special Constabulary is conducive
to temperance and sobriety amongst the
members of that force?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think I might
have notice of that question?
Mr. M'GUFFIN: In consequence of the
unsatisfactory nature of the answer I will
feel compelled to raise the question on the
motion for the adjournment this evening.
EXTENSION OF UNEMPLOYMENT
BENEFITS.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is in a position to state
what further provision by means of legislation or otherwise the Government propose
to make towards unemployment, seeing that
the 5th April is the first date on which
those who have drawn the first six weeks'
extension will be out of benefit, and
whether a statement will be made on this
subject before that date?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I am in frequent communication
with the Minister of Labour of the Imperial
Government, but I regret that I am not yet
in a position to make a statement on the
matter. I certainly hope, however, that
the statement will be made well before
April 5th. In the meantime I may say
that it has been decided by the Cabinet
of Northern Ireland that we should make
the same provision in Northern Ireland in
regard to unemployment benefit as is made
by the Imperial Government.
Mr. DONALD: Thank you.

THE PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw): I regret the occasion on
which it becomes necessary for me to move
the Second Reading of this Bill. Unfortunately, the Attorney-General, to whom the
task has been entrusted, is unwell, and so
the work devolves upon me. I regret as
much as anyone that it has become necessary to introduce a Bill of this kind, but
we must realise facts, even if they are disagreeable, and not make the same mistake
as the Imperial Government, who tried to
form facts in accordance with their
wishes. Our task as a Government is a
very difficult one indeed. This morning's
papers, apart from anything which may
have occurred before, would leave one under
no delusion on that head. We have got
to undertake the task of governing North-
-Second Reading.
Special Powers Bill

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Megaw]
ern Ireland not light-heartedly, but on the
other hand we shall do it courageously,
and the first thing which is recognised by
all that we have got to do is to restore the
supremacy of law and order within our
area. One of the most serious difficulties
which affect us is the legacy which arises
from past maladministration. Vacillation
and ineptitude almost beyond belief have
characterised some of the past government
of our country, and the result is that a
firm administration and a consistent policy
seem to be absolutely beyond hope. Vigorous statements have been made in the
Imperial House of Commons from time to
time. So strong were they that we occasionally thought that another Cromwell or
another Napoleon had arisen. Most of us
would have been content with an Abraham
Lincoln, a man who was strong to act and
who dared not lie. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear!") After these declarations we had
vigorous action for a week, followed by the
squeals and whines of rebels, and criminals,
and their sympathisers. Then a fortnight's
lethargy would ensue and the police would
not know where they were. After that a
report would go abroad that some emissary,
lay, or more probably ecclesiastic, had been
seen in the neighbourhood of Chequers
or Downing Street. Then there would be
an almost unanimous demand for conciliation. You know what conciliation means,
the gaol doors thrown open, criminals set
free and treated as if they were the
saviours of their country, while the men
who had done their duty had to seek
another country. That is not an unfair or
highly-coloured sketch of the Imperial
Government's policy for the last five years,
and it is not unnatural that Government
and politicians should be regarded under
such circumstances with suspicion and distrust. That makes our task in Northern
Ireland all the more difficult.
Let me give you a brief sketch of our
own history. This Government was formed
in June of last year. I need not recapitulate the circumstances or the promises that
were given to us. We were given promises
in very great measure, but for a long time
we were given no powers. As a matter of
fact one of those periods of conciliation to
which I have referred had arisen, and it
was part of the conciliation that our
Government should get no powers. That
was bad enough, but worse was to follow.
The Government that would not give us
powers took on itself to exercise a stronger
prerogative, as has already been mentioned
in this House, than any of the Stuart kings.
Within a month of the meeting of this
House that Government practically suspended law in Ireland. Parliament had

the
Repowers granted to it under
storation of Order in Ireland Act, the
very powers we are asking you to entrust
to us in this Bill, but the Government had
said from that time, We will not use
those powers. So long as you are, or so
long as you call yourselves politicians, you
cannot commit a crime." Crimes with
them were merely high policy. That seems
to have been their ethical conception of
crime. Then we may ask what was their
idea of law? Apparently rules only to be
observed and administered when convenient,
and to be flouted and disregarded when
inconvenient. In a state of freedom law was
an incumbrance. Freedom knows no law,
and so the law was superseded. Then in
the course of the negotiations between the
British Government and Sinn Fein a thing
called a Truce was arranged, and haphazard
administration ensued. Was there ever
such a Truce in the history of the world
between the Government on the one side
and its subjects on the other, and that not
a signed agreement, each party to it giving
its own construction to what the Truce
meant? I can understand well why there
was no signed agreement. If there were a
constitutional lawyer in the Government
he would be aware of what that meant.
Such an agreement, apart from an Act of
Indemnity, would have exposed its authors
to a criminal indictment. When at last
we took over Government that was the
situation of chaos. Law was suspended.
Illegal instructions had been given to the
police. We were met by statements from
time to time about liaison officers. I looked
into my text books on law, and I could find
nothing in them with reference to liaison
officers, and being old-fashioned, and by
profession a lawyer, I never could find out
what the position of the liaison officers
was, and I declined to have anything to
do with them in any of the administrative
acts which came before me.
Then we had the illegal orders that were
issued to the police. These were more
serious still, and gave very great trouble,
especially as the police were only partly
under our control. It was absolute defiance
of law to issue instructions of that kind to
the police, and it was a work of some
difficulty to convey to them that they were
expected for the future to enforce the
ordinary law of the land.
We may examine the counterparts that
were signed by each of the parties to the
agreement I have referred to. One term that
might have been extracted from both was
that no new forces for the British or for the
Sinn Fein Government were to be raised by
either party to the agreement. Ulster, as we
all know, was not a party to the " Truce."
But during the period from July to Novem-

ber the British Government had still control

Happily, we have the best evidence with

The amount of arms and ammunition that

It is clear that the so-called Truce was

aided powerfully the conspiracy that is
directed against our

very existence.
have got to meet that conspiracy.
It has

by

on Dublin

This is an exceptional time and requires
exceptional measures. We may require
stronger measures still. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear) Those we ask now, though
exceptional, are not new. They are in
nearly every case exercisable by the military
at this moment. But it is felt that the
civil authorities should have the same
powers as the military had. They do not
supersede ordinary law. The powers
now ask for are for the most part contained
in Regulations. Some of these Regulations
are scheduled to the Bill. Other Regulations
can be made, and will be made, by the
Minister of Home Affairs from time to time
as may be necessary, these having got to be
we
laid on the table of the House. They will
have exactly the same force as Regulations
that are contained in the Schedule.
These offences that are made by the
Regulations are not in the same category as
ordinary crimes. Some of them would not
be offences against law at all if it were not
for the Regulations, and they are treated
by somewhat different tribunals from those
that exist in the administration of the
ordinary law. Now the offence in each of
these cases consists of a breach of the
Regulations, and the court that has been
established here, that is to correspond to the
court that deals with offences under the
Restoration of Order in Ireland Act, is a
court consisting of two resident magistrates
sitting together, and these will have power to
deal with all offences against the Regulations and to impose penalties amounting to
imprisonment for two years and a fine not
exceeding £100. Now in addition to the
powers that were given to the military by
the Restoration of Order in Ireland Act,
there has been in one case a new departure
made in the Bill, that is the imposition of
flogging for certain specified crimes. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Now, I think the
House will agree with me with regard to
those cases in which flogging is introduced,
that there are good reasons for taking the
power to inflict this new form of punishment. The use of bombs and explosives is
one of the most nefarious means that one
can think of in the commission of crimes.
Under no circumstances that you can
think of could a civilian have a
bomb for the
purpose of defence.
It is always intended to do injury
to life or property, in the most
cowardly, sneakish fashion, and the person
who is so degraded as to use a bomb certainly
merits no leniency at the hands of justice. If
very much more severe penalties were inflicted
I think society in general would feel the
benefit.
Now we have introduced flogging not only
with regard to explosives, but in one case in
which, I think, there was an omission in the
Larceny Act. The Court has power to inflict
flogging in case of robbery with violence. We
have extended the law to some extent. Where
violence has not actually been used, but where
there have been menaces that are equivalent
to violence, we have asked you to give leave
to have the same punishment inflicted as in
the case of robbery with violence. There are
altogether under the Schedule 30 Regulations,
and these Regulations are all contained in
the Regulations that have been made under
the Restoration of Order in Ireland Act.
Some, perhaps, have been omitted that should
have been included, and probably more
should have been made than have actually

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Megaw]
been made. We do not want to ask too much

for dealing with crime-these special
phases of crime that are growing among us

Mr. LYNN: I am sure the House feels
under a debt of obligation to the hon. and
learned Gentleman who has just moved the
second reading of this Bill. He has done it
in very lucid fashion. Those of us who know
his great legal ability could only expect that.
But there was more than that; there was a
ring of courage behind the words that must
appeal to every Member of this House. We
are living not in normal, but in very ab
normal times. And yet the demand that the
Government is making of this House is not
an extreme one at all, because I think there
is scarcely a Regulation or Clause in this
Bill, or a Regulation that will be made under
it, that every civilised Government does not
hold at the present time. If I had one
criticism to offer, it is that the Government
has not gone far enough. I think the situation
is such that we need much more stringent
Regulations than have been placed here. This
is no time for indulging in legal hair-splitting. The only thing we have got to ask
ourselves is this:-Is civilisation going to be
allowed to exist, or is there going to be
anarchy? It is quite clear that our opponents are out to create anarchy in Northern
Ireland. I am not quite sure whether the
outrages that have been committed of late
have been directly instigated by the Provisional Government, or whether they have
been instigated by that hybrid body, Dail
Eireann. But the Provisional Government
either instigates these crimes, or it is unable
to prevent them.
Not very many weeks ago we thought that
Ireland had reached the cross-roads, and that
there was going to be peace in the country.
The Prime Minister met Mr. Michael Collins
in London and discussed the whole situation
with him. I know there were people who
strongly objected to the Prime Minister meeting Michael Collins, but I for one did not
agree with them. I think it was the wisest
step the Prime Minister could have taken. I
also think it was true statesmanship, because
the Prime Minister realised that in meeting
Michael Collins he was taking his political
life in his hands. He was offending some of
his best friends. And yet in the interests of
peace he met him, and did what he could to
create peace in Northern Ireland and in
Ireland as a whole. I think it cannot be
suggested that the Prime Minister, the Members of the Government, and the Members of
this House have been anxious for anything
save peace, not only for our own province,
but for the whole of Ireland. We have done
our very best to create a peaceful feeling.
We have done our best to meet our opponents.
Crimes have been committed that are
outrage on the laws of man and on the laws
of God Himself. No Government that is
worthy of the name could allow these things
to go on without taking adequate steps to deal
with them.
an
The hon. and learned Gentleman referred
to the question of flogging. That question of
flogging is not a new one. I know there are
some sentimentalists who think that you
should not flog a man who happens to throw
bombs into a tramcar, or commits other cruel
crimes. Surely, if stealing with violence is to
be punished by flogging the use of bombs
ought to be punished in a much more stern
fashion. I think the Government should
make provision whereby any person found
with a bomb should render himself liable to
capital punishment. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). After all, two years' imprisonment,
even when preceded with a dose of the cat, is
no punishment for a man who throws a bomb
into a crowd of innocent people, knowing too
well that it must kill or maim someone. As
the hon. and learned Gentleman has said, no
man carries a bomb for personal protection,
and, therefore, any man who is found with a
bomb or any person found with bombs in his
house should be, I think, subject to capital
punishment, and the sooner the Government
take that step the sooner we are likely to get
into peaceful waters.
I am sure there is not a Member of this
House who is not anxious to help the Government in every way. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I am sure the hon. and learned
Gentleman is anxious that helpful criticismbecause here will be nothing else offeredshould be offered, so that when the Bill is in
Committee it may be strengthened and improved, and made a more efficient instrument
for grappling with this very serious crime.
We may have differences on this or that
point. Personally, I have criticised the
Government in the past, and I hope to have
the privilege of doing it in the future, if
needful, but on this question there can be
no difference of opinion. We are here as
one, as a body, to rally round the Prime
Minister, to give him and his Government
every support that is necessary for suppressing crime and maintaining law and
order. We all recognise the enormous
burden that is thrown on the Prime
Minister and thrown on the Government at
the present time, but I think it is only
right to let him know that he has our
sympathy and whole-hearted support, and
any service that is necessary will be rendered
by every loyal subject in Northern Ireland.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

and I do not think up to the moment in

and if this Bill had no other reason to

The Government have tried from time to

Something more drastic was necessary, and

There is a tendency at the present time,
and perhaps to a degree it is the aftermath
of the Great War, to look with a sort of
levity on death. People are not asking
now "Who is killed?" They are asking
"How many
are killed?" They are not
really concerned about the crime itself, but
how many times it has been committed.
We read our papers in the morning, and
almost congratulate ourselves if there has
been only one murder or one assassination
during the night or previous day. There
was a time in the history not alone of this
country but of the British Isles when to
hear of a revolting crime shocked the whole
heart of society, and the entire history of
that crime was followed with the most
curious expectancy. That has all disappeared now. How are we going to get
back to the normal conditions under which
we used to live, and which we used to regard as the best? The great defect
of this Bill-and after all it is not a defect of
the Bill if properly administered at all-is
that it is impotent so far as producing
witnesses-any evidence-against those who
commit these crimes. We cannot, for the
moment, take a man and say to him " You go
into the witness-box." We have to find, first
of all, the witnesses. That is a very difficult
thing to do at present, due to the fact that we

which a man is not permitted, or is afraid, to
give evidence, even though he may have witnessed the crime. Therefore, we hope well
for this Bill, and I am sure it will have the

House. We cannot see the Government of

vigorously and up to the present so conscientiously by the Prime Minister-we cannot see it brought to confusion because of

consideration for our Government, and I
think Sir Henry Wilson was right when he

It is utterly impossible that we could provide the necessary police to protect and
guard so wide an area, and I hold it is a

My hon. and learned Friend referred to

year this Parliament has been severely

late the Prime Minister, who foresaw what

will, I hope, be of a constructive nature.
I feel very sorely what has taken place
and what is taking place in Belfast and
the Six Counties. What is the position of
the city at this moment? Business people
are handicapped. What happens when they
send men out with horses and carts? My
sympathy goes out to the carters and those
who have got to go round the city with
horses; numbers of them have been shot
in the execution of their duty. Take, for
instance, East Belfast. You go over the
Queen's Bridge with a horse. You go as
far as Memel Street and deliver your goods.
But you have got to come back. You go up
the Sand Quay, round the Albert Bridge,
down Templemore Avenue, and back to
Newtownards Road in order to continue
your business. I hope this Bill will do
something to give protection to these people,
so that no one, however great or small, can

the position of affairs at Bridge End,
because no man can pass that corner without taking his life in his hands. What
happened the other day? Almost a dozen

Dr. MORRISON: Before dealing with the
measure that we are considering to-day, I
would like to say a word or two with regard
to what has fallen from the Member for
Antrim (Mr. Hanna). I cannot for the life
of me understand what position he takes up
with regard to this Bill. It may be due to a
lack of intelligence on my part, but he seem?
like a man hesitating between two opinions.
In the first place he made reference to a conference. There was a conference, and the
conference failed. I think it was a wise and
a reasonable thing for the Prime Minister
of this Northern Area to attempt to settle
this thing by a conference, but it failed, and
now the Member for Antrim (Mr. Hanna)
talks about a conference without proposing that we should lay aside this measure
and go into a conference. He is doubtful, he is hesitating, and he is hesitating also on the only alternative that
is before this House, namely, that of force.
He made some reference to backbone, and 1
must say that so far as I have been able to
see there is very little evidence of backbone
in his contribution to the debate or to the
serious state of affairs that exists in the SIX
County Area at the present time.
Dealing with the Minister's reference to
the Bill, I am-and I am sure the Members
of the House are with him when he regrets
that it should be necessary for us in the
Northern Area to introduce a measure like
this. There are three rather important questions, three broad questions, in connection
with it that I would like to refer to. The
first is in connection with the first section.
It states here clearly and distinctly that the
Civil Authority may do certain things, and
there are very wide powers being conferred
on the Civil Authority under this Bill. But
the next paragraph says:-
Provided that the ordinary course of law
and avocations of life and the enjoyment
of property shall be interfered with as
little as may be permitted by the exigencies
of the steps required to be taken under
this Act.
It appears to me that that is just evidence of
the vacillation that damaged all action by
past Imperial Governments. You had first
severity, and then you had conciliation.
There is no use in us passing a measure like
this-we have no option but to pass it-and
putting in a clause that the regulations are
to be carried out so that you are not to interfere with the enjoyment of liberty as far as
possible. I think the Ministry are only asking for trouble by putting in this clause.
There is an unctous rectitude about it that I
thank should be eliminated, because, having
made up our minds to do a certain action
that we regret, but that we are forced to do,
I would get rid of all this sentiment and say,
"We cannot help ourselves. We are up
against a wall, and we must make a fight for
our lives"
Next I would like to say I listened with
very great pleasure to some of the Belfast
Members when they described the appalling
conditions that exist in this city. I do not
know anything about them, but I know the
conditions that prevail in the country districts. I see here in Clause 6 there is power
to-

either absolutely or except in such circumstances or on such conditions as may be

allow me to say it, that it is a very unwise
thing to abolish Coroners' inquests.

holding of inquests."
Mr MEGAW: It is only " may
" prohibit.
Dr MORRISON: I am only making this
Euggestion to the Home Office. I find that
publity is the best solvent for abuses. I

no discredit will be done to the constituted

opinion is this, that while our police, that
is the Royal Irish Constabulary and the

to make the offering of drink

on duty, either by a licensed trader or by a

friend, a violation of the regulations.
would not make it subject to whipping, but
subject to two years' imprisonment and a

I assure this House and the Minister of

or a revolver he should have a clear mind

this trouble is coming on us-and I think
it is I want to use clean instruments in the

some irresponsible member of the police
force. If we can make up our minds to go

SUPERANNUATION BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): It has been
deemed advisable to introduce a short Bill
for the amendment of the Superannuation
Act of 1921. Hon. Members will be aware,
of course, of the conditions under the 1920
Act, whereby existing Civil Servants in the
Irish service were transferred to the service
of Northern Ireland, and all their rights,
which they enjoyed in their former positions
under the Civil Service Acts, were continued
to them, and the service which they had
given previously in the Imperial Service
counted as service for Northern Ireland.
Doubts have arisen, however, in the case
of what we call "specially appointed
officers." Those were officers who had not
hitherto been employed in the Irish service,
and consequently did not come to be transferred under the Act. They were especially
those gentlemen whom we considered to be
possessed of that special knowledge which
would enable us to institute our different
Departments, and we induced them to come
over from England to take up service under
the Northern Parliament. The particular
point which we consider requires correction,
and which we endeavour to overcome, in
this very short Bill, is to secure to them
that the service which they have given under
the Imperial Service prior to their joining
the service of Northern Ireland should be
counted when reckoning any gratuity to
which they might become liable. I hope
this is a contingency which is not likely to
arise, because in order to qualify for these
benefits the servant has to die within five
years of his taking up service under the
Northern Parliament. Still, it is only right
that they should be safeguarded in this
matter, and that the privileges which they
have earned under the Imperial Parliament
should be safeguarded to them notwithstanding the fact that they have now come
over to Northern Ireland. The other point
which it is thought necessary to amend is
a slight ambiguity in the Act. That was
that apparently under the Act this gratuity
could only be payable to the servant himself,
whereas, of course, the Act should have
been so worded that it should be payable to
his executor or lawfully appointed successor.
You will understand that the Bill does not
confer any additional benefits than were intended to be conferred under our own Act of
1921. It is merely to clear up a doubt as to
the legal interpretation of that Act and to
prevent what would be a very real hardship
if the interpretation were put on our Act
of which it is apparently capable. I beg to
move.

should be a ruling upon it.

of the Clock, Mr. Speaker in the Chair.

Mrs. CHICHESTER (by private notice):
asked the Minister of Home Affairs with
regard to the recent outrages in County
Derry, and particularly in the neighbourhood of Maghera, will he state what precautions, if any, were taken in the R.I.C.
barracks to guard against attack, and
how it is possible for large bodies of men
to have entered and held up the town of
Maghera and taken possession of the
barracks without any resistance by the

receive warning on the Sunday morning of

did he take to deal with the situation?
Will he also state what steps will be taken
and how soon to prevent the repetition of
such outrages in towns similarly situated,
and to protect the Loyalists in these areas?
information to hand regarding

Is any
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In answer to the first
question put by my hon. Friend, every
possible precaution is being taken to prevent
the repetition of such outrages and to pro
tect the Loyalists in these areas. Certain
measures are being taken which it is
inadvisable to announce publicly. I very
much regret that no trace has yet been
found of Sergeant M'Kenzie. In answer to
the second Question, the matter is at present
the subject of inquiry, and if the hon.
Member will put her Question on the paper
I will give the reply as soon as the necessary
particulars are available.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I should like to remind the Committee that in the December sittings of the
last Session of Parliament my hon. Friend,
the Parliamentary and Financial Secretary
(Mr. Barbour), presented Estimates and
Supplementary Estimates to provide for the
services of the State to the end of the
current financial year now rapidly approaching its close. If I may judge from the
official report, my hon. Friend performed his
task with a brilliance and lucidity which
justly earned him the commendation of the
House. (Hon. Members: "Hear, hear!")
The moneys which were then voted and the
moneys represented by the Supplementary
Estimates which the Committee considered
yesterday cannot be used legally for any
purpose whatsoever after the 31st day of
the present month. It therefore becomes
necessary in order to ensure continuity in
the supply of the services that Parliament
shall adopt one of two courses-either these
Estimates must be passed in their entirety,
or, alternately, Parliament must agree to
a Vote on Account. It would be opposed
to all Parliamentary procedure-indeed I
think it would be lacking in respect to the
Committee to expect that the multifarious
details contained in this volume of the
Estimates could be examined, and analysed,
and, I suppose, criticised by hon. Members
in the six Parliamentary days which remain
of the present financial year. It is the
practice, as I understand it, in the Imperial
House to distribute the consideration of the
Estimates over a large part of the Session,
and I think we may follow that course with
propriety. It is a great advantage that
hon. Members should be in possession of the
information which is submitted in the
Budget of the revenue and expenditure of
the Province to enable them to judge the
proper relation that exists between the
expenditure embodied in the Estimates
and the revenue of the State. There
are, however, one or two small departmental Estimates, which, I think, may
conveniently be disposed of, and there are
also some minor Estimates in the larger
Departments which may be suitably con-

sidered by the Committee and passed,

In submitting the Motion that the Committee vote a sum on account of the necessary supplies for the coming year, I do not
propose to enter with any detail into our
prospective financial situation or requirements. Indeed, any statement I might
submit on the subject would be largely
speculative, and, therefore, it would be
misleading in the absence of the full details
of revenue, for which we are entirely dependent upon the Imperial authorities. The
House will remember that fully 90 per cent.
of our
revenue and a not inconsiderable
portion of our expenditure is carried out in
connection with the reserved services, such
as the Inland Revenue, Customs and Excise
and the Post Office, all of which are reserved
to the Imperial Parliament. Information
on these heads cannot be obtained until the
Imperial Chancellor has finally settled his
Budget scheme. The Chancellor on the
first day of this month said that he could
scarcely imagine anything more imprudent
than for a Chancellor of the Exchequer to
announce before the end of the current
financial year, when he did not know results,
what taxes he proposed to impose in the
following year. Some apparently circumstantial reports have been circulated in the
Press that the Chancellor had in contemplation a reduction in the Income Tax by a
shilling in the pound, and possibly a reduction of the duties on beer. I think
too much reliance should not be placed on
a statement of that kind in the meantime.
Until the year has run its course the
Chancellor will not be in a position to know
what his reserves are, and it will, therefore,
be, impossible for him to determine his
policy, except such policy as will be determined by the political situation.
I need hardly remind the Committee that
the decision of the Chancellor is of very
serious moment to us. One shilling reduction in Income Tax would affect our revenue
to the extent of £700,000, and 3/- per barrel
on beer would mean another £100,000. We
are thus so dependent on the convenience
of the Imperial Government, the Committee
will appreciate the fact that it is impossible
for me to frame any complete Budget scheme
of our own State revenue for next year
and expenditure before the end of April
or early May, and when that period is
reached I hope to be able to review at
length the whole financial outlook of the
Province. At that time I will also be in
a position to report to the House with
exactness the results of our four months'
experience from 1st December till 31st
March, and whatever deductions may
be drawn from this experience. But I can
say now that assuming the revenue returns
of Income Tax for the next eight days are
normal, we shall be able to finish this
broken period of a full year with a surplus
of £30,000 to £40,000.
The Committee will, therefore, understand
that the Estimates we now submit are
limited to the cost of services which we
control. These are calculated on the basis
of current rates except where commitments
which have already been made involve
increases. Teachers' Salaries, Housing, etc.,
are in the latter category. There are
also new charges, such as the additional grant to Intermediate Teachers,
and the setting up and development
of Agricultural Stations. Of the latter
we expect to get a large refund from
the Imperial Government, as part of equipment expenses for which that Government
is liable. I should have liked, had it been
possible, to have given the Committee
Comparative figures of the expenditure of the
present year to guide it in considering the
Estimates now submitted, but there are so
many adjustments which have been made,
and changes in the methods of accountancy,
it would only have been misleading.
As an example of what I mean, there are
now provided in our Estimates charges
which were hitherto met from the Endowment Fund of the Department of Agriculture
or the Church Temporalities Fund. Moneys
from these Funds went directly to the
Department concerned, and did not appear
in the National Estimates. I propose that
the receipts, not only from these funds,
but from every other source shall come
direct into the Exchequer. This is a reform
which I regard as sound accountancy, and
very essential to the easy comprehension
of all sources of revenue on the one side
and the total expenditure of the Province
on the other. There is only one valid
method of comparison for us and that is
with the year 1920-21, upon whose Estimates
the financial clauses of the Act of 1920 were
based. I call this year for purposes of easy
description the basic year. In a few
moments I will present some interesting
comparisons of the figures of that year
compared with our present Estimates.
My hon. Friend in his admirable statement in December submitted comparative
figures of the Estimates for the past two
years as calculated by the British Treasury.
But I would remind the House that however
useful these figures may be for purposes

Estimates and not ascertained results. When
we entered our protest in 1920 against the
unfairness of the demand for a contribution
of £18,000,000 from Ireland as a whole,

As a fact, they only received

acceptance of the Treasury Estimate by the
Government is at the root of our financial
worries to-day. I do not question the right
of the Minister, who was acting with Cabinet
authority, to prefer the calculations of his
own technical experts to those of a Committee of lay men, but I certainly urge that
when he discovered the egregious miscalculations of his officers he was bound by
every canon of honour and honesty to exert
himself to remove the difficulties that arose.
I was innocent enough in those days to
believe that the promise of a British Minister and English gentleman was sacred and
inviolable, and when we had the assurance
in conclave that Ulster would have a surplus
of £2,000,000 after all her services were provided for, and when that assurance
repeated in the Parliament of the nation
with all the force of Government authority,
and when Parliament passed the measure
with this assurance ringing in their ears,
I had no doubt the undertaking would be
implemented.

I have learned something, however, since
then. I know that the Minister in question
-now one of His Majesty's principal Secretaries of State-is a man of honour, and
I have not given up hope that when the

is submitted to Parliament it will contain

I can now give some comparative figures,
which I think will interest the Committee.
The figures which appear in these Estimates
are, with a few exceptions, legacies from

are reflected in some of the Votes which

Education Estimate is a type and there

As regards the cost of our Parliament
and our administrative services, no doubt
Members will recall how pessimists and
croakers-friendly and unfriendly-predicted
that by reason of the smallness of our area
the splitting of the administrative Departments centralised in Dublin would involve
us in heavy additional expense, which
would add to the burdens of our people.
I am glad to be able to report to-day that
all these doleful prognostications have been
falsified. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). By
the savings which we have been able to
effect in the costs of our administrative
Departments, not only are the expenses
of our Parliament and Government covered
but in addition a substantial margin of
saving has been accomplished.

I come now to a very important feature of
our liability-the Unemployment Insurance
Fund-and I think it is necessary that I
should submit to the Committee some details
in regard to this very serious liability which
we must undertake. This Fund was established in 1910, on the same general principle
as the National Health Insurance Fundthat is to say, the contributors were the
employer, the employee, and the State. The
theory of the scheme is that during normal
and prosperous trade conditions such an
accumulated Fund can be created as will
provide for the necessities of those who cannot find employment in periods of trade depression. The industrial community, as a
whole, provides and pools the bulk of the
Fund, but the general taxpayer bears that
part of the burden which is represented by
the State's contribution. Unfortunately the
scheme had not been established sufficiently
long to permit of the accumulation of funds
to meet the drain which has recently resulted
from the unexampled depression of trade
and the consequent magnitude of unemployment. Under exceptional and trying circumstances, when the fund was exhausted
and no money was available, the British
Government agreed to advance a sum up to
twenty millions by way of a loan to the
fund, so that a continuance of the grants
might be ensured until unemployment was
less acute. The Government, however, made
it clear in the Act giving the necessary power
to make advances, that the loan was to be
regarded as a first charge on the Fund, to
be repaid when it was re-established on a
solvent basis.
The proportion of this twenty million loan
applicable to our Northern Province has not
yet been finally determined. It may be possibly £500,000 to £750,000, but as Ulster has
been created an autonomous State, although
the power to borrow is provided by the existing United Kingdom Act of Parliament, the
actual cash has to be provided by the
even
advances
to
made before the appointed day-1st January.
This would have been a very heavy and unforeseen burden for a new State to undertake, and in the ordinary course would have
involved borrowing by the Northern Government in order to be able to make the advance. Fortunately there has been a counter-balancing factor in quite another direction, where the Imperial Government has
met us by a very fair concession which
represents an addition to our revenue of
approximately a million pounds. The British authorities imposed the important condition in respect of this concession that, in
order to conform to similar conditions in
Great Britain, the advance to the Unemployment Fund of Northern Ireland must be in
the nature of a loan to be repaid when present exigent conditions disappeared, and the
Fund became solvent. The sum therefore
remains a loan; a loan by the general taxpayers of Northern Ireland to the Unemployment Insurance Fund during times of
exceptional unemployment, and it is repayable for the benefit of the community generally as soon as the Fund becomes solvent.
If, unfortunately, unemployment should
continue to remain at its present high level,
it will be necessary to consider what action
shall be taken to re-establish the Fund on a
solvent basis: that is to say, whether to
increase contributions, or reduce benefits, or
increase the State grant-in-aid. This question is already receiving the attention of the
Imperial Parliament, whose decision in the
matter we shall probably be compelled to
follow, both to ensure that our burdens and

In regard to finance, it will be remembered that our Prime Minister, in his
correspondence with the British Cabinet,
pointed out a third alternative to the two
proposals of that body-namely, a fiscal
status for Ulster equal to that of Southern
Ireland. This was refused, and, therefore,
we continue-as I think most of our people
desire-in close fiscal relationship with
Britain.
If a frontier is to be created in Ireland
between North and South, it will be a
British frontier, under British protection;
but if wisdom and good sense guide the
leaders of Southern Ireland there is no
reason why, in the common interest, some
measure of accommodation cannot be devised. If they are wisely directed, the
Southern Government would adopt the
British standard of taxation for some
probationary years, so as to learn exactly
its effects on the material interests of the
country; but if they allow their judgment
to be disturbed by sentiment or prejudice,
and a system of tariffs against British goods
is instituted, the policy will be a constant
menace to the peace and prosperity of the
country. Probably such a policy would have
a much less injurious effect on our Province
than on Southern Ireland, because we
more self-contained, and will continue to
have a free market with the forty millions
of people at our doors. Although the Councii
of Ireland is non-existent, there is at least
hope that some other link of communication between North and South may he forged
which will help us to deal with the difficult
questions of our fiscal relationship with the
South.

Our position in regard to the British
Exchequer is clearly defined by the Act, and,
as I have already stated, the financial clauses
of that instrument have been so drawn that
they embarrass us not a little, for under it
there is no question of any adjustment for
two years. Meanwhile, we are called upon
to pay from a diminished revenue towards
an expense which has also been materially
reduced (namely, the expense of the Army,
Navy, and the National Debt). So unjust

referred the matter to the Joint Exchequer
Board, who fortunately are still functioning,
and I am not without hope that some proper
basis of adjustment may be arrived at in the
near future Meanwhile, our contribution
for the four months of the current financial
year is calculated at one-third of the yearly
amount.

the aid of the workman that is quite unrealisable and inconceivable at the moment.
The situation, as the Minister of Finance
has said, is not improving, and I think
the Minister of Labour would agree even
to that, though the statistics of unemployment are coming down. On the authority
of the masters themselves matters are not
improving, and that is more important for
us to consider than the fact that the register
is lowering in the Exchanges. I congratulate
the Minister of Finance on being present
again in the House. We missed him while
he was away, and we are glad to be reassured as to his improving health by his
presence amongst us once more. Whatever
has happened I do not think his mental
powers have been in the slightest degree
impaired by his absence. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. POLLOCK: I should just like to say

services, the public works of the entire Province,
all the revenue services, the

purchase annuities. All these services come
under the head of the Ministry of Finance
for an expenditure of £70,000. If my hon.
Friend would analyse the numbers of
officials who are employed under the various
heads I think he would discover that probably it was not a very extravagant expenditure. But the main fact stares us in the face,
that we have been able to consolidate all
these services under one head and to save a
very considerable margin as compared with
the administration of these services when

centred in Dublin. Similarly in the

the prisons, constabulary, reformatories,

Mr. LYNN: I am sorry to interrupt my
