The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): My right
hon. Friend the Minister of Finance indicated in the course of his very excellent
address on the present state of finances his
intention of introducing at an early date a
Bill to authorise borrowing on the part of
the Exchequer in order to meet certain occasional sums outside the normal expenditure of the year. As such money Bills must
have their origin in Committee of Supply,
these resolutions are now asked for in order
to enable that Bill to be brought in in due
time. Since these resolutions were put on
the paper we have received from the Treasury a note of the form of guarantee that
they are willing to give us in respect of loans
which we may find necessary to issue. A
part of these loans will be the Ulster Savings Certificates, to which allusion has already been made. This communication from
the Treasury only reached us to-day, and
notice of an amendment has already been
handed in which I now beg leave to propose. I ask the indulgence of the House
in bringing in this amendment in this way.
It is only to give effect to the guarantee
which we hope to receive from the British
--and Local Loans.
22 MARCH 1922.
Special Powers (Money). 138
Treasury. The amendment is added to this
resolution in the following words:
"And if any such loan is guaranteed by
the Treasury of the United Kingdom in
pursuance of any Act of the Parliament
of the United Kingdom, the aforesaid
charge and any sinking fund payments in
respect of the loan shall have priority
over any charges on the said fund existing at the date of the Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, and any
sum due to the Treasury of the United
Kingdom under such guarantee, together
with interest thereon, shall be charged on
the said funds immediately after the
charges in respect of the loan."
That is legal phraseology, I suppose, and
I think hon. Members would like to know
what it means. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It simply means that in respect of
this guarantee that we constitute any loan
and any interest thereon absolutely a first
charge on our Exchequer. The involved
paragraph that I have just read out is intended to carry that into legal effect. I quite
agree with what has been said that it would
be very nice if we could meet these unusual
charges on our funds out of revenue. Still
if we were to raise our annual taxation to
the sum which would enable us to meet a
very heavy strain of a temporary character
on our finances I think we might be very
properly charged with overtaxing the taxpayer. There is no doubt that non-recurrent expenditure is very justifiably met by
means of a loan and a suitable sinking fund,
so as to enable the loan to be repaid in easy
stages. One purpose for which borrowing
would be necessary would be for loans to
local authorities. We never can tell what
loans we may be asked to make.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Are there any applications
at the moment?
Mr. BARBOUR: We have heard of one. It
has not been put before us in definite form.
Then there are loans to the Unemployment
Fund. I sincerely hope this matter may be
tided over. We hope that in due time that
fund may be put on a solvent basis. And
then there is another reason for borrowing,
and that is, the uneven flow of revenue into
the Exchequer and out of the Exchequer
account. While the year may balance at the
end of the twelve months we may be overdrawn in the early part of the year and
have to borrow in order to meet out-goings,
though the loan may be repaid during the
currency of the same year. The first loan
which will actually be made in connection
with this Bill will, of course, be the Ulster
Savings Certificates. The expenses of raising any such loan will be borne on the votes
of Parliament rather than on the Consolidated Fund, as is the custom in the United
Kingdom. This is to secure to the House
of Commons an opportunity of discussing
estimated expenses before the event rather
than after they have been incurred. I beg
to move the first resolution.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: On a point of order, is
that really an amendment or is it a new
resolution? It confuses me at the moment.
The CHAIRMAN: It is obviously a condition attached to the resolution and becomes
part of it.
Question as amended agreed to.
Resolved:

That it is expedient to authorise the
issue from the Consolidated Fund of any

Such Council, Commissioners or Guardians

Mr. BARBOUR: Members of the Imperial
Parliament, and possibly of this House and
others who follow National finance, will be
familiar with the expression Local Loansthat is, loans provided for local authorities
which, as a rule, are raised for that particular purpose. As we are not on so grand
a scale as Westminster we do not think it
necessary to have a special loan for that
particular purpose. We propose that loans
should be raised for general purposes, paid
into the Exchequer, and then issued for such
purposes as may be required. I think that
is the only explanation that hon. Members
will require. I beg to move the third resolution.

THE ENGINEERING DISPUTE.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: There is a matter that I
would like to bring before the House, and
particularly I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Labour to it. We are
all aware that a very serious crisis obtains
at the moment in respect of the engineering
industry. An attempt is being made to
bring the employers and the representatives
of the workers together in order, if possible,
to adjust the difficulty. We all hope that
good may attend that effort, but up to the
moment the British Parliament have not
felt themselves warranted in intervening in
the dispute. It is rather regrettable that
they should have taken that course, because
there at at least two alternatives that could
be adopted with respect to it. There are at
least two boards that could be called in to
intervene in the situation. What I want to
bring before the Minister of Labour is this.
While this difficulty is still pending, and
while arrangements are being suggested with
respect to bringing it to a solution, acrimonious criticism is being indulged in from
one quarter and another, and in particular
with regard to the attitude of the workers.
It has been suggested that they have been
provocative in the past, that they have
assailed from time to time the position of
the employers and challenged their rights
upon the managerial principle. Well, I
want to say, as one associated with the
Union that is at the moment locked out,
that we deny those allegations-we absolutely deny in respect of that that the engineers
of this city have been in one instance guilty
at least for the last ten years. I think the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) will
admit, and perhaps the House will agree,
that during the war there could have been
no better record than that achieved by the
industrial forces of this city. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We did as efficiently, and
we achieved as much, as any other centre in
the three Kingdoms, and in some particulars
we excelled all other centres in our contribution to the winning of the war. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Under those circumstances, to be charged
with a provocative attitude, with aggravating the situation, and with bringing about
the present impasse is, I think, a most regrettable thing. I have had a communication, I may as well say to the
House, from the Amalgamated Engineering
Union (Belfast Committee), who have
invited me to put a question to the
House, and to ask the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) if he will concede
to us a Court of Inquiry, or let me say Committee of Inquiry, to look into the question
of these allegations. The communication
reads:-
"We here in Belfast have never had at
any time any trouble with the Belfast
Employers' Association."
I want the Minister of Labour to mark that.
That is a specific statement on the part of
the Union, and they disclaim any
responsibility.
"We here in Belfast have never had at
any time any trouble with the Belfast
Employers' Association on the question at
issue, and are assured if an inquiry were
held the same could be said of many other
centres, which would go to show that the
employers have no ground for their present
attitude."
the
Now, I want to support that attitude on
the part of the District Committee of the
Engineering Union. I want to take up that
attitude and support it with the testimony
of my own experience. I would only ask the
right hon. Gentleman to take this into consideration, though as perhaps he knows the
Imperial Parliament, particularly
Minister of Labour, has declined to intervene at the moment or to set up a cominittee.
Well, in view of the fact that other alternatives were open but not adopted, it would
be only fair to the engineering union if he
constituted a committee that he will be
absolutely free to nominate, and whose
umpire or chairman he will be free to nominate, too. I think it is only fair that he
should take into consideration the suggestion

made by this Committee and set up a Comittee of Inquiry to look into this
case and see how far the allegations made
with respect to the engineers in this matter
can be supported. It is not asking too much.
Perhaps, the Minister of Labour would be
prepared to make a statement and give us
an opinion with respect to the matter, or if
he cannot see his way to set up a committee
now on account of the present dispute, if he
will say that at some future time he will set

matter and decide on these allegations, I
am sure, as representing the Union, I will
be obliged.
Mr. TWADDELL: I would like to support
the appeal made by my hon. Friend for
North Belfast (Mr. M'Guffin). The Minister of
Labour has been so successful in connection
with these labour disputes that I feel if he
agreed to set up such a Committee, good
would result therefrom. I suppose it is
within the knowledge of most Members of
this House that some years ago a great industrial dispute of this kind happened
throughout the entire country, but we at
least managed to escape the troubles of a dispute and strike. I feel that if the Minister
of Labour would agree to set up this Committee of Inquiry we might be quite confident that through his good services the result
would be most satisfactory, and to the
advantage of the whole community.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): If the Government thought that
such an inquiry would be productive of good
and lead to a settlement, they would most
heartily agree to form such a Committee, but
on the other hand my view at the moment
is that the setting up of such a Committee
would prolong this dispute rather
than bring it to the end which we all
desire. The Minister of Labour in the
Imperial Government was asked to form a
Committee of this kind, and he refused.
I would feel in a difficulty in taking a different course, especially as this trouble is
not a local trouble, but a national trouble.
There is no local trouble. In fact, the circular from the Amalgamated Engineering
Union (Belfast District) which my hon.
Friend has read, and of which I have a copy
here, points out clearly that we here in
Belfast have never had at any time any
trouble with the Belfast Employers' Association on the question at issue."

That being so, I really fail to see why we
should form a Committee, or what the
terms of reference would be. It is true, as
my hon. Friend has said, that certain
statements detrimental to the interests of the
engineers have been made in the Press by
certain individuals. I do not think that
this House would agree to take notice of
such statements. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The point really is that this is not
a local trouble, but is, as I have said, a
national trouble. Indeed, I was able to arrange with our employers here and the local
representatives of the Union referred to that
provided the local employers were able to
obtain the permission of their Federation in
the United Kingdom to allow them to withdraw the notices there would be no lock-out
in Belfast and district, subject to the condition that whatever settlement was agreed to
in Great Britain would be binding on both
parties here.
Unfortunately, and to my great disappointment, the local employers were unable to obtain the permission of the Federation in Great
Britain to adopt this course, and so the lockout notices were kept up. However, I see from
the Press that this matter is receiving considerable attention across the water, and I
hope that a settlement will be brought about
at no distant date. I feel that if we were to
set up a Committee now while ballots are
being taken across the water it would prolong the trouble here. I think I ought to
point out to the House that this dispute is
the result of the men refusing-of course
within their rights-refusing to accept the
advice of their own leaders in Great Britain.
A vote was taken, and I think I am right
in saying that only about 70,000 voted out of
a total membership of 400,000.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: 21 per cent.
Mr. ANDREWS: About 21 per cent. of the
whole. Of course if a large percentage had
voted we would have had a proper indication-
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Might I point out to my
right hon. Friend that the vote upon which
the conditions were established was only an
18 per cent. vote, so that we improved the
vote in respect of this matter.
Mr. ANDREWS: I think that bears out
my point and strengthens my argument that
so few voted that a poor indication was given
of the real feelings of the men themselves.
I am satisfied now, however, that conciliation
is at work in Great Britain, and I am very
hopeful that this trouble will be brought
to an end quickly. In the capacity of a
negotiator I would be pleased to do all I can
to bring about that very desirable result.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. DONALD: I only wish to say a word
or two generally on the question of the lockout. Having some previous experience with
regard to industrial matters as they concern
us locally I fail to understand the attitude

It was always held that they were not members of the Federation. Indeed, for 20 years
or more the Belfast shipbuilding and engineering firms carried on while a national
strike took place on the other side. If there

breaking of trades unionism, then I, for one,
will take up a very different attitude, because I have some experience of what the
rights of the workers should be. I think,
in my humble judgment, the employers in
Belfast have no grievance whatever,

23 MARCH 1922.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 23rd March, 1922.
The House met at a quarter after Two of
the Clock, Mr. Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
BELFAST PRISON DISCIPLINE.
1. Mr. WILLIAM GRANT asked the
Minister for Home Affairs whether there
have been complaints from residents in the
vicinity of Belfast Prison respecting undue
noises and disorder; whether strict discipline is being maintained in the Prison,
and whether the Regulations are being duly
enforced? What is the position of affairs
with respect to prisoners who have been
sentenced to hard labour for so-called political offences, and whether any distinction
is made between them and persons sentenced
to similar terms for ordinary offences?
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): No complaints have
been received for some time as the Prison
has been quiet. Strict discipline is being
maintained, and the Prison Regulations are
being duly enforced. Certain prisoners who
have been sentenced to hard labour have
refused to work and have been confined to
their cells. The only concession made in the
case of certain so-called political prisoners
was to allow them to receive two parcels
of food per week and to receive and write
a reasonable number of letters. This has
been continued only to that class of prisoner who were committed before we took over
the administration of the Prisons, but prisoners convicted by the ordinary Courts are
now subjected to the ordinary prison regulations irrespective of whether the offence is a
so-called political offence or not.
PROPOSALS OF GEDDES COMMITTEE.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has received any protests
against the proposals of the Geddes Commitee on National Expenditure to impose a
fee of 10s on each annual valuation return
sent to the Chief Registrar of Friendly
Societies; if so, whether he will state the
intention of the Government with regard to
this matter?
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The answer to the
first part of the question is in the negative.
The Northern Government have deferred
consideration of the question of the imposition of any such fee pending the decision of
the Imperial Government regarding the proposals of the Geddes Committee on this
point.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
seeing that some dissatisfaction has arisen
with regard to this question and others
arising out of the Report of the Geddes Committee on National Expenditure, may I ask
the Prime Minister if he will give an early
day to discuss the Geddes Report?
The PRIME MINISTER: I am afraid we
could hardly give a day to discuss the Geddes
Report in this House. I am sure the hon.
Member will get a day in the Imperial House
of Commons, of which he is a Member.
Mr. DONALD: I quite agree, but as
matters in the Report refer to the Services
of this country I think it would be quite in
keeping that this House should have an
opportunity of discussing it with reference
to those Services which are not now under
the Imperial Parliament.

CIVIL AUTHORITIES OF NORTHERN
IRELAND (SPECIAL POWERS) BILL.
Considered in Committee.
[MR. MOLES in the Chair.]
Clause 1 (Powers for preserving peace and
maintaining order.)
1.-(1) The civil authority shall have
power, in respect of persons, matters and
things within the jurisdiction of the Government of Northern Ireland, to take all such
steps and issue all such orders as may be
necessary for preserving the peace and
maintaining order, according to and in the
execution of this Act and the regulations
contained in the Schedule thereto, or such
regulations as may be made in accordance
with the provisions of this Act (which regulations, whether contained in the said
Schedule or made as aforesaid, are in this
Act referred to as "the regulations"):
Provided that the ordinary course of law
and avocations of life and the enjoyment of
property shall be interfered with as little
as may be permitted by the exigencies of the
steps required to be taken under this Act.
(2) For the purposes of this Act the civil
authority shall be the Minister of Home
Affairs for Northern Ireland, but that Minister may delegate, either unconditionally or
subject to such conditions as he thinks fit,
all or any of his powers under this Act to
any officer of police. and any such officer of
police shall, to the extent of such delegation,
be the civil authority as respects any part
of Northern Ireland specified in such
delegation.
(3) The Minister of Home Affairs shall have
power to make regulations-
(a) for making further provision for the
preservation of the peace and maintenance
of order, and
(b) for varying or revoking any provision
of the regulations;
and any regulations made as aforesaid shall,
subject to the provisions of this Act, have
effect and be enforced in like manner as regulations contained in the Schedule to this
Act.
(4) All regulations made as aforesaid shall
be laid before both Houses of Parliament as
soon as may be after they are made, and, if
an address is presented to the Lord Lieutenant
by either House within the next fourteen days
during the session of Parliament after any
such regulation is laid before it praying that
the regulation may be annulled, the Lord
Lieutenant may annul that regulation and it
shall thenceforth be void, without prejudice
to the validity of anything done thereunder,
or to the power of making a new regulation;
and regulations made as aforesaid shall not
be deemed to be statutory rules within the
meaning of Section 1 of the Rules Publication Act, 1893.
Special Powers Bill.

CLAUSE 2.-General Provisions as to
Offences.)
(1) It shall be the duty of every person
affected by any order issued by the civil
authority or other person in pursuance of
the regulations to comply with that order.
and if he fails to do so he shall be guilty of
an offence against the regulations.
(2) Any person who attempts to commit, or
solicits or incites or endeavours to persuadé
another person to commit, or procures, aids
or abets, or does any act preparatory to, the
commission of, any act prohibited by the
regulations, or any order, rules, or other instrument made thereunder, or harbours any
person whom he knows, or has reasonable
grounds for supposing, to have acted in
contravention of the regulations, or any
order, rules, or other instrument made thereunder, shall be guilty of an offence against
the regulations.
(3) It shall be the duty of any person who
knows, or has good reason for believing, that
some other person is acting, has acted, or is
about to act, in contravention of any provisions of the regulations to inform the
civil authority of the fact, and if he fails
to do so he shall be guilty of an offence
against the regulations.
(4) If any person does any act of such a
nature as to be calculated to be prejudicial
to the preservation of the peace or maintenance of order in Northern Ireland and
not specifically provided for in the regulations, he shall be deemed to be guilty of an
offence against the regulations.
(5) Where the offence against the regulations is committed by a corporation or company, every director and officer of the
corporation or company shall be guilty of
the like offence, unless he proves that the
act constituting the offence took place without his knowledge or consent.
(6) Where under the regulations any act if
done without lawful authority or without
lawful authority or excuse is an offence
against the regulations, the burden of prov
ing that the act was done with lawful
authority or with lawful authority or excuse
shall rest on the person alleged to be guilty
of the offence.
(7) Sections one to four, inclusive, of the
Criminal Evidence Act, 1898, shall apply in
the case of a person charged with an offence
against the regulations.

CLAUSE 5.-(Special Punishment for Certain
Offences).
Where after trial by any court a person is
convicted of any crime or offence to which
this section applies, the court may, in addition to any other punishment which may
lawfully be imposed, order such person, if a
male, to be once privately whipped, and the
provisions of sub-section (6) of section
thirty-seven of the Larceny Act, 1916, as to
sentences of whipping shall apply accordingly.
The crimes and offences to which this
section applies are as follows:-
(1) Any crime under the Explosive Substances Act, 1883, as extended by section 18
of the Firearms Act, 1920.
(2) Any offence against the Firearms Act,
1920, in relation to the having, keeping or
using of firearms.
(3) Any offence against the regulations in
relation to the carrying, having, or keeping
of firearms, military arms, ammunition or
explosive substances.
(4) Any offence against section 30 of the
Larceny Act, 1916 (which relates to demanding with menaces, with intent to steal).
Mr. BEST: I beg to move in clause 5, page 4,
line 27, at end insert:-
Special Powers Bill.
-Committee.
23 MARCH 1922.
"Provided that this section shall not be
deemed to apply to any crime or offence
committed before the passing of this Act."
In Clause 5 we propose to assign new
punishments to old offences. At present we
have no power to punish offenders who are
guilty of offences under the Explosive Substances Act or the Firearms Act of 1920 by
whipping, and we have no power also to
punish by whipping those offenders who demand money with menaces with intent to
steal. Under section 23 of the Larceny Act of
1916 the court has power to order whipping
where there is robbery with violence, but we
wish also to give the Court power where money
has been demanded with menaces. A man
goes into a public-house and pretends he has
got a revolver, and really the threat that he
makes is quite as good as if he had
a revolver, and he demands money with
menaces. We wish to make a case like that
punishable by whipping. This Amendment
has reference only to offences of this nature
that may occur after the passing of this Act.
We have a number of people, for example,
awaiting trial at the moment, and we do
not wish, if those trials did not come on
until this Act is passed, to make this Section
apply to them. We only wish that in
future people will know what is up against
them, and therefore the Act in that respect
should not be retrospective.
Mr. DONALD: What is the law in respect
to the person who refuses to recognise the
Court?

therefore it could not be competent for the

it applies to
"Any offence against the regulations in
relation to the carrving, having, or keeping of firearms, military arms, ammunition, or explosive substances."
Am I warranted in thinking that it is
within the power of the Court to impose
whipping in connection with the carrying
of arms?
Mr. BEST: Certainly.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: I would think that
would be exceeding the limits of the necessity of the case. (Hon. Members, "No.") I
differ with the Committee on that matter.
It is not every person to whom a permit will
be granted on application, and there are
many people who feel that a revolver is
necessary under the present circumstances
for their own protection. They might do
that secretly without any intention in the
world of injuring any person, or of invading
the rights of anyone. It seems to me if
they were apprehended in the city and
brought to Court it might be possible that
they would be subjected not only to the
corporal punishment, but to the humiliation
of having the whip used upon them.
Now I think there should be a modification
of this Bill. Suppose I myself could not
obtain the right to carry a revolver, but
thought it necessary to carry one for my own
protection. have no intent to use it against
any person, yet, if I am apprehended on the
street, I am summarily dealt with. I think
that is going beyond the necessities of the
case. I would ask the right hon. Gentleman
to consider that matter and see if that particular Section could not be modified in such
a way as to release respectable citizens from
being dealt with in that manner. It would be
humiliating, to say the least of it. Why,
the circumstances of the moment would
almost warrant one in protecting himself
against imminent danger.
Mr. LYNN: The most serious trouble at the
present moment is the carrying of firearms.
Surely the first business of the Government
is to use whatever means are necessary to
end that practice. I quite realise the position
of my hon. Friend (Mr. M'Guffin), but a wise
Government is not going to prohibit lawabiding citizens like the Member for North
Belfast from getting a permit to carry firearms. Indeed a stage may be reached when
it will be necessary for the Government to
arm all law-abiding citizens in order to maintain civilisation in the country.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: I do not wish to move an
amendment. I simply want to see if the right
hon. Gentleman could take the matter into
consideration. If he is not prepared to do so
I waive my objection.

Dr. MORRISON: I would suggest to the
Attorney General that in the first paragraph
of Clause 6 he is asking unreasonable power,
namely the power to abolish absolutely
coroners' inquests. I do not think that is
necessary. I would be quite willing to give
him any powers which are necessary, or which
he thinks, on consideration, are necessary.
The power to hold an inquest by a coroner
who is attempting to obstruct the law, or
bring discredit on officials connected with the
law, should be taken from him, but I think
the holding of inquests is a very necessary
thing under ordinary and other circumstances
that may arise. They satisfy public opinion,
and I believe where inquests are necessaryas I hope they will not be our people will
come out of the proceedings with credit. I
consider that the right hon. Gentleman has
ample power if he retains the right of abolishing the power of a coroner to hold an inquest
in any particular case. If he can see his way
to meet us in this respect he will not lessen
the efficiency of his Bill.
The CHAIRMAN: Do you propose any
definite Amendment?
Dr. MORRISON: No; I only make the
suggestion.
Mr. BEST: I am sorry it is impossible for
me to meet my hon. Friend in this matter.
The matter has been considered very carefully
indeed. I may say there is no intention of

The Clause is:
"For the purpose of preserving the peace
and maintaining order, the Minister of
Home Affairs may, by order, prohibit the
holding of inquests by coroners on dead
bodies in any area in Northern Ireland."
We cannot shut our eyes to the fact that
there are some areas where the coroners are
not in sympathy with us-where they are
absolutely hostile to us, and the Minister of
Home Affairs wishes, under these circumstances, to be able to prohibit inquests from
being held in those particular areas.
Although the Minister of Home Affairs is
under no obligation to do so, he does me
the honour of consulting me about these
things. I give him the best advice I can,
and I give it solely in what I conceive to
be the public interest. The hon. Member
for Queen's University may rest assured that
these powers will not be abused either by
my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
or myself.
Dr. MORRISON: I am satisfied.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I would like to point out
that the carrying out of this particular
Clause might reflect discreditably on ourselves. If we take over the powers to prohibit inquests you may arouse suspicion
amongst a certain section of society, that
there is something of a secret nature behind
it-whereas, on the other hand, an open
investigation into the cause of death and the
verdict, even though it were given by a
partial coroner, would satisfy public opinion.
We may incur a greater risk to our reputation as a Parliament and Government if
you persist in the present course. Under
the circumstances, I think it would be wiser
to have discretionary power and not absolute power.
Mr. BEST: Under Regulation 81 of the

Mr. ROBB: I find a difficulty in knowing
what the policy of the Government is under
this Section as it stands. Do they intend
that persons whose property and rights are
interfered with shall have a right of bringing
in the County Court, under the rule that has
been made, an action to recover compensation,
or is there to be some prior sanction to be
given by some person for bringing any proceedings? The first Sub-section says this,
"Where, under the powers conferred by
this Act or the Regulations, any lands,
buildings, or property are taken, occupied,
or destroyed, or any other act is done
involving interference with private rights
of property, compensation may be paid by
the Civil Authority."
If you stop there, and compensation was a
thing that was to be decided by the Civil
Authority, it would be simple enough to
understand, but the next Sub-Section says
this:
"If any question arises as to the liability
of the Civil Authority to pay compensation
under this Section, or as to the amount of
such compensation, the question, if not
settled by agreement, may be referred for
settlement to the County Court or an
Arbitrator to be appointed by that Court,
and such questions shall be settled in
accordance with such procedure as may be
prescribed by rules made by the Lord Chief
Justice of Northern Ireland after consultation with the Civil Authority."
Suppose the Civil Authority says this is a
case in which compensation ought not to be
paid, but the claimant says it is a case in
which compensation ought to be paid? A
question has then arisen as to the liability
of the Civil Authority to pay compensation,
and it is not settled. Apparently it is then
to go before the County Court. I do not
understand the meaning of the Section as it
stands. Suppose the County Court disagrees
with the Minister of Home Affairs, and says
this is a case in which compensation ought
to be paid? Who is to prevail? You have
said under the first Sub-Section of this
section that the Civil Authority may pay,
but under the second Section the County
Court may apparently say, no matter what
the Civil Authority thinks, that they shall
pay and they must pay. Is there to be a
right in the subject whose property is taken
to receive compensation, or is there to be a
right to obtain compensation only in those
cases in which the Civil Authority thinks
compensation ought to be paid? The Section
does not make it clear. The Government
ought to make up its mind which line of
policy it wishes to adopt. I can see a great
many arguments in favour of the Civil
Authority saying they will not pay compensation, because owing to the information they
have they do not think the owner or occupier
of the property was free from implication in
the civil disturbances. I suggest to the
Attorney-General that in consultation with
the Government he formulate definitely in
his own mind which of the two methods he
wishes to adopt, and, having made up his
mind, to make it quite clear in the Section
what it is he wants done.

RAID ON ST. MARY'S HALL.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That this House do now adjourn." (Mr.
Burn.)
Mr. HANNA: The Attorney-General has
said nothing about the raid on St. Mary's
Hall a few days ago, and I think it will
be in the public interest to know whether
he is going to have an inquiry into the
matter. The House should know what
Fower the right hon. Gentleman had in this
regard. Section 6 of the Explosive Substances Act, 1883, says :-
Where the Attorney-General has reasonable ground to believe that any
crime under this Act has been committed
he may order an inquiry under this
Section, and thereupon any justice of the
county, borough or place in which the
crime was committed or is suspected to
have been committed, who is authorised
in that behalf by the Attorney-General,
may, although no person may be charged
before him with the commission of such
crime, sit at a police court or petty
sessional or occasional courthouse or police
station in the said county, borough, or
place, and examine on oath concerning
such crime any witness appearing before
him, and may take the deposition of such
witness and, if he see cause, may bind
such witness by recognizance to appear
and give evidence at the next Petty
Sessions or when called upon within three
months from the date of such recognizance,
and the law relating to the compelling of
the attendance of a witness before a justice
and required to give evidence concerning
the matter of an information or complaint,
shall apply to compelling the attendance
of a witness for examination and to a
witness attending under this Section."
Now, the right hon. Gentleman has power
to direct an inquiry to which every person
who has any interest in St. Mary's Hall
where these bombs were found can be
summoned and made to answer any
question put to him touching his knowledge
of the presence of these bombs. We have
spent the whole of this day giving special
powers. Here you have powers to deal with
a situation that has arisen, and the right
hon. Gentleman has the information now
that these bombs were there. I respectfully
suggest that it is the duty of the Government to make and prosecute every inquiry
they can with a view to bringing these
people to justice. I only ask if it is intended to take any steps. We are not even
told that I took the opportunity yesterday
or the day before to warn the House when
we were dealing with the Civil Authorities
of Northern Ireland (Special Powers) Bill
that all power would be taken away from
this House, and here we have an instance
of it to-day. We will be told when we ask
a question about the administration of the
new law exactly what I have been told in
regard to the old law-" that it is not in
the public interest to let you know whether
we intend to do anything or not." I do
not think, under the circumstances, that is
an answer which the right hon. Gentleman
should give to any Member of this House.
We are entitled to some assurance that it
is the intention of the Government to
exercise the powers they have, and to
prosecute those who had the custody of
those weapons of offence used with such
deadly aim all over Belfast and other parts
of Northern Ireland.
Mr. BEST: I am surprised at my hon.
Friend persisting in this matter. I could
quite understand a layman but I cannot
understand a lawyer taking up the attitude,
where a crime has been committed, and
where investigations and inquiries must be
made, that before these inquiries have been
fully carried out the world must be told
what steps are being taken or may be
taken. I decline to answer my hon. Friend
in any other way than the way I have
already answered him, namely that in my
opinion it is entirely out of keeping with
the public interest, that I should disclose
what steps, if any, I intend to take in the
matter.

serious matter. The Member for Queen's
University, referring to it the other day

a Special had a right to have a drink just
as well as the ordinary individual." I think
it would be a serious deprivation of privilege

into consideration what the House cannot

cannot but think that if hon. members would

circulated in regard to our Police Force. The

but I think that if the hon. Member took
more interest in the Special Constabulary he

the manner in which these wet canteens are
conducted. I would like to explain to this
House the method under which these canteens are run. First of all, no spirits are
allowed to be sold-only beer and stout.
They are only allowed to be open within
certain specified hours; they are managed by
the men themselves, and every month the
Commandant of the Constabulary inspects
the accounts, which are also constantly
checked by officers, and by that means they
are able to ascertain whether, as some hon.
members have suggested, the
men overindulge themselves, and I am glad to say
that there has not been a single instance of
over-indulgence.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: That is not the point we

strictly sober. I would ask the right hon.
Gentleman to address himself to the moral
aspect of the question.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps the hon.
Member will allow me to finish. The District Commissioner has always taken up the
attitude of providing comforts and recreation for the men and, in practice, the result
of having these wet canteens, properly
managed and controlled, has been to prevent

entertained by their so-called friends. I do

Constabulary he would realise these things.
Apparently he has never been inside a barracks, otherwise he would not have said he
only now learned with surprise that these
canteens have existed in barracks. In addition to these wet canteens we have dry canteens, and in the management of these dry

Mr. M'GUFFIN: I take the opportunity
that is afforded me by this motion of saying
how much we regret that affairs in the city
have not very much improved. Last night
we had a very serious outburst by which four
persons lost their lives, and in all probability
the death-roll will be increased by the three
who were wounded; while at mid-day yesterday, in broad daylight, two of our Special
Constabulary were assassinated in the public
street. We were discussing a Bill, the terms
of which are calculated to effect a repression
of these very dreadful crimes, and I was
wondering if I might ask the right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs, if
it would be possible to make adequate
provision for the protection of life even
during the hours of Curfew. We all
have the opinion that no man. with
even the suggestion of humanity about
him would be guilty of these horrible outrages. They are committed by miscreants
who, up to the moment, have evaded the law,
but who we hope will be apprehended in the
future as a result of the measure that we dealt
with yesterday. I would like the right hon.
Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) to say if it
would be possible to make further provision
in this matter to prevent a recurrence of these
horrible scenes in the night-time. We all felt
a sort of assurance that we were quite safe
during the Curfew hours, but if these crimes
continue to occur we will feel that under no
circumstances are we safe.
Another thing that I would like to mention
is that in connection with yesterday's debate,
particularly the closing part of it, some heat
developed with regard to the discussion of the
question of wet canteens. I assure you that,
as one who instigated the discussion, and who
is to that degree responsible for it, I did not
intend to be, and I hope I have not been, in
any sense offensive to the Minister involved.
I brought before him, as I thought I was
entitled to do, a question of urgent public
importance immediately concerning his Department. I do not remember the exact
terms of my criticism, but I am quite sure of
this that I did not exceed the limits of discretion or indulge in the language of offence.
But I think we are entitled to bring a matter
of this sort before the Minister of a Department, in order that we may hear what he has
got to say with respect to it, and no person
should be regarded as in any sense implying
maladministration, or even negligence, on the
part of the Minister responsible, because, forsooth, he happens to bring objections or
criticisms against his particular policy. I
assure the right hon. Gentleman that was not
implied.
I do not think it would be advisable to say much more upon this mat.
ter. I am more particularly concerned
about the peace of the city at the
moment, and, seeing that the Prime Minister
is present, and in view of the recent occurrences which are of such an atrocious and at
the same time startling character, I wondered
if it would be possible for him to give the
House some assurance with regard to the protection of life and property during the hours
of Curfew.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): May I say on behalf of the
Government how much I deplore the occurrences of yesterday and last night? For some
time past we have been increasing the number
of "C" men and mobilising them for duty
in the streets, and I can assure my hon.
Friend (Mr. M'Guffin) that every possible
step is being taken with the object of bringing these murderers to justice, no matter to
what class or creed they belong. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
With regard to the discussion that took
place yesterday, if in the course of my reply
to the remarks of my hon. Friend, the Member for North Belfast (Mr. M'Guffin) I used
an expression which he may have thought
conveyed other than what I really meant,
may I say that I had just heard the news of
the murder of two members of our Special
Constabulary, and I had read an attack in
one of the Nationalist newspapers accusing
specially the "B" men of entering publichouses and indulging in drink. Perhaps 1
replied in a more heated way than I would
otherwise have done. I do not want to re-

Mr. M'GUFFIN: Hear, hear. That is what

Sir DAWSON BATES: There is one point
I did not mention yesterday, and in regard
to which I think there is some misunderstanding. It should not be assumed that
there is a wet canteen in every Special Constabulary barracks. Such is not the case.
The camp at Newtownards is a joint camp.
The troops there have a wet canteen and a
dry canteen, and hon. Members will understand there is a great deal of difficulty in
differentiating between a special constable
and a soldier who are in the same camp. I
do not wish to say anything more in regard
to the matter.

Mr. POLLOCK: I beg to move. The House
will remember that in my statement submitting the Vote on Account on Wednesday
last I entered with some elaboration of detail
into the capital requirements of the Government during the coming year. These were
particularly for the purpose of advancing
money to Local Authorities for their public
schemes, advances to the Unemployment Insurance Fund, and any possible deficiency of
revenue that might arise particularly in the
early part of the year, which is generally
described as the lean months of the yearthat is to say, when revenue does not
flow into the Exchequer in sufficient
amount to meet the liabilities. The
object of this Bill is to deal generally with
the subject matter that I have referred to,
and, specifically, first for borrowing for the
Exchequer Account, and secondly for issuing
from the Consolidated Fund all the loans to
which I have just made reference.
We only require power to issue an occasional loan to local authorities because the
issuing power is already granted or will be
sought for by means of a separate Bill; that
is to say, a separate Bill will be introduced
to extend the power of issuing for the Unemployment Fund. The Consolidated Fund Bill
will give power to issue for any deficiencies
of revenue that may arise. This present Bill,
therefore, so far as it relates to the Unemployment Fund, is an extension of the means
of borrowing, and if we remove the legislative phraseology the borrowing powers of the
Bill refer to the new issue of Ulster Savings
Certificates. I explained the main features
of the Ulster Savings Certificates on the Vote
on Account, so I do not consider it is necessary now to enter into any further detail,
but there may be some necessary amendments to the scheme in order to meet local
requirements which can be discussed later.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Is it the right hon.
Gentleman's intention to issue these Certificates immediately?
Mr. POLLOCK: On the 1st April. The
discontinuance of the issue of National
Savings Certificates oa the part of the Imperial Authorities takes effect on 1st April,
and it is intended that our Savings Certificates should be immediately issued in substitution of the earlier
ones. Any further
details that are required in regard to this
question of the necessity of borrowing I shall
be glad to give in case any Member desires
it, but the Bill itself is of such a simple
character an so easily understood that I do
not think it will be necessary to detain the
House at any length in elaborating it. I beg
to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill read the Second Time.

As I have said in the printed foreword to

they had already assumed at the time these

at Westminster. They have advised us as

action has been deferred. It is only when.
that final transfer takes place that we will

is it right and proper and fair and

people should be asked to contribute to taxation in order to maintain these positions?
Candidly, I think it is not. I do not think it
is fair. I do not think it is just and right,
and consequently I enter my most humble
protest.

charge which will come in course of payment during the year ending 31st March,
1923, for the Salaries of the Department of

Mr. M'GUFFIN: Personally, I do not
think I can take exception to this vote.
But there is one thing in connection with
it here that I should like to pass some
observation upon. I find there are five
Cabinet Ministers, with £500 inclusive,
£2,000 in all. I think on another case
I remarked that I would very much prefer
that the amount should be consolidated
into a grant of £2,500. I do not see why
we should have that £500 inclusive. It
seems in the first instance to be a degradation to the Minister to have it paid in the
form of a bonus. I feel that in dealing with
this financial matter that we should suggest
that it should be altered. Of course it is
open to the criticism that the Minister need
not necessarily be a Member of the Cabinet
and that you should have, as it were, five
Members of the Cabinet with £500 a year
constituting the Cabinet without Ministerial
responsibility. I hope I have made my
position clear. That is what I mean to
say at any rate. I think it is not the
proper way to proceed. If the Committee
is of the opinion that a Cabinet Minister
who holds a portfolio is entitled to £2,000
a year, I, for one, will not demur. It is
just the policy that is being pursued by
the Executive. Now, the other objection
I have is with regard to the matter of the
Prime Minister's Secretary in connection
with what is called the Secretariat of the
Cabinet. That was a question that was
under consideration and criticism in this
House. The House took strong objection
to the adoption of the principle of a Secretary to the Cabinet. I do not know
whether there is any precedent for that.
It does not obtain across the water. The
point of my objection is this: I think when
the Prime Minister came to reply he stated
that he wanted it provisionally adopted and
to that the House assented. I find the word
"permanent" is placed in front of it. I
think it is going to be a permanent institution in this House. My objection
is this: You have a person present in the
Cabinet listening to the most important.
discussions, who is privy to everything that
takes place, and is not responsible to this
House. Cabinet secrets are always very
important matters. I understand there are
no minutes kept. Under these circumstances we can see the very great importance of having no person present at the
Cabinet meetings who is not in some degree
responsible to the House so that we can
hold him answerable for any dereliction of
duty of which he may be guilty. Then
we have, as a necessary consequence, the
assistant secretary. This represents further
expense. I am not going to cavil over the
matter, but I would rather it were presented
in a different way. In so far as the appointment of the secretariat is concerned,
if we get the assurance that it is not going
to be a permanent secretary-a permanent
institution in connection with this Parliament-it will disarm much of the criticism
I have made. I know that at the outset
of the Parliament and with such a tremendous undertaking as the Prime Minister had
in hand something in the nature of that
office was almost necessary. But while that
would be a justification at the moment, if
it is going to be declared a continuous policy
then my objection holds good, in view of
the fact that it does not exist in the Imperial Parliament.
The PRIME MINISTER: With reference
to the first criticism of my hon. Friend (Mr.
M'Guffin) on the question of how the extra
£500 for Cabinet Ministers appears in the
Votes, I think perhaps I should call his mind
back to the fact that this was an arrangement
of the House itself, not of the Government.
The House set up its Own Committee to
deal with these matters, and it was
a specific recommendation from the
Committee that Cabinet Ministers should
have the £500 in addition to their Ministerial
salaries. The Cabinet at that time were faced
with the alternative of either accepting the
report that was brought in by Members of
the House, or rejecting it, or amending it.
We decided, and I think rightly decided,
that, as we had asked Members of this House
to go into the whole matter, to go over to
London-to consult experts and authorities,
and to take all the difficulties and trouble on
their shoulders of dealing with the matter,
it would only be wise and reasonable on our
part to back up that Committee and to embody their findings in our Estimates. That
remains to-day as it did last year in exactly
the same position, but, of course, as all Votes
can, and properly can, be revised from year
to year, my hon. Friend can raise the point
from time to time. We still think it would
be wiser to adhere to the recommendations of
the Committee, for if we had deviated from
them in one respect we might have had to
deviate from them in other respects, which
would have caused considerable discontent
and trouble.
With regard to the second criticism, dealing with the Permanent Secretary of the
Cabinet, the hon. Member says there is no
precedent for the position, but he must know
there is not only one but many secretaries of
the British Cabinet-a Permanent Secretary
and a regular secretarial staff. Consequently we are not creating a precedent by

I would like to say with regard to the
Civil Authorities of Northern Ireland
(Special Powers) Bill, that owing to the
various amendments that were put down by
the Government when it was under discussion
yesterday, we felt it would be unfair to the
House to discuss the matter to-day, when it
would only be possible for Members to consider the Amendments in manuscript and not
see them upon the paper. Consequently the
Government decided that on the whole it
would be better to postpone this matter until
Tuesday next. There will not, I think, be
any undue delay in consequence of that course
being adopted, because if we can manage to
get through with the Bill the Senate will be
able to take it up on Wednesday, and we will
endeavour to get the Royal Assent at the
earliest possible moment.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 28th March, 1922.
The House met at a quarter after Two of
the Clock, Mr. Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
CONFERENCE WITH IMPERIAL
GOVERNMENT.
THE PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT.
Dr. MORRISON, by private notice, asked
the Prime Minister of he is in a position to
make a statement with regard to the Conference which is to be held in London tomorrow?
The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend
has asked me to make a statement with regard to the Conference that it is proposed
should be held to-morrow, and I will crave
the indulgence of the House if I have to
cover a considerable amount of ground. In
the first place, I would like the House to
understand that this is an invitation to meet
His Majesty's Government, and the policy
that we laid down very early in the controversy over the Free State Bill was that we
were always ready to present our case to the
British Government, that we had a good
case, and that we were not afraid of any
arguments that might be brought up against
the policy which we have pursued consistently from the beginning, which policy has
never been changed, and from which policy,
I personally never intend to deviate one inch.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
There may be critics who will say that it
is an error of judgment to go into any such
Conference, and there are other critics who
say we should lay down conditions before
going into such a Conference. That may be
so. I do not deny that the time might come,
as a time has come before when we refused
to go into such a Conference to discuss the
question of an All-Ireland Parliament in
which Ulster would be involved, and that
situation, or a similar situation, might
arise again. But, in the meantime, the
Government of which I am the head, have
carefully considered the whole matter, and
have come to the conclusion that in the best
interests of Ulster and of peace, which we
all desire, we should accept the invitation
extended by His Majesty's Government.
I would not to-day have made any statement on the subject at all had it not been
for the serious charge made against me esterday by Mr. Collins, to overlook which
might cause dissatisfaction amongst my loyal
supporters in Ulster-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and might at the same time allow an
unfounded impression to get abroad that I
had not honourably stuck to my word, and
had not done my utmost to carry out the
Agreement that he and I entered into. I
notice various discrepancies in Mr. Collins'

last? The Agreement is well known to everyone, but, before I read the Agreement, may
I read Mr. Collins' comments upon my attitude? He said:

Unfortunately Sir James Craig has not

He has neither kept his undertakings

When I came back from London, pleased

To secure the return of the Catholic workmen into the Belfast shipvards is a matter
which no Government as Government
could undertake. There is no law, as far

compelled to work alongside somebody else
whom he desires not to work alongside-in

many men may bring the horse to the pond,

The Government is always prepared to give

Therefore, I divested myself of the position

Those conditions were being drawn up

trade revives, and we have the old activity

creating the Special Constabulary necessary to
guard our Borders. I wonder that the health
of my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
stood the strain, never ending day or night,
of all the reports brought in, and taking a
grip of the situation which at one time seemed
hopeless, and which, I am glad to say, to-day
is very much better. I believe we will, in a
short time, show to the Government across the
water, as well as to the people here, that when
the Ulster people take a matter of this kind
in hand they can do it well-even better than
the Imperial authorities themselves. Now,
let me just say this-there are charges flung
about that we do not, in our speeches, sufficiently sympathise with the victims of these
outrages, or sufficiently condemn the outrages
which take place in our midst. That is
another wanton statement which it pleases the
Opposition Press to make, and most of the
Press is, unfortunately, in opposition to
Ulster. We cry inwardly to ourselves when
we hear of the widows created and the young
families left fatherless after these foul assassinations take place. And it would be a count
against us of insincerity if we were to repeat
that from day to day. Our condemnation of the
outrages has been made on frequent occasions
by different bodies and persons. Our clergy
have, as usual, entered into the spiritual side,
and done their utmost in these difficult
times, but our energy must be spent in
overtaking the difficulties and troubles in our
midst. We have had a pause. I believe there
was nothing to stain the name of our city
last night or this morning. Murder is a
terrible thing, and it is almost impossible to
place any variation on one type of murder
more than another. I say, standing at this
Table, that there can be no more foul murder
or assassination than the next one that takes
place in Belfast. The next murder will be
one of the foulest crimes that any citizen
could perpetrate, and let the person who
dreams of such a thing search his heart. It
may not be one man who may be murdered,
but hundreds, and perhaps thousands. On
the man who starts this thing, either by
speech, pen, or word, will rest the guilt and
sin. I earnestly pray that this slight pause
that has taken place will continue, and that
a better day will dawn for the citizens
of the city generally. But I am
going to have no charge laid upon the Protestant population as a population. In no city
in the world will you find a finer picture of
better self-control and self-restraint than has
been exhibited in Ulster. It is very easy for
editors in London offices and others to sit
down and write glibly about the Protestants
of this great city of ours. The long and the
short of it is that I will always say the Protestants are not to blame.
Mr. DONALD: They are too loyal.

The PRIME MINISTER: They are too
loyal to the Crown and Constitution, and too
loyal to their Protestantism, ever to allow
themselves to lose their self-restraint. I
know of no other body which has stood what
they have stood under provocation unparalleled in the history of the whole world. If
people only knew of that provocation, if they
thought for a moment what it means to have
two of our gallant men, while doing their best
to preserve the peace of the city, shot dead by
assassins who steal up behind them in broad
daylight and pull the trigger that leaves them
both lying on the ground The least said
about these things the better. The only way
to stop these outrages is for the South and
West to keep themselves in hand, for the
British Government to give them all the aid
they can to set their own house in order, and
not be constantly irritating and inflaming
passions amongst the Protestant community
of the North.
Now might 1 counsel moderation on the
part of public speakers. Let no man have it
laid upon him that by any unreasonable word
spoken on a public platform, he once more
started this sordid business. It is a time for
public men to practice self-restraint, coupled
with energy and effort to help the Govern-
Inent. At one time there was no Government.
Now there is a Government, firmly constituted with proper authority, with Police and
Specials who will be produced in any
numbers. Therefore, may I appeal to the
people for confidence, courage, and selfrestraint. Mr. Collins I presume, by his
speech, intended to create an atmosphere
before he went across to London. That is
what it is called in modern times; trying to
create an atmosphere before a meeting takes
place. I am going to create an atmosphere by
my concluding words, and that is to express
an earnest desire even at the eleventh houreven if I may say so on the stroke of twelvethat vindictiveness and hatred in Ireland
should give way to reasonableness and a sense
of proportion leading to peace. I want to
create an atmosphere of a helpful nature,
and not of an obstructive nature. God knows,
the difficulties and troubles through which
we are passing are heavy to a degree. Losing
one's head or heart will not solve the difficulty. What will solve it is what has solved
Ulster's difficulties before-that is the rallying of the people and of the spirit of the
people round their leaders in these trying
times and even placing greater restraint on
their private conversations. Let them stop
the criticising of little things which may take
place from day to day; let them take a grand
conception of their duty and help in the
great struggle between those not alone in our
midst but in the South and West of Ireland.
Let us daily and hourly pray that peace may
descend upon our land, peace for those at the
I believe that there is a possibility of
speedily wiping out the worst characters in
our midst. It may be more difficult to get
rid of the extremists and worst characters in
the South and West, but let us be no party to
backing up the extremists in these great and
dangerous times. Let us where we can see an
opportunity, even half a chance or no chance
at all, still talk to one another to endeavour
to save life and bring peace to our country.
That is the atmosphere which I hope will
surround us in London, the atmosphere which
I hope the British Government will welcome,
an atmosphere that we should allow all
that has passed to remain behind us-
I will not say to be forgotten, for it
is hard to forget some of the dreadful
things that have been done but I would
say let us start by thinking less of the
wrongs of the past and more of the great
possibilities that lie in the future. This is
a time above all others for men to do their
utmost to grapple with a serious situation,
to speak for peace, to work for peace, and,
if I may say so in all solemnity, to pray
for peace to pray for peace in the Churches
and in the home, so that God may hear us
when we ask Him to send His blessing upon
our land.

economic basis, and in asking that question
I would also like to ask the Minister of

I am probably accused of being as loose in
my statements as other people, but I want
to say here that, since the Provisional Government was set up, and since matters took
any definite shape, I do not think anybody
can point to where I made a speech in any
way provocative, or denunciatory of the organisation that ought to, and we hope may,
come into power in Southern Ireland. I want
to say at once we are in sympathy with any
power that will grip the situation, control
and govern the people of the South, and bring
them into ways of industry and peace. We
are with any such Government heart and
soul, and we are not here to taunt them, to
pick holes, or by word or act to say or do
anything provocative that might in any way
make wider the unfortunate breach that
exists between the two peoples.
Mr. COOTE: I should like to have some
information, if I may, on the question of the

able unrest, and to some extent a

ment, and there is very considerable dissatisfaction in the City and in the Province that

May I also draw attention to another fact
-at least it is alleged it is a fact-that there
is considerable waste of officers and men in
the Constabulary Depot at Newtownards. I
am informed, on very good authority, that

months ago, but was never sent there, and

ought to be given by a gentleman who is in

there as amount to waste. I hope the
Minister in charge will say whether or not

were brought to my notice by a gentleman
whose word I have to accept until I find
there is proof to the contrary. Might I revert to a few facts on which I should have
liked to have made a statement immediately
after the speech of the Prime Minister, but
which, owing to the manner in which it was
taken up, precluded any general discussion
by the Members of this House. I share with
the Prime Minister the feeling that this is a
time when we ought to bridle our tongues,
But there have been some statements made
which give us a perfect right to intervene in
defence of our own people. Statements have
been made, for instance, that the loyal people
of this city or the people of the Protestant
denomination are committing murder for the
love of murder, and I think it is time we
refuted these statements, if we can. From
reading the speech which Mr. Collins delivered on Sunday, and which was reported in
yesterday's papers, one would be led to think
that the Protestant people are entirely to
blame for all that is happening in the city
of Belfast, but he forgets that the methods
adopted by the Provisional Government are
something like this. Some time ago a communique was issued by the Provisional Government finding fault with a certain officer
of a regiment stationed in the city, and just a
few days after attention was drawn to this
man he was done to death. A few days later
the police were mentioned in another communique, and following their mention by the
Provisional Government five policemen were
shot in the city. Three of them were Roman
Catholics who were shot down in Roman
Catholic districts, entirely removed from
Protestant influence.
Then in connection with the troubles
on the Border, surely it is unfortun
ate that the loyal people of Tyrone and
Fermanagh should be blamed for a condition of things brought about entirely
by Southern Ireland. It was not the local
people who did the kidnapping.
There was
absolute peace on that Border. The Border of
South Tyrone was one of the most peaceful
districts in Ireland. It was so peaceful that
in connection with all the party demonstra
tions held in the old days, either on the 17th
March or the 12th July, it was not necessary
to draft in an extra policeman. There never
was any party bitterness of such a nature as
to lead to a breach of the peace. But, suddenly, without any notice, twenty-two peaco
able citizens were taken from their homes

ing, and they have to steal out in the nigh;
time to leave food for their cattle Only the

the other day charged Commandant O'Duffv
with making all the trouble on the Border
Commandant O'Connor is a Republican,
charging O'Duffy, the Free State Commandant, with making the trouble on the Border,
and O'Duffy says it may be true, or it may
not be true. He does not deny it. So far as
the Loyalists are concerned, their hands are

stare the community in the face now.
We would like, if we could, to impress upor
our own Prime Minister the necessity of
taking stronger measures for the protection
of the Border. When peaceable citizens are
done to death while attending to their cattle,
the time has come when the force of
authority should be so strengthened as to
give the necessary protection to people of this
kind. We believe that if the British Government, who are still responsible for the
government of the Free State, would put a
line of military inside the Free State, ind
declare a radius of two miles on the Southern side out of bounds, so that the Sinn Fein
snipers from that side could not send their
bullets across to Northern territory, it would
probably have the desired effect, or would
at least mitigate very much of the trouble.
Meantime we look with very great suspi-
Icion on this Conference in London. We fervently hope it will do good, but we believe
that it is a herring being drawn across the
trail, and that when the British Government
find themselves in a difficulty they will
always try to get Ulster to intervene to take
them out of the abominable position in
which they find themselves. We believe the
British Government are humiliated before
every British citizen, and we hope and we
believe that our Prime Minister, and those
associated with him in his mission to-night,
will be exceedingly wary of the gentlemen
with whom they have to deal, not only on
the side of Southern Ireland, but more particularly on the side of Great Britain itself.
We have no faith whatever in the British
Government. The only hope we have is that
they will soon be relieved of office, and that
they may never hold the reins again. Our
position is to try to enlighten the British
people-the British people are all right--as
to the condition of things in this country, in
the hope that we may get a Government with
some backbone, with some desire to maintain
law and order, and to preserve some form of
civilisation in the North and the South of
Ireland.
We believe, further, that this may be
another move on the part of the Southern
Government to weaken our own authority
here in the North. We believe that the
Government of Northern Ireland are now
gripping the situation; that, although things
look black to-day in the city and Province,
it is the beginning of the end of the Bolshevist and the gunman, and that in a very
short time, if our Government go on firmly
and steadily, supported by the great mass
of the people, Ulster will yet be a fit place
for decent people to live in and go about
their business. But we are afraid of anything that will in any way arrest
the hand of authority in tracking
down the murderer, be the murderer
Protestant or Catholic. That is our position. We want to assure the Government
that we are behind them in all their efforts
honestly and squarely to maintain law and
order, but we do view with very great suspicion this Conference in London. We hope
it will lead to no weakening of the means
taken here to protect the loyal citizens of
this Province, no matter what is their religious persuasion. We must be pardoned
when we say we have no faith in the British
Government or in any of their attempts to
restore order in Ireland, because they, and
they only, are responsible for the disorder
and for the terrible inheritance they have
handed on to the people of Northern Ireland. They only are responsible for it, and
we believe they have neither the backbone
nor the inclination to put down murder
North or South. They simply are drifting,
and they are now anxious to have us brought
in that we may to some extent take the responsibility off their shoulders and bear it
for them, a responsibility which will go
down in history as theirs, for the maladministration of things in Ireland.

Clause 3 (Trial of Offences)-
3. (1) A person alleged to be guilty of an
offence against the regulations may be tried
by a court of summary jurisdiction constituted in accordance with this section, and
not otherwise.
(2) An offence against the regulations shall
not be prosecuted except by such officer or
person as may be authorised in that behalf
by the Attorney-General for Northern Ireland, and in accordance with such directions
as may be given by the said Attorney-
General.
(3) Any person aggrieved by a conviction
of a court of summary jurisdiction for any
such offence may appeal in manner provided
by the Summary Jurisdiction (Ireland) Acts.
(4) A court of summary jurisdiction when
trying a person charged with an offence
against the regulations shall be constituted
of two or more resident magistrates, and a
court of quarter sessions, when hearing and
determining an appeal against a conviction
of a court of summary jurisdiction for any
such offence, shall be constituted of the
recorder or county court judge sitting alone.

Where any enactment or other provision

power by, or imposes any duty on, any

Mr. BEST: I beg to move in Clause XI.,
page 6, line 10, after the word "were" (were
exercisable by) (were imposed on) to insert
the word "also," in each place where that
word occurs.
The effect of this section is to provide that
certain powers hitherto exercisable by the
Royal Irish Constabulary can be exercised
in future by any constabulary that may be
established by the Northern Government.
As the Clause stood originally it might
possibly be open to the interpretation that
while those powers could in future be exercisable by the new Force, they could no
longer be exercisable by the old Force. Of
course that was not intended. Therefore, to
make the matter clear I propose to insert the
word "also ' immediately before the word
"exercisable," and also immediately before
the word "imposed." Then the effect will
be that where a provision or enactment
allows certain specified members of the
Royal Irish Constabulary to do certain
things-
That enactment or provision shall in
Northern Ireland have effect as if the said
power were also exercisable by, or the said
duty were also imposed on the corresponding officer or member (by whatever title
designated) of any police force under the
management and control of the Government of Northern Ireland.
It is to make clear the point that these
powers can be exercisable by our own police
force as well as by the existing Royal Irish
Constabulary that the Amendment is
proposed.

It is a new Regulation, and one which I
think will be of very great service to us by
way of procedure. It may possibly be that
an offence has been committed in a disturbed
part of the country, and it might be very inconvenient for a Court to be held in the particular place where the offence took place.
Under this provision it will be possible for
a person having, for example, jurisdiction in
the city of Belfast-the Resident Magistrates
in Belfast-to deal with an offence which has
been committed in a disturbed part of
County Down, or a disturbed part of County
Armagh, or any of the Six Counties.
In other words, the Magistrate will have
jurisdiction wherever the person may be
found at the time. It is a very important
matter, and we think it may be of great service, and I accordingly beg to move that this
be added to the Regulations.

Mr. McGUFFIN: I am sure I am only
voicing the opinion of the entire House when
I say that we regret very much the necessity
for the introduction of a measure of this
description, particularly at so early a stage
in the history of our own Parliament. The
Parliament itself was instituted in the midst
of civil commotion, and its existence has
been challenged ever since by a series of
social upheavals. The object of this Bill
is, as far as possible, and as soon as possible,
I presume, to effect a restoration of law and
order, and by that means bring about a state
of society which is more consistent with our
idea of civilisation. What I am afraid of
is that we are attaching too much importance to this Bill, and expecting too much
to result from it. It may be that I am quite
astray with respect to the matter, but I want
to impress upon the House that the repression of crime does not always imply the extirpation of the criminal tendency. It was
always said in regard to Crimes Acts, in
their application to Ireland in many years
gone past, that they did not affect the situation, they did not create a new feeling, or a
new tendency, or a new desire, or a new
aspiration in connection with the individual.
What they simply did was to drive crime
below the ground to reappear on some other
occasion. Therefore, so far from thinking
that it is exactly a legal difficulty, and one
capable of being solved even by the intensive
measures which are incorporated in this Bill,
so far from thinking that the situation is

soluble through that I am inclined to think
that our difficulty at the moment is a moral
difficulty. None of us, who have been reflecting upon the grave transpirings in connection with the Northern area, and, indeed,
throughout the whole of Ireland I might say,
can hide from ourselves the fact that there

will be able to do all that is promised of it;
but unfortunately men are very easily led
into criminal tendencies and criminal pursuits, and I think the words of the poet
Cowley never more truly applied than at the
present time
"The way to hell is open night and day,

In this a task of mighty labour lies."
We are lapsing in respect of recognition of
moral responsibility, and until this can be
arrested on the part of the community, and
until they can be brought to realise that they
personally are responsible in many instances
for the things that are transpiring round
them, I do not think that we have any just
grounds to hope for the good results which
are anticipated from this Bill. When
want to effect a great social or political reform we establish a propaganda, and sometimes we think that no expense is too great
for this particular purpose. We send emissaries abroad throughout the country and
print any amount of excellent literature, but
here is a case where we are anticipating
great results from a Bill which is merely of
a coercive character, or of a repressionist
character, and we are making no effort practically to raise the moral tendency of the
people.
The reason I introduce this point is this,
