Mr. COOTE: I merely rise for a moment
to refer to some matters on this Bill. I am
sure we all realise how very grave is the issue
and the circumstances under which this Bill
is introduced and which I hope will pass into
law. We realise it is no ordinary measure.
It is not to meet ordinary circumstances that
we are asked to past this measure. This Bill
is only for those who break the law-those who
persist in trying to destroy society, no matter
by what name they may be called. We are
trying to make an honest effort at stamping
out not ordinary crime, but diabolical crime
-crime the like of which this city has never
had the experience in its history before. We
have a heritage given us by the British
Government, a state of things rendered
unbearable because of the misgovernment
under which we have lived and laboured for
the last 15 years in Ireland.
The Constabulary, one of the finest bodies
of men, and the most honourable, at least
quite as honourable as any in any civilised
country in the world, were our pride until
1906. After 1916 they tried to do their duty
in Ireland, but they were hamstrung. They
were abused. Their recommendations were
thrown into the wastepaper basket. No action
was taken on their reports, and they were
însulted by the authorities in Dublin Castle
until, very naturally, the force relaxed its
efforts in finding out crime. Then our Secret
Service and I lay particular emphasis on it--
was practically abolished. I say to those who
are responsible for law and order in the
Northern area that we shall never have crime
stamped out until we have an efficient, keen,
fearless Secret Service working in this Province, until we are able to find out the dens
where these crimes are hatched, and are able
to lay our hand on the criminals, and those
intended to be criminals, practically before
they carry out their diabolical intention
For this purpose we must have this special
Act of Parliament. Does any hon. Member
of this House think that if a man is found
with a bomb in his pocket he has that bomb
there for a plaything? May the man found
with a bomb in his pocket not be a treble
murderer instead of being guilty of the
murder of a single person? Who can know
what may be the harm that this infernal
thing will do in the hands of a criminal?
When he throws the bomb he himself does
not know. Therefore, we must deal sharply
with the man or individual who carries in
in his house
his possession or harbours
infernal things of this sort with which to
destroy his neighbour, no matter what his
particular beliefs may be, or what his
political beliefs may be.
I suggest to the Ministry that there ought
to be a time limit given, and it ought to be
made more clear that the most drastic action
will be taken against those who are actually
armed without licence, or against those who
will harbour infernal machines of this kind.
I am afraid it has not been brought home to
their minds sufficiently that the Government
are absolutely in earnest to put down crime.
There should be a proclamation issued and
rendered as emphatic as possible calling
attention to the fact that atter a certain
date any people found with bombs in their
possession or in their houses, or traceable to
them, will be dealt with in as drastic a
manner as this Bill will give power to do. I
appeal to any man of conscience. or any
man I do not care how tender his religious
beliefs inay
be-is he doing right by his
countrymen, by the citizens of this city; is
he doing right by the community if he will
allow people to get off with the carrying of
these infernal things that are for the destruction, and the destruction only, of his
fellowmen?
I hold that we would not be honest, or
courageous men, and have no right to be here
if we will not band ourselves against crime
of all sorts, and take the proper machinery
to stamp it out. It is all very well to talk
of peace and of compact. The Prime Minister
never intended in the latter portion of his
speech that we were to hang up the Bill,
because he hopes that there may be some
conditions of peace resulting from the Con-

go about their business without fear of bomb
or rifle, or these abominable outrages to which

ference. If you believe that then you must
make Mr. Collins, the representative of
Southern Ireland, amenable. In my opinion
the Prime Minister never intended anything
of the kind. This Bill is made for those who
break the law within our border. (Hon.
Members-Hear, hear.) It has nothing
whatever to do with the Conference. It has
nothing to do with the greater and wider
national and international questions on
which the Prime Minister is our representative in any Conference that may be held in
London to-morrow.
No; we have been playing with crime too
long. The British Government have been
playing with it for years, and we have the
right to take the instrument necessary in
order to stamp it out. No man, if he is a
law-abiding citizen and well-meaning enough,
will come under the purview of this Bill
unless he has committed, or is about to
commit, and it can be proved he is about to
commit, deeds that are an abomination to
everyone of us. No man will be hurt by this
Bill. Therefore, I say it is necessary to have
it. I say if a man has got a bomb in his
hand and is about to throw it, and a policeman shoots him down, he is absolutely justified
in doing so. He is doing an act of mercy
to the community. Is anyone in this House
going to say we should not have a provision
in this Bill in order to make it impossible
that these crimes should be perpetrated? We
are tired of this mawkish teaching that is
going on that you are not to grip crime. If
there was not a rod in all our homes when
we were youngsters I am afraid we would be
worse people than we are. I do not think
any of us pleased our fathers and mother's
when they had to bring the rod into use.
Who to-day in our Empire is looked upon as
the strongest man? General Smuts' Why?
Because he gripped the Bolshevists in South
Africa, who were trying to destroy the very
foundations of civilisation, and to pass their
principles on to other colonies and other parts
of the Empire. He gripped the situation, and
thus did much to shorten the sum total of
destruction of human life. He ended in a
few days that which might have gone on for
years and put South Africa on a par with
Russia. Heaven only knows where it would
have led to. Contrast South Africa with
Russia. In Russia men came in and, there
being no strong man to resist them, they
taught methods of revolution, and used them.
So have Russia to-day committing
cannibalism. We do not know the horrors.
If we do not do our duty with Ireland we
are going to have another Russia-Bolshevism
and men simply robbing and destroying and
preying upon society. Things are more
serious than they appear, and it is up to us
to do our part, and let the South do as they
please. Let us see that the law is obeyed,
and that well-meaning citizens are allowed to
we
CHICHESTER :
Mrs.
Before this Bill
passes its Third Reading I should like to say
a few words on the subject. I fully agree-I
do not always agree-with the hon. member
for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) on
this occasion, for certainly I can endorse
every word he has said to-day. Some days
ago the hon. and gallant member for Down
said he thought it only right that every section of the House should express its opinion
honestly. I fully agree with what he said,
and would like to assure the Government
from the section which I represent-at any
rate I am one of the representatives from
Derry-that they are with them heart and
soul in their endeavours to stamp out these
abominable crimes which are being committed in our midst. (Hon. Members-Hear,
hear.) I speak as one of the representatives
of my sex, representing thousands of women
in the Six Counties, and I feel I can say that
they have been shocked within the last few
days by the terrible outrages, bloodshed, and
violence. We feel that the strongest measures
are absolutely needed now, and that in the
present state of the country it is only the
very strongest measures which can strike the
necessary fear into the hearts of the criminals. We hope and pray and feel assured
that once this Bill is passed the law will be
ruthlessly and impartially administered and
that criminals will be brought to justice, no
matter to what side they belong and no
matter what their political convictions or
religious denomination may be. Unfortunately, we all realise that these terrible
outbursts of crime are not confined to one
side or the other. May I just add---and I
hope it is not out of place-that we wish the
Prime Minister God-speed on the journey
which he has undertaken to-day.
I can
assure him that, as he knows, he has our
unswerving and unbounded confidence. We
are grateful beyond expression to him for the
fight which he has made for us ap till now,
and all along. We know that he is fighting
not only for us in the Six Counties, but for
Ireland and the whole Empire, and we feel
that our future and our honour lie absolutely
safe in his keeping.
Mr. GRANT-I desire to make one or two
remarks, but before doing so, I would like to
know from the right hon. the Attorney-
General how this Bill is going to affect
Press correspondents. When he gives his
answer I will make one or two remarks.
The DEPUTY-SPEAKER-I would call the
hon. Member's attention to the fact that he
cannot address the House twice. He has now
resumed his seat, and there is no possibility
of his further entering into the debate.

The House met at a quarter after Two of

BILL PRESENTED.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BILL.

To amalgamate the rates of contribution
end the rates of benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Acts, 1920 and 1921, and the
Unemployed Workers' Dependants (Temporary Provision) Act, 1921, in their application to Northern Ireland, otherwise to
amend the Unemployment Insurance Acts,
1920 and 1921, and to repeal the Unemployed Workers' Dependants (Temporary
Provision) Act, 1921, in their application
as aforesaid, and for purposes connected
therewith."

(Mr. Andrews), supported by the PARLIA-
MENTARY SECRETARY TO THE MINIS-
TRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Megaw).
Read the First time; to be read a Second
time to-morrow, and to be printed. (Bill
No. 5.)

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour); I hope the Committee will understand the necessity of
bringing this in at rather short notice. It is to
enable the Exchequer to issue sums of money
to the Ministry of Labour in order to make
payments under the Unemployment Fund.
Without such authority from the House the
Exchequer would not be justified in paying
sums out of the Exchequer at all on or after
the 1st April, so this is simply to carry out
the procedure with which the Committee is
already perfectly familiar. I beg to move.

Funds after the 1st April? If not,

the term. Are we to be governed by the
British House of Commons' measure without
the matter coming before this House, or must
we not have powers from this House to carry

Mr. ANDREWS: I think it would meet with
the approval of the Committee if I answered
the question. The hon. Member (Mr. Coote)
is quite right in saying that a Bill is at the
present time going through the Imperial
House of Commons dealing with the question
of Unemployment Insurance. The present
term ends on the 5th April, and until the new
Bill becomes law no further payments would
be payable to those who have exhausted their
benefits on that date. It is proposed, I under.
stand, that the Bill should be effective on
the 17th April. That is, there will be a period
of about a week and a half when no benefits
will be payable to those who have exhausted
their benefits on or before the 5th April.

know the

Mr. COOTE: In this Vote at page 54, I see
an item, I Commission to Constabulary for
Collection of Parental Moneys, £200," and
then down at the bottom under the heading
of "Receipts there is the item, "Estimated Receipts from Parents of Children
sent to Reformatories and Industrial Schools,
£800." I should like to know why this commission is paid to the Constabulary for collection of these moneys. Surely, a constable
is paid a salary; and if in addition he is to
be paid commission for collecting moneys, I
think it looks a very anomalous business
altogether. I should like to know how much
is collected by the Constabulary, or does it
follow that this £800, receipts from the
parents of children is money collected
by the Constabulary. We should like
some enlightenment on these two matters.
Especially do I take exception to officers and
men who are paid very fair salaries, being
paid commission on any special undertaking
in connection with their work, paid commission for the collection of sums of money
which, I suggest, ought to be collected by the
Constabulary without commission.
Sir DAWSON BATES-In connection with
the point raised by the hon. member for
Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) this
Government is only following the practice
adopted by the Imperial authorities, under
which the police collect the amount chargeable against each parent of a child who has
been committed to an Industrial or Reformatory School. It is no part of the duties of
the police to collect that money, but the Imperial Government came to the conclusionand I think rightly so that the best means
of collecting that money was by the police.
The amount of £800 represents the sum
which it is hoped will be collected from the
parents.
Mr. COOTE: Is that the entire amount
which is to be collected?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, the entire
amount.
Mr. COOTE-Surely the Government is not
going to pay 25 per cent. commission to the
Constabulary for collecting the money for Industrial Schools? If £800 is the sum to be
collected, and they are getting £200 for collecting it we might all turn into collectors.
Because the late Government did certain
things I hope it is not going to be taken for
granted that this Government will follow
suit. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) If they
do they are going to get into the bog. The
time has come when we might well clear up a
lot of these things. We are now considering
the reconstitution of our whole police force,
and I think this is a matter which might
well be looked into just now. Surely this
work of collecting this money, which they
have been doing, if they ought to do it,
ought to be done as part of the day's work.
In normal times the police have not very
much to do. Unfortunately, just at present,
they have a lot to do; but in other times
this is work they might very well be doing,
and they are well paid, I submit, with £200
for the collection of £800.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think I might
clear up the point now raised by my hon.
Friend (Mr. Coote) at once. In addition to
the £800, which I have mentioned, you will
see under sub-head "B" that there is a

these funds.

Mr. McGUFFIN: I am sorry that it is
necessary for me to intervene so frequently
on the Motion for the Adjournment, but the
occasion really calls for some remarks. We
are all sorry that better success has not
attended the efforts of the negotiating Committee to bring about a settlement of the
very regrettable crisis in the Engineering
Trade. I do not know whether the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Labour, has
any recent specific information with
respect to how matters stand at the
moment. Unfortunately the Committee
that was appointed to negotiate in
the interests of the Engineering Unions
have failed to effect a settlement, and at the
moment it is rather regrettable that by
reason of the complications that may ensue
there is a prospect of a greater number still
being added to the industrial unemployed.
We all appreciate the efforts that have been
made by the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Labour, to effect a settlement
locally, and we do appreciate his co-operation
with the Minister of Labour across the water
to bring about a general settlement. It would
be most regrettable if in addition to over
30,000 engineers, half a million workers in
kindred trades were also, effected. Grave
insinuations have been made, particularly by
one public body, with respect to the attitude
of the District Committee of the A.E.U. with
regard to an application made to the Board
of Guardians for relief in respect of the
unemployed. I am sure the Minister of
Labour feels that affairs are sufficiently complicated without an outside body interfering
in the matter with a suggestion of a most villainous nature-I characterise it so strongly
-with respect to the attitude of the District
Committee of the A.E.U. The action I refer
to is in connection with a deputation that
attended before the Board of Guardians and
invited the Board to assist the unemployed
by way of relief, and it is alleged that we had
dissipated our funds in political propaganda,
and that our intention in sending a deputation to the Board of Guardians was to secure
an advance of lock-out pay. That is a most
unfair and unjust suggestion to come from
any public body, and it gives a political
significance to the movement which does not
characterise it. To rebut that suggestion I
would point out that from January to December, 1921, the Union referred to had paid out
in unemployment benefit £2,162,187. Does that
look as if the funds had been used for political propaganda? And yet we have an insulting statement made to the effect that we were
approaching the Guardians for funds to be
used as lock-out funds. It is a most unworthy
suggestion. We may have a very grave crisis
in the industrial world before the present
difficulty is settled. I am not speaking
menacingly or prophetically, but as things
are it looks as if we are going to have a
grave crisis, and it will not alleviate the
situation if suggestions such as I have referred to are introduced in connection with
the dispute. I would like the Minister of
Labour to say if he has any more recent information with regard to how the dispute
stands at the moment, and if he has any hope
of an immediate settlement. Up to the
moment we have not had any information oi
a very reassuring character, but probably the
right hon. Gentleman, who is continually in
touch with the Minister of Labour across the
water, may have some more recent information.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I am very disappointed that as
yet no settlement has been reached. The employers here, as I have already told hon.
Members, were very anxious to get
separate treatment extended to them by
their Federation, SO that they might
keep the work going on here notwithstanding the troubles across the water.
I have twice, on behalf of the employers, petitioned the Executive in Great
Britain to give its permission, but on each
occasion that permission has, I regret to say,
been refused. I see from the newspapers that
continual negotiations are in progress in
London. It seems to me that they meet every
forenoon and fall out every afternoon, and
then meet the next day to try to find a
formula of agreement. I do not know
whether that is the best way of bringing
about a settlement or not. I have found
during my short experience that the best way
to effect a settlement is to keep both sides at
it night and day until they come to an agreement, and then they are generally very glad
to shake hands. It is not for me to criticise
how these meetings are arranged in London.
It is only for me to express regret that this
being a National trouble we are still involved
init. As regards the extract from the letter
written by the British Empire Union to the
Board of Guardians in reference to this un-
Adjournment.
29 MARCH 1922. -Unemployment Benefit.
fortunate dispute, I have no sympathy with
what has been said in that document, and I
am sure hon. Members have no sympathy
with it. At the same time I do say that I
feel it is primarily a matter between the
Amalgamated Engineers' Union and the
British Empire Union, and not a matter with
which this House can deal. The hon. Member (Mr. McGuffin) has said that the Union
expended over two millions in giving unemployment benefit to its members in 1921. That
is perfectly true, and I am aware of the fact
that in other benefits to its members, altogether independent of labour disputes, the
same Union has given to the extent of threequarters of a million, so that personally I
do feel it is unfair that they should be
attacked in the way they have been. As
regards the trouble in the shipyards across
the Channel, all I think I ought to say at
this stage is that so far there has been no
trouble in Belfast or in Derry, and I am
very hopeful that as we have been able to
avoid a stoppage up to the present, the spirit
of reasonableness and generosity, if I may
say so, which has been shown by the employers in this matter will prevent a stoppage in the near future at any rate, and I am
hopeful that before the matter becomes really
critical some settlement may be arrived at on
the other side which will prevent trouble
here. We all recognise what a disaster it
would be if our already large number of unemployed in this city-which, I think,
numbers about 30,000--were added to by about
20,000 shipyard workers. The consequences
of such a large general stoppage of work would
be of a far reaching character, and I think I
am justified in repeating that it is probable
that it may be avoided.
Mr. COOPER: May I ask the Minister of
Labour if he is aware that people who joined

I.R.A. police are in receipt of wages, and

Mr. ANDREWS: I am aware of the fact
that there is considerable difficulty at the
boundary or frontier in connection with this
as well as with other matters. All I can say is
that I am doing what I can to get over the

There is a great difficulty in this way: that
men work on one side of the frontier but
live on the other side. I am hoping, however,
that some arrangement will be made between
the Free State Government and the Northern
Government similar to that which has been
made already between the Northern Government and the Imperial Government, namely,
a reciprocal arrangement subject to adjustment which makes it possible for the
Imperial Government to meet the liability
in Great Britain while we meet the liability
in Northern Ireland. Some arrangement,
no doubt, will be made with the Free State
Government as time goes on, an arrangement
which I feel is necessary and which will be

Ireland to come in here when they happen
to get out of employment in Southern Ireland
and draw money from the unemployment
fund here.
Mr. COOPER: These people are in employ.
ment and are receiving money from the Irish

when the services of the Department

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
M'KEOWN): I have been asked by my right
honourable Friend the Minister of Agriculture
to deal with this question.
When the powers and duties of the Department of Agriculture and Technical Instruction in so far as they related to Agricultural
Services in Northern Ireland were transferred
to this Ministry, accumulated balances of

to the credit of each of the Six Counties.

ATTEMPTED MURDER AT JOY STREET.
2. Mr. DONALD (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs what information he can give regarding the attempted
murder of a workman, named Lyle, at the
corner of Joy Street and Ormeau Avenue in
the city this morning; and in view of the fact
that Lieutenant Bruce was recently murdered
convenient to the spot on which this murder
was attempted, will he state whether special
precautions can be taken to preserve life in
this neighbourhood?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): At 9.10 a.m. to-day,
James Lyle, Protestant, and native of Dromore, Co. Down, was fired at by several men
with revolvers at corner of Ormeau Avenue
and Joy Street, Belfast, while going to his
work at Messrs. M'Kinney & Co.
He was
seriously wounded, and taken to the Royal
Victoria Hospital. I am glad to say that I
understand he is progressing favourably. This
is one of the localities which is causing the
authorities considerable trouble, and honourable Members may rest assured that all possible steps are being taken, with the resources
available, to preserve life.
HOLD-UP OF A TRAIN AT ADAVOYLE.
3. Mr. DUFF (by private notice) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he has
received a report regarding the holding up
of the train at Adavoye on the night of the
28th-29th instant, and can ha give particulars
for the information of this House?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yesterday morning
about one o'clock the goods and mail train
proceeding from Belfast to Dublin was held
up at a place known as Cloghogue, 2 miles
North of Adavoyle Station. A red light was
exhibited to the driver by about 100 armed
men. The driver did not, however, observe
the danger signal, owing to the fact that the
goods train from Dublin was passing the
place at the same time. The raiding party,
who had evidently well prepared plans, had
removed a rail, with the result that the
engine, sorting carriage, passenger guard's
van, and two goods wagons were derailed,
fortunately without injury to the staff of the
company or Post Office. Seven of the wagons
were set on fire and destroyed, and in addition
a large number of consignments were thrown
out of other wagons on the permanent way,
and afterwards burned.
The police, who were in the neighbourhood,
proceeded to the spot, when they found that
the train was not proceeding on its normal
course, but the raiders had decamped.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask my right hon. Friend if any arrests
have been made in connection with this
dastardly occurrence?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Not yet.
Mr. DONALD: There have been no arrests?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
CAPTURE OF BELCOO BARRACKS
4. Mr. M'GUFFIN (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs what information he can convey to the House regarding
the capture of Belcoo Barracks, County
Fermanagh, and whether any of the police
who have been kidnapped have been released?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received a
report from the police stating that a few
minutes before ten o'clock on the night of
the 28th instant the police in Belcoo Barracks
were surprised by the entry of about twenty
armed raiders. The raiders rushed into the
dayroom from the front door shouting
"Hands up," and captured two sergeants and
eleven constables. Four constables who were
in the kitchen escaped into the yard, and
were not noticed by the raiders.
All revolvers, rifles, equipment, ammunition, and contents of the men's boxes were
stolen. The raiders stayed about two hours,
and then drove off in three cars to Blacklion,
bringing the captured police with them.
While the raid was in progress the village
was surrounded by sentries. One constable
returning from a walk was halted, but
escaped.
Two Special Constables were alo halted
and taken to Sergeant Flannery's house,
where the sergeant was on sick leave, and the
three of them were then taken to Blacklion.
Sergeant Flannery was subsequently released
on account of illness. It is thought that the
raiders came into Belcoo on foot, and that
the cars came later when the barrack was
captured. The raiders were not disguised.
Apart from Sergeant Flannery, none of the
men who were taken have yet been released.
The total strength of the barracks was three
sergeants and nineteen constables. Sixteen
of these were captured, of whom one, Sergeant
Flannery, was, as stated, released; the others
escaped.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask the right hon. Gentleman if he
thinks that where an attack of this sort can
be carried out with such deliberation, skill,
and expedition, sufficient vigilance i being
observed by those who are in control of the
barracks?
MI. DONALD: Before my right hon.
Friend answers, may I ask him if it is his
view that these happenings are in the nature
of reprisals for what has occurred in the City
of Belfast; and, if So, what steps the
Government are going to take in view of the
speech that was made in the Imperial House
the other night?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure my hon.
Friend, the Member for North Belfast (Mr.
M'Guffin) will understand that, having regard
to the fact that the men are in the custody
of these raiders, it is impossible for the
Government to get information in order that
fuller inquiry may be made as to the cause
of the raid, and as to whether or not there
was any negligence on the part of the police.
I am sure the House will not expect me to
give an answer to a question of that sort at
the present time.
MURDER AND WOUNDING OF POLICE
AT CROSSMAGLEN.
5. Major SHILLINGTON (by private
notice) asked the Minister of Home Affairs can
he state the circumstances in connection with
the murder and wounding of police at Crossmaglen, and whether he has any information
which shows who is responsible for this
dastardly outrage?
Sir DAWSON BATES: A patrol of Police
left Crossmaglen about 10-0 o'clock yesterday
morning. At about 11-30 a.m, they were ambushed at Culloville within our area. The
patrol consisted of Sergt. Patrick J. Early,
R.I.C., and six Special Constables.
Sergt. Early was shot dead.
Special Constable Harpur, shot dead.
Special Constable Samuel Dougall, wounded
in left elbow.
Rest of party uninjured.
Ambushers numbered about fifty, with two
machine guns, one on each side of the road.
Survivors returned the fire and believe they
wounded several of the ambushers.
Arms and ammunition taken from the dead
policemen.
This is part of the attacks being made by
the I.R.A.
Mr. DONALD: I would suggest to my right
hon. Friend that these questions be submitted
by telegram to the Prime Minister at the Imperial House.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I will undertak
have that done.

The object of the Bill, which is very simple,
is to empower the Minister of Finance
to make advances to the Unemployment
Insurance Fund, so that these donations that
are given to men out of employment may be
provided for.
It is in the nature of a loan
to the Fund. I need not recite all the
different circumstances under which the Unemployment Insurance Fund finds itself today by reason of the unexampled depression
in trade and the unusual amount of unemployment. The Fund, for the time being,
has become insolvent, and, therefore, it has
been necessary for the State, and for ourselves
following the other side, to make provision
by way of advances to the Fund to carry it
over the period of depression, which is very
acute now, but which it is hoped may be
ameliorated before any considerable time.
The limit of finance, as hon. Members will
see by the first Clause of the Bill, is
£1,000,000, but, of course, it is hoped that it
will not be necessary to make any such
provision under these deplorable circumstances. We can only hope that the conditions of trade and of commerce will exhibit
such an improvement that it may not be

finances of the Northern Government to the

Members are concerned, is really for reference. If a debate is taking place to-day, and

Report lies in the fact that it serves as a
handy reference; but if it is to be used simply
as a memorial of the proceedings of the
House then I submit that it is a question for

Ing the Hansard under such circumstances.

Mr. McGUFFIN: We have not yet been

regulations just as other colleagues of theirs,

more duty than it is capable of discharging.
If you do you will have a mutiny in the
ranks of the shorthand writers. Therefore,
let us dismiss them out of our calculations
for the moment. The other difficulty is the
real difficulty. You must realise that the
Labour market in respect of the printing
trade in Belfast is entirely different from
the Labour market in the same trade in
London. In London there is always a floating
population which can be called upon at once
to case or linotype to meet any emergency.
More, and this is by far the greatest difficulty, his Majesty has a Stationery Office,
which includes a printing department of its
own, and that makes all the difference in
the world. In Belfast there are not, in fact,
in the ordinary course of newspaper production enough linotype operators to go round.
Trade union regulations forbid more than a
given period of overtime in the entire week.
If you are going to produce your Hansard
at night so that it can be perused by Members
in the morning, it can only be done by violating Trade Union rules in respect of overtime,
so that precludes that being done. What is
the alternative? You can import from other
centres linotype operators, but if you do this
follows: no firm will import linotype operators to keep them idle for six months of the
year in order to employ them for six months
to produce your Hansard. If they do, they
must include the cost of keeping those men
the other six months in the charges they impose in respect of the production. Therefore
as a simple matter of business work and de.
tail you have to come down to hard facts, and
that involves that you must produce under
day labour and not under night labour, because the latter is not possible; but if you
produce under day labour you cannot deliver
the Report between the interval of the sitting
which concludes at six o'clock at night and
its resumption on the following morning.
Therefore it becomes a practical difficulty. It
was imperative from the point of view of
the printers to consider whether, as you
were producing a Hansard under these
changed conditions, you should not produce
two or three or four days together at very
much reduced cost, and as there has been
such a great cry for economy-I do not say
that it came altogether from that particular
quarter of the House, and I am not suggesting I do not sympathise with you-but

up against these facts and has dealt with

Oral Answers to Questions.
COMMITTEE ON LABOUR EXCHANGES.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour if he will state when the Report of
the Advisory Committee on Labour Exchanges will be made public?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The Committee has not yet concluded its deliberations, but it has completed the taking of evidence, and is considering the various matters raised by the
Terms of Reference. The honourable Member, however, will be glad to know that the
Committee has just presented an Interim
Report recommending the establishment of
Local Advisory Committees in connection
with Employment Exchanges in Northern
Ireland similar to the Local Advisory Committees in Great Britain. This Interim
Report will shortly be made public.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask the hon. Member if these Committees will be provided
for in the Unemployment Insurance Bill at
present before this House?
Mr. GORDON: In reply to the hon. Member, I may say we are giving that matter
serious consideration, and the possibility is
we may provide for these particular Committees in the Bill which has already been
introduced to this House.
UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF GRANTS.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state the amount
received by the Government of Northern
Ireland under the Unemployment Relief
Grants for expediting Road Construction
and Road Improvement Works?
Mr. GORDON: I have been asked by my
right honourable Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs, to reply to the honourable
Member's question. No sums have as yet
been received by the Government of Northern Ireland for these services, but the
Imperial Government will shortly pay to the
Government of Northern Ireland a sum
of £42,000 to meet the cost of current works
approved under the Unemployment Grants
Committee Scheme during the period subsequent to November 22nd, 1921, when Northern Ireland became responsible for its own
finances.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask if the £42,000
referred to is part of the £500,000 to be provided by the Imperial Government for relief
work?
Mr. GORDON: In reply to the hon. Member, I have to say that the £42,000 that is
mentioned in the answer I have given is distinct and apart from the £500,000 which is
to be provided for the relief of unemployment.
LAND PURCHASE ANNUITIES.
3. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will state the amount
collected in respect of Land Purchase Annuities under the Government of Ireland
Act, 1920?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The amount collected in respect of
Land Purchase Annuities in Northern Ireland from 22nd November last to 31st March
is approximately £252,000.

The PRIME MINISTER: I feel quite confident that my colleagues and I have had the
deepest sympathy of every Member of the
House during the past few days in
the delicate and difficult business that
we transacted in London. It is unnecessary for me to review all that
has taken place during the past year leading
up to the deplorable state of affairs with
which we have been confronted. It is unnecessary for me to enter into all the condemnation that many of us feel towards
individual Members of His Majesty's
Government or the Government at Westminster collectively, or against those in the
South and West of Ireland who by factious
troubles and difficulties have added very much
to the gravity of the situation, deplorable in
the extreme, which up to quite recently has
disgraced, we might almost say humanity,
throughout our particular part of the
country. All that is not our fault.
have as a House here and as a Government
done our utmost from the moment that we
took up office to stabilise government, to
insist upon the restoration of law, and
to appeal to all fairminded persons to come
to the assistance of the authorities with a
view to establishing peace in our midst.
We
I have been from time to time faced with
complicated and with
very difficult
questions. It has been my duty to protect
to the fullest extent all the citizens of
Ulster. It has been my duty to see that
nothing took place which infringed upon
the rights and privileges of this House.
The House and the country are well aware
that the greatest infringement, the greatest
transgression, occurred on the day when His
Majesty's Government settled with a third
party behind our backs a term or an
article in an agreement whereby grave risks
were run, to the territory which was handed
over to us constitutionally under the Act of
1920, upon which Act we have since been
functioning. From that day to this it has
been my earnest endeavour to point
out to the British Government the
serious consequences of the steps
they took that day behind our backs, and it
has also been my anxious endeavour to come

to some further agreement whereby this delicate, difficult business regarding our borders would be settled amicably without
friction and without detriment to the interests of Northern Ireland. On the last
occasion I was hopeful, as I said to the
House before I went away the other day,
that the agreement that we entered into was
an agreement that would in the long-run
tend towards the accomplishment of that
particular object.
It broke down, and as I was careful to
point out to the House, it broke down without anything on my part having been done
to imperil the arrangement that was by that
further agreement entered into between the
Southern Provisional Government and our
own. However, this whole thing is so involved that it becomes almost impossible to
go back upon even a month or two without
feeling confused as to how it is better results did not ensue. I accepted the invitation of His Majesty's Government to meet
the Provisional Government again in London,
and the outcome of that further endeavour
on all our parts is a document which is now
known as the Agreement between the Provisional Government and the Government of
Northern Ireland. Now, it is not my intention to go through this Agreement to-day
clause by clause or item by item. It stands
there for everyone to read, and if there is
any question that any hon. Member desires
me to elucidate, or anything that may appear
obscure, I will do my utmost to clear it
up.
Let me point out, first of all, one or two
essential features. Before putting one's
signature to a document of this kind one is
always wise to ask oneself what would occur
if the worst happened as it did before-the
very worst, what would happen if the Agreement were put in the fire, torn up, and discarded on all sides. So far as we are concerned
we would have to go on exactly in the old way,
and I am determined that we shall go on in
the old way. In other words, nothing has
been sacrificed so far as we re concerned,
and I am not desirous, and I hope no one
here will be desirous, of claiming this document as either a triumph for Ulster or a
triumph for the South The document was
not intended to be that. It was intended to
be an earnest endeavour on the part of the
signatories to the Agreement to bring peace,
not alone to Ulster, but to the whole of Ireland.
Now, in approaching the subject from that
point of view, let us probe into what has
actually been accomplished. In the first
instance the House will bear in mind that
one of the gravest difficulties with which we
were confronted, and especially my right hon.
Now,
Friend the Attorney-General, and my right
hon. Friend the Home Secretary, was the
non-recognition of the sentences of our Courts,
and I emphasise here, as I have done on
several occasions in London, the utter
impossibility of carrying on government in
any country unless the foundation of society
was recognised by all classes of the inhabitants. The Courts must ran The sentences that are imposed by our Judges must
carry, and must not be overriden by any
other authority. I believe in this document
we have at last secured the very necessary
elemental foundation of society. If hon.
Meu bers will turn to Clause 10 they will see
that no offences committed after the 31st
March shall be open to consideration
that is agreed to by the 'rovisional Government, by the British Government, and
by ourselves. Hitherto we
have had
great difficulties, because it was possible
for our Judiciary to be weakened or flouted,
our jurors to be weakened or flouted, because
they had undertaken their duty with that
impartiality &nd that fairness which
have always characterised the Ulster
jurors. I defy anyone to point the
finger in any deprecating way at a single
one of those who adorn the Bench in Ulster
to-day. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I
had
to safeguard them; safeguard the
categories to which I have referred, and
having done that I believe I have done a
service not alone to Northern Ireland, but
to the whole of Ireland, because it is a
recognition by the Provisional Government,
as well as by ourselves, that you cannot
govern a country unless it is recognised that
the Courts run, and that justice shall not be
interfered with. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Now, that is the first, and I believe the
fundamental issue really at the bottom of this
document so far as we are concerned. But
the second important point is this, that for
the first time, if I may use a hackneyed
expression, we have sorted out the sheep
from the goats. None of us could tell either
when there was an incursion into our territory or an outrage committed within our
borders, whether that was officially sanctioned by the Provisional Government or
whether it was the work of desperadoes
belonging to the Republican party or
acting upon their own. This document
settles that in my opinion once and for all,
because it recognises here by
Article 6-" Irish Republican
activity to cease in the Six Counties."

them to do, and to come forward and

experienced lawyer as to when the month ran
in which this Parliament was to vote itself
into the Free State or to vote itself out of
the Free State. That has been set at rest by

The new wording satisfied my legal advisers

Well, then, that brings me to the portion of

"Whether means can be devised to secure

That, again, is hardly a question that it is

Having cleared out of the way what I may
call these primary points in the Agreement, I
want to show the House that the Agreement,
as it is, carries us really nowhere at all unless

"Peace is to-day declared."
Peace was the earnest desire of everyone
round the table that day. Peace was what

for, and what we trust will now gradually
come to us in Ulster. But I was never for
a moment under the impression that by ringing down the curtain you could cut off the
So far as the Border is concerned, I think

The Clause relating to the Borderland reads

:-
Failing this,"

There is good in those few words. Article

chance to discuss the matter.
Now, before I close, may I refer to the very
important meeting which was held yesterday
in the city, when leading business men, representative of all parts of our land, met
together and passed a series of resolutions.
Whether those resolutions were passed or

Charter was that a British subject was

One of the real reasons why Britain
has become great, why the freedom of
Great Britain is unequalled in any other
country in the world, is that Clause of the
Great Charter. Yet at the dictation-well,
probably dictation is too strong a word, let

I can claim that all of them are personal
friends of mine, and during over three years
in the Imperial House of Commons I have
had opportunities of being in daily touch
with at least two of them. Therefore, wher
I deal with this it is not because I have not
the greatest faith in the Lords Justices, but
I say it is a recognised principle of British
law and the British Constitution that a man
shall be tried before a jury. Why should we
depart from that? I agree with the Prime
Minister that there have been cases where we
have had to make departures, but why were
those departures made? Because jurors have
been terrorised and afraid to do their duty.
Can anyone tell me that there ever has been
a jury in Ulster that has been terrorised or
afraid to do its duty? I have never met with
a case. Therefore. 1 for one object very
much to this departure. I pass over the next
paragraph, which proposes to set up a Press
censorship. That, of course, I need hardly
tell the Prime Minister, is a thing that a
Committee representing Northern and Southern Ireland and the Imperial Government
cannot do. No self-respecting journalist, no
self-respecting newspaper editor is going to
take his reports of outrages or anything else
that happens in his community from any
Committee (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
however high-minded or however excellent
that Corimittee may be. The independence
of the Press would be struck at if such a
thing were tolerated. Therefore I pass that
paragraph by saying that it is absolutely
unworkable.
I was glad to hear the Prime Minister
state his views so clearly with regard to the
question which comes under Article VII. A
good many people I know have been perturbed-and rightly perturbed-not because
they do not feel absolute confidence in the
Prime Minister, but because of what has
happened on the other side of the water.
Adjournment.
-Peace Negotiations.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Lynn]
Because of the treachery of the British
Government our people undoubtedly are
neasy in regard to any negotiations that are
going on. I was glad the Prime Minister
made it so clear that he who runs may read
that there is no idea whatever of Northern
Ireland going under a Sinn Fein Parliament.
(Hon. Members-Hear, hear.) The Prime
Minister says if the people of Southern Ireland want to live on neighbourly terms with
us we are prepared to live in unity with
them If they want us to co-operate with
them in promoting the highest interests of
Ireland we are ready to unite in that work.
We will do anything in our power to facilitate and promote the peace, and happiness,
and welfare of Ireland, but on one thing
we have made up our minds, and that is
that we are not going under an Irish
Parliament. I do not think anything is
to be gained by camouflage in a matter
of this sort. It is better to state the truth.
The Prime Minister has said-and I believe
him-that if anyone wants to lead Ulster into
a Sinn Fein Parliament he will not be
that leader. I would like to see the man
who would attempt to lead Ulster into a
Sinn Fein Parliament. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) For thirty-five years we have
put up a stern fight because we mean to
stick to Great Britain, and that determination is stronger to-day than ever it
was. Therefore, let no one be deceived. In
reading the speeches of Mr. Collins and Mr.
Griffith one gathers that they are under the
impression that we are tumbling over
one another in order to come under I do not
know whom. Because we have made all these
concessions for peace-and I have said before,
and I repeat that the Prime Minister deserves
every credit for the efforts he has made
for peace-what are we offered on the other
side of the account? We are told of course
in the first paragraph that
"Peace is to-day declared."
I am sure, as far as our Prime Minister and
his colleagues are concerned, nothing was
nearer to their hearts, and there was nothing
they desired more. But what were the other
two signatories able to do for peace? What
control have they over the I.R.A.? Why, at
Castlebar on Sunday they drove Mr. Collins
himself away. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
My impression is that, as far as the other
two signatures to this Agreement are concerned, they carry no more weight than the
signatures of the three Tooley Street tailors.
I do not believe that Mr. Collins and Mr.
Griffith speak for the South and West of
Ireland. I am sorry it is so, because amongst
extremists they are less extreme than the
other people, and I think probably if they
had the opportunity they would co-operatewisely co-operate-with our own Prime
Minister for peace in the interests of Ireland
But they are not able to prevent the Repub
licans from holding an armed parade in
Dublin. They are not able to hold a meeting
of their own in Castlebar. They are not able
to protect the British arms and ammunition
in Cork. Look over the South and West of
Ireland to-day, and who are the people who
can sign an agreement with any binding
effect? Why, of course, the people who control the men who have got the guns. After
all, it is not reason and it is not sentiment
that prevail there. It is the men who have
got the automatics and the bombs, and, unfortunately for Ireland to-day, De Valera's
people have got the guns and have got the
ammunition. If there were going to be lasting peace I would say I was glad that the
Prime Minister had agreed to get rid of the
political prisoners. But since 1916 about every
six months we have had to release the Irish
political prisoners. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Each release has only resulted in the
situation becoming worse. I hope the Prime
Minister will see to it that those who have
been convicted are not released until he is
absolutely sure that Mr. Colline and Mr.
Griffith are able to deliver the goods, because
if he did not it would only weaken the hands
of his own forces, only depress those who are
rallying round him and want to help him,
and it would only be a new cause of trouble
in the districte. We have certainly had
enough trouble, but I think, looking over
Ulster as a whole, that Sinn Fein is fairly
well done. My own impression is that
Belfast is the worst spot in the whole of the
Six Counties at present. My inquiries rather
point to the fact that a great many of the
Sinn Feiners are discovering that the game is
up, and if they find that they are up against
a strong Government that is going to maintain law, that is going to administer the law,
and that is going to stand no nonsense with
crime, then I think that fairer weather will
be encountered, and the Prime Minister
will find that that peace, which I know
he has worked for and wishes, is not so
far away.
But I do implore him, and I
implore him as one who wants to help in
every possible way, to remain absolutely
firm, to let the murderer-it does not matter
what his colour is or what his name isbe suppressed with a strong hand, and
let them see that so far as we in Ulster
are concerned, while we are anxious for
peace with honour, one thing we are not
going to submit to is a peace dictated by
murderers. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. COOTE: When we meet with the
responsibility of speaking on this question, as
we do to-day, I think we agree with the senti.
ments of the Prime Minister in all that he
Adjournment.
-Peace Negotiations.
4 APRIL 1922.
are
said with a view to extending a neighbourly
hand to any power in the South of Ireland
that can deliver the goods. We have not
been breakers of the peace or of the law, but
when you read this whole Pact from start
to finish you find that it refers practically
only to Ulster, and that Ulster is to be
labelled before the world as the only troublesome spot in Ireland and in the United Kingdom. The people who are suffering from the
incursion of the murder gang, whose business
is being destroyed, whose undertakings are
being held up, and who are holding their
breath wondering what is to happen next,
are being penalised under this Agreement as
if they were the aggressors, instead of the
people imported into our midst who
deliberately trying to destroy the functioning
of the Northern Parliament. It is an unfortunate Pact. It savours very much of the
practice of the Government of the United
Kingdom-when they come to the solution of
a problem, when they are within reasonable
distance of enforcing the law, some rearguard
attack is made on the institutions of law
and order, everything is scrapped or set
aside, and the powers of dieorder prevail.
That to my mind seems to be what is happening in Northern Ireland. We sat here for
days while the Minister of Home Affairs and
the Attorney-General piloted the Special
Powers Bill through this House, with the
whole-hearted assent of the Members, and
after that is done the signature of His
Majesty is given to the document. Then
our Prime Minister goes over to London with
his Cabinet and they agree to things that set
aside the most important provisions of the
Act, that require alterations in it, and that
practically break it up. Trial by jury is
abolished under certain conditions. Speaking
for this House of Commons, I say that we
object to be made the tool of intriguing parties over in London. We are being used in
this matter simply to further the interests of
the British Government in their policy of
surrender and of scuttling out of Ireland,
while by implication they make grave charges
against the honourable acts of our Special
Constabulary and against the Constabulary in
general. While they practically allow it to
be said that our people are breaking the law,
and are out for disorganisation and riot, there
is not one word said about Southern Ireland,
and the fact that the loyal population there
are being driven from their homes, their
farms, and their businesses. The private
letters of those people to us-I wish we could
only read them out before the public and give
their names are pathetic beyond measure,
and yet there is not one sentence in this
Agreement pleading for better conditions for
our friends in the South and West.
I hope the Prime Minister is not serious in
expecting us to pass the Pact in this House.
There is not a motion before the House
to-day, but if there was, I am afraid there
would be very great trouble in getting a
unanimous vote, if he got a vote at all. The
feeling in the city and in the country is such
that he would be a very bold man who would
give assent to this Pact in its present form.
I want to refer to the words of the Prime
Minister at the great meeting of business
men held in Belfast yesterday. There was no
Pact publicly-I believe there was privatelyin the air when that meeting of business men
was called. That meeting was called for a
different, a bigger, and a greater purpose, and
I protest against making it subservient to
this issue, making it a tool of Lloyd George
and his surrender pack-I cannot call
them by a more respectable namethe men who have surrendered everything and have humiliated not only
Ireland but Great Britain before the
world. I object very strongly to the use that
the Prime Minister made of that meeting, and
I say that that use will recoil upon his own
head, if he persists in it. I am very sorry to
hear that in that meeting there was
engineered a committee of Peace with Honour,
when the gallant men who are out night
after night patrolling our city and the
country at the risk of their lives, free,
gratis, and for nothing, are being scrapped,
because the other side would not come
in and help to bring about peace, because
they wished that these men should be
humiliated, as they have, in fact, been
humiliated, by this Pact in London. Does the
Prime Minister think that that great meeting
yesterday would have stood by anything of the
sort, if it is implied that these men are to be
insulted and despised for having done their
duty, that their arms are to be taken from
them, and that they are to be sent about their
business? No; they meant nothing of the
kind. There is no honour there; there is
neither peace nor honour. The meeting at
which this motion was promulgated yesterday
will turn in disgust when they come to see the
use made of it. They will certainly object to
any such thing being made out of the great,
big, hearty meeting that took place yesterday
in the city of Belfast. I have dwelt on the
Special Constabulary and the insult meted out
to them, and I am sure no one knows better
than the Prime Minister the great work that
these men have done for the peace of Ulster,
both Roman Catholic and Protestant, in the
last few years.
In a certain place in Ulster,
certain members of the British Press, representatives of cross-Channel newspapers, called
upon a local Roman Catholic priest, and they
asked him had he any complaint to make in
regard to these Specials, and he bravely said,
"No; neither the 'A' nor the 'B' Specials;

they have treated me and my people with
the greatest respect." I believe that is
the feeling in the hearts of the most respectable Catholics throughout this province. They
have felt secure in their beds, because they

Catholic
We knew there was something in the air,
and that there was some dodge to try and
break up the solidarity of the Loyalist portion
of the community, and especially to destroy
the efficiency and power of the Department
of Home Affairs. They were getting too close
to the murder gang, and therefore there must
be a herring drawn across the trail. The
Specials are to be weeded out, and there is
to be a system which will be absolutely
unworkable put in its place. Does anybody object to have Roman
Specials? (Hon. Members: No.) Do we
object to Roman Catholics in the Constab
ulary? (Hon. Members: No.) We have
given our answer in the Interim Report of
the Committee on Police Reorganisation
which will come before this House tomorrow'. In that Report we recommend
that the ratio of Roman Catholic to Protestant policemen in the old Force should
be adopted, and that Roman Catholics
should be taken into the Ulster Force
according to their proportion of the population. Therefore, there is nothing partisan
or arbitrary in that.
Mr. McGUFFIN: All the same it is sectarian.
Mr. COOTE: We object not only to a
Roman Catholic Committee being set up in
order to select members for the Force, but
we object to any religious denomination
selecting them. We should object as much
if it were a Presbyterian, a Methodist or
a Church of Ireland Committee. These
people should mind their own business.
They have no right to dictate to us as to
whom we shall take or shall not take to
serve in the Ulster Constabulary.
The PRIME MINISTER: I think my hon.
Friend is working himself up into some heat
over a misapprehension. The Interim
Report of the Committee, of which he is a
member, deals with the Royal Ulster Constabulary, the new force to be formed. He
himself and others have suggested-I think
quite rightly-that two-thirds of that Force
should consist of Protestants and one-third
of Roman Catholics. If he will look at the
Agreement he will see that it has nothing
whatever to do with the Royal Ulster Constabulary. He is reading into it something
that it does not deal with.
Mr. COOTE: I did not say that.
The PRIME MINISTER: The point is
this, Catholics in Belfast are now prepared
to join the "B" Specials, to take the oath,
and to show their anxiety to help in putting
down murders and disturbances. We do
not know these men. Therefore, we are
suggesting that they should form a committee, and that that committee should
make recommendations to the authorities as
to the Catholics in the city who may be
trusted to help to maintain law and order in
their own districts. That is really the point.
I do not want my hon. Friend to mix up
the two questions. They have nothing
whatever to do with the Royal Ulster Constabulary..
Mr. COOTE: I am not mixing them up.
Nothing was further from my mind. I
merely gave an illustration of the fact that
we wish to be fair to the Roman Catholics
of Ulster, and said that we are prepared
to do in the Ulster Constabulary what was
done in the old Royal Irish Constabulary
in regard to the proportion of Catholics.
We do object, however, to any church
setting up an advisory committee through
the channels of which men should come into
this Force.
The PRIME MINISTER: But my hon.
Friend knows perfectly well that under our
present system with regard to the "A" and
"B" Specials a committee is set up in order
to prevent people getting into them who are
known not to be on the side of law and
order. It is impossible for us to choose,
and we have asked them to set up a committee similar to that at present existing
under the "B" system.
Mr. COOTE: Our committee is absolutely
a business committee. It is not a religious
committee. The fact that Roman Catholics
will not act upon the committee does not
make it a sectarian committee.
We are
was
very sorry they take up that attitude., but
it was not set up as a sectarian committee.
and the Force was not set up as a sectarian
Force, although it was inevitable that it

ludicrous. You cannot possibly have a

There is another point that is insisted on

in this Agreement, which I think is a very
serious matter, although apparently vary
small. I refer to the fact that the Constabulary are to be numbered, or, in other
words, they are to be a real, proper, visible
target for the gunmen who come here from
other parts of the country. Say a gunman
comes here from the South to look for
Brown, or White, or Black. He does not
know Brown, or White, or Black. He knows
there is such a name, but he cannot connect
the name with the personality. With the
use of numbers all he has to do is to take
up a certain beat, and No. 1, No. 4, or No..
6 is the man he wants. It is quite easy
for the gunman to find out the number,
and then use his revolver. He has not
to identify the personality. Is not it a
fact that the numbers on the uniform of
the old Constabulary had to be taken off
for that very reason? Here the Members
of the Northern Government have included
in the Pact the provision of a real, visible
target, so that the gunman can identify
his man by the number, instead of having
to identify the personality. I think that it
is a very serious mistake, and that it is
fatal to the efficiency of the force. It is
not fair to the men who are risking their
lives for the peace of the city that the
representatives of Southern Ireland should
suggest to our Government what we are to
do with our police, and how they are to
be marked. Why, the thing is ludicrous.
If we had sent so many children away to
London they could not have behaved in a
more puerile fashion. They simply allow
themselves to be played upon every time
by these men who cannot deliver the goods.
My hon. Friend, the Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Lynn), has dealt with the
question of trial by jury. I agree with
every word he said, and I will not take
up the time of the House by mere repetition, but we do hold very strongly that men
charged with crime involving capital
punishment, or with other serious offences,
should be tried by a jury of their fellowcountrymen.
In regard to the activities on the Border,
the signatories to this Pact, just by a stroke
of the pen, have settled them all, and we
hear that for the last twelve hours or so
the Border is at peace. I hope so. I want
to ask the Prime Minister and the other
Northern signatories to this Agreement if
Mr. Michael Collins and the other Southern
signatories are speaking the truth in other
places? What can they do to relieve the
situation on the Border? They say the
I.R.A. operating on the Border does not
belong to them. They have a wonderfully
convenient way in the South of Ireland, when
they do an illegal thing or commit an overt
act of illegality, of having somebody else to
blame, and so they deceive us all the time.
I submit that if the Members of this House
were living on the Border in constant fear
and dread, and realised that their only help
was the "A" and "B" Specials especially
the "B" Specials, the countrymen who are
doing their work in the fields by day and
going out and tramping the roads at night
in order to protect the people they would
be slow to make any changes on the Border
until the I.R.A. is taken away, root and
branch. There is another way of settling
the Border problem. The British Government could easily settle it by putting
garrisons in four or five of the towns on
the Southern side of the Border, and the
civil population would be allowed to go on
with their ordinary avocations. But there
is no provision in this Agreement in reference to the Border further than the word
of Mr. Michael Collins and his confederates
that the activities on the Border are to
cease, when they admit themselves that the
people operating on the Border do not
belong to them.

The PRIME MINISTER: Really, I am
afraid of my hon. Friend's words causing
the very effect that I am sure he and I
are desirous of preventing that is uneasiness among the population on the Border.
There is no intention whatever in the
ruinds of the Government of relaxing
their efforts on the Border until the
peace that is aimed at in this Treaty
is carried into effect. Obviously if there is
mobilising, firing, and abominable outrages
on the other side of the Border against our
people, then our A" "B" and "C" men
and the Army will come to help'us to deal
with the situation. But the whole point of
the Agreement is that Mr. Collins has the
authority to stop all this warfare upon the
Border line. Provided he does that, all
that this document proposes is that the
B's" should be gradually withdrawn to
their homes. To say for a moment that I
or my Government would relax any effort
to hold what we have is of course a suggestion for which there is not the slightest
foundation.
Mr. COOTE: My point is this, that prior
to the Truce between His Majesty's Government and Southern Ireland, in which
Northern Ireland was included-I never
could understand why it was there was
a similar state of things. There were outrages and depredations, and but for the
excellent services of the "B" men in the
Border Counties the peace would not have
been kept, even as it was kept. Then there
was the declaration of the Truce, and the
British Government believed it was going

to assuage the anxiety of the people in
these counties who are in terrible fear
to-day lest the only force they have for

It may be that our Government for the
moment believe people will deliver the
goods who are not in a position to do so.
Now I come to Clause VI., dealing with
the Boundary question. I cannot accept
the explanation of the Prime Minister.
I really think, if you will allow me to say
So, quite respectfully, that the weakest
point in his whole speech was his attempt
to explain why sub-section A of Clause VII.
was put into the Pact and signed by the
representatives of the Northern Government.
In order to show the harm it is doing, and
the use that is being made of it, I take a
letter written by a gentleman who is not
an officer of De Valera, but who is a follower
of Mr. Michael Collins. Mr. Louis Walsh,
writing to the Dublin Press, said:
"The agreement arrived at in London is
good-not so much for what it contains
as what it implies. The break-up of the
Ulster 'Specials,' as we knew them, the
release of our prisoners and the provisions
for the relief of the unfortunate Catholics
of Belfast, are big material gains, and
represent a tremendous climbing down
on the part of the Craig Administration.
Mr. Justice Wilson has been taught that
even his sentences of ten or fifteen years
are not so infallible a remedy for the
pacification of Ulster as he evidently intended they should be. And we have
given nothing material away. The army
is still in being, and only its activities
restricted. So that we have a substantial
guarantee for the carrying out of the pact
on the other side.
But more important than any immediate gain is the promise of national
unity which the agreement holds out.
The fact that the Northern leaders went
into the conference at all after all their
denunciations of Lloyd George and his
colleagues for 'shaking the blood-stained
hand of Michael Collins, and that they
conceded so many things that they vowed
they would never concede is proof positive
that even the dullest of them now realise
that they cannot go on as they have been
trying to do, and that some form of
national unity must be arranged if there
is to be peace in the country.
That is how the Free Staters are interpreting this sub-section A of Clause VII.
a
"Whether means can be devised to
secure the unity of Ireland."
Does the Prime Minister not believe that
the average man-in fact, every man-must
read this as some means by which we
can have a United Parliament in Dublin,
to put it in plainer language? Is not that
the meaning taken out of it by every man
south of our Border? Is not that the

is that every means must be exhausted with
view to achieving that end, probably
before the discussion of the Boundary Commission. I want to call your attention to
the fact that the next sub-section is to come
into operation only if sub-section A fails.
I hold that if the Prime Minister does not

and definitely here to-day he does not believe in it-it is not fair to Ireland, it is
not fair either to the North or to the South
that that language should be used there.
It is simply camouflage of a very dangerous
type, a type that may lead to further bloodshed in Ireland, and further economic
pressure on Ulster in order, if possible, to
drive us into a United Parliament in Dublin
before the question of the Boundary Commission is discussed. Sub-section B says-
"Failing this, whether agreement can be
arrived at on the Boundary question otherwise than by recourse to the Boundary
Commission outlined in Article 12 of the
Treaty."

about the poor refugees in Cork, Limerick,

None whatever. That is my attitude.
say they have no right in view of the way

provision for the trial of persons charged
with serious crimes in Northern Ireland,
and for purposes connected therewith.

(Sir Dawson Bates), supported by the

Report of Police Committee,
MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn." (Mr. Burn).
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In accordance with the
undertaking I gave to this House at the
time the Report of the Police Committee was
laid on the Table I think this would be a
suitable opportunity to enable hon. Members
to discuss the terms of that Report. Before
referring to the Report itself, I would like
to take this opportunity of expressing the
thanks of the Government to the Committee,
and in this connection may I especially refer
to the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Lloyd Campbell) the Chairman of the Committee for undertaking a task which was
both arduous and difficult. No one except
one who was on the Committee, or who was
in close touch with it, could possibly realise
the enormous amount of work involved, and
the extent of the investigations which had
to be undertaken by the Committee. The
object of referring this matter to a Committee
was in order that the Government might get
the combined views of representative men in
Ulster, so that, based on their Report, a Bill
might be brought in setting up a new Police
Force which would be a credit to Ulster, and
which would, above all, enjoy the confidence
of the community. I believe that in this
Report we have these essentials.
The Report is in the hands of hon. Members, but I would like to take them very
briefly through the main recommendations.
The first point to which I desire to refer is
the question of pay. In 1920 a Committee
was set up by the Imperial House of Commons
under the chairmanship of Lord Desborough
for the purpose of inquiring into the various
police forces in England, Scotland, and Wales,
and making certain recommendations. The
result of their Report was that certain standards of pay were set up for the police forces
in England, Scotland, and Wales, and these
standards were subsequently adopted by the
Royal Irish Constabulary. I think any hon.
Members who have had any connection with
the Royal Irish Constabulary will realise
that up till that time the terms of pay of
that force were entirely inadequate. In the
Report which is now before the House it will
be seen that the Committee recommend that
in the new force about to be set up, and
which is limited to a total of three thousand
men, the pay should be the same as that now
paid to the Royal Irish Constabulary, and I
suggest to this House that this is a
reasonable and adequate amount. A policeman has to display many qualificatione. He
has, unfortunately, more especially in this
country, frequently to carry his life in his
hands. He has to have-and this is a point
which I think the public do not quite realise
-a good knowledge of criminal law, and,
above all, know how to apply it. His occupation imposes upon him many restrictions
which do not exist in the case of ordinary
employment. He is liable to be called upon
for duty at any time. He is restricted not
alone in his mode of living but in where he
lives. Therefore, having regard to the nature
of his work, the pay should be sufficiently
good to attract to the Force men possessing
these qualifications.
There is another reason why I suggest that
this standard of pay should be adopted. It
will be found that the Committee recommend
that two-thirds of the Force should be
recruited from the members of the Royal
Adjournment
5 APRIL 1922. -Police Committee's Report.
Irish Constabulary, and one-third from the
Special Constabulary. I think hon. members
will agree that it is essential at the outset of
our new Police Force that a large proportion
of its members should be fully trained policemen. In order to attract a sufficient number
of the men of the Royal Irish Constabulary
it is suggested that they should receive an
allowance of one-sixth of the pension to which
such members will be entitled on disbandment as members of the Royal Irish Constabulary. Members of the Royal Irish Conetabulary will also retain their existing ranks
when they join the new Force. In regard to
the Special Constabulary-and may I say
that no body of men has done more to earn
the gratitude of the people of Ulster than the
Special Constabulary-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear) it is recommended that one-third of
the recruits for the new Force should be
taken from their ranks. Members of that
Force will all enter as constables, but any
member of the Force who has served as an
officer, or who has served for a period of six
months or more in the rank of headconstable, will be granted for the purposes
of pay, and pension, and seniority six years'
service, and any member who has served six
months in the rank of sergeant will be
deemed to have served four years. In addition, members of the Special Constabulary
joining the new force will be entitled to have
the benefit of their service in the Special
Constabulary. In regard to the age limit it
is proposed that for members of the Special
Constabulary the age limit should be 32, and
in the case of those who have served in any
other of the forces of his Majesty it should
be extended to 35. In the case of ordinary
candidates the age limit should be 27 years.
With regard to the scale of pay of officers
it is also proposed to follow the rates of pay
now in force in the R.I.C. After the senior
officers of the Force have been selected a
Selection Board will be set up consisting of
the senior officers of the Force, who will thereupon select the head constables, ergeants,
and constables of the new force. In regard
to the general question of pay it is proposed
that after the first 3,000 men are recruited a
lower rate of pay may be introduced for new
recruits, but that will be a matter for future
consideration. It is further recommended
that one-third of the new Police Force should
be recruited from the Roman Catholic members of the R.I.C. and Special Constabulary,
and the balance of one-third (1,000) from
Protestant R.I.C., and the remaining onethird (1,000) from the Special Constabulary.
Under the arrangement which this Government has entered into with the Imperial
Government the R.I.C., as regards the members of that Force serving in Northern Ireland, will be disbanded at a date not later
than the 31st May. The Government proposes
to introduce a Bill setting up the new Force
prior to that date.
Before I conclude may I say that it is hoped
that His Majesty will consent to allow the new
Force to be styled "The Royal Ulster Constabulary," and while I regret it has been
found necessary to disband the old R.I.C.
with its traditions of loyalty and work well
done, I can express no greater hope for our
new Royal Ulster Constabulary than that
they may continue to carry out those traditions. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Before
sitting down I should invite criticisms from
all parts of the House, and I can assure hon.
Members that they will receive very careful
consideration, at the hands of the Government.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I would like first
of all, on behalf of the Committee and myself
personally, to thank the Minister of Home
Affairs for the kind words he used towards us,
and I can assure him and the other Members
that if we have accomplished any good we
have done it with a will and a half. Now, I
would like to pray the indulgence of the
House for a few moments to read, if I may, a
few extracts from what was called the Desborough Report. The Desborough Report is
the report of a Committee which was set up
in England, Scotland, and Wales, presided
over by Lord Desborough, to inquire into the
whole question of the police system there, and
I think the few lines that I wish to quote
bear very much indeed on the point that we
are discussing here this evening:-
"The primary function of the police is
the maintenance of law and order and the
preservation of the peace. . . . We consider it important also to bear in mind that
the constable, even in the execution of his
duty for the preservation of peace, acts not
as an agent of the Government, exercising
powers derived from that fact, but as a citizen, representing the rest of the community,
and exercising powers which, at any rate in
their elements, are possessed by all citizens
alike. The citizen is still bound, at the
direction of a magistrate or on the appeal of
a constable, to take his part in the preservation of the peace and suppression of disorder, and, in this country, the whole power
of the constable rests on the support, both
moral and physical, of his fellow-citizens.
We desire to emphasise this point as, in our
opinion, it has an important bearing on the
relations between the police and the public
-as to the consideration to which the police
are entitled on the one hand, and their
obligations to the public on the other.

In considering the standard rate of pensionable pay which we should recommend,
we have taken into account not merely, or

even mainly, the rates of pay in force before
