his calling and distinguish him from other
public servants and municipal employes,
and we consider the police entitled thereby
to special consideration in regard to their
rate of pay and pensions.
"A candidate for the police must not only
reach certain standards of height and physical development, but must have a constitution which is sound in every way. The
duties the police have to perform are varied
and exacting; they are increasing, and will
probably still increase in variety and complexity, and a man cannot make a good
policeman unless his general intelligence,
memory, and powers of observation are distinctly above the average. His character
should be unblemished; he should
humane and courteous, and generally, he
should possess
a combination of moral,
mental, and physical qualities not ordinarily
required in other employments. Further,
be
when he becomes a constable, he is entrusted
with powers which may gravely affect the
liberty of the subject, and he must at all
times, be ready to act with tact and discretion, and on his own initiative and responsibility, in all sorts of contingencies. The
burden of individual discretion and
responsibility placed upon a constable is
much greater than that of any other public
servant of subordinate rank."
I am sure the House will forgive me if I
continue this. I consider it is very important
from our point of view:
"The police also stand in a special relationship to the community. Each constable
on appointment becomes one of the duly
constituted guardians of law and order for
and on behalf of the citizens as a whole, and,
as we have pointed out, he makes a declaration of service to the Crown as such. He
undertakes special responsibilities in regard
to the prevention and detection of crime,
and while he does not relieve the citizen
from all responsibility for the protection of
his own property and for bringing offenders
to justice, he claims to be and is the principal agent in the prevention and detection
of crime of all kinds, and generally holds a
position of trust which it is important he
should be able to maintain. We consider it
essential that the sense of obligation to
the public should be preserved in the police,
and the reason we dwell on these considerations at some length is that they are fundamental to the views we have formed as to
the status of the police and the pay they
should receive."

Mr. DONALD-It has been amended.
Mr. CAMPBELL-The Committee in dealing with this matter, as the Minister for
Home Affairs has said, had considerable difficulties, and although we might almost call
our report an unanimous report, still at the

which make it not a unanimous report.
Therefore, in addressing the House this evening I feel in rather a delicate position as
being the Chairman of the Committee and at
the same time an individual member of this
House, and the remarks I am about to make
I purpose to make as an individual member
of this House. I would just like to add
to what I have read from the Desborough report as regards the duties of a policeman.
Some people seem to think that a policeman
has, in common parlance, a soft job. But take
the ordinary working man. He is at a job;
something crops up in the job which he does
not understand; he can turn to his foreman
and consult him, and if the foreman does not
understand it he can turn to the manager and
consult him. They can get consultation on
the matter, and eventually decide what is to
be done.
Take the case of the ordinary policeman out
on beat duty. He is by himself; something
crops up; he has got to act on his own responsibility and on the moment. He, in addition, takes the responsibility on his
shoulders for the way in which he
acts, because, bear in mind, a policeman is
not free from responsibility as regards his
action. Another point is that a policeman
must know the law. I do not mean to say
intricate law, such as a barrister or solicitor
is acquainted with, but the general principle
of law so far as police duties are concerned.
Another point is that he is always on duty.
He cannot go to an evening party; he may
be called away in the middle of it. He may
go to his bed, and be called up in the middle

of the night. He is on duty from the 1st

in
Now, we had two main factors to contend
with. The first, and in my humble opinion
the most important, was efficiency. The
second I would say was very important indeed-economy.
Now, it would be the most
fatal mistake that any Government could
make to take and enrol and build up a force
of underpaid men. It is absolutely essential,
order to get efficiency, that the
men should be properly paid. As soon as
that point of pay is reached, then we can
turn to consider economy. It would be false
economy, indeed, to try and have a force of
underpaid men. Across in England there is
a system of policework by which each city
and borough and county has its own police
force. Now, we consider here that for our
Northern area it would be much better,
indeed, from every point of view-from the
economical point of view, from the efficiency
point of view-that we should have one force
for the whole area. It makes for economy
in the maiter of having one headquarters
for the whole area. It makes for economy
in the purchasing of supplies. It makes for
economy if one area is peaceable to move a
man from that area into another area which
may not be so peaceable.
Further, there is a point which I should
mention which is not mentioned in the report, but which we discussed in Committee,
and that was for the whole area there
should be one ladder of promotion. At present, I understand, a man is promoted in his
own county, and that has led to some hardships, because the promotion in one county
happened to be quicker than in another.
Probably when the Committee sit again we
will recommend that promotion shall take
place through the whole area, and therefore through the whole force. Now, there
were several points in the R.I.C. system
with which the Committee did not agree, and
in connection with which we certainly
would have liked to have made some change,
but there is an old proverb and a very good
one that it is not a good time to change
horses when crossing the stream. Therefore we felt that in the recommendations we
were to make to the Minister of Home
Affairs we should make
as few radical
changes in the existing system as was possible to make.
There were several things which we discussed, and which we hope to report on
later for instance, what the number of
Headquarters Staff would be; what the pay
was to be; the allocations of the police to
each county; as to whether the present
system, by which if a county gets extra
police in it has to pay for the extra cost
of those police, should be done away with
and a common pool made for the whole area;
also certain variations in other ways.
We
were, however, much rushed at the end
owing to the marvellous manner in which
the Imperial Government thought fit to
treat us as regards the present Force, and
we have left all these matters over for
further consideration. What we really have
given is only the mere skeleton of the new
Police Force. Now, the pay that we have
recommended is the pay which has been
paid in connection with the old R.I.C., and
the pay which is in existence at present
across the water.
I may say perfectly honestly that we considered the pay of a policeman is rather
high, but it is what is being paid across the
water at present, and what is being paid here
at the present time, and we considered that
it was necessary to continue that pay.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: May I ask the hon.

Mr. SPEAKER: Hon. Members should not

Mr. CAMPBELL: That pay, as I say, may

Now, I would like to try and explain what
is certainly a rather complicated mathematical problem, and that is the question of
pension. But let me say at the outset that I
have not yet seen-I do not know whether the
Prime Minister has seen more-any binding
document produced by the British Government with regard to the R.I.C, on this question. We have heard a lot of things, but no
Act of Parliament has been passed by the
Imperial Parliament yet as far as I know.
However, we have reason to believe that
certain things are going to take place. As
far as I can understand the way the financial
question of the R.I.C. was settled for a certain
number of years was as follows: In the
Imperial House there was on the estimates
a Police Vote for the police of Ireland. The
amount of that Police Vote included pay,
upkeep, and all that sort of thing,
and, in addition, it also included the
actual amount of money which would be
expended during that year in paying pensions. In other words, as far as pensions
were concerned they were simply working out,
with the result that at the end of the financial year across the water they, in conjunction
with our finance people, drew up the financial
arrangements for the 1920 Act. They said:
"The police force in Ireland is costing so
much, which includes the pensions paid
every year; you people in Ireland will be
credited with that amount, and you will have
to pay the pensions yearly out of that
amount."

Mr. COOTE: I should like in the first place
to ask the House to acknowledge their indebtedness to the hon. Member who has just
sat down (Mr. Campbell). I sat on this Committee as far as my Parliamentary duties permitted me, and I was astonished at the infinite
patience and good temper and industry displayed by the Chairman of this Committee.
This House does not understand the tremendous task he undertook when he accepted the
chairmanship of the Police Committee. and I
congratulate the Minister of Home Affairs on
the selection he made. In my judgment he
could not have made a better one. So far as
I can see the discussion on this Report can be
confined to two points, namely the question of
pay and the composition of the Force. On the
question of pay I admit there were very conflicting opinions in the Committee, and some
of us, especially the Members of Parliament
who have to face the taxpayer, realised what a
serious situation this was, and what a serious
undertaking it was to pay the Force on such
substantial lines. I hope the House will bear
with me if I try to visualise the situation.
We have a Royal Irish Constabulary who are
to-day enjoying certain pay and emoluments,
and they are about to be disbanded. It is of infinite importance that we should have as many
of them in our new Force as we require,
and I hope we shall get all we require, and to
offer them less pay than they have up to now
been receiving would, I think, be an excellent
way of defeating the ends we had in view.
Assuming that we are going to get a certain
number of R.I.C. men, we then come to the
question of linking up the Special Constabulary. Realising that they have very handsome
pay, although it is only temporary, and realising also that they have been two years in our
service, taking very serious risks, and risks
which most of us would rather not run, the
question occurred to our minds, and I hope to
our consciences, "can we ask these men to
come into the new Force for less pay than the
flat rate of the R.I.C.?" We felt that we
could not. To have the R.I.C. with one rate
of pay and the A" Specials with another
rate of pay-two classes of men walking the
street on different scales of pay-would be very
anomalous and unworkable, and no business
man would recommend anything of the kind.
Therefore, taking into consideration the wider
and bigger interests of the community, we had
to take our courage in our hands and suggest
a unified rate of pay for both sections of the
force. But you may say there is an extra inducement offered to members of the R-I.C.
For the first six years' service there will be a
year added to their pension, and for the next
twelve years another year will be added. I
confess there was a difficulty in the minds of
the Committee on this point, and you will find
when you read the Report and the criticisms
of some of the Members that there was not
unanimity. I do not see that we ought to give
any further inducement than the present
salary enjoyed by the R.I.C. and the twelve
years which is to be added to their service for
the sake of their pension. We should not go
further because it is creating an evil you wish
to avoid. It is not unifying the pay of the
whole Force, and I do not believe it will be
any deterrent to the men coming in. In the
face of the dangers to which they are subject
we desire the police force to be content and to
enjoy reasonable pay, and, in fact, to have
pay better than that given to other ranks of
the same type of men outside, but if we go

further than this we are making a mistake.
Some of us differed from the majority of the
Committee on the question of the pay that is
to be offered to officers of the new Force. I
submit that the officers of the Force stand in
an entirely different category. The House
will be aware that there is a glut of officers
offering themselves for service. We are inundated with applications, and the pay for officers is much too high, especially for the young
officers. The recommendation signed by Mr.
Duggan and Mr. Hill Dickson, with which I
personally agree, suggests salaries that are
quite sufficient, and I hope that the Minister
of Home Affairs when he comes to frame his
Bill will take this recommendation into consideration, because this Bill will be subject to
very searching inquiry and opposition going
through this House. A County Inspector in
the old days only received a salary of from
£500 to £600, and only in very rare cases did
it exceed £600. Now you propose to give him
a salary ranging from £700 to £900. We suggest that this should be cut down by a hundred pounds in every grade, from the County
Officers down to the humblest District
Inspector. With regard to the composition of
the Force, I am in agreement with the Chairman of the Committee when he says that every
member of the Committee wishes to do justice
to every section of the community in relation
to the religious composition of the Force. Personally I object to fixing a figure and laying
it down that there are to be so many Roman
Catholic constables and so many Protestants.
If the Roman Catholic population refuses to
join the new Force in the proportion specified
are you to leave the Northern area without
police simply because the Roman Catholics
will not or dare not join? If the Roman
Catholics will not join your Force, surely it
will be the duty of the Ministry of Home
Affairs to fill up the ranks with Protestants.
To bind us to a hard and fast line was not the
intention of the Committee, although so far
as the Report goes that impression is conveyed.
The Force will be brought into existence no
matter what the religious persuasion of the
candidate may be, and if certain people will
not join, others will be put in their place.
Another point on which we feel strongly-and
I believe there will be great sympathy in this
House with the objections I make when the
Bill comes up for discussion-is with regard
to the numbers you are going to take from
the
old R.I.C. and the numbers you
propose to recruit from the Special
Constabulary. Originally the Committee
thought of taking 75 per cent. of
the old R.I.C. and only 25 per cent.
of the Special Constabulary. Then
they amended the latter number to one-third.
I had an amendment down at the Committee,
but I could not be present-some of us could
not attend all the meetings-and so I could
not divide the Committee on the matter. They
were nearly all officials who were there apart
from the Members of Parliament. I make no
aspersion on their work, but I feel I must
say that there was a very great desire to do
the very best possible for the old R.I.C. It
is only natural for an old official to stand by
the old guard with whom he soldiered all his
days. We do not blame them, but we want
this House to try and maintain a proper sense
of proportion. Here are these Specials, who
came in and stood in the breach, and did
splendid service for Ulster when we were
afraid the Constabulary Force would be burst
up in this country, and we say it is only fair
and right that fifty per cent. of the Special
Constabulary should be asked to join the
new Force. We think it is only fair to them,
and I am sure that when this matter comes
up for discussion on the Bill, which the
Minister for Home Affairs will bring forward,
there will be very, very strong opposition to
the proposal of the majority of the Committee. I submit that this should also apply to
the junior officers of the new Force-the men
who soldiered in France, the men who stood
before the guns-that fifty per cent. of the
officers of the new Force should be taken from
the officers of the "A" Special Force as it
exists to-day. Surely we are not asking too
much. We realise that you must keep a due
sense of proportion, that you must have as
many of the old Constabulary and the old
officers as will run the new machine, and run
it effectively and properly, but surely fifty
per cent. is enough and more than enough.
If we keep a proper balance the result will
be a very effective Force, because in the "A".
Force you are getting the young men, the
ambitious men, the men with their futures
to make, men who are as keen as mustard,
and who are trying to do the best they can
for their country. These will be the men
who wish to get on, and will not be waiting
merely till their time is up to enjoy
their pensions. They will not be simply
putting in the remainder of their days, but
will have their careers before them, and I
hold that they should not be left out in the
reckoning of the proportions of the composition of the new Force.
The other point I wish to make is in regard
to the Selection Board. If you look at Clause

says:
"That in the formation of the New Force
the Minister of Home Affaire should appoint the Officers after consultation with

That is all the comment I wish to make on
the Report at present. I confess that the
salary is a good salary for the Constabulary,
but let us remember the conditions which
prevail in our country round us. It is up to
this House to see to it that under every
reasonable circumstance they will have
Police Force to cope with any disorder that
may face us and which is facing us every day.
It is not suggested that this is a salary laid
down for all time. I do not agree with the
Chairman (Mr. Lloyd Campbell) when he says
that these 3,000 men must have this salary
guaranteed to them for the rest of their days.
I hold that it should be subject to the fluctuations of the cost of living as is provided in
the Desborough Report, and if it is not in
the Report of this Committee it ought to ne
put in. It would be a very anomalous condition that any class of men should be supported by the State, high and dry, above all
the laws of the fluctuation of prices and the
cost of living, and enjoy a salary that was
fixed in war time, when the cost of living was
at its height, and that that salary could never
be brought down. Apply the rule to the
Civil Service and you will land yourselves I
know not where. I hope the Minister of
Home Affairs will not make it an iron rule
that we are never to reconeider the salaries
of these 3,000 men. They must take their
chance just like any other people in the community, and if the Desborough standard is
lowered in England, Scotland and Wales, then
-and I know the police are quite agreeablethe scale must be revised here. We must not
by anything we do have the police charge us
with not playing the game. Let us speak our
minds at once, and let it be understood that
they must come in under the same scale as
all other Civil Servants. I hope the House
will also understand that the salary suggested
here only affects the first 3,000 men, and the
Committee have yet to consider what should
be the salary of the men coming after. We
suggest that it should be very much lower.
There is no dissentient voice in the Committee on this point. Some of us think it
should be very considerably lower, and I
suggest to this House that we ought to be
very careful in fixing that salary in view of
the outlook in the trade and industry of this
country. I am afraid we are coming to such
a state of finance and business procedure in
this country as will bring the cost of living
and prices generally very much down, and
you will be offering very much lower salaries
to these men than your minds lead you to
think of at the present time. Let us remember that the salary of a policeman before the
war was only something like £85 a year. His
salary now is over £200 a year. Do you think
that this will go on? Do you think that we
will be able to pay £700,000 or £800,000 to our
Police Force? These are suggestions I am
making, but the Committee feel as keenly as
any Member of this House that the permanent
salary, the future salary, of all outside these
first 3,000 men ought to be well and
seriously considered when the Report comes
finally before this House. There is nothing
further I wish to discuss in this Report. The
Committee gave every attention to all the
ramifications of the whole situation, but no
one gave anything like the amount of

devoted to the task. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

upon which the members of the Constabulary were paid was very low-exceptionally

It was increased during the period of the
war, but, if it was, it was done upon the
cost of living-and I would like the right
hon. Gentleman to mark that point-and the
increments, just as in the case of the industrial classes, were based upon the cost of
living. Now you are fixing the basis of pay
for these men irrespective of the cost of
living. Unfortunately, the industrial
classes cannot insist upon a condition of
that sort. The hon. Gentleman who has
presented this Report (Mr. Lloyd Campbell)
is an employer, and, in his particular way,
I would suggest a model employer; but, all
the same, he is quite aware of the fact that
at the moment large cuts are being made in
respect of the wages of the industrial
classes, and these are the taxpayers upon
whom will devolve the payment of the
standards set forth in the Report. I, for
one, will regret very much if there is such
an alarming contrast to be made between
the pay given a policeman and the wages
that will be given to a skilled tradesman.
It has been suggested by the hon. Gentleman that it would take anything from two
to seven years to make an efficient policeman. I would suggest to him that it would
take just as long a time to make an efficient
tradesman, and that is not taken into consideration when the industrial conditions
make a reduction in wages necessary; but it
is of importance when we are considering
the remuneration of policemen.
Then there is the question of the selection
of the members of the R.I.C. to serve in
the new Force. It has been suggested that
they should be selected from the entire R.I.C.
of Ireland, that is to say that the policemen
in the Southern area should be eligible just
I
the same as the police in the North.
do not demur to that suggestion, or to the

They may be a very special class of men,

Now we come to deal with a very crucial

that is the sectarian question. I am very
sorry indeed that this forms any part of
the recommendations of the Committee. I
am quite tired hearing about sectarianism.
It has wrought havoc amongst us here. I
wish above all things in connection with

It would not matter for service in the Army
so why should it matter here? And, if it

I now come to the question of policewomen, and I know I will have the support
of my two hon. Friends, the ladies who are

Let me give the House some figures as to
the splendid work that is being done by

total number of people assisted by the

They found shelter for 6,454, and they

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw): I wish on behalf of the Ministry of
Home Affairs to say a few words in reply to
the criticisms that have been put forward by
hon. Members in regard to the report on
Police Reorganisation. In the first place, I
should like to make it absolutely plain that
HOUSE OF COMMONS. -Police Committee's Report. 376
Adjournment
[Mr. Megaw]
the Government welcome all these criticisms,
and that all the criticisms that have been
made to-day will be taken into very careful
consideration by the Government before the
matter in the report is embodied in the Bill.
I should like to say a few words with regard
to the criticisms that were offered by the
hon. Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr.
Coote), who himself was a member of the
Committee, and whose criticisms, which follow the ordinary report, certainly require
very careful consideration. The first point he
made was that there should be a flat rate of
pay for all policemen that are taken into the
new Force. That would be a very useful
thing, if it could be done in full measure, but
one has got to recognise this fact, that the
R.1.C. who are being disbanded to-day are entitled to retire absolutely with 12 years added
to their service for the purposes of pension,
and they can then enjoy that pension at the
expense of the Northern Government, so that
in the case of every R.I.C. man who is taken
on in the new Force we are actually saving,
I think, something like £80 a year by having
him employed in the new Force.
What are we giving in exchange for that?
We are adding one-sixth to his pension, and
if I calculate aright that makes a sum of
about £16 a year, so that instead of having to
pay his full pension we have only to pay £16
a year in respect of it, and that is all he gets
for the first six years, in addition to what his
pay is above that of the ordinary member of
the 'A" Force or the ordinary constable who
is taken on in the first instance. So I think
the report of the Committee is entirely justified so far as that is concerned. He goes on
to deal with the pay of the officers. The same
criticism may be offered with regard to that,
because we are compelled by the Government
of Ireland Act, 1920, to take, at any rate, a
certain proportion of the existing officers of
the R.I.C. Now, if that is so, the only alternative that we have is to pay them the pensions that they are allowed under that Act.
They would be getting their pensions on the
basis of their present salaries. The salaries
that are now offered for officers are the existing salaries, so that for each of such officers
that we take into the new Force we are saving the amount that would go on his pension.
We have to look at the financial position as
well as the rate of pay that would be payable
in the future. The hon. Member went on to
deal with the composition of the Force and
referred particularly to the religious basis. I
do not think there is one of us here who likes
the idea of that religious basis (hon. Members: Hear, hear)-either being embodied in
the Report or in the Act of Parliament, but
unfortunately sometimes we have to make
some concession to expediency, and I do not
know that there is at present any fairer
method of dealing with what is a very vexed
question than the way the Committee have
done. The basis is certainly as equitable
a basis as can be taken if you once admit
the principle that religions are to be considered at all. The basis is that of the
existing population, which is, as my hon.
Friend the Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Lloyd Campbell) pointed out, the relation of
one to two, or thirty-three per cent. to sixtysix per cent.
He also found fault-indeed I should hardly
say he found fault-with the constitution of
the Selection Board. What he did was to
suggest that all interests should be represented on that Board. I am sure that the Government will be very anxious to do that. If
the Report is read you will see that the
Selection Board is to consist of Senior Members of the existing Police Forces in Ireland,
and I am sure that the Minister of Home
Affairs, when these matters come to be considered, will take all the advice that is offered
to him, and will be very glad to bring the
administration of the Force into accordance
with the views of hon. Members as far as it
is possible. The hon. Member mentioned
that the salary should not be a salary for all
time. I am not sure whether anything else
in regard to the first members that are chosen
would be feasible. Of course all these things
will be taken into consideration as I have
said, but one has got to remember that at
present the existing members of the R.I.C. are
entitled to retire on a fixed pension for all
time on the basis of their present pay and
the pay that will be offered to each officer
of the new Force, so that if a fixed term is
to be made for the men who are joining I
hardly see how it will be possible to make an
arrangement with them that, after a certain
period, the pay that they are enjoying at
present should be reduced. Of course I have
no doubt that this will also be very carefully
considered before the Report is embodied in
the Bill.
We next had some very useful criticism
offered by the Member for North Belfast (Mr.
McGuffin), who seemed to be afraid that the
whole Report was to be embodied in the Bill.
That is not the case. The Report is a very
valuable basis for consideration of the materials that should be in the Bill, but it
is not intended, at present, at any rate,
to embody all the recommendations of the
Committee in the Bill. The hon. Member
found fault with the addition of the one-sixth
of the pension to the pay. I have dealt with
that already. It is easy to be seen that
if we are to attract any considerable numbers
of the existing R.I.C. they should get some
recognition of the amount of their pension.

6 APRIL 1922.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 6th April, 1922.
The House met at a Quarter after Two of
the clock, Mr. Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
UNEMPLOYED. MEN IN BALLYMENA.
1. Mr. M'MULLAN (for Mr. CRAWFORD)
asked the Minister of Labour if he will state
the number of unemployed men in Ballymena, according to last returns; if a portion of the £500,000 granted for relief works
in Belfast and neighbourhood will be available for Ballymena, and if so, what steps
would be necessary for the Ballymena Coun
cil to take in order to participate in the
grant?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
ANDREWS): I regret to have to inform the
honourable Member that on April 3rd there
were in Ballymena 655 men totally unemployed and 249 men on systematic short time.
In reply to the second part of the Question, the honourable Member is probably
aware that the £500,000 grant for relief
works in Belfast and neighbourhood was obtained from the Imperial Government in
consideration of the very exceptional position
in Belfast. This grant is not available, therefore, for the country districts.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Arising out of that
answer, I would like to ask the right hon.
Gentleman if he would contemplate making
provision of some sort for those who are
necessarily unemployed through no fault of
their own, by reason of the present stress in
the trade union world? I think they are entitled to some consideration, and if something could be allocated-
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think that arises
out of this Question, which refers to Ballymena.
CIVIL SERVICE COMMITTEE.
2. Mr. ROBB (for Mr. Twaddell) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs if he is aware that
a number of officials in the service of the
Belfast Corporation have applied, in accordance with the provision of Section 8 of the
Local Government (Ireland) Act, 1919, for the
sanction of the Civil Service Committee to
their resignation of service, the Commission
having been substituted by Section 68, Subsection (2) of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, for the Local Government Board, and
that the Committee, though repeatedly applied to, have ignored the applications, and
in consequence prevented the officials from
obtaining the pensions to which they are
entitled on resignation of service under the
provisions of the first-named Act, and what
steps he proposes to take to enable officials
to obtain the necessary sanction when they
are entitled to same?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The facts generally are as
stated by the hon. Member, and several
instances, not only in Belfast, but in other
parts of Northern Ireland, have come under
the notice of this Ministry of officials who
have applied to the Civil Service Committee
for permission to retire, but who have received no reply from that Committed owing to
the fact that the operations of the Committee
have, for some reason not known to this
Government, been temporarily suspended.
Repeated representations have been made to
the Imperial Treasury urging that the
Committee should deal with these cases, but
I regret to say there representations have
been so far without result. The injustice
inflicted on these old officials is entirely due
to the failure of the Civil Service Committee
to discharge the functions imposed on them
by Statute.
PORTAVOGIE PIER.
3. The ASSISTANT PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Burn) (for Mr. Mulholland)
asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he
is prepared to extend the existing pier at
Portavogie in order to provide safe anchorage
for the fishing fleet of that port?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY to
the MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
M'Keown)-I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply-The harbour and pier at
Portavogie are vested in the Down County
Council, who have not made any proposals
to the Government of Northern Ireland with
respect to an extension of the pier. The
Government, however, has no funds available for any such work, and at the present
moment has no powers in respect of Fisheries.

Orders of the Day.
Criminal Procedure Bill.
STATEMENT BY THE ATTORNEY-
GENERAL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed, "That
the Bill be now read a Second Time."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
It will be within the recollection of Members
of the House that the Prime Minister made
a very important statement on Tuesday
dealing with an Agreement that had been
entered into between the Northern Government and the Provisional Government, and
countersigned by representatives of the Imperial Government. The Bill, of which I
have the honour to move the Second Reading,
is concerned really with one particular clause
of that Agreement, Clause No. IV. Might I
say, in answer to my hon. and learned
Friend, the Member for the University (Mr.
Robb), who spoke just a moment ago, that
we have been frightfully pressed in connection with the preparation of this Bill. I
myself am personally aware that the
draftsman has been working at very high
pressure indeed. This is a Bill of a novel
character, one for which there is practically
no precedent to be found. I say practically
no precedent, because there is one precedent
at least. The greatest care had to be taken
to make provision, as well as could be done,
for carrying out the words contained in this
Bill. I know that SO far as the
draftsman is concerned the draft left his
hands yesterday afternoon, and it was sent
to the printers. I do not know whether they
were asked to do overtime-we heard a lot
about overtime the other day-but I understood the Bill was to be ready by 12 o'clock
to-day However, I myself, who am
cerned with moving the Second Reading of
the Bill, have only had the Bill in my
hands for about ten minutes. Therefore if
hon. Members are at a disadvantage they
will remember that I am to a very large
extent at the same disadvantage. May I
read Clause IV. of the Agreement that was
entered into? It is as follows:-
con-
66 'A Court to be constituted for the trial,
without jury, of persons charged with
serious crime, the Court to consist of the
Lord Chief Justice and one of the Lords'
Justices of Appeal of Northern Ireland.
Any person committed for trial for
serious crime to be tried by that Court:
(a) If he so requests, or
a
(b) If the Attorney-General for Northern
Ireland so directs.
Serious crime should be taken to mean
any offence punishable with death, penal
servitude, or imprisonment for a term
axceeding six months. The Government of
Northern Ireland will take steps for
passing the legislation necessary to give
effect to this Article."
Now, that is the article which has given
rise to the present Bill, and as far as I have
had the opportunity of considering the matter, and, of course, I have been in consultation with the draftsman, who gave me every
assistance that he could, I think the Bill
which is before the House, and which will
-Second Reading. 386
Criminal Procedure Bill
1922.
6 APRIL
now, I hope, be read the Second Time, carries
out the agreement contained in Article 4.
The Bill consists of five clauses. The first one
in the words of this very Clause 4 of the
Agreement provides-
"Where any person charged with a
serious crime is committed for trial, he
shall
(a) If he so requests, or
(b) If the Attorney-General for Northern
Ireland so directs
be tried by the Court established under
this Act."
Now, if as a lawyer I had been asked, shall
I say, to give my blessing to a clause of this
description, I might have had great difficulty indeed. (Hon. Members; Hear, hear.)
But it is in the Agreement, and I take it
that this House is prepared to carry out the
Agreement. Up to the present, whatever
may be said against the Government of
Northern Ireland, it cannot be said that any
promise which has been made by us has been
unfulfilled, and I hope that so long as we do
carry on this Government that same observation will apply Once we have passed our
word, that word will be as good as our bond,
and in the very letter and in the very spirit
we shall proceed to carry out our engagements. If he so requests, a prisoner when
committed for trial may require that he shall
be tried by this special Court which is to be
set up, instead of being tried by a jury of his
peers. I listened with great interest to my
hon. Friend the Member for West Belfast
when speaking on the motion for adjournment on Tuesday, and he complained-and in
certain circumstances the complaint would
have great weight in it-that this was to a
large extent doing away with a provision of
Magna Charta, and that it was depriving
Irishmen, shall we say, of that sure shield
which has always protected them-trial by
jury.
a
Is there any ground for complaint if
prisoner himself, the person who is committed
for trial, does not wish to be tried by a jury?
If he thinks that is a tribunal which may
be dispensed with to his own advantage, then
there may be an objection undoubtedly from
the point of view of those who have to carry
out the law and administer the law, but there
can be no objection put into the mouth of
that man such as was put by my hon. Friend,
namely, that he is being deprived of trial by
jury, because, although I have no definite
information on the subject, I am perfectly
certain, as anyone must be certain, that this
provision was never put in at the instance
of
the Northern Government. (Hon.
Members: "Hear, hear!") The Northern
Government have nothing to fear from the
way in which juries have done their work.
They have done it magnificently, and I
believe that in the future they will do it
magnificently, too. Therefore, so far as
the objection arising from the deprivation of trial by jury is concerned, there can
be no objection if the person charged so
requests.
I admit that there may be something to be
said against Clause B, which I have just read,
"if the Attorney-General for Northern Ireland so directs." Well, I do not know what
is thought of the present Attorney-General
for Northern Ireland, whether he is a reasonable man or not, but speaking for myself,
and, of course, without giving any binding
pledge or anything of that kind, would like
to indicate what my attitude would be in
reference to cases that may come before me
to be dealt with under this Clause. I am
perfectly satisfied up to the present with
the way in which juries have discharged their
duty. They have discharged their duty
without fear, favour, or affection. (Hon.
Members: "Hear, hear!") If they continue
to do that, then I think I might go so far
as to pledge myself, as far as I am concerned
personally, while I hold the reins of office
of Attorney-General I shall be quite satisfied
to allow that state of affairs to continue, and
to deprive no man of his right to trial by
jury, unless it should happen that jurors
through fear, through intimidation, through
cowardice, through partisanship, or for any
other reason, should fail to do their duty; and
if they fail to do their duty ought there not
to be a remedy?
If such a serious departure has been made
in Clause A as to allow a person to select his
own tribunal, surely it is not a very great
thing to say that the Attorney-General of the
day, the Officer responsible for the administration of law, more responsible than anyone
else for the administration of law and order,
should be allowed to say in particular cases,
"This is a case that could not fairly be tried
by jury, this is a case in which trial by jury
must be withdrawn." I take it that hon.
Members will give the Attorney-General of the
day credit for trying to do his duty to the
utmost of his ability. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The Crown never seeks, and it is no
part of the Crown to seek, for victims. They
want to see that the law is administered, and
administered fairly and impartially, and as
Long as the ordinary tribunals are prepared
to carry out their duty then the Crown
ought to be, and will be, satisfied with that
duty so carried out. So much, then, for the
request which may be made by the prisoner,
or for the direction which may be given by
the Attorney-General as to the withdrawal of
the trial from the jury and the sending of it
to the Special Court to be set up.

[Mr. Best]
The second Sub-clause simply provides:-
"There shall be established for the purposes of this Act, and for such time as this
Act continues in force, a Court to be called
the Special Court, which shall be constituted
of the Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland and the two ordinary Judges of the
Court of Appeal, with the consent of the
said Lord Chief Justice and Judges; and
the Special Court, when trying any person
charged and committed as aforesaid, shall
consist of two Judges sitting together, of
whom the said Lord Chief Justice shall
always be one, and shall sit without a
jury."
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Is that in the sense of an
Appeal Court?
Mr. BEST: No, not at all; there is no
appeal from this Court. Sub-Clause 3 provides:-
"For the purposes of this Act, a serious
crime means any crime or offence punishable
by death, penal servitude, or imprisonment
for a term exceeding six months, and being
a crime or offence specified in the Schedule
of this Act."
The opening words in that are the identical
words contained in Clause 4 in the Agreement,
but the words-
"and being a crime or offence specified in
the Schedule to this Act."

are words which are added, and, in my
opinion, rightly added by the draftsman,
because, let us go back for a moment to the
kind of crime to be provided for and the trial
so to be provided. Imprisonment for a term
exceeding six months." There are hundreds
of cases, I might almost say thousands of
cases, in which imprisonment for a term
exceeding six months can be awarded, and I
take it that it never was intended in Clause 4
that a man charged, say, with an offence
under the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act of
1885, a man charged with forgery, a man
charged with perjury, a man charged with
simple larceny, a man charged with embezzlement, in each and every one of which the
imprisonment may exceed six months-it
never was the intention of the people who
drew up the Agreement that crimes such as
these should be withdrawn from trial by jury.
I do not use the word political offence or
political crime, because, in my opinion, there
is no such thing. (Hon. Members:
"6 'Hear.
hear.") In my opinion, there is no such
thing. A crime is a crime. (Hon. Members:
"Hear, hear.") A certain state of things
gives rise to crime, and for my own part I
would decline to defend political crime, or
to have anything to do with political crime,
but I take it that what was intended in Clause
4-I may be entirely astray-was any crime
which is committed by people who are dissatisfied with the order of things as they are
established at present, and who wish to overthrow that order.
We know that for the purpose of overthrowing that order murders have been
committed, arson has been committed,
various other things have been done which
are set out in the Schedule to the Act;
assaults have been committed, robbery with
violence has been ommitted, offences against
the Explosive Substances Act of 1883 have
been committed and also against the Firearms Act of 1920, and there have been conspiracies to carry out one and all of these
crimes. Therefore, we say instead of indicating in the Schedule the crimes which are
not to go to the Special Court, and which
would probably have made the Schedule four
times as long if they had been inserted, we
have put in the Schedule what we conceive to
be the crimes that were in contemplation in
this Article 4 of the Treaty. I may say, how.
ever, that we are not wedded to the Schedule,
and if any hon, or hon. and learned Members
suggest that there is some other crime which
should be put in the Schedule so as to bring
it more into conformity with the provision of
Section 4, then the suggestion of bringing
that crime into the Schedule will be considered favourably, but we believe we have
given the most careful consideration to the
Schedule, and that the crimes set out in the
Schedule are the crimes to which reference
was intended to be made by this Article 4 of
the Agreement.
The second Section is really a procedure
Section: I said there was scarcely a precedent
for setting up the Special Court. Well, there
was a precedent, and it is a well-known precedent to lawyers. I have often thought since
I heard of the new Agreement whether the
same fate will apply to the Special Court
which is now being set up as applied to the
Court which was set up in the
year
1882. In 1882 juries refused
to do their duty. They were intimidated.
Every conceivable form of pressure was
brought to bear upon them to prevent them
doing their duty, and the result of
the agitation that went on then was
that the criminal law broke down, and
broke down completely. It has not
broken down with us, and I see no
reason why it should break down with us.
In the year 1882, as I have said, a Special
Commission was set up, and it was to consist
of three judges of the High Court. From
that Court an appeal was given to a Court
of Criminal Appeal consisting of five other
judges of the High Court. Of course none
of the three who had sat in the trial could
sit on the appeal, but from the first moment
that Act became a dead letter. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) A most distinguished judge resigned his position, and
389 Criminal Procedure Bill

refused to be any party to having anything
to do with the carrying out of that particular Act.
The Act became a dead letter, and I am
speculating as to why any person, who could
be tried by jury, would select two judges,
even though they might be the most fairminded judges on the face of the earth. I
have had some experience, and my hon.
and learned Friends have had some experience of defending prisoners. I have been
at the business now for shortly over a
quarter of a century, and during that time
I have defended a great many prisoners,
and on any charge against me the one
tribunal in the world I would select, unless
I wanted to commit hari kari, would be a
jury. I am no longer concerned in defending prisoners; I am trying to hunt them
down. No, arguments and considerations
will weigh with juries that would not hold
for one moment before a Court consisting
of judges, and I wish those who have
selected this tribunal luck of their experience. I am perfectly and absolutely certain
that all the judges will give prisoners a
most fair and most impartial trial, and
every consideration will be given to them,
but when all is said and done, if I, in defending a prisoner, want to get my man
off, give me a jury in preference to a Court
consisting of judges alone.
As I say, Clause 2 is concerned with procedure. May I run quickly through its
various headings? It constitutes the Special
Court, and says:-
(1) The Special Court shall have all the
powers, authorities, and jurisdiction which
would, apart from this Act, have been
vested in a Court of Assize or other Court
or Commission sitting for the trial of any
such crime or offence, and shall have power
to determine any question and to find any
issue or verdict which would, apart from
this Act, be required to be determined or
found by a jury.
We had a difficulty as to where this Special
Court should sit, and we came to the conciusion that, on the whole, Belfast would be the
best place. But, while we came to that conclusion, we did not wish that the Judges or
the Court should be tied down to Belfast,
and, therefore, in sub-section (2) we provide
that:-
The Special Court shall have an office in
the City of Belfast, and shall sit, for the
trial of crimes or offences under the provisions of this Act, in the County of the
City of Belfast, or in such other County as
the Special Court in any particular case
shall direct.
•
Prima facie, therefore, the place of trial would
be the City of Belfast; but if, for considerations which may be put before that Court-
I take it either by the prisoner or by the
Attorney-General, or moving from the Court
itself-they come to the conclusion that some
other place than the City of Belfast would be
more appropriate for the place of trial, then
the Special Court has power so to direct;
and the Special Court shall, whether
sitting in the county in which the crime
or offence was committed or in which the
accused person was returned for trial or
elsewhere, have the same powers, authorities and jurisdiction as if sitting in the
county in which the offence was committed, or in which the accused person
was returned for trial.
The next Sub-section is:
(3) Subject to the provisions of this Act
and to any rules made thereunder, the
existing enactments, procedure, and practice relating to the trial by a Court of
Assize of any crime or offence, or to
matters preliminary to such trial, shall,
so far as the same are applicable, and,
with the necessary modifications, apply in
the case of the trial of any crime or
offence by the Special Court.
Sub-section (4) was put in to deal specifically with the case of a sentence to death.
It may be that no people will be sentenced
to death by this Special Court, and it may
be that a great many people will be
sentenced to death. In certain cases I think
it would be very advisable that if a man
were sentenced to death his place of execution sould be as near as possible to the
place where the crime was committed.
Therefore provision was made in Sub-section
(4) as follows:
Without prejudice to the powers, authorities and jurisdiction herein before conferred upon the Special Court, sentence
of death passed by the Special Court shall
be carried into effect in such county
place and by such sheriff or other officer
as the Special Court shall direct.
or
I hope that that provision will commend
itself to the House. Now we come to the
time when the request by a prisoner has
to be made. Sub-section (5) says:
A request to be tried by the Special
Court shall be made forthwith upon the
committal for trial of the person charged
with the crime or offence, and shall be
made to the justices so committing such
person for trial.
In other words the procedure will be this:
A man is indicted, say, for murder. Depositions are taken in the case, and the
prisoner is asked does he wish to call any
witnesses; he is asked does he wish to say
anything, and after all the preliminaries
have been gone through, and everything of
391 Criminal Procedure Bill

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
-Second Reading.
[Mr. Best]
that kind has been done, he is then committed for trial. Suppose a murder were
committed in County Derry, the prisoner
would be committed for trial to the next
Assizes for County Derry in the ordinary
course, if this Bill and its provisions were
not to come into operation. But under this
Bill the prisoner, if he thinks it would be
more advantageous to him, or for any other
reasons, if he wishes to be tried by the
Special Court rather than by the Court of
Assize, must signify to the Justices cominitting him that instead of being tried by the
Assize Court-which would have tried him
in the ordinary course, if this Bill had not
come into operation-he wishes to be tried
by the Special Court, whereupon the necessary steps will be taken to have the
depositions returned to the central office,
and the necessary arrangements made to
enable the trial to be carried out by the
Special Court. Sub-section (6) says:
Any direction by the Attorney-General
for Northern Ireland for the trial of a
person by the Special Court shall be given
not later than fourteen days after the
person charged with the crime or offence
shall have been committed for trial, and
notice of such direction shall be forthwith
given to such person.
it is obvious that some time must be given
to the Attorney-General to give the necessary
directions for the trial. As a matter of
fact when a prisoner is returned for trial,
say, to the Assizes, the proceedings so far
as the dispositions are concerned is that
they are sent forward by the committing
Justices, or by the Clerk of Petty Sessions
to the Clerk of the Crown and Peace. The
Clerk of the Crown and Peace makes out
copies of the depositions, and he sends them
to the Crown Solicitor for the particular
place where the crime was committed. The
Crown Solicitor then sends them to the
Attorney-General to take the directions of
the Attorney-General as to whether the
person is to be prosecuted, and how he is
to be tried, and so on. That, obviously,
all requires time, and the similar procedure,
which will have to be adopted under
this new Bill, will also require time.
Therefore it was thought appropriate that
some substantial time should be given to the
Attorney-General to enable him to have the
papers put before him, and also to enable
him to go fully into the case, that some time
like fourteen days should be given to him so
that he might be able to say whether or not
a particular case was to go on in the ordinary
way or to be tried by the Special Court. As
I said before, we are not wedded to the fourteen days, but in my opinion it is a reasonable time. As you see there is the difference
that the prisoner must make his request at
once, because he is there on the spot, and
will be able to make up his mind before he is
returned for trial, but obviously it would be
impossible for the Attorney-General to make
up his mind instanter, because he would not
have the necessary facts before him.
Sub-section (7) provides that:
The Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland, after consultation with two ordinary
Judges of the Court of Appeal, may make
all such rules as may be necessary for
carrying this Act into effect
and in particular

.
(a) For adapting for the purposes of this
Act the procedure on and preliminary to
the trial of criminal cases, including the
forms of indictment or other documents,
and for prescribing the forms of and manner of dealing with, notifying, or transmitting to the special court informations,
depositions, examinations, statements,

sworn, taken, acknowledged, made or given
in any case which is to be tried by the

(b) For prescribing, and, if necessary,

for regulating the employment of officers
for such duties,
and generally for laying down the procedure
in reference to trials. Clause 4 provides that
This Act shall continue in force for one
year and no longer, unless Parliament
otherwise determines.
I do not think I have anything more to say
at present. There will be an opportunity
later on to discuss these matters more in detail, and I simply content myself now with
moving the Second Reading.
Mr. LYNN: There is no Member of this
House, and very few people, 1 think, in
Ulster who are not aware of the brilliance of
the Attorney-General as an advocate, and also
of the great ability he always shows in crossexamination. I have had the pleasure once,
and only once, of being cross-examined by
him, but I only wish that the procedure in
this House would allow me in turn to crossexamine the Attorney-General in regard to
this Bill. Unfortunately it does not, but
there are a great many questions I would
have liked to put to him. I came to the conclusion that if I knew nothing about this
thing, and I had only listened to his brilliant
speech-and it was a brilliant speech
-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-I would
vote against the Second Reading, because if arguments were necessary to show
that this Bill should not be read the Second
Time, those arguments have been provided
Criminal Procedure Bill
-Second Reading.
6 APRIL 1922.
by the learned Attorney-General. He began
by saying that it is a novel Bill. That is a
very polite way of describing it. Then he
went on to say that there were precedents
for it. I had a recollection that there was a
precedent, and evidently the learned
Attorney-General realised that I would refer
to it if he did not. But what a precedent!
In 1882, when the jurors of the South of Ireland were terrorised, and failed to do their
duty, Parliament was forced to bring in a
Bill setting up a Commission of three
Judges, and, as the learned Attorney-General
very fairly admitted, the whole thing proved
a dead letter. Therefore, because this precedent proved a dead letter, it is one which
is going to be adopted by the Government of
Northern Ireland. I should say that this
precedent is not one which ought to
be followed, or which is in any way useful.
The Attorney-General was also fair enough
to admit that if he had been asked as a lawyer
to defend this Bill he would find it very difficult to do so. I can well believe it. He says
Magna Charta is not impinged upon because
a prisoner has the right of saying whether he
shall or shall not be tried by this Special
Court. I never knew of a criminal who
had any desire to be tried by any Court,
special or otherwise, and I did not know
that it was the duty of Parliament to
consult merely the wishes of the criminals
concerned. If we are to make this change
-and it is a serious change, though only for
twelve months- in the criminal procedure of
the country surely some substantial reason
should be given why we should make it.
I could understand the learned Attorney-
General coming to this House and saying
that the jurors of Ulster had failed in their
duty through fear, or through partisanship,
or for any cause like this, that the jurors
had failed to carry out their oath to give
a verdict according to the evidence-I could
understand the learned Attorney-General
coming to the House then, and asking us to
set up a special Commission under those
circumstances. But he has not given us
a single case where a jury in Ulster has
failed to do its duty. Not only so, but I
challenge him now to give us a single
instance even in these terrible times in
which we are living-where an Ulster jury
has failed in its duty. If he were able to
do that there would be some justification
for asking us to pass this Bill, but I submit
that under the circumstances, and the juries
having done their duty, there is no case
whatever for departing from the ordinary
procedure.
I agree with the learned Attorney-General
that crime is crime, and that it is an absurdity for us to start to classify crimes as
political crimes. Whether a man shoots
another man because of his political opinion,
because he has got some personal spite
against him, or because he wants to rob him,
surely that is murder, and I do not know
why we should go into different classes of
murder. To me there is only one class of
murder, and all murders are equally black
and equally detestable. Further, I do not
see why, because a man calls himself a
political murderer, some special provision
should be made in his case that is not made
in the case of an ordinary citizen. I would
like the learned Attorney-General to tell us
what is going to happen in case the two
judges disagree.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. LYNN: There must be two judges,
one of whom must be the Lord Chief Justice
of Northern Ireland. Suppose they disagree
what is going to happen? Why, one of
the two judges will always come back
on the case. You are not going to get
a fresh tribunal. I would like whoever
replies on behalf of the Government
to tell us what they are going to do in a
case like that. Is the prisoner to be released? Releasing prisoners is a very
popular thing nowadays. You may murder,
burn, or do what you like, but after a week
or two, or sometimes after a day or two,
you are released.
I do not want to waste the time of the
House by traversing ground which has been
gone over already. I object to this Bill on
two very simple but very important grounds.
The first is that it interferes with the great
Charter under which our nation has grown
up, under which freedom has developed as
it has developed in no other country in the
world. The second is that under present
conditions this Bill is an insult to the jurors
of Ulster who in all circumstances and under
all conditions have faithfully discharged
their duties. What are we going to get
in return for abrogating Magna Charta even
for twelve months, or for casting a sluralthough I am sure it is the last thing the
Prime Minister wants to do on the jurors
of Ulster, because inferentially there is a
slur cast on them, and it is being done in
order to please two gentlemen who, to use
a phrase common some months ago, are on
the run. To-day, Mr. Collins and Mr.
Griffith have got no influence whatever in
the South of Ireland. They are unable to
defend themselves or their friends, but yet
we are making this grave change in the
constitution of the law in order to please
two politicians who, as I say, are on the
run and who are unable to carry out the
pledges they have signed and agreed to. I
do not want to hamper the Government in
any way, I do not even want to force this
matter to a division. I have my own im-
Criminal Procedure Bill
-Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Lynn]
pression as to what would happen if there
was a full House and it came to a division,
and I know the feeling of the people as a
whole in regard to this matter, but I realise
the difficulties of the Government and I do
not want to add to these difficulties in the
slightest degree. Therefore, after making

The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps my hon.
Friend (Mr. Lynn) would not object if I
were to explain to the House my view of
this particular article which is included in
the Agreement. In the first instance my
hon. Friend is perfectly correct in saying
that it is by no desire on my part that
any such arrangement was ever suggested.
But it was not suggested by Mr. Collins.
It was suggested by certain Roman Catholics
in Ulster itself who were very desirous of
having peace. They approached me with
regard to that and many other matters, all
tending towards one end-that this sordid
and terrible cycle of crime, going on day
after day and adding not only death to so
many households in our midst, but adding
to what was becoming a bad name for Ulster
and a bad name for Belfast, should cease.
They themselves put forward in the first
instance many suggestions which with my
advisers I considered to the best of my
ability. Eventually these suggestions found
their way to the Conference table and some
of them were embodied in the Agreement
that we arrived at. I quite agree that if
it had been left to the Government we would
never have introduced this Bill at all. I
quite agree that there is no part of the
United Kingdom where, under more difficult
circumstances, the jury system works better
than it does here, and I hope it will go
out, as it has done from my hon. Friend
(Mr. Lynn) and from me and my Government, that this is no reflection whatever
upon the jurors or upon the jury system
in the Six Counties. It is in some ways
a compliment.
Mr. LYNN: A queer one.
The PRIME MINISTER: It is a queer
one, I agree, but at the same time it cannot
be taken in any sense other than that the
Government itself is advocating the continuity of the old jury system that has proved
so successful in the past. I will go a step
further than the hon. Member for West
Belfast and say that it is a very Irish Bill.
I cannot be quite sure whether he himself
when he was speaking, did not see a certain
sense of humour in the fact that whereas
in 1882 the Government of the day
were proposing something of this sort,
in 1922, it is the very people who
objected to it in 1882 who are asking
for this Bill which we as a Government
propose to give them in the hope that, added
to the other Clauses in the Agreement, we
may be able to bring peace to our community. But may I point out two things
which will, I hope, somewhat allay feeling
in the House and outside. First of all my
hon. Friend asks what will happen if the
two judges do not agree. What happens
where a jury fail to agree?
Mr. LYNN: A new trial.
The PRIME MINISTER: And when they
do not agree?
Mr. LYNN: A new trial.
The PRIME MINISTER: And when they
do not agree?
Mr. LYNN: A new trial. There is a new
trial three times.
seen
The PRIME MINISTER: My right hon.
and learned friend (Mr. Best) says that
where you cannot get an agreement the
prisoner is discharged. I have frequently
cases where a prisoner is discharged
when the jury fail to agree, and in Scotland
when there is a disagreement the case is
marked "not proven." At all events let us
look at it from this point of view. First
of all we have a splendid judiciary. I do
not believe myself that a man who commits
any of the offences referred to in this Bill
will get off a bit more lightly because he
goes before two judges than if he goes
before a jury. If that had been the
object of the Bill I would not have
consented to it, and I only consented
to it because I felt that if it was
said in England or in the Colonies or in
any part of the world that Ulster would
not allow prisoners who so desired to be
tried by the judges of her own High Court,
and would smash the Agreement for peace
in consequence, it would go very much
against us. Therefore I have to ask the
House when considering this Bill to bear
in mind that it is part of the general
Agreement for arriving at peace.
It may
be of some interest to the House to know
that since I arrived here I have received
further assurances that the other side intend to enforce peace themselves, and the
prospect seems to me to be even better than
it was yesterday. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I must also point out to the House
that we have brought the Bill before the
House in the way we have done although
--and this is a point I hope my hon. Friends
will bear in mind it is part of the Agreement that we should do this-I arranged
that we should do this because I wanted
this House to have the first opportunity of
discussing the whole matter frankly and
openly. I always try to be as frank an open

Criminal Procedure Bill

as I possibly can, but at the same time this
is really a matter for the British Government. As the hon. Member for Queen's
University (Mr. Robb) knows, the judiciary
is a reserved service, and the British
Government could have passed this legislation over our heads as part of the Agreement. But I said "No. Let us in the
first instance bring in our Bill, thrash it
out in the House, get the most searching
criticism, and if it passes our House we
will hand it across to you and you can pass

action we have taken the most open
and frank way of meeting the people
here. I hope the House will not take the
matter too seriously. I will tell you why.
I have the feeling that the provisions of
the Bill will hardly ever be called upon. I
do not myself believe that it will be taken
advantage of, because I think the public as
and
whole, both Protestant
Catholic, in the Six Counties are perfectly
satisfied with the jury system and with the
measure of justice that has been meted out
to them. I believe hat the very people who
have asked for this Clause to be inserted
will be the first to prefer the ordinary jury
system when it comes to a question of trial.
Therefore to carry out the terms of the
Agreement entered into for the purpose of
promoting peace I ask the House to give
us a Second Reading of the Bill, the details
of which can be thrashed out in Committee,
because I personally could not enter into
the details of such a legal measure.

very glad of the Prime Minister's intervention in the Debate to explain how it
came about that this Special Court was

if the exact constitution of this Court was
suggested by Mr. Collins. The only defence there could be for the introduction of this Court at all would be,
my hon. Friend, the Member for West

They have been complimented by Judges of

cumstances. If it was proved that they were

I am like my hon. Friend, the Member for
West Belfast, I have never been able to distinguish between ordinary and political
crime. Crime is crime, no matter what
the motive. But might not the particular
section of society in whose interests this
Court is provided be themselves somewhat
suspicious with respect to it? They have not
been consulted. Their so-called leaders have
decided. I am not at all sure that if I were
a Roman Catholic I would like to be tried by
two Judges. The suggestion was made by the
right hon. and learned Gentleman himself
in introducing the Bill that he would expect
much more from a Court where a jury was
in operation than from a Court constituted
of Judges. I quite agree with that. There
is nothing to appeal to where two judges
are presiding at a Court. There is nothing
to appeal to but their direct standard
of the law. No mitigating circumstances are taken into consideration. The
human element-the human sympathies-are
in some degree eliminated. That would not
be so in the case of an ordinary jury. I
would argue, therefore, that in the case of
those for whom this Court is to be a special
protection there is an awful danger that
it may prove quite otherwise.
The PRIME MINISTER: The hon. Member should bear in mind that they are not
bound to go to it; they have the option. I
hone he bears that in mind-that there is an
option.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I am keeping that before
me. But if the Attorney-General so directs
or decides he can challenge the choice. Is
not that the effect of sub-section (b) ?
Mr. ROBB: No, no.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I am afraid that his
discretionary powers are such as to make the

The question is this, and to my mind it is a
very pertinent question, what will happen
when the Court constituted by two Judges
disagree? Now we will have to have that
question answered. We know what happens
when a jury disagrees. But when two Judges
disagree what will happen? Will it happen
as has been suggested by the Prime Minister
sometimes happens in the case of Scotland,
that the case will be marked "Not Proven "?
Or, will it be adjourned indefinitely? When
Criminal Procedure Bill

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. M'Guffin]
two Judges disagree and there is no higher
Court of appeal, what can happen? I am
sure the right hon. and learned Gentleman
has the means of answering that question.
It will be very interesting to know what the
answer is. And one of the two must always
sit. That is a very important point.
There is just one other aspect of the
question to which I wish to refer, and which
I suggest that the right hon. and learned
Gentleman should note. Is the idea in connection with these Courts to expedite trials,
that is to say, to give the prisoner shorter
shrift? I do not know whether that is the
intention or not. I am sure that two Judges
will deal with a case more quickly than a
jury. A jury will retire into their room and
ponder over all the evidence, take into consideration all the circumstances, take into
consideration every detail of the evidence.
I am not suggesting that the Judges will not
do so. But Judges will determine a case
much more summarily than a jury. I suppose
the Court will receive distinguished occupants of the Bench of Northern Ireland. A
great many things might be said in the way
of comparison with the different Criminal
Court under the 1882 Act. When the right
hon. Gentleman was inquiring what precedent there was, I was wondering if he would
refer to the Star Chamber. I do not think
that was present in his mind at the time. It
was the Courts that were constituted to deal
with crime in 1882. Other objections to this
Bill with respect to the Schedule can be discussed during the Committee stage. I mean
to say that in glancing through the Bill there
were many things that arose to me as points
of criticism that, I may say in compliment
to the right hon. and learned Gentleman,
have been fully elucidated in his speech. I
am very glad that they have been. I think
that after we have dealt with this Bill in
Committee we shall be more agreed with regard to the necessity for its provisions. I
can only hope at any rate that it will have
the effect-we have got the assurance of the
Prime Minister-of leading to the permanent
peace that is necessary to the prosperity of
the city.

Reading. The speech that has been made
by the learned Attorney-General and the
statement made by the Prime Minister seem
to me absolutely to justify the Second
Reading of the Bill. It has been founded
not on any will of the Northern Government to put through the Bill but on a bargain which the Prime Minister on our behalf
entered into with the Provisional Government of Southern Ireland and the Imperial
Government. Also, might I say that had
it been my privilege earlier in the day to
have heard the lucid statement of the learned
Attorney-General with regard to the several
Clauses of the Bill, I might not have objected to the Motion moved earlier in the
day. It is one of those unfortunate things
that happen. I do not seek to blame the
Attorney-General or anyone else. I recognise the high pressure put upon the Government with regard to the preparation of this
Bill. I think it was right when the Bill
was introduced that Members should not be
asked to swallow it at one gulp. (Hon.
Members: Hear,, hear.) With regard to the
Bill itself, I would like to suggest for the
consideration of the Attorney-General
or two particulars. In Section 1, Sub-section
(2) a Court is set up with the consent of the
Chief Justice and Judges. I would like

in each case?
one
Mr. BEST: Generally. In cases of this
kind where new duties of à most frightfully
involved character are put upon judges and
where in our case we cannot make them
do the work if they do not wish to do it,
it is always put in with their consent. The
judges have given their consent to act under
this Bill.
Mr. ROBB: That is exactly what I wanted
to have brought to the knowledge of the
Members of this House. I think, perhaps,
it would be well if the Attorney-General
would consider before the Committee stage
whether he ought to put into the Bill some
provision with regard to what is to
happen in case the two judges disagree. If
a case has been brought and tried before two
judges of the greatest possible experience,
and these two judges disagree about the guilt
of the prisoner then I think the principle
of English law ought to apply, that the man's
innocence is to be presumed, the Crown having failed to prove his guilt. There is one
other point, and that is I am not quite sure
that it is fair that the prisoner should forthwith upon committal request to be tried by
special Court. I think he is entitled to some
time, possibly a week would be enough. We
know how these things happen. Very often
before the magistrates he has no one to defend
him. He is committed for trial; he has no
means of employing advocates to defend him.
I think that some time should be allowed,
even after his committal, during which on
the advice of his friends or on legal advice
he may have an opportunity of requesting
that he should be tried by special Court and
not by a jury. I offer these suggestions to
those in charge of the Bill. I heartly support the Second Reading.

the Prime Minister, who is in a better posi-

Clause 8.-(Powers of Police in Northern
Ireland).
Senate Amendment:
or
After Clause 8 insert as a new Clause-
"The provisions of section fourteen of the
Petty Sessions (Ireland) Act, 1851, in relation to the readings of depositions as
evidence upon the trial of a person
charged with an indictable crime
offence, shall extend so as to authorize the
reading of such depositions as evidence,
where it is proved that a witness is so ill
as to be unable to travel; or, where the
attendance of the witness cannot be procured, owing to the prevalence of a state
of disorder or otherwise."
Mr. BEST: I beg to move, "That this
House doth agree with the Senate in the
said Amendment."
This is a very important Amendment, and
perhaps the full significance of it does not
appear from the words that are upon the
Paper. My hon. and learned Friends will
appreciate the full significance of it.
Section 14 of the Petty Sessions (Ireland)
Act, 1851, provides that where a deposition
has been taken and a person has been re
turned for trial, and where the person who
has made the deposition dies before the trial
is carried through, then on proof of certain
formalities that deposition may be used
upon the trial. Of course the person who
made the deposition cannot be there; he is
dead and gone. What is proposed in this
new clause is that that provision should be
extended so as to include depositions taken
before a magistrate, and that we should be
authorised to read those depositions as
evidence where it is proved that a witness
is so ill as to be unable to travel, or where
the attendance of the witness cannot be procured owing to the prevalence of a state of
disorder or otherwise. It is a curious
matter, but it is a fact, that the first of the
new provisions is already used in English
statutes. In other words, in England, where
a witness has made a deposition, that deposition can be used upon the trial either
in the case of the death of the witness or in
the case where the witness is so ill as to be
unable to travel. But that latter provision
has never applied in Ireland. We want it
to apply now, and further, we want this
Amendment, namely, where a witness has
been kept back from a trial, where threats
have been resorted to and intimidation has
been used against him, we wish to have the
power of using the deposition made by that
witness, so that the effect and value of his
evidence shall not be lost. It has been
found most effectual where depositions have
courtsbeen taken, particularly before
martial, and where a warning has been
given. Now if anything happens to this
witness, if this witness is kept out of the
way, still his sworn statement can be used.
When that becomes known it will mean
there is no good trying to intimidate a witness because his deposition can still be used,
and the accused will not have the advantage,
if it be an advantage, of having the witness
there for cross-exmination.
Question put, and agreed to.

CRIMES AND OFFENCES TO WHICH

(1) Treason or Treason Felony.

(3) Assault which either causes actual

committed with intent to cause grievous
bodily harm,
(4) Arson whether by common Law or by

involving (a) the breaking into, firing at or
otherwise attacking or injuring a dwellinghouse; (b) larceny or robbery with threats

to or destruction of any property whatsoever,
including any crime or offence under the
Malicious Damage Act, 1861.
(6) Any crime or offence against the Explosive Substances Act, 1883, or the Firearms Act, 1920.

any of the said crimes or offences or being
accessory to or aiding or abetting in the
commission thereof.

Motion made, and Question proposed:
