The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I beg to move that the Bill be
now read a Second time. If I had been told
a year or so ago that I would to-day in a
Northern Parliament, as Minister of Labour,
be responsible for moving the Second Reading of an Emergency Unemployment Insurance Bill, affecting, approximately, a
quarter of a million insured persons, about
one fourth of whom at the present time are
unfortunately unemployed, I would have
said that such a chain of circumstances was
almost impossible, and that my friend was
a false prophet. However, as we get olderand in this respect at any rate I am making
progress-I think we feel that our lives are
in large a measure portioned out for us.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) In the first
place, I should tell the House that (except
in two of its clauses to which I will refer
later) this Bill is drafted on parallel lines
to the Bill which has just passed the Imperial House of Commons. This is in comformity with the decision of the Cabinet of
Northern Ireland, of which I am sure Hon.
Members will all approve, namely, that our
unemployed persons should be dealt with
similarly to those who are unemployed in
Great Britain.
This Bill amalgamates the Unemployment
Benefit authorised by the Unemployment Insurance Acts of 1920 and 1921 with the Grants
authorised by the Dependants Act of last
year.

[Mr. Andrews]
that before July, 1923, arrives, the acute
emergency period will be past. In this
attempt to deal with a difficult problem, I
think I can count on the sympathy of all
honourable Members.
Mr. LYNN: Hear, hear!
Mr. ANDREWS: During the last month or
so I have kept in close touch with my right
hon. Friend, the Imperial Minister of Labour,
and, although this Bill is in the main his
child, I feel I can say, without any breach of
faith, that on certain matters of importance
he has not entirely shut his eyes to my viewpoint. Once again I am pleased to express
my indebtedness to him for the valuable help
which he has given me in this and in
other matters since my appointment in June
last. Of course, I know this Bill will be
criticised. Probably every Bill should.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear!) It is easy to
say that it does not fully deal with the position; but it can be viewed, I admit, from
another standpoint altogether. For instance,
a few days ago I was talking to two working
men on the subject. One of them, whom I
will call Mr. B., said to me that the present
contributions were too high, and the other, on
my left, whom I will call Mr. C., said :-
"Oh, that is not what I object to. What
I object to is that the benefits are far too
small," so I said to Mr. B.:" I suppose you
are working?"
"Yes," he replied, "I am."
I turned to Mr. C., and I said, "I suppose
you are out of employment?" "Yes, that is
true," was his answer. You will see it is
just how you approach this question. It is
the old story of the producer wishing prices
to be high, and the consumer wanting them
low. It is impossible to please everyone.
Personally, I am not going to attempt the
task. You have probably heard of the story
of the old man and his ass. I am not going
to fall off that animal. I feel that this Bill
is an earnest attempt to deal with a great
national emergency, and it can be said with
truth that no other Government
in any
country in the world has ever gone so far
before Of course, I am aware that thoughtless people talk about pauperising the nation,
because those who, through no fault of their
own, are out of employment, receive during
periods of commercial depression, by means
of a contributory insurance system, that to
which they are justly entitled. Changes in
form and alterations in amount are sure to
take place as the years roll on, but instinctively I feel that insurance against starvation and dire want due to unemployment has
come to stay, as one of the factors upon
which our industrial and our social systems
must necessarily rest in the future. Apart
altogether from the human factor-which
should not be lost sight of-it must not be
forgotten that this ever-fluctuating reserve of
labour must be cared for and preserved
during times of depression, so that it may be
available for and capable of performing
useful work when more prosperous days
come round.
I desire to take advantage of this opportunity of again appealing with what strength
and little influence I may possess to employers
in Northern Ireland to do all that they can
to provide work for our people. It is work
which our people want, and, believe me,
Northern Ireland cannot for very long afford
to have idlers in any class. Some employers,
I know, are hard pressed at the moment, and
can give little help in this direction. Others
-I say it with some hesitation-might do
more than they are doing.
In this connection, I feel that Messrs.
Harland & Wolff are an example to us all.
Owing to the influence, power, business
ability, and the unparalleled energy of Lord
Pirrie, ably supported by his faithful staff,
the firm to-day are employing as many persons
in Belfast as they did before the war. Beyond
all doubt, Lord Pirrie is the greatest com.
mercial magnate that this country has ever
produced, and to him this city is indebted
more than to any other man. This new
Ulster of ours has many difficulties to face,
both industrial and political, but I am
satisfied that we will weather the storm, and
that by work and through the will power of
our people, Uister will become greater and
more prosperous still
The present unemployment situation will
be very materially relieved by the relief
grant of £500,000 which has just been made
by the British Treasury for works to be
carried out in Belfast and neighbourhood.
The House can be assured that this money
will be wisely spent. On the basis that the
Fund will find 50 per cent. of the wages paid
on relief works, and that the money is all
spent within 12 months, continuous employment will be found for somewhere about 6,000
people. In addition there will be an increased
volume of employment, which cannot, however, be measured, due to the additional
spending power of the persons employed on
the works. Further, there will be more
employment produced by the manufacture of
the necessary materials which will, as far
as possible, be provided from Ulster. This
relief of unemployment will naturally ease
the strain on the Unemployment Fund. I
have almost completed the appointment of
a very representative Committee to advise
me in connection with this all important
matter. The names of this Committee I hope
to announce in the Press to-morrow or the
next day. I will be much disappointed if
some of these relief works are not started
within a week from to-day.
417 Unemployment Insurance Bill 11 APRIL 1922.

-Second Reading.
The House will remember that, some
months ago, I appointed a Committee to
advise me on the question of Labour Exchanges and Unemployment Insurance in
Northern Ireland. This Committee, under
the very able chairmanship of the honourable
and gallant Member for Armagh, has presented an Interim Report unanimously recommending that Local Employment Committees, the same as in Great Britain,
should be associated with our Labour Exchanges. With this recommendation I am
in entire agreement, believing that it will
lead to both increased efficiency and
economy. I propose to establish such Committees as soon as possible, and by Clause
(8) of this Bill we ask for powers to confer
certain duties upon them. This Bill is
designed to help those who, owing to unemployment and through no fault of their
own, are temporarily at the bottom of the
ladder. In this spirit, therefore, and with
implicit confidence, I recommend it to the
sympathetic treatment of the House.
Mr. LYNN: I think hon. Members and
the House will admit that there are two
outstanding features in the character of the
Minister of Labour. One is honesty, and
the other is lucidity of expression. He
has dealt with a very complicated subject, and
he has dealt with it, if I may say so, in
an exceptionally able and lucid manner. I
have listened to a great many speeches on
unemployment insurance, and I am free to
admit that on most occasions I knew less
about it when the speech had ended than
I knew when it began. It is not so on
this occasion. I think the right hon.
Gentleman has made this Bill perfectly
clear to everyone. I think it is right-and
I am glad to hear him say it-that the
Cabinet of Northern Ireland has agreed to
place unemployment insurance in the same
position in Ulster as it is in in Great Britain.
After all it costs as much for an unemployed
person to live here as it does in England
or Scotland. The unemployed person has
got his wants here just as he has in any
other part of the United Kingdom or of
the Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
And therefore it is right that an unemployed person should be in the same position
here as in any other part of the United
Kingdom.
I agree with the right hon. Gentleman
that there is a great difference between
unemployment insurance and what he calls
pauperising the people. Under a scheme
of unemployment insurance the working
man is making provision against conditions
such as unhappily we are passing through
at the present time. The employer is also
helping, and the State is helping. I think
it is right that they should help in order
to tide the community over periods of this
sort. Instead of pauperising, the unemployment insurance scheme is the very antidote
to pauperism and helps to maintain that
virile independent spirit which we want to
see maintained amongst our people.
I am sure every member of this House will
join with the right hon. Gentleman in the
appeal he has made to employers to do the
best they can for the unemployed. It is
wonderful how much can be done when there
is a little optimism about, and if all employers shared the optimistic spirit of the
Minister of Labour I think there are a
great many difficulties that might be got
over, and a different atmosphere might be
created. I for one join heartily with the
Minister of Labour in the tribute he has paid
to Lord Pirrie. I have had my political differences with Lord Pirrie in the past, and it is
possible I may have political differences with
his lordship in the future, but no political
differences one may have should be allowed
to obscure the fact that Lord Pirrie is a
great Ulsterman and not only a great Ulsterman, but, as the Minister of Labour has
said, a great commercial magnate and
great asset to this part of the United Kingdom. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am
sure every Member of the House is deeply
grateful to Lord Pirrie for what he has
done, because if he had not thrown his great
ability and great energy into those shipbuilding works of his probably the Minister
of Labour would to-day have had to deal with
more unemployed than is the case, and,
therefore, the public as a whole must feel
grateful to Lord Pirrie, and we do hope that
others will follow in his footsteps.
a
The right hon. Gentleman quite rightly
says that there are many things in this Bill
that could be criticised. I have not seen
many Bills, except the last one (Criminal

This old system of Unemployment Insurance
is complicated, and if I wanted to deal
purely in criticism I think I could find a

the system. But I do not blame the right
hon. Gentleman, because he has inherited a

sure that if he and his

the Government could have got rid of them.
There has to be an individual account kept
of every one who comes under the scheme.
It is not really a mutual insurance scheme;
it is an individual scheme and thus it adds

Mr. ROBB: I only wish to ask the right
hon. Gentleman a question. In presenting
the Bill he stated that except with regard to

has just been passed in the Imperial House.
He told us he would explain what those two

Mr. M'GUFFIN: I would like to join the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn)
in offering congratulations to the Minister of
Labour for the very efficient, very clear, and
adequate way in which he has presented this
Bill to the House. It is most important that
this Bill should pass as quickly as possible.
There is very little criticism that can be
offered, because the Bill runs on parallel lines
to that passed in the Imperial House. There
are a great many lapsed claims in connection
with our system of insurance, and it is very
desirable that as soon as possible, by means
of a Bill of this kind, claims for the resumption of payment should be provided for. I
was in company one evening which was discussing the question of which is the most experimental of the sciences. Some said that it
was biology, others said it was chemistry, but
a more intelligent individual than the rest
suggested it was law. In connection with
this question we have had eleven Bills in the
course of as many years, all tending to
improve the conditions of insurance and the
position of the worker. I was very pleased,
in reading the discussion that took place in
the Imperial House the other night, to see that
the Minister of Labour took occasion to clear
away a very false impression that existed in
the House to the effect that unemployment
insurance constituted a dole. I want to protest against that. I think I have even heard
it suggested in this House. It is by no means
a dole; and, in view of the fact that the
system is contributory, I fail to underst ind
how any person can regard it as a dole.
From November, 1920, until the present time
£80,000,000 will have been expended by the
Imperial Parliament on insurance benefits,
and of that £80,000,000 the Government will
have contributed £16,000,000. That is to say,
the Government have contributed about
one-fifth, and, therefore, the workers and the
employers are entitled to the credit of having
contributed four-fifths of the entire amount.
To talk of that system as conducted on the
basis of a dole is, to my mind, preposterous.
I quite agree with my hon. Friend (Mr. Lynn)
that there are many respects in which the Bill
might be criticised, but, considering that it
has got through the Imperial House, where it
was subjected to very few criticisms, and in
view of its urgency, we will accept the Bill,
and put it through the House as quickly as
possible. We are glad to know that it is
only a temporary measure, and that the right
honourable Gentleman has in contemplation,
through the assistance and advice of the Committee which he set up, an even better Bill.
However, this Bill has to run for fifteen
months from now, and it will be the end of
June, next year, before that period will have
elapsed. I am quite sure that during that
time the Minister of Labour will focus his
attention on this matter, and give it every
possible consideration, and that he will then
introduce to this House a Bill that will be
worthy of our position as a new Government.
There is one particular in which an improvement might reasonably he effected, and that
is the amalgamation of Health and Labour
Insurance. If that were done, valuable
economy could be achieved, and that is very
desirable, because, at the moment, our financial status is very uncertain, and the amount
of our income is even more problematical.
In view of that fact, I think it is very necessary that the Minister of Labour should see
that the system of Unemployment Insurance
in the Northern area is carried out with the
greatest possible economy.
There is another respect in which the Bill
might very usefully have been amended, and
I am sorry that the Imperial Parliament did
not see its way to adopt the amendment that
was proposed, and thus in all probability
have secured the advantage to us. I refer to
the disqualification that takes place through
strike exigencies. Take the case of a man
who is employed in one section of a firm.
The workers in another section of that firm
go out on strike, and, because the first section
I mentioned is dependent on the second section for the supply of the necessary material
to carry on their work, they are thrown out
of employment. Those who are thrown out of
employment in that way are deprived of their
work through no fault of their own, but,
421 Unemployment Insurance Bill

under the present Bill, they are not entitled
to benefit. I think that is very regrettable,
because those men have been paying their
insurance contributions, and under any other
circumstances would be entitled to benefit.
Then there is the matter of increasing the
benefit paid to the wife and to the children
through the Emergency Act that has been
amalgamated with the ordinary Acts. I do
not take very much exception to the 5s paid
to the wife, but I think 1s is a most inadequate amount to pay in respect of a child.
Take the case of a man who is married. He
is entitled to £1 a week, but if he has a wife
and two children he only gets 22s. That is to
say, for the two children he is only entitled
to 2s. extra.
The Government would have been well
advised if they had modified the sum payable
in respect of the wife, and allowed more to
the children, because I am of the opinion that
the greatest hardship exists where children
have to be provided for. When you work it
out, it means 1d. per day to provide meals
for a child. That is absolutely inadequate,
and it is a pity the Bill could not have been
improved in this respect. The amount
allowed to children during the war was something like 6s. and 3s. per week, and as my
hon Friend (Mr. Lynn) has said, it requires
as much to support a child now as it did
during the war. Yet you are making the
miserable provision of 1s. a week for him,
whereas during the war you paid him 6s. and
3s.
We are all glad to know that prices are
falling, but they are not falling to a degree
that enables us to say that we are better off
now than we were prior to the war. On the
whole, we are worse off.
The Imperial Government contemplate
paying £60,000,000 in respect of insurance
benefit within the next fifteen months. That
represents a great volume of relief, and
under present circumstances the question
that suggests itself is: how did we manage
prior to 1910 or 1911 when these measures
were first introduced? When a worker was
suddenly displaced he had no resources unless
he had made a little provision out of the
rather inadequate pay with which he was remunerated at that time. Now we find that
provision is made, and I regard it as the
duty of the State to provide for the workers
just as they do for soldiers. After all, our
workers are the backbone and the basis of
the riches and prosperity of our nation.
Where would we be without them? When a
serious strike occurs and certain utilities are
cut off, we know immediately how the mass
of the workers stand in relation to us. If
soldiers are useful in protecting us during a
period of war, the industrial worker, whom
I may call in the circumstances the industrial soldier, is just as important for our
maintenance during the years of peace. The
need of the moment is to get the Bill through
this House as expeditiously as possible. We
trust the House will deal with it in the
spirit of the appeal made by the right hon.
Gentleman who moved the Second Reading
(Mr. Andrews). We all feel the greatest
sympathy with those who, through no fault
of their own, find themselves unemployed.
We were glad to hear from the Minister of
Labour that things are a little more hopeful
particularly in the North of Ireland, and
we hope the time is not far distant when
normal conditions will return, though at the
moment I am very sceptical as to what may
happen within the next two or three years.
However, a Bill of this description, when it
becomes law, is certainly of great advantage
to the industrial classes. They recognise that
fact, but they do not like the benefit to be
given to them as charity or a dole, and if you
are administering an Act for the benefit of
the workers you are not to detract from its
advantages by associating it with an insult.
Workers have independent minds just like
other people, and they are entitled to anything towards which they contribute. Under
the circumstances 1 think we would be well
advised to push this Bill through as speedily
as possible.

Mr. MARK: After listening to the Debate
that has taken place here I only wish to
add a few words of comment. I did not
want to intervene at an earlier stage, but

of Labour, who has done his best to maintain industrial peace in the Six Counties.
The part of this Debate that struck me
more than any other was the reference
made by the hon. Member for Tyrone and
Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) to the administration of these funds. Nowhere in the Six
Counties is the state of affairs he referred
to better illustrated than in the city of
Derry. What is there to prevent any man
coming in from Donegal, and after a few
weeks asking for unemployment benefit? I
have known instances where men have had
the cheek to come into Derry to ask an employer to sign their cards although there
have been weeks in which they had never
crossed the threshold. That is done in
Derry city. Recently in Derry city two
local people, one an ex-soldier minus a leg,
were turned out of the labour exchange, and
two others, one of whom was not a Six
County man, were appointed in their place.
These things naturally create friction in
the district, and I think that in drafting
a Bill such as this something should be inserted which would prevent an imposition
of this sort taking place.
It has been stated that an inspector of the

case of an I.R.A. man having received unemployment benefit. I am afraid the inspector could not find out who the I.R.A.
men were, but notwithstanding what the
inspector reported I am strongly of opinion
that in all the Counties there are I.R.A. men
receiving benefit from the Six County funds.
It was a matter of comment at the recent
Revision Sessions in Derry that twelve or
fourteen young unmarried men who were
not born in the city but had come in during
the last few years were getting votes in respect of two rooms. Surely there is something wrong when these men can come in
and hold up the street corners while at the
same time drawing unemployment benefit
from us.
There are men employed in agriculture who are receiving benefit and they
never contributed anything towards it. Take
the case of the men employed on the new
Basin in Derry. These men are all farmers'
sons who are engaged daily looking after
their blackfaced sheep on the hills, and they
come into Derry once a fortnight or once a
month, and because they have been working.
a few weeks on the new Derry Basin they
can get benefit, although they have been
working on their fathers' farms. Some limit
should be put on the drawing of this benefit,
and I think we should not have followed exactly in the footsteps of the Imperial Parliament. We should have gone back on the
old system of 10s a week for a married man
and doubled the allowance for the children.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE (MONEY)
Considered in Committee.
Mr. Moles in the Chair.
Resolved: "That, for the purposes of any
Act of the present Session relating to insurance against unemployment, it is expedient
to authorise the payment, out of moneys
provided by Parliament, in respect of the
period between the seventh day of May,
nineteen hundred and twenty-two, and the
end of the deficiency period. of an increased
contribution towards unemployment benefit,
and any other payment to be made out of the
Unemployment Fund, not exceeding the
amount determined by the Ministry of
Finance to be approximately equivalent to
the sum which would be produced by weekly
contributions paid in respect of insured
persons at the rate of threepence in the case
of men and twopence in the case of women,
boys, and girls."-(The Minister of Finance
(Mr Pollock).

forthwith."

allowance for the child. It is not a very
big sum for the area under the jurisdiction
of our Parliament compared with what the

in the same position as the wife who has
no children. The latter is able to give her

the House was to see if two shillings could

and everything is improving, and I am quite
sure my right hon. Friend will have our
sympathy in putting forward this question
of giving an extra shilling for a child to

ing it is only a shilling for the child. After

Mr M'GUFFIN: I do not think it is necessary to discuss this matter any further, but
there is one object I have in view in rising,

present at the Committee where that has
been a matter of grave discussion, and it was
admitted by the Minister that though the
Bill was proceeding he was not quite sure of
the financial soundness of the measure. I do
not know how the right hon. Gentleman
stands in the matter, for he can forecast
nothing. I cannot suggest very much, as we
have no power to interfere, and yet, forsooth,
we have been looking forward to a Bill in the
near future. I hope in presenting the Bill he
will not too slavishly follow the Imperial
Parliament. There seems to be some risk. I
was going to suggest the more the better.
With regard to support of the workers, the
attitude seems to be if we can give them as
much as will prevent a tendency towards
revolution we have done all that we are
entitled to do. There will be a splendid
opportunity afforded to the right hon.
Gentleman, in his distinguished position as
the head of a very important Department, for
breaking new ground in this matter. I think
the more risk you take it will be the better
for all concerned, even for the Parliament,
if not with respect to the expenditure of that
particular Department, at least with respect
to the expenditure of the Government as a
whole. The Minister of Labour will undoubtedly contemplate now the preparation
of the new Bill. We are glad to think that
he will have the advantage of the adjournment to think the matter over. I do hope
that he will not delay the introduction of the
Bill. I hope it will be introduced early, and
that the House will have ample opportunity
of examining it in detail, and eliminating
everything that is objectionable OT not
according to the interests of all concerned.
The early introduction of the Bill would not
mean its immediate application. It could be
held in suspense until the expiration of the
present Act. I hope the right hon. Gentleman
will find it expedient in the course of his
consideration to enlarge his sympathies with
respect to the claims of the industrial classes.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 13th April, 1922.
The House met at a quarter after Two of
the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
FIREARMS FOR "B" AND "C" CLASS
SPECIALS.
1. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister for
Home Affairs if he will state whether "B"
and "C" Class Specials are entitled to keep
firearms for their protection at home?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I would refer the hon.
Member to the Notice which has appeared
in the Public Press. The applications for
permits for this purpose should be addressed
to the County Commandant concerned.
FLAX PRODUCTION.
2. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Minister of
Agriculture if he can state the number of
tons of Flax produced in Ireland in the years
1920-21; if he can also state the number of
tons likely to be produced in the present year.
Also whether the Ministry has taken any
action to encourage the farmers to put in
more, in view of the certainty of a great
shortage?
The ASSISTANT PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Burn): I have been asked
to reply to this question on behalf of my
right hon. Friend. The number of tons of
flax produced in Ireland in 1920 was 17,020
and in 1921, 4,788 tons. It is not practicable
at this stage, when the seed has not yet been
sown, to estimate what weight of flax fibre
is likely to be produced from this year's crop.
There is no reason to anticipate that the
area under flax in the 1922 season will vary
to any great extent as compared with the
area in 1921. The Minister has had the
matter under consideration, but the question
of extending the area under flax depends
almost entirely on the factor of price, viz. :—
whether the farmer is satisfied that it will
be more remunerative for him to grow flax
instead of some other farm crop.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of that
question, might I ask the hon. Gentleman
if representations on this matter have been
made by the North of Ireland Spinners'
Association with respect to a great shortage
of raw material, and if he can say if they
anticipate a larger import from Russia than
has been the case for the past four or five
years?
Mr. BURN: I am unable to answer the
supplementary question put by my hon.
Friend (Mr. McGuffin) but I will have it
brought before the Minister of Agriculture.
ADJOURNMENT OF THE HOUSE
(EASTER).
Resolved: "That this House, at its rising
this day, do adjourn till Tuesday, May 16th,
provided always that if it appears to the
satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the Government, that the
public interest requires that the House
should meet at any earlier time during the
adjournment, Mr. Speaker may give notice
that he is so satisfied, and thereupon the
House shall meet at the time stated in such
notice, and shall transact its business as
if it had been duly adjourned till that
time." (Mr. Burn.)

Tuesday, 16th May, 1922.
The House met at Three of the clock, Mr.
Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
JOINT RAILWAY COMMISSION.
1. Mr. M'GUFFIN (by private notice)
asked the Prime Minister whether his attention has been called to a statement by Mr.
M'Grath, Minister of Labour (Provisional
Government), quoted in the local Press, to
the effect that he declines to consent to the
Joint Railway Commission, as agreed
upon with the Minister of Labour (Northern
Ireland), upon the ground that the London
Pact" has been broken by the Government
of Northern Ireland; whether a Joint Railway Commission was a part of the said Pact;
also whether he is aware that the Chairman
of the Commission appointed by the Minister of Labour (Southern Ireland), which is
sitting at present, has stated that the inquiry which he is conducting related to all
the railways in Ireland; whether any communication has passed between him and the
representatives of the Provisional Government with respect to this matter, and what
action he proposes to take in respect of this
effort to ignore the authority of the Northern Parliament?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James
Craig): The answer to the first part of the
question is in the affirmative. Notwithstanding that my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour, and Mr. M'Grath,
Minister of Labour in the Provisional Government, were for some time in complete
accord as regards all matters in connection
with the Joint Railway Commission, the
Provisional Government have refused to
honour the agreement arrived at last February between the two Ministers of Labour
and the representatives of the Railway Companies and the Trade Unions. As regards
the alleged reason for breaking this agreement, this Government has carried out the
London Pact, but I should point out that
the terms of that Pact have no connection
whatever with the agreement to set up a
Joint Railway Commission. The Chairman
of the Commission for Southern Ireland is
in complete error when he states that the
Southern Ireland Commission has any authority to deal with Railway matters in Northern Ireland. My right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour, is at present making
arrangements with the representatives of
the Railway Companies and the Trade
Unions to set up a Commission for Northern Ireland, and he hopes to be in a
position in a few days to announce its personnel and terms of reference.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Arising out of that

The Estimate differs from that
which was submitted to this Committee in
December last, as not only since then has the
transfer of the various offices to this Ministry
been very nearly completed, but, in the
working out of the details of the Government
of Ireland Act, certain other duties have
been undertaken which were not foreseen at
that time. Certain reciprocal arrangements
have been made between the Imperial Parliament and that of Northern Ireland
whereby each undertakes for the other certain duties where it has been found convenient and more economical so to do. This
has necessitated in some of the Departments
of our Ministry the engagement of a larger
staff than was at first contemplated, and, on
the other hand, has obviated the employment of certain other officials to do that
work which the Imperial Government now
carries on on agency terms for us.
I hope I may be pardoned if I remind
Members of the Committee of the various
duties of this Ministry, as they are more
varied and comprehensive than one would
usually associate with the term "Ministry
of Finance." They include not only
administrative, but also operative-or I
might almost call them productive
features. They were enumerated in the
"Belfast Gazette " of June 7th last,
and are shown in diagram form in the Official
Directory. The most important of these
duties is the supervision and control of all
financial matters, and of the operations of
the Government so far as they affect the
financial position. This consists not merely
of the direct official administration of
certain departments, but also involves the
control of the operations of other
Ministries. This Ministry has to regulate
the banking arrangements, issues from the
Consolidated Fund, and the personnel of the
Civil Service in all departments in its recruitment, general conditions of service,
such as salaries, hours of work, holidays,
sick leave, subsistence and travelling
allowances, so as to ensure uniformity of
terms throughout all the Ministries. Under
the heading of productive departments I
would include the revision of valuation of
all ratable tenements, the collection of land
purchase annuities, and the collection of the
revenues arising through estate duties,
stamps, licences and other provincial taxes
as these have to do with the basis or determining of the actual collection of revenue.
As regards the operative or routine section,
I would include in it the registration of
births, marriages, etc., the preparation and
supervision of general statistics, and the
maintenance and equipment of public buildings. In addition to these there are minor
services, such as the Ulster Savings Certifi-
To carry out the entire work of the
Ministry as at present constituted the
establishment that is considered necessary
is as shown in the Estimate, and amounts to
187 officials exclusive of Ministers. Now this
staff has been gathered to the extent of 83
by the transfer of existing Irish
officers under the Act. There have been 9
officers specially appointed, and 95 have been
recruited meanwhile as temporary clerks.
To classify this staff, professional, technical, and mechanical officials amount to 45.
These are shewn under Sub-head "A" in
the Estimate, and the description set against

telephonists, and charwomen amount to 37.
This number, I hope, will be capable of

accommodation can be found. This leaves .
altogether 105 who are engaged in the administrative and clerical work of the Ministry of Finance proper in all its branches.
As regards the particular duties on which
the various members of the staff are at present engaged, owing to the very varied nature
of the work requiring to be dealt with day
by day one could not definitely divide them
into compartments. Adaptability and

put; but a computation has been made of the

and a comparison made between such numbers and the number of staff engaged previously either in Dublin or in London on
purely Irish work. On a population basis
the proportion or percentage of the staff in

£29,500, and if you deduct from that the fall

the case, and not to state anything more
favourable than that to which we consider

And now to touch upon some matters
which are of general interest, and affect

candidates from a very large number of local
men who had offered for service under the
Northern Government, and in making this
selection preference has been given to exservice men, special regard having been
given to their military record, their educational attainments, and any special qualifications they may have had for the post
to which they might be appointed.
This Committee has already held upwards
of 25 meetings, and has approved of 130
temporary clerical appointments, 70 typists,
2 telephonists, 3 typist-telephonists, and 40
messengers. All these appointments in the
meantime are of a temporary character, but
from now on-now that the supply of transferred officers from Dublin has practically
terminated-definite appointments will come
to be made gradually out of this number,
and out of a still further number to be
recruited.

CLASS I.-No. 6.-STATIONERY AND
PRINTING.
Motion made and Question proposed:
That a sum not exceeding £1,650 be granted
to His Majesty for the service of the period
ending 31st March, 1923, to defray the expenses of providing stationery and printing,
paper, binding, books and office supplies for
the public services and for the Houses of
Parliament and for the production of the
"Belfast Gazette."

Mr. BARBOUR: I beg to move. It will be
seen that the net amount of the Vote required for this is £2.250. The gross total is
£23,175, and the amount £20,925, the
difference between the gross and net, represents the recovery to be made from the various Departments for printing. Hon. Members will understand that this particular
account shows the entire expenditure on
stationery and printing incurred by the various Ministries, each Ministry or Department
being charged with its appropriate share, and
then the charge to that Department is set
out under receipts appropriated in aid."
In the main, this represents the expenditure
on printing and stationery with the exception of a sum of £1,000, which represents
stock on hand at the end of the year which
has not yet been appropriated to any Department. The sum of £550 is set out as being
the loss on the "Belfast Gazette," but I am
very pleased to be able to state that since
drawing up this Estimate there is reason to
believe that the receipts from the sale of the
'Belfast Gazette" will go very much further towards paying the cost than was anticipated at the time the Estimate was drawn
up.
Then there are other statutory publications, the loss on which is estimated at close
on £700, but these returns have to be prepared and have to be available for the public,
and maybe in due time the receipts will go
further towards reducing the expenditure.
As regards our stationery and printing we
have come to the conclusion that the most
economical way of supplying ourselves is to
rely on His Majesty's Stationery Department
in London. We get the benefit of all the contracts they place over there. They place the
orders for local requirements locally, and

stuff. This arrangement should work out
economically and satisfactorily.

Mr. COOTE: I should like to ask a few

F there is to be a small grant made for the

Are workhouse teachers not under the category of teachers treated under the National
scheme?
Mr. MEGAW: It is a purely speculative
grant. There have been no applications made
up to the present, and this is a purely
nominal sum.
Mr. COOTE: Then why put it in? Is it
not a temptation to put in a little sum of
money that someone may nibble at, because
they will find it out, and these are not the
days when we should tempt people with regard to expenditure. Under the heading of
"Grants payable to Local Authorities to meet
charges on Loans," I should like to ask the
hon. Gentleman if the new Local Government
Board of Northern Ireland is keeping its eye
upon the amounts that should be transmitted
to us from the late Local Government Board
of Ireland in respect of the unexpended
portion of the money granted by the
Imperial Parliament under the Labourers
Acts for the erection of houses, and the granting of certain land to soldiers and sailors
There is an unexpended portion which we
ought to enjoy in the North of Ireland, and I
believe there is a time limit within which
if we do not receive this money, we shall lose
it altogether. To me it is a very important
matter because there are many soldiers and
sailors who are most anxious to have homes
built for them, and they feel that this grant
may be filched away from this portion of Ireland by another part, or may be left in the
British Exchequer. I am sure I am
voicing the feelings of the Members
of this Committee when I congratulate
the Ministry on the decision taken
by the Local Government Board not
to subsidise the building of new houses.
Surely we have come to the time when the
country can do its own work in this respect
and when we should not call upon the taxpayer to build houses for other people. But
there is a larger question involved. The
hon. Gentleman commenced his statement by
saying that he did not introduce any revolutionary measure, and we congratulate him
on avoiding such a thing. When we consider
that for a number of years the Local Government Board of Ireland has been introducing
revolutionary and senseless measures that
were very extravagant, we should hope that
the Local Government Board of Northern
Ireland will go closely into these matters,
and particularly the Health schemes. In
connection with Tuberculosis you have a
grant of 50 per cent. of the net approved
expenditure incurred by Insurance Committees of County Councils. We who serve
on Committees of County Councils are made
to realise that this is very largely a waste of
money, because there is no complete scheme
to combat tuberculosis. You erect a sanatorium and you bring your patients in, but
when they get so far advanced as to be incurable they are sent back to their homes
just when they are spreading the disease
more than they were in its early stages. As
the scheme at present exists it is a great
waste of money. We believe you can have a
more efficient system with greater economy,
and the same applies to other of the Local
Government Board schemes. We do hope
that when the Minister gets settled in his
office he will apply that Northern economical
and practical mind of his to bringing in such
reforms in our Local Government system as
will make his name and his term of office
memorable. He has a great field before him,
and if he uses his opportunities he can not
only curtail needless expenditure but secure
greater efficiency.
There is another matter with regard to the
grants to hospitals. Here, again, I think the
Minister will admit there is room for reform.
You are subsidising Workhouse Hospitals,
and the rates of the various counties are sub
sidising County Hospitals, and the whole
system is a source of expenditure which is
very largely wasted. Our people who are not
compelled to go into the workhouse will not
avail themselves of the workhouse hospital,
and we have to keep large staffs to comply
with the rules of the Local Government
Board. We should like you to inform the
Local Government Board that the people are
getting tired of these sources of taxation by
which expenditure is going on without efficiency being secured. While we do not wish
to challenge any Vote at the very inception
of the work of the Local Government Board
of Northern Ireland, and while we congratulate the Minister on keeping the expenditure
at the level at which it is, we do hope that
when he comes to perfect his organisation
and to consider in what way he can improve
the Local Government of Northern Ireland,
he will pay some attention to these matters,
which are being very much discussed by
people outside.

we do not blame him for the condition in

formerly costing £1,600 were built for £900
by subsidy. I regret the discontinuance of
the subsidy, and that it will not apply to the
forthcoming year. It is one of those things
upon which perhaps there might be
diversity of opinion, but my own view is
that it has been an advantage, and that if it
were continued until housing accommodation
had become more adequate in the city, it
would be to the advantage of the industrial
classes at least. That is all I have to say
with respect to this matter. I look upon it as
a very important estimate. There are other
matters one would care to refer to, but as
they are not of a
very objectionable
character, I content myself with simply
offering this short criticism.
Dr. MORRISON: I desire to say a word or
two with regard to this very important
matter, the treatment of tuberculosis, and at
the beginning I would like to refer to what
the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford)
has said with regard to it. I have a good
deal of experience of tuberculosis, of the
difficulty in dealing with it, and of the
methods that have been taken to deal with it.
There are goodnatured men, whose hearts
are filled with kindly impulses, who think
that if they spend money they are doing good
and are providing a remedy. That is a fatal
mistake. I think that you are only doing an
injury. You may have kind-hearted men who
subscribe here and there, and they are
encouraging idleness, and waste, and improvidence. Often some well-meaning men
by spending public money in this fashion are
demoralising and injuring the cause of reform. I think that is the attitude of men like
the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford)
I do not say it in any offensive way.
In County Antrim you have a very active
County Tuberculosis Committee. I do not
know the exact amount of money they spend
on it, but they do their work in a most efficient fashion, and if the County Antrim
people were working on a system that could
do anything more or give more to the tuberculous people, I believe they would have done
it. They have gone about their work in a
most systematic and practical fashion, and
they have intelligence for carrying out any
work. I give them credit for all that. But
I say, and experience will tell any man who
knows what this institution means, that they
are attempting the impossible. By the
methods by which they are working in County
Antrim they will not stamp out tuberculosis
till the crack of doom. We have in County
Derry practically no scheme, and if you take
up the returns from which the hou. Member
quoted, and which I got from the Registrar-
General through our own Home Office with
the object of educating the people as to the
danger of this and as to the folly of our present methods, you will find that in County
Antrim, where they have an elaborate, wellworked scheme, they have no better results
than in County Derry, where they have practically no scheme. I think that is conclusive. What is happening in County Antrim
is happening all over Ulster, and it is this:
You have consumption produced by a
microbe, and no man is attacking the microbe

which is causing the whole trouble. He is

So you have an endless chain going round

We hear a large amount of talk about

It is an
object lesson of what is going on in the

what little practical common sense I had I

under the headings of travelling expenses
and loss of remunerative time amounted to
far more than what the doctors got for working the Act.

That is the system. I may be liable to be

This part is dealt with by one Department,

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 17th May, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker in the chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
EXTENSION OF CURFEW.
1. Mr. GRANT (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
inform the House why Curfew has been
altered to 10 p.m. over the entire City, whilst
disturbances are confined to small areas?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The disturbed state of the
City demands that during non-Curfew hours
the number of police on duty shall be greatly
in excess of normal. It is, therefore, necessary
to restrict free movement of the populace
earlier to enable the police to obtain adequate
rest. At present strength the police are
working at an average of twelve hours per
day. Owing to disbandment of the R.I.C.,
which is now taking place, the number of
trained police in Belfast is being, and will
still further be, materially reduced.
Mr. GRANT:-Arising out of that answer,
I would like to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs if he considers that men who are
engaged at their work during the day, and
have agreed to the Summer-time Act for the
benefit of the extra hour of light, and are
devoting that hour to working in their plots
in different parts of the City and suburbs,
should be punished by this particular Order,
which is unfair to those who are law-abiding
citizens?
Mr. DONALD: The Minister of Home
Affairs says that the Royal Irish Constabulary
are overworked. May I ask my right hon.
Friend if he will take into consideration the
advisability of enrolling "B" Specials, who
will be delighted to give their services free
for this particular work?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Unfortunately, as
I explained in my answer to the hon. Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Grant), the "B"
men are not trained men in the sense that
the Royal Irish Constabulary are.
Mr. TWADDELL: Arising out of the
answer of the Minister of Home Affairs, has
he taken into consideration the fact that all
these outrages which have been committed
have been perpetrated during the daytime?
For instance, the robbery of the bank on the
Falls Road, the shooting at Corporation
workmen on Saturday morning from the
tower of the Roman Catholic Chapel at the
head of the Falls Road-
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member cannot
do more than ask one specific question. I
think it is very likely that this matter may
be discussed later, but we cannot enter into
a debate on it now.
Mr. LYNN: Arising out of the answer of
the Minister of Home Affairs, may I ask him
whether he has considered the advisability of
applying this extended Curfew simply to the
districts in which disorders are taking place?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That has already
been done in the case of the Marrowbone and
Ardoyne areas, where Curfew operates at
Nine o'clock. Unfortunately, with the
number of police at our disposal we cannot
do that all over the city. The police are
overworked at the present time, and must
have rest.
Mr. LYNN: In view of the unsatisfactory
replies of the Minister of Home Affairs I
beg to give notice that I shall raise the whole
question on the adjournment.
OBSERVANCE OF EMPIRE DAY.
2. Mr. DONALD (by private notice) asked
the Prime Minister whether any scheme for
the observance of Empire Day has been
arranged. If so, whether an arrangement is
being made with the local authorities for a
general observance, also an arrangement with
State-provided schools in Northern Ireland.
and the hoisting of the Union Jack on all
public buildings.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Prime Minister
has asked me to reply to this question. The
attention of local authorities is being drawn
by circular to the question of the observance
of Empire Day, and it is hoped they may be
able to give the matter every consideration.
As regards schools, I understand that the
Minister of Education has only power to enforce a holiday upon those schools directly
under the management of the Ministry,
namely, the Model Schools. He can only
proceed in regard to other schools by request
that a holiday be observed and by giving his
sanction that the holiday taken shall not be
included in the normal school vacation which
is limited to 40 school days. In this connection a notification is being inserted in the
Press by the Ministry of Education to-day.
The Union Jack will be hoisted on
Government buildings on Empire Day.

CLASS II. No. 4.
I. PRISONS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding Fifty-five
thousand six hundred and sixty-two
pounds be granted to His Majesty for the
service of the period ending 31st March,
1923, to defray the expenses of Prisons."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This is an estimate
for the cost of the prisons in Northern Ireland, of which there are only three-Belfast,
Londonderry and Armagh, the last-named
being used for female prisoners only. These
prisons were handed over to the Northern
Government in a very poor condition.
Belfast and Derry, as you are aware, had
suffered severely from the damage done by
Sinn Feiners, while none of the three
prisons are at all up to modern requirements
The Imperial Government, which spent
large sums on bringing the Scotch prisons
up-to-date, spent nothing on the Irish
prisons, most of which, according to the
Royal Commission of 1884, were of an antiquated type devised for an obsolete system of
discipline. This affects all Irish prisons, but
a point which affects us particularly is the
fact that the stocks of requisites in these
prisons, such as clothing, bedding, etc., had
fallen to a very low level, so that this
Government has to incur extra expenses in
bringing the stocks up again to their proper
level. As regards the staff of the prisons, we
were placed in a difficult position owing to
the serious illness of the Governors of both
Belfast and Derry Prisons. Their duties
have been discharged by two officers of the
Special Constabulary with marked efficiency,
and I must express my gratitude to these
officers for the admirable way in which they
have carried out the task imposed on them.
The staff generally have had a heavy task,
but I trust the decision to revert to ordinary
prison discipline will remove many of the
difficulties which have thrown an increased
burden on the staff. I may say that this
decision applies to all prisoners committed
after the 31st March, without distinction of
creed or class.
II
Prisons.

Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
As will be seen, nearly half the estimated
cost of the prisons goes in pay and allowances. The rates of pay were fixed before we
took over control and were assimilated in
1920 to those of the English prison service.
The staff cannot be considered excessive, as
the number of prisoners in custody has
increased considerably, owing to the activity
of the police. Since the 1st December, over
1,900 prisoners have been committed to
Belfast Prison alone. As regards victualling,
the average cost at Belfast and Derry is £18
per head, practically 1s. a day, which, I
think, is very moderate, having regard to the
dietary allowed. The provision for clothing,
etc., is increased to some extent by the
renewals rendered necessary by the malicious
destruction of property by Sinn Fein prisoners.
The sub-head dealing with repairs and new
buildings, etc., are also increased by the
amounts necessary to repair damage done by
Sinn Fein prisoners. I am referring to the
time prior to the period we took over.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Is the Imperial Parliament responsible for any portion of that?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would like to consult the Minister of Finance in regard to
that matter. I certainly hope we will get
something from them. One wing in the
Beifast jail, which was completely wrecked,
has been completely restored, and I think at
an extremely moderate cost. It was done
by prison labour under the supervision of
artisan warders. Owing to the fact that
there is no convict prison in Northern Ireland, and no Borstal Institute, it has become
necessary to arrange to send a certain number of convicts and Borstal inmates to
Scotland and England respectively, and this
accounts for part of the amount shown
under the head of escort and conveyance and
for the cost of maintenance of prisoners in
other countries. Although the conveyance of
these prisoners throws a small extra cost
on this Government, the arrangement is on
the whole economical, and has given us time
to consider what can be done to provide a
convict prison and Borstal Institution. As a
matter of fact, the maintenance of a convict
in the Scotch Convict Prisons is very much
less than the cost of a convict in the South
of Ireland prisons. I think the cost in
Scotland is something like one-half the cost
of the maintenance of a convict in Southern
Ireland.
I would like to add that officials of this
Department have visited England and Scotland, and discussed the question of prison
accommodation with the English and Scottish
Prison Commissioners, to whom I am much
indebted for the help which they have already
given us, and for the assistance promised.
We have to consider the provision of a Convict Prison, a Borstal Institution, a place of
Preventive Detention, an Inebriate Reformatory, and a Central Criminal Lunatic
Asylum. At the present time criminal
lunatics have to be sent to Dundrum, in
County Dublin; but these questions are being
very carefully gone into. I referred before
to the fact that our prisons are very much
out of date, and I would like to see them
more up to date.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: More comfortable?
a
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
may disagree with me, but I am most anxious
be
that while imprisonment should
deterrent to the wrongdoer, the importance
of its reformative side should not be lost
sight of. Since this Government took over
the jails we tried to restore prison discipline,
with, I may say, a great deal of success. I
am glad to say that practically all the
prisoners in the jails are now working. I

Motion made and Question proposed:
That a sum not exceeding £1,249,812 be
granted to his Majesty for the service of

I
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
M'Keown): I desire to remind hon. Members
that, notwithstanding the fact that the
educational services are entirely under the
control of the Northern Administration, the
various systems under which these services
are administered are the same as when the
Estimates were previously before this House.
This will continue until a measure of reform
is presented to and approved by this House.
The Advisory Committee, under the excellent
chairmanship of the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Lynn), is working hard, and it
is expected that an interim report will ere
long be presented. We intend immediately
to apply ourselves in an earnest way
to that valuable report, and we hope that
measure of reform can be presented to
this House not later than the autumn of the
present year. It is not my intention, therefore, to go into the details, but to try to
bring as clearly as I possibly can before the
Committee the more important matters in
connection with the administration.
would like to tell hon. Members that the
Estimate of the salary charges for the year
1921-1922 of the administrative and inspection
staffs for the whole of Ireland was £190,566.
Our Estimate just now before the House is
for 28 per cent. of this amount. It is, therefore, a fact that under the Northern
administration the cost of the service is
actually less than if this Service had
continued to be administered from Dublin.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is also well
for hon. Members to bear in mind that the
administration has no assistance from local
School Boards, as in the case of England and
Scotland, but has to do all the details of the
work of administration, inclusive of the
payment of the salaries of individual
teachers. From statements recently made it
would appear in England and Wales that
of the total amount provided from the
Parliamentary grant and local rates only
14/- in the pound actually goes to the payment of the teachers, and the remaining 6/-
goes to administrative charges, such
as

training colleges, etc. Of the entire vote
now before the House, 18/- in every pound
will go to the payment of teachers in Northern Ireland, and if we exclude Queen's
University the cost of the administration in
Northern Ireland is something less than 11d.
in each pound.
Coming now to the sub-heads under une
vote, I desire to draw the special attention
of hon. Members to the vote for training
colleges. In all Ireland there are 7 training
colleges. Only one of these St. Mary's,
Belfast-is in Northern Ireland. The total
estimated grant for the whole of Ireland is
£104,000, and if this is shared between
Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland in
proportion to the number of teachers in
each, £32,600 would be our share, and that
is inserted in the Estimate. I regret, however, to have to inform the Committee that
when we approached the Provisional Government so that we might co-operate with them
in the Easter examination for monitors,
pupil teachers, and candidates for admission
to these training colleges our representations
were more or less ignored. Moreover, in
regard to the course of training at the
colleges, the Provisional Government, without
any reference to the Government of Northern
Ireland, decided to alter existing arrangements, and to hold the students' examinations
at the colleges a month earlier than usual,
so that the pupils could have the last month
of the session to devote to the study of the
Irish language, literature and literary history. Hon. Members will readily realise
that we could not fall in with such a proceeding as that. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We thought such action was unfair,
and I am sure that in the public estimation
it will be considered unfair. We, therefore,
had no alternative but to make independent
plans. I would like just now to remind hon.
Members that although in the Estimates
before the House there is a provision for
the post of Organiser of Irish Language in
Northern Ireland, that post is now vacant,
and it is not the intention of the Ministry
to fill it at present. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We hope to be able to get the
necessary work done by one of our inspectors.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Would the hon. Gentleman (Mr. M'Keown) say what substitute he
has made for training colleges, and where
teachers are being trained at the moment?
Mr. M'KEOWN: If the hon. Member will
allow me I am just coming to that.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: I am sorry.
Mr. M'KEOWN: It was stated by the
Provisional Government that this month for
the study of the Irish language would be
welcomed by the students throughout the
whole of Ireland. I think, to put it mildly,
that may be considered a misrepresentation
of the facts. We held successfully our own
Easter examinations (hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and now the question of making provision for the training of candidates is very
acute. It is, as a matter of fact, necessary
to make independent arrangements, and I
can assure hon. Members that arrangements
will be made for the training of teachers
in Northern Ireland, and they will come
into operation not later than the beginning
of the session in September of this year.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Will that be in Belfast?
Mr. M'KEOWN: In Belfast. I am happy to
be able to inform hon. Members, that we have
hopes that a grant will be made by the Imperial Exchequer in aid of the capital expenditure and equipment of a training college.
I now come to the question of the salaries of
national school teachers, which absorb such a
very large sum. Hon. Members are aware
that in November, 1920, an agreement was
come to between the Treasury officials, the
Commissioners of National Education, and
the teachers, whereby improved scales of
salaries and capitation grants were fixed.
The last instalment under the arrangement
came into force on 1st April of this year, and
it means an advance of the salaries of the
teachers of £170,000 over the preceding year.
It is interesting, and hon. Members should
know that the average income of teachers
from State sources in Northern Ireland now
stands as follows:
For men teachers, £354;
Women teachers, including
£266;
principals,
Junior assistant mistresses. £134.
It is difficult to compare these salaries with
the salaries of teachers in England and Scotland, but I think it may be assumed that the
salaries paid here are not inferior to those
paid in England and Scotland. One thing
which it is necessary to point out is that the
salaries here are subject to deduction for
superannuation, which is not the case, as
hon. Members know, in England and in
Scotland.
Mr. McGUFFIN; It was very nearly being
the case.
Mr. McKEOWN: We heard something of
that last night. The whole question of the
salaries of teachers in Northern Ireland will,
at some time, receive the earnest consideration of the House, as also the desirability of
maintaining them at their present level, and
increasing the standard of efficiency of the
teachers. We also hope to save money in our
administration at the same time through the
amalgamation of schools and in other ways.
I come now to the question of intermediate
education, and I would touch upon it shortly.

The grants are the same as formerly, with
the exception of the interim grant, which is
now £24,000 as against £12,000 when we took
control. The £18,000 appearing in the Esti
mates is accounted for in the note which is
attached to this particular Estimate. I may
point out that the various grants will, in all
probability, be administered as they have
been previously administered with the exception of the interim grant. We have made
an effort to make the application of this grant
fairer to the teachers, and, as a matter of
fact, it is well known that it was devised for
the teachers. Forms were sent to all schools
throughout Northern Ireland, and these were
to be filled in giving what was in the opinion
of the Administration necessary information.
Acting on that information we are adopting
what we believe will be an improved method
in the administration of this interim grant,
which, as I said, will make it fairer to the
teachers concerned. This grant was formerly
paid in one sum at the end of the session.
It is now hoped that the interim grant of
£6,000 will be paid at the end of the present
month, and that the balance-£12,000-will
be paid at the end of the session. We expected in the administration that we could
co-operate with Southern Ireland in the
intermediate examinations, but the same
thing occurred there as occurred in the case
of the Easter examinations. The Provisional
Government wished to give undue prominence to the Irish language in the Intermediate Examinations. This could not be
accepted by our Administration, and I am
glad to say, though it necessitated very considerable work, we will be able to hold our
own independent examinations in Northern
Ireland during the coming month. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
There is very little to be said at the
moment regarding technical instruction.
We inherit the rules and regulations of the
Department of Agriculture and Technical
Instruction, and the administration is being
carried out on the same lines. With regard
to the vote for the Queen's University, I
would remind hon. Members that under the
Irish Universities Act of 1908 £18,000 was
granted, though afterwards this sum was increased under the Government of Ireland
Act to £26,000. There is also £10,000 from
the Church Temporalities Fund, and this
amount will be paid into the Exchequer of
Northern Ireland.
I have tried in a very simple way to bring
what I consider the important matters regarding our Administration before the hon.
Members. I should like to say before
sitting down that we are very fortunate in
having a very valuable Permanent Secretary,
and also that the principal permanent
officials of the Administration are giving

Mr. LYNN: I do not intend to occupy the
House for more than a few minutes, and I am
certainly not going to introduce into any remarks make any of the heat that unundoubtedly exists outside. I want in the
first place to draw the attention of the
Minister of Home Affairs to the Curfew
Order, which I understand comes into operation to-day, altering the hours from eleven to
ten o'clock, and from five to six o'clock. J
am sure there is no Member of this House
and there is no law-abiding citizen in this
City or in this Province who is not prepared
to make any reasonable sacrifice that may
be necessary in the re-establishment of law
and order. but when we see Orders made that
can have no effect whatever except to penalise
the law-abiding and the law-respecting
citizens, we want to enter at least a mild protest. I for one fail to see any advantage that
the city is going to gain from the peace point
of view by reducing the hour from eleven to
ten o'clock. Remember, when you do that
we are one and a half hours ahead of the sun,
and you are going to cut off a very good fart
of the evening for the people. You are
going to inflict a serious hardship
small shopkeepers, especially
Saturday evening, and you are going to
inflict a hardship on the people who live a
long way from what we may call the plague
spots of the city, spots where there has been
disorder and murder and trouble.

on
a
It would be very interesting if the Minister
of Home Affairs were to provide the House
with a chart showing the hours when the different crimes have been committed in this
city since he took charge of affairs in
November. I think he would discover that
even the ordinary Curfew has not been of
much avail. A great many of the murders
took place during the Curfew hours. A good
deal of the disorder has taken place during
Curfew, and a great many other murders
took place early in the afternoon, and some
in the morning. I have the gravest possible
doubt as to the benefit the city is going to
get from Curfew. Perhaps my right hon.
Friend will be able to convince me I am
wrong, but I am afraid he will have trouble
in convincing the vast majority of the
citizens. We want to help. There is no

Sir DAWSON BATES: May I say in the
first place how much I appreciate the
temperate way in which the case has been
put before the House. With regard to this
recent Curfew Order I say at once that there
appears to be a great deal of misunderstanding. Sometimes, as in the case of Ardoyne
and the Marrowbone, which have been referred to, it has been found necessary not
alone to put on a very close Curfew, up to
nine o'clock in the evening, but also to surround these areas and restrict the movements
of people going in and out. That has been
found very satisfactory in regard to that
particular quarter. But to do that takes a
very large number of men. The general
men.
system of Curfew for the whole city, which
is taken exception to by this House, is not put
into operation for the purpose of penalising
the city. It is done because we have not got a
sufficient number of trained
Hon.
Members must surely be aware that the Royal
Irish Constabulary is in process of disbandment at the present time, and we never had
fewer trained policemen in the city than we
have to-day. To surround one of these bad
quarters takes a very large number of men.
People say, "Why is this Curfew put on?"
The effect of taking an hour off under the
Curfew is that you release 400 trained men
for the purpose of doing duty in the disturbed areas and of protecting the lives and
property of the people outside the peaceful
areas.
This Curfew was not put on in a lighthearted way as some of the hon. Members
have suggested. It was done on the advice
of our military adviser, General Solly Flood.
General Solly Flood is entirely in control of
all the forces which are at the disposal of
this Government, and so long as I am in the
position which I occupy, I am not prepared
to disregard the advice tendered by
General Solly Flood, and from what
I know I can say that the General would not
remain here a day if the advice
which he tendered were not carried out.
But I will say this, that there is no one who
realises the difficulty and hardship which
this Order imposes, especially on the working classes, more than General Solly Flood,
and I can assure this House, speaking on his
behalf, that this Order will be removed at
the earliest moment. I would appeal to my
hon. Friend, the Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Grant) to have a little patience until we
see if this matter can be approved of, but for
the moment this Order will have to remain.
The hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn)
referred to recent Orders which were made, as
he suggested, for window-dressing. No Order
that has been issued from the Home Office
has been issued for the purpose of windowdressing. He referred, I think, to the recent
Order under which a man must sleep in his
own house. Anyone who has studied the disorders that have taken place must realise
that no outrage is committed in the district
. in which the man lives, and it is for the purpose of restricting the movements of these
outlaws that this particular Order
issued. I can assure this House that the

licensed premises, except between the hours

Sir DAWSON BATES: That may come yet.
I can assure this House that if the Government think it necessary to do so they will
not hesitate to do so. With regard to the
question of the firearms permit, this Government went into the whole matter very carefully, and acting on the advice of Field-
Marshal Sir Henry Wilson and General Solly
Flood they decided to restrict the issue of
permits to hold or keep firearms to members
of the Special Constabulary. There are two
reasons why this arrangement was arrived
at. First, to ensure that no one who was not
a loyal citizen in the Province should have
firearms. Secondly, we felt that it was not
too much to ask any citizen to come forward
and enrol himself in some branch of the
Special Constabulary, no matter in what
category that might be. To meet the cases
which, I think, were referred to by my hon.
Friend, the Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Twaddell), we introduced a special category
to provide for old men and invalids.

Sir DAWSON BATES: No, they are not.
If a crisis comes in the history of this Province, as it is coming-it is perhaps closer
than some of the Members of this House
realise we expect everybody, whether he is
delicate or not, to come forward and help the
Special Constabulary in some form. I resent
the suggestion and the sneer that because a
man is delicate or is an invalid he is unable
to help this Province.

I wanted to know what their status was.

Mr. McGUFFIN: I am obliged to the right
hon. Gentleman for saying so, because I
would not like to be misrepresented before
the public in such a way. I did not intend
it as a sneer, but if there were honorary
members of the Constabulary I wanted to
know if they would be called upon to serve.
In the case of an active member I know
what the position is. My hon. Friend the
Member for Queen's University (Dr. Morrison) hopes to be able to join, but believes
he is an invalid at the moment. I cannot
see in what capacity he can serve, but he
hopes to comply with the condition that
will make it possible for him to hold firearms. With regard to the general question,
I would like to remind the right hon. Gentleman that grave criticism is being directed
against his Department on the ground that
he is taking measures to prevent the coming
into the city of firearms. Pickets are posted
at the suburbs, and I was held up myself
on Saturday evening, and saw civilians held
up, in regard to firearms. It is quite right
that that should be done, but it is being
done too late. Unfortunately, the city is
stocked with arms now. After this remissness on the part of the authorities people
are entitled to cavil to some extent, for these
are rather serious restrictions that are being
put upon their liberty. On the whole I would
say in regard to the Curfew that I think it is
necessary. I am sorry that the restriction
is being imposed, but I would suggest to
my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
that it should be confined to the districts
affected rather than to the entire city. That
would be much more beneficial and much
more to the point. I would ask the right
hon. Gentleman to bring this matter to the
notice of the Military Adviser, and ask him
if the restrictions would not have more
effect if applied to the disturbed districts
rather than to the entire city.
Question: 'That this House do now adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Twenty
minutes before Six o'clock.
