able to do so.
The object of the Regulation is a simple
one. It is an automatic test, first, whether
the man is on the side of law and order,
and secondly, whether he is willing in so
far as in him lies, to give active assistance
in restoring law and order.
While there may be many cases in which
the individual may not, owing to his
physical condition, or, in limited and
exceptional circumstances, the condition of
his employment, be able to undertake
active duty on the streets or in the country,
the time may come when the whole manhood of Ulster may have to be mobilised,
and we will need men in different
capacities. If we have a record of these
men it will be of invaluable assistance to
us.
We cannot and will not allow exceptions.
I assure the House that if we once allow an
exception in one single case, it opens the
door to others, and the regulation will break
down. Naturally no one will be asked to
undertake any duty beyond his physical
powers but, under the guidance of the most
expert soldier in our country, we are most
anxious to make our provisions so clear that
they can be understood by the whole public,
and the whole public must back us up in
what is considered necessary for the safety
of our Province. I might just say with regard to the question of this particular force—
and it refers also to the "A" and "B" classthat General Solly-Flood is very anxious to
get as many willing young officers as possible,
and he has asked me specially to use my
position in this House to-day to appeal to
Belfast and the Six Counties to help him in
every way they can. There are numerous
young people about who in the ordinary
course if a call is made to them in the
interests of their province will come forward
and lead, as they did when officers in the
army, the men who in their own neighbourhoods are taking such risks and responsibilities. I do hope that all to whom my
words penetrate will recognise that Ulster is
making her preparations now-not in any
provocative spirit, but simply because of the
necessities of the case-to defend herself, and
we want stout hearts and the youth of Ulster
as we required them in 1914 for a similar

the gallant General in the onerous task that
he has before him.
Well, then we come to the delicate question
of how are you ever going to carry on such an
enormous force with the limited resources
which Ulster possesses. That is a point that
was raised a few days ago. I was busy negotiating with the British Government on the
subject at the time and I wished as little said
about it as possible. However the view that
I take is a very simple one. Ulster fought all
her days to remain part of the British Empire,
under one Parliament, one Flag and one King.
The Parliament of Great Britain came to us
and said-we will not go into the reasons-the
Government came to us and said:
Will you
help Great Britain and the British Empire,
take a Parliament of your own to manage
your own affairs to a limited extent?" and they
brought forward the 1920 Act. We took that
Act as an Act which was balanced by having.
half of it delegated to the South and West.
And when we took the Act the South and
West were to function exactly as we were to
function and to have their Parliament, and

there were two reasons for irritation and for

was reflected in an even more intensified

the other the country depending upon

I was somewhat hurt-I use the word deliberately-because I was hurt at the large
number of protests that were poured in upon
me and upon Members of the Government
on the subject of the Curfew. I know well
all the difficulties that the people of Belfast
suffer under at the moment. No one knows
better. But again I say, take the wide view.
Our Specials are overworked in many instances, our Police are overworked. There is
no doubt that when Curfew falls it enables
the police authorities and the military authorities to deal with outbreaks very much
better than when the streets are thronged
with the passing population. I do hope that
the public will not think that the Curfew
or the other regulations which may be necessitated by the case later on are put on in a
vindictive way or because somebody thinks
it would be a good thing to do. All these
questions are threshed cut by us here, by all
of us, and we consider what is the best thing
to do under the serious circumstances. We
have often information in our possession
which is not in the possession of the public.
I would have the public understand that my
right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates), on
whom so much of this business falls, is in
the position towards this Government that
the Chief Secretary used to be in with regard
to the Irish Government, and that is that
the blame for everything falls upon the
shoulders of my right hon. Friend. I should
like to clear one point straight away, and
that is if there is any praise or any odium
to be poured out upon, or borne by, anybody
it is shared equally by all my colleagues.
There is no such thing as this being a oneman Government. This is a Government of
all the people here whom you see in front of
you, all of whom take equal responsibility,
and all of whom are moved by only one desire to carry out the Government to the very
best of our ability in the interests, not of one
section or another, but in the interests of
the peace and prosperity of our country.
And therefore I do hope that my right hon.
Friend, who has such a terrible burden to
bear at the moment, who has awful decisions
to take, and difficult problems to solve, will
be backed up by the people of Belfast, that
they will rally round him, that they will
come to him and say: What can I do to
help?" and not ask why some Special was
moved from one district to another, and
things like that? Those are the kind of
things which, in my opinion, spread through
the city and cause disaffection, and I
say that there has been no time in the
history of Ulster when, not one man, but the
whole of the Government requires so much the
rallying of you who represent your constituencies and the people themselves to help us
through unparalleled difficulties which would
crush many a stout heart. They will never
crush ours-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)—we
will carry through all right, but we require,
and we demand, the help of every person who
wishes to see this Parliament hold out against
the enemies in our midst.
I have very little more to say. Some critics
may point out that I might have said much
of this before. It was impossible. There are
certain things which one dare not give away
to one's opponents. There are certain things
which may make us dissatisfied with the
organisation to meet eventualities. I dared
not reveal our weakness. We are now
strong, and 1 have no hesitation in
revealing our strength. But there is a
reason for all these things, which I need not go
into, and I am quite sure that the Houseevery man in it-is at my back in desiring
that I should hold my tongue for the service
of Ulster and only speak when there is reason
and when it is necessary. I have mentioned
practically everything which I think is necessary to meet the future. I have no hesitation whatever in saying that we can meet
the future with calm hearts, clear consciences,
and strong right arms. I believe that the
organisation, at the end of which we have now
almost arrived, will be ready against any combination of circumstances, and that, with the
Boundary Commission off our minds and off
our shoulders, we can go forward to meet anything that may come against us.
"6
Before I close I would like to make comment on the fact that we had a great
many detractors over a year ago. Many
men told us, You will never establish
your Parliament "; and when it was
opened by His Majesty the King, the
same persons said, You will never be
able to carry on "; and when we carried'
on they said, "You will be swamped by the

and we will still remain here; and we simply
say to those, who hitherto have been such ill

prophets regarding the future of Ulster, that
we are prepared to go forward for another
year with the same confidence and the same
determination that those privileges, which
were given to us by the Imperial Parliament,
shall not be impaired, and that we shall
stand by the trust which was imposed upon
us by our people. That has only been made

themselves. They have been splendid. They
have been grand. They have stuck by us.
Crisis after crisis has occurred, and they
have come along and surmounted them, and
placed us in the position of being able to
hold up our heads among the Parliaments of
the world. Not only have the people been
splendid, but they have been generous in
overlooking the shortcomings of the Prime
Minister and his colleagues who sit upon this
bench. I have always invited discussion, and
I have always invited criticism in this
House. I think it would be fatal for this
House either that we should become a
mutual admiration society, or that the public
opinion outside should not be allowed to
penetrate inside our walls, or that hon. Members should not be allowed to tell us exactly
what is happening outside.
I
The next point I want to deal with is that
wish to pay a special tribute
to the magnificent bearing of those
who have taken up arms on our behalf. I
hope the people will realise that those men
have taken up arms on behalf of each individual in the whole community. Especially
would I like to pay a very great tribute to
those who were so sorely pressed in the attacks recently made, especially in the two
instances of Castlewellan and Martinstown.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) A few years
ago if seven or eight barracks had been attacked I almost venture to say that fifty
per cent. of them would have been surrendered and would have fallen to the enemy.
The other night these barracks were all attacked, and not one of them surrendered.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I say it is a
magnificent tribute to the stuff which we
have in our Special Constabulary. The story
of the defence at Martinstown is almost an
epic. I only gather up information like the
rest, but somebody told me that a little man
from the Shankill saved the situation. There
are plenty of men on the Shankill to save the
situation in other barracks, and in other
parts of the country, and in the city of Belfast-(Hon Members: Hear, hear)-and the
hearts of the men in other parts are just as
sound as those which beat on the Shankill.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is a pleasure to me, and to all of us, I am sure, to
think that when the Ulster people are asked
to do something, and to take responsibility
and to take risks, there is nothing that they
will not do. Their gallantry in the field
fighting the common enemy, or in little barracks isolated by so many miles from other
places, holding forth against long odds,
shows this. What is the spirit which does
it? It is the spirit which says there will be
no surrender to the traitors in our midst.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That is what
makes me perfectly confident that we will
carry through the future no matter what it
may hold for us.
My last word is to the House and to the
country. To-morrow will be Empire Day.
Let us celebrate Empire Day to-morrow as
we never celebrated before. Let every person who has the Union Jack or the Red,
White, and Blue, bring it out and fly it from
their windows, and let them show that, even
after all the attacks made on us, the blood

In time that our Minister of Home Affairs is

inen who support him we have most

The policy that the Prime Minister and his
Cabinet have adopted in the serious conditions in which we find ourselves is
suported by two main pillars. The first
pillar-and it led to misapprehensions, it led
to misconceptions, and it led to suspicionswas a desire on the part of the Prime
Minister to work in conjunction and in harmony with the British Government and the
British Cabinet. I think that is a policy that

clean honest government for every man who
was loyal and law-abiding. When you come

10 exception could be taken to them. I
would like to say a word or two with regard
to that in connection with the constituency
in which I have a post of considerable
importance that is, Londonderry. County
Derry has to face at the present time a bill
for something like £100,000 for malicious
injuries done in that county within very
recent weeks, because up till a very short
time ago Londonderry was one of the most
law-abiding counties in the Northern area.
In South Londonderry, in which I live, and
where I know a great many men of both

There have been, I think, 14 murders, and

men who admit to me that the policy on
which they are embarked in County Derry is
bound to be ruinous to the ratepayers and
ruinous to the prosperity of the country, if

come forward and help us we will be glad to
receive them and to try and produce such a

and discontent, and produce general
prosperity.
I think on the whole the people of Ulster
may face the future with an easy mind. In
my opinion-and I think it is the opinion of

raid to which we have been subjected has
done us more good than it has done us harm.
I remember long ago, when we were fighting
this great question, Ulster was the top dog.
We had no sympathy because we were
believed to be an ascendancy party. If anything, we are now the under dog, and I

I am glad that the Prime Minister was able
to make such a reassuring statement to us
to-day. I hope that in the near future the

prosperity will again shine upon our
province. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

Wednesday, 24th May, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker in the Chair.
THE BUDGET.
FINANCIAL STATEMENT, 1922-1923.
Motion made and Question proposed:
That this House approves the proposals of
the Government for meeting the financial
requirements of the year."

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am sure the House will join with
me in my feeling of regret that my right
hon. Friend the Prime Minister (Sir James
Craig) will not be able to be present at our
sittings to-day, owing to indisposition. I had
a telephone message from my right hon.
Friend's private secretary informing me that
he is laid aside with a very sharp attack of
laryngitis, and that the doctor absolutely
prohibits him from leaving the house or
taking part in any public proceedings. It is
an additional subject of regret, because I
know that my right hon. Friend was anxious
to be here and to join in the discussion on
the financial proposals. I have also been
charged by the Prime Minister with a message relating to the protection of the Province. I purport reading this message when
I reach the question of special expenditure
in the progress of my statement.
When the Prime Minister reminded us
yesterday in happy language that this was
Empire Day I could not avoid feeling that it
was a happy omen that the presentation of
the first Budget of Northern Ireland should
synchronise with the anniversary of that
fateful Empire Day a year ago when this
Parliament was elected and when Ulster
made such a resounding declaration both for
country and for Empire. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
When submitting the Vote on Account of
the cost of the services of the State for the
present year I expressed the hope that when
I presented the Budget I would be able to
report to the House with exactness the
financial result for the period which began
on the 22nd November, 1921, and ended on
the 31st March of the present year. This
was the first four months of our financial
control.
At that time I had no completed returns of
revenue, but I ventured to forecast that,
given certain normal receipts for the period
still to run, we should be able to close our
accounts with a surplus of 30/40,000. I purpose now to submit to the House a statement
as to how the accounts have actually worked
out.
The House will readily understand that it
is not an easy task to calculate the exact
amount of revenue attributable to Ulster,
in view of the fact that the taxes are
collected in Great Britain, in Southern Ireland as well as in our own territory. The
adjustments necessary to apportion our share
of these taxes are of a most complex and
delicate character, and in several matters
resort has to be had to a population basis of
distribution.
The Transferred Revenues collected by our
own Government offer no difficulty. In the
four months we received:

respect of other taxes such as Excise Duty on

And when we recall the fact that in addition to these overlappings the adjustments for
the period I am discussing are concerned with

it needs no colouring to visualise the complexities of the problem of allotting to Ulster
her proper share of the collected revenues.

Corporation Profits Tax;

Postal Services.

House of the methods of arrangement with

theory is that at the end of the year the Imperial Treasury gets together into one amount
all the taxes appertaining to Ulster, amounting as a fact to something like £12,000,000.
From this is deducted first the Contribution
that we make to the Imperial Services, the
Army, the Navy, and the Air Force; and,
second, the cost of the Services which they
operate, the collection of taxes, the cost of
the Judiciary, which is a reserved service,
and so on. The amount is then deducted
from the taxes collected, and the balance is
understood to come to us. But obviously that
operation is of no value whatever to us, because we must have money during the year to
pay for our liabilities as time passes, and so
the Imperial Authority arranged to pay us
sums of money monthly on account of the
estimated results which I have just indicated.
During the four months we received from
the Imperial Treasury a sum of £1,250,000 on
account of our share of the taxes collected
by Britain, after deducting the costs of collection, and our Imperial contribution, at
the rate of £7,920,000 per annum. When all
the accounts were made up it was found that
the Treasury had somewhat overpaid us,
arising, as was alleged, from the unsatisfactory payment of Income Tax in the
Province. In view, however, of the difficulty of disentangling the accounts and the
admitted fact that our contribution was too
high, the Treasury agreed that the amount
of £1,250,000, which we had received, should
stand as a settlement of our transactions
with the British Government up to the 31st
March.
I regard this arrangement as a fair and
generous one, in the circumstances. It will
save an enormous amount of trouble and
negotiation, and I cannot do less than acknowledge the excellent spirit in which the
Chancellor of the Exchequer has met us in
this matter.
Adding this agreed sum of £1,250,000 to
our own local collections of revenue, namely,
£755,159, we arrive at the total receipts on
revenue account for the four months of our
control of £2,005,159.
I have thus far dealt with revenue only,
and I ask the attention of the House for a
few moments to consider the expenditure side
of the account during the four months I
am discussing. It is unnecessary, as I think,
to occupy the time of the Committee in
detailing each item of departmental expenditure, but in order that Members may be
fully informed as to the disposition of our
State Funds, I have laid on the Table a
detailed statement of the total outlay on the
services of the State up to 31st March,
amounting to £1,940,439. If we deduct this
sum from the revenue side of the account,
So far as a calculation can be made for the
short period of our own State control which
I have just reviewed, our revenues have been
prejudiced to an even greater extent from
trade conditions analogous to those obtaining
in Great Britain, as well as from causes that
are purely local.
This affords eloquent proof of the lack of
foresight in determining our statutory obligation to Imperial services definitely for
practically three years ahead in the midst of
such startling and revolutionary economic
changes. Having regard, however, to the disturbed political conditions of the country,
and the general confusion, in the midst of
which our baby State was cradled, I feel that
I am not exceeding the limits of Parliamentary decorum in congratulating the House
and the Province on the outcome of our first
experiment in State finance. (Hon. Members: "Hear, hear.")
With the single exception of the Special
Force necessary to preserve the safety of the
State, we have been able to effect economies
in the cost of every Department, over which
we had effective control, and if we had been
permitted peacefully to work out our own
destiny we should even now, at this early
stage of our existence, have been engaged in
developing measures designed to promote the
well-being of our people. (Hon. Members:
"Hear, hear"). These, however, must wait
until happier conditions obtain in this distracted country.
If I may make any deduction from the
added knowledge and experience which I
have gained from endless investigations and
close study of the fiscal and financial relations of Great Britain and Ireland, I am
riore and more convinced that these two
islands, whether regarded from the standpoint of geographical proximity or racial and
lingual uniformity, or whether from the
point of view of commerce and finance, cannot be other than one economic unit.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Their social
and financial relations are so interwoven it
will pass the wit of man to disentangle them
without injury to both, and certainly disaster

EXPENDITURE, 1922-23.
I have now taken leave of the last financial
year, and I begin to look forward with great
hope, and some not unnatural fears, to the
days that lie ahead of us. My hope lies in
the prospect of a return to such happy conditions in our province as will enable us to
work out our own destiny, untrammelled by
the malign influences of uncivilised warfare.
My fears are that the policy of the British
Government has planted such
a crop of
anarchic weeds in Ireland it will be difficult
to purge and purify the soil for many a day
to come. Pessimism, however, never accomplished anything in this world, and I have
confidence that our Ulster people will live up
to the traditions of their race, and see this
thing through, (Hon. Members: 'Hear,
hear.") It is in this spirit of confidence that
I submit my statement of the financial out.
look for the year which still largely lies ahead
of us.
I propose to divide my balance sheet for the
year into three separate Departments, in
order that the House may have a clearer
understanding of our exact financial obligations, and how it is proposed to meet them.
The first Department treats of our normal
receipts and expenditure; the second is concerned solely with special and, as I hope, nonrecurrent matters; and the third sets out our
capital obligations.
I begin with an analysis of our ordinary
revenue and expenditure, taking the expenditure side of the account first, and thereafter
submit the estimated revenue necessary to
meet this expenditure.
The Consolidated Fund services include the
statutory salaries of the Speakers and that of
the Comptroller and Auditor-General, etc.,
amounting to £4,350, and, in addition, a provision of £50,000 for interest. I am bound to
contemplate the necessity of borrowing for the
Unemployment Insurance Fund. and the
interest on this advance and the creation of
a nucleus to meet the interest on the
National Savings Certificates justify me in
putting aside £50,000, which I regard as
ample for these purposes.
The Houses of Parliament and the Cabinet
absorb £34,000. This is a very small percentage of our revenue, and, I think, needs
neither comment nor justification, particularly as we have been able to effect such
savings in our Departmental expenditure as
far more than covers the expenditure on our
Government and Parliament.
The Estimate for Old Age Pensions, at
£1,156,000, shows a reduction of about £24,000
on the cost in 1920, accounted for by closer
supervision. I propose to institute administrative changes in this service when conditions are more settled, and it is expected that
these changes will effect considerable savings.
At present the administrative cost of the Old
Age Pension scheme is quite too high. (Hon.
Members: Ilear, hear.")

The Ministry of Finance, with all its
adjuncts and diversified services, is responsible for £121.000.
The Ministry of Home Affairs requires the
substantial sum of £503,000 for grants to the
Local Authorities, whilst the administration
of its varied Departments costs £173,000.
Under the head of "Labour," the contributions to Health and Unemployment Insurance
amount to £316,000, whilst the administrative
costs, including £42,000 to close up the Imperial unemployment schemes, are £218,000.
The varied activities of this Ministry necessarily entail a heavy burden on the community, and so long as the administration of
the Unemployment Insurance Fund involves
such heavy work, the liability in respect of
this Department is not likely to be lessened.
Education is also necessarily a very heavy
State charge. The payments are estimated
to reach £1,720,000 for the year, and the
administration costs £80,000.
The outlay on Agriculture is estimated at
£111,000. I may say that I do not know of
money that could be better expended, or a
Department that is more efficiently administered. Commerce, which is a new
Ministry, will require £22,000.
These services which I have enumerated
are all under our own direct control, and
require a total provision of £4,454,000.
The new Royal Ulster Constabulary, for
which we have now assumed responsibility,
is estimated to cost the State for the ten
months of this year £725,000. During the
first two months of the year the Royal Irish
Constabulary policed the Province, and the
charge for this service was initially paid by
the Imperial Authority, but will be deducted
from our revenue which is collected from
Whitehall.
The Imperial Authority incurs charges for
Northern Ireland which, in the aggregate,
amount to £2,026,000. This amount is deducted from our revenue, and includes such
charges as the

Also the cost of our Judiciary and the collection of Inland Revenue, Customs and
Excise, etc. The total of these expenses,
amounting to £2,026,000 as I have just mentioned, is deducted from the revenue collected by the Imperial Authority, as well as
our State contribution to Imperial services.
On the expenditure side of the account, I
have allowed £150,000 for Special Supplementary Votes. I anticipate such savings
on the ordinary departmental estimates as
will balance any liability for ordinary contingencies. I think it is wise that we should
lay aside a considerable sum of money for
any special contingency that may arise in
the course of our year's working.
The Imperial contribution is by far the
largest item on the expenditure side of the
account. The amount of the liability for
all Ireland under this head was fixed by the
act of 1920 at £18,000,000, of which it fell to
the North to provide £7,920,000. I think we
are quite familiar with that amount. The
injustice, not only of the total Irish contribution, but more especially of the apportionment, was apparent to the Northern
representatives from the moment of its
submission. A fundamental mistake was
also made in fixing for two years by Act of
Parliament the amount based on the revenue
at an exceptional period of violently fluctuating and prosperous trade conditions at the
close of the Great War.
As I have mentioned earlier, eloquent
proof of this lack of foresight was afforded,
during the first year of our constitutional
existence, in the reduction of the United
Kingdom revenue by no less a sum than
£91,000,000 below the estimates. The
revenue of our Province naturally suffered
in like proportion. The Imperial Government has admitted the changed conditions,
and in order that Northern Ireland shall not
be penalised, pending the decision of the
Joint Exchequer Board, it has been arranged
that the Treasury deduction from the
revenue shall be at the rate per month of
one-sixteenth of the statutory contribution
instead of one-twelfth for the first
four months of the financial year. This,
in effect, means that our contribution
would be three-fourths of £7,920,000-a reduction of £1,980,000. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I consider that I am justified, therefore in calculating as our liability for Imperial
Services a sum of £5,940,000 for this year.
Although we claim that the reduction should
be considerably more than one-fourth, the
arguments advanced to the U.K. Chancellor
have borne fruit to the extent that for the
time being advances are being made on the
basis of the 25 per cent. reduction. Therefore,
although the exact contribution is not definitely settled, it would be improper to let our
liability stand in my Estimates at £7,920,000.
I think I should read the important terms
of reference to the Joint Exchequer Board in
regard to the matter of our contribution. I
should also like to say that an arrangement
was made by our own Prime Minister with the
Imperial Government and that the right
hon. Gentleman displayed such courage and
pertinacity in his prosecution of this claim
that it reached the happy result that I now
propose to read to the House.
"The British Government agree to refer to
the Joint Exchequer Board the amount of
the contribution which should be made by
Northern Ireland for Imperial liabilities for
the years 1922-23 and 1923-24, for their consideration, in the light of the Budget Estimates for 1922-23, and to ask them to report
whether any modification could properly be
made in the present statutory sum, and, if
so, what steps would be necessary to give
effect to their recommendation."
This brings our ordinary Budget expenditure for the year to a total sum of £13,636,000.

The final items on the revenue side are

£160,000, and repayments by the Imperial
Treasury of £127,000 against our outlay on
Government Buildings. Both items are

These figures, which I have given, make up
a total revenue of £13,705,000, and if from this
evenue we deduct our Budget expenditure of
£13,636,000, we arrive at an estimated surplus
on our year's accounts of £69,000.
Returning for a few moments to the
subject of taxation, I should inform the
House that I have not taken any account of Excess Profits Duty. As all
business men know, there are heavy
claims being made on the State under this
head for repayments, and until all these
claims are determined it would be unwise to
reckon on any great amount of revenue
accruing from this tax. It is just possible it
might realise up to £100,000, but I prefer to
take no chances on this head.
The apportionment of our revenue derivable from Customs and Excise is determined on a population basis. From its
nature and the diffusion of the collections no
other course is feasible. The presumption is
that the inhabitants of one area consume on
the average as much spirits, beer, tea, sugar,
tobacco, &c., as those of another, and taxes
paid on these articles form, as will be seen,
our most important source of revenue.
Income Tax is giving us a good deal of
concern, and it also furnishes a large proportion of our income. There was a deplorable falling off in this revenue during
the four months of last year, and this was
the cause of a good deal of difficulty and
negotiation with the Treasury Authorities in
settling up the accounts for the four months
of last year.
There seems to be a great deal of misapprehension regarding Income Tax payments. I am bound to say I have never
known anyone keen on paying this tax, but
when it has to be paid it may as well be paid
promptly. And I wish to impress on our
people that whether they pay the tax in
London, in Dublin, or in Belfast, the money
belongs and inures to the benefit of our
province.
There is at present a suspicion of Dublin,
which is perhaps not unnatural-(Hon.
Members: "Hear, hear ")-but the House
should remember that the Imperial organisation which has existed for many years still
functions there, and must continue to do so
until the business of claims and repayments
is cleaned up.
But it may tend to reassure our people if
I state that we have made arrangements
which justify the hope that by the 1st July
the whole Income Tax Department will concentrate in Belfast. (Hon Members: "Hear,
hear.")
I have reckoned upon the arrears of last
year, which are considerable, being paid
promptly. Otherwise the financial machinery
of the Government becomes deranged. My
estimates of revenue will be falsified if these
arrears are not paid up during the year, because I have based them on this presumption.
When I am on the subject of taxation, I
should like to remove some misapprehension
which seems to exist in respect of our powers
in this Department.
When honourable Members of this House,
who are assumed to be well informed, inveigh
against the alleged Government extravagance,
and predict additional taxation, it is not unnatural that the Man in the Street should
dread the same result.
I wish to remove that fear. Seven-eighths
of our taxation is imposed by the Imperial
Parliament, and in no single case could we
add to it. We may relieve the burden of Income Tax if we have the money, but only by
way of rebate through the same machinery
that collects it.
With regard to taxation which this House
controls, the produce is so relatively small, no
increase could appreciably assist us, even if
we contemplated such a policy. Death Duties
are abnormal, and in my judgment are sufficiently high. Those who pay Entertainment
Tax are groaning at present under an alleged
burden, and claim that their business is being
ruined. Stamps are also high enough. The
produce of these taxes imposed by us is only
£900,000 in a total revenue of almost
£14,000,000.
What new tax, then, could we impose? I
do not know of any. If honourable Members
who are interested in fiscal problems care

to turn their inventive genius to account and
can discover a tax which will produce any
considerable revenue without imposing too
great a burden on the community, I warrant
that the British Government will pay handsomely for the patent.
In almost every country of the world the
most experienced fiscal authorities are endeavouring to discover new means of taxation to
meet their national necessities, but it is generally found that every avenue is exhausted.
From every point of view it is an advantage
to have our taxation uniform with that of
Great Britain-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)
--and I wish, therefore, emphatically to dispel any idea in the minds of our people that
there can be any tax superimposed upon the
present system.

I now come to what I regard as the most
important part of my statement.
The expenditure shown in the second Department is
exceptional in its character, and such as it
is to be hoped will be non-recurrent.
are outgoings in the Unemployment Scheme
to the extent of £500,000, to be administered
by my right honourable Friend the Minister
of Labour, the details of which have been so
fully discussed as to require no further
com.ment.
Another important provision has also been
made in this Department, that is, an amount
of £750,000 to meet malicious injury claims
during the currency of this year.
The last and most important item of expenditure is that contained under the head cf
Special Police," amounting to £2,562,000.
""
On the other side of this special account
will be found the credit of amounts payable
by the British Government to provide for the
cost of the Unemployment Scheme (£500,000)
and the malicious injury claims (£750,000).
There also appears a Grant-in-Aid by he
Imperial Government of £1,000,000, designed
inter alia to defray the cost of the Special
Police for the half-year ending 1st October.
Any further liability of the British Government under this head will be determined as
circumstances further develop. If it should
be necessary to conduct further operations,
the cost of this service must increase, and our
claim on the British Government will doubtless exceed the present estimated deficit of
£1,562,000, but the whole position in Southern
Ireland at present is so chaotic it is obviously
impossible for any Finance Minister to estimate calls on his Department which the circumstances may demand.
I make no apology for a diversion at this
point to take the question of Special Police
out of the atmosphere of cold finance, and for
raising it to the plane of Imperial sentiment,
Imperial honour, and Imperial duty. (Hon.
Members:" Hear, hear.") We regard Jlster
to-day as the keystone of the arch of the
British Empire. This may seem a grandiose
claim, and I have no desire to exaggerate the
importance of our little State; and I would
remind you that the importance of States is
frequently in inverse ratio to their area and
population. (Hon. Members: "Hear hear.")
Fierce and bloody wars have often been undertaken either to overthrow or protect the
liberties of States smaller or less important
than Ulster.
Belgium is a comparatively small State, but
for centuries it has been the cock-pit of
Europe. On its soil monumental battles have
been fought to vindicate or establish principles far transcending in importance the
mere question of the integrity of Belgium.
Ulster to-day has been selected as the cockpit of strife by those whose object is the
destruction of the British Empire rather than
the mere acquisition of Ulster. Here, in this
province, the whole principle of Empire is at
stake. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Attacks such as are now being planned or
carried out on Ulster, if attempted in New
Zealand, would arouse the whole Empire to
fury, and yet we pay our full share of the
cost of our protection, which New Zealand
does not.
We are the children of the Empire-we
Ulster people. It is no exaggeration to say
that, in proportion to our relatively small
population, we have done more than our fair
share in upbuilding those great communities
that own Britain as their mother. Where
the Red Ensign of Britain flies-whether
under the Southern Cross or in the colder
regions of the Northern Hemisphere-there,
be sure, the Ulsterman and his brother Scot
are found, peaceful, law-abiding, and adventurous citizens.
But I am satisfied the British people are
quite sound on this question, and that the
British Government is now alive to the
Empire's danger. They are pouring additional troops into Ulster, and this is all to
the good. The appearance of British troops
in the streets of Belfast imparts a great sense
of security to our people, who love and
fraternise with the British Tommy.
But the problem cannot be solved by military operations, as the British Government
fully appreciates from its experience in
Southern Ireland; and I think the Government also realises that the disease can only
be cured by those on the spot, who are able
to diagnose the symptoms and apply the
remedy. Be this as it may, there is general
agreement that the cancerous growth must be
uprooted and the law vindicated.

The Prime Minister asked me to inform

from

the British

He hopes the House will not press for

THIRD DEPARTMENT CAPITAL
COMMITMENTS.
I pass on now to the third department of
my financial statement, which is concerned
solely with Capital Commitments.
On the credit side of the account, I have
a surplus of £64,000 from last year, and
there is a small repayment by a local
authority on account of a recent loan of
£1,0000. But the salient feature of this side
of the account is the estimated receipts
from Ulster Savings Certificates. I have
assumed these receipts at £350,000. I believe this to be a conservative estimate, in
view of the fact that up to the present the
applications have been coming in at a rate
considerably over £400,000 per annum of
cash.
The most gratifying feature of the Savings
Scheme is the volume of small investors
who are taking advantage of this suitable
class of investment, which aims, as one of
its objects, in developing habits of thrift
amongst our people.
On the other side of this account, the
Unemployment Insurance Fund has needed
to be financed to the extent of £160,000 as
at 31st December, and we reckon that this
Fund will require a further loan of £700,000
during the current year.
The Local Authorities will probably draw
on us for loans to the extent of £50,000,
so that the total of these advances, which
amount to £910,000, will leave us with an
amount of £495,000 to be met by borrowing.
The nature of the borrowing, of course, will
have to be determined as the circumstances
arise, but, as money is cheap, and I hope
will continue to be cheap during the year,
it may not cost so much in interest as we
anticipate.
I have now submitted a complete forecast
of the financial position of the Province for
the year in which we stand, and have shown
that the ordinary revenue and expenditure
account should show a surplus of £69,000.
I must, however, remind the House that
all Budgets are Estimates, and any Chancellor taking on himself the role of a prophet
moves in the region of conjecture. As the
Finance Minister of this Province, I encountered peculiar difficulties in dealing with
the revenues of a State subject to the many
uncertain conditions of pioneer organisation
without any figures of the past to guide me.
I would, therefore, remind the House that
trade conditions may affect our revenue
either favourably or the reverse, and that
our contribution to the Imperial Services
has still to be determined by the Joint Exchequer Board.
But, summarising the statement as a
whole, I believe it presents a fair and,
indeed, conservative estimate of the financial
conditions of the Province.

CONSTABULARY BILL.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed, "That
the Bill be now read the Second time."
:
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw) The circumstances in which it
becomes necessary to bring forward this
Constabulary Bill are fresh in the minds of
the Members of this House. They will remember that by the Government of Ireland
Act the Royal Irish Constabulary, which had
been the Constabulary in Ireland for so many
years, was made a reserved service, and it
was contemplated by that Act that within
three years after the appointed day the
Imperial Government should transfer that
existing force, part to Southern Ireland and
part to Northern Ireland, and the administration of the force was to be transferred
simultaneously. There were elaborate provisions made in that Act by which the rights
of the various members of the Force should
be preserved, and by which a proper division
of it should be made between Northern
Ireland and Southern Ireland. What was
contemplated was the division of the existing
Force, and not the constitution of new Forces
in both Northern and Southern Ireland, but
circumstances have changed, and the change
of policy has required a change of plan. It
was soon found that the Irish Free State,
which has come into being since the Government of Ireland Act, would have nothing to
do with the old Royal Irish Constabulary,
and on our side the situation was made very
difficult indeed, because while the Force was
in existence in Northern Ireland we had
practically nothing to do with the management and control of it. It was, as I said at
the beginning, a reserved service under the
control of the Imperial Government.
Our Ministry, when we were given some
control over its movements, were treading on
very dangerous ground, very precarious indeed, for when dealing with the Royal Irish
Constabulary we had to find whether our
decisions in regard to it would be honoured
or not by those who were in actual
control. But now we are face to face
with the disbandment of the Royal Irish
Constabulary, and a Bill is before the Imperial House which, I think, will result in its
disbandment on the 31st of this month. It
has become necessary to have a substitute
Force in our Northern Province to replace
that Force, whose operations here have been
known so well. Against the day of disbandment, the Minister (Sir Dawson Bates) took
what I think would seem a very wise precaution indeed. He appointed a strong and
representative Committee to inquire into the
whole circumstances of the Force which it
was proposed to establish, and that Committee
has presented a very valuable and very exhaustive Report. That Report was considered by the House here, and a discussion
took place on the findings of the Committee.
The Government have taken into consideration all the recommendations that were made
in that debate, and they have done what they
can to embody the findings of the Committee.
These they have practically adopted in every
particular in the measure that is now presented to the House for Second reading.
The features of the Report are, first of all,
that it establishes a single control for all the
Province. This was agreed upon unanimously by the members of the Committee,
and I think very wisely, because at this
time it is absolutely essential that the
Government should have control over
the Police Force, and I think that
when the details of the Bill are examined
it will be found to be not only in the interests of the efficiency of the Force, but also
in the interests of economy. The next feature that will characterise our new Force is
that it is to be of the same name as the old
Force, but with the change of locality sug
gested that is, that the Royal Irish Constabulary will become the Royal Ulster Constabulary. It was hoped when the Report was
prepared by the members of that Committee
that we should obtain the Royal Assent for the
use of this name, and I am happy to say it
has been given. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Just as the Royal Irish Rifles, the regiment
which was so associated with our area, has
become the Royal Ulster Rifles, so the Royal
Irish Constabulary will be known in future as
the Royal Ulster Constabulary. The next
thing that was mentioned in the Report was
the numbers of the Force, and the recommendation of the Committee has been adopted,
and is embodied in this Bill. The Committee
reported that a Force of 3,000 would be neces
sary. That number is a little over the
strength of the Royal Irish Constabulary in
the Six Counties in normal times, but we are
not in normal times at present, and we think
the recommendation of the Committee was a
very wise one indeed. We propose to adopt
it for the present, but, of course, that will
Constabulary Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Megaw]
not prevent us in any way when more peaceful times come from reducing the Force if we
find that such is possible.
The Bill before the House deals really with
three matters:-
First, it deals with the establishment of
the Force;
Secondly, it provides for a slight modification of the law with regard to Resident
Magistrates. The House will remember that
the Resident Magistrates occupy a rather
anomalous position in the administration
here. They have been established by the
Constabulary Act, and it is only by the
adaptation of that Act they are dealt with
under the present Bill.
Thirdly, the Bill deals with the position of
the Specials.
Much has been said, and very rightly said,
in praise of the work that was done in the
In
past by the Royal Irish Constabulary.
their palmy days they were a magnificent
force, they were splendidly efficient, undaunted in their bravery, and absolute in
their loyalty, but latterly dark days and sore
trials came upon them. When law was disregarded by those who were administering it
it was perhaps to be expected that the loyalty
of the Force should not be encouraged and
well-meant and proper executive acts were repudiated by thosa in command. It is surprising, however, how sound the moral of the
Force remained, exposed as it was on the one
hand to bitter and barbarous enemies and on
the other to being let down by those who
had it in control. I think this House is paying the highest tribute to the worth of the
Royal Irish Constabulary by what is being
done to-day. Imitation is the sincerest
flattery, and we are practically adopting here
the constitution of the Royal Irish Constabulary for the Constabulary that is now
to be formed. Pursuant to the recommendations of the Committee we have modelled our
Force on the old pattern. This Government
does not break readily with the past, and
there has been eighty-five years' experience
of the work of the Royal Irish Constabulary.
Changes have been introduced from time to
time, changes in the way of improvement in
regard to organisation, in regard to its discipline, and in regard to the management of
the Force generally. We have tried so far as
possible to use the results of that experience,
to garner the fruits that have resulted from
the working of the Force during those eightyfive years, and we have made some changes,
but those changes have been introduced very
cautiously, and I will mention them in
detail when I come to deal seriatim with the
provisions of the Bill.
In the personnel we have followed the same
policy. We have tried not to break too far
with the past. We have tried to induce the
men who were tried and proved in the Royal
Irish Constabulary to enlist in our new Constabulary, and we have made special provisions for these men. I am glad to say that
the result so far has been very satisfactory,
and we shall have a very fine leaven of the
old men in our new Force. The Bill applies
the enactments and regulations of the Constabulary Acts with some necessary modifications, and I propose in detail to deal with the
various clauses of the Bill.
The House will see, by Clause 1, the new
Police Force is to be established, which, as I
have mentioned, is to receive the name of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary. Just as the
Royal Irish Constabulary had its government
and direction vested in an Inspector-General,
so we propose that the supreme control of
the Force here that is, the general government; of course, the Ministry is still responsible is to be in an Inspector-General, and
the number of officers is set out in the First
Schedule to the Bill. As I have said, there
are to be 3,000 in the Force, both officers and
men. Sub-section 3 applies the enactments
relating to the Royal Irish Constabulary,
under the change of name, to the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, and we have not, therefore, to
make a new code in that respect. We have
a ready-made code, which, of course, is still
subject to alteration, but we have it at present
to govern the administration of our special
Force. In the same way, Sub-section 4 applies
the ranks of the various members of the old
Force to the new conditions. As in the past
the appointment and removal of officers rested
with the Lord Lieutenant, so it does at present. It is essential to the Force being a Royal
Force that the Lord Lieutenant should be the
responsible authority, but of course, as in all
constitutional matters, he will act on the
advice of the Home Minister (Sir Dawson
Bates) in this respect.
Section 2, Sub-section 2, is an adaptation of
the Constabulary and Police Act, 1919,
enabling the Minister to make regulations
with regard to the rates and scales of pay.
That is merely adapting Section 4 of the Constabulary and Police Act to the new Force.
Sub-section 3 suspends the operation of one of
the clauses of that Act for a period of twelve
months. The reason for that is this: That
Act provided that when there were rates of
pay and scales of pay and pensions to be considered, a representative body of the men
should be consulted in the matter, but as
there is no representative body, and cannot
be any representative body, till the Force
is formed, it is impossible that that should
be done, and so the operation of that clause
has been suspended.
Now, coming to Section 3, it is, I might
say, one of the economic provisions of the
Constabulary Bill-
Second Reading.
24 MAY 1922.
reserve
Bill. It has been modelled on the already
existing Acts dealing with the Royal Irish
Constabulary. They have been enacted at
different times and in a somewhat muddled
condition, but here the provisions are made
by a distinct enactment as to how the Force
is to be distributed throughout the various
counties. By Section 3, sub-section 1, you
will see what is referred to as the free
quota. Free quota means this, that for every
county and county borough there shall be
established an additional force-a
force-of which numbers can be sent
to one county or another
as the exigencies and conditions of law and order
require. The free quota has been determined in the past on a number of conditions.
First of all, there is the population of the
county, its valuation and its area. All
those things had to be considered. After
considering those things it has been the
practice to allot a definite number of police
to every county and to every county borough,
leaving, as I say, a proper number that
can, as a reserve force, be sent to one
county or another as the case may be. Of
course the sub-section provides that it does
not expect a greater number than 3,000 to
be formed in the force altogether, but subsection 2 deals with the additional force.
That additional force is defined in the definition Clause which you will find at
Section 9. Section 9 defines the additional
force as a force,
"Which, by reason of its being stationed in a county or county borough,
causes the total number of sergeants and
constables in that county or county
borough to exceed the free quota."
That additional force is the force that
is moved from time to time from one county,
or one county borough to another. The meaning of all this is that the free quota of police
in any county or county borough is to be
maintained altogether by the moneys provided by Parliament. That is, that this
House is responsible for the free quota in
the various counties-for the full charges,
but so far as the additional force is concerned that will be dependent to some extent
on the order that obtains in the county
itself, and if the county or county borough
needs a larger number it will be partly
responsible, because of the state of order
there, for the upkeep of the force in that
particular county. That is provided for by the
financial clause, which says that one half
of the cost of the additional force shall be
borne by the county or county borough as
the case may be. That is dealt with in
Section 4. Sub-section 2 of Section 4 deals
with the boroughs of Belfast and Londonderry. It abolishes the enactments in force
with regard to those boroughs. There were
some rather complicated provisions about
night watchmen and higher officials.
How
that arose was, that in the history of the
Police Force it was formerly the case that
Belfast-I am not sure about Derry-had
a Police Force of its own. That was up
to 1860, and I am not sure that it was
satisfactorily managed. They were glad in
that year to come in and have the Constabulary Acts applied to Belfast itself. Since
that date, 1865, Belfast has been policed
by the Royal Irish Constabulary, but there
are some old provisions remaining, about
the case of night watchmen and one or two
officers. It is now proposed to do away
with these and make the whole Police Force
uniform and under one uniform control. As
I have said, that is the unanimous report
of the Committee that was appointed by
the Ministry, and I think that it is a very
sound conclusion to come to.
Sub-section 5 deals with what is called
the fine or fee fund of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, enabling the fines that are
imposed in matters of discipline to be used
for rewarding or benefiting members who
have shown exceptional ability and deserve
special commendation. Sub-section 6 of
Section 4 deals with administrative provisions. Section 5 provides for the transition
stage, so that we may be able to retain a
sufficient Force until the members of the
new Force are sworn in. For a period of
three months it will be possible to retain
any of the members of the old Constabulary
to keep things going until our own Force is
in full working order. Section 6 deals with
the question of Resident Magistrates. At the
present time the jurisdiction of a Resident
Magistrate only extends to the county to
which he is appointed and to the adjoining
county. This Section enables the Ministry
to have a Resident Magistrate sent to any
county in which his services may be urgently
required, and gives him jurisdiction over
every county in our area. Section 7 is
really carrying through the policy of applying the former Acts to this new Act. I need
only draw attention particularly to subsection C, which deals with the form of
oath that should be taken by the new
Constabulary. That oath has been drawn
out after careful consideration, and it is
hoped that it will be found satisfactory.
The only change that is really introduced
in this oath is more or less to make
it explicit. It sets out explicitly what was
inferentially contained in the old Constabulary oath. It inferred that the oath of
allegiance to the King implied an oath of
allegiance to His Government, and that all
orders of the Government would be obeyed.
It was thought it was as well to have this
set out expressly, and that there should be
no ambiguity on the subject. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) It was also thought,

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Megaw]
with regard to our police becoming members
of any association, that it was only fair
they should be allowed to become members
of proper or legal associations just as
ordinary citizens, but that their attention
should be called to the oath, that anything
in the nature of a seditious or illegal
association would not be tolerated, and that
members of the Force could not take part
in such.
Class D of Section 7 reduces the age from
40 to 35 years.
Under the former Acts, the
Constabulary might be chosen up to the age
of 40. It has been thought that 35 is a
better age, and, accordingly, it is proposed
that the age of 35 should be the maximum
from which recruits for the Police Force
should be taken. I do not think there is
really anything more that requires attention
so far as that section is concerned. As
regards Section 8, I mentioned in the earlier
part of my speech in introducing this
measure that there was a provision with
regard to Special Constables. The chief
effect of that section is to remove the limit
that was set by the Special Constables Act,
together with the War Emergency Laws
(Continuance) Act, and make it for all
practical purposes a continuing measure and
have it on the Statute Book so as to be
able to use the Special Constabulary when
we require them. This is no time to
disband or to lose any opportunities we
have of using the services of the Special
Constabulary. The effect of this section is
to put them on that basis, and to have them
while embodied on as close relationship to
the existing Royal Ulster Constabulary as
possible. Sub-section 5 of that section is
intended to remove any difficulty that may
have arisen through illegality from time to
time. Because of the congestion of affairs
in regard to the Special Constabulary Force,
there had to be very strict regulations, and
sometimes it became absolutely impossible
to have full compliance with these regulations from time to time, and this House
is asked in this measure to pass such
legislation as will remove any danger from
irregularities that may occur.
I need not refer to the matter any further.
I think I have explained pretty fully what
is the effect of the measure. As I have said,
it is proposed to establish in Ulster a force
that is constituted in the same way as the
Royal Irish Constabulary was, and I believe
that the measure will meet with the approval
of this House. I have much pleasure in
moving the Second reading of this Bill.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. LYNN: I am sure other Members like
myself are grateful to the hon. and learned
Gentleman who has just sat down, for his
very full explanation of the Bill. Personally, I am grateful to him, especially because
I only received a copy of the Bill when I
came into the House to-day. I notice a
habit growing up in this House, and it is one
I think which we should protest against
at once, and that is putting a Bill into your
hand a few minutes before you have got to
discuss it. I do not think it makes at all for
good legislation, and I do not think it is
helpful to the Government. I do appealthis is not the first occasion, as my hon. and
learned friend for the University (Mr. Robb)
protested some weeks ago with regard to

allow the Members to have the Bill in their
hands for a few days so as to enable them
to go through the different clauses and make
themselves familiar with it. To get a Bill
and to try to gather its contents inside a
few minutes is one of those things that the
average Member must find rather difficult
Having made this protest, I would like to
join with my hon. and learned Friend in the
tribute he has paid to the old Royal Irish
Constabulary that is now going out of existence. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) In the
profession to which I belong I have had opportunities of seeing the Royal Irish Constabulary in all sorts and conditions of
weather. I have seen them in the early
morning and I have seen them at night; I
have seen them in peace and I have seen them
'n riots. I say no tribute that could be paid
to the Royal Irish Constabulary does justice
to that Force, and I think when the history
of Ireland is written, when Irishmen look
back in a calmer frame of mind than they
are in at present they will be sorry that the
old Royal Irish Constabulary have disappeared. My right hon. Friend the Home
Secretary is bringing this Bill in and establishing this Force under exceptional circumstances. We all recognise the exceptional
circumstances under which the new Force
is being established, but I would like
Members to look particularly at the Schedule to this Bill, and to ask themselves do
they not think that the higher command
is rather overweighted. It strikes me that
for a small force of only 3,000 men you are
establishing a headquarters staff that is
much too large for the work it has to do. I
commend this to the House. It may be
there is no point in the objection. I have
an open mind myself. I am prepared to be
convinced that every officer recommended
in this Bill is necessary, but the Home
Secretary will have to convince
me that
really the staff he is going to set up
is not too large. If he convinces me I shall
vote for it, but if he does not I shall at
least enter a protest.
Constabulary Bill-

With regard to the County Inspectors,
I know at the present time it will be
necessary to have a pretty large force, but
is it really necessary to have a County Inspector for each of the Six Counties if we
happen to live in normal conditions? I do
think that this point might be looked into.
There is another point I would direct the
attention of the Home Secretary to. I am
sure other Members of Parliament like
myself have been getting complaints to the
effect that it is not going to be an Ulster
Constabulary at all, that so many people
are being brought in from other parts of
the Empire that it will only be the Royal
Ulster Constabulary in name and not in
reality. There may be no justification
for that complaint. I cannot tell. I do not
know. The Home Secretary must know, but
the complaint is being made, and it is being
circulated very strongly in the city that
there are so many Englishmen being brought
into this Force, and that they cannot know
anything of local conditions. It would be
much better either to have Ulstermen in
charge of the Force or to have Irishmen who
served in other parts of Ireland and who
know Irish conditions.
This is a point that I commend to the
right hon. Gentleman. We must know
whether there is any justification for the
complaints that are being made, and I pass
the complaint on to him as it has been
given to me.
I am sure that the best wish every
Member of this House can have for the new
Constabulary Force is that it may live up to
the high traditions of the one that has preceded it. If the Royal Ulster Constabulary
is as good as the Royal Irish Constabulary,
then we who are going to originate that
Force to-day, or at any rate in a few days'
time, will have every reason to be proud.
Looking back over the other Force, it is a
Force that we are justly proud of, and we
hope that the new branch will be grafted on
to the old stem, and that the old principle,
the old tradition, their impartiality, their
fairness in dealing with different-even
acutely divided sections of the communitywill be exemplified in this new Force. When
the Committee stage is come to there
will be opportunities for going into
details, and I only throw out these
two or three suggestions that have been
impressed on me by people who are anxious
to help the Home Secretary, just as anxious
as I am, and by people who are anxious that
this Force shall be made a great success.
Mr. DUFF: Permit me to emphasise the

These are only two points I wish to draw

are to make them easy in the future it is

mentioned here about women in the Force.
It may be said that we should not have
women in the Police Force, but it was clearly
pointed out by the hon. Member for South
Belfast (Mrs. McMordie) that good work was
being done by the two present members of
our Force, and we should not altogether
follow the decision which has been come to
lately for the abolition of the women in the
Force on the other side. Now that we are
establishing a new Force, provision should
be made in this Bill for the inclusion of
women in the Force. They can do very
useful work in our cities and in our Courts
looking after young persons, and dealing with
women, and they can do it in a very much
better way than men would be capable of.
There are other matters I would like to
bring before the House but, like my hon.
Friends, having had such a short time at my
disposal, I am not in a position to criticise
the whole Bill, but between this and the
Committee stage, and having had the experience of serving on the Committee on the
Police Bill in the Imperial House, I will go
into these matters and see if I can help my
hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Megaw) by
making suggestions or putting down amendments in order that we may get this Bill as
up-to-date as possible. We are in a transition
period at the present time, and undoubtedly
difficulties will arise-probably in the course
of the next few months-and then we will
wish we had put this and that in the Bill.
I think this House should thoroughly discuss
the Bill and offer all the suggestions possible
in order to save these difficulties arising in
the future. Those are the only observations
I wish to make at the moment, but I hope
the suggestion I have offered will be taken
into consideration and that we will be given
a little more time to draft amendments in
order to help the Government in the constitution of the new Force.
Mr. GRANT: I would just like to say that
I agree entirely with the hon. Members who

Mr. MEGAW: I wish to say a few words
in reply to the criticisms of the
various hon. Members who have spoken
on the Bill. I regret very much that hon.
Members have not had more opportunity of
studying the Bill. The House can have very
little conception of the high pressure which
exists at present in the Ministry of Home
Affairs. The Royal Irish Constabulary are
in course of being disbanded, and there are a
great many other matters which have got to
be attended to as well as this Bill. The
measure has only been drafted very lately.
I myself only had an opportunity of seeing
the first draft at the end of last week, and
it was only when I came into my office today that I was able to see the final draft,
which is before the House. I would ask hon.
Members to have more consideration for the
high pressure at which we are working at the
present time. As a matter of fact, we are
very considerably under-staffed just now, but
we are doing the best we can. It has become
necessary that this Bill should become law
before the 31st of May, and we must ask
the indulgence of the House to enable us to
secure that.
Hon. Members have dealt with this Bill in
no unfriendly way, and I think the criticism
is very largely deserved. They should have
had more opportunities of reading and
digesting the provisions of the Bill, and I
feel that perhaps some of the criticisms
which were offered would not have been
made to-day if that had been the case, because a good many of the matters which have
been referred to would not necessarily appear in a Bill at all. They are matters for
regulations to be drawn up by the Ministry.
We recognise that the Police Committee's
Report was an interim Report, and it was,
and is, the intention that that Committee
will come together again. Their recommendations will be very carefully considered, I
am sure, in the preparation of the regulations which may be made from time to time.
But we had to do the thing in a very hurried
way, and I feel that it would hardly have
been possible for us to have the Committee
brought together again and for us to have
their findings before the 31st May, when the
R.I.C. will be disbanded.
With regard to the criticisms which were
offered by the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn), with reference to the great
number of higher officers who were in the
Force, I may say at the outset that we hope
that in normal times there will not be anything like such a large number of officers;
but, just as we in the Ministry are working
under high pressure, so the police in Belfast
and in Ulster are working under very high
pressure at the present time, and they require
far more officers than would be necessary in
normal times. As a matter of fact it is almost impossible to get the ordinary police
work which is requisite from day to day carried through. Some of our constabulary are
working twelve or fourteen hours a day, and
the officers are overworked too. Hardly a
man of them ever gets a holiday at any
time, and at present we cannot come before
the House and ask for a smaller number of
officers than that proposed in this Bill.
As I indicated myself before the criticism
was offered, we hope it will be possible to
have the number reduced in more normal
times. That is really all I have to say with
regard to what the Member for West Belfast
said.

matter of fact that is provided for in the

As a
So far as the Women Police are concerned,

It may
be necessary by way of regulation--or one
can do it without a regulation at all: it can

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 25th May, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION ACT.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour whether it is the intention of the
Government to introduce a Bill this Session
to amend the Workmen's Compensation Act,
seeing that the War Addition Acts expire at
the end of this year?
LABOUR (Mr.
The MINISTER OF
Andrews): I am aware of the necessity for
amendment of the Workmen's Compensation
Act in view of the impending expiration of
the War Addition Acts. No doubt my hon.
Friend will have observed a statement by
the Imperial Home Secretary in the Imperial
House of Commons recently to the effect that
he hoped it would be possible to prepare an
amending measure before the end of the
present Session, which would be acceptable to
all parties. I am anxious for obvious reasons
that as far as possible the law relating to
Workmen's Compensation should be the same
in Northern Ireland as in Great Britain,
and I am in communication with the Im
perial Home Secretary on the matter. Some
weeks ago I stated publicly on behalf of the
Government that the workers of Northern
Ireland would not be placed in a less advantageous position in this connection than
their fellow-workers in Great Britain.
MOUNTPOTTINGER Y.M.C.A.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister for
Home Affairs whether his attention has been
drawn to the great inconvenience caused to
members of the Mountpottinger Y.M.C.A.
by the authorities taking over the whole of
the building, thereby depriving over a
thousand young men of shelter or recreation
in any part of the building, and whether it
is a fact that a wet canteen has been established, which is quite contrary to the principles and regulations of the Y.M.C.A.?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I have most carefully considered this matter and have consulted the
Military Adviser as to the possibility of
meeting the wishes of the members of the
Association, but I extremely regret that it
has not so far been possible to allow them
the use of part of the building or to find
alternative premises. If this
Parliament
agrees to the abolition of wet canteens for
the R.U.C., as proposed in the Constabulary
Bill, the wet canteen in question will be
closed forthwith.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my right hon.
Friend if it would not be possible to set
aside at least part of the building, in view
of the large number of young men there? I
appreciate very much the latter part of the
answer, as the matter has been practically
settled now.
man

existed in the Y.M.C.A. during the occupation of it by the soldiers, and previous to the

Home Affairs whether it is the intention of
the Government to introduce legislation
dealing with the whole basis of taxation of
motor vehicles, and whether this question
will be one for the consideration of the Departmental Committee?

Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand that
this problem is being considered in Great
Britain, and in the event of fresh legislation
being undertaken in that country, the
question of assimilating the law in this
country will be carefully considered. While

CONTRACT FOR BLANKETS.
4. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Mr. Hanna)
asked the Minister for Home Affairs if he
has recently entered into a contract on behalf of the Government for the purchase of
14,500 blankets; and if so, will he state the
name and address of the supplying firm, and
the full particulars of the contract?
Sir DAWSON BATES: An order has
recently been given to the firm of Messrs.
Hepworths & Haley, Ltd., Dewsbury, Yorkshire, for 12,000 blankets for the Constabulary in Northern Ireland, being portion of
the contract mentioned. In accordance with
the usual Government restrictions, this
tender was accepted, as the price quoted was
below that of any other firm tendering. It
is contrary to all practice and undesirable
to publish the particulars of the tenders
sent in by different firms, but, if the hon.
Member so desires, I will send him a copy of

are not concerned in this business at all, that

business, and were given a contract for

that.

RESUMPTION OF DEBATE.
Order read for resuming Adjourned Debate
on Question: "That this House approves the
proposals of the Government for meeting the
financial requirements of the year."-(The
Minister of Finance.)
Question again proposed.
Mr. LYNN: I do not intend to delay the
House for any length of time in going into
the very exhaustive and very interesting
statement that was made by the Finance
Minister yesterday. It may be a fact that
under other circumstances I should have
been inclined to enter into some detailed
criticism on the Budget statement, but I
realise that we are living under conditions
which make criticism, even the most friendly
criticism, rather out of place, and certainly
not in keeping with either my own feelings
or, I am sure, the feelings of the majority of
the Members of the House, because Ulster is
being attacked. Ulster, as I pointed out two
days ago, is in very serious danger at the
present moment, and whatever differences
we may have in regard to the financial
ability or otherwise of the Government, this
is not the time for dealing with these matters. Our business is to strengthen the
hands of the Government, to let it go out to
the public that we stand not even with the
shadow of a shade of difference, but that we
stand as a united House and as a united
Province. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It
is in this spirit I rise to-day. I was referred
to by the Minister of Finance as one who
assumed to have some knowledge. I am
quite sure from what I know of my right
hon. Friend he did not intend it as a sneer,
but I would say that possibly, like himself,
I have spent a great many weary days and
weary nights going through Finance Bills.
I just want to clear up one point. There
may be an impression in the House that the
Government cannot possibly go in for
extravagance, because seven-eighths of the
taxes are levied by the Imperial Parliament.
If my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)
will refer to the Act of 1920 he will find,
as he knows very well, and his highlyqualified understudy (Mr. Barbour) knows
also, that you cannot increase any of the taxes
levied by the Imperial Parliament, but you
can do what is much more important-you can
reduce any tax imposed by the Imperial
Parliament. But that is not the whole
matter. This House can, if it so desires, levy
extra taxes, and I put it to my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) that if his Budget
statement did not balance, and if he had not
been in the satisfactory position of having a
surplus of at least £69,000, if instead of a
surplus he had a deficit of £69,000, I presume,
then, the House would have had to levy fresh
taxation. We are very fortunate, and we are
very thankful to the Finance Minister for
the fact that under very difficult conditions
he has made his Budget to balance, and has
a small surplus. I congratulate him as
heartily as anyone in this House on that fact.
I know the enormous amount of work he and
my hon. Friend opposite (Mr. Barbour) have
done. The general public have no idea how
heavy a burden has been placed on them, and
