The Budget-
[Mr. Lynn]
Finance Minister before the British Cabinet,
they will give a most sympathetic reply to my
right hon. Friend.
I congratulate them both and the whole
Finance Department very heartily on their
very excellent work.
I have a recollection a few months ago,
when Government hats were flying in the air
at Westminster, when the wires were red hot
with messages about the new and loyal opinion
created in another part of this country-I
rather think at that time we were told that
Ulster would have to go into a Southern Parliament, because in a Southern Parliament
there would be practically no taxes to pay.
It may interest the House to know that since
I came here this afternoon I have been told
on very good authority that the Postmaster-
General of Southern Ireland has just told
some people it will be impossible to make the
postal reductions that come into force in
Great Britain and in Northern Ireland on
Monday next, because he has no money. That
should be a warning to those short-sighted
people-fortunately there are very few of
them--who are under the impression that if
they go under a Dublin Parliament Income
Tax will become a thing of the past, and that
in fact we will be paid for living rather than
having to pay for being allowed to live.
The Finance Ministry is to be congratulated on the fact that going through such a
serious crisis, serious from two points of view
-serious from the financial point of view,
serious from the political point of view--they
have been able to present the statement the
House heard yesterday. I would like to join
in my humble way with the Chancellor in
appealing to the British Government to
revise the whole financial agreements with
reference to Northern Ireland. Those of us
who are members of the Imperial House, and
who had a good deal to do with the fighting
in 1920, pointed out the difficulties that have
really arisen. The mistake was made that
our contributions were fixed at a time when
income was abnormal. It must have been
clear to most people that the income of 1919
and 1920 was an income that could not
possibly be kept up, and, therefore, we have
suffered. I have said often in the Imperial
House and I repeat it here so far as the
loyal population of this Province are concerned, they have never hesitated to pay
their full share of the Imperial contribution;
whether that contribution has had to be in
hard cash or in blood, Ulster has always done
its duty-(Hon. Members-Hear, hear)—and
we do not ask anything from the Imperial
Government that is unfair or unreasonable.
We only ask to be treated as an integral part
of the United Kingdom, because we are that;
and, as my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Labour pointed out in another place last
night, we do not mean to be divorced from
the British connection. I do think when the
case is put, as it will be well put by the
The real, serious part of the business
here to-day is undoubtedly the anarchy that
exists in this country. We in this House
are not responsible for the conditions that
exist either here or in any other part of
Ireland. I am sure no one is more anxious
than my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance that the dove of peace should settle
down, North and South. We are anxious
for peace.
We do not want murder and
fire and anarchy, either in the North or
South. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We
want to see the whole country settled down
to hard work, because after the great war
that has upset the whole of Europe-indeed,
the whole civilised world-after a war like
that what we want is a long period of
peace, and so far as we are concerned we
are very anxious for peace. We say in
all seriousness to these people that no good
whatever can come out of a campaign of
murder, a campaign of arson, and of
sowing weeds of anarchy it will take whole
generations to uproot. The Government
would fail in its duty if it did not take
whatever steps are necessary
in order
to protect Ulster against the attacks that
are being made, and so far as I am concerned it does not matter how much the
Government say they must have in order
to stamp out crime, I, for one, am prepared
to vote for it. There may be some details,
indeed there are details, where I think
there could be savings, but I am not going
to enter into this now, because I believe we
should show in spirit and in our every effort
we are united. Where we think there is
any unnecessary waste, instead of ventilating the subject on the floor of this House
and perhaps creating a false impression
outside, it is much better that these facts
should be brought before the Finance Mini.
ster in private or before Members of the
Government. There are points, as I say,
where there could be a saving and I shall
mention them afterwards to the Prime
Minister, but to-day I appeal to the House
to show that Ulster was never more united
than it is at this moment. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I want the feeling to go out
that we must all pull together, that we
must all pull the same way, that we
must use the whole united forces of
Ulster, first of all to repel the wanton
attack that has been made upon us, and
secondly to restore peace and good order.
I heartily congratulate my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) on the very interesting statement he made yesterday, a statement that is not only interesting on account
The Budget-
Adjourned Debate.
25 MAY 1922.
of the £69,000 but interesting because of

So, where?
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: I wish
to give expression to a few thoughts that
have been passing through my mind. I do
not wish to criticise the Budget. On the contrary, I desire to congratulate my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) most heartily.
When my right hon. Friend has taken the
matter in hand I am positively certain we
will not be disappointed and that at the end
of the financial year there will be the surplus
he anticipates of £69,000. As far as the
expenditure is concerned, I do not think it
can be reduced. No doubt there is a strong
feeling outside that this Parliament has been
set up on too extravagant a scale. Perhaps
the salaries of the Government Ministers are
too high. I do not wish to raise that
question. I only wish to point out to the
public that the entire salaries are only a
fraction of the cost; they do not really enter
into the larger question. They are not
worth considering. There is also a feeling
outside that there are too many officials
employed. There, again, I think they are
wrong, because you must necessarily have
sufficient to carry on, and while we are told
that the largest numbers of those officials are
employed in a temporary character, I have
never yet in my public career known temporary officials to have been dismissed. As a
rule, they become permanent officials, and
possibly the Government will require them.
My feeling is that they cannot be reduced
very much. I think the Government will
require all the officials they have. I only
make that observation because I do not think
the Government can reduce their expenditure
on that side.
It has been said that possibly, when we
are housed in the new Parliament House,
there will be a reduction. I cannot possibly
see it, because you must bear in mind that
the Imperial Government have undertaken to
provide suitable Houses for this Parliament,
and they are to-day paying the rent of the
official offices occupied by this Parliament.
Consequently, I do not think we can look
for any reduction in that direction. If it had
not been for what I think was the generous
treatment of the Imperial Treasury, we
could not possibly have gone on, and our
Chancellor could not have presented his
Budget, because you have to go to the
Treasury and ask them for grants in certain
directions. Of course there are unforeseen
circumstances.
Now the rev-
And now I come to the point, to which the
Minister of Finance referred yesterday, about
our contribution to Imperial funds. Nobody
knows better than the right hon. Gentleman
that some of us had very strong opinions on
this matter and, having given full consideration to it we felt convinced that the figure
arrived at was absolutely wrong. We
pointed out that the figure of 18 millions for
Ireland was altogether out of proportion. The
Imperial Government pointed out that they
were at that particular time receiving that
amount in revenue. That was quite right,
but that was based upon the peak year, when
everything was at its highest, and when we
discussed this with the Prime Minister in
London every man knew perfectly well that
the commerce of the country was at its highest point. As a matter of fact we were over
the other side with regard to receipts, and
we were gradually going down.
enue has fallen to an alarming extent, and
the figures which were then discussed will
not for a moment hold good. I hold the view
strongly that the highest contribution we
in Ulster should make should not exceed
three million pounds, instead of £7,920,000.
The Government proved that they have already realised that when they gave us a
rebate, or an allowance-call it by whatever
name you like of almost two million pounds
during the financial year. I am firmly convinced that, if the Government is about to,
or has set up the Joint Exchequer Board to
determine the amount which Northern
Ireland ought to contribute, that amount
should be settled definitely for a given period.
While I agree with my hon. Friend the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) that we
do not in any degree desire to shirk cur
responsibility, and that there are certain
services to which we are entitled to pay a
certain sum, I hold that that sum should be
one which we are able to pay, and our Government should not be placed in the position
of having to go to the Imperial Treasury and
beg them to give us more or to make us an
allowance. That should not be, because the
time will arrive undoubtedly, sooner or later,
when the Government in England will
The Budget-
Adjourned Debate.

change, the pendulum will swing, and a new

If they take up that position you cannot

I will give you any assistance I can in my

While I agree with my hon. Friend, the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) that we
have no power to increase the taxes, I think
we have some power to super-impose. We

As I have already said, you cannot in my

In my
opinion that is now at the minimum amount
which will enable you to establish your

after carrying out many useful reforms, 1

alone. There are many useful reforms which
will have to be carried out, but we hope we

before the House-six months ago--robed in

We can
raise it I know in Committee of Supply, but

informed that he has seriously considered the
liabilities the scheme involves us in, and also
the fact that there are abuses in connection
with it.
Any man who knows the working of the
Old-Age Pension Scheme will admit that
there never was a more admirable law passed
than that for giving a pension to keep old
people out of the Workhouse. Everybody
approves of it. It was a thing that was far
too long delayed, but in the country there
are large numbers of people who own portions
of land worth, perhaps, £200 or £300 who are
drawing that pension. Nobody grudges
giving it to working people, but the people
to whom I refer are diverting to their own
use funds that should go to deserving working people. These people who own this land
die, and probably leave property worth £200,
£300, or £400, which goes to their friends.
Not only that, but in many cases people who
own land assign it to their friends so as to
qualify for the pension. I am not saying a
single word against the scheme, because I
thoroughly approve of it. It is the first and
primary duty of the State to provide for its
infirm workers, and I was glad to hear the

and economised on the administration of the
fund, which I think is just as costly as any
other form of administration in connection
with this House. I hope the Finance
Minister will look closely into this question.

duty, having taken hold of this Government,
to set to work and try to carry it through
on the lines laid down for us and to try to
make a success of our Northern Parliament.
But we realise that in each step we take we
are necessarily following along the line of
dissolving those financial ties, whether they.
are personal, commercial, or even national,
which unite this country with the sister
countries of England and Scotland, and with
whom, it seems to me, our destinies, whether
financial or political, are so indissolubly
united. Be this as it may, we have to carry
out the duties that have been entrusted to
us. They are complicated to a degree, and
we are very far from having seen the end of
that disentanglement which must necessarily
take place.
I quite agree with what the Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) has said, that in
our Budget, where our power to raise revenue
is restricted, our attention must in the first
instance, and always in a greater degree, be
directed to reducing our expenditure, the
great item in which stands out as £7,920,000,
which I regard as being only provisionally
fixed as the amount of our contribution
towards the debt service, and the Army,
Navy, and Air Forces of the Empire. Abuse
of British institutions does not come with
any facility to my lips. 1 have always had
the very warmest regard for England and
Englishmen, and although we may feel
strongly at times the way our interests here
have been treated, still, however they may
appear publicly and no matter how apathetic
they may be to what we consider the
very serious issues in
our affairs over
here, I think there are many occasions
on which we have to regard their attitude towards us and their treatment
of us financially as generous and very
friendly indeed. As a matter of fact they
have already departed to some extent from
the strict letter of the law as laid down in
the Government of Ireland Act. Hon.
Members who have touched on this matter of
our contribution and the manner in which
it should be arrived at have been in a large
measure correct, but the provisions as laid
down in the Act have since been modified,
generally speaking in our favour. They have
agreed that it will not be necessary for us
to wait for two years before we begin to feel
the benefit of any reductions which the Joint
Exchequer Board may consider we are
entitled to. In the meantime they are
only deducting from our revenue as it is
collected one-sixteenth of that sum instead of
one-twelfth, and we are encouraged by that
move
on their part to hope that our
contribution of £7,920,000 may be reduced by 25 per cent. Even then
we shall not accept that readily.
We shall, as my hon. Friend the Member for
South Belfast has stated, continue to watch
every point and study it closely to see that
our contribution is fixed at a fair and
equitable figure. I do not know whether we
should adopt any fixed sum unless we were
sure that it would be favourable to us and
that we were making no mistake, but with
the variations that recessarily take place in
taxation or reduction of debt or
even in
reduction of armaments, naturally policy
changes from time to time so that we must
resort to some sort of sliding scale to fix the
contribution from the Northern area to the
United Kingdom.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Do I understand the
hon. Gentleman to say that he hopes the
reduction will be 25 per cent.? Is it not
already 25 per cent.? I hope he will assume
it will be 50 per cent. instead of 25 per cent.
Mr. BARBOUR: I am sorry I did not make
myself quite clear. I said the Imperial
Government were only deducting one-sixteenth of £7,920,000 each month from our
revenue as collected, instead of one-twelfth.
The reduction from one-twelfth to onesixteenth is 25 per cent., but there again I
stated that even the £7,920,000 is only a
provisional figure, and, while I hope that the
reduction may be 25 per cent. or better what
I wished to convey to Members of this House
was that they would not be justified in
accepting this as a finality. It is subject
to the ruling of the Joint Exchequer Board.
Although the matter of our contribution falls
more particularly within the duties of the
Minister of Finance, I am sure no one will
more readily than myself accord to our Prime
Minister our very hearty thanks and great
appreciation of the very great personal acti-
Adjourned Debate. 674
The Budget-
25 MAY 1922.
vity which he himself has taken in arranging
these matters with the Imperial Parliament.
Sanguine and optimistic as we may be in
the Ministry of Finance, we have sometimes
been surprised at the greater degree of
optimism which he has brought into the
negotiations and the very successful issue he
has achieved in so many important matters
which we have had under consideration.
There are one or two questions which have
been raised, some by more than one hon.
Member, and one is largely concerned with
unemployment relief. Altogether there have
been three sums touched upon, one of £42,000,
another of £500,000, and the other of £50,000.
The £500,000 and £42,000 come entirely from
the Imperial Exchequer, and pass through
our accounts. The question was raised as
to the £50,000, and where it appeared. There
was no desire to conceal this item or treat it
with any degree of ambiguity. As a matter
of fact, it was a decision arrived at almost
within a few hours of the statement being
presented to Parliament, and the item
which it is included is one of £150,000 under
the heading of payments against provision for
Supplementary Estimates. This £50,000, as
you will see, becomes a charge upon the
finances of the Northern Parliament. As
you are aware, the sum of £500,000 towards
unemployment relief was a free gift to the
Northern Parliament from the Imperial
Parliament to show their desire to try to do
something to alleviate the feeling of unrest
in Belfast, which maybe was the root of a
great deal of this discontent and outrage
with which we have become so sadly familiar
with in the last few months in Belfast.
in
It was a free gift on the part of the
Imperial Parliament, and they were able to
dictate the terms upon which that gift should
be made. My right hon. Friend the Minister
of Labour is administering that fund on the
lines laid down to you, but it was stipulated
at the time the gift was made that that fund
should only be made available for Belfast
and the immediately contiguous neighbourhood. The Cabinet of Northern Ireland have
realised that these difficulties which exist in
Belfast exist, though possibly not in SO
acute a form, in other portions of the Six
Counties, and they decided it would be right
from their own funds to grant a sum of
£50,000 to be administered in as nearly as
possible the same manner as the £500,000
given by the Imperial Parliament, but that
this sum from the loan fund should be
available throughout the Six Counties in
Northern Ireland. As regards some items
that were criticised I think the criticism of
these details falls or should fall more conveniently to such debate as may take place
on the different Estimates, and it would not
be right to go into matters of minor detail
at the present time.
There was one question raised, however,
and that was as to how the savings to which
we refer in our statemnt were arrived at
owing to the fact that we have no figures
of a previous period with which an exact
comparison can be made. I explained in introducing the estimate for the Ministry of
Finance that although we had no figures of
our own every care had been taken to endeavour to ascertain from Dublin and from
Westminster the cost of conducting the Irish
Services in previous years. These are capable
of ascertainment, but not with any degree of
precision, but they have been taken out as
carefully as the conditions permit, and it
is with figures taken out in that way as compared with our own estimate that any figure
as to savings or otherwise is arrived at.
Generally speaking, I should like to refer
once more to the sentiments expressed by my
hon. Friend the Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn), and I can only assure him that
that patriotic spirit which he has shown in
refraining from any criticism which might
tend to embarrass or in any way hamper the
Government in dealing with the more serious
issues with which we are immediately confronted will be as a spur to us to endeavour
to respect his wishes in other respects, and
that is that every possible economy that can
be effected should be studied, and I hope
achieved, in carrying out the expenditure
which we are now budgeting to you.
Members: Hear, hear).

675 Referees and Arbitrators Bill. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. BARBOUR: The object of this Bill,
the Referees and Arbitrators (Procedure)
Bill, is two-fold. Sections 33 and 34 of the
Finance (1909-10) Act, 1909, provide for the
hearing of appeals in regard to Mineral
Rights Duty and Estate Duty by Referees
taken from a panel of persons appointed by
a Reference Committee. Article 9 of the
Government of Ireland (Adaptation of Taxing
Acts) Order provides that there shall be a
separate Reference Committee and a separate
panel of Referees for Northern Ireland. The
Reference Committee for Northern Ireland
shall consist of the Lord Chief Justice and
the President of the Surveyors' Institution,
or some member of the Council of the Institution nominated by the President, having
special knowledge of valuation in Northern
Ireland. The Referees appointed need only be
part-time officers and are paid by fees.
Difficulties have arisen in regard to one of
the qualifications of the representative of the
Surveyors' Institution, viz., that he should be
a member of the Council of the Surveyors'
Institution; and Section 1 (2) of the Bill
makes provision that the person appointed
need not necessarily be a member of the
Council. As steps have already been taken
by the Lord Chief Justice to appoint a panel
of Referees, the Bill makes provision so as to
give covering authority for these appointments without going to the inconvenience of
reappointment.
a
Section 1 of the Acquisition of Land
(Assessment of Compensation) Act, 1919,
provides for the appointment of official
Arbitrators, to be taken from a panel of
persons appointed by a Reference Committee.
These arbitrators arbitrate on questions in
regard to compensation for land taken over
by Public Departments. As in the case of
the arrangements under the Finance Act,
a separate Reference Committee and
separate panel of arbitrators, similarly
constituted and with the same qualifications,
are set up for Northern Ireland. The arbitrators under the Acquisition of Land Act
must be whole-time officers, but in Northern
Ireland there is insufficient work to occupy
the time of one official, either under this
Act or combined with the duties under the
Finance Act. The Bill, therefore, proposes
to remove the qualifications in regard to the
whole-time, and provides for remuneration by
way of fees instead of salaries. Moreover,
the distinction which exists in the original
Acts and which has been maintained in the
Adaptation Orders under the Government of
Ireland Act between these two Reference
Committees and their subsidiary arbitrators
or referees is now abolished, one committee
and one set of referees being made to do
duty for both. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
whole House for to-morrow.
Live Stock Breeding Bill, 676
Live Stock Breeding Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read the Second
time."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): The subject of this Bill
has been before the country for a very long
time. When the Government started the
Department of Agriculture and spent a lot
of money in the country it was found that
the full results of all their expenditure
could not be obtained. Sires were allowed
to produce stock that could not be sold in
any fair or market in the country, and as
long ago as 1906 the matter was brought
forward by the Council of Agriculture. The
resolution of the Council of Agriculture was
very much on the lines of this Bill. In
1907 and in 1909 it was again brought
forward, but they found the only chance
they had of securing the object in view was
bringing in a Bill for stallions only.
They tried that, but the difficulty of getting
time for Irish business in the House of
Commons in London was so great that it
was unavailing. They continued to press
for it. In 1918, owing to England, Scotland
and Ireland joining together they brought
in the Horse Breeding Act, and they tried
to get the Bill which the Ministry is bringing in to-day at the same time, but it was
not possible. They pressed again in 1919,
and it was thought then that the war being
over there was a chance of getting it passed,
but they found there was too much business.
In 1921 they pressed again. It has been
six times pressed by all the Boards of Agriculture. They tried to get the three other
Boards to co-operate, and there was a good
deal of progress made in the year 1921, but
it was again found that the difficulty of
getting an Irish Act pure and simple through
the House of Commons was too much. In
1922 we found the opinion of this country,
when we had a Government of our own,
was so strong that the Ministry, although
they had a great amount of other work on
hands, were forced to consult all the various
Committees in the country. We consulted
every kind of Committee, the Royal Ulster
Agricultural Society, the Ballymena Agricultural Society, the North-West Agricultural Society in Derry, and the Ulster
Farmers' Union. They every one of them
pressed us to bring in this Bill on the lines
suggested by them. It was then put before
the Cattle Advisory Committee which has
been set up by the Ministry, and also the
Consultative Committee on general agricultural subjects, and they made some
suggestions. It was then put before a full
meeting of the Executive of the Ulster
Farmers' Union, and I am glad to say they
went through it section by section, and my
hon. Friend, one of the Members for Derry
677 Live Stock Breeding Bill-
Second Reading. 678
25 MAY 1922.
(Mr. Mark) made some exceedingly useful
suggestions which we were able to incorporate in our Bill.
Of course, it entrenches a little bit, some
people may say, on the liberty of the subject,
but we have the Horse Breeding Act to work
upon, and we have no intention of putting
it in force severely or to do any harm to
any man. On the Continent it has been
in force in Switzerland for many years, and
there is never any trouble about it. There
is no trouble about the Horse Breeding Act
at the present time, and I am certain when
this Act is worked in a sympathetic manner
by the Ministry, which they intend to do,
and with the full assistance of the various
agricultural societies and the various County
Committees that no one will be injured at
all in any shape or form. It is not meant
to hit any man who is trying to benefit
the country; but what we do want to stop
is the indifferent farmer using a bull which
is really more like a goat than a bull or
anything else of that sort.
a
I believe this Bill will improve the price
of our store cattle enormously, and give
springing heifers that can be bought. I
know men about the country who when
they get a lot of heifers send them to
England or sell them to their neighbours
and have no calves for their own rearing.
They do not care twopence what sort of bull
it is that runs with those heifers, and the
produce is not at all to the benefit of Ireland
or to the benefit of the purchaser of these
cattle. This is very well-known fact,
and we are determined if possible to stop
that work. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The restrictions we are putting on are very
moderate. A person who owns or has control of a bull is subject to a fine not exceeding £20 unless the bull is licensed or he has
a permit. The licence can be obtained at
a fee, and a copy can be given to a man
at a fee not exceeding 5/-. The fee will be
about 2/6 an animal. Surely no one can
complain about that. Anyone who wishes
to fatten a bull and only keeps it for that
purpose can get a permit for a fee not exceeding 2/-. We do not intend to charge
than, I
suppose, 1/-, but there
must be some small fee for a bull kept for
that purpose. Anyone who is in control of
a bull must produce a licence if he is
required to do so, or he is subject to a
penalty not exceeding £5. Anyone who has
got a bull and does not submit it to inspection or does not produce the licence and show
it to the person going to him and asking
for it, is also subject to a fine not exceeding
£5. That is under Section 6.
obstruct a man entering your premises to
see if the bull is registered-we have an
official told off to do such a thing-you are
subject on summary conviction by Section
7 to a fine not exceeding £20, and if you
more
If you
alter a licence or forge one you are subject
to the same penalty.
The Ministry does not propose that this
should be enforced until the 1st January,
which is the appointed day for having these
licences. That gives time enough for farmers
round the country in backward districts to
acquire the knowledge that they must have
licences for their bulls, or if they have a
bull of a sort to get rid of it, or act as
required in the Bill.
Mr. MARK: I would like at the outset to
congratulate the Ministry on the pluck they
displayed in bringing this Bill before the
House. I know it has been long in expectation in various parts of the United
Kingdom, but for Northern Ireland to be
the first to have such a Bill says a great
deal in favour of the Ministry we have here.
Undoubtedly the Bill is a crying necessity
at the present time. Only last week the
need was glaringly brought before my notice.
A neighbour of mine who has the best herd
of shorthorn cattle in the three Kingdoms,
at least in Ireland, with bulls costing up to
£1,000, saw the other morning that his
neighbouring farmer had let the grazing of
his farm to a cattle dealer, who had put in
a lot of blue, and grey, and black bulls
beside his heifers. If that sort of thing
can go on I do not know what damage will
not take place in the future. However,
we have now got a Bill which will brand
such a man as a criminal, and we can get
him fined at a court of summary jurisdiction.
The Minister of Agriculture rightly states
he has the support of the farming community
all over the Six Counties. The matter has
been brought before the various breeding
societies, agricultural societies, and show
committees in Ulster, and has been
thoroughly approved by the Ulster Farmers'
Union. I have spent, as he says, a whole
day going over this Bill in company with
some other farmers. We suggested some
improvements which we thought might be
put into the Bill, and the Ministry at once
agreed and have done everything in their
power to do what is fair and reasonable.
Some people may think it is not quite
drastic enough. Some may think it interferes
too much with the liberty of the person,
but I think, properly administered, it will
be an excellent Act. I hope the Ministry
will see it is lived up to and is not more
honoured in the breach than in the observance. There are some things in it not
quite complete, but I see powers have been
reserved for the making of regulations for
the carrying out of the Bill. One thing I
notice is that the Bill does not say when
a calf becomes a bull and when a man
becomes responsible for having a bull.
Probably the Regulations will set all those
matters right. The Ministry will have power
to make those Regulations, and I am sure

[Mr. Mark]
they will make them in conjunction with,
and with the approval of, the other bodies
concerned. I am sure the Act will have
the support of the farmers and will be lived
up to in the future.
Dr. MORRISON: I want to say a word or
two of approval in regard to this Bill. I
want in the first place, if you will allow me,
to state my claim to speak on this matter.
I think it is questioned if I have any authority to speak on agricultural matters and it
is said when I do speak on this subject I
should go lecturing. I am not ashamed
that in the last twenty or twenty-five years
I have been lecturing to farmers on these
matters. The Minister of Agriculture will
tell you he received a communication from
the Committee of one of the biggest cooperative societies in County Derry, representing a turn-over of £30,000 a year, telling
him on behalf of six hundred farmers that
I was a man who could give advice on agricultural matters. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Therefore, I hope without any
suspicion of jealousy to add my little experience to the collective wisdom of this
House without offence.
The Minister of Agriculture has said this
Bill might infringe on the liberty of the
subject. In this matter of the liberty of
the subject, we have listened to far too much
humbug and nonsense. The liberty of the
subject must always be subject to the welfare
of the community. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
There need be no apology for restricting any Act that has a tendency to
injure the community. The Bill is admirable
in nearly every respect; but I think in regard
to this question of fines, any man who is
familiar with what goes on in the administration of justice in our Petty Sessions
districts knows that the weakness of the
administration there is the leniency of the
bench of magistrates, a leniency that in my
opinion is becoming a crime. Punishment
has no value if it has not deterrent action,
and to inflict fines of 2s. 6d. or 5s. for a
serious offence, or reducing a heavy fine, or
recommending its reduction is very bad
policy.
What I think should be done in regard to
violations of this Act is that a minimum fine
should be fixed the same as it is in regard
to an offence against the fishery laws of £5.
So for a violation of this Act, there might
be power of appeal or making a recommendation to the Minister of Agriculture and
letting him settle it. Then you put it into
the right hands. If you leave it in the
hands of the magistrates, even if it was a
fine not exceeding £20, they will say, "Well,
now, he is poor, we will reduce the fine."
It is very easy being generous at other
people's expense, and they may regard the
circumstances with geniality and sympathy
and reduce the fine to 10s.
I would fix it
at £10, and make the recommendation subject
to the approval of the Minister of Agriculture. I think the Bill is a useful one.
It is much needed. I am glad to know the
Ministry have taken it up, and so far as I
know, speaking with my limited knowledge,
and on behalf of the important community
of farmers whom I represent, I beg leave to
commend it to the House.
Mr. M'BRIDE: I would like, on behalf
of the community which I represent, to
thank the Minister of Agriculture (Mr.
Archdale) for the introduction of this Bill.
I am glad he has had the manliness to intro
duce such a measure because the breeding
of inferior cattle has been detrimental to
this country for many years past. I hope
with the hon. Member for Derry (Mr. Mark)
and the hon. Member for the University
(Dr. Morrison) that once it is passed it will
be thoroughly carried out. Leniency, as
the hon. Member (Dr. Morrison) said, would
be a very great disadvantage at the present
moment. The use of inferior animals for
breeding purposes has caused the country
to suffer the loss of many thousands of
pounds in the past. In the locality from
which I come many inferior animals have
been thrown on the country by farmers,
and because they are cheap people go to
them and breed cattle which are neither
useful to the farmers themselves nor to the
people who are depending upon them to
bring in money. Therefore I would urge
upon the Minister of Agriculture that, now
that he has introduced this Bill, he will see
that it is thoroughly carried out, and that
there will be no leniency for any infringement of the law.
Mr. LYNN: Like my hon. Friend the
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
it is with some trepidation that I rise in
face of the hon. Member for Derry (Mr.
Mark) to speak on agriculture. I can plead
that I have been interested in Agriculture
since I have been interested in anything,
and I am hoping some day to induce the
Minister of Agriculture to arrange a contest
between the hon. Member for Londonderry
(Mr. Mark) and myself with regard to agricultural matters. I have risen now simply
to say how cordially I approve of this
measure. It is not one of those Bills which
lend themselves to oratory or purple passages, but it is one of those very sound
practical measures which when carried out
will add immensely to the wealth of the
community for which we are responsible.
As the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Archdale)
has pointed out, attempts have been made
again and again to get such a measure passed
through the Imperial House, and if it had
been passed we would have gained enormously. I have been told by practical

CONSTABULARY BILL.
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
Ordered, That Clause I. (Establishment of
Royal Ulster Constabulary) stand part of the
Bill.
Clause II. (Appointment, Removal, Pay,
and Pensions of Constabulary).
Sub-section. (2) The power conferred on
the Minister by the Constabulary and
Police (Ireland) Act, 1919, as applied and
modified by this Act, to make orders as to,
and prescribe the rates and scales of, the
pay, pensions and allowances of members of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary shall extend
so as to enable the Minister to provide by
any such order for recognising, for the purposes of such pay, pensions and allowances,
the rank, period of service or record of any
such member in the Royal Irish Constabulary, Special Constabulary, or other police
force specified in such Order.
Mr. DONALD: I beg to move, on page 2,
line 35, after the word
order "
(at the end
of Sub-section 2), to insert the words:
"It shall be lawful for the Minister to
make regulations as to the government pay,
allowance, pensions, clothing, expenses and
conditions of service of the members of the
Police Force of Northern Ireland, and the
Police Authority shall comply with the regulations so made."
In moving this amendment I do so, as I
stated on a previous occasion in this House.
with the object of making this Bill as simple
and as complete as possible and with a view
to assisting the Government in the administration of the Police Force. That is why I
put down this amendment. It is a draft
amendment, and although it may be said that
it gives the Minister further powers, I contend that practically the whole of these
powers should be placed in the hands of the
Minister. I have listened to many debates
in another place when a similar Bill was before that House, and I do not see anything
objectionable in including this amendment
in the clause, and I hope my hon. and
learned Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary
to the Ministry of Home Affairs, will accept
it. It may be said that we have regulations,
and that these matters come under the
regulations. I contend that this House
should be responsible for the legislation that
passes through it dealing with this Police
Force, and that while we are held responsible
for financing the Force, we should also be
responsible for its administration. We have
been told time and again that this House
should legislate in line with the Imperial
Government, and I may say that that is why

Mr. DUFF: I must ask the indulgence of

for the purpose of the Government as distinct
from the local or civic requirements, a considerable number of Constabulary will be
necessary for work which should not be imposed as a charge upon the local authorities.
It, therefore, must be obvious that these considerations should be taken into account when
the free quota is being fixed, but our difficulty
is that there is nothing in the Bill to show
on what principle this free quota will be
fixed, and we do not know whether it will be
fixed by geographical area, per caput, or by
taxable capacity. At the present time Belfast
is the exception to the other Six Counties. I
am not sure whether Londonderry is also
an exception, but leaving out Londonderry
the city of Belfast is the only city which is
at present paying a very large special sum
in addition to its taxation for the upkeep
of Constabulary, and I am informed, and
further I know from some bitter experience
during the past few years, that the city of
Belfast has had to fight year after year on

free quota. The actual circumstances at the
moment are that Belfast's free quota is 900,
and we have to pay at the present time for
322 extra men. I am instructed that under
this Bill there is nothing to prevent a similar
state of affairs happening in the future.
There is nothing to show that the whole of
the 2.718 men will be allocated as free quotas
(for the Six Counties, and my remark yesterday on the Second reading that the mobile
column can only under this Bill be something
like 155 was not correct. It was a very

speech on the House, and I am going to start

with Section 3. It really has some
bearing on it, but the bearing that I wanted

2 in Section 4 made us suspicious of

more than that to take off £60,000. If you

that we have very good reason to look into

through a very severe mill, and you will have

cific in some of the questions we ask.
We are going to ask a very simple and innocent question. You mention additional force
in the second part of Sub-section 1 of Section 4.
We would like to know where is such an additional force to be drawn from? At one time,
when the Royal Irish Constabulary consisted
of 10,000 men, there were supposed to be free
quetas given all over Ireland, but the strange
thing was that they only distributed 9,000 of
the 10,000 as free quotas, leaving 1,000 as a
burden on the Force. What was done was
this, that a considerable number of that spare
1,000 was shifted into the City of Belfast, and
the actual reason given by the official in Dublin Castle was they did it to economise.
stead of bearing the burden of 1,000 men they
thought they would try a few of them on Belfast, and they shifted the burden of a considerable proportion of that 1,000 spare men on
to the City of Belfast. Well, we are afraid from
a careful reading of this Bill that it will be
within the power of any official or of the
administrator-because after all, mind you,
you may make a statutory rule, you may
Inmake a statute, you may get promises from
the men who are passing this statute, and
after that the administration of the statute is
in the hands of entirely different men,
who
are guided not by the promises of the Ministers when putting the Bill through, but by
the actual terms of the Act that they are
administering, and we would like to know
where this additional force is to be drawn
from?

like to know. You say here, when a free
quota is to be charged to anyone,

the general Bill I want to make-

Sub-section 4 says,

We feel that in all the Clauses there is an inordinate power given to the Minister. The

question, where the additional force would
come from as distinct from the quota? The
additional force, as I understand it, will
first of all be drawn from the reserve force,

there is a quota in a county which is not
necessary, part of it may be drawn away and
may be used as an additional force if
another part of the country requires its
services, but I should say that it would only
be on occasions when there was a very considerable need for the force arising from
difficult circumstances in the area that
wanted the force for the time being.

Oral Answers to Questions.
HEALTH AND UNEMPLOYMENT
INSURANCE.
(1) Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Labour:-
(1) What are the amounts contributed by
employers and employees, and also by County
Councils, during the past year ending 28th
February for each of the Six Counties in
Northern Ireland-
(a) For Health Insurance?
(b) For Unemployment?
(2) What amounts have been expended under
each head?
(3) What amounts have workers received?
(4) What amounts have been spent on
salaries and administration?
(5) What balances are in hands of Approved
Societies?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I regret that I am not in a position
to give figures for the year ending February
28th, 1922, since my Department was not
responsible for the administration of the
funds during that period, and no separate
figures were compiled for Northern Ireland.
I propose however to circulate in the official
report of to-day's debate a statement of the
estimated expenditure for an average year,
but I should say that our experience of these
funds is short, and our first estimates may not
be as accurate as they would be with longer
experience. No separate figures have ever
been compiled for the different counties, but
figures associated with each Employment
Exchange could be given if desired.
It is not possible at present to state the
amount of the reserves of Approved Societies
until the valuation of the Societies has been
completed.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Arising out of that,
has there not been a valuation since these
things came into force? Can the right hon.
Gentleman say where these balances are
invested, and what is the rate of interest?
Mr. ANDREWS: I believe the last
valuation available is 1918. That audit, I
understand, was only completed a few days
ago, and has not been circulated yet. I
regret to say that these audits, which are
conducted by the Imperial Ministry, are very
slow, so far as the publication of the returns
is concerned. As regards the rate of interest,
that has varied recently, according to the rise
and fall of interest, but a large proportion of
the funds of those Approved Societies are
invested in War Loan.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that, may
I ask the right hon. Gentleman if a Bill will
be introduced in this House shortly on the
question of Unemployment Insurance, when
he will have an opportunity of giving us facts
and figures?
Mr. ANDREWS:-I do not quite understand the hon. Members' question. As regards
Unemployment Insurance-
Mr. DONALD: Health Insurance.
Mr. ANDREWS: We propose to proceed
on parallel lines with Great Britain for the
present, and if a Bill is introduced in the
Imperial House dealing with Health Insurance we will introduce a somewhat similar
Bill here. There is a Bill being considered
in the Imperial House dealing with the
transfer of medical certificates. The liability
at the present time is attached to the taxpayers, and the Approved Societies in Great
Britain have taken that obligation on
themselves. I am pleased to be able to say
that the Approved Societies here have agreed
with me to take upon themselves a similar
obligation. That will mean a saving to
Northern Ireland of £28,000 a year; but until
the matter has been further dealt with in the
Imperial House I do not propose to take
action here.

TRAINING COLLEGES FOR PRIMARY
SCHOOL TEACHERS.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Education if the Ministry of Education,
whilst proposing to establish a Training
College for Primary School Teachers within
the Northern Area, has entered into an
arrangement to recognise and subsidise a
Training College, situated within the Free
State, which is also denominational in its
character; if this will not be prejudicial to
the proposed Northern Training College,
lessen the number of students who will avail
themselves of it, and necessitate a larger
capitation grant for their training than
would otherwise be required, and act as an
incentive to other religious bodies to claim
that preferential treatment shall be given to
them also; if he will state why the Ministry
has adopted a policy of this kind without
reference to Parliament, and why, in partieular, it has done so before receiving the

THE PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
M'Keown):
(1) It is presumed that the reference in the
first part of the question is to the Church of
Ireland Training College, Kildare Place,
Dublin, one of the recognised Training
Colleges for National teachers hitherto in
connection with the Commissioners
National Education. The Ministry proposes
to continue the arrangements with this
of

College, whereby candidates from all parts of

INCREASE OF RENTS ACT.
3. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of Home
Affairs if the Government is considering the
introduction of legislation to modify the Increase of Rents Act, in view of the considerable reduction which has already been
affected in the wages of the artisan classes.
.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates) The question of introducing
legislation restricting rents or modifying existing Acts has been carefully considered by
the Government of Northern Ireland.
The Government have had strong representations made to them from various sources
and interests, from which it would appear
that any legislation, if introduced, would be
of a most controversial character, The
Government also feel that any further legislation on this question might act as a check
to private enterprise, and they feel that it
is only by free and unrestricted building
operations that rents will ultimately be
lowered.
The Government of Northern Ireland have
kept in close touch with the Imperial Government on this important subject, and understand that that Government have decided
after careful consideration not to introduce
any further legislation on the subject of rent
restriction.
It appears to the Government of Northern
Ireland that, in the present condition of
trade and industry, any differential legislation in Northern Ireland and Great Britain
on matters of this sort might be prejudicial
to the best financial interests of Northern
Ireland.
In all the circumstances, therefore, it has
been decided that it would be inadvisable to
introduce any legislation on this subject.
Mr. DONALD: Is my right hon. Friend
aware that it would have been a very good
job if there had never been any legislation on
this question, and then the matter could have
righted itself in a proper way? That is where
the Government failed at the beginning.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Motor Vehicle Races [S] Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read the Second time." (Sir
Dawson Bates.)
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of the
present Bill is to confer upon local authorities powers to enable them to close roads in
their particular areas for the purpose of holding Motor Races for a period not exceeding
three days in one year. It will be within the
recollection of hon. Members of this House
that in 1913 the famous Gordon Bennett Race
was held in the South of Ireland. To enable
races to be held on that occasion a special
Act had to be passed, but that only remained
in force for one year. With regard to the Bill
itself, the public are safeguarded, inasmuch
as that, under Clause 1 sub-Section (2), any
Order made by a County Council must contain
the necessary provisions approved by the
Ministry of Home Affairs for the purpose of
protecting the public, and no Order can be
made without the consent of the Ministry. I
would suggest that this Bill should meet with
the approval of the House, because it does not
impose any additional burden either upon the
taxpayers or the ratepayers. Any expense will
have to be borne by the promoters of the particular enterprise.
I am sure that hon. Members will agree
that as a Government we should do everything
possible to help to develop tourist traffic in
the Six Counties, and not only will races of
this kind help the tourist traffic generally,
but, by doing so, will help hotel keepers, farmers, and others, and will generally bring
money into the country. It is estimated that
something like £200,000 was spent annually in
the Isle of Man in connection with the races
held there. I am sorry it will not be practicable to hold these races in the immediate
future, but I hope, before long, when more
lawful conditions are resumed within our
area, we will have them. I can only say that
so far as this Government is concerned we
intend to support everything of this kind
which will bring money into the country. I
beg to move.
709 Motor Vehicles Races Bill.

get a reduction in the taxation of motor

measure, and I do not want to offer any opposition, but I think my right hon. Friend

as to when he gives permission for these races.
I think it should not be given in the near
future, at any rate, until the country becomes
a lttle more settled. I am very pleased to see

in order that Northern Ireland may benefit
by such competitions. We are all lovers of

If I may say so, I think the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) made a very wise

With regard to the question raised by the

JOINT NURSING AND MIDWIVES
COUNCIL [S] BILL.
Order for Second reading read
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read the Second
time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to amalgamate the Joint Nursing
Council for Northern Ireland and the Central
Midwives Board for Northern Ireland. The
Midwives Act of 1918 established a Board for
the whole of Ireland, and in 1919 an Act was
passed establishing a Joint Nursing Council
for Ireland. These Councils correspond generally to the General Medical Council and the
recently established Dental Board. These
Boards are not in any sense Government
departments.
are
They
entirely selfsupporting, and the expenses are defrayed
out of the fees of applicants who seek to be
registered under the Act. Following on the
passing of the Home Rule Act, and the
necessary transfers being made, two separate
Boards had to be set up for the Northern
area. Having regard to the limited means
which these bodies possess, it has been felt
that there should be an amalgamation of
both bodies and thereby save a great deal
of unnecessary expense caused by the duplication of the various offices.
After very
careful consultation with the various
interests affected the constitution of the new
body has been worked out, and I think it
will be found that it allows for very fair
and adequate representation of the interests
concerned.
Taking the Bill in detail, Clause 1 provides
for the formation of the Council. It is a
corporate body and will have a seal. Subsection (2) of Clause 1 sets out the constitution. This only applies to the first three
years, that is the constitution on its formation. Four persons shall be appointed by
the Ministry, of whom one shall be a medical
officer of the Ministry, one a person appointed
by the Ministry after consultation with the
County Councils and County Boroughs, and
two registered medical practitioners, who
shall be appointed after consultation with the
various medical organisations. The remaining six shall be appointed by the
Ministry, and they shall all be nurses, but
two of them must have special qualifications
in regard to midwifery. These will all be
appointed after consultation with the various
nurses' organisations. The first Council
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
will remain in office for three years, and
future Councils will exist for five years, but
the future Councils will be entirely elected,
except in regard to two of the officers, namely,
the medical officer of the Ministry and
the representative of the County Councils and
the County Boroughs; that is to say, the
two registered medical practitioners will be
elected by the registered medical men and
women in the Six Counties, and the six
nurses will be elected by the registered nurses
in the area. Sub-section (3) is a formal
section to enable the seal to be approved, and
sub-section (4) is consequential, putting an
end to the existing Councils. Clause 2 is for
the purpose of protecting nurses who are
already registered. I do not think there is
anything further to which I can draw the
attention of hon. Members. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the whole
House for to-morrow.

MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £40,963 be
granted to his Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge that will
come in course of payment during the year
ending 31st March, 1923, for the salaries
and expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture."
The MINISTER of AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The Estimate for the Ministry of
Agriculture is divided into three sections-
No. 1, the salaries and expenses, which we are
taking now; No. 2, Agricultural Services,
which were passed the other day; and No. 3,
the Surveys, which will come on after this.
In No. 1, which you will see at page 84, the
whole salaries are set out, and the estimate
which we made up till the 31st March last,
when the services were not properly transferred, shows that we were almost exactly
correct. We find, now that we have them in
working order, that they are almost the same
as they were in March last. In sub-section
"B-Travelling, Subsistence, and Removal
Expenses," less than half is for the travelling
of officers on departmental work, and the
larger half is for the expenses of removal of
officials from Dublin and other parts of the
country. Their retention expenses will, of
course, only be for this year, and that is very
carefully supervised by my right hon. Friend
the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock).
Printing and postage stamps too are
expensive, but I would ask the Committee to
bear in mind that when setting up a new
Department there is a tremendous amount of
printing required, and you want it afterwards. You have to get all the new forms,
all the circulars, and all the leaflets which
we issue all round the country, and that
estimate, of course, will afterwards be much
less. One thing of great difficulty is the
collection of agricultural statistics. That
accounts for the printing being so much. Up
to four years ago the police in the Six
Counties collected the statistics. That source
of collection is now unavailable. The services
of the police will not be available owing to
the present state of the country, and we have
to send 400,000 forms to all the farmers asking them to send particulars to us. It is one
of the most important parts of the work of
the Ministry to be sure that the whole area
is cropped. The Government have to know
exactly what the farmers are doing about the
country, and to be sure that some crops most
necessary for the feeding of the country are
not allowed to go down altogether, or that
some such thing as flax, which hon. Gentlemen are interested in, is not allowed to go
down. We want to know exactly the area
and quantity. It is a thing we take particulars about, and we are sending the forms
to every farmer we can think of.
As to forestry, we are only taking over the
work which was being carried on before un
this country. We are not having an expert
head forester, as we have had before, as we
do not think the Six Counties are big enough.
The forestry we have to do is not large
enough to employ the services of a highly
capable expert, but we have arranged with
the Forestry Commission in London to get
the loan occasionally of a man to come over
and see that our work is being carried on in
a proper way. We are not acting extravagantly, and are not losing money. You will
see that is one of the things that we get
receipts for. We have at the present time
the biggest collection of young trees in the
United Kingdom. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). We hope to get a considerable sum of
money from the sale of these in England,
Scotland and other places in a short time. I
do not think there is anything more I can
say. I will be very glad to answer any questions on Estimate No. 1. I beg to move.

Mr. M'GUFFIN: I want to offer a few observations with regard to this measure.
I am
not going to criticise its principles or its
details. With that I have got nothing to do,
but I do want to say that it is rather surprising that in the grave condition of affairs
which exists at the moment this House should
be content to discuss a Bill which merely
makes provision for pleasure and enjoyment.
It seems as if we were oblivious to the real
situation in which we are living. I do not
mean to say it is true of the Prime Minister,
but it is true of us as a House if we discuss
things of this kind in the midst of so many
urgent difficulties. I cannot see what urgency
there can be in a matter of this sort, and I
do say that when a Bill such as this is about
to be introduced in the House, the House
is entitled to have the Bill circulated. I have
brought this matter before the House on another occasion, and I have shown that in a
particular instance it was intended to read a
Bill a Second time before it was printed.
With regard to the Constabulary Bill I
pointed out that we were entitled to receive
a copy of it and it was agreed that it would
be circulated. I am not sure whether my hon.
Friend, the Junior Whip, gave me that prɔmise, but until this moment I have not received a copy of it. The same applies to the
Bills we are discussing here to-day. We have
not had an opportunity of looking into them
to see what principle is involved. So far as
the details are concerned it may be that we
will be able to agree with them, but the
main and important point is the Second
Reading. It is at that stage that the principle of the Bill is examined and it is upon
the principle of the Bill that it is frequently
defeated, and it gives us absolutely no chance
when we are asked to pass a Bill like the
Constabulary Bill without having it in our
hands. From the remarks made by the hon.
Member for North Belfast I understood that
certain suggestions would be incorporated in
the draft of the Bill, but apparently no
notice was taken of them and we have not
had an opportunity of seeing how far the
recommendations contained in the Police
Committee's report were adopted or recognised. I invite the Prime Minister, if he is
disposed to do so, to give the House an assurance that when a Bill does not imply
urgency it will be circulated sufficiently early
to give us an opportunity of examining its
principles and seeing how far we can subscribe to or support them. I think this is
a very important matter.
It is the usage
which is observed on the other side. There

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James

has been raised by both my hon. Friends
(Mr. M'Guffin and Mr. Donald) first? The
Bill in question, as I suppose they are both
aware, followed exactly the same course as
was followed in the Imperial Parliament.
In other words, it was introduced in the
soon as the Senate was
Senate, and as
finished with the Bill it came to this House.
It is quite true that the period between the
Bill being dealt with by the Senate and its
coming to this House was very short; but we
thought that, on the whole, as the Bill was
non-contentious, and also as it was fulfilling
a pledge given by my right hon. Friend (Sir
Dawson Bates) to the motor industry-if I
may use that broad expression-it would be
to the advantage of the House to go straight

go on, we naturally took the Committee
stage and the Third Reading to-day. I can

think the hon. Member (Mr. Crawford) did

reading of the Bill. On a previous occasion

What appeals to me most of all is the organised attempt which is being made to prevent

I am not quite sure what is meant by
racing. I have never made a bet in my life,
not even on a horse, or on a Parliamentary
election, which is much more exciting,

efficiency of engines; to see how quickly

i3 one which ought to be fostered in Northern

think the Government are to be congratulated

of the House, and I hope the House, in passing

Geo. 5, c. 96), 2 (Provisions as to Register of
Nurses and Midwives Roll), 3, (Interpretation), 4 (Short Title), stand part of the Bill.

the Bill.

SUPPLY.
ESTIMATES-1922-23.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
Class 2. No. 8.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £735,864 be
granted to His Majesty to defray the charge
which will come in course of payment
during the year ending 31st March, 1923, for
the salaries and expenses of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary."
Sir DAWSON BATES: In presnting this
Estimate for the expenses of the Royal Contabulary for the remainder of the financial
year, I would like, before proceeding to make
a summary of the various items in the Estimate, to express the great regret which I,
and I am sure every Member of this House,
and indeed every Irishman, feels at the
of
passing
that great and historic
Force the Royal Irish Canstabulary,
Force, which for close on
cause of law
century has upheld the
and justice impartially and fearlessly. While
we all have that feeling of regret, at the
same time this event has given to Ulster an
a
opportunity of having her own Police Force,
and I feel certain that that Force will carry
on with the same efficiency the work of the
Royal Irish Constabulary, and that the great
traditions of the Royal Irish Constabulary,
from which the new Force will largely spring,
will be safe in the keeping of our new Force.
Hon. Members are aware that His Gracious
Majesty has been pleased to bestow upon our
new Constabulary Force the title "The
Royal Ulster Constabulary." That Force
will never disgrace its name, and, composed
as it will be of all that is best of the Royal
Irish Constabulary and our own Special
Constabulary it will, I venture to say, make
a Force that any country might be proud of.
It only rests with the people of this province
to give the new Constabulary their support
and goodwill. Without this, no matter how
excellent a Police Force may be, it must
suffer and its efficiency be impaired. I think
I can promise for the people of Ulster and
for this Government that our new Police
Force will never be subjected to the treatment which the Royal Irish Constabulary
received. (Hon Members: Hear, hear ").
With regard to the Estimate it is, to a
large extent, self-explanatory. As hon.
Members are aware, we are simply continuing, at any rate for the moment, the existing
Royal Irish Constabulary Estimate. To take
any other action for the present would be
impossible. Better adhere to the old tried
machinery than make hasty, and perhaps
disastrous changes. Any modifications
which we may require later on, and which
may be found desirable, can be made gradually from time to time.
Provision has been made to meet the
various recommendations of the Police Committee. It will be observed that in the
Headquarters and Depot Staff we have a
number of redundant officers. These are for
the purpose of meeting the very heavy additional work which must necessarily be accomplished in setting up and training a new
Force, and to meet the emergencies of the
present grave situation in Ulster.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Have the redundant officers been engaged on the understanding that
their positions are only temporary ?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly not. I
will deal with that question afterwards.
While the R.I.C. who join the Royal Ulster
Constabulary will be, of course, trained, it
will be remembered that at least one-third
of the new Police Force, which is drawn
from our Special Constabulary, will require
a period of training in technical police
duty. Once the Police Force is running cn
normal lines, and the condition of the
country becomes more normal, I hope it will
be possible to dispense with the services of
certain of these officers indicated for this
special purpose, and they will be absorbed
in the Police Force with a consequent reduction in the numbers.
Royal Ulster Constabulary. 726
Supply-
30 MAY 1922.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman in what way they will be
absorbed. I cannot understand it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
will understand that we are taking over a
certain number of the old R.I.C. officers who,
in course of time will go out on pension,
some sooner and some later.
I might point out that we have decided a
City Commissioner should be appointed for
the City of Derry. We feel that the importance of Derry, lying on the North-West of
our Province, warrants that such an appointment should be made.
It is impossible in this year's Estimate to
forecast with precision the amount payable
in respect of pay. This depends very largely
upon the number of Royal Irish Constabulary who join the Force and the period of
service which they carry into the new Force.
The amount has been taken, however, on an
average basis. It should be pointed out that
the existing scale of pay only applies to the
first 3,000 men. In many cases the figureshaving regard to the fact that we had no
previous Estimate to go by-have been taken
from an Estimate furnished to us by the
Royal Irish Constabulary authorities with a
proportional increase in respect of the increase in strength. The strength of the
Royal Irish Constabulary in Ulster was something like 2,700; that of the new Force will be
3,000.
The Estimate under the head of Clothing is
taken on a lower basis than that furnished
by the Royal Irish Constabulary, as it is
believed that owing to falling prices
there will be a reduction in this head.
With regard to arms, in the ordinary
course a comparatively small amount is
necessary to cover this cost, but in the
present position of the new Force it is necessary to provide for the complete equipment
of a proportion of the Force.
Under the head of Rent, it will be observed
that a nominal provision has been made for
the establishment of a Depot. It is essential,
in order to ensure that the training of
recruits is carried on under proper conditions, that a suitable Depot should be provided for, and we hope that a Depot will be
established this year. Meanwhile, the work
is being carried on at Newtownards Camp.
Provision will have to be made for the
repairs to barracks. A great deal of necessary maintenance work seems to have been
postponed by the Imperial Government pending the disbandment of the Police Force, and
nothing has impressed me more-and I think
our Prime Minister referred to it himselfwhen going round the country than to see the
condition of the barracks in many of the districts. The Government feel that it must be
one of its first duties to see that the members
of their Force and their families are housed
in a reasonable degree of comfort.
Regarding damages to property, provision
has to be made for the damage done by
members of the Force by accident.
Special Advances.-In the case of members
of the Force being injured and claiming from
the county, it has been found necessary to
advancé, either to the constables or to the
dependants, moneys pending the payment of
the claim to which they may become entitled
under the Malicious Injury Acts.
With regard to the Appropriations in Aid,
this is the amount estimated by the Royal
Irish Constabulary authorities and consists
of payment for ex-police.
With regard to the payment to ex-police,
in accordance with the undertaking given by
my hon. Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary, the Local Authorities will be consulted
before the free quota is fixed.
I have dealt very briefly with the various
items, but I cannot close my remarks without adding a tribute to those already given
to the members of the Police Committee,
whose assistance in this important and
difficult problem-the establishment of a new
Police Force-has been invaluable. I feel I
owe a personal debt of gratitude to them all
for the time and labour which they bestowed
upon this question.
Mr. DUFF: There are just one or two
points that I wish to draw attention to.
under the heading "N-Criminal and
Investigation Expenses." Some of us think
that that amount is totally inadequate to
meet the present situation, and we feel impelled to say to the Ministry that if they
spend four or five times that sum under
present circumstances they will have the
support of almost every business man in the
Six Counties. When we come to the subhead "U-Appropriations in Aid" we reach
a very peculiar situation, because some of
us, who are somewhat new to Parliamentary
matters, may not quite grasp why it is that
an item is put into the Estimates that has
been practically thrown over by the
Ministry. This amount of £30,700 can be
easily calculated by anyone who has been
in contact with the finances of the police
during the past few years. The period for
which those Estimates are calculated is a
period of nine months; but I would suggest
that I am correct when I say the sum of
£30,700 is calculated for a period of six
months, and I can give you my reason.
These Appropriations in Aid are rendered for
six months, and I suggest that this period of
nine months covered by the Estimates only
covers a period of six months so far as this
sum is concerned. When we reason in that
way, from what we might term bitter experience, we again suggest to you that notwithstanding the fact that my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Home Affairs,
and my hon. and learned Friend (Mr.
Megaw) have both given us an undertaking
which we accepted in good faith, it is not
Royal Ulster Constabulary. 728

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Duff]
carried out in the Estimate. During
the Second Reading I made a remark which
drew forth what was a characterisation of
undue suspicion from my right hon. Friend
when I said it was possible a Statute might
be enforced and a promise given by the
Minister during the period when that
Statute was being fixed, and that later on
when the details of the administration were
in the hands of a different set of men
altogether that promise might not receive
the due and thorough weight it deserved.
That appears to me to be exactly the situation as detailed in these Estimates, because
here we have exactly the sum of £30,000
provided for, and duly deducted from the
Estimates. I submit a further statement is
required. Unfortunately, that is a statement
we cannot get, because we cannot pass a
deduction of £30,000 in the Estimates in the
same breath as you would receive an authoritative statement that you never intended to
get it.
But that is actually the position as it
seems to us, and we have gone very closely
into these figures. I would suggest this
£30,700 was perhaps put into the Estimates
before the undertakings were given by the
Ministers. I would further suggest that this
figure was given by the Administrative Staff
of the Royal Irish Constabulary, expecting
innocently-of course, they did not know what
the Ministers were going to say, but stating
that this was the amount which they expected
-to get in reduction of the actual
cost of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
for the nine months. These are the
only remarks I have got to make,
but they are pertinent, I think, and
very clear. I admit they are impossible of
answering without stultifying the Estimates,
but I will assume if we shut our eyes to them
and pass these Estimates that the Minister
will take steps that our unfounded fears and
suspicions will vanish into thin air.
Mr. DONALD: I should like to make one or
two observations under Sub-head "A." I
hope my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson
Bates), when he is recruiting the members of
the old Royal Irish Constabulary for our new
Force, will take into consideration-probably
he has done so-
-the years of service of each
man. He has already said himself it will undoubtedly take time, and that these men
should have a highly technical police training
in order to fit them for the work they will be

service, and twenty-two had less than three
years' service. The point I want to make is
that some of our officers serving to-day called
Specials are just as qualified for Lae
new Force as these officers. With regard to

The Specials are entitled to more than onethird in view of the service they rendered
during the past twelve months, which would
be more in keeping with the numbers I have
given. Then 6,222 men in the old Force have
less than three years' service, therefore they
cannot have a very
or

technical
training.
There is another important point with regard to these men if they join the new Force
and are taken over, and I do not know
whether my right hon. Friend has considered
it. It is the question of the allowance these
men are to get, and here is a very important
point, the question of finance. In the case of
an officer with less than three years'
service, or with one year's service, or oneand-a-half, or two-and-a-half years' service,
transferred to the new Force and serving side

find that an officer with one year's service
gets a minimum compensation allowance of
£107 for a number of years. Then an officer

the old Force gets under the disbandment conditions £115 18s.
The CHAIRMAN: We are getting rather
far away from our Estimates.
What may
have happened to members of the old Force
upon disbandment by the Imperial Parliament is a question with which we have nothing to do. What is to be done with the new
Force to be created and paid for under these
Estimates is quite a different matter. It is
the specific matter we are discussing. We got
rather far away from that.

think this is a question which would give the

they can do SO as cheaply as,

agree, but, from the inquiries I have made, I

These blankets probably will serve only a few

washed. If you paid a little more, and got a

to this Government. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I wonder did my right hon. Friend
sce in the market for auction 7,000 blankets.
I saw those blankets, and I am informed they,
are far superior to the blankets you have got.
They are old blankets, but they would stand
washing, and would give some of our widows
whose husbands have been murdered employment in washing them. This would be better
than their being practically in a state of
starvation. I think this matter in regard to
these contracts has been rushed through far
too quickly. What is the use of standing

country? Surely our Ulster people, even if it
cost a penny more-I have not seen the specification. I do not know the price, but I know

The fibre is so short you could not pull it. I

Surely, after what has occurred here to-day,

not turn round and give away the contract
for sheets. I understand they have advertised a contract for sheets. When we boast
of having the greatest linen industries in the
world, surely the sheet contract will not go to
Er gland.
Public opinion is very strong on this question, and I am only voicing it. Even it had
cost a penny or twopence or sixpence a
blanket more we could have given employment to our own people. There is one point
you have not noticed, but you know how
hard our traders have been hit by the boycott, and here is a matter of great importance where you could have thrown money
into our own till and given employment to
some of our people who are on the streets at
the present time. I will not detain the
House any longer in criticising any of these

Friend to take into consideration before

I will leave that at the moment as I think
that other hon. Members will be dealing with
that matter.

With regard to the appointment of these
different officers, I hope we will not be told

hope that an Irishman will be appointed as
the head of this Force. I hope that an Irishman will not only be in the first position, but
that one will be in the second position. Irishmen are quite capable of filling all these
positions without bringing people from across

the
Of course, if it is a matter of price, that
is 1s. per blanket-the small blanket like
what they were using-then I really do think
those who had the giving out of the order
could not conscientiously give it to an Irish
firm if an English firm was 1s. per blanket

the blankets are delivered they will be seen
