Mr. McGUFFIN: I regret very much that
I have not had time to look into the Constabulary Bill that was submitted to the
House a day or so ago.
I did not get a
copy until an hour or so ago. There are
many things in connection with it that I
would like to have looked into regarding
which I had grave suspicions, but in dealing
with this Estimate here I am more troubled
about what is called the redundant officers
than perhaps any other portion of the
Estimate. It is no justification as far as
I can see for the appointment of redundant
officers to say that we are in a phenomenal
position or up against an extraordinary
difficulty. It is not necessary that you
should have redundant officers because of the
position. It occurs to me that what you
require to do is to see that there are
sufficient subordinate places in order to
carry out the instructions of the one chief.
But to create a deputy inspector-general
and other deputies until you have in
regard to the headquarters no fewer
than eight to transact the business
of the Six County area is in my opinion
quite absurd.
I am not going to say anything with
regard to the salaries that have been
allocated to these officers, because I have
not had the opportunity of comparing
them with what is ordinarily paid to
men occupying similar positions in the
Royal Irish Constabulary. I have the
figures at home, but I had not the opportunity of making a contrast, and I cannot
say just now what it is. I am persuaded of
this, however, you have paid them enough.
Take for instance a county inspector with
£700 rising to £900. All I can say is if you
are organising the police on that grandiose
system I do not know when the culmination
of expenses is going to be reached. I think
it should be taken into consideration that
there is a fall in connection with all salaries
and wages.
You do not seem to have
recognised the necessity of that in the salaries
you have allocated to these officers. It occurs
to me that it does not sound a democratic
Estimate, because you are paying munificently men in high quarters and in
authoritative positions. Well, I have got
nothing to say with regard to the amounts
you are allocating to the ordinary men. They
are reasonable enough, but they are not on
the munificent scale you are paying the
officers.

Mr. HANNA: When I came into the House
to-day, I came with the intention of taking
the opportunity to raise on the adjournment
of the House the question of this contract
that has been alluded to by my hon. Friends
in this debate. If it is in order to discuss
that contract, perhaps it would be a convenient time for me now to say what I
have got to say. I hold in my hand correspondence that passed between the Ministry and
persons seeking the contract, and I hope that
what occurred in placing the contract for
these blankets will not occur in the allocation
of contracts in any other matter required
by the Constabulary or by the Ministry.
In reply to those who answered the advertisement for tenders a letter was sent with
a sample pinned to it. That sample was not
of what was wanted. It was stated deliberately in the letter that what they wanted
was not to be in accordance with the sample.
The sample contained no wool, whereas they
wanted all-wool blankets. When those who
answered the advertisement offered sample
blankets they were told that under no circumstances would sample blankets be received
or looked at. Patterns were all they wanted,
and yet when the contract is given out to
an English firm letters come from the Ministry to all those who had tendered noting
the Ministry's regret that they could not
accept their tenders, and telling them that
the sample blanket would be sent backthe thing they said they would not have
and which they did have. I read with very
great interest a letter written by Lord
Carson to the Press, in which he suggested
that we here have cause to complain of the
treatment we are receiving across the water,
even from our Loyalist friends, and pointing
out that the British nation was spending
lots of money on the Jews in Palestine, but
would not spend any in relief of the Irish
Loyalists, and yet here we are giving this
contract to the Jews of Bradford. The firm
which has received this contract-Messrs Hepworth & Eady-is, I am informed, a Jewish
firm. I do not complain of that, but I do
complain that the contract was given to
Englishmen in Yorkshire when we here have
no less than five different woollen mills
inside the Six Counties, which were all
engaged during the war in making blankets
for the Army, and which had all got special
machinery fitted for the purpose. My hon.
Friend (Mr. Lavery) has told us of one mill
at Newtownards. There is one at Broughshane, there is one at Kells, there is one
in Fermanagh, and there is one in Tyrone.
I take a different view from my hon. Friend
(Mr. Lavery). I hold that, even if the
blankets manufactured by an Ulster firm
cost a shilling apiece more than those of
the firm to whom the contract was given,
we would know that they were manufactured
here, that they would be what they were

Would it be fair for a moment to the men

With regard to these particular blankets,
I may say that, roughly, the tender accepted

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 31st May, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
INSTRUCTIONS TO CORONERS.
1. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Finance if he is satisfied that the directions
of the Registrar-General as to the cause of
death in inquest cases are of such a nature as
to enable the Government and the public to
determine accurately the direct and indirect
cause of many of the cases, and, if not, will
he issue new instructions to Coroners regarding this very important matter.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): My right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) regrets
that he is engaged on a Committee at the
moment, and he has asked me to reply to this
question on his behalf.
The instruction referred to by the hon.
Member was apparently inserted in the
Certificate simply for classification purposes,
to be used in the compilation of the annual
statistics issued by the Registrar-General's
Department.
The Minister will be glad to consider any
suggestions my hon. Friend may have to make
as to the proposed alteration of the existing
instruction.
Dr. MORRISON: I beg to give notice that
I will raise this question on the motion for
the adjournment.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
BENEFIT.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour if he will state the conditions of
benefits under Section 3 of the Unemployment
Insurance Act relative to single men and
women, seeing that some misunderstanding
exists regarding young persons maintained
wholly or mainly by their relatives, and
whether he is aware of the great hardship
caused to many families by this decision.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The special conditions applicable
to claims to Unemployment Benefit, irrespective of stamp contributions, by single persons,
whether juvenile or adult, who are residing
with parents or other relatives, are proof,
firstly, that when in employment they support
themselves; and, secondly, that when unemployed they cannot reasonably look to their
parents for support.
The first condition is satisfied when a
claimant establishes that when he is employed
he supports himself, although he lives with
his parents or relatives. The second condition
is fulfilled when a claimant proves that his
parents or other relatives are unemployed, or
if employed are not in a financial position to
support him.
The misunderstanding to which my hon.
Friend refers would not arise if the distinction were borne in mind between benefit
payable. irrespective of stamp contributions,
and that which is payable on the basis of the
contributions standing to the claimant's
credit. In the latter case the conditions
above mentioned do not apply, and a claimant
would receive the amount of benefit to which
his credit of contributions would entitle him.
I am not aware that hardship has been
caused by applying these conditions, which
seem to me to be eminently reasonable when
a single person without any dependants
claims Unemployment Benefit and he has no
stamp contributions to his credit. Parallel
conditions are in force in Great Britain.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
does my hon. Friend not think there is a
very great hardship, say, where there is a
family of a father and three sons, and the
three sons are unemployed, and are not
entitled to a halfpenny of benefit? With
regard to the other question might I ask my
hon. Friend if he will be good enough to see
that when these deserving cases come before
the Minister of Labour they will receive
special consideration when the parents are
not in a position to support the family?
Mr. GORDON: In reply to my hon. Friend,
I have already stated in my answer to his
question that if a claimant can prove that
members of his family are unemployed he is
entitled to benefit and accordingly benefit is
granted to him.

Motion for Adjournment.
STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House at its rising this day, do adjourn
till Tuesday, June 20th.-(Mr. Burn).
The PRIME MINISTER: I think this
would be an opportune moment for me to
make a statement regarding the grave affairs
that have once more agitated our area. The
House knows that not only has an incursion
been made into our territory on this occasion,
but that those forces from the South have
had the audacity to seize and hold on to that
territory--an offence the gravity of which no
words of mine are needed to emphasise. If a
happening of this sort were to take place in
any other part of our wide Empire, it would
be classified without hesitation by the Government and the people as an out-and-out
749 Motion for Adjournment.

31 MAY 1922.
declaration of war. Ulster has stood provocation on more than one occasion in a manner
which has redounded to its credit, and
it is necessary for me to-day, as perhaps one of the most patient of
the Ulster people, to simply say that
patience is never a sign of weakness,
We have gone along the most peaceful lines
with the earnest and heartfelt hope that by
such means, and by negotiations and putting
out views before Great Britain and before
those in the South and West of Ireland,
our country might be rescued from ultimate
chaos.
I
We have done all that, month after month,
and many a time against my own inclination
and my own feelings, but all the time in
the true interests of the Ulster people.
have done what I could to preserve the peace
and secure better feeling throughout the
length and breadth of our country. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Unfortunately a
Minister is not always in a position to put
the whole of his cards on the table. Sometimes Ministers are blamed and have to
take the blame for this and that, when an
explanation in the House and in the country
would clear away the mystery which seems
to surround some of our deeds and what are
classed as our misdeeds, but nothing of the
kind ever influences me in the slightest. I can
only repeat what I said a few days ago in
this House that, taking a wide view of
this Ulster question, the people are perfectly
safe. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
An incursion, a nipping off of a place here
or a place there is an operation against
which we will take special precautions in the
future, but which, owing to one cause and
another, it was extremely difficult to prevent in the case which has just occurred. I
am not going to say what I think regarding
the actual loss of the territory; but I am
going to assure the House and assure the
people in that locality that they will be
restored to their homes. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) There is no question whatever about
that, and they will be restored to their homes
intact as far as this Government can do
it. I hope that no one in this House will
press me as to how that is to be done.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I assure them
of it; but, in case there should be a feeling
of uneasiness outside, may I in that connection take a letter-an anonymous letterwhich appears in the "Belfast News-
Letter" this morning as somewhat typical
of the feeling of certain persons
throughout the Six Counties. It is
true that letter is signed by a Radical, and
I presume he and some of his friends were
instrumental, in the first instance, in
getting us into the position in which we are
to-day. (Hon Members: Hear, hear.) That
probably did not occur to the writer when
he signed the letter. At all events, he says
that he might possibly exonerate this
Northern Government, and he wants to put
the blame on to the Imperial Government.
I have felt all along it was much more to the
interests of the Ulster people to bring the
British Government along with us in the
hard task that lies before us, rather than
constantly to irritate them by saying it is
part of its duty. It is no small thing for the
Imperial Government so far to have trusted
the Loyalists of Ulster as to have undertaken
on the one hand to supply as many troops as
are necessary to deal with whatever situation arises, to have sent the "Dauntless"
to guard our shores, to have sent the Warwick" up to the Foyle, and also to have sent
other vessels to Carlingford Lough and
above the bridge on the Foyle, which my
hon. Friend (Mr. Mark) knows was done
immediately it was asked for. It is no small
matter for them to say to us:
"We look upon

your territory as British territory, and any
incursion into it is an incursion into Great
Britain." (Hon. Members: Hear hear.) And
although, of course, there is and always will
be the difficulty of getting one Government
to see eye to eye with another, still I bear
testimony here in this House to-day that,
in response to every reasonable request that
we made for assistance in the hour of
our trouble and difficulty, the Imperial
Government has come forward and helped
us. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I admit, of course, and admit frankly,
that in order to secure that consummation
it required a good deal of argument and, I
may say, skill on the part of myself and my
colleagues who were with me; but believe
me, reading as I have just read the speech of
the Secretary of State for the Colonies in the
Imperial House this morning-believe me
when I say that running all through that
speech there is not a single word that would
cause the slightest misconception or misunderstanding in Ulster. There seems
to be running all through it the
right tone of dealing with those who would
in any way attempt to overthrow the honourable undertaking that was arrived at under
the Treaty. I have received from the Government a telegram asking that I should cross
over to London to have a talk with them, not
on this immediate situation so much as upon
the future which will develop of course when
action is taken in connection with recovery of
our territory. My reply to the Government
is that Lord Londonderry, who so ably, as my
colleagues are willing to admit, backed me up
in the most delicate negotiations with the
Government, and myself, would cross over tonight-I quote from the telegram-
Motion for Adjournment-
Prime Minister's Statement.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]

On the distinct understanding that we
are not asked to meet the delegates from
Southern Ireland."
(Hon. Member: Hear, hear.).
I make that statement public, because I see
no chance whatever of having negotiations,
either directly or indirectly, with a body of
persons so composed of Republicans, who in
my opinion are out to bring about the fall of
Ulster. I can put no stronger words upon it
than that. Therefore we have accepted this
invitation, which the House will quite readily
understand we could not refuse. It would be
ungracious on the one part, unncessary on the
other, and be repugnant indeed to my own
feelings that where a Government-the great
British Government-has held out every
assistance to us in our hour of trouble, we
should refuse to go across to consult with
them as to the best way they can help and to
clear up misunderstandings which are sure to
have arisen after their being closeted for a
week with Mr. Collins and his colleagues.
Therefore, the House and the country may
rest assured that neither the Noble Lord nor
I would leave our place here for one moment
if we did not think that we could do better
service to the cause of Ulster talking to the
Ministers of the Crown, who are helping us,
than being here. The only other comment I
have to make on this dangerous situation is
this: We shall easily win through. I have
not the slightest doubt about that. Remember that the situation as regards Sinn Fein in
Ulster is very different from the situation in
the South and West of Ireland. In the South
and West the British troops were up against
not only those who were actively engaged with
bomb and pistol, but up against a hostile community. Throughout the whole length and
breadth of that part of the country there was
a hostile community against the troops and
police. In Ulster, as everyone is aware, it is
exactly the opposite. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.). The troops, the police, and Specials
are welcome in the castle and cottage, and
every assistance that can be given to bring
about the old state of peace is being given by
the local inhabitants. In the South and West
it was dangerous for a Loyalist to possess arms
to defend his house and home. In Ulster,
owing to our system of A, B, and C Constabulary, there is no reason why every Loyalist
should not have arms to his hand, legally
agreed to by the Government. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.).
The consequence is that, instead of having
to take away arms from those holding them
for the protection of their life and property,
we are able to say to them:
"All of you come along, all join in order
to have some sort of record and some control over affairs; all come along, and you
can be armed in defence of your own country."
That is a great difference. Another thing
from the psychological point of view is the
grit of the people against whom the Sinn
Feiners are up. They are up against Ulster.
Nobody has ever been against Ulster without
finding that they were knocking in vain in
this way against the people's will, and I can
only repeat what my predecessor (Lord Carson) in the leadership of the Ulster people
repeated on many a platform:
"Time will reveal that the Ulster people
can never be coerced-they can only be
won."
How long it will take the South and West
to learn that lesson I do not know; but
whether we are in for a short, sharp campaign
in order to bring them to a realisation of that
fact-whether it is long or whether it is
short, the Ulster people, I am perfectly certain, will wear them down. As far as I am
concerned and as far as my colleagues are
concerned we are quite unruffled by any of
these foul attacks which have been made on
our liberty, and we are only nerved to
go on and on in our preparations to
meet whatever eventualities may come.
They are trying every dodge, they are trying
every nefarious scheme, not for the benefit of
Ireland-not a bit of it, that is the last thing
these men seem to think about-what they
are aiming at is, as I said before, the fall of
Ulster, so that Ulster may be brought to the
same welter that exists in the South and
West. Ulster will put up such a stern resistance that these persons will be sorry they
ever attempted it.
to rest

My last word is to ask the people of Ulster
once more for absolute confidence, for courage
to stand up to anything that may come along
on the one hand, and on the other
assured that, whether it be in
or whether it be on the

Mr. LYNN: The Prime Minister, in his
opening remarks, I think quite rightly
pointed out that this was an occasion on

even those few words ought to be very estrained. It would be very easy to make a
fiery speech, and it would be very easy to

tieme measures, so much the better. I was
glad to hear the Prime Minister say that out
they must go. Beyond that I do not wish
to say anything. So far as the Prime Minister
and the Government are concerned, one thing
on which they can rest assured is that the
whole Loyalist population of Ulster stands
behind them in this crisis. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Whatever minor differences
there may be, or whatever we may think of
this or that that has been done in the past,
we have only one thought now, and that ne
is how to help the Government to see this
thing brought to a successful conclusion.
The Prime Minister is justly entitled to say
he has shown an enormous amount of
patience, and his patience has been shared by
the people of Ulster generally, and he has
added, and rightly added, that that patience
is no sign of weakness, that the patience
exercised in the hope of bringing peace not
only to Ulster but to the whole of Ireland, in
no way points to Ulster weakening, or to
Ulster hauling down the flag. I was glad the
Prime Minister paid the tribute he did to the
Imperial Government. The Imperial Government is very often abused-often rightly
abused, often wrongly abused. From my
knowledge of the Members of the Imperial
Government, and especially of the Colonial
Secretary, I make bold to say believe they
are determined to carry out in the letter and
in the spirit the Agreement so far as Ulster,
and, indeed, so far as the whole of Ireland,
is concerned. Part of that Agreement is that
we are to be left alone.
Mr. Churchill in his speech to the Imperial
House today pointed out that the Treaty
must be honestly carried out. How can the
Treaty be honestly carried out so long as attacks are being made on Ulster as have been
made for the last few weeks? I do hope, and
I appeal to Members of this House who have
not so much experience as some of us have of
the Imperial Government to refrain, even
when they are smarting under some tempoiary annoyance, from attacking the Imperial
Government and the English people. The
Imperial Government, I believe, are determined to give us any and every assistance they
can. I have too high a regard for the British
Parliament to imagine for a moment that a
country that put nine and a half million men
in arms in order to protect Belgium from the
attacks of Germany are going to leave their
best friends in this part of the Empire to be
attacked by their worst enemies. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I do not believe
it. I cordially re-echo the words of the Prime
Minister to the Imperial Government. He
has asked for confidence and courage. Well,
so far as courage of the Ulster people is concerned, that has been demonstrated too often
to need anything to be said about it; so far
as confidence is concerned, he can rest assured
that so far as this House is concerned, and I
think I speak for thousands outside this
House, the Government have their confidence
and they will have their help in whatever
steps they may take in order to bring to an
end these attacks which have been made on
the Province.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Before I begin to deal in detail
with the Estimates that I have the honour to
lay before this Committee to-day, I would
like, with your permission, to make a short
general statement in reference to the work
of my Department in order to remove some
erroneous impressions which, I fear, exist
amongst some of our people as to the work
ZZ

Ministry of Labour.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Andrews.]
that the Ministry of Labour is called upon to
perform. There are those who think that we
are merely a spending Department, called
upon to shovel out from the public exchequer
on all occasions to all persons large sums
regardless altogether of Statute. That obviously is not so. We are bound not only by
Acts of Parlament passed by this House, but
also by Acts of the Imperial House, and we
have to administer those Acts in strict in
strict accordance with the terms laid down
in them. My hon. Friend the Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison), who is quickly
gaining for himself, owing to his genial and
humorous personality, an outtanding position
in this House, stated the other day that the
first dometic duty of a State was to look after
its old people. I quite agree, but I think
that consistently he might have gone a little
further and coupled with the old people, if
I may say So, those who are broken
down in health and also those who,
through no fault of their own, are deprived of the opportunity of earning their
daily bread through unemployment. These
two latter problems it is my Ministry's duty
to deal with. But, as I have said, we are
not merely a paying-out Department.
We
have placed upon us very many other
duties of a constructive character. We have
to deal, for instance, with the Factories and
Workshops Acts, the Trade Board Acts,
Workmen's Compensation, Employers' Liability, Trade Disputes, Conciliation, and the
Industrial Court Acts, and in addition to
these we have placed upon us from time to
time quite a number of odd jobs, such as
taking charge of relief works, Railway Commissions, etc. I think I may claim that
looking at it from the industrial standpoint
we have reason to congratulate ourselves.
Since we started to function in June
last, we have not had a single commercial or
industrial disturbance worthy of the name,
with the exception of the engineering trouble.
That engineering trouble has given me a great
deal of anxiety. I think I ought to say that
generally speaking there is a great spirit and
desire for accomodation amongst our people,
both employers and employees. That spirit
has been invaluable to my Department and
has on many occasions averted troubles which
might have been disastrous. Suppose, for
instance, that that spirit did not exist in the
shipyards, we might have been involved in
Northern
Ireland in a strike of a most
serious character. I have said this engineering trouble has given me a very considerable
amount of anxiety and I go further and say
that if there had been more reasonableness
shown across the Channel the trouble
might have been ended long ago. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) And a point which
this House may have to consider sooner or
later is how long it can permit negotiations
to go on in a case of this kind without our
Government being represented, in consideration of the fact that both the Exchequer of
Northern Ireland and our workers are seriously affected. I think it is unnecessary
that I should say in a general way, and I,
propose, therefore, to deal briefly with the Estimates under Head 1.
In the first place there is a very substartial sum of £170,315 placed opposite salaries.
wages, and allowances. That is an Estimate
by the Imperial Ministry, and it is probably
reasonably correct, but I would like to inform the House that for so far we have not
appointed more than two-thirds of the
staff which we ask for power to do.
We are conducting our Department, I hope,
on business lines, and the House may rest
assured that our staff are not tripping over
each other, and that we will not appoint men
unless we have work for them to do. So
far from their tripping over each other,
I regret to say that many of the staff,
especially those in positions of high
importance, have been over-pressed with
work, and almost overborne by it, but I
hope that there are somewhat easier times
ahead for them than there have been during
the last few months.
The next item is that of £8,000 for

him most heartily on the work he has done

whole community suffers by any industrial
upheaval. I am not going to follow him
in regard to whether his staff
are not tripping over each other.
T certainly never said of him what
was said of a well-known British statesman, that "He never did anything and
it always took ten or a dozen people to help
him." That is not true of our Minister of
Labour, who, I know, works hard himself,
and from what I know of him I am quite
sure he will see that his staff also have to
work hard. But I would suggest to him
that between now and the time for bringing
in his next Bill he ought to go into this
whole question of the Labour Department,
and see whether it cannot be greatly simplified, whether he cannot do away with what
was referred to rather naively yesterday in

officers." I do not know whether he has
any redundant officers, but I think this whole
question ought to be simplified.
The right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews)

was due to some long-sighted statesman who

classes, and, indeed, amongst all classes

Dr. MORRISON: I want to say a word or
two in connection with a reply which was
given to me with regard to Registrars of
Deaths in inquest cases. I have got to sit as
a Coroner, and as a man having practical
experience of the statistics available in connection with these inquests, I can say they
are wholly misleading. This is a very serious
statement to make with regard to any public
statistics. We have, and I have attempted to
have the practice extended, to get statistics
of the deaths of our cattle. That is a very
necessary thing, because no remedy can be
devised for certain diseases if you do not
know the actual extent of the problem with
which you are dealing. I think every Meinber of this House will admit the first consideration of Parliament should be the health
of the people. In order accurately to determine that you must have a correct record of
the death rate and the causes that produce it.
In the Registrar-General's Returns you will
find very accurate descriptions of nearly all
diseases. You will find tuberculosis classified
under three or four heads, infant mortality
analyzed, and all the other information you
wish to secure except this very important
question of deaths investigated at inquests.
Parliament, as I have said, must have a
knowledge of these facts before they are able
to provide a remedy.
With regard to the question of inquests, it
is an unfortunate thing that one of the
amenities of this House under present conditions is that some of us may die a violent
death, and it will explain the position if I
tell you what is going to happen if this rather
awkward contingency should arise. In the
first place we are asked by the Registrar-
General to state the primary cause of death
and then the secondary cause of death. Now,
the primary cause of death in an ordinary
case of wounding is shock and hemorrhage,
and to this you will probably add heart
failure. That defines exactly where you are,
but it gives no information to the public as
to how this death arose. The Registrar-
General in his instructions says you should
put down the primary cause of death and the
secondary cause of death, and then you
classify them under three heads-suicidal,
homicidal, or accidental. I maintain that
under these headings the public are entirely
at sea as to what in many cases is the direct
cause of death in inquest cases. It misleads
the public, it misleads this House, and it
prevents a remedy from being found for the
deplorable condition which I say exists in
these statistics. Let me give you one or two
concrete cases. I held an inquest on the
bodies of three persons who, according to the
evidence which came before me, went down
the street in one of our towns under the
influence of drink, got into a boat and
capsised it before they had gone a mile. The
result of the inquest was that asphyxia was
the primary cause of death. It was classified
"Drowning; asphyxia; accidental." I think
is is fairly obvious to any man that any
person reading these three case of accidental
drowning from the Registrar-General's Returns will be absolutely incapable of
diagnosing or telling what really was the
cause of death. In another case a man who,
according to the evidence, was so drunk
in a public-house that he was unable to put
a glass of whisky to his mouth, walked out
of the house and stumbled and fell on the
tramway. A tram went over him nd
smashed his legs, and he died some time
afterwards. I had to hold an inquest, and
the primary cause of death was put down as
"fracture of the legs," and the secondary

case like that? The third case in
which
was called upon to hold
an inquest was that of a man who, when

a very small cut. As people will do under

to hold inquests in something like 236 cases,
probably nearly 250 cases, and I would think
that in 50 of those 250 cases these misleading
returns occur.
I think that in public statistics which are
drawn up with the object of enabling Parliament and our people to put their fingers on
certain sores, there should in cases of death
be accuracy. I maintain under this system
it is wholly inaccurate, and the people are
blinded and cannot possibly do anything for
themselves. No man goes so far as the man
who does not know where he is going. I do
not want to indulge in sentiment in regard
to this matter, but I want it put on a
scientific basis, exactly in the same position
as tuberculosis and infantile mortality.
Thomas Carlyle said, "The British Empire
consists of thirty millions of people, mostly
fools." I am inclined to believe there is a
very large amount of truth in that statement,
although it is not altogether true.

Oral Answer to Question.
REGISTRATION OF TITLE, CENTRAL
OFFICE.
1. Mr. ROBB (for Mr. Hanna) asked une
Minister of Home Affairs if he will state
when the Northern Ireland Central Office
for the registration of transactions under
the Local Registration of Title (Ireland) Act,
1891, is likely to be set up and operating;
and if, in the meantime, he will take steps
to prevent the serious inconvenience occasioned to persons interested in the completion of such transactions by the great
delays experienced in dealing with the
Central Office in Dublin?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have arranged with my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Home Affairs
to reply to this question. It is anticipated
that the Central Northern Ireland Registration of Title Office will be in a position
to operate at a very early date. So far as
I am aware, all possible facilities have been
given to the public in Northern Ireland by
the Central Office in Dublin, but doubtless
that Office has been considerably hampered
of late by reason of their Records not being
available owing to the occupation of the Four
Courts by irregular forces of the so-called
Irish Republican Army.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): I have been asked by the Minister
to introduce this Estimate which makes
provision for the salaries and expenses of
the Administration, and in doing so, I desire
to remind hon. Members that owing to the
suspension of the Civil Service Committee
about the end of January of this year, the
final allocation, as between North and South,
of the existing staff employed by the various
Education Boards up to 1st February, 1922.
is still in many respects incomplete, and that
this circumstance has greatly hampered the
Ministry in arranging its staff satisfactorily
on a permanent basis. The staff, from the
Assistant Secretaries downwards, provided
for in the Estimate is the total staff which
has been already transferred from the three
Educational Boards in Dublin, or which the
Ministry has reason to believe will be transferred when the Civil Service Committee
resumes its operations. With regard to the
Inspectorate, it has been found that there
are considerably more volunteers for Northern Ireland from the all-Ireland staff than
there are vacancies under the Northern Administration. This involves consideration
by the Civil Service Committee of individual
claims a work which is still incomplete.
Education in Northern Ireland, pending
the introduction of a measure of reform, is
being administered under the same system
as when the administracion was in Dublin.
Knowing the relatively larger cost of the
higher administrative posts, which is unavoidable in a scheme which deals with a
comparatively small portion of the all-Ireland
area, as compared with the like charges
under a scheme which dealt with the whole
country, we were anxious to keep the cost
of administration as moderate and reasonable as possible. Hon. Members will, I am
sure, agree with me that we have succeeded
when I point out that the Estimate of the
salary charges for the year 1921-22 of the
administrative and inspection staffs of the
Education.

Regarding Sub-Head "B," the gures inserted have been arrived at by as careful an

previous year. Hon. Members are aware

National schools and of teachers' residences,

vested in the Ministry. Provision is made

Under Sub-head "D," provision is made for

Schools in Northern Ireland. The figures
under "E," "F," "G," "H," are somewhat

Sub-head "I" provides for the expenses

West Belfast (Mr. Lynn), has done and is
doing such valuable work, and for any
further enquiries which it may be found
necessary to make. Hon. Members will be
pleased to know that the Interim Report of
this Committee is now in the hands of the
Ministry. I am satisfied that the work
of the Ministry is being carried on under
existing conditions as economically as possible. It is hoped, however, that when we
have a more practical, and probably more
simple system, co-ordinating the various
services, it will be possible to make still
further reductions in the cost of administration. I beg to move.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I desire to move that
this Vote be reduced by £1,000. I do so
for the following reasons. I cannot agree
with the Parliamentary Secretary of Education that this thing has been administered
more cheaply than it has been previously.
I have facts in my possession which go to
show that I am not taking up an unreasonable position. I find from the report of
the Commissioners for the year 1920 that
there were 8,000 schools altogether in Ireland.
In this Northern area there are about 2,000
schools-one-fourth of the number in all
Ireland. The total funds at the disposal of
the Commissioners for 1920 amounted to
£3,250,000. If our Government charges anything it would be reasonable to say that
they should ask for only one-fourth of the
funds which the Commissioners had at their
disposal. That would be £812,500, but our
Ministry asks for £1,520,000. I know the
teachers are paid more now than they were
paid that year. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I hold, however, it should be the same
amount-one-fourth-plus the amount of increase given to the teachers. If we look
at the office staff, we find that in the year
1921-22 the estimates provided for 191 of
a staff in Dublin. We have got one-fourth
of the schools. These 191 officials adminis
tered 8,000 schools, and as we have got only
one-fourth of the schools under our control,
one-fourth of 191 would be 48. Yet if we
look at Section A, page 77, you will see that
the Ministry of Education asks us to provide
money for 92 officials. If 191 in Dublin were
able to manage 8,000 schools why should
our Ministry ask us to provide for 92 officials
to look after 2,000 schools? I hold that we
ought not to be over-staffed and that the
Ministry are unreasonable in asking us to
provide for 92 officials in Northern Ireland.
The total cost for the 191 in Dublin-I want
hon. Members to take this in-for the year
1921-22 was £70,215. One-fourth of that would
be £17,554. Yet they ask us for £32,719,
and the Parliamentary Secretary tells us that
they are doing the work more cheaply than
in Dublin. Come now to the question of
Inspectors. We find there were 85 inspectors
for the whole 8,000 schools. Six of them were
for the Irish language. We do not want inspectors for that in the Northern area. Deduct
the 6 from the 85 and you have 79 inspectors.
One-fourth of that would be 20 in round
numbers, and yet the Ministry of Education
asks us in page 77 to provide for 36 inspectors. They ask as a matter of fact for
37, one being intended for the Irish language.
I deduct that and say 36. The total cost of
inspectors for the year 1921-22 was £60,946.
One-fourth of that would be £15,000 odd,
and yet the Ministry asks for £28,927 for
inspectors. In the face of that they say
they are managing things more cheaply than
Dublin. The travelling expenses for the 80
inspectors in 1921-22 was £22,440. One-fourth
of that would be £5,610, and yet they ask
us to give £10,750. You will find that in
Section B, page 78 in the Estimate. If you
take this sum for travelling and incidental
expenses you will find as regards the 36
inspectors it works out at £300 for each,
or 30/- for each person per day. When you
take into consideration that one-seventh of
our schools are in the City of Belfast I hold
that it is a complete waste of money to ask
so much for travelling expenses for inspectors.

If you divide 2,000 schools by 36 you have
only 58 schools for each inspector, and under
the old system you had 80 inspectors, each
of whom had 100 schools. Under the proposed system you propose to have one for
every 58. There are only 200 school days
in the year. That would give these inspectors an opportunity of paying two visits to
each school, and would only take 116 days
of their time. I hold that it is not a
satisfactory way of managing the affairs of
the Education Board. I am not raising any
objection to the salaries being paid to the
inspectors, and I am not raising any objection
to the way in which they do their work,
but I hold as one who has given a little
consideration to the matter that it is an
unreasonable thing to ask that the taxes
of this country be spent in such an absurd
manner. It may be that they have had to
take these inspectors over on account of
the transfer of services. If so I would ask
them to give us an assurance that no more
will be appointed. I would like to ask what
the scale of travelling expenses is, or how
it comes that each inspector should get 30/-
per day for travelling expenses? I need
not labour the question very much. I have
put the facts before the Committee, and I
ask the Ministry to give an assurance that
the number of inspectors will be reduced
and that the business of the Board will be
worked in an economic manner. The only
way to do that is by reducing the funds at
our disposal, for if we vote this money they
will spend it. I move that this Vote be
reduced by £1,000.

objected; I said I would have nothing to

CLASS II, No. 1.
MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £38,599 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1923, for the
Salaries and Expenses of the Ministry of
Home Affairs." (Voted on Account £12,500).
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In introducing this Vote
I feel that it is unnecessary to amplify to
any great degree the explanation which 1
gave in December last in regard to the internal organisation of the Ministry of Home
Affairs. I then pointed out that there are
two main divisions in the office; one which
deals with the services formerly administered
by the Chief Secretary's office in Dublin,
and the other dealing with those services
formerly carried out by the Local Government Board and the Ministry of Transport.
The Estimate which is before the Committee
provides for a staff of 100 officials, and I
can assure the Committee that when this
was drawn up it was hoped that this would
be sufficient. It is only right, however, to
say that since the Estimate was prepared we
have been obliged to increase the numbers
of some of the minor classes of officials. On
the crime side especially our activities have
been greatly increased, and the work has
developed far beyond our anticipations. It
will be appreciated that the criminal activities which are going on in our midst must
necessarily impose a very heavy additional
burden upon the Home Affairs Branch of the
office, and we have been obliged to augment
the staff accordingly. I would like, however,
to point out that these extra officials only
hold their appointments temporarily, and I
hope, when we get back to normal times and
normal conditions, that we will be able to
dispense with their services.
In
I would like to remind the Committee that
my Department is faced with exactly the
same difficult problems as confronted the
Chief Secretary's Department in Dublin
These
during the last three or four years.
problems are precisely of the same magnitude,
and officials who have been transferred to my
Department from the Chief Secretary's office
have told me that the number of papers
coming daily into the Home Affairs Registry,
relating to Home Office affairs, far exceeds
that which had to be dealt with in the Chief
Secretary's Department in Dublin. In regard
to that, I might point out that the Chief
Secretary's office in Dublin was provded with
two Under Secretaries, and a total staff of
over 200. We have only one Secretary and
a total staff of 56, dealing solely with Home
Affairs, other than Local Government.
connection with Local Government work, in
addition to the intern staff, we have only
one General Inspector for our Local Government work as compared with 13 in Dublin;
2 Medical Inspectors as compared with 9 in
Dublin; 3 Auditors as compared with 20; and
one Engineering Inspector as compared with
9 Engineers and Architects. The services
we have to attend to are, I may say, the
oldest of all the Irish services. The roots
of the Chief Secretary's Department were
deep down in Dublin, and I can assure you
it was no easy task to pluck up these roots
and to transplant them here. Many difficulties were placed in our way, and one of
the greatest difficulties lay in securing the
transfer of properly trained men
However, I am glad to say that we have
overcome those difficulties, and I venture to
say that we have now got some of the best
officials in any branch of the Civil Service.
In addition to setting up a fresh office
organisation, we have had to establish our
new Police Force, and 1 can assure the
Members of this Committee that that was
by no means an easy task. Again, we found
our prison administration in a hopeless condition when we took it over, and I think I
may claim the credit for a substantial
strengthening of this branch of our administration. Might I also remind the House
that since we took over, Parliament has
imposed on us many difficult and troublesome
duties. The Civil Authorities Act, with its
wide powers, has imposed upon us a great
many duties which we had not anticipated.
The Act empowering us to dissolve local
bodies imposes very troublesome duties.
am glad to say that that Act has been a
most successful one, and from all parts of
the Province I get communications to show
that the Commissioners whom we have uppointed are doing their work well and
economically, and many of the ratepayers
to

would be sorry to revert to the old condition
of affairs. In addition to that, we have
got the new Nursing Act, and now the new
Local Government (Northern Ireland) Bill,
which I hope to introduce to the House
next week, will impose further additional
duties upon our Department.
I am also glad to be able to announce that
we have almost completed arrangements with
the Imperial Government for taking over,
as an agency service, the administration of
the Irish Land for Sailors and Soldiers Act
in Northern Ireland. We have been continually pressing the Imperial authorities
to hand over to us the administration of this
Act as an agency service, and our efforts
have at last been successful. I think I may
confidently say that we will in a very short
time be in a position to carry out the administration of that Act. Out of a total of 3,500
cottages which has been allotted for the
whole of Ireland, we in Northern Ireland
are to have 1,000. We are not satisfied with
this proportion, and are pressing the Imperial
authorities further to see that that proportion is increased more in comparison with
the number of men we sent out from Ulster.
Additional staff will be required for this
work, but the cost will not fall
on the
Government of Northern Ireland. The Imperial Government have promised to place
at our disposal a sum not exceeding £250,000
for the purpose of carrying on this agency
service for the present year. I think the Members of this Committee will readily understand that all this involved a very heavy
addition to our work. The staff we have can
certainly not be described as excessive, and
I may safely say that there is no one in the
whole office who is not pulling his whole
weight. Many of them, and especially the
higher administrative officers, work early and
late, Sunday and Saturday, and the strain
upon them is very considerable. I would like
to testify my appreciation of the work
which my staff is doing. I would like particularly to refer to the new recruits from
Ulster who have joined our staff.
Members: Hear, hear.) I think it is very
promising to find that in the recruits I have
got from Ulster in my Department we have
as good men for our Civil Service as could
be obtained anywhere. I beg to move.
(Hon.
Dr. MORRISON: In the absence of any
other person to speak on this matter I desire
to make a few remarks. In the first place
I think an extraordinary amount of work
has been placed on the Minister of Home
Affairs. In addition to looking after justice
and prisons and the other multifarious duties
he has to do he has the whole of the
Local Government Board work to attend
to, and I cannot really perceive how it is
possible for one man to do so unless he has
specially equipped and capable, efficient servants to carry out the work imposed on him.
I think the Minister has met that difficulty
by getting men who are specially qualified.
There are men behind him who are capable
of running the Local Government Board, and
running it more efficiently, in my opinion,
and more cheaply than it was run in Dublin.
There are, as far as I can judge, three or
four departments under him. He has a very
serious responsibility, the most responsible
position I think of any Minister in the
Cabinet. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do
not think if he were not provided with the
capable business men he has behind him it
would be possible for him to carry on the
work as efficiently as he has done. I have
been in and out of his office and have been
brought into contact with him and I gladly
bear testimony to this fact.
With regard to the Minister of Home
Affairs himself, the fact that he stands in
the front rank at this crisis in our history,
that practically his office is responsible for
dealing with all the criminals in the community-and God knows they are very
numerous and very active-brings naturally
on him criticism criticism that is very often
ill-considered, and, in my opinion, very unjust. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) My
opinion may not carry much weight, because
as I told the House on an earlier occasion
the public do not always take you at your
own estimate. I have laboured under that
disability all my life, but I venture to give
this opinion, and at least I hope that the
public do not consider I am altogether a
fool, that in this matter of the way our
Home Minister is looking after the serious
affairs that come before him he has displayed
grit and determination. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Any man in Ulster, especially
in Unionist circles, who thinks that he is
weak or timid or hesitating is making a very
huge mistake. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I venture to make this prophecy, that if he
is supported as I think he will be by this
Committee he will be able to put down crime
and restore normal conditions in the Six
Counties. I have no doubt whatever about
that being the result.
There is another matter, and I am a little
bit timid about beginning it. In this report
which he has submitted he has made reference to work done under the Local Government Act, and he has made reference to
inspectors. I take it I am in order in offering
some criticism with regard to this matter.
I take the two medical inspectors who represent the Local Government. What amazes
me in connection with the figures I see here
is that those two medical inspectors start
at the modest salary of £500 a year. Now
in the medical profession it has always been
admitted that the man who became a Local

CLASS III, No. 4.
UNEMPLOYMENT GRANTS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £552,000
(including a supplementary sum of £550,000)
be granted to His Majesty to defray the
charge which will come in course of payment during the year ending on the 31st
March, 1923, for grants to local authorities,
etc, in Northern Ireland for assistance in
carrying out approved schemes of relieving
unemployment." (Voted on Account
£40,000.)
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews): The total of this Vote which the
Committee are now called upon to consider
is £552,000 for works for the relief of unemployment in Northern Ireland. It is
made up of three sums. First, £42,000 from
the Lord St. David's grants for relief works in
Northern Ireland approved by the Unemployment Grants Committee in London. Of
this sum £14,000 still remains to be applied
to schemes under the altered conditions to
be approved by the Minister of Labour
in Northern Ireland. The second sum is
the very substantial one of £500,000 which
was obtained under the London agreement,
and the third is £50,000 which you are
asked to grant on behalf of the Northern
Government, making a total of £592,000 in
all.
Of this amount £40,000 was voted by
this Committee on the 22nd March last, so
that the total sum which the Committee are
asked to vote is, as I have already said,
£552,000.
I feel that this Committee and the general
public ought to know that these large sums
have been obtained mainly through the influence and exertions of the Prime Minister.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Therefore,
thousands of our unemployed in Northern
Ireland are deeply indebted to him in this
as in many other respects. As regards the
£500,000 which came to us under the London
agreement, I think it is necessary that I
should speak at some length, because
I am aware that certain wrong impressions
exist in some of the minds of Our
people. When the responsibility for dealing
with this large sum was placed upon me I
felt there would be a considerable amount
of criticism, due to the unfortunate fact
that we have in Belfast and neighbourhood
about 20,000 unemployed men, while under
these schemes we cannot find work for more
than 6,000 of them for a period of about
twelve months, under the most favourable
circumstances. It is only natural that
those who do not get work under
these schemes should feel disappointed,
but, after all, we cannot take more
Unemployment Grants. 794
Supply-
21 JUNE 1922
out of our purse than we put into it,
and although the sum is very substantial,
the need, I regret to say, is greater still.
I observe that Mr. Devlin in the Imperial
House is making very unfounded statements-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-about the administration of this Fund, and I feel it
my duty to-day to explain to hon. Members
the machinery which I brought into being
in order that this Fund should be distributed
in accordance with the pact, and absolutely
impartially as between the different creeds in
this community. In the first place, I brought
into being an Advisory Committee, composed
of 23 Members, of whom nine represented the
Catholic community. I must say that the
members of this Committee, one and all,
have given me invaluable assistance and that
they have co-operated with me and with
each other in a spirit of accommodation and
with a desire only for the public good. Mr.
Devlin takes a different view.
I absolutely
deny in this House the statements which he
has made in the Imperial House, and I
venture to say to him to-day that he would
be playing a more manly game if he would
come into this House and make these statements here, where he could get the answer
which he deserves. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
I am very glad to observe by this morning's
papers that Mr. Churchill has decided to
send over here to investigate this and
other matters, a very distinguished public
servant with a career of which any man might
be proud-Mr. Tallents, C.B., of London.
I welcome Mr. Tallents, and I court his
inquiry. I only hope that when Mr.
Churchill gets his report he will give it
publicity so that those who run may read,
and that the people of Great Britain may be
made alive by a distinguished public servant
of their own to the way in which the people
of Northern Ireland and the Government of
Northern Ireland are misrepresented. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I am sure Hon. Members would like to
know something of what has already been
done as to the allocation of this substantial
sum Thirty-four relief schemes have
already been sanctioned and most of them
have already been started. The Committee
will recognise that it is impossible to get
all the schemes started at once because the
public bodies are obliged to get forward the
necessary materials to permit of the work
being done. For instance, take the case
of the Water Commissioners. They cannot
begin to open the streets and give employment to our labourers until they get
the pipes from Glasgow, but I am absolutely satisfied that although it is true that
only 740 men have so far got work under
these schemes, the rate at which they
now obtain employment will be very quickly
increased. I, personally, will be very disappointed if within a month from now that
number is not, at any rate, quadrupled. I
would like to say that the schemes which
have been authorised amount in the total
to £615,766; the total wages bill of the
schemes authorised amounts to £209,404, and
the grant towards wages from this Fund is
£111,913. Therefore, already rather more than
one-fifth of the total sum available has been
granted. I ought to tell the Committee that
I appreciate very much the spirit in which
all our public bodies have co-operated with
me in connection with this matter. They
have all realised their responsibilities. They
have all come forward with schemes, and are
all doing their best to get the work started
as soon as possible. I feel they have shown
an example to the other public bodies
throughout the Six Counties which, as I shall
be able to say later on, is being followed by
the public bodies of the counties themselves.
The public bodies are putting up more on
their own behalf than they are getting from
the Fund owing to the arrangements which
we have made with them. In other words,
while from the Fund we are giving from
50 to 60 per cent of the wages, the local
authorities are putting up the balance plus
all the materials, so that in that way we
have increased the £500,000 voted by the
Imperial Government to a sum of about one
million and a half, all of which will be given
to the relief of unemployment in the City
and the neighbourhood of Belfast.
As regards the £50,000 referred to, I would
like to explain that the Government of
Northern Ireland felt that while so much was
being done through the instrumentality of
the £500,000 grant for the unemployed
in Belfast and neighbourhood, it would
be unfair to the unemployed throughout the Six Counties that something
should not be done for them.
I may
say on behalf of the Government that wo
never forget that we are a Government for
the Six Counties and not a Government only
for the City of Belfast. The £50,000, therefore,
which you are asked to vote is for schemes
to be carried out in conjunction with our
local authorities in the Six Counties. I am
very glad to tell you that already the public
bodies have put up a very large number of
schemes, and practically without exception
every county has put forward its schemes,
and many of our Urban authorities have
done SO also. In all, about eighteen
schemes have been authorised, and a great
many of them have already been started.
Personally, I think that the importance of
this whole effort to deal with unemployment
cannot be over-rated. A great many people
object to National Insurance against unemployment, a great many people carp at what
they call the dole, and have always said,
"Give the people work."

SITUATION ON THE BORDER.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn." (Mr. Burn).
Dr. MORRISON: I desire to raise a
question with regard to the order of business.
I understand we considered and definitely
decided that the House should not sit on
Mondays, and I understood also that it
should sit on Fridays. I hear now that there
is business arranged for next Monday. There
fore, I presume the House will sit on that
day, and I would like to know where we
are, and, if the arrangement I have referred
to has been made, has the House been consulted with regard to the change? I would
also like to refer, not in the way of serious
complaint, to the fact that country Members
are put to some inconvenience by the manner
in which they are summoned here. They find
that matters which appear on the paper and
which necessitate their attendance in Belfast,
are not discussed at all on that particular
day. I refer particularly to the Local Government (Northern Ireland) Bill.
We are
led to expect that it will be considered on
a particular day only to find that it is
adjourned. Many of us, thinking it was
an important matter, made an effort to be
here. I think more attention should be paid
to the country Members by the Whips of
this House. I believe the complaint is
general in the other House as well as in this
House.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps my hon.
Friend will allow me to say that the proposal to skip over this Friday, to meet on
Monday, and on Monday to take the Bill
dealing with Proportional Representation,
was adopted in order to meet criticism which
has frequently fallen from different parts of
the House that sufficient time was not given
to hon. Members to study Bills before they
were brought forward for Second reading.
It was felt by my colleagues and myself
that if we took the Second reading of the
Proportional Representation Bill to-morrow
we might in a friendly way be charged with
rushing the Bill when there was really no
necessity to do so. Therefore, we decided
that it would be more convenient to hon.
Members to have till Monday to consider the
various Clauses in this Bill and to consult
their constituents or others interested in the
Measure. It is a Measure of first-class importance and one that requires very careful
consideration from all quarters of the House,
although I believe I am right in saying that
the desire for the Bill is a unanimous one
from all the authorities concerned. That
is the explanation, and I hope it will satisfy
my hon. Friend. With regard to his further
criticism on the subject of the agenda, I
hope he will bear in mind that although the
Paper of our House bears upon it a longer
list of Measures and proceedings than it is
intended to take each day the Whip sent
out will keep him right as to the actual
business the Government propose to take on
that day. The reason it appears in full upon
the Paper is to enable the Government to
adjourn it from day to day in order to suit
the convenience of the House, and I can
assure the hon. Member and other Members
that in arranging the business of the House
the Government are entirely in the hands of
the House and only desire to meet the wishes
and convenience of Members from all
quarters, because we are on the spot all the
time, and it is convenient to us to meet
practically at any hour and take such
Measures as hon. Members may decide. I
hope that explanation will be satisfactory
to my hon. Friend (Dr. Morrison).
Mr. MILLER: I am afraid the Prime
Minister has made a slight mistake. It was
really the Whip that the hon. Member for
Queen's University (Dr. Morrison) was complaining about. It was the Whip which
brought us all here yesterday to find that
we had nothing to do. The Whip said this
most important Local Government Bill was
to come on to-day. I quite agree with the
Prime Minister when he says that the Bill
should not be rushed until we have had time
to consider it. It might also be remembered
that at present the posts of the country are
in such a state that you can never depend
on getting anything within two or three
days of its despatch. For instance, I expect
I will get the Whip for yesterday's meeting
of the House some day next week. You can
have no idea of the delays which are taking
place at present. I was sent some documents
from the Library on Friday last, and they
were not delivered until Tuesday morning.
I would also like to ask the Prime Minister
a question which I will not expect him to
answer unless he thinks it is advisable.
There is a great deal of uneasiness in my
part of the country on account of the situation on the Border. People think it is an
extraordinary thing that they cannot go, for
instance, from Omagh to Derry without being
turned out of the train and their pockets
searched, and if there is the slightest
reason, the contents taken away. There

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
Naturally the House will understand that
I have had no private notice that this matter
would be raised, but I fully realise the great
importance of the subject and the keen interest that the two hon. Members, representing the zone which is affected, naturally take
in the position. I wish to weigh well any
words that may say, but the hon. Member
for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr. Miller) and
the hon. Member for Derry (Mr. Mark) may
take back to their constituents a message
that the Government have under consideration the very serious state of affairs that
has arisen in connection with these predatory
raids upon the railway which passes in and
out of our territory, and out and in of the
territory of the Free State. The intolerable
situation must be brought to an end-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)--and the Government
have various schemes under consideration.
One reason why I refrained yesterday from
making a statement, as it is generally called,
at the beginning of the sitting of the House
after a break, was because so much hangs
upon what is taking place at the moment
in the South. I felt, and Ministers of the
House of
Imperial
Commons also felt,
that with fuller information-to put it
on no higher ground than that-we

early next week. I felt, as they felt, that
it would be much better to have all that

or in a much better position than we are in

In dealing with this serious railway situation, I may say that what I hope will be a
satisfactory arrangement is being come to
with regard to what is known as the Belleek
salient, and, if the experiment which we are
endeavouring to apply to the Belleek salient
proves successful, it may be possible to try
the same scheme with regard to that portion
of the county to which my two hon. Friends
have referred. But, there is one answer that
I may make emphatically, and that is, that
if any attempt is made to interfere in such
a way as was suggested by my hon. Friend,
the Member for Derry (Mr. Mark), with the
transferring of goods inside our own area,
exactly the same prompt measures will be
taken as were taken when the Free Staters
or Republicans invaded Ulster territory.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There can be
no doubt whatever about that. Wherever
there is a direct challenge of that kind to
the authorities of Northern Ireland, then
Northern Ireland will reply at once. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I hope at the same
time that saner counsels may prevail. The
result of the elections in the South and West
at all events indicates one thing, and that
is, that the general body of the people want
peace. Whatever other lessons may be learned
from the elections, they mean that the general
body of opinion in the South and West, like
that of the North, wants peace, and if the
leaders therefore are desirous of properly
interpreting the voice of the people of the
South, it may lead to peace. At that result,
of course, we here in the North will rejoice
with everybody else throughout the country,
and if peace does come then some of the
problems will be solved for us without our
taking any action whatever. That type of
solution of the problems of course will be
much more agreeable to our Government
than any other solution. But, at the same
time, do not let there be any mistake.
determination of this Government is to deal,
as they have done before, with the problems
as they crop up. I give this message of

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Captain
Dixon): I do not complain at all of the
criticism which my two Friends have made
of the Whips' Office. I think it was very
just and fair, because, when hon. Members
are brought down here for certain Bills, if
possible we should put those Bills before
them. In the case of the Proportional Representation Bill, which deals with a subject
in which the hon. Member for Fermanagh
and Tyrone (Mr. Miller) is keenly interested,
we could not take it to-day because we had
not the actual Bill to put into the hands
of the Members in time. We thought that
the Bill was so important that it would be
very unfair to rush it on the Members of
the House without giving them due time to
consider it, and, therefore, when the question
came up yesterday as to whether we should
bring this Bill before the House to-day or
not, we decided that, as we could not have
the Bill in the hands of the Members we
would put it off until such time as would
enable the Members to study it before it
came before the House. I have only to add
that we do everything we possibly can to
meet the wishes of the Members, because
we are really the servants of our party in
this matter, but there are times when
physical difficulties of printing and otherwise
defeat us, and when we are defeated we gladly
get up and apologise.

UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF GRANTS, AD-
MINISTRATION.
1. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Labour if his attention has been called to
the questions put in the Imperial House of
Commons on the 14th June by the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) to
the Secretary of State for the Colonies in
connection with the administration of the
£500,000 Relief Grant, and whether he will
make a statement about the administration
of this grant?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have read the official report of
the question put to the Secretary of State
for the Colonies by the hon. Member for
West Belfast, who, I regret to say, was
quite misinformed as to the facts. I would
refer the hon. Member to the statement which
I made yesterday when moving the estimate
for this grant.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
is my right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) aware
that these people are placed in a very high
and unique position in view of the fact that
the amount of this £500,000 allocated to them
places them in exactly the same position as
ex-Service men? I see no reason for complaint by the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) but on the contrary.
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not know to whom
the hon. Member (Mr. Donald) refers as
"these people."
Mr. DONALD: The question arises out of
the statement made by the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) complaining about
the granting of this money to a certain section
in Belfast. That is why I refer to "these
people." I think the Roman Catholic section
are getting exceptional treatment.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member must
ask a question. He knows quite well he
cannot make a speech or a statement at this
stage.
CONDITIONS GOVERNING GRANTS.
2. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of Labour
if any applications have been received from
the various County Councils for a portion
of the £50,000 granted by the Northern
Government to relieve unemployment through.
out the Six Counties, and if he will explain
the conditions of the grant?
Mr. ANDREWS: The grant of £50,000 for
the relief of unemployment in Northern Ireland outside Belfast and neighbourhood has
been provisionally allocated to the six County
Councils in Northern Ireland, to the Borough
of Londonderry and to certain Urban
Councils, due regard being paid to those areas
which are bearing the heaviest burden of
unemployment. I am glad to inform the
hon. Member that almost all of the local
authorities are co-operating in a publicspirited manner. The toal cost of the Relief
Schemes which have been sanctioned under
the grant is about £33,000 up to date. The
total amount to be spent on wages is about
£16,000, and the total subsidy from the grant
is about £9,000.
With regard to the second part of the hon.
Member's question, the conditions governing
this grant are in the main the same as those
governing the £500,000 grant, namely, schemes
are subsidised to the extent of 50 per cent.
of the wages of unemployed men who are
engaged on revenue-producing works, and
60 per cent. in the case of non-revenue producing works; all labour must be engaged
through the local Employment Exchange in
order to ensure that preference is given to
ex-Service men and expelled workers, with
priority to those who have been longest unemployed and who have the largest families.
The wages to be paid to all men employed
on unskilled work will be the local authority's
rate for such work, and skilled workers will
be paid the current Trade Union rate of
the district.
FLAX AND HEMP TRADE BOARD.
3. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of Labour
if he has decided to abolish the Trade
Board in the flax and hemp trade?
Mr. ANDREWS: On June 12th I published
in the Press an announcement of my intention
to make a Special Order withdrawing the
flax and hemp trade in Northern Ireland
from the operation of the Trade Boards Acts.
Objections to this course may be lodged
during the period of 40 days from June 12th
and any such objections will be considered in
the manner prescribed by statute. I took this
step in consequence of an agreement reached
between representatives of the Flax Spinners'
Association and the Trade Unions concerned.
The agreement provides for the recognition
of the principal of collective negotiations
and for the constitution of a joint body to
deal with general questions affecting wages
and working conditions in the trade. It also
contains an agreement as to a reduction of
wages and stabilises the reduced wages until

the end of this year. Further, it contains
some valuable provisions relating to the
future settlement of industrial conditions in
the trade.
The request for the withdrawal is very
properly accompanied by a statement that
it is without prejudice to the policy of the
Government as a result of whatever report
may be made by the Advisory Committee
on Trade Boards which is at present sitting
and which, I hope, will very shortly report.

Chamber of Commerce, demanding an investigation into the funds and administration
of the National Health Insurance Act, and
protesting against its anomalies and injustice
to employer and insured, and if he proposes
to grant an investigation?
Only
Mr. ANDREWS: My attention has been
called to the resolution in question.
one valuation has yet been made of the
assets and liabilities of Approved Societies
and that valuation certainly disclosed considerable surpluses existing as at the 31st
December, 1918. It should be stated, however,
that all Societies which were certified by the

benefits to their members. The Northern
Ireland Societies, like Societies in Great
Britain, have also undertaken to relieve the

I am prepared to give every consideration
to any representations such as that of the
Portadown Chamber of Commerce with regard to the finances and administration of
the National Health Insurance Scheme, and
I will not overlook the holding, at the proper

the initial years of the National Health
Insurance scheme were abnormal owing to
the conditions created by the war, and until

under normal conditions.
Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of that reply,
I would like to ask the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Andrews) if he recognises that that is
root and branch condemnation of an Act
which is costing us £500,000 a year, and
which has been in force for practically
twelve years?
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not at all admit that
is is condemnation of the Act in question.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) On the contrary, as I think I have pointed out, owing
to the abnormal conditions through which
we have been passing we have not a sound
basis to go on to say whether things are
right or whether they are wrong. As far
as we know they are right, but I would like
to point out that I think a great deal of
the criticism directed against this Act is due
to misunderstanding. Only a portion of these
surplus assets are available for additional
benefits, and the Societies acting in Northern
Ireland are all paying additional benefits at

TUBERCULOSIS SECTION, ADMINIS-
TRATION.
5. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Labour how much of the £50,000 granted
yearly to County Committees who administer
the Tuberculosis Section of the National
Insurance Act in Northern Ireland is spent
with the object of preventing infection from
Tuberculosis, or of enabling the people to
protect themselves and their children from
this disease.
Mr. ANDREWS: The sum which is available out of the National Health Insurance
Fund for County and County Borough Insurance Committees in Northern Ireland to
enable them to carry out their powers and
duties in connection with Tuberculosis is
about £18,000 a year. The main use which
is made of this money is the provision of
treatment in Sanatoria and in other suitable
ways for insured persons suffering from this
terrible disease, and this treatment in itself
tends to protect the public from infection.
In addition, Committees have discretionary
powers to spend money on the education of
the public by measures designed to prevent
the spread of the disease, and I am glad to
say that, thanks, I believe, to my hon.
Friend's influence, the Londonderry County
Committee has done useful work in this
direction. I may say that the whole question
is engaging my attention at the present time.
Dr. MORRISON: I beg to give the Minister
of Labour notice that I will raise this question
on the motion for adjournment.
