ESTIMATES, 1922-1923.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
CLASS I, No. II.
PUBLIC FUNERAL OF MR. TWADDELL.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £130 be
granted to His Majesty to defray the
expense of the public funeral of the late
Mr. W. J. Twaddell, a Member of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland."
The PRIME MINISTER: I have asked my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance
to be kind enough to allow me as the head
of the Government to move this motion in
the Committee to-day as a special tribute
to the memory of our late colleague, Mr.
Twaddell. I should say that immediately the
sad news reached my ears that this foul
assassination had taken place I communicated
with the bereaved widow, expressing
the deep regret and sorrow of all Members
of the Government, and at the same time
I said to her that there was no way in which
the Prime Minister, the Cabinet, or the
Government could express their sympathy
except by offering to her what is tantamount
to a State funeral. Broken with grief she
and the other members of our late colleague's
family acknowledged at once the right, I may
say, as well as the privilege of his old colleagues, to pay him this last respect, and
they were kind enough in the midst of their
grief to acquiesce in the proposal.
This is one of those instances where the
Government cannot at once ask for permission.
but I felt at the time I would be voicing the
sentiments of all the Members if I took on
myself the responsibility of incurring this
small charge, not only on behalf of the
Government but on behalf of the whole of
Ulster. It is not necessary to make a long
speech to the Committee. It is true that the
first horror of this dastardly outrage may
have passed way, but the memories of Ulster
people are long, and I am sure there is not
a Member of this first House of Parliament
of Ulster who will ever forget the tragic end
that met our dear friend who has departed.
I do not think any further words are necessary in moving that this sum be granted
as a tribute to the memory of our old colleague. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
OBJECTS OF ESTIMATES.
STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I think it would be convenient if
I made a short explanatory statement upon
the general character of the Estimates and
Supplementary Estimates, which I understand are in circulation and probably in
the hands of all hon. Members. These Estimates are very largely of a formal character,
and they are directed to attain several
objects. The first object in view, although not
necessarily the most important, is to regularise the whole accountancy system or arrange-
Supply-
Criminal Injuries.
22 JUNE 1922
ments between the Imperial authority and
ourselves. The second object, and also one
of some importance, is to distribute the
different liabilities from the Ministry of
Finance to their appropriate departments;
and the third, which I am sure hon. Members
will agree is not less important than any
other object to be attained, is to enable hon.
Members to be fully seized of the various
financial transactions and activities of the
Province.
As regards the first, that is to say, the
harmonising of the accountancy system of
the Imperial Treasury and our own, I think
I can recall that in my Budget statement I
dwelt at some length on the extreme perplexity of the financial movements that took
place as between the Imperial Treasury and
ourselves. The Imperial authority makes
payments direct and on its own, but they
ultimately reach us by way of deduction
from the revenue which that authority collects,
matters such as customs, excise, income tax,
etc. Then again they have to arrange with
our Ministry of Finance to act as agents
in regard to expenditure on buildings and
their maintenance for which they are liable.
Again, they ask us to meet expenditure for
which we are liable, but for which initially
under the Act they are primarily responsible.
An example of this is the case of certain County
Court Officers. Then again we have to undertake our own expenditure direct, which is the
simplest operation of all. But all these
things taken together will convey to hon.
Members' minds the great difficulty and complexity of the arrangements necessary to
harmonise all these matters and to bring
them before Parliament, so that all hon.
Members will be in a position to grasp fully
the nature of every financial transaction-no
matter of what character-how large it may
be, or how infinitesimal it may be. Everything must appear here before Parliament,
and hon. Members are brought into direct
relation to them.
A
The second object I mentioned, that is to
say, the distribution of the various items
of expenditure emanating from the Ministry
of Finance and relating to the different
departments, is necessary for various reasons.
One of the most important is economy, and
a proper and thorough supervision of the
various departments' items of expense.
good example of this is the Stationery
Department. I only mention this in order
that hon. Members may grasp the point. We
differ in our arrangements from the methods
adopted by the Imperial Parliament in respect of this department, and we do so
deliberately because we think our arrangements much more businesslike and offer much
greater opportunities for exercising a rigid
supervision which naturally will develop
economy. In the Imperial system Parliament
votes a lump sum to the Stationery Department, which supplies the various departments
with stationery requisites without charge. ln
our case it distributes its material over the
whole of the various departments of the Government, but charges each department with the
cost of the stationery it requires, and these
amounts must appear in the Estimates of
this department which are presented to
Parliament. Therefore, it is necessary in
this case that the Estimates I am presenting
to-day for distribution over the various departments and emanating from the Ministry
of Finance should be brought before the
House.
The third object needs no elaboration, as
I touched upon it, that is to say that all
these matters require to be brought in full
before the House. In regard to these Estimates, if hon. Members will refer to the
first page they will see a small Estimate and
various large Supplementary Estimates making a total sum of £1,400,000. This may seem
rather a large sum to present in the shape
of Supplementary Estimates, but I do not
think hon. Members need have any perturbation in regard to this. In the first place,
of the £1,400,000 it will be found that
£1,250,000 represent Imperial grants intended
for distribution in the Province. The first
is a sum of £750,000 which hon. Members
will recall is part of the grant made by the
Imperial authority for the purpose of meeting
the claims for malicious and criminal injuries. The second is a sum of £500,000
which is being demanded by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Labour, in regard
to unemployment, the estimate for which
was passed, if I recollect rightly, yesterday.
In regard to the balance between this
£1,250,000 and the amount of the Estimates,
the Committee may recollect that in my
Budget statement I made a provision for
Supplementary Estimates to the extent of
£150,000. I foresaw at that time that there
was definite expenditure which would require
to be provided for, and therefore it was
necessary to include it in the calculation of
our expenditure for the current year. The
first of these items was a sum of £98,000
additional State contribution to Unemployment Insurance. This was necessitated by
the passing by this House of an Act known
as the Unemployment Insurance (Northern
Ireland) Act, 1922, and which was passed
subsequent to the preparation of these
Estimates. In addition, there was a sum of
£50,000 which the House agreed should be
allocated to my right hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour, for expenditure in different
parts of the Province outside of Belfast for
which the larger sum was appropriated.
These two items in effect made up the
Supply-
Criminal Injuries.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

£150,000 which appeared as supplemental

In regard to the other matters which will
appear on the Estimates, I think possibly it

reach the Estimates themselves. There is

to refer to in view of the information I
conveyed a few minutes ago as to the agency
services we perform for the Imperial Government. The item of £250,000, which was
alluded to by the Minister of Home Affairs
yesterday, is a sum of money devoted by the
Imperial authority for the provision of houses
for ex-Servicemen. The position of that
matter is this. A sum of £600,000 was
provided by the Imperial Parliament to cover
their liability in regard to these houses for
soldiers and sailors for the whole of Ireland.
But a difficulty has arisen in regard to the
apportionment of this amount as between
Northern and Southern Ireland. Our claim
is that the apportionment should be made
in proportion to the number of ex-Servicemen
who joined up from Northern Ireland-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear and not upon the
basis of population. The ratio of population
is 28 per cent. for Northern Ireland, and the
Chief Secretary, who has purview of this
matter, proposes to allocate that £600,000 in
the proportion of 28 per cent. and 71 per
cent. We resent that apportionment, and
although we are proposing, through the
machinery of the Home Office, to carry out
this arrangement with the Imperial authority
and prosecute the scheme for the erection
of houses for ex-Servicemen, the whole matter
is still sub judice and under discussion, and
I can assure the House it will not be for
want of any effort on our part if we do not
succeed in securing a larger proportion for
Northern Ireland.
There are other agency matters of a somewhat complicated nature which I think can
be better explained when we reach the Estimate involved-matters relating to Clerks of
the Crown and Peace, County Court Officers,
Resident Magistrates, and such like, but I
think I have indicated sufficiently the general
nature of these Estimates which I propose to
submit without detaining the
House any
further in regard to the general question. I
will, therefore, when you call upon me, deal
with the Estimates in detail.
CLASS II, No. 9.
CRIMINAL INJURIES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £750,000 be
granted to His Majesty to defray the charge
that will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1923, to provide
recoupment to local authorities in Northern
Ireland in respect of payments made by
them on foot of Criminal Injury decrees."
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps it will
be for the convenience of the House if I
took charge of this particular Vote as I
probably know more about how we came to
arrange this than any other Member of the
Government. My right hon. Friend and
were faced with the fact that very large
sums of money were being demanded in our
Six-County area in connection with the
criminal loss that was sustained in all
quarters by the murders and burnings that
had been going on. An arrangement was
come to by the Imperial Government with
the Provisional Government in Southern
Ireland to set up a Commission to inquire
into all the cases which had arisen there
where compensation might be claimed, and
the suggestion was thrown out that we here
in Northern Ireland should also have a
Commission to sit and inquire into all the
claims that had been made with a view to
the same amelioration being got out of the
Imperial Exchequer. I pointed out at once
to the Government that the difference between
Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland was
this: that our Courts were running; that
claims for malicious injury were all being
tried by the County Court Judges throughout
the length and breadth of our area, and
that these claims, therefore, had already been
the subject of the most meticulous inquiry
before a decree was given, and consequently
we were in a position to know exactly where
we stood for the period for which this particular grant was made. I argued also with
the Chancellor of the Exchequer in Great
Britain that the horrors that filled pages of
our daily papers were quite sufficient without
having a re-hash of all these sordid happenings which had taken place during the
period to which these Votes refer, and to
have a Commission sitting, and going back.
for instance, to the terrible murder of
Inspector Swanzy at Lisburn, recalling in
one's mind the horrible details, and all being
served up for the relatives and friends, and
also for those in whose midst these terrible
crimes were committed, was not, in my
opinion, a very suitable arrangement to make
when the passions of the people were sufficiently high. Therefore, after very close
consultation with my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance, we both came to the
conclusion that it would be better to take
a hard and fast sum from the Imperial
Government-something approximating to
two-thirds of the whole of the claims-than
to have a Commission sitting and inquiring
into them and in the end perhaps not dealing
so generously with us as we have been dealt
with under this grant. At all events, two
moieties of £750,000 are to be paid. One
moiety has already been lodged to my right
hon. Friend's credit which he is now prepared to dispense with in accordance with
the claims put in by the Local Authorities,
Supply-
Supplementary Estimates.

be lodged to his credit on 1st June next

the Vote to go any further at the moment,

of a similar character with regard to those

I do think this House would like me
to say, and not in any niggardly way, that
we really are grateful to the British Chancellor of the Exchequer for the way he has
met us in regard to this matter.
Members: Hear, hear.) I know well the
feelings that are stirred up in the hearts
of all of us when we think we have been
deserted or forgotten or maltreated by Great
Britain, but in this case His Majesty's
Treasury have met our wishes in the matter
to the fullest and most generous extent. They
came forward with the suggestion that our
local Recorders and our County Court Judges
should allow their decrees to be taken as the
standard on which this sum was based. They
have met us most generously in regard to
the £750,000 lodged to our credit, and the
£750,000 that will be due to us on 1st June,
1923. If there is any other point in respect
of this matter that the House wishes to
discuss, my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Finance, will be only too glad to answer
any particular question.

Mr. POLLOCK: The Estimate which I now
present is one of an exceedingly complicated
character and requires some explanation.
The Vote, as hon. Members will
see, is
directed to the provision for County Court
officers' and magistrates' salaries, allowances,
and travelling expenses. A part of this
service, that is to say the salaries of all
existing Clerks to the Crown and Peace and
the payment of bonus to Recorders and County
Court Judges, whose salaries are charged or
the United Kingdom Consolidated Fund, were
to be paid in the first instance by the Im
perial Government under Section 54 (I) of the
Government of Ireland Act, such payments
to be recovered by deduction from the Northern Irish residuary share of reserved taxes.
This necessitated an Imperial estimate for
this expenditure, which was formerly accounted for by the Paymaster-General's Department in Dublin Castle, but which was
transferred to the Irish Office in view of the
recent changes which, as we all know, have
taken place in the Government of Ireland.
Arrangements have now been made at the request of the Treasury whereby the Ministry
of Finance examine and check claims in respect of the above, issue payments on behalf
of the Irish Office, receiving an advance by
way of imprest from that Department, the
exact balance being adjusted subsequently
with the Irish Office in accordance with a
certified statement of expenditure to be rendered by us.
The second point is that the remaining part
of this service, which is administered directly
by the Northern Government, that is to say,
salaries of Valuers, Registrars, Process
Servers, the Assistant Recorder, Belfast,
travelling expenses of County Court Judges,
etc., etc., was, at the time the Estimate for
1922-23 was framed, accounted for by the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and the Vote passed
by the House-Class 2, No. 3-appeared with
the Ministry of Home Affairs as the accounting Department. The Ministry of Finance,
however, has now been substituted for the
Ministry of Home Affairs in regard to this
part of the service for the following reasons-
(1) The County Court Vote has always been
a Treasury Vote.
(2) There were possible objections to payments to the Judiciary or its officers being
made by the Executive instead of by a
purely financial department.
(3) The Ministry of Home Affairs undertook an additional burden on the accounting
side with the addition of an Ulster Constabulary Vote to its list,
so that the Ministry of Home Affairs had
quite enough on its hands in regard to these
matters without making this addition to its
burdens. The substitution of the Ministry of
Finance for the Ministry of Home Affairs in
this connection consequently necessitated a
revised estimate in order to bring the change
of responsibility before Parliament. That is
really the gravamen of my statement. This
revised Estimate has been laid on the table of
the House and circulated to Members. It

most complex and complicated arrangement

I beg to move.

823 Assassination of Sir H. Wilson. HOUSE OF COMMONS. Statement by Prime Minister 824
Assassination of Sir Henry Wilson.
STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to move
that the House do now adjourn. I have
to break sad news to the House. Field-
Marshal Sir Henry Wilson has been
murdered. (Hon. Members: Shame, shame.)
I am sure this
Parliament of
young
ours is getting many a sad task to
perform. Sir Henry Wilson has laid down his
life for Ulster. Of that we have no doubt
whatever. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) A
short time ago, as is in the memory of the
House, I had occasion to ask his assistance in
our hour of trial, and trouble, and difficulty,
and his answer was very characteristic-no hesitation, no thought necessary.
He said,
"You need hardly have asked me. Now that
you have, all that I can do for you shall be
done for the cause of my country." (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I believe the acceptance of that request has cost him his life, and
I am sure he would not have it otherwise.
A more gallant or a finer soldier never stepped.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). To his widow,
we as a House tender our profound and
deeply-felt sympathy. The news has only just
come through. I have barely heard it myself.
There are no details. There is no doubt Sir
Henry has been murdered and assassinated.
He has laid down his life just when he was
emerging after a long term of service to the
Empire and to the country that he loved, looking forward as many men would have looked
forward after escaping an honourable death
upon the battlefield-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear)--to some relaxation, some quiet, some
peace, after all the arduous work he had performed. That has been denied him. He has
been called away. I suppose he was one of our
greatest men. It has often been said that
Ulster has produced men who have lived in
her very midst who were an honour to their
country, to their Empire, and yet their greatness was not recognised by the people among
whom they lived. And that may be true to
some extent, or may have been true, with
regard to the gallant Field-Marshal up to a
short time ago. I do not believe that the people
of Ulster appreciated what a great man he was
till he retired from the Army-I should not
say retired, for a Field-Marshal never retires
from the Army, but from active service with
the Military Forces of the Crown. His name
is really a monument amongst the whole of
the countries of Europe. They recognised in
him a great man, and they knew that towards
the winning of the War no single person lent
so much as our late comrade and friend,
Field-Marshal Sir Henry Wilson.
I have counted him a close personal friend
He
for many years.
most lovable
was
a
character, and the people of Belfast had a
deep reverence for him. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Strange to say, one of the last
letters that passed between him and myself
was with regard to the seat rendered vacant
by the death of Mr. Twaddell. The Committee, through our Chief Whip, asked me to
communicate with him to say how honoured
they would be if he would allow his name
to go forward as the standard-bearer of the
Loyalists in that division. He was unable to
do so. He felt that his work lay more in giving advice to us on military matters, and advice to the Government in London on Imperial matters. I mention the incident to
show that here in this great city of Belfast
his marked qualities were appreciated by the
people. They loved him. He is one more
stalwart fallen in this desperate battle which
we are fighting. But it will make no difference to any man in this Assembly. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. DONALD: We will carry on.
The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend
the Member for the East Division says we
will carry on. We will carry on more vigorously. We have now the death of Mr.
Twaddell and the death of the Field-Marshal
always before us. Guiding lights they will
always be to us--the one in a humble capacity, lovable, the other in a higher position,
equally lovable. They have been carried
away. I am sure everyone in this House will
think it would be ill-fitting for me to say any
more on the subject. I have hardly recovered
from the terrible shock, and I am sure the
House will not like to proceed with any further business. Even had we had the news
earlier in the day I would have proposed an
adjournment, but it has come in at the end
of the day's work. It is all very sad. I feared
when I spoke last of the loss of our late
Member (Mr. Twaddell) that he would not be
the last to be taken away from us. The realisation of that fear has come sooner than I
expected. I know that my colleagues feel with
me, that the situation has become additionally
grave, and it should now be clear even to
those men who through prejudice have had
blinded eyes with regard to our position, or
through ignorance have failed to understand
it, that this foul murder which has taken
place in London proves beyond all further
argument that there is a wide conspiracy
against those who are fighting the battle of
Ulster.
I do hope and trust that there will be no
further doubt in the mind of any man that
what Ulster is engaged in is a battle not for
Ulster alone, but for the Empire, and if any
thing is needed to steel the nerves and hearts
of Ulster people it is the fact that they are
battling not for a selfish cause but for one
825 Assassination of Sir H. Wilson.
22 JUNE 1922
which affects the whole of the people of the
great Empire to which they are proud to belong.
I have just had the following further particulars handed to me:-
"Field-Marshal Sir Henry Wilson was
returning from unveiling a Memorial to
War heroes at the Great Eastern Railway
Depot, where he wound up a moving speech
by quoting from Kipling's "Recessional,"
and he was approaching his house in Eaton
Place when two men approached and fired
three shots, all taking effect. The crowd
rushed at the attackers, who fired again,
Statement by Prime Minister. 826
two policemen being wounded. One of the
assailants, seeing he could not escape,
turned the weapon on himself and was taken
to hospital badly wounded. His accomplice
was captured."
I have nothing further to say, except once
more on behalf of this House to tender to the
widow, whom I personally count as a friend,
the deepest sympathy of the Parliament of
Northern Ireland.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Monday, 26th June, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.

Oral Answers to Questions.
MAILS FOR BELLEEK-PETTIGO DIS-
TRICT.
1. Mr. MARK (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Minister of Commerce if he is aware that the
people residing in the Belleek-Pettigo district
have received no mails for at least a fortnight; whether these mails are accumulating
at Omagh, and by whose orders the mails are
held there, and if he will have an inquiry
instituted into the matter?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
M'Keown): I am aware that there was a sus
pension of deliveries of letters from the
Belleek, Letter and Pettigo Post Offices for
about a fortnight from the 1st of June owing
to the stoppage of trains from Omagh and the
military operations in the district. The
mails were necessarily held by the Postal
Authorities at Omagh until arrangements
could be made for their delivery.
The control of the Postal Services in Northern Ireland remains in the hands of the
Imperial Government. On the matter being
brought to the notice of my Department,
however, representations were made immediately to the Postal Authorities, and I am informed by those authorities that instructions
were given to the Postmaster, Omagh, to
make immediate arrangements for correspondence addressed to places within the Northern Ireland area, and hitherto delivered
from Pettigo Post Office, to be delivered from
an adjacent office within the Northern area
pending the re-opening of the Pettigo office,
and that arrangements were also made for
the delivery of correspondence addressed to
Belleek and Letter. I now understand that
the Pettigo office has been re-opened within
the past few days.
REGISTRATION OF GOVERNMENT
MOTOR CARS.
2. Mr. MARK (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether the Government has recently purchased a large fleet
of motor cars, which are being used without
registered numbers, and without paying taxes
in the counties in which they are being used,
and whether he is prepared to have this state
of affairs remedied?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Government has recently
received a large number of motor cars which
are being registered as rapidly as possible.
Under Section 12 of the Roads Act, 1920,
vehicles belonging to the Crown are exempt
from Motor Licence Duties.
INQUIRIES IN LIEU OF CORONERS'
INQUESTS.
3. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Home Affairs-Who is the Commissioner
appointed to hold inquiries in lieu of
coroners' inquests in Northern Ireland;
what are his qualifications for the office;
what is his remuneration, and does he supersede the Coroners? Also, in view of the fact
that there are already efficient Coroners for
all districts in the Six Counties, is not the
appointment of a Commissioner to discharge
the same duties an unnecessary expenditure
of public money?
Sir DAWSON BATES: There has not been
made any permanent appointment as Officer
to hold inquiries in lieu of Coroners' inquests.
A Solicitor or a Barrister has been
appointed to hold inquiries in a few cases in
which the circumstances were such as to
render it undesirable to ask either juries or
the local Coroner to act.
For instance, in the cases of the recent
murders near Newry, it was considered it
would not be right in the turmoil of local
feeling to ask either the local Coroner or a
Jury to act.
The professional gentleman appointed will
be paid £10 10s for each inquiry, but his fee
is limited to this sum where the inquiry is
into more than one death at the same time
and place.
When the nature of the duty, and the
circumstances in which it is performed are
considered, as well as the fact that there are
frequently adjournments, and that more
than one day's work is necessary, it will be
seen that the fee is not excessive.
It is essential to secure the services of a
gentleman whose qualifications are beyond
dispute.
Each case is carefully considered in all its
aspects. including that of economy, and it
is only in exceptional cases that the Special
Inquiry is ordered. In all other cases the
ordinary inquests are held. The Coroners
have not been superseded.
a
The policy of holding these Special
Inquiries was adopted by Parliament
couple of months ago, and it is this policy
which is being carried out.
It must be remembered that before the
passing of the Civil Authorities Act, Military
Inquiries were generally held in similar

In all these circumstances it is considered

careful control is being exercised.
Mr. LAVERY: With regard to this query
would the right hon. Gentleman inform the
House what is the fee for each inquiry that
is held?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I explained in my
answer that the fee is ten guineas, regardless
of the time occupied. A case might occupy
one day, two days, or three days, but there
is a fixed fee of ten guineas to cover the
inquiry.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT (NORTHERN
IRELAND) BILL.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read the Second time."
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw): My right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs, who has so many
pressing duties to attend to, has asked me
to take charge of this measure, and I consider in the circumstances it is a pleasure
as well as a duty to relieve him of any of
the heavy burdens that are on his shoulders
at the present moment. The primary object
of the Bill is to abolish Proportional Representation so far as it affects Local Government. Till a short time ago only a few
who might be styled political philosophers
knew anything of what was meant by Proportional Representation. Yet the principle
is not a present-day invention. In his work
on "Representative Government," John
Stuart Mill, whose life was spent in trying
to reduce mental and political problems to
hard and fast laws, discussed the theory which
had been promulgated some time before
by a gentleman called Mr. Haire. The conclusion of John Stuart Mill with regard to
Proportional Representation was that in no
other way which it seems possible to suggest
would Parliament be so certain of containing
the elite of the country. Of course
he was there speaking of the Parliamentary
representation, and I think that hon. Members should appreciate the compliment that
they are chosen after the best fashion on
which political science could form a theory.
Notwithstanding the great authority of Mill,
the system of Proportional Representation
remained a theory till modern democracy
came into contact with the constituency of
Sligo. Sligo has a very unique political
history. It has proved something of a
stumbling-block to those who believe in the
infallibility of the collective wisdom of the
people. Long ago it was disfranchised in
the Imperial Parliament for corruption and
bribery. Afterwards, when the Household
Franchise was introduced in Local Government, Sligo remained true to its traditions,
and held the palm for wasteful and inefficient administration, giving a lead that
was followed later by Poplar. The result
of this was that bankruptcy stared the
Council of Sligo in the face, and something
had to be done. The Government in power
shirked any course that would suggest a
doubt on the theory that all Irishmen were
fit for self-government. Something had to
be done, and someone suggested Proportional
Representation. The suggestion was adopted
and we had a typical instance of the old
maxim:
"Fiat experimentum in corpore vili."
It was said that the result was good, and
that some respectable men got elected, whereas, it could not well have been worse than
it was before, and under any system of
government the probability is that a better
Council would have been returned for Sligo.
The doctrinaires who had been promulgating
this theory regarded it as a panacea for
all the evils of the State, and they proceeded
to fresh achievements. The new franchise
had just been introduced by the Imperial
Parliament which would apply to Local
Government, and even the most firm believer
in majorities was somewhat afraid of what
might happen in Ireland. The proposal
then was made to apply the system of
Proportional Representation that had turned
out, as they said, well in Sligo to all Irish
self-government, and the Local Government
Act of 1919 was accordingly passed. It was
intended to give an opportunity to moderate
men to take part in the business of Local
Local Government Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Megaw]
Government. There was no popular demand
for it. Sane politicians had become rather
despondent of the future of local government
in Ireland seeing that at that time it had
pretty well broken down, even under the
old franchise, because one body after another
was defying the law, and the Local Government Board was led to bring writs of
mandamus and other proceedings in the
Courts to try to induce them to do something
like their duties.
As
This Act of 1919 changed the previous
system of elections and introduced new
electoral districts so as to give Proportional
Representation free scope. I should have
mentioned that it had been previously
adopted in regard to some of the University
seats for the 1918 election; but I think
Proportional Representation was more made
for academic constituencies probably than
any others, because University people are
trained in allotting percentages and marks
They are
at competitive examinations.
accustomed to that sort of thing, so the
study of the various points of the candidates
would give them pleasurable excitement.
But I think this House will consider that
experience is the best test of any theory,
and I am bound to say that neither in
Southern nor Northern Ireland did the
great things prophesied for Proportional
Representation fructify. We heard a great
deal about the highly educated minorities
getting representation. These highly educated minorities may have existed, but we
did not see members of the Councils who
I do not
seemed to reflect their influence.
know that there would be any better example
of that than the Dublin Corporation.
you know, of course, I myself have an experience of Dublin extending over a great
Dublin contains a very large
many years.
number of learned men of all professions;
it is also the seat of the Government,
and naturally it contains a great many who
might be supposed to make a leaven for the
But the
representation on the Corporation.
results of the 1920 election reduced the
Dublin Corporation to something worse than
it ever was before, and it had the same
effect in the constituencies in Southern
Ireland. At the previous election the local
authorities had been bad, but those which
were elected under Proportional Representation were worse. You may remember that
after these various new bodies were elected
all through Southern Ireland, they defied
the law. The Local Government Board,
as it had practiced before, tried again to
reduce them to something like order, but
it did not press the matter to anything like
a serious head, and the result was that local
government broke down all through Southern Ireland-and that was with the local
bodies which had been elected under this
system of Proportional Representation.
are
In the North we did not fare so badly,
but I think anyone who has had experience
of it will say that most of the electors
and candidates-successful and unsuccessfuldisliked the system, which by its complication lent itself to manipulations by clever
electioneering agents. It was not generally
understood, and the House will remember
that lectures had to be given all through
the country by those who were qualified to
instruct the various officials as to how its
administration should be managed.
As a
result, the percentage of voters who went
to the polls, except in the counties of Tyrone,
Fermanagh and Derry, was very small
indeed. The areas were so unwieldy that the
candidate was frequently not known in the
parts distant from his residence. The
theories about the electors welcoming the
best known public men were falsified very
largely in practice as the candidate who
provided the largest number of motor cars
and had the most pressing canvass got the
Number 1 preference. Comparisons
invidious, but I think there are few who
will contend that even in the North the
local bodies elected under Proportional Representation were an improvement on their
predecessors. You will remember that a
few of them in some parts of the Northern
area defied the law and have been suspended
by our own Government. There can be no
doubt as to the experience of the last
Parliamentary election. Hardly anyone
wants the system to be continued. All of
us who have gone through the mill-and
we all have successfully-know how deeprooted the aversion to Proportional Representation is. The English Lord Chancellor
after the late Southern elections has been
very loud in his encomiums of the system,
but his observations have been from a
distance. I hope he will have cause to
retain his complacent admiration when he
has had experience of the mental and moral
equipment of the Members of the Southern
Parliament who are chosen under the system
which has been regarded as the panacea for
all the ills of the Commonwealth. It has
been found more costly both to the candidates and the ratepayers. I am informed
on good authority that the elections under
Proportional Representation have cost two
or three times as inuch as under the old
system. The elections themselves are cumbersome, and they often lend themselves to
freakish incidents and results.
Perhaps, however, the feature of Proportional Representation which calls for
most criticism, and is most objectionable to
the average elector. is not the mystification
as to how the result is arrived at, but the
fact that he has no member whether for
his rural district or county council, as the
case may be. It is said that he has four
or five members, but none of these is in
a position to voice the claims of a par
Local Government Bill-

26 JUNE 1922
Second Reading.
ticular district, and this is the essence of
local government. The electoral areas are
so large that there are certain to be different
interests for different parts, and the result
is that responsibility to the electorate is
largely taken away. The essence of local
government administration centres in the
word "local" and the areas represented
should be local and not unduly large. For
Poor Law relief the Guardian should be in
a position to ascertain the circumstances of
any applicant for that relief within his
constituency. The County Councillor should
know the roads and road management of
the constituency which he represnts.
I am
taking these as examples, but if any Member
of the House cares to examine the functions
of local Councillors, he will find that the
same argument applies to most of them.
For good local government there should be
local specialised interest on the part of the
Councillor, which is dissipated perforce in
big areas with large numbers. In our
system we should aim at commanding the
respect and confidence of the people, that
they should understand the system and feel
that it is their affair. Consequently, simplicity is essential, and it is only by an
intelligible system that proper representation
of local interests may be obtained. In the
Six Counties we had a system of voting
which gave satisfaction. We may have had
voters whose sense of responsibility was not
what it might have been, but there was no
complaint as regards the system. It worked
satisfactorily, and we are asking the House
now to revert to it.
Having mentioned in general terms what
our proposals are and the reasons for them
I would ask hon. Members, to examine more
or less generally the more salient features
of our Bill. The whole essence of the Bill
is contained in Clause 1, which provides that
on and after the ordinary day of election
of next year the members of local authorities in Northern Ireland shall be elected
under the system which was in force prior
to the passing of that Act of 1919, which
I have mentioned, and that the various local
authorities shall be elected for the electoral
divisions, wards, urban districts, or towns,
instead of for the local areas which were
formed under that Act of 1919; that is, we
are reverting to the system of the old electoral
units and the new electoral areas which
were promulgated by the Local Government
Board in Dublin in their various electoral
orders shall no longer be applicable for local
elections. Sub-Section (2), to which I would
call the attention of hon. Members, is consequential. It repeals Section 1 and Section
10 of the Act of 1919. Clause 1 of that
Act was the Clause which introduced the
system of Proportional Representation.
I would call the attention of hon. Members
to the fact that Section 11 of the Act of
1919 repealed the old system, which was in
force in the boroughs, by which one-third
of the members of the Council retired annually on each election. The effect of the
repeal of that Section brought it about that
the elections in the boroughs, just as in
the counties and rural districts, take place
only once in three years, and the Bill as
it is now introduced leaves that new system
in force. We are not wedded to it as a
Government. We are ready, if it is the
view of the various Members representing
the borough districts, to revert to the old
system by which one-third of the members
should retire each year; but under the Bill
as it stands at present, and if it were passed
without amendment, we should have the
system introduced by which all the members
would retire triennially. Section 11 also
dealt with the election of Aldermen. Under
the new system of the Act of 1919, the
Aldermen were those who topped the polls
at the one election, that is there was the
same election for Councillors and for Aldermen. They were elected in one body and
those who headed the poll were styled
Aldermen, but they retired at the same time
as the Councillors did. Now, I think there
is a good deal to be said for that, not
perhaps as it exists under Proportional
Representation, but that there is a direct
election where all the voters can vote for
all the candidates who come before them.
It is, I think, not a bad idea at all
that the man who heads the poll should
be styled "Alderman," if there is any
particular honour attached to that title.
I should have said that sub-Section 3 of
Clause 1 is to be read with Part 1 of the
Schedule to the Bill, and that the two wogether are substituted for sub-Sections 2
and 3 of Section 4 of the Act of 1919. The effect
of the substitution is to provide an improved
method of electing Aldermen and Councillors. Instead of having the election of
Aldermen separate there is one election for
both, as I have mentioned before.
Sub-Section 4 of Clause 1 is to be read with
Part 2 of the Schedule, and the two of these
read together make provisions for re-enacting
the necessary provisions of the Local Government Act of 1898 repealed by the Act of
1919. They have general relation to the
election of County Councillors for each electoral division, Rural Councillors for each
rural district, and Guardians for each Urban
District. There is one other matter that is
embodied in this Bill which I have not
mentioned up to the present. Under the
old system in rural districts two Councillors
represented each district. That had the
effect of making rather a large body, I think,
in the rural districts, and it is now proposed
to continue the method, at least to continue
the principles approximately that were sub-

divisions, and so forth, and it tells the conditions under which that can be done
Criticism has been made that though this
has been done in regard to county boroughs
and in regard to county electoral divisions
it has not been done in regard to rural
districts. As a matter of fact that nas
already been provided for by the Act of
1898, and we have power to do so. Therefore
it has not been considered necessary to
re-introduce that in this measure.
Sub-Section 3 contains regulations that in
the carrying out of that duty to which I
have referred the various bodies that are
interested should be consulted so that the
Home Ministry should have an opportunity
of hearing what may be said by the various
local bodies in regard to the changes that
are proposed to be made. There is just
one other thing in the Bill that I want to
call attention to, and that is in the second
paragraph of the third sub-Section of
Section 2. Hon. Members will see there
is a clause that the 15th day of November
has been fixed as the time when it is necessary to have the register of electors made
up. That is only for this year, because it
would be absolutely impossible for the
Ministry, if this Bill is passed, to have the
register made out in the constituencies that
will have to be fixed by Order of the Home
Ministry. Now, Clause 3 does not require
any comment from me. Let me just say
in conclusion that in bringing in this Measure
the Government has no desire to preclude
Hon. Members from making suggestions as
to how the Bill may be improved. The
broad scope, as I have said, is to restore
the old voting, as to which practically unanimous representations have been made from
all parts of our area. We shall be glad to
consider in Committee any suggestions that
are made that are not at variance with the
principles of the Bill, so that the measure
may tend to the promotion of efficient Local
Government throughout Northern Ireland.
I beg to move.
Mr. LYNN: It is with some trepidation
I rise to take part in this discussion, because,
as you know, in 1919 my hon. Friend the
Chairman of Ways and Means and I spent
a very weary Session trying to fight this
Bill at every point. We did keep it hanging
up for about three months. We fought it
at every point, but we were always voted
down by people who never took the
trouble of listening to debates or of making
themselves acquainted with the arguments
for or against the Measure. My hon. and
learned Friend opposite (Mr. Megaw) might
have mentioned that when the Act was
passed there were only two Irishmen in the
House of Commons who voted for the Second
reading. I think that of itself is a striking
commentary, because, after all, if Irishmen
want a thing they are not slow in asking
for it, but when this Bill was brought in
only two Irishmen could be induced to vote
for it, and let me say with respect to both
of them they neither of them understood
the Measure. The Measure was really forced
upon the Government in order to give some
assistance, some help, to the minority in
Southern Ireland. The then Attorney-
General, Mr. Justice Samuels, was very enthusiastic about it. He had the impression
that we were going to get something new
and valuable into public life, but the result
of the Measure itself has shown how hopeless
it is. My hon. and learned Friend (Mr.
Megaw), who is always very polite in his
expressions, referred to the people who
carried this as political philosophers. Some
of us who are blunter are inclined to describe
them as cranks. I think anyone who has
watched the operations of this Measure in
Ireland knows very well that it is not a
Measure that has made for the benefit
of political life. It has not benefited
the voter, the taxpayer, or the unfortunate
person who devotes his time to public
service. Sligo, of course, was the instance
that was always given, and I am not going
to follow my hon. and learned Friend with
regard to Sligo, and, indeed, I think Rory
O'Connor could have given them a better
Council at the point of the revolver than
any they could have got under Proportional
Representation or any representation. So far
as we are concerned it has been a hopeless
failure. There is only one point on which
I disagree with my hon. and learned Friend
opposite (Mr. Megaw), and that is that he
seems to think that the Universities got
some satisfaction out of it. May I point
out to him there is one University in Northern Ireland-I believe he is a member of it
himself and that the percentage of spoiled
votes in the elections of 1920 was much
higher in that University than in any of
the other constituencies? It was a very high

There are three points that were very ably
and eloquently made by my hon. Friend the
Chairman of Ways and Means in the Imperial House, and the first was, if I re
collect aright, there was no mandate for
this change, the second was that several

Parliament but had been rejected, and the

purpose for which it was intended. We know
it has failed, and for the reasons which my
hon. and learned Friend has given. I know
from the Parliamentary point of view it
gives us much too large a constituency. I
agree with my hon. and learned Friend that
it is essential in order to get work well done
the representative, whether he be in Parlia
ment, in the Corporation, the Board of
Guardians, or any public body, should really
know his constituency well and that his
constituency should know him if that were
possible. When there are four members or
more for a constitueney, the question is,
how are the constituents to visit the sins
on any member, or how are they to appraise
or give him credit? You get hopelessly
mixed up. You do away with the control
that the constituents have over the members,
and in that way you weaken public life.
For that reason I am glad that in this
Bill we are going back to the old principle.
I think the old principle worked very well.
I know theorists can work out all sorts of
things for Proportional Representation, but
look at the practical working of it and see
if any of these theories ever fructify. I do
not know that they have. I am glad to hear
my hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Megaw)
saying they are prepared to accept amendments in Committee that do not interfere
with the principles of the Bill. For instance,
I notice in looking through the Bill
that the Minister of Home Affairs may

Parliamentary rights, have also got their
If
constituency divided into fifteen wards.
the Home Secretary was to change the

There are other points with regard to this

sure will

my hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Megaw)

Rates have increased enormously. It is

in controlling expenditure. As I said some

Sir CRAWFORD M'CULLAGH: I desire

to express the indebtedness of the House

and I am not in any way speaking for the

So far as the City of Belfast is concerned

amendments. While you repeal the Act of

Under this Bill all the members of the
Belfast Corporation will go out of office in
January and there will be a new election
for the whole of the 60 members. My great
objection to that is that you will lose the
continuity of the present work of the Corporation. You will have 60 members retiring
at once, so that you may have the entire
personnel of the Corporation changed and
you will get some freakish results I think
it would be much better to go back to the
system of annual elections, that is to say,
to have an election every year. The City
of Belfast, as my hon. Friend the Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) has said, is
divided into fifteen wards. I suggest that
those fifteen wards should be retained, because they represent all the different classes
in the city, and by having four members
for each ward you get the full membership
of the Corporation, which consists of three
Councillors and one Alderman for each ward.
Of course I quite understand that you will
have to have an election for the entire 60
members in January, but I will suggest in my
amendment that in 1924 fifteen Councillors,
one from each ward, should retire. It may
be said that it would be a hardship in the
case of men who had to fight another election
within a year, but experience has taught us
that where a man has served his city well
for twelve months he is very often returned
unopposed. Then in 1925 I suggest that
fifteen more members should retire, and in
1926 the remaining members who would by
that time have completed: their three years'
service, should retire. That would complete
the rota. Under this Bill I cannot see any
difference between an Alderman and a
Councillor. In the old days an Alderman was
elected for six years, but now if you get
the largest number of votes you become an
Alderman, and yet retire after three
years. It is a very doubtful compliment,
and what I suggest is that having elected
fifteen Aldermen in 1923 you allow seven to
retire at the end of three years. That could
be easily arranged by the Corporation under
the Act of 1896. When they are re-elected
they would remain in office six years, and
after another three years the Aldermen
elected in January would retire after six
years' service. That would establish the roca.
I am firmly convinced that so far as the
City of Belfast is concerned it would be
better to have an election every year, so
that if there was any question of great importance before the public, as there usually
is, the opinion of the citizens could be
expressed upon it. I do not think I need
dwell any further on the matter to-day
because I shall have an opportunity of going
into the question in detail on the Committee
stage, but I do hope the Government will
seriously consider the suggestions I have
made. I might also say that another proposal in the Bill to which I strongly object,
is that if a casual vacancy occurs the Corporation should fill it from the ranks of
the Councillors and declare the seat of the
selected Councillor vacant. Where a vacancy
occurs for an Alderman I think the constituency should have an opportunity of saying
who their Alderman shall be, and I suggest
that instead of co-opting an Alderman from
the ranks of the Councillors the Alderman
should be selected by the constituents as
under the Act of 1896. I think such a
change would improve the Bill. I have only
given an indication of the amendments I
intend to move, and I hope to have an
opportunity of going more fully into the
details on the Committee stage.

I am not at all satisfied with the Bill as

against the wall trying to make a minority
a majority, and when we saw this little
unwanted infant you are doing to death

However, having shed a tear on the coffin
of this poor little unwanted bantling, I must

a convert to proportional representation,
but I find from statistics that it was only
under proportional representation that the
loyalists in Southern Ireland had a solitary
chance of being returned. (Hon. Members:
None). Let me quote where they have been
returned. In every county there are men
returned under proportional representation
who would have had no earthly chance
under minority representation.
We have all a right to take a wider view
of this question. The truth of the matter
is I question very much if the bringing in of
this Bill will not rather tend to turn the
minds of the people. Have the people been
consulted before you, brought in this Bill?
I was at two meetings, and what was the
result of one of them? There were only
ten for and eight against. At another
meeting I went to there was really no
majority or anxiety shown that they were
wanting a change in the method of election
at all. You know we are living in very
troublesome times, and I think in all
fairness the people should have been consulted. I may be told that the representatives of the different divisions met in consultation, but I am sorry they did not
invite me. I am here with a perfectly open
847 Local Government Bill-

mind, but if the speeches that have been
made were of the tone of the speech of my

indication that proportional representation
would meet the very views he has expressed,
that certain people in certain areas would
conveniently be brought in under this Bill.
That is all I have got to say about the
Bill. I think we are rushing this thing just
rather quickly, and it is causing expense.
I am satisfied in my own mind that we could
have carried our next elections with great
success under proportional representation.
It is just as fair to one side as the other. I
have in my mind that at one of the last
Local Government elections a member was
actually returned who only received in the
first count 302 preference votes. One other
member received over 700, and another over
600, but the member with 302 was elected.
Therefore, it is just as fair to one side as
the other, and that applies to every division
in the city of Belfast. Now, it may be said
that I am like a voice in the wilderness,
but I speak as I feel at this time, and I
believe that every hon. Member of this
House should get up and express his candid
opinion. The people have not been consulted. I do not consider one meeting I was
at was really a meeting; it was really a committee. I do not consider it was a representative view that could be accepted when only
ten voted for and eight against. So far as
I am concerned while I said I was going
to criticise the Bill I am not going to oppose
it, because it is useless to do so. This
House will undoubtedly pass it, but it is
unfair to bring in the measure at this time
because the expenditure will be such that we
could very well do without it.

Mr. LAVERY: I rise to congratulate the
Government on introducing this Bill. I think
it is high time to put an end to the Chinese
puzzle that another Government prepared for
us. If I remember correctly when going
round the various towns and villages in the
County of Down twelve months ago the loyal
people were all agreed to a man-and to a
woman-in favour of the repeal of this
Act, and a promise was given that if the six
candidates were elected undoubtedly
Bill of this kind would be introduced and
run through the House at the earliest date.
Therefore, the promise then given is being
kept faithfully and well. There are one or
two matters in the Bill that I should like
to refer to. I am very strongly in favour of
the one-third retiring annually. It will enable us to have continuity in our councils
whether they are rural or urban. For years
past we have felt the want of that, because in the town from which I
come we have, unfortunately, a special Act—
and it was very wrong indeed to have such
a thing, but personally I voted against it,
and was out voted-and we put ourselves in
the position that for years past the entire
Board retired every third year. We found
it a great want in continuity, particularly
when there were any special things on hand.
By this suggestion of one-third retiring
annually, which I think the House will receive very favourably indeed from what I
have heard, the importance of these things
will be looked into and sustained from year
to year.
So.
Another matter has been mentioned, and
that is with regard to limited liability
companies, directors and such like not

been mentioned, that the rates are high.
Why should these people who start business
and give labour to hundreds and thousands
of employees not have votes in connection
with their establishments? We have power
now to make that right, and we ought to do

Mr. MEGAW: I wish to say only a few
words in reply to the criticisms that have
been offered by hon. Members who have
taken part in the debate. My friend, the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) spoke
about the position of the Belfast Water Board.
There will be no difficulty whatever with
regard to the division of the wards, and we
shall have before us the position of the Water
Commissioners. It is almost consequential.
So far as the question of the franchise of
limited liability companies is concerned, that
is entirely foreign to the system of regis
tration of voters, and I hardly see how that
could be brought into a measure of this kind,
because unless you introduce a franchise
such as is used in connection with the Harbour Commissioners you could not have
anything like a cumulative vote. Members of limited liability companies have their
votes as individuals, and the vote could not
possibly be given to them as members of
limited liability companies themselves.
My hon. Friend, the Member for South
Belfast (Sir Crawford M'Cullagh) mentioned
the question of triennial elections. It seems
to be the view of the Members representing
the Urban constituencies that triennial
elections should be introduced, and, I think
I may say on behalf of the Government, that
they will accept an Amendment to that
effect. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). With
regard to the position of aldermen, as to
whether they should be elected for three
years or six years, we will take that into
consideration.
The next speaker was the Member for
Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr. Miller), who
dealt with the size of the rural districts.
There is no question whatever that the
Ministry has already the power of dividing
the rural districts and altering their
boundaries, under Section 68 of the Local
Government Act of 1898. The question was
raised of the position of the "A" and "B"
Specials. As a matter of fact, the "A" and
"B" Specials are not disqualified by the
fact that they are members of the "A" and
"B" Specials, but I think the point of the
Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone was that
there are difficulties put in the way of their
registration by the fact that when they are
taken into training they are removed from
the constituency to which they belong, and
that between the two stools they fall to the
ground and do not get their votes. I am not
sure whether that can be remedied. If he
can suggest a proper remedy, we shall be
very glad to introduce it into the Bill. He
also made a strong point with regard to the
members and officers of the Council taking
the Oath of Allegiance. Some members of
the various councils have defied the law. The
declaration that they took in accepting office,
that they would administer the affairs of the
body according to law, was in effect an oath
of allegiance. They seem to think that that
does not apply to the recognition of a legally
appointed Government, and notwithstanding
that declaration they have seen fit to declare
their allegiance to an illegal council. I
think the time has come when that should
be remedied, and that the members on
taking their seats should explicitly give a
declaration of allegiance to the Government
under which they serve. We shall accept
an Amendment that will require officers
appointed by local bodies as well as the members themselves to give a declaration of
allegiance to the Northern Government.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The next criticism offered was that of the
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald), who,
I think, was speaking to some extent under
a misapprehension as to what the Bill proposes to do. He said that the Bill entailed
a Commission for the fixing of boundaries.
It does essentially nothing of the sort.
FFf.
Local Government Bill. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Supply.
[Mr. Megaw]
It gives power to the Home Ministry, when
it is required, to fix boundaries. There is
no suggestion that Belfast is going to be
divided straightway into wards different
from those that exist at present. All that
the Bill provides is that the Ministry of
Home Affairs may from time to time make
orders dividing a borough, urban district or
town into wards. That does not mean that
everything is in the melting pot,
and that there will be a new division
of Belfast now. There will necessarily
ble divisions of places that have
been fixed under the Act of 1919, where
very large areas were fixed for the purposes
of Proportional Representation, but that will
not affect the question of existing wards. No
doubt one or two wards that were put together for the purposes of Proportional
Representation will be interfered with. The
hon. Member also suggested that this measure was being introduced in some way as
against the Labour party.
Mr. DONALD: No.
Mr. MEGAW: He is entirely mistaken-
Mr. DONALD: I did not put it that way.
I said that it was certainly against the
minority getting representation. I had in
my mind that hon. Members (when they
were supporting this Bill, were afraid of that
minority, the Labour Party. I said that I
was like Lord Carson-I was not afraid of
the Labour party.
Mr. MEGAW: This Bill has nothing to
do with the Labour party. As a matter of
fact the Labour party through its Central
Council at the quarterly meeting in Portadown, having delegates from Larne, Lurgan,
Comber, Newtownards, Londonderry and
Belfast, passed a resolution calling for this
measure that is introduced here to-day, so
that it cannot be suggested that this is in
any way antagonistic to the Labour party.
As to the statement that it will mean
additional expenditure, how would it cause
expense? I rather think my opening statement cannot be controverted that elections
under Proportional Representation cost two
or three times as much as they would under
the ordinary system with which we are all
familiar.
So far as the hon. Member for Down (Mr.
Lavery) is concerned, I think the points
he raised, with the exception of the question
of the franchise, have already been answered
by me. Regarding the franchise, I am afraid
that the scope of the Bill would hardly include the franchise. However, the matter
will be taken into consideration, and if there
is any general desire for it, we can see if
the thing can be done in Committee. At any
rate we are open to consider the question.
Question, "That the Bill be now read the
Second Time," put, and agreed to.

Clause 2 (Power to Grant, Suspend, or Revoke Licences and Permits).
(1) The Ministry of Agriculture for
Northern Ireland (in this Act referred to as
the Ministry) shall have power to grant,
revoke and suspend licences and permits
for the purposes of this Act, and a licence
or permit shall remain in force until suspended or revoked by the Ministry.
(2) The Ministry shall, on application
being made in the prescribed manner, at
the prescribed time, and on compliance
with the prescribed conditions as to inspection and examination, grant to the
owner of any bull a licence in the prescribed
form in respect of the bull and also, if so
requested, a certified copy thereof on payment of such fee (not exceeding five
shillings) as may be prescribed:
Provided that the Ministry may refuse
to grant a licence or may suspend or revoke
a licence in respect of a bull if it appears
to the Ministry that the bull-
(a) is calculated to beget defective or
inferior progeny.
(b) is affected with any contagious or
infectious disease;
(c) is affected with any other disease or
defect prescribed as a disease or defect rendering the bull unsuitable for
breeding purposes;
(d) has proved to be inadequately prolific; or
(e) is of a breed or type unsuitable for
the district in which it is kept, and
is not a pure-bred bull belonging exclusively to a single individual and
kept for the service of cows belonging
exclusively to him.
(3) The Ministry may, on payment of such
fee (not exceed two shillings and sixpence)
as may be prescribed, and in compliance
with the prescribed conditions, grant to the
owner of a bull intended to be fattened
off for slaughter a permit authorising the
keeping of the bull for such period and
subject to such conditions as may be specified in the permit, but the permit shall not
be transferable from one person to another.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 27th June, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
DISEASES OF ANIMALS ACT.
Mr. MILLER (by private notice) asked the
Minister of Agriculture who is the authority
at ports in Northern Ireland under the
Diseases of Animals Act to grant licences for
the export and import of live stock?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): By Order in Council of the 1st
of April last the powers of the Department
of Agriculture, Dublin, which would have
gone to the Council of Ireland became
exerciseable in Northern Ireland by the Chief
Secretary or his agent. At the request of
the Chief Secretary I agreed that my Department should act as agent for him under
Section 63 of the Government of Ireland
Act, and he had the following telegram sent
to each of the Veterinary Officers whom he
placed at my disposal:-
"Chief Secretary desires me to inform
you that he has appointed Ministry of
Agriculture for Northern Ireland as his
agent for purposes of administration of
Diseases of Animals in Northern Ireland,
and you should, therefore, comply with all
instructions received from the Ministry of
Agriculture for Northern Ireland relative
to the administration of those Acts in
Northern Ireland."
All officers so notified have been retained
by me and no officers except those employed
by the Ministry of Agriculture have authority to issue licences for Northern Ireland.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I thought that perhaps hon. Members would
understand that this was an extremely unfavourable moment to raise the question of
the expenses of the Special Constabulary.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) After all, the
Special Constabulary is to a very large
extent, if not wholly, paid by the British
Government, and unless an hon. Member
has some very specific question to raise regarding the Special Constabulary I think it
would be more fitting if this House allowed
the Vote to go through without discussion.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There is more
than one reason for that line of conduct at
the moment. I am sure the House desires
to help the Government in every possible
way in these anxious times, and I am perfectly certain that in the autumn when this
whole matter is taken under review an
opportunity will be given to hon. Members
to discuss it. It would be more feasible to
do it then than to-day.

Wednesday, 28th June, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions
UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour if a person who is in receipt of unemployment benefit, and who is arrested and
remanded for seven weeks and eventually discharged, is deprived of unemployment benefit
for the period above mentioned?
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR
Andrews): The Unemployment Insurance Acts
provide that benefit is not payable to anyone
whilst he is an inmate of a public institution,
such as a prison, and is maintained at the
public expense.
I assume that the case which my hon.
Friend has in mind is that of a person who is
detained in custody during remand If this
is not so, or my hon. Friend is aware of any
other particulars relating to the case in question which appear to take it outside the statutory conditions, by which, of course, I am
bound, I will give it the most careful consideration on his sending me all the facts, and
will submit it to the Umpire if it is a case
requiring his decision.
PAYMENT OF MEMBERS.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Prime Minister
whether the Government will now consider the
question of payment of Members of Parliament?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I presume that the House, as a whole, is in
favour of the principle of the payment of
Members. (Hon. Members: "No, no," and
Hear, hear."). In the circumstances, then,
I think the best procedure for the Government is to put down a Resolution dealing with
the subject for some day convenient next
week, when the question can be thoroughly
discussed in all its bearings, and if the House
comes to a decision that the principle of the
payment of Members should be established in
this House we can set up a Committee to deal
with the whole matter.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw): I beg to move:

In Clause 1, page 1, line 9, at end insert
the word immediately" ("which was in
force immediately ").
I think it will be perhaps for the convenience of this Committee if in moving this
amendment I make a general statement
with regard to the Government's policy
affecting the various amendments which
have been tabled to this Bill. As I stated, in
moving the Second reading, the Government
are anxious to have the assistance of the
House in making the Bill as full and complete as possible, and in rendering it
consonant with the wishes of the various
local bodies. There were certain amendments suggested during the debate on the
Second reading, and the Government have
taken these into consideration. I stated
myself when I was replying to criticisms on
the Second reading that there were certain
of these amendments which the Government
Hon. Members
were prepared to accept.
have tabled quite a number of amendments,
and it was felt that perhaps it might be
convenient if some of the Members of the
Government met and discussed as far as
possible these amendments before coming to
this Committee, and try to see that they were
put in the best form possible, and find how
we could accommodate as far as possible our
own proposals to those put forward by hon.
Members. The general effect of what has
been done is this: Some criticisms were
offered with regard to the position of the
Water Commissioners of Belfast, and the
Government was prepared to embody this in
the present Bill. An amendment has been
tabled by an hon. Member (Mr. Lynn) in
regard to this, but the Government has also
an amendment which, I think, will suit all
the requirements of the case, and will meet
the undoubted grievance the Belfast Water
Commissioners would have had if there had
not been some such provision made in this
Bill.
Then, on behalf of the Belfast Corporation,
it was put forward that the old system of
electing councillors and aldermen was preferable to the new, and it appeared to be
generally accepted that a triennial election
was disadvantageous in a good many ways,
and so far as the borough of Belfast itself
was concerned it was quite clear that they
wished to have an annual election in respect
of one-third of the whole number of councillors retiring each year. This has also
been provided for as we have brought
forward an amendment which will put in
force the Belfast Local Act, and leave the
position exactly the same as it was before
the 1919 Act was brought into force. The
same has been done with regard to the
election of aldermen, and I may say here
that, so far as the urban districts are
863 Local Government Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Committee.
[Mr. Megaw]
concerned, it will be possible, if the amendment which has been tabled by the
Government is accepted, that any borough
council or any urban council may, if it
chooses, make representation to the Minister
of Home Affairs who may then apply that
system of annual election to any of the
other urban constituencies.
The next matter to which I wish to call
attention is the Declaration of Allegiance.
It seemed to be the mind of the House
generally that there should be a Declaration
of Allegiance (hon. Members: Hear, hear)—
and this, as I promised in my reply on the
Second reading, has been accepted by the
Government. The form of it, as we are
asked to deal with it to-day, is not quite
the form which appears in the Schedule
Part III. We thought something of a
simpler nature would meet the requirements
of the case, and, in addition to the Declaration, which is taken by Members
accepting office, we have introduced a clause
by which both a member accepting office
and an officer, whether newly appointed or
whether already existing, should have to
take a Declaration to this effect:
on
"I,
will render true and faithful
allegiance to His Majesty King George V,
his heirs and successors, according to
law, and to his Government of Northern
Ireland."
We think that would meet the circumstances
of the case instead of the form which has
been set out in the Schedule. I do not
think there is very much more to which
I need refer except a new clause which has
been introduced with regard to the consent
of candidates to serve as members when they
are nominated. Under the orders in force
under the 1919 Act, I understand it was possible for some very grave malpractices to
occur in the case of nomination of members,
by which any member may be baulked of
standing for the constituency in a rural
district for which he desires to be nominated.
All that is necessary is that some enemy
may put in a nomination paper for him,
and, according to the present rule, he is
bound to stand for the constituency for
which he has been nominated first; so that
all that is really necessary to prevent a man
being chosen for any particular board is to
have him nominated for a place in which
he has no earthly chance of being elected,
and then he is disqualified from standing
for any other constituency in the district.
This Bill provides a remedy for that. It
provides that a candidate on being nominated shall consent to his nomination, and
he cannot be nominated without his consent.
I rather think there has been a failure to
deal with one aspect of the case. I think
that not only the member but his agent
should have the power to consent to the
nomination, because it may happen that a
man is away for the time being and he
may have an agent, and that agent should
be able to give consent on his behalf. However, that is a matter of detail. The other
point introduced is to save the expense of
useless elections, and to prevent candidates
who have no earthly chance from coming
forward. The same system has been adopted
as in the Parliamentary elections, by which
candidates on being nominated will be
called upon to pay a deposit to the Returning
Officer. The deposit fixed is not large, but
it will prevent a man from standing for a
multiplicity of constituencies. The amount
provided in the amendment of which I have
given notice is a sum of five pounds for
rural and urban district councils, and ten
pounds for county and borough councils.
I am not sure whether that is large enough.
An amendment has been tabled by an hon.
Member by which ten pounds and twentyfive pounds respectively are suggested,
but when the matter comes forward we
will be better able to deal with it.
I think that this covers the general scope
of the amendments. I have mentioned the
amendments that the Government are prepared to accept and the way in which they
are prepared to accept them. I beg to move.
Amendment agreed to.

New Clause (Declaration of Allegiance of
Members and Officers of Local Authorities)—
(1) A person elected as a member of a
Local Authority shall be deemed not to
have accepted office, and his office shall
be deemed to be vacant, unless he has,
within the time required by law for
making and subscribing a declaration of
acceptance of office, also made and subscribed the Declaration of Allegiance prescribed in Part III of the Schedule to
this Act.
(2) Every officer holding an office of
profit under or in the gift of the council
of a county, borough, urban or rural
district, Board of Guardians, or Commissioners of a town, shall make and
subscribe the said declaration of Allegiance-
(a) in the case of an officer holding
office at the date of the passing of this
Act, within one month after that
date; or
(b) in the case of an officer appointed
after the passing of this Act, within one
month after his appointment.
No such officer shall enter upon the duties
of his office until he has made and subscribed the said Declaration of Allegiance,
and if an officer fails to make and subscribe the Declaration within the said
month, his appointment shall be void and
of no effect.

I need not recapitulate what I said on
the motion for the Second Reading of the
Bill or what I said regarding the necessity
for having such a provision. We have
found here that some of the local authorities
have considered it consistent with the declaration they have already taken to recognise
an authority different from the authority of
Northern Ireland, under which they hold their
office. There can be no misunderstanding with
regard to that point. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). Every local authority and every
officer who is drawing pay under any local
authority will understand that they do owe
allegiance to this Northern Government,
and I think what has taken place where
it has become necessary to dissolve some of
these bodies shows absolutely the necessity
for having some such clause put into force.
The clause as it was drafted would, I think,
be considered too cumbersome, and that
which I propose will, I think, meet the
necessities of the case. As to the policy of
the clause that I propose I can see no
answer.
