WAYS AND MEANS.
Resolved: "That this House will, tomorrow, resolve itself into a Committee to
consider of the Ways and Means for raising
the Supply to be granted to His Majesty."
(Captain Dixon.)
ROYAL ASSENT.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig)
(at the Bar of the House) reported that His
Excellency the Lord Lieutenant, in the name
and on behalf of His Majesty the King, has
been pleased to give his assent to the
following Act agreed upon by both Houses-
Local Government (Northern Ireland) Act,
1922.
THE PRIME MINISTER'S
STATEMENT.
Work of the Government.
Motion for Adjournment.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn." (Captain
Dixon.)
The PRIME MINISTER: I think that all
Members of the House will agree with me
that we meet to-day under more satisfactory
conditions than on any occasion since we
undertook the responsibilities of self-government. Although it is quite impossible to
probe far into the future, and there are so
many unstable elements prevalent in the
country, we do know that since the rising
of the House in the summer there has been
a slow but steady progress towards that end
for which we have been striving, and striving
under the most inauspicious circumstances.
We find ourselves to-day more cheerful at
heart, perhaps, than at any time I can recollect since His Majesty entrusted us with
the government of our own affairs.
The people throughout the Six Counties
have to be, first of all, thanked most
heartily for their co-operation, their steadfastness, and loyalty to the Government of
the day, and I personally must take this
early opportunity of tendering my appreciation of the cordial manner in which each
and every Member of this House has carried
on and assisted and encouraged the people
and shown them their duty through trying
times.
me
I think it would be advisable for
to-day, not only for the convenience of Members of this House, but for the convenience
of the public outside, to cast my mind over
the various Departments of State, endeavour
to make some explanation of those matters
which appear still to be misunderstood, if I
may say so, regarding the Government, and
to clear up some of the mis-statements that
have appeared from time to time.
Prime Minister's Statement. 940
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister.]
Trade depression still continues, as it continues not only here but across the water,
and practically in every country in the
world, and when one takes a broad view of
the situation, no matter what country one
may touch upon, one finds that conditions are
still in a chaotic state. I can only say that,
perhaps, on the whole, if we take the past
few months as some indication of what we
are all hoping and praying for, Ulster, after
all, is not the worst place in the world to
live in at the moment. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
I have been consulting my Ministers specially with regard to my statement to-day, and
the Minister of Agriculture assures me-and
I think I am right in touching, first of all,
upon what after all, is the greatest industry
in our part of the country-that, provided
we have a continuance of good weather, we
shall have a fair average harvest this year,
and in his opinion a better harvest than in
England or Scotland. To say that it will
be a bumper harvest, of course, would be
to exaggerate the condition of affairs, but
it is satisfactory to know, at all events, that
in that Department-and I shall refer to it
later on-we are faced with, we hope, comparative prosperity among the farming
classes.
Unemployment in our midst with regard
to other industries is still rife, and I am
sorry to say that the index figure is somewhat higher than that across the Channel.
However, there again, I shall refer in more
detail to the matter at a later stage.
I would like, before I go into any details,
to announce to the House that his Excellency
the Lord Lieutenant has expressed his desire
to visit us on the 24th, 25th and the 26th
of this month-(hon. Members: Hear hear)—
primarily in connection with the unveiling
of a war memorial in Enniskillen, but he
has placed himself in my hands with regard
to several other functions, and full details
of his programme will be announced in due
course. I feel confident in assuring him
beforehand of the hearty and royal welcome
to which he is entitled as the representative
of the Sovereign. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
With regard to the immediate business of
this House, I would like to state that we
endeavoured to so fix our business that we
shall be able to release Members of the
Imperial House of Commons for their duties
at Westminster, beginning about the 13th
November, although it may be necessary
to overlap that by a few days. The House
is aware that the first business in the Imperial Parliament must be the introduction
of a Bill to consummate the Free State Treaty,
and, as that involves very many important
Ulster interests, it is absolutely necessary
for our Imperial Members to be there in
full attendance to watch over our interests.
We propose during our Sittings to introduce
a Solicitors Bill. It is to make legal where
it is necessary the Charter which has already
been obtained by the solicitors' profession
in Northern Ireland. There will be an
Unemployment Insurance (No. 2) Bill, the
full details of which, of course, my right hon.
Friend beside me (Mr. Andrews) will
explain to the House at the appropriate
moment. There will be a Local Government
Elections Bill in charge of my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Home Affairs (Sir
Dawson Bates an explanation of which will
also take place when that Bill is introduced
for Second reading. There will be a Finance
Bill, an Expiring Laws Continuance Bill.
and a Uniformity of Laws Bill.
I may
say with regard to the last two mentioned
that the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill i
one which will take those Acts which in the
first instance were intended to be only temporary, or on trial, and which it is necessary
to carry on further in accordance with the
public convenience, and, of course, each of
the Bills which it is proposed to continue
will come under the purview of hon. Members
who will have full opportunity of discussing
them.
With regard to the Uniformity of Laws
Bill, that will be a Bill to bring us here
in Ulster up to the same position as
Great Britain, where measures have been
passed in the Imperial Parliament which
would be of value to us in keeping us pari
passu with the legislation which they
undertake. There again hon. Members will
have an opportunity of deciding whether
they will allow the whole Act, or part of
the Act as the case may be, to be embodied
in one Bill in order to save a long discussion
on the merits of various matters which have
already been well determined and thrashed
out in the Imperial House of Commons, or
whether they will prefer to drop some
of the things out of the Bill and re-introduce
into this House a comprehensive Bill going
over clause by clause the same Bill as has
been passed by the Imperial House of Commons.
time to
It is proposed at the sia me
set up or rather I should say to ask leave
to set up-a Royal Commission to deal with
the subject of Temperance, on which it is
hoped it will be possible to effect legislation
in this House. With regard to that matter
I would like to make one or two observations.
I myself personally, and I believe also the
majority of my colleagues here, are pledged
to some form, at all events, of temperance
reform. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
believe that I voice the sentiments of all
Members when I say that those pledges were
entered into with all sincerity and were
intended to be carried out. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) It will probably cause some
controversy in the country, that is obvious,
but there are two points in connection with
it which I think it is well to make perfectly
clear. Up to the present time the Govern-
10 OCTOBER 1922 Prime Minister's Statement. 942
Adjournmentment and the Members of this House have
been working under extraordinary difficulties.. They have really had no time to
go into the merits or demerits of a measure
of that kind, because they felt it was so
essential to have the full backing of the
whole Loyalists of the Province during those
critical times, and we as a Government felt
it would be unwise to cast into the troubled
waters one more cause of friction amongst
any section of the population. It is a sign
at all events that we are over the worst
and that we consider we are gradually but
slowly coming into calmer waters that we
propose now to ask for the setting up of
this Commission in order to deal with
matter which I think has been demanded by
most of the people of Northern Ireland.
a
At the same time I would like to point
out that in my experience-and I have
travelled some of my time I have been
about our own country of Great Britain a
great deal, I have talked to many from
abroad, and putting the information at my
command into concrete form I would say
we suffer less in the Ulster area from the
abuse of drink than perhaps any other part
of our Empire. It is a most remarkable
thing how one can pass to and fro in the
streets of our great cities and of our local
towns and with the exception of an odd case
note how very little there is to complain
about in that direction. At the same time
there are undoubtedly points that require to
be inquired into and dealt with, and we hope
the Commission will fulfil that function in
an able manner. I do trust that the best of
good nature and good temper will be exerrised by both sides and that there will be
no unnecessary controversy over it.
I hope
that the people will believe me when I say
that many a good cause has been absolutely
ruined by the extremists, and that if men
and women are anxious for reform in the
direction of temperance they will be guided
by me to this extent, that if their demands
are moderate they are pretty sure to be
carried, but if they are exaggerated it may
be impossible for this House to get the legislation through.
I now turn to the general situation, and
although, as I have said in my opening
sentence, we have passed through times of
great anxiety that have taxed the courage
and energy of our own people, the splendid
spirit which animates all sections of the
community has carried us through to the
present position in which we find ourselves.
A word of warning is somewhat necessary
at this stage. Just as the passengers and
the crew on board an Atlantic liner look to
the captain and to his officers in storm and
stress to see them through, not one of them
venturing to interfere with the management
of the ship, so Ulster looks to her leader
and his colleagues in the storm and stress,
whenever it may be, to guide them wisely
and carry them over the perilous times
which lie ahead. But just as in the case
of the captain and his officers, when the
storm has died down somewhat, when calmer
waters have been reached. it may be that
some murmurs of discontent from the passengers, or some rumblings from the crew
below reach his ears. And it may be that
harm is done if the captain does not immediately enquire into the cause of the
discontent amongst the passengers, or the
rumblings among the crew, and I would like
if I can to-day to deal with some of those
murmurings which have reached me from
various quarters and which I have observed
in the Press and heard from friends who
have come to talk to me. In the first instance I
may say that nearly all the
criticisms that have come to my ears have
been couched in the most courteous terms.
I have no complaint to make on that score.
The criticism, such as it has been, has been
intended in a most friendly way. But at
the same time there are certain gross
exaggerations and malicious mis-statements
going about the country, and if one were
asked to trace their source I fear it would
take some cleverer man than I am to do
So. I often wonder whether our enemies,
having failed by direct action, are attempting to sow little seeds of discord amongst
the population at the moment in order to
attain their ends in some other manner.
do not know, but I would ask the people who
hear these criticisms in the first place to
cast their eyes back eighteen months and
picture the condition of Ireland and the
condition of Ulster, and then to sum up tolay exactly where they stand, and by drawing that picture understand properly how
much they have to thank God for at finding
themselves in a more stable condition to-day.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

With regard to finance, may I turn to my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance
(Mr. Pollock)? Little rumours, little stray
words have reached me about the burden
of debt, about the fear of increased taxation,
even about bankruptcy. There is not one
word of truth in it. There is no debt upon
Ulster whatever, and I see no prospect of
creating any debt. There is no taxation in
Ulster above the taxation of our brothers
in Great Britain. We are all in the same
boat as far as that is concerned, and there
is no intention or suggestion on the part of
the Government to put one penny of extra
taxation upon the people of Northern Ireland, nor is there any necessity for it.
Further than that, last year with all the
heavy expense that fell upon our shoulders
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) not only
balanced his budget but had a small balance
on the right side, and I am as confident
as I was last year that my right hon. Friend
will perform exactly the same miracle
this
year. In other words, in spite
Prime Minister's Statement. 944
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister.]
of all we have to carry
and do
he will be able to show a balance in
favour of the Northern Ireland Exchequer.
There are very few countries in the world
can say the same thing. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) When one looks at the vast
upheaval in the financial world throughout
the whole length and breadth of Europe
and considers the discount to which credit
has fallen in the various countries, and
compares it with our own centre here where
credit is as high as ever before the war-all
that should reassure the people that our
financial stability is unquestioned, that the
prospects up to the end of the financial year
are as bright as they were last year in spite
of the depression that has taken place.
Therefore, I do hope that some of the criticism with regard to finances in that direction
will cease, and that the people will be satisfied that we are not going in any way to
lessen the high standard that we set ourselves when we first undertook our particular
duties.
With regard to some of the charges that
are levelled against the finances of Ulster,
1 would say let us be content to-day with
that broad statement of mine and rely on
my right hon. Friend here (Mr. Pollock) to
go into more details where specific questions
are raised at a later date.
As to agriculture and commerce, I have
already stated that my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Archdale) is fairly optimistic about
the future in regard to agriculture. When
I touch upon commerce I hope I will not
weary the House, but I look upon Our
position with regard to trade and commerce
as of far-reaching interest to every man,
woman and child within our borders, and
I cannot too strongly emphasise the importance of conveying to Great Britain, and
especially to her commercial centres and
those of Scotland, that trading with Ulster
is just as safe as trading with Norfolk or
Suffolk or Essex or Kent-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear) or may I say with Glasgow,
Birmingham, Manchester, or with Leeds?
I cannot emphasise too often that we are
and will remain part and parcel of Great
Britain, and we might as well talk of Great
Britain and Norfolk as talk about Great
Britain and Ulster. They both mean one
and the same thing. Traders, bankers, all
classes of commercial men, and shopkeepers
may understand that in carrying out contracts with us here in the North they may
rely upon the same commercial integrity and
stability as in the past. And I may say
that the Ministry itself-the Ministry of
Commerce-has performed splendid work
along with the Belfast Chamber of Commerce
and the Ulster Association in convincing the
British public that there can be and must
be no differentiation between them and
ourselves. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I cannot here enumerate the number of
instances where trouble was experienced and
immediately tackled by these three bodiesthe railway despatch of goods, the registry
of postal packages, the bankers' embargoone might almost say, on trading with us
unless on cash on delivery. Numerous other
cases of hampering our close commercial ties
with the other side could be instanced. They
were all tackled speedily and satisfactorily
by my right hon Friend (Mr. Archdale), the
Chamber of Commerce, and the Ulster Association. I emphasise this particularly in
order that we may clear the air as far as
we are concerned. We have surmounted the
difficulties, we have secured the peace, we
have brought ourselves down now to be able
to forget some of the instances of the past
and to be able to concentrate ourselves upon
the business which lies to our hand.
I now turn to the Labour Ministry and
hope I will not be wearying the House if I
go into some details in order to reassure the
great mass of the working classes in our
midst that as a Government we are constantly keeping in mind the very serious
problems that confront that part of the
community. My right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) has supplied me with figures not
only of interest to Members here but to the
public at large regarding unemployment.
The number of persons registered for employment at the Labour Exchanges and the
branch offices attached on the 10th January
last was 58,410; on the 25th September,
47,596, an improvement of 10,814.
Mr. DONALD: That is for the whole Six
Counties?
The PRIME MINISTER: For the whole
Six Counties. The number of persons
working systematic short time on 10th January, 1922, was 17,495; on 25th September,
8,073, an improvement of 9,422. The number
of complaints received by my right hon.
Friend has fallen for the week ended 25th
September last to the small number of 20,
that is to say, the number of complaints
regarding non-payment of benefits and so
forth, of which there were many charges
made last year and early this year. They
have got down to the very low number of
20. Under the relief work scheme it will
be interesting to know that the number of
schemes approved of at the end of September
was 61. The total estimated cost of the
schemes was £836,713. The total labour cost
was £312,625 and the grant sanctioned from
the half million in the hands of my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) was £179,067.
The number of workmen employed at the
end of September was 1,036, and the additional number to be employed on schemes
approved but not yet begun is 1,300, making

Adjournmenta total of 2,336, employed or re-employed on
schemes already approved. That shows that
the grant from the half million Unemployment Fund of £179,067 has resulted in the
promotion of schemes to the total value of
less than £836,713-large figures, and
figures, I think, which entitle us to congratulate my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) on the success which has pursued
his administration of the Unemployment
Fund. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

In the Six Counties the number of schemes
approved at the end of September was 64, the
total estimated cost, £104,267, the total
labour cost, £50,863, and the grant sanctioned
from the £50,000 was £29,270. The number
of workmen employed at present is 300 and
the number of individuals who have been
employed, 642, showing in the country districts that an expenditure of £29,270 from
the Fund has resulted in the promotion of
schemes to the total value of £104,267. In
addition to this unemployment work, the
House is aware that His Majesty's Office of
Works and the Treasury have given their
sanction to proceed immediately with the
building of our new Parliament House. Of
course, it may be that hon. Members may
think that there has been undue delay. I
can only say that the delay that has taken
place is owing to no shortcomings on our
part. The delay was occasioned by most
cautious investigations in the interests of
the case, the necessity of deciding as to the
foundations, drawing up plans and specifications, and, I presume, taking out
quantities. However, I am glad to say that
this matter has been settled, and the first sod
will shortly be cut, and with all the power
that we command the work shall be in full
swing before the winter fully sets in-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-in order that every
avenue possible may be made open to pick
up those persons who are in dire distress
owing to unemployment.
My right hon. Friend intimates that the
administration of the Health Insurance
which was taken over on 1st March, 1922,
has been continued on similar lines to those
previously followed in the United Kingdom.
Α consultative committee of approved
societies has been set up to advise the
Ministry in close relationship between the
Ministry and the societies in Northern
Ireland. As the schemes of Health and
Unemployment Insurance have been brought
together under one Ministry, it has been
found possible to effect many economies by
the combination of duties of officers, records,
etc.
There are about 300,000 insured persons
in Northern Ireland. In a normal year,
under present conditions the contributions
by employers would be about £197,000 and
by employees £180,000, the State paying, in
addition, two-ninths of the cost of the benefits paid out by the societies.
With regard to industrial relations, the
number of disputes since the Appointed
Day has been remarkably small, and those
which have occurred have been quickly
settled. I would like to make comment on
that that I hope all industrial disputes can
be as readily settled, and if my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) were in the position
in some other parts of the United Kingdom
which he occupies here I believe there would
be less industrial troubles in the country.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The railway
position, he tells me, has been giving him
keen anxiety for some time past. However,
no stoppage of the railways has taken place,
and that is a matter on which we are to be
congratulated. During the stoppage in the
shipyards in Great Britain, work was carried
on here the same as usual-a matter of great
importance to this industrial centre. The
services of the Department in the conciliation of industrial disputes have been
extended to Londonderry, Coleraine, Ballymena, Lisburn, Newry, and other centres.
With regard to Advisory Committees, in
order to ensure as far as possible that in
matters of general policy he was acting with
the approval of the community, my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) established Advisory Committees on certain matters. He
had a committee called the Trade Boards
Committee, presided over by Lord Dufferin.
This committee has presented a unanimous
report, and legislative proposals based on
that report will be submitted to you in due
course. The Employment Exchanges and
Unemployment Insurance Committee, presided over by my hon. and gallant Friend,
the Member for Armagh (Major Shillington)
has already presented an interim report recommending the establishment of Local
Employment Committees. It has reached
an advanced stage in its deliberations, and
its final report is expected shortly. The
Advisory Committee on Health Insurance
Approved Societies is a standing committee
under the chairmanship of my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) himself, and it advises him from time to time on matters
affecting the approved societies. The Cost
of Living Committee, under the chairmanship of my hon. and learned Friend, the
Member for the University (Mr. Robb), was
set up to explore the vexed question of the
cost of living in Northern Ireland, and it
has recently, as is well known, begun its
labours. The Belfast Relief Grants Advisory Committee, the constitution of which
is well known to us all, has advised the
Minister in respect of all the schemes to
which I have just referred. The Railway
Commission is under the chairmanship of
the right hon. Mr. Justice Brown, and it is
hoped it will shortly present its report.
Then the Local Employment Committees, to
which I have just referred, are getting under
way, and we will be able to give further

information to the House concerning them
at a later date.
I am glad to be able to say in regard to
this Ministry that, in spite of the vast
amount of work which it has to do, there has
been a considerable economy in administrative expenses. The Ministry is saving
actually on staff as compared with the staff
employed by the Imperial Ministry itself.
The headquarters work is done by a substantially less staff in proportion as a result
of the grouping of several of the services
under one head. The total Employment
Exchange staff when the Ministry of Labour
assumed control on the 1st January was 532.
On the 2nd inst. the figure had dropped to
412, a reduction of 120 in numbers and an
economy in money of approximately £19,000
a year. This reduction is, of course, in
part due to the fall in unemployment, but
the bulk of it is accounted for by the increased amount done by the staff itself, and
by the speeding up and perfection of the
Department. The cost of the Courts of
Referees in the month of January was £886,
giving a yearly rate of £10,632. By the
improvements which have been introduced,
the cost for the month of July fell to £418,
which works out at a yearly rate of £5,016,
a considerable saving in that direction, and
the introduction of the Local Employment
Committees, it is hoped, will obviate the
whole of the charges altogether.
With regard to Health Insurance, an Act
passed last July relieved the State of the
cost of the certification of sickness, saving
some £30,000 per annum, while the Health
Insurance Commission, and a special medical
and legal staff which have hitherto been
considered necessary in Ireland, have been
dispensed with altogether, and this means
a saving to the Department of, roughly,
£10,000 a year.
I mention these matters in
some detail in order to show the public
outside that the loose charge of extravagance
in the Departments is unfounded and that
the Departments themselves are slowly but
surely making improvements which save a
considerable sum to the country in various
directions.
Mr. DONALD: Did my right hon. Friend
mention the Roads Advisory Committee?
The PRIME MINISTER: That does not
touch upon my right hon. Friend's (Mr.
Andrews') Department. I was dealing with
his Ministry, and the Road Board comes
under the Ministry of Home Affairs. Now,
I would like to touch upon Education. The
first remarks I would like to make are with
regard to the general administration. My
right hon. Friend (The Marquess of Londonderry) has conveyed to me information of
which I think it only right that the House
should be in possession at the earliest possible moment because of the great importance
of this matter almost upon the eve of its
occupying the attention of the House in regard to a Bill upon the subject. He says that
the general administration of the department
of Primary Education has proceeded smoothly upon the accepted lines, and the control of
the Ministry has been loyally accepted by
all Protestant managers and teachers, and
the same willing spirit of co-operation has
been shown by the great majority of the
Roman Catholic managers and
teachers.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) A satisfactory
report, he says, may be given of the Intermediate side of the Ministry. The increased
interim grant has been distributed to the
teachers, and it is felt that those who are
engaged in this highly important branch of
the educational system of the Province are
looking forward with renewed confidence to
the future of Intermediate Education under
the Ministry. They have successfully held
the Intermediate Examinations for Northern
Ireland. The percentages of passes and
honours compare favourably with those
shown in the recent results of the Intermediate Examinations for the whole of
Ireland. Unfortunately, in this branch of
the Ministry, certain of the schools, in fact,
the majority of the schools, under Roman
Catholic management have taken up an
attitude of opposition to the new administration. Technical Schools, under the lively
influence of local administration, have shown
a wide appreciation throughout the Province
of the advantages which may be derived by
students at these institutions. The Minister
has hopes that the present attitude of the
recalcitrant schools under Roman Catholic
management, both Primary and Intermediate, will be discontinued in the near future.
With regard to the Training College for
teachers, it was recognised at an early date
that some immediate provision should be
made, even if only of a temporary nature.
for carrying on the work of the training of
teachers, as it was found impossible to make
satisfactory arrangements with the Training
Colleges already in existence in Dublin. A
special committee was, therefore, appointed
for this purpose, and a Training College has
been established in Belfast, whose first
session opened on the 4th inst. with 200
students of all denominations on the rolls.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The Minister
wishes to acknowledge a deep debt of gratitude for the assistance given in establishing
the college by the Queen's University and
the Belfast Municipal Technical Committee.
The accommodation at present is merely provisional, and it is intended at the earliest
possible moment to establish a Training College and hostels on the Stranmillis House
estate, which has been acquired by the Government from the University for that purpose, so that we will be second to none in
Adjournment-
Prime Minister's Statement.
10 OCTOBER 1922
that highly important department of education.
The Departmental Committee, under the
chairmanship of my hon. Friend the Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) presented
an interim report at the end of June dealing
with matters requiring legislation, and
this has been published as a Command
Paper, though, unfortunately, publication
was delayed by the printers' strike. Doubtless hon. Members have already seen the Report and read it with as much interest as I
havo. That report has not only been welcomed by the Government and by the Ministry concerned, but I feel from the criticisms
which have appeared that it has been received very well indeed by the community
as a whole, and that is a very important
matter. Immediately upon the receipt of the
interim report the work of drafting a comprehensive measure of educational reform
was commenced by the Ministry. The wide
scope of the measure and the magnitude of
the task can only be appreciated by those
who have studied the interim report of the
Lynn Committee and its recommendations.
Such a measure must involve every other
Ministry, and there must necessarily be an
interval for Cabinet and inter-departmental
discussion before a Bill of this importance
can be brought before Parliament. It is intended, therefore, to introduce the measure
at the earliest possible moment of the next
Session of the New Year. Those who are
clamouring for immediate legislation during
the present Session must be reminded that,
while piecemeal legislation might be possible, only a comprehensive measure
satisfy our educational requirements.
I would like to add also that the Committee

Another point in that connection is this:
It is not good for us to talk too much in
public as to what our plans are, or what is
the size of our Force or organisation. If I

provocative. Provocation does no good at

down to trusting those who have the heavy
burden to carry on their shoulders; and I

those men who became redundant will

There is a good deal of loose talk about
a want of policy. Has any Government ever
had a more settled policy than the Ulster
Government? That policy is to retain a
Parliament of our own, and not to come
under a Dublin Parliament. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) We have done all that human
ingenuity and courage could do in order to
reach the position in which we stand. That
is our policy to-day, and that will be our
policy so long as I have the honour to stand
at this table. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
There is no Dublin Parliament for us.

very
interesting. I certainly do not doubt his

necessary offices at Stormont, and they are
also going to erect at their expense the
necessary offices in the heart of the city of
Belfast to provide for all the requirements
of the Northern Government. That is very
satisfactory. The other question I wish to
refer to is that of finance. It is most
interesting to know from the Prime
Minister's statement that we are in a healthy
condition financially, that the necessary
expenses of the Government will be met, and
that the Chancellor of the Exchequer will
probably be able to present a budget with a
balance on the right side during the next
financial year. But the question of the
financial relationship between this Government and the Imperial Government has yet
to be cleared up, and I should like to hear
from the Government what has been done
in that direction. Has anything of a
character likely to be lasting, likely to be
permanent in its nature, been established
between the British Government and ourselves? We all know the unsatisfactory
position we were placed in by the Act of
1920, and although I believe the British
Treasury has dealt generously with us on
the whole, yet we have to face the future.
British Governments come and go. This
Government may go on for ever, but I am
doubtful. What is going to be our position
from a financial standpoint? It is well
known to this House that when the settlement of 1920 was arrived at we were assured
by the Minister then in charge of the Billand his views received the sanction of the
British House of Commons-that Ulster
would probably have a surplus of over
£2,000,000. I do not think the Chancellor of
the Exchequer will deny that. Are we
negotiating with the British Government on
that basis, claiming that what was held out
to us when the statement was made will be
assured to us by some permanent arrangement in the days that are to come?
I view with the gravest concern the future
financial arrangements with the British
Treasury. Everything may be working in a
satisfactory way at the moment, but I wonder
if the present British Government will bring
in some Bill upon this question, or upon
other matters that must be cleared up, so
that we will know exactly where we stand.
I may be somewhat of a revolutionary,
although you would not think I was, but 1
can foresee the time when some statesman in
Ulster in the coming days will raise this
question in a very acute form, and I would
not be at all surprised if that statesman in
Ulster said to the British Government, "Will
you please tell us what our share of the
National Debt is"? It is going to be
apportioned, and has been apportioned by
arbitrators in Southern Ireland.
Tell us
what our proportion of the National Debt is
and we will pay it. And if we should
develop and expand our resources, the same
statesman will probably ask the British
Government a similar question. If we are
going to have Imperial protection tell us
what price we have got to pay and we will
pay it. I think the time is coming, although
perhaps not immediately, when Ulster will
collect her own money and insist upon spending it after dealing in a fair and right way
with British trade. I do hope some
permanent arrangement will be come to with
the Imperial Government at a very early
date. I trust the Minister of Finance may
be able to tell us exactly what has been
accomplished and what the prospects are, if
he has any information on that particular
subject. I do not think I should refer to
the various other points raised in the Prime
Minister's speech. He dealt exhaustively
with the Labour Department, with Commerce, and with the Home Office. He
covered the ground very fully, and gave us
a lot of very valuable information. I have
no doubt that other Members will take up
these various points and deal with them, but
to-day I would rest satisfied with the
criticism I have made in regard to the
special points in which I am personally
interested. All I can say is this. I think
we are met to-day under very happy circumstances. We have surmounted many
difficulties, and J believe that the
difficulties which still lie ahead will be deal
with wisely and firmly, that we will
establish the Parliament of Ulster upon a
firm and sure foundation, and do our work
in a way that will contribute to the salvation, the prosperity, and the welfare of our
people as a whole.

the Labour representatives I have the

Dr. MORRISON: I should like to say a
word or two with regard to the speech
of the Prime Minister. Before I refer to
any question he has raised may I express my
dissent from the views put forward by the
hon. Member for Derry (Sir Robert Anderson) and the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn) with regard to the holding up
of the Local Government Act. I think if
you look at this question you will see that
there are two sides to it. It dealt with what
I think is a most important matter in connection with this country-the treatment of
minorities. While I approve of the Act-1
voted for it-nevertheless I think it was the
duty of the Imperial Government to hetate, and to weigh the whole question before they sanctioned the repeal of the Act,
which was specially introduced by them with
the object of protecting minorities, both in
the South and in the North. When we consider the fact that any outbreak of disorder
here or in the South is to be met, and the
expense is to be paid for, in large measure
by the Imperial Government, I think it is a
right and proper thing for them to look well
before they sanction an Act which, in their
opinion, might bring about results that are
not to be desired. I do not like this constant
carping at and denunciation of the Coalition Government and of the Prime Minister
of England, and I dissociate myself from it.
With regard to the questions raised by the

£9,500,000 is spent on drink. I state that as

There is one matter to which the Prime
Minister referred to which I wish to make
a brief reference, and that is the matter of
National Health Insurance. He told us it
cost something like £550,000-the workers
paid £180,000, the employers £197,000, and the
State £173,000. That is a matter that has
been before this House on several occasions.
I have raised it. I do not know if anybody
else has taken much interest in it, but I have
taken an interest in it because I am in touch
with its working, and I know where the shoe
pinches. I spoke here, not against the
National Health Insurance Act, because I
think it is a necessary, and wise, and proper
Measure, but I spoke against the way in
which it is administered, and the way in
which the insured are treated by the Societies
which represent them. The Prime Minister
stated that the Minister of Labour had
arranged with the Societies to form
Advisory Committee, of which he himself is
the chairman. I take it these Societies are
going to keep him right. This is entirely a
reversal of any conception I had of what were
the duties of the Minister in dealing with this
question. I think his position is to keep them
right. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) When
he takes this position it seems to be an
extraordinary anomaly. All over the Six

Dr. MORRISON: I think that this might

While I speak bluntly on this matter, because

The latter part of it I would be inclined to

It is an extraordinary thing that he

Is there no consideration for the huge numbers of workers in our Six Counties area who
have no court to which they can go, and who

area? Have they no right to be represented

What is the fact? When the Act came
into operation, six or eight years ago, I soon
found that this Society was hedged with protection, and that the people who were injured
were so helpless that it was absolutely impossible to do anything to remedy their
grievances. I found also there was no use in
fighting. I am in for a fight if necessary,
and I approve of fighting, but I am judicious
enough to know there is no use in kicking
against the pricks, if you want to go back to
Bible phraseology. I found these people were
so hedged round and in such a position that
protests were rendered useless. I made
friends with the Society, and the result was
that for five or six years I wrote to the
doctor or the Secretary of the Society regarding every cose in my district that there was
any doubt about, and what I recommended
went through. Hon. Members will agree
that that condition did not prevail in other
dispensary districts, and that these people
were consequently at the mercy of
an unfair agent or unsympathetic
Society. Let me take a case: The Minister
of Labour mentions this is ancient history.
The Prime Minister wrote to me asking for
these details, and I gave him a sample of the
injustice that was done in one particular
case.
It was a case where technicalities were
raised that enabled the Society to refuse payment, and the aggrieved person was compelled to fall back on a Court that is of
absolutely no value. The case I gave was
that of a man who was riding his bicycle
after his work was over. He fell off his
bicycle and injured his knee. The insurance
people raised the point that it was a case
coming under the Workmen's Compensation
Act. The result was that for three months
that man got no benefit.
I put it to the Members of this House, is it
fair that a working man with a family,
struggling through life, should not get
benefit from a Society to which he has been
contributing, that he should be excluded
from benefit for three months by the frivolous excuse that the accident came within
the Workmen's Compensation Act and not
within the Insurance Act at all? I can
plove to you that that man had to ride on
three occasions no less than 100 miles
appealing to Court after Court in order to
seek redress. It ultimately ended in the
National Insurance Commissioners being
written to, and they insisted on his being
paid. The fact remains that that thing is
going on, and I have used that as a sample
of what is going on all over Ulster. In the
explanation I have given this House I think
I have exhausted all the possibilities of the
English language to make my meaning clear
I think it is clear to every man of ordinary
intelligence. I was not dealing with an individual case.
It did not matter whether the
man's case was right or wrong. It remains
true that it is the type of case that is general
ali over Ulster. What means have you taken,
or what provision are you going to make to
prevent it occurring in the future? Here is
what he (the Minister of Labour) writes to
me:--
"
As regards Harbinson's case, I understand the difficulty was as follows:-The
Health Insurance Society would not pay
until they were absolutely satisfied that
the man was not entitled to Workmen's
Compensation. As soon as they had satisfied themselves on that point they paid."
That is, that the Society is blameless. Yet
they kept this man waiting three months
while they determined a simple elementary
question like that. You have here a man
who represents the Labour Department, who
poses I should hardly use the word poseswho claims to be a representative of Labour
in his capacity as Minister, and who is, I

If that is the attitude to be taken up by
this President of the Unionist Labour Association, it is not the attitude that I take up,
and I hope it is not the attitude of the

I do not know what the explanation of this

Immediately some point was raised, namely,

Mr. CRAWFORD: I would like, in a word,
to express the great pleasure I had in listening to the illuminating speech delivered by
the Prime Minister. It is needless to say I

I had the opportunity of addressing public

advice that the people should have patience
with the Government and have absolute confidence in them. Consequently, I say those
who are in favour of temperance legislation
deserve a little more consideration at the
hands of the Government. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I believe it is one of the things
that the people are ripe for, and there is no
necessity in the wide world to appoint a Commission to inquire into it. I do not agree-I

the Prime Minister that Ulster is freer from
the drink traffic than other parts of the world.
I have had the opportunity on several occastons of visiting a great many countries, and
so far as I can judge, Ulster is worse in the
atter of the drink traffic than any other
country I have been in. I said before in this
House and I say it again; of all the causes
that contribute to crime and the misery of

Government would be doing a good job for
themselves and a good job for Ireland if, instead of putting this into the hands of a Commission, which may perhaps bring in minority
and majority reports, or which may be so
formed that it will not be sympathetic towards temperance legislation at all, they took
action at once and brought in temperance
legislation.

Mr. DONALD: I wish to make a few
observations arising out of the very exhaustive statement of the Prime Minister this
afternoon, and the first question that is
uppermost in my mind naturally is that of
unemployment. I think the Prime Minister
should have dealt more fully with this important question. No doubt the Minister of
Labour has dealt with the powers vested in
his Department with regard to this vexed
question. The percentage of unemployment
is very much higher here than in any part of
Great Britain. I want to say here and now
that I never agreed with the policy regarding
the £500,000 which was allocated to us. After
the lapse of all these months only 1,036 people
are actually in employment under it, and
1,300 are about to be employed. I repeat
what I said in this House before, that until
some better method is introduced of dealing
with this unemployment question I can see
no rescue, so to speak, from the present
position. This Government is not grappling
with the situation as it ought to do. I have
told this House before that I was talking to
the head of a big shipbuilding concern. Wha
did he tell me? That they cannot compete in
the market owing to the high price per ton
of the building of ships, and that unless the
Government came to their assistance to take
them out of the difficulty the men will have
to remain on the streets. For the life of me,
I cannot see why this Government and the
Imperial Government cannot take up this
question. For £50,000 I question if we could
not get 4,000 or 5,000 men off the streets at
once. We must quote less than £10 per ton
for shipbuilding to-day, when other people
are quoting something like £8 per ton. The
numbers unemployed to-day are something
over 47,000. I am afraid that other means
will have to be adopted very soon for dealing
with this matter.
I was a member of a deputation which
to-day brought this problem before another
public board which has not touched the question in a real, practical way up till now. We
reminded that public board that they have
laws which give them power to borrow and
expend money for the purpose of finding
employment for these people. Up till the
present they have made no attempt to put the
powers they have into execution. I hope that
something will be done by that body in the
near future to help the Minister of Labour.
The Prime Minister's speech from beginning
to end was really an apologetic speech. How
can the people be happy if they are starving?
I feel very strongly on this question. I can
tell the Prime Minister that there are people
starving in Belfast, and the people who
are starving are not the class who do not
want work, but the class who are
looking for work and cannot get it. Only
two days ago a young couple came to my
house. The husband has been idle for
eighteen months, and his funds are exhausted. Not a halfpenny is coming in, and
on the top of that the husband gets a notice
to quit the house in which he and his wife
live. Here is a question that the
Prime Minister never touched upon
to-day. We have a Rents Restriction
Act which
expires next year. Then
what about the housing question? Why
cannot we get a move on and expend some
of this money in building houses in order to
get our people off the streets. I know of no
problem that has cut so deeply into the
minds of the working-class people. There
are many who, even when in employment,
are haunted night and day by the spectre of
unemployment.
I leave that matter, and I come to the
question of Temperance Reform. Was not a
pledge given, when his Gracious Majesty
opened this House, that a Bill would be
brought in to amend the licensing laws?
What is wrong with this House that it
cannot deal with temperance legislation on
moderate lines? I am not an extreme maa
in any sense of the term, but I do say that
the time has arrived when the Government
should keep its pledges-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and not refer the matter to a Commission, a step which will have the effect of
shelving it. Leave the question to the good
judgment of this House, and I will be satisfied. We are here as the representatives of the
people, and I see no reason for setting up a
Commission of this description. This House
is quite capable of dealing with the problem.
By setting up a Commission the matter will
be deferred till next year. Then you want a
contented people. These people got a prɔmise from the Noble Lord who was the leader
of Ulster previous to my right hon. Friend.
The Noble Lord said this was one of the first
questions he would deal with. I know y
right hon. Friend (the Prime Minister) would
be as anxious to keep that pledge as the
Noble Lord would himself. I see no reason
why Temperance Reform cannot be openly
introduced into this House and dealt with
early next year. That is one of the things
that is causing unrest in the minds of the
people.
I now come to the question of Education.
I cannot understand why the question of
Agriculture being taught in the Primary
Schools has been omitted from the Interim
Report. The Prime Minister himself said

I take it, it will be well on next year before

is necessary, but would my hon. Friend, the

I come to the question of Special Constabulary. No one admires more than I do
what is being done by our gallant Special
Constabulary, whether A's, B's, or C1's, but,
when the Prime Minister was telling of the
inducements offered to the officers to come

men. The men who have already been disbanded have only added to the number of

You were paying them far too much, 70/- per
week, in comparison with the skilled worker
in the workshop.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps my hon.
Friend (Mr. Donald) would allow me to explain to him that the pay was fixed by the
British Government before we took over
charge of the administration of law and
order, and that, from the time we took over,
the area that we have to control was so disturbed that we thought it would be unjust
and ungenerous to ask those who were fighting our battles to take a lesser wage than
had been fixed by the Imperial Government.
But, when we saw there was an opportunity
of curtailing expenditure, we decided to
make a reduction in order to spread what
there was over as many as possible. That
was the reason.
Mr. DONALD: I quite appreciate the statement made by the Prime Minister, but this
House has it in its power to deal with this

The PRIME MINISTER: The pay has

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

I say he is not. I have pointed out again
and again that people who committed
greater crimes in Ireland are walking about
free men to-day, while we have men lying in

were in a crowd and those in authority had

Truce persons who are ying in prison?
This is the cause of a good deal of trouble.
What is the good of the Government talking
about peace when the people are knocking
at the door for the release of innocent
persons who are in prison.
I have a letter in my pocket from a young
man who says:-"Do you think I would
screen anyone whom I saw doing foul deed:
I am innocent" His wife and three children
would have been in the Workhouse but for
voluntary help. These are things that the
people are thinking about. I am quite willing that a fair percentage of these posts
should go to Englishmen and Scotsmen, but
what did we tell our gallant officers who
went out to France and Flanders? What
treatment is meted out to them now in regard
to the positions in the R.U.C.? Ulstermen's
claims have been largely overlooked, and the
same applies to the rank and file. Much of
the discontent in our city to-day is due to the
fact that justice has not been done to those
who stood loyally by the Government and the
people of Ulster and did their duty. Then we
are told it does not pay to be loyal. It does
not pay to be loyal, and I am prepared to
prove it. (Hon. Members: "Shame.") Some
people have been appointed over the heads of
others when they should not have been
appointed. I am expressing the opinion of 75
per cent. of the public to-day, and I am
prepared to give you facts and figures to show
that the claims of those who were entitled to
appointments have been overlooked, simply
because they were loyal. No one can question my loyalty, but I want to see that justice
is done. We always boasted that the
Ulsterman was capable of accomplishing
anything. He is not getting a chance in
connection with these appointments. Ulstermen are not getting a fair look in, and I am
prepared to prove my statement to any branch
of the Government. I want to close by
quoting a few lines I read the other day from
a Prime Minister who is supposed to represent the Imperial Government. He said :---
The old world was one where unemployment, through the vicissitudes of industry,
brought disaster to multitudes of humble
homes. If we renew the lease of that old
world we shall betray the heroic dead.
The old world must, and will, come to an
end. No effort can shore it up much longer
If there be any who feel inclined to maintain it, let them beware lest it fall upon
them and their households in ruin.
I wish the gentleman who uttered these
words would practice what he preaches
What is the state of the world to-day? What
is the condition of things in the Near East?
What is the state of our country, and where
is the effective legislation passed through this
House for the benefit of the people? That is
what the people are asking. We pass
financial resolutions in order that we can
carry on. We want to do something effective
that will give the people something to think
about, and will enable them to say that after
all their Government is doing something for
their benefit. This Government is simply
marking time, and bringing in estimates in
order that the machinery may be kept in
motion.

We are waiting for a lead." I thought the

annual report to the Orangemen of County
Tyrone 1 referred to the matter, and I said,
"In my opinion you will find your lead in
the 30th chapter of Isaiah, 15th verse :-
quietness and in confidence shall be your
strength.'' Then I proceeded to form a "B"
force of my own, without 26 brigadier-generals, with the motto, "Be quiet, be confident,
be strong, be ready when your leader calls."

When I was younger and more energetic
than I am to-day, I had one or two hobbies,
and one of them was amateur gardening. I
learned that there were some plants that
could not be forced. Now, confidence is a plant
that cannot be forced, and I would ask the
Government to try to retain our confidence by
giving us more of their confidence. The
Prime Minister told us a short time ago of
certain Bills that he was going to bring in.
From what he stated, I think I know what
they contain. But six weeks ago a member
of a political party with which I have nothing
to do could tell a member of a political
party with which I have a great deal to do
that that Bill was to be brought in. I would
ask the Government whether they cannot see
their way to take some of us backwoodsmen,
if you like, more into their confidence. 80
that we can confidently say, as I said to my
brother Orangemen, In quietness and in
confidence shall be your strength."

enternow
go
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): It is
nearly two years since there was transferred
to the Parliament of Northern Ireland that
portion of the revenue which came under
our own immediate jurisdiction. We have
the duty to levy and collect that reserved
revenue, to make our own arrangements for
the collection of it, and the proceeds
directly into our own Exchequer. But during
the interval that has elapsed it has been
found necessary in the Imperial Parliament
to make certain modifications in the laws
and regulations under which those taxes were
collected in order that the administration
of the law should carry out more fully the
intentions of the drafters of those regulations. The particular Clauses which I now
rise to move have to do with the Entertainments Tax, but I say that, in addition to
dealing with this feature of the revenue at
the present time, it is intended to deal with
other matters with which it has been found
necessary to deal in the Imperial Parliament
at Westminister. I should like to assure
hon. Members right away that it is not considered that these new regulations will in
any way add to the taxation. They will
clarify the regulations and remove dubiety,
which has existed, I think, owing to certain
conditions not having been kept well in mind
at the time this tax was originally produced,
which was as far back as 1916. The Entertainments Tax, so far as we are concerned,
brings in a revenue of about £80,000 a year,
and the conditions which have required the
passing of this resolution at Westminister
obtain almost entirely on the other side of
the Channel. I do not know whether we
will be greatly affected by their adoption,
but, as in all other things, we consider it
wise to follow the lines of Westminster,
and so, although there may not be any immediate necessity for the adoption of these
Clauses at the present time, it is always
well to benefit by their experience and be
ready for such conditions should they arise.
The first Clause will read:
"payments for admission to an entertainment made to a person other than the
proprietor of the entertainment;"
11 OCTOBER 1922
In Committee-

Entertainments Tax.
Then, we are anxious to tighten up the
collection of the revenue in one way by
restricting the exemptions from the Entertainments Tax to the following undertakings,
namely, that
where the whole of the takings are devoted
to philanthropic or charitable purposes
without any charge on the takings for
any expenses of the entertainment;
where the entertainment is of a wholly
educational character;
It was clearly the intention when this Act
was passed that all admissions to entertainments should bear this tax, but it has been
found, owing to the wording adopted, that
it has been possible for people to derive
enjoyment from an entertainment without
actually having paid for admission to the
proprietor or promoter of that entertainment.
It may be difficult to see how this could
arise, but I could illustrate it by taking
the case of a certain society or club which
was promoting a regatta on a river, which
occupies a large space. The promoters of
the regatta might have their own enclosure,
for admission to which they would charge,
and of course that would bear the tax; but
there might be someone with a lawn or premises convenient thereto, who had nothing
whatever to do with the promotion of the
regatta, and yet might be able to erect a
stand and charge for admission to that
stand. Under the old regulation there was
dubiety as to whether the tax was leviable
on that stand so erected.
Similarly the second Clause reads:
"payments of rent made in respect of an
interest in any premises which is primarily
acquired for the purpose of securing admission to an entertainment."
I think this also has to do with customs on
the other side of the Channel. I believe on
some very large racecourses there are boxes
in the stands which can be rented, and the
person who rented those boxes might entertain his friends there, and yet that rent
would not be subject to taxation under the
Entertainments Tax, whereas it was clearly
intended that all admissions, whether by
means of rent for part of the premises or by
the purchase of an individual ticket, should
be subject to this tax. Another matter which
requires clearing up is that of exemption
from taxation, or the repayment of the tax
charged on admission. Under the present
law every ticket for admission to such an
entertainment should bear clearly imprinted
upon it the price of the ticket, and whether
or not that price includes the Entertainments
Tax. In many cases it is the custom to sell
tickets of admission in advance of the date
of the entertainment itself, and if by any
chance the purchaser of those tickets did not
make use of them, and did not present them
at the barrier for admission, it meant that
the promoter of the entertainment derived
the benefit of the tax instead of the State,
so that is the necessity for making this read:
"payment for admission to an entertainment."
instead of, as the Act read formerly,
"each person admitted for payment."
You will see we wish to make all tickets,
whether the person is actually admitted or
not, subject to this Entertainments Tax.
where the entertainment is intended for
the amusement of children, and that the
charge is not more than one penny for
each person:
Also,
that the entertainment is provided for
partly educational or partly scientific purposes by a society, institution, or committee
not conducted or established for profit.
It is proposed that exemption from taxation shall be restricted absolutely to those
classes of entertainment to which I have
referred.
Then we have to safeguard ourselves in the
matter of refund of entertainment tax where
in the first case that entertainment tax has
been collected. Under the law as it has stood
hitherto entertainment tax is only refunded
in cases where the expense of the entertainment did not exceed 20 per cent., and all the
balance goes to the charitable or philanthropic object in aid of which the entertainment has been promoted. It has been found
in actual experience that this limit of 20
per cent. is rather too narrow a margin on
which to work, and therefore it is proposed
in future that this shall read 30 per cent.
That will be introduced in the Finance Bill
which will be duly brought before this House.
Then we wish to make clear that in the reklemption of the tax the tax so refunded must
go towards the charitable object for which
the entertainment was promoted. As the
law stands at present, the refund of the tax
is made to the proprietor of the entertainment, whereas it was intended that the
charity alone should benefit. In the majority of cases the tax so refunded has been
handed over to the charity, but where this
has been a matter of goodwill in the past
we wish to ensure in the future that it shall
reach its proper destination. There are some
matters in connection with the collection of
motor taxation which require to be dealt
with. Where the tax has been paid on a
motor, and during the lifetime of that license
that motor is so transformed that it is
rendered liable to a higher rate of duty,
as soon as that motor is so transformed, it
shall immediately become subject to the
higher rate of duty. Then it is intended to
extend the privilege which is at present

enjoyed by dealers and agents who have a

Then there is another matter of accounting
in order to simplify matters. In the execution of certain documents the Government
at present has to affix stamp duty to these
documents in accordance with the law which
covers original documents of Commerce.
That has been settled in the past by debits
and credits between the different Government
Departments, necessitating book-keeping, and
there is no money passed into the Exchequer
as a result of this. It is proposed now to
take a short cut and simply exempt Government documents from stamp duties, and that
will do away with all this accounting. Then
we go on to another section which I do not
expect is of much real importance in
Northern Ireland, and that is to take advantage of that law which protects us from
having to pay double death duties in respect
of taxation in various British possessions.
It is proposed, under the Bill which is about
to be introduced, that certain of the Malay
States should be regarded for this purpose as
British possessions. This thought did not
originate with ourselves, I need hardly say,
but we are taking advantage of this Bill
which will be brought in, if you approve of
the financial resolution which I am now
moving, in order to bring ourselves in line
with Westminster. On the one hand, speaking for the Exchequer, I am sorry it does not
mean any additional revenue for Northern
Ireland, but, on the other hand, the taxpayers will be relieved to know that it does
not impose any additional burden, and that
they are simply maintaining the position of
equality with the taxpayers of England and
Scotland. I beg to move.

The PRIME MINISTER: I have been very
carefully considering the result of my statement yesterday with regard to the proposals

of the Government to ask for a Royal Commission to inquire into and report on the
whole subject of temperance so far as our
Northern area is concerned, and I notice
that some of my hon. Friends took grave
exception to what might be a delay in connection with a matter which is of such importance that it has always created great
interest in the Six Counties. I have not
had very much time since yesterday to
analyse the whole position, but I would like
to make an offer to my hon. Friends who
seem to think that this would cause inordinate delay, that they should communicate
with me, put their heads together-those who
are more vitally interested in the question
than some other Members of the Houseand come to me at any time with proposals.
If those proposals can be accepted by the
Cabinet I will endeavour to have a Bill
framed on the lines which they desire-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-and if possible to
start this year and to give it very early
priority in our legislation next year if it
is impossible to get it through this year. I
throw that out with the hope that there
will be no recrimination and no excitement
created in the country. We in this House
are all of one mind with regard to certain
parts of temperance legislation, and if it is
satisfactory to those who approached me on
this subject, as I gather it is, I can assure
one and all that they will receive the utmost
possible sympathy from my Cabinet and
myself. This proposal will enable us to get
the work through either at the close of this
year or very early next year. I hope my
hon. Friends will take this in the spirit in
which it is meant, as going a long way to
meet them, and if they will take an opportunity of approaching me at any time we
will have a frank discussion on the whole

Oral Answers to Questions
THE ULSTER MONTH.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Prime Minister
whether he will state the actual position, so
far as it can be surveyed, regarding the ratification of the Treaty with the Irish Free
State, and when does the month begin to
run during which Ulster may exercise her
option of contracting herself out
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
The Treaty providing for the setting up of
the Irish Free State was signed on behalf of
the British and Irish Delegations on the 6th
December, 1921. The Articles of the Treaty
were given the force of law as from the 31st
March, 1922, being the date of the passing
by the Parliament of the United Kingdom
of the Irish Free State (Agreement) Act,
1922.
Articles 11 and 12 of the Treaty stipulated
that if before "the expiration of one month
from. the passing of the Act of Parliament
for the ratification of this instrument" an
Address were presented to His Majesty by
both Houses of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland, Northern Ireland should continue
under the Government of Ireland Act and be
outside the Free State. The question was
raised in the House of Commons at Westminster whether the Irish Free State (Agreement) Act was the Act of Parliament for the
ratification of the Treaty. No satisfactory
assurances were forthcoming in Debate, and
eventually the question was set at rest by
insertion in the Act itself (Section 1 (5)) of
the following words:-
"This Act shall not be deemed to be the
Act of Parliament for the ratification of the
said Articles of Agreement as from the
.
passing whereof the month mentioned in
Article 11 of the said Articles is to run."
Accordingly, the month runs from the
passing of some future Act, and it does not
seem to be open to doubt that it will run
from the date of the Act of the United Kingdom Parliament, which will, in effect, finally
ratify the Treaty by confirming the Constitution of the Irish Free State. This Constitution is at present under consideration in
the form of a Bill which is proceeding
through the Provisional House of Parliament
in Dublin. When that Bill receives the
effect of an Act of the Provisional Parliament it will be submitted as part of a Bill
to be introduced at Westminster when Parliament reassembles next month.
The Westminster Bill must receive the
Royal Assent early in December in view of
the Agreement expressed in the last Article
of the Draft Constitution of the Irish Free
State, which is as follows:-

"The passing and adoption of this Constitution by the Constituent Assembly and the
British Parliament shall be announced as
soon as may be, and not later than the 6th
day of December, 1922, by Proclamation of
His Majesty, and this Constitution shall
come into operation on the issue of such
Proclamation."
Accordingly, as far as can be foreseen, the
Ulster" month will begin to run from a
date subsequent to the reassembly of Parliament at Westminster, but in any event not
later than the 6th of December next.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask the Prime Minister whether he
has seen in the Press statements by Mr.
Cosgrave, in reply to a point raised by Mr.
Figgis, that there was in the Treaty a special
machinery which would deal with the extension of the Free State. On that principle,
he said, his Government was going to stand
or fall. He further said that no interference
would be permitted with the clause in the
Treaty dealing with the setting up of a
Boundary Commission, in accordance with
the Articles which set forth what should be
done in the event of the North "hopping"
out?
The PRIME MINISTER: Of course. as my
hon. Friend is aware, I keep a careful eye
on the Press notices of the meetings that are
taking place in Dublin, but my hon. Friend
will bear in mind that neither this Government nor this Parliament was any party
whatever to the Treaty which was entered
into by Great Britain and certain representatives of Southern Ireland.

The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend

HOUSES FOR EX-SERVICE MEN.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister for
Home Affairs if he will state what progress
has been made regarding Housing under the
Irish Land (Provision for Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919; whether sites have already
been selected, and, if so, where; and whether
building operations will soon be commenced,
in view of the great unemployment.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): It would not be possible to
compile a satisfactory statement giving the
information asked for by the hon. Member in
the short time available, and, with his permission, I propose to circulate a detailed
statement on the subject in the course of the
next couple of days.
I can assure the hon. Member that sites
have been selected and that building operations under the Act have been in hands for
some time in Northern Ireland and are now
being carried on as rapidly as possible.
Mr. LYNN: Will that statement be circulated before the Vote is taken for the Department that is dealing with this question?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That Supplemental
Vote is being taken to-day.
Mr. LYNN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman whether he does not think that
we ought to know if this Department is
doing anything before we are asked to vote
it money?
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of the answer,
may I ask my right hon. Friend whether
any arrangement will be come to, similar
to the arrangement in Great Britain, whereby
the ex-Servicemen will get employment in the
construction of these houses?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Every consideration
will be given to that subject, and, so far as
possible, preference will be given to the ex-
Servicemen in the matter of employment.
RENTS RESTRICTION ACT.
3. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister for
Home Affairs whether it is the intention
of the Government to appoint a Committee
of Inquiry to deal with the questions arising
out of the Rents Restriction Act, and to
advise what steps should be taken regarding
the Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question of
legislation amending the Rents Restriction
Acts has been engaging the serious attention
of the Government of Northern Ireland and
the Imperial Government for some time past.
The latter Government have set up a Committee of Inquiry to deal with the matter,
and it is hoped that that Committee will
present a report during the next few weeks.
This Government feels that any differential
legislation in Northern Ireland on matters
of this sort will be highly prejudicial to
Northern Ireland, and the Government of
Northern Ireland are therefore awaiting the
report of the Imperial Committee.
The hon. Member may rest assured that
a close watch is being kept on this important
matter and that legislation will be undertaken in this House before the present Act
lapses in the event of the Committee not
having reported in time.
Mr. LYNN: May I ask my right hon.
Friend whether the Government have taken
into consideration the fact that the Rents
Restrictions Act has practically killed all
private enterprise in building, and whether
he thinks it is possible to get the houses
that are really needed as long as private
enterprise is being penalised in this way?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is a matter
of opinion, and it can be thrashed out when
the matter comes before this House in the
form of legislation.

Address to the Lord Lieutenant.
PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That an Humble Address be presented to
His Excellency the Lord Lieutenant,
followeth :-
as
Your Excellency, we, His Majesty's most
dutiful and loyal subjects the Commons of
Northern Ireland in Parliament assembled,
towards raising the necessary supplies to
defray His Majesty's expenses in Northern
Ireland, do, as from the appointed day for
the purposes of the financial provisions of
the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, freely
and voluntarily give and grant unto His
Majesty the several duties and taxes existing at the said appointed day, and
available for raising the said supplies by
virtue of grants made to His Majesty from
time to time by the Parliament of the
United Kingdom, being duties and taxes in
respect of the imposing, charging, levying
and collection whereof the Parliament of
Northern Ireland has, as from that day,
power to make laws."
The PRIME MINISTER: In case there
should be any misapprehension as to what
is the exact meaning of this rather legal
formula, I think it right to explain to the
House that I myself had some little difficulty
in probing into it when it was first put before
me. However, there is no precedent for it.
It is the advice of the legal side of our
Ministry of Finance that this should be done
in order to maintain the rights and privileges of this House in exactly the same way
as the rights and privileges of the House of
Commons of Great Britain is exercised over
purely financial matters. It is following
constitutional practice declared by the Bill
of Rights in the year 1688. It has been the
custom, when a new tax was imposed, for the
Commons of the United Kingdom Parliament
to grant freely and voluntarily the proceeds
of that tax to His Majesty. Thus, immediately prior to the establishment of the Parliament of Northern Ireland, all existing
taxes, including those which are now known
to us as transferred taxes, were, at the time
they were imposed, granted to the Crown.
The setting up of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland introduced a new element, inasmuch
as the power to impose, levy and collect,
Sittings of the House.

certain taxes, namely, the Entertainments,
Stamps and others, was transferred to us
in pursuance of Section 21 of the Government of Ireland Act, These transferred
taxes must be regarded in the light of new
taxes as between the Parliament of Northern
Ireland and the Crown. It is, therefore,
necessary for the Commons of Northern Ireland itself to grant the taxes to the Crown
in order to regularise the constitutional position and preserve the authority of the
House of Commons of Northern Ireland over
transferred taxation. The formal resolution
now before the House is intended to achieve
this object. I merely give that concise explanation in order that there should be no
misapprehension outside that there is any
other motive behind the motion except to put
us in exactly the same position as the Imperial House as regards taxation. I beg
to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Excellency by such Members

Council in Ireland.

Mr. LYNN: Would the Prime Minister
take into consideration the advisability of
giving us more work to do when we come
here for a day? I do not mind whether you
sit two, three or four days a week, but really

Looking over the sittings of the House, I

The PRIME MINISTER: I quite agree
