PRISONS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£83,865 be granted to His Majesty to defray
the charge which may come in course of payment during the year ending 31st March,
1923, for the expenses of prisons."
Sir DAWSON BATES: In asking this Committee to pass this supplementary Vote it will
at first sight appear somewhat unusual that
the amount asked for should so greatly exceed the original Estimate, but hope to
satisfy hon. Members that I am justified
in coming before the Committee and in asking
them to pass it. When the original Estimate
was framed we had nothing to go upon
except the existing conditions, and we accordingly adopted as an average 470 prisoners
as the population for the jails. Owing, however to the better enforcement of the law
and the offences created under the Civil
Authorities Act the number of ordinary
prisoners, as distinct from those to which
I will refer, increased from 470 to 830. That
is an addition of 360 ordinary, convicted
prisoners, and this Estimate makes provision
for that addition in respect of ordinary
prisoners. But apart from these ordinary
prisoners we have something like 500 prisoners who are interned under the Civil
Authorities Act, SO that as against the
original Estimate of 470 prisoners we are
now budgeting for an additional 860. With
the exception of one item, which I will refer
to later, the amount that I come to this
Committee for is entirely due to this increased prison population.
As hon. Members know we have only three
prisons-ordinary prisons-in the North of
Ireland, and at one time, if I may use the
expression, we were dangerously near
breaking point, but when the Civil Authorities Act came into operation we had to look
round for further accommodation. After
very careful consideration in regard to this
extremely difficult subject we came to the
conclusion that the most efficient way to
deal with the case was to put these prisoners
on to a ship, and accordingly the Government
purchased a vessel known as the "Argenta,"
together with its tender. The Press, hon.
Members know, was full of propaganda
against the scheme. Horrible tales were told
of the atrocities perpetrated against the
prisoners and their awful sufferings, but
imitation is, I suggest, the most sincere
form of flattery, and we find that the Provisional Government who were perhaps our
most hostile critics have now adopted the
same method as we adopted to deal with
the situation in the South of Ireland. So
far as I can see, and having regard to the
health of the prisoners, and from economical
grounds in addition, it has proved an unqualified success.
The "Argenta" was at first moored in
Belfast Lough, and that was done for reasons
of safety. You all realise the conditions

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[Sir Dawson Bates]
prevailing at the time that vessel was brought
into commission. But on the ground of
economy, and also because it has been considered that a vessel of this size cannot very
well remain in the fairway of Belfast Lough
during the winter it has been decided to
remove the vessel to Larne, and as a result
we have been able to effect a great many
economies in the meantime--a reduction of
the crew and in other respects. Unfortunately, the accommodation in the Argenta "
was not sufficient for the purpose, and we
had to turn our attention to another method
of dealing with the situation, and the Larne
Workhouse being vacant and it being the
property of the Ministry we decided to convert that into an auxiliary prison working
in conjunction with the Argenta." Hon.
Members will see that in the Estimates the
cost of converting this workhouse hospital
into a prison amounts to £5,000. Hon.
Members will realise that converting any
building into another purpose is an expensive
thing, but more particularly converting a
hospital into a prison. Now, as a result of
these two prisons, the "Argenta" and the
Larne Workhouse prison, we have accommodation for 500 internees, and I do hope
and pray that may be sufficient for the
purpose of the Government, but if it is not
sufficient the Government will have no hesitation in coming to this House to ask for
further accommodation.


Now with regard to the different items,
we have had to find a complete staff for
the 'Argenta" and Larne prison, and in
addition we have had to increase slightly
the ordinary staff in the two male prisons,
Belfast and Londonderry. The items for
provisioning, clothing, and fuel and light
speak for themselves. We have endeavoured
to effect as many economies as possible, but
dealing with certain classes of prisoners such
as we have got to deal with there is more
destruction in prison clothing than otherwise
would be the case.
Coming down to sub-Head O, which is for
the maintenance of prisoners in prisons outside Northern Ireland, I would like to remind
Members of this Committee that we have
not got a convict prison. Therefore, we
have entered into arrangements from time
to time with the English and Scotch authorities for housing our convicts. In the
original Estimates we provided for 50 convicts. Now we come and ask for an addition
of 20, and that increase is also due to the
fact that at the time this Government took
over the administration of the prisons there
were a number of prisoners in Scotch and
English jails who had been sent there for
reasons best known to the Imperial Government, and, therefore, they were not in our
custody at the time we took over administration.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Has it been added to
since?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, I am budgeting for a further 20. With regard to these
old prisoners sent over prior to us taking
over administration, the Imperial Government have now suggested that we should
pay for their maintenance at the present
time. I am not prepared to admit the equity
of their claim, and negotiations are going
on in regard to it. This Committee may
rest assured that this Government will do
its utmost to prevent itself having to pay
for the maintenance of these prisoners. At
the same time if we fail it is necessary
to make provision for that amount.
With regard to the original Estimate,
which was presented, that works out at a
cost for 470 prisoners of something like £127
per head per annum, and that figure is lower
than is charged or what it costs in Scotland;
but in the present Estimate which is now
before the Committee, that is in respect of
the 860 additional prisoners, if one deducts
from the total Estimate of £83,865 first of
all the capital cost of the "Argenta" of
£19,000, the cost of fitting up the workhouse
of £5,000, and the amount for the prisoners
maintained in England, £17,000, a total of
£41,920, we find that the actual cost of the
maintenance of these 860 prisoners, which we
are budgeting for to-day, works out at something like £47 for nine months or £63 per
head per annum. I do suggest that those
figures speak for themselves. I think they
illustrate in a practical way that we have
endeavoured to provide as economically as
possible for our unwilling guests.
When this Government took over the
administration in December last the condition
of our jails was deplorable, but I am glad
to say that has been completely altered. I
think the most satisfactory change is the
complete restoration of prison discipline.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We have had
an extremely uphill task, but our Governors,
some of whom were new men and inexperienced, and our warders, many of whom were
new and inexperienced, have risen to the
task, and I would like to bear tribute to
the way in which they have restored prison
discipline. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The old familiar hunger strike which disgraced Irish administration is now entirely
a thing of the past. I do not think we are
likely to have a recurrence of it. I have
not touched on the absence or the necessity
of providing a convict prison. Sooner or
later that will have to be dealt with, but

per head. I ask the Members to agree to

[Mr. Donald]
I speak strongly on this matter. I do

men will conduct themselves in the way they

I am
prepared to follow that up because I think

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Dr. MORRISON: I would like to say one or
two things in connection with this Vote, and
I think it has been received with a considerable amount of satisfaction and that no Member has very seriously criticised it. We are
dealing with a very serious state of affairs.
I remember when the Prime Minister was addressing this House and talking about the
protection of the Frontier, he said that if it
was necessary he would not hesitate to tax
the Ulster community to the very last penny
they would be able to carry, and the House
cheered him. I remember my hon. Friend
to my right saying on a subsequent occasion
that if it were necessary he would welcome
conscription by the Government.
Mr. LYNN: Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: He still says it. My
point generally is this: that revolution or
actual war is destructive of all civil institutions and civilisation in any community, and
I say also that the regime of crime and
murder and bloodshed such as we have had
in Ulster, and such as we have specially had
in Belfast, is equally destructive of any
civilisation. And if we are called upon to
pay a little extra in the shape of taxation for
dealing with this question it is infinitely less
than that contemplated by the Prime Minister
or by my hon. Friend.
I think we should give every credit to the
Minister for Home Affairs for dealing with
this matter in the effective and complete manner in which he has done. I would suggest that
it would ba a very wise thing for people to
learn, like the Americans, to take their medicine without making faces. We have a rather
unpalatable pill to take in the shape of extra
taxation with regard to these supplementary
estimates, but if we have to take our castor
oil we can satisfy ourselves with the knowledge that it will have a beneficial influence
and that the body politic will profit. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I would like to say one thing with regard
to the appeal that we listened to here yesterday, and listened to again to-day, from Members with regard to leniency to the prisoners.
I think that Members and public men like
ourselves have a very great responsibility
placed upon us. We pass these measures for
the restoration of order here with great reluctance. They were passed to meet a very
grave state of affairs. We gave power-very
large powers-into the hands of our Ministers. I think for any public man to petition
or to make an appea! in this House on insufficient knowledge is, in my opinion, a very
grave indiscretion. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I would think that ordinary prudence
would suggest to any Member that before taking a step like that he should come to the
Minister in question and ask for the reasons
for the interning of these people. I know
that the Minister of Home Affairs has, without murmuring, borne abuse and censure
when he had in his hands--and has in his
hands at this time-a sledge hammer with
which he could knock down any hon. Member, including Members who have made these
appeals.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: I pass a farmstead near
my home owned by a man whom I do not
know, but whose friends I know and respect.
His hay is lying broadcast to the world, and
his crops are being neglected. I think it is
a deplorable state of affairs. I said to the
Minister of Home Affairs that if without any
danger to the public this man could be set
free, that I would be glad to know that it
should be done, but that the responsibility
was his, and I was not asking him to do any
thing he did not think he was justified in
doing. He told me and it is well that the
public should know this-that there is an
Advisory Board, and that this man refused
to lodge a claim or appear before the
Advisory Board. That Advisory Board does
not consist all of Unionists or Protestants.
There are Roman Catholics on it to see that
justice is being done. This man could go
free if he made a declaration that he is a
law-abiding citizen. He declines to appeal
and have the protection that otherwise he
might have. I do hope that hon. Members
of this House will not use undue influence
with the object of setting men free when interned by the Government. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) The Government know the
facts, and if some of the Members addressing
the House in the interests of leniency knew
the facts as the police know them, they would
be ashamed to open their mouths in the defence of these people. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It is not confined to one section of the
party or one section of the population. I
only heard from what took place in this
House that there is a set of men who
deliberately plotted and deliberately carried
out the murder of unoffending Roman
Catholics; and I say if such men exist, it is
the duty of the Government to put a stop to
it. I will never raise my voice to have them
protected.
I think that the Home Minister has met
this great crisis that has taken place in our
history very effectively. He has done it in
the most economical fashion, because he has,
as compared with treatment in England, been
able to support these prisoners on half the
cost of what it is across the water. He met
a great emergency. People state, and stated

are in the market, but prison ships are not.
If they had been I would have been only too
glad to have hired a prisonship, and if I
could not have hired one, to have purchased
one. At the same time I do not think that
the sum of £19,000 has altogether been lost.
I hope that when the shipping trade improves we may be able to make a profit out
of the vessel, and perhaps hand it over to the
Southern Parliament as a prison ship.
Mr. DONALD: Do I take it that this ship
cost only £3,000? There is an item of £2,500
for repairs.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Those are subsequent repairs for the accommodation of extra
prisoners.
Mr. DONALD: No one objects to that.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to the
question as to whether or not it would have
been better to have a camp rather than a
ship, we have many reasons for having a
ship. I think a ship is a great deterrent.
Many of these internees have been
accustomed to enjoy the luxury of an internment camp, but I think they find that things
on board a ship are not quite so pleasant, and
many of them try to avoid going on a ship
who would otherwise be only too glad to
enjoy the life in an ordinary internment
camp. With respect to the question of wages,
the wage of the captain, who is a qualified
skipper, is £10 a month and food, with an
allowance of 7s 6d per day.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: £10 a month or week?
It
Sir DAWSON BATES: £10 a week.
would be absolutely impossible to maintain a
ship of that kind without a proper captain.
As to the question of why we do not have
convict prisons they have to be dealt with
on different lines to an ordinary prison. Of
course, it is quite open to us to send our convict prisoners to the South of Ireland, but I
could not guarantee that the Provisional
Government would retain them, and I do not
believe you will think it is desirable I should
have adopted this course. Having no convict
prison of our own, it is necessary to send
prisoners to some other convict prison. It may
be necessary later on to have a convict prison
in the North of Ireland, but I would like

As to the question of warders, they are
temporary warders, and are engaged as the

Mr. M'GUFFIN: Are they paid 29s a week?
Sir DAWSON BATES: They are paid that
with bonus. If the hon. Member refers to
the Estimate he will see the figures. With
reference to the question raised by the hon.
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald) in regard to these internees, during the last six
months we have interned something like 500
persons, and this is the first occasion on which
any Member of this House has ever raised
the question of interning persons without
trial. I think the hon. Members who have
raised this point seem to have forgotten the
circumstances under which this Act was
passed. Six months ago this Government
came to the House at a period when the
machinery of the law was practically at
breaking point, and they asked for these
drastic powers.
At that time murder and
outrage had been committed throughout Belfast and the Six Counties, and not a man had
been brought to justice. We asked for these
powers, and I do suggest that the peace we
are enjoying to-day is due to the fact that
the House entrusted these powers to the
Government, and that these powers have
been carried out impartially and fairly.
Surely the hon. Member does not suggest
that because one set of persons belong to one
creed they are to be treated in a different
way to persons belonging to another creed?
Mr. DONALD: If my right hon. Friend
refers to me, I state quite openly that the
treatment that was meted out to prisoners in
one part of Ireland was entirely different to
the treatment meted out in this part of Ireland. How long are these prisoners to be detained in custody without trial? That is my
point. I do think that the same justice should
be meted out all round. Hundreds of men have
been released in the Free State under the
Free State Government, yet our Prime
Minister himself told us distinctly-

Sir DAWSON BATES: If the hon. Member refers to the Act he will see it gives
power to intern prisoners, and not
specific charges. As I said before, in one
month alone 90 murders were committed in
Belfast, and not a man was brought to
justice. The people knew who committed
those murders, but no one had the courage
to come forward and give evidence. The result was that this House gave the Government these very drastic powers of internment,
and in order to safeguard the interests of
persons interned it was provided that an
Advisory Board should be set up.
Advisory Board consists of the Deputy Recorder and one other barrister and an exsoldier, and I can assure hon. Members that
if their friends, or the men they refer to, are
as innocent as they think they are, and they
will come before the Advisory Board, and the
Advisory Board recommend they should be
discharged, I shall be delighted to allow them
to go. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) This
House has a right to see that the Government
maintain law and order, but it is very
embarrassing to have allegations made
against the Government that they exercise
these powers wrongly and unjustly. Personally, I object to the principle of internment,
and I hope that the day is not far distant
when this Act will be repealed, but so long
as it is on the Statute Book I intend to
endeavour to carry it out impartially as regards all creeds and classes. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

Regarding the staff of the Home Office, in
the original estimate we asked for 100, which
has now been increased by 35. I should like,
however, to make it clear that a large proportion of our staff is' temporary, and in fact
at the moment, out of a total of 135, 56 are

have not therefore, committed ourselves to

is remembered that half the total expenditure
in Northern Ireland is accounted for by the
Ministry of Home Affairs no one, I think,
can reasonably suggest that the staff of the
supervising department can be described as
excessive.

RELIEF FOR PENSIONED TEACHERS.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance whether he is aware that sixty
pensioned teachers have less than £20 per
annum, and some of these pensioners have
pensions of only £13 per annum. Whether
some immediate relief will be granted to these
deserving people until legislation is introduced regarding this matter?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The total number of ex-teachers
receiving pensions of less than £20 per
annum from the Northern Ireland Teachers'
Pension Fund is 54, and of these 18 are in
receipt of not more than £13 per annum.
These sums are in some cases supplemented
by the State Old Age Pension. The smallness of the Teacher's Pension is usually due
to one of the following causes, namely:-
Shortness of Service,
Previous commutation of part of the
Pension, or
Non-compliance with the statutory, qualifications required for the increase of Pension
under the Pensions (Increase) Act, 1920.
Regarding non-compliance with statutory
qualification, the main qualification is that
the pensioner must prove that his means, including pension, are less than £150 per
annum if unmarried, or £200 per annum if
married.
I am not aware that any considerable
hardship exists, and any additional payments
would require amendment of the law. An
amendment of the law by this House presents many difficulties, inasmuch as the Act
under which increases are granted is of
general application throughout the United
Kingdom not only to pensioned teachers
but to persons in receipt of pensions from
local authorities, civil servants, army and
navy pensioners, and so forth, and differentiation in treatment would undoubtedly cause
great discontent.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Arising out of that
answer, might I ask the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) if, in view of the splendid
services performed by these teachers now
upon the pension list, and in view of the
fact that they have received such small remuneration for those services, and at the
moment have retired with a very inadequata
pension, in some cases not amounting to
more than £20 per annum, he would consider the advisability of receiving a deputation on their behalf to present their case,
or, alternatively, in the event of the Bill
about to be introduced increasing their pension, will he see that that provision is made
retrospective as from 1921 ?
Mr. POLLOCK: I may say at once that I
have no objection whatever to receiving a deputation on the subject, but I would point
out that the cases of hardship, if any, are
comparatively few.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Some of them are in the
workhouse.
Mr. POLLOCK: It has to be remembered
that if a teacher commutes part of his pension for a capital sum he thereby automatically reduces the balance of the pension to be
received. The greater number of these people,
as I have indicated, now belong to that cate
gory.
PRICES OF HOUSE COAL IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he will furnish a statement showing the retail selling prices of
house coal delivered to the consumers in
Belfast and the various centres, and the
items of cost included in the retail selling
prices, from the pit-head to the consumer?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): My hon. Friend (Mr. Donald) will
have observed that the prices of coal to the
consumer have recently been reduced, and,
accordingly, the information which he seeks
is as follows:-
The net retail prices of house coal in Belfast range from 39s. to 49s. per ton, delivered to consumer. These prices are made
up of an initial cost to the merchants of 258.

to 35s. f.o.b. at port in Great Britain, according to the district from which the coal
is drawn, to which must be added freightage
of 5s. to 10s. per ton according to the geographical position of the loading port, and
distribution costs of 10s. to 13s. per ton, according to the quantity of coal delivered,

DRIVING OF CROSSLEY CARS.
3. Mr. COOPER asked the Ministry of
Home Affairs if he is aware that a number
of accidents have occurred in Northern Ireland through the negligent driving of Crossley cars, and that many people of moderate
means have suffered considerable losses, and
have been unable to obtain either compensation or inquiry into their cases. Whether
any remedy exists against the Government
other than by Petition of Right, and, if not,
whether he is prepared to introduce some
remedy, having regard to the fact that such
proceedings are a luxury which cannot be
borne by the pocket of the ordinary citizen?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): It is true that a number of
accidents have occurred, though it must not
be assumed that most of these accidents are
due to negligent driving. Close inquiry is
made in all such accidents, and where negligence can be established the person responsible is either prosecuted at Petty Sessions,
or if the offending person is a member of the
Police Forces, disciplinary action is taken
against him. Instructions have been issued
that every precaution shall be taken to prevent reckless driving, and the Police authorities will, to their utmost ability, carry
these instructions into effect.
In regard to the latter part of the question, no legal remedy exists against the Government, but the Government is always willing to consider an application for compensation where legal liability would attach if
the car were the property of a private owner.
Of course, proceedings can always be taken
against the driver if he has been guilty of
negligence.

Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of the answer,
I should like to ask has it not frequently

Mr. POLLOCK: I think it is rather an

is this, that a farmer must be protected
against liabilities that would exceed ten times
the amount of the annuity for several reasons.

materially weaken the security of the Government in regard to the payment of the

of a holding or the owner of a holding could
mortgage his property to an unlimited extent.
I do not think it desirable that transactions
of the kind indicated by my hon. Friend

Solicitors Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this Bill be now read the Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill, the
Second reading of which I have the honour
to move, is one for adapting with the necessary modifications the provisions of the
Solicitors (Ireland) Act of 1898. The
Solicitors Act, 1898, applied to the whole of
Ireland, and provided for, amongst other
things, the keeping of a roll by the Incorporated Law Society, in which were entered
the names of all persons entitled to practise
as solicitors. It also gave authority to the
Incorporated Law Society of Ireland to make
regulations with respect to persons seeking
to be admitted to the profession, and provided
for the holding of preliminary examinations
and the general legal training, and the holding of the final examinations prior to these
candidates being admitted to the roll of
solicitors, which enabled them to practise as
such in Ireland. The Act also provided for
the oversight of solicitors by the Incorporated
Law Society, and for investigating charges of
misconduct, if that ever took place, and in
suitable cases bringing them before the Lord
Chancellor with a view to having such
solicitors punished by being suspended or
struck off the roll, as the case might be.
There were certain other subsidiary divisions
incidental to the regulations with which I
think it is unnecessary to trouble this House.
As a result of the passing of the Government
of Ireland Act of 1920, and the setting up of
a separate judiciary in Northern Ireland, the
Northern Law Society applied for, and
obtained, a Royal Charter, under which they
became incorporated in the name of the
Incorporated Law Society of Northern Ireland. That being the case, it became necessary that legislation should be provided for
making adaptations of the Act of 1898, which
I have referred to and which applied to the
whole of Ireland, enabling them to carry into
effect the provisions made in that Act, and
also to make certain other necessary amendments in the Act to suit the new conditions
of affairs.
(E) provides for
in lieu of the
With regard to Clause 1, Sub-sections A,
B, D, and F, these are adaptations of the
principal Act with the necessary modifications. Clause 1 (C) gives power to the Incorporated Law Society to hold only two examinations in the year. Under the principal
Act, it was necessary for the Incorporated
Law Society to hold at least three, but it is
considered that having regard to the lesser
number of solicitors' apprentices coming
forward it may not be necessary to hold
more than two. Clause
the giving of certificates
Benchers' certificates to barristers of five
years standing to enable them to become
solicitors. Clause 2 (1) gives power to the
Incorporated Law Society, the new society
of Northern Ireland, to take under its
control existing apprentices who are in the
North of Ireland, and arrange for the completion of their term of apprenticeship, and
to provide for their legal education during
that period, and for the holding of the
necessary examinations. With regard to
Clause 2, Sub-section 2, and Clause 3, Subsections 1 and 2, under the old Act, it is provided that graduates of certain specified universities were entitled to be admitted as
apprentices without having to pass a preliminary examination, and under those condi-
Solicitors Bill-
17 OCTOBER 1922
Second Reading.
by the Minister of Home Affairs.
tions there was a reduction to three years
of the term of apprenticeship, and in the
case of apprentices who passed a matriculation or entrance examination to certain
specified universities, they were also allowed
the preliminary examination. Under this
new Clause, it is felt that having regard to
the fact that several new universities have
sprung into existence since the Act of 1898
was passed, the examinations and degrees of
those universities ought to be recognised,
subject to the necessary requirements being
met by the Incorporated Law Society. Clause
3, Sub-section 3, gives power to the Lord
Chief Justice of Northern Ireland, who takes
the place for practical purposes of the Lord
Chancellor of Ireland, to grant total or
partial exemptions under certain conditions
from the preliminary examinations, but
that power
can only be exercised on the
recommendation of the Incorporated Law
Society.
With regard to Clause 4, a rule-making
authority was formerly constituted by the
President of the Incorporated Law Society of
Ireland and certain members of the Supreme
Court of Judicature in Ireland. We are substituting for that the President of the New
Incorporated Law Society and certain members of the Judiciary in Northern Ireland.
Clause 5 transfers the rules and regulations
already existing to the jurisdiction of the Incorporated Law Society here, and also the
rules that have been made by the new ruling
authority. It also gives authority to the
Council of the new Society to make temporary regulations during the transitory
period. I think those are the main points
in the Bill, which I beg to move.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have no
intention whatever of following my right
hon. Friend in the detailed speech he has just
made to the House on this very interesting
subject. I do not know that the House, as
a whole, will be intensely interested in the
question of law and lawyers. There might
have been more interest in the question of
solicitors' bills instead of a Solicitors Bill
such as is on the Order Paper here to-day. I
think the House will be satisfied with the
statement made by my right hon. Friend.
Some of us have read the Bill, and I think we
have a fair, general idea of what is intended
and I suppose we will trust the lawyer
friends that have drafted this Bill to see that
it is perfectly correct. I see no reason why
the House this afternoon should not give this
Bill a Second Reading right away, and thus
place it on the Statute Book without any
further delay.
Mr. DUFF: I confess that I have not been
able to follow all the technical details, which
I assume have been very clearly explained
My friend
the Member for Derry (Sir Robert Anderson)
made a jocular reference to fees. I am
perhaps a little more serious-minded, and I
am going to ask a serious question about fees.
I cannot see anything in this Bill by which
the fees of solicitors can either be increased
or decreased. I understand that those fees
have statutory force. If this Bill is intended
to give to the Incorporated Law Society most
of the powers that solicitors have in England
or Scotland is there any means by which we
can get these fees either reduced or increased?
In other words, is there any application of the
law by which the Incorporated Law Society
can do this, or will it require a separate
Bill to be passed in this House?
Mr. COOPER: I am afraid the hon. Member
for East Belfast (Mr. Duff) must have lost
his case, as he is so hard on the question of
fees. I want to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs if a solicitor will now have to pay
a licence duty for practising in Northern
Ireland and another for practising in
Southern Ireland, because it seems to me
that there may be a certain hardship in that
respect, and I would like to hear something
about it.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Might I urge Members
of the House to pass this Bill quickly and
let us get on to something more useful. I
have heard that at the commencement of a
period of great prosperity in Russia Peter the
Great banished all solicitors in the Kingdom
except one, whom he put in prison, and that
the country was exceedingly prosperous for
a long time afterwards. If the authorities
think this is a wise measure we should pass
it at once.
Sir DAWSON BATES: By leave of the
House I would like to reply to the question
raised by the Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Duff). I am sorry he has had such an unfortunate experience, but I can assure him
that unfortunately the solicitors profession
has nothing to do with the fixing of fees.
This Bill does not alter the present condition
of affairs. If the hon. Member desires at
some subsequent date to introduce a Bill in
this House I am sure it will receive very
careful consideration on the part of Members.
With regard to the point raised by the hon.
Member for Fermanagh (Mr. Cooper) I can
only say that if a solicitor desires to enjoy
the luxury of practising in both Northern
and Southern Ireland, as apparently he
wishes to do, I am afraid fees will be payable
in both areas.

We found, however, that the urban electoral areas did not present that very serious
difficulty. The Act, itself, especially with
regard to Belfast and with regard to Derry
and the other urban areas, made it rather
easy to make any of the necessary Orders.
The underlying idea was to return as far as
possible to the state of things that was
in existence prior to the passing of the
Proportional Representation Act, 1919.
In many cases the areas in urban districts
for election were for the whole constituency;
that is to say, a single constituency returned
as the case may be 9, 12, 16 or 21 Members.
We felt that the provisions of the Act, if
it were passed, could be easily put into
force with regard to the cities, and with

districts a very different state of things met
us. There were some hundreds of electoral

incongruities of a very startling character.
We were told something of them during the
passage of the previous Bill in this House,
and the discussions which involved the idea
that there would be redistribution showed
the necessity for it, but certainly for myself
I had no idea that the state of things was

It must be remembered that many of the
electoral divisions were fixed something like
80 years ago, and there had been no general
scheme of redistribution since then although
there have been radical changes in the
population. While those changes in the
population had occurred nothing has been
done to meet it by way of changing the
electoral areas throughout any of the
counties. I should like the House just to
realise how unfair and unjustifiable the old
arrangement of seats was. It was not confined to one county. We heard a good deal
about the Counties of Fermanagh and Tyrone
during the course of the discussion, but
every county from Antrim to Fermanagh
showed exactly the same state of affairs. It
showed examples of unequal representation
especially in the rural districts. I want
the House to have a few instances, typical

not calling attention to at all. In County
Antrim, in the Lisburn Rural District,
Derriaghy has a population of 3,373 according to the 1911 census. It has the same
representation as Tully rush in the same

500. That is, every voter or ratepayer in
Tully rush has seven times the voice in the
expenditure of rates that his neighbour in

753. In the Downpatrick rural district,

A study of these figures shows that the task
before us was one that required very sweeping changes in the redistribution, and while
the assent to the Bill was hung up we were
driven to the conclusion that it would be
impossible with our staff to-day to effect
redistribution in the time that was left at
our disposal, that is we would have the
space of about two months 1ot only to arrange things with regard to the urban and
county boroughs, but these hundreds of
cases arising in the rural districts. We
recognised at once that the task was beyond
us, and that some other course would have
to be taken with regard to the elections
that were coming next year.
A study of the question showed certain
alternative courses, and the ones that presented themselves to our minds were these-
First of all, to let the elections proceed
with the electoral divisions as they were
in existence before the P.R. Act. The second
would have been to ask the House to pass
a Bill suspending the operation of P.R. for
a year. The third was to ask the House
to postpone the elections until redistribution
can be effected. As regards reverting to the
old electoral divisions, we felt that in the
face of the inequalities disclosed we could
not justify the course. We would make it
more difficult to re-arrange the divisions
afterwards if we had proceeded to have elections in these divisions as they had been
before the Act of 1919, and indeed the House
had assumed that there would be redistribution. It had laid down cardinal principles
as to county areas. These areas were to be
drawn from rural district areas. If a county
area was to comply with the conditions of
the Act in regard to equality of population
you had to see that the rural areas of
which it was composed had also been dealt
with in the same way. After our experience
of the mind of the House as to proportional
representation we felt that it would be im-

The only other provision of the Bill that I
need call attention to is Clause 3, which is
the Declaratory Clause. Its purpose is to
remove doubt as to when the preliminary
meeting of any local council shall be held.
The provisions that were made by the Pro
portional Representation Act, raised a doubt
as to when these meetings should take place,
and this section of the Bill is to remove any
ambiguity on that point. I beg to move.
Mr. LYNN: The hon. and learned Gentleman who has just moved the Second Reading
of this Bill was, as usual, very lucid in his
explanation, but I could not help thinking

far from convincing and certainly not very
logical. Personally, I see no reason why
Clause 2 should be passed by this House, and
I hope, in Committee, the Members will
agree to eliminate it altogether. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) These recalcitrant
councillors had no regard whatever for the
needs of the ratepayers. They defied the
law, they defied the Government, and they
let the interests of the ratepayers go by
default. Now my hon. Friend (Mr. Megaw)
proposes that these people who have treated

House this is a case where these people
should not be reinstated by Act of Parliament. If they are ever to be reinstated, they
should be reinstated by the votes of the
electors themselves, and, therefore, when we
come to deal with this Bill in Committee,
I do hope that the Members will insist on

Mr. ROBB: I would like to say a word or
two also on Clause 2 of this Bill. I cannot,
I think, agree with the view put forward
by the hon. Member who has just spoken.
The alternative to his view seems to me to
be this, that the Ministry shall continue to
administer the areas which were administered
by these recalcitrant councils until the year
1924, necessarily by a commissioner. I do
not think that administration by a commissioner is a good principle, although the
administration may itself be good. The
alternative which has been suggested is that
there should be a fresh election. The hon.
Member who has moved the Second Reading
of this Bill (Mr. Megaw) has shown us in fact
there cannot reasonably be a register ready
for a fresh election before 1921. The alternatives, then, are two: to reinstate these
recalcitrant councillors, or such of them as
show penitence; or to continue the administration by a commissioner. For myself, I
prefer that the discretion of the Ministry
should be exercised in the reinstatement of
those who are prepared to show that they
are now penitent for the position they formerly took up. I think it is more
democratic, surely, that any area should
be administered by those members of the
original council who are willing to carry
on their work now. They may have been
wrong in the past, but, surely, if they are
willing, now and for the future, to do their
duty they should be given an opportunity
of doing so. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
But there is one difficulty in the section as
it stands, although, possibly, it is a matter
more for the Committee than for the House,
and that is this: The Ministry is given power
to reinstate all or any of the persons who
held office as members of the local authority
immediately before its dissolution. I see
grave objection to the power being given to
the Ministry to constitute a county council
or a district council of a very small number
of those who originally held office. Supposing there were originally thirty members,
are we to count twenty, or ten, or five such
persons as sufficient to constitute the new
council? Apparently the Minister would be
satisfied with five out of thirty. From this
five they can reconstitute the council. I do
not think that is a wise discretion to entrust
to the Ministry. So much upon that part
of the Bill.
I would like to ask the Parliamentary
Secretary one other question. The first part
of this Bill deals with the re-distribution of
seats in local areas. Apparently it is contemplated by the Bill that the Minister shall
make, once and for all, final orders distributing seats in any or all of the areas with
which he chooses to deal, and there does not
seem to me to be any opportunity for
representations being made to the Minister
as to the inequalities that may be existing
in the Orders he does make. I think it
would be wise that this House should insert
in the Bill provision whereby Provisional
Orders for redistribution should be made,
with a limited time for objections, and the
Order only becoming final after the expiration of a period within which objections to
the Provisional Orders should be made.
Subject to these two observations, I heartily
support the Second Reading of this Bill.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: With regard to the

that it has been thought necessary to reward

punishment in the way which is suggested in
this Bill. I note that the condition for
reinstatement shall be "as the Ministry
thinks fit," and I presume, as has been
stated, that one of the principal conditions
will be that the members who wish to return
should take the oath of allegiance. I wonder
whether hon. Members will think that sufficient. We know what importance some of
them at any rate attach to an oath of this
kind. We have only got to refer to some
of the speeches made recently in Dublin to
realise that their idea of loyalty to government, even if this oath of allegiance be taken,
is not our idea. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) One of the Roman Catholic Bishops
said quite recently that
An Edict of the State might be in conflict
with God's law, and then resistance was
not only lawful but a duty.
Are they going to define what they call God's
law. He further says
If a law or tax was patently unjust, it
might be resisted even with violence.
Are you going to put this power to judge
whether a law or a tax is unjust into the
hands of people who argue in that manner?
I cannot help remarking further that if
these members wished to return or wanted
to be forgiven why did not the members
of the real Opposition-those who were returned in order to champion their own sidecome into this House and urge the case of
these people? (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Their view of the oath of allegiance is
perhaps an example of what the view of the
reinstated members of these councils would
be. They took the same oath, at any rate
they took the oath in the Imperial House.
How have they kept that oath? What
guarantee have we that the others will not
do the same? (Hon. Members: Hear hear.)
Before we reinstate them let us hesitate.
Let us not forget-and again I say that I
speak with great feeling as a former member
of one of these Boards-let us not forget
the insults which we had to endure in the
past, and the tyranny with which they
ground the minority under their heel.
May I remind hon. Members that I come
from an area where I think I am quoting
the figures correctly-247 labourers' cottages
were built, and of these only 47 were given
to Unionists. That is the Board which would
be reinstated under this Bill. We have had
to sit there and listen to our King being
insulted, to our Government being derided.
We have been told that killing was no
murder unless committed by the foreign
invader. At another Board, of which I am
not a member, I remember a scene in which
one of the majority said that rather than
recognise the Northern Government the
hillsides would be running red with our
blood. I ask you again to hesitate before
These councils knew
you pass Clause 2.
what we would do. They were warned. They
staked everything, believing that our Government was weak. They lost. Our Government
was strong. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
hope that our Government will continue to be
strong. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) How
can you treat children reasonably, how can
you instil discipline unless you punish, and
punish adequately? Perhaps we may be satisfied as to the other conditions in the minds
of the Ministry, which they may consider
it possible to impose, but I would make just
one suggestion-of course I quite realise that
this will all be discussed in Committee-and
it is: Could we not wait till May, 1923, the
date when, in the ordinary course of events,
a new election would have taken place,
before we reinstate, if we reinstate then,
any of these rebellious councils? I do hope
that it will not become necessary to sacrifice
the loyal element in our area to the disloyal.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. COOPER: I think that the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. Megaw) in introducing this Bill gave us some of the most
powerful reasons why it should not be
passed. Take County Fermanagh. He told
the House of the great differences there were
in the voting powers in the division. He
showed that in one division sixty votes
equalled 500 in another. I can tell you
that the Council which was dissolved never
at any time represented the electors of County
Fermanagh, and if there were an election
to-morrow morning the County Council which
has been dissolved would not be returned.
Under these circumstances are you going to
reward this Council which has been dissolved by setting it up for an extra year
and a half? This Council will go out of
office in the ordinary course in a couple of
months. What you propose now to do in
this Bill is to give them another year and
a half of life to misrepresent the ratepayers
of Fermanagh. It seems to me that that is
an extraordinary suggestion for this Government to adopt. I do not want to say anything further at this stage, but when the
matter comes up in Committee I will move
that this Clause be struck out of the Bill
altogether, and I hope the Government will
see its way in the meantime to agree that
this Clause should be struck out.

Mr. POLLOCK: My hon. Friend the Parliamentary and Financial Secretary (Mr. Barbour) on Wednesday last submitted
financial resolution, which was a preliminary
to, or perhaps I should say the foundation
of, the Bill of which it is now my duty to
move the Second Reading. My hon. Friend
(Mr. Barbour) in moving the resolution
entered in some detail into the character of
the measure, but as hon. Members at that
time laboured under the disadvantage of not
being in possession of the text of the Bill,
and, therefore, perhaps, might not have been
able to follow my hon. Friend's (Mr. Barbour's) quite lucid explanation, it may,
perhaps, be found convenient if I enter now
into some details, not of too great prolixity,
in order to elucidate matters which may
have seemed obscure to hon. Members. The
Bill itself is divided into five parts, none
of them, it may be said, of superlative importance, but yet valuable, and to some
extent necessary if only to assimilate the
legislative enactments of Great Britain with
those of Northern Ireland. There is general
agreement as to the advantage of such a
course, and the Government, therefore, think
that a measure of this character should be
submitted to the House at the earliest possible moment.
Let me take the Clauses of the Bill categorically and endeavour as far as possible
to make their meaning clear. The first part
of the Bill relates to the Entertainments
Duty, and the first sub-section of the first
Clause of the measure, if hon. Members have
the text of the Bill in their hands, will be seen
to refer to a simple adjustment of words in
order to make clear what the intention of
the measure is, that is to say that not only
must each person admitted for payment to
an entertainment pay the tax, but that also
each payment made shall be subject to the
tax. Now the meaning of that is obvious.
As hon. Members know in very many cases
tickets are sold greatly in advance of the
entertainment, and often many of them are
not used, although the tax has been included
in the charge. The only person thus receiving any advantage from the tax that has
been paid is the owner or proprietor of the
entertainment, and it is to amend that that
the substitution of these words is made in
the measure, namely that-
For the words "each person admitted
for payment" there shall be substituted
the words" each payment for admission";
and for the words " the number of admissions" there shall be substituted the words
the number of payments for admission."
I hope that makes that part of the Clause
sufficiently clear, and I think hon. Members
will agree that it is necessary in the interests
of fairness and also for the protection of
the Treasury. In regard to the second subsection, which may appear somewhat cryptic,
it eliminates a part of the Finance (New
Duties) Act of 1916 in order that the intention
of the Act may be made more clear as far
as Northern Ireland is concerned. Its real
intention is to provide that in all cases of
entertainments, whether they relate to sports
or entertainments indoors, there shall be the
same measure. The elimination of the paragraph to which I refer will place all those
who attend entertainments on the same
footing.
Passing on then to the second Clause in
respect of entertainments for charitable or
philanthropic purposes, it is the intention
of the Government that they should be wholly
exempt from duty. That has been the case
in the past, and it is intended that that
should be continued. In other cases of
charitable entertainments repayment is made
where the expenses of the entertainment do
not exceed twenty per cent. of the receipts.
That has been the custom in the past. I
think hon. Members will realise the meaning
of that provision, the object of it. I do not
suppose we have any proprietors of entertainments in Northern Ireland who would
be guilty of it, but it is quite conceivable that
Second Reading.
Finance Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
abuses may take place if such a provision
were not in existence. In order to make the
matter clear, let me submit a supposititious
case by way of example of the point which is
involved. It is a very interesting point.
Assume that an owner of a house of entertainment announces a performance in aid of
a particular charity, and has sold £100
worth of tickets. Let us assume that the
owner alleged that in order to provide the
entertainment his payments to his permanent
staff and his standing charges absorbed the
whole of the £100, and that, therefore, the
charity did not benefit by the entertainment.
Where the receipts have been entirely absorbed by the charges, in order to protect
the charities and in order to protect
the revenue, it was considered necessary that
a limit, a maximum, of charges should be
imposed. It has been found from experience
in many cases of bona-fide entertainments for
charities the expenditure has ranged from 20
per cent. to 30 per cent., and it was felt
in that case a grievance existed that repayment could not be made to the charities concerned under such circumstances.
therefore, proposed in this Measure, and in
the Clause which I am discussing, that the
maximum should be increased from 20 per
cent. to 30 per cent. The primary object of
the people who attended these entertainments,
of course, was to benefit the charity, and the
amendment of the Clause would have the
effect of assisting philanthropic and charitable entertainments when the limit of
charges is increased from 20 per cent. to 30
per cent.
It is,
I have reached Clause 3. This Clause is
simply a repetition of a Section in the Imperial Finance Act of 1922, and it is merely
chosen to clear up certain ambiguities, and
to remove doubt as to the scope of the existing law. It has happened not infrequently
that payments for admission to charity entertainments are taken by persons who are
not proprietors of the entertainment at all.
For instance, it is no uncommon feature at
race meetings-this applies more to Great
Britain than to Northern Ireland, where
race meetings are not so frequent-that some
of the stands are under the control not of
the race committee, but the proprietor of the
entertainment is some person who has
erected or rented a stand upon the ground,
on which he has either acquired the right
of a proprietor or rented from the Race Committee. It is unfair that the Race Committee should be liable to entertainment duty
for admission to a stand, but some other
person for admission to another stand should
not be liable. Some points may arise in
either case, and it is desirable at any rate,
although it is not of such significance in
Northern Ireland, that this matter should be
harmonised and made uniform with that of
Great Britain. In regard to Sub-section B
of Clause 3. occasionally happens a person
rents the whole of a stand for the purpose
of entertaining his guests at a race meeting.
There is no reason why the payment for an
individual seat on a stand should not be
liable to entertainment duty while a person
can have a whole stand and escape liability.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) In cases payment of rent is made, not for the purposes
of acquiring the stand for the purposes of
securing admission to an entertainment, but
of sub-letting. (As I say, these cases in
Northern Ireland are negligible, but for purposes of uniformity it is desirable that this
provision should be introduced in the Measure
I am now submitting.
I have dealt with the Entertainments Tax
so far as it relates to Northern Ireland, and I
come now to the second part of the Measure,
which touches upon the Licence Duty on
mechanically propelled vehicles. The 1st
and 2nd Clauses are taken from the Imperial Finance Act of 1922, the British
Measure. It will be seen that it has been
designed to cover the case of vehicles which
have been converted or diverted from commercial vehicles to vehicles of pleasure, the
rate of duty in the one case being higher
than in the other, and if the transformation
takes place the enhanced duty becomes payable. In the following Clause motor agents
have, under the existing law, the privilege
of paying single licence duty to cover all
cars which they manipulate for the purpose
of their business, and this Clause that I am
now discussing extends the privilege to
motor car repairers, who in a great number
of cases are also agents and dealers in motor
cars. That is the only part of the Measure
that touches upon the motor mechanically
propelled vehicles.
I come now to part 3, which refers to
stamps, and this also is not of any considerable importance. Under the Alkali Works
Act, 1906, there were certain registration fees
imposed in order to cover the cost of the
investigation and inspection of these works,
There are some 26 works to which this
tax is applicable in Northern Ireland
and it is proposed to change the tax,
following the British precedent of £5 in the
casa of Alkali works, and £3 in the case of
other works, to £10 and £6 respectively; in
other words to double the fees. It has been
found by experience that the fees charged
in these cases were insufficient to cover the
cost of inspection, and the change is only
made in order that the Government may be
recouped for the cost of inspecting these
works. There is only one Alkali works, as a
matter of fact, in Northern Ireland, and the
remaining works to which the Measure will
apply are mainly gas works. Therefore the
change will not be anything like a heavy
burden upon the institutions, and it only involves an additional amount of £80. I come
Finance Bill-

now to the fourth part of the Measure, Estate
Duty. It is also a matter rather more of formality than of any really valid importance.
The reading of the Clause itself will practically inform hon. Members of what is wanted,
that is to say, to avoid the payment of double
death duties in respect of property situated in
British possessions passing on the death of the
deceased person. The present Clause grants
to certain of the Malay States, a very far
away possession under the British flag, the
status of a British possession for Estate Duty
It is not anticipated, of course,
purposes.
that many cases in Northern Ireland will
arise in which persons holding property in
the Malay States will make any such claims,
but for the sake of uniformity in this legislation with Great Britain it is desirable we
should keep side by side in all financial matters. The last part of the Measure deals with
general matters, such as construction and designation, and does not, I think, need any detailed explanation from me. I beg to move
the Second reading of the Measure.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: I think the House is at
one with the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Pollock) in the intention he has in the introduction of this Bill. I quite agree that the
British Parliament contains some very
clever financiers, but I do not think they are
always wise men. I have never had very
much sympathy with the entertainment tax,
and I think the Government would be well
advised if it could avoid as far as possible a
slavish imitation of the institutions that
obtain in the British Parliament. The
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Finance (Mr. Barbour) has told us that this
does not involve any extra taxation-we are
glad to know that-but that it may lead to
the taxation in some instances of other
sources of revenue. The reason I object to
the Bill is that in the first instance this was
introduced as a war tax, in 1916, I think;
and that was so with the income-tax, which
has been built up stage by stage until to-day
it is 5s, and it was recently 6s. I would be
afraid that a similar course might be pursued
with respect to this, seeing that even so far as
the Northern Parliament is concerned it
now amounts to £80,000 per annum.
That, you will admit, is quite a large proportion of the revenue we have got
here. I object to it again upon the ground
that it is au undemocratic tax. The right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) made
reference to race courses, which are so much
more popular in England than they are
here, but we have other forms of sport and
entertainment that are subject to the tax
here, and where this tax is made more incident upon the working man than upon
better off people. At the present it is imnow.
possible for one to attend a place of amusement or go to a rendezvous of sport without
meeting the tax, and it is a direct tax.
It is one that he must be aware of, because
in every instance it is included in the price
of admission. He is aware of the tax; and
when it was imposed, I would like the
right hon. Gentleman to remember that men
were earning very much larger wages then
than they are to-day, and that they could
afford the tax. I suppose that was the reason
they did not grumble at the time. They
found that they had resources to meet the
tax. These resources have sadly disappeared
Yet we have a continuance of the
tax. It has been stated, and I think all
authorities. will admit, that sport is a very
necessary exercise, especially to those who
find no pleasure in reading or study. You
cannot have a drab existence. You must
have some outlook. But then, unfortunately,
you will be taxed-taxed at every avenue.
The tax represents one of the transferred
revenues that we have here in the Northern
Area, and therefore can be dealt with by the
Minister of Finance or by this House. I
simply want to say that so far as I am concerned I would welcome very much a modification of the tax in the interests of the
working people. Young men come out from
their work on Saturday evening and they are
anxious to get away to football, or cricket,
or some other sport, but before they enter
they must pay the tax. Their resources are
much less than they were. I. therefore,
appeal on their behalf to the Minister that
when he will have it under review he will
be prepared to make some modification of
this tax in respect of our area. That is all I
want to say except that so far as the motor
tax is concerned I have always thought it
should be upon fuel. I think it is only fair
that that should be so. You take a man with
a motor that he has no occasion to use often.
He is taxed, and the man who uses it every
day is taxed no more. If you pay upon petrol
each man will pay according to the use or
service that is performed by the motor. We
would not object to the tax on that basis,
but as it is at the moment it appears to be
absolutely unjust. I compliment the right
hon. Gentleman on the very reasonable
statement he has placed before the House.
I hope in his next Budget in respect of
income and expenditure he will keep in remembrance the suggestions made here this
evening.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance (Amendment) Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): This Unemployment Insurance
Bill, No. 2, which I have the honour to bring
before the House to-day for Second reading,
is a very simple measure, notwithstanding the
far-reaching importance of the great social
problem with which it deals. Hon. Members
will remember that, when this House rose on
the 5th July last, the Imperial Government
had not made up its mind as to what it proposed to do in regard to the third and fourth
special periods in the Unemployment Insurance Act which was passed at the beginning
of the present year. It was felt by hon.
Members generally that the matter might become urgent during the time that this House
was not sitting, and, therefore, in an informal
way, they gave me power to follow on parallel
lines with whatever was done at Westminster.
Acting upon that expressed wish of this
House, I arranged to follow exactly on the
lines adopted by the Imperial Parliament,
with the result that I increased the fifteen
weeks' benefit period so payable to twentytwo weeks, and reduced the gap period from
eight weeks to one week. This Bill, in the
first instance, gives statutory authority to the
action which I took at that time in connection
with this matter.
Hon. Members will also probably be aware
of the fact that a few weeks ago it was
brought before my notice by several very important deputations that a very great hardship would be inflicted upon certain covenanted persons owing to the fact that for them
there would be a gap period of seven weeks
at the end of their twenty-two weeks' continuous benefit. I was able to arrange, on
behalf of the Government, that four weeks
would be transferred from the fourth special
period to the third special period, and that
arrangement, I think, eased the situation to
1003 Unemployment Insurance Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Andrews].
a considerable extent and lessened the hardship which these covenanted persons would
At the same
ctherwise have had to bear.
time, it has not cost the Fund anything appreciable. There may be a small item for
interest, but that is all the additional financial liability which will be placed upon the
Fund. This Bill will also give statutory
authority to that action.
In the third place, it deals with the situation
which may arise during the coming months.
The Imperial Government-if there is an
Imperial Government-at the moment has
not decided whether or not they are going
to make any changes in the Act of 1922 in
regard to the fourth special period. and this
Bill will give me power-of course in consultation with my colleagues-to follow along
the lines which the Imperial Government
take, if they are in a position to take any
action at all. If they do not take any
action, it will be left for us as a Government
to decide how we are going to deal with the
matter.
From an administrative standpoint there are
considerable difficulties in reference to these
Unemployment Acts, because at the same
time we are administering the Act of 1920
which deals mainly with covenanted persons,
while under the Acts of 1921 and 1922 we are
dealing with a great many more persons who
are brought into insurance, and who obtain
free benefit. or uncovenanted benefit as it
is called, owing to the exceptional circumstances arising from the industrial depression through which this, and
other, country is passing at the present
time.
every
Some hon. Members may wonder how it
is that this Government follows, in what
may be called a somewhat slavish way, in
the footsteps of the Imperial Government in
this as well as in some other matters. After
all, we all want to be considered part of
Great Britain, and we are not above following a good example. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Besides, there are other very important considerations which should not be lost
sight of. First of all, I am sure that every
Member of this House desires that the
people here should not be worse treated than
their brothers and sisters across the
Channel. In the second place, I am sure
it is also generally recognised that if we
were to attempt, for a time at any rate, to
do better for them, we would be thereby
attracting a great many unemployed visitors
from Great Britain, and probably also from
the Free State, to come and settle in our
midst to obtain these better conditions.
There is another serious matter which I
feel I ought to refer to in this connection:
that while in Great Britain at the present
time the contributions are sufficient to meet
the benefits payable, we are unfortunately
continuing to pledge the future to an extent
of between £50,000 and £60,000 per month.
That is due to this cause. It is true that
in some of the large cities in Great Britan
unemployment exists to an even more serious
extent than it exists here, but after all, we
cannot compare city with city-we must
take area with area-and in Great Britain
the average they are dealing at the
present time with 12.2 per cent. of unemployment amongst insured persons, while in
Northern Ireland we are obliged to deal with
20.22, or a difference against us of rather
over 8 per cent. That is, as I have said, a
serious matter, the importance of which I
am certain hon. Members will recognise.
Therefore, we are pledging the future to a
greater extent even than they are doing at
Westminster.

I would like to refer to another aspect
of this
Our Government
content to deal with this subject
by paying benefits to unemployed persons.
What as far as possible we want to obtain
for our people is work-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and that is, I think I am right in saying, beyond the shadow of a doubt what the
vast majority of our people desire. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) But the difficulty
which we find here is really an international
difficulty at the present time, and that is
to find work to keep our people going.
often I am asked in the streets and elsewhere
"Why not wind up this unemployment benefit
business altogether?" Well, my answer invariably has been this: Let us find employment
for our people, and unemployment benefit will
automatically end. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) In this connection, as I have said,
our Government are doing all they can. The
Ministry of Commerce has taken a very deep
and a very keen interest in the revival of
trade, and I am sure our whole community
greatly appreciates the efforts they have made
in connection with the United States Tariff
Bill, which has created such a serious position
for our linen trade in the North of Ireland
during the last few months. Personally
speaking I am very hopeful that the worst
of our industrial crisis is past. I remember
the figures-I do not think I will ever forget
them-when I was appointed Minister of
Labour, now more than a year ago. At that
time there were totally unemployed in Northern Ireland about 78,000 persons. On the 1st
January, when we took over, the figure had
fallen to about 58,000 persons totally unployed, and to-day, I am glad to say, it is
rather below 47,000. Of course 47,000 totally
unemployed is a huge total for an area such
1065 Unemployment Insurance Bill- 18 OCTOBER 1922

Second Reading.
as ours, the seriousness of which, I can assure
the House, I do not underestimate. However,
it is satisfactory to feel that trade is reviving
and that the position, at any rate, is not
as serious as it used to be.
There is another way in which the Government are trying to do what they can for
our unemployed persons, and with the permission of the House I would like to refer
to it. We are providing relief schemes both
for this city and for the Six Counties, and
owing to the influence and exertions of our
Prime Minister we received from the Imperial
Government the very substantial sum, as
hon. Members know, of £500,000. In addition
to that this House voted £50,000 for relief
works-or, as I would prefer to call them,
assisted schemes of public utility-in the Six
Counties. This work is being carried on, and
already we have been able to obtain, with
the help of our public bodies not only
throughout the Six Counties, but also in the
city of Belfast, work amounting to the very
substantial total of between £900,000 and
£1,000,000. I would like to say that I know
perfectly well-probably nobody feels it
more than I do-that the administration in
connection with these reliet schemes is a particularly difficult and thorny path to have to
tread, because, while it is perfectly true that
those who receive work under these schemes
are satisfied provided the conditions of employment are reasonable, it is also true that
the vast majority of our unemployed, for
whom we have not been able to find work,
are naturally-very naturally-doubly disappointed. We have all, if I may presume to
say so, got to take a long view and a broad
view of this problem. We have got to emember who these men are whom we are
striving to help. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) First of all there is the ex-Service
man, to whom this country owes a debt
which can never be repaid; then there
is the expelled worker, who naturally wants
back to his old employment; and then, in
the third place, there are a great many
tradesmen, who for the time being are
obliged to exchange the chisel and the hammer for the shovel and the pick, and who
are naturally very disappointed with their
position at the present time. In the administration of these funds not only have I received very valuable help from my very taithful staff at the Ministry of Labour, but I also
want to say that I feel very deeply indebted
to the Advisory Committee, which was called
into being in order to help me to disburse
these vast sums. On that Committee we have
capitalists and Labour representatives, we
have Protestants and Catholics working together in friendly co-operation for the benefit
of the whole community, and I do hope
earnestly that that spirit will be fostered and
extended in our midst, for I believe I am expressing the feelings of every hon. Member
when I say that Ulster will not be able to
reach the full measure of her share of returning commercial prosperity unless our
ways are ways of reasonableness and our
paths are paths of peace. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I beg to move.
