in connection with the peace of our city that
our young men should be taken off the streets
and given some useful work. I hope before
this House rises to-day we will have a satisfactory answer from the right hon. Gentleman and his Department that something wit
be done in the way of bringing work of this
nature to the city.
Mr. DUFF: I do not know that the
remarks which have been made by the last
three hon. Members have a real reference to
the Bill under discussion, but as a member of
one of the public Boards which are making
very serious and earnest attempts to work
with the Ministry of Labour with a view to
lessening unemployment I think I have a
right perhaps to ask one of two questions.
My colleague in East Belfast (Mr. Donald)
has, I presume, with a certain amount of
responsibility made the statement that if
£100,000 is guaranteed to shipbuilders in the
City of Belfast that will at once secure the
employment of 5,000 men in the shipyards.
Now I do not wish in any way to cast any reflections whatever on the remarks made in
this House, but if the Member for East
Belfast is in a position to guarantee the
truth of such a statement then he ought
to get busy at once and see that that state
ment is brought before the proper authorities.
Mr. DONALD: I do not wish to interrupt
my hon. Friend, but a deputation, I understand, met the Prime Minister and the
Government from the Shipbuilding Federation
on this very question.
Mr. DUFF: I do not deny that for one
moment, but as a man interested in Belfast
and knowing the number of unemployed here,
and as a member of a public Board who
knows the great difficulty of getting schemes
afloat on a business basis that will not
ultimately be a very heavy burden on the
backs of the ratepayers of Belfast, I say
if the Member for East Belfast can guarantee
that by a dole or a guarantee he does not
describe the guarantee, whether it is a gift
or a guarantee-but I will assume that he
weighed his words when he came here before
us-to appeal to us if by a guarantee of
£100,000-which I suppose is a mere bagatelle
in the turnover of the shipyards of Belfastif by any Ministry or Parliament
guaranteeing £100,000 it will ensure the employment of 5,000 additional men in the
shipyards then he has before him one of the
greatest services he has ever rendered to
the City of Belfast. And if he will concentrate on that one point until he gets to
the bottom of it--if it has any bottom-
(Laughter) then he will be doing a very great
service not only to his constituents but to
every public man and to every earnest-minded
citizen in Belfast. But on the contrary if
he is not in a position practically to prove
and guarantee the truth of the statement
then I appeal to him in the interests of the
peace of the City not to come and make
such statements from a privileged position
in this House.
Dr. MORRISON: I would like to make a
remark or two on this question, and I think
that on the Second Reading you are allowed
a certain amount of latitude. The last
speaker thought the area of discussion was
narrowed. I understood that on the Second
Reading we could go into a fair amount of
discussion. I would like in the first place
to try to direct the Members of the House to
a fact that up till now seems to have escaped
the attention of this House-that there are
other sections of the community as well as
Labour who deserve consideration, and that
there are other portions of our Six County
area than Belfast. Now I think that these
are two things that should be considered.
I think that up till now from certain clearly
defined causes Labour has been stressed. A
large burden is borne by other sections of
the community that have not been stressed.
I listened to the painful stories about
starvation of children in Belfast, and
confess I have very great difficulty
in believing or swallowing statements
like that. I have looked up, since
I first got in the way of these things,
to that modern institution, the Belfast Board
of Guardians. I think the Belfast Board of
Guardians does its business in a way that
has made it remarkable among poor-law
institutions. I saw not very long since, and
I
1073 Unemployment Insurance Bill- 18 OCTOBER 1922

Second Reading.
it struck me, that they granted 25/- a week
outdoor relief to one family, counting at the
rate of 5/- per child. I am aware that they
have relieving officers, and you have intelligent people in Belfast who know that they
can get relief, and for a man to stand up
and tell me seriously that a child is dying
from starvation in Belfast is to put a tax
on my credulity that is, I must say, too great.
This unemployment benefit, which
Minister for Labour has been explaining to
us to-day, is, I think, a very necessary and
very wise provision on the part of the Government. He says it can only be wound up
when employment is plentiful and when
there is work for every man and that it
will only stop then.
the
I venture to dissent from that. I state
here and I know that I am incurring a
certain amount of responsibility and criticism-I state here that in my opinion this
unemployment insurance--and in the opinion
of a great many men amongst whom I have
included myself-has created a new class who
will live on the unemployment doles. I am
not making any charge against decent working men; I am making a charge against a
class that is being created by these unemployment doles, and who do not want to work
and are perfectly satisfied to live on these
doles We have reached this stage in the
humanitarian provision for the necessities of
the poor that we have passed certain fundament laws that govern our attitude; and
one of these laws is that the producer of
wealth, the creator of the State, should be
the first charge on that State. Everybody
admits that that is so. We act on it in
diffe nt Parliaments and different laws that
deal with economic questions. The second
fund mental law is that the State should
do for the people only what the people cannot do for themselves and to stop there.
Now I should like to ask what has occurred
in this country. The old beggar we used
to see wandering about is gone, but his or
her place is being taken in the country
towns and in the country districts by men
who live on unemployment benefit, by men
who claim from the National Insurance Act
benefit that they are not entitled to receive,
by men who have been in the Army and
have got real or imaginary diseases that
would not prevent them from working if
they chose, but who make a special system
of this and are able to get a living out of
it without working, by people who defraud
the Old Age Pensions Act and have property
while they are getting the pension-property
amounting perhaps to £500 or £1,000, and
they draw the pension. These things are bad;
I
they are injurious to any community.
think it is necessary that somebody should
protest against it. This course is injurious
to the deserving working man and to the
deserving poor personally. They are a charge
on trade, a charge on industry. Take for
instance what happens in my own district.
I have this from respectable working men
who can testify to the facts. A man in that
district is able by special employment to earn
£9 a week, and on Monday morning when
he begins his second week's work he has to
borrow enough money to get a refresher from
the public-house before he tackles his job.
They told me of a man who went to receive
a gratuity from the employment bureau. He
got £2 10s. for his weekly dole.
He may
have had some from something else than
from unemployment, but he got from public
funds £2 10s. He had a child waiting by
his side. He gave that child £1 to take home
to keep the house. The other 30/- he spent
in the public-house. A ship coming in to
discharge a cargo in that little port, I am
told by workmen in the town, employs men,
and the workers spend £50 of that in the
public-house for every ship that comes in
to have a cargo discharged
All this proves that strict administration
is necessary. But you must set a limit to
this expenditure if possible. The hon. Member for Derry told us here, and I could
hardly credit it, that Irregulars who were
fighting in the Irish Republican Army came
in regularly to Derry City, and got their
unemployment benefit. I have since heard
through independent sources that he was
strictly accurate in that statement. Things
like that are going on over the whole country.
It is injuring the ratepayer, injuring industry, injuring the working classes themselves. I for one in the interests of the
taxpaying community who belong neither to
Capital nor to Labour, hope that the administration of this Act will be done so
carefully that these frauds will be limited
and finally eliminated.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr. Gordon):
No real arguments have been put forward by any of the speakers against
the Second Reading of this Bill, but
several observations have been made by
Members who have spoken on the floor of
this House, and I think it would be necessary
that I should offer some correction, more
especially to the hon. Member for the
University who has just sat down. During
the course of his observations he stated that
unemployment insurance was creating a new
class, a class of workless men, and from his
experience he knew of one man who received

£2 10s. a week from public funds. Did I

from Unemployment Insurance?
Dr. MORRISON: I did not. I made that
clear. From public funds.
Mr. GORDON: If he received it from the
Unemployment Insurance Fund I do not think
that any Member of this House would raise
any objection, because in order to obtain
such an amount of money it would be absolutely essential that he should be possessed
of 30 children. The hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) during the course of
his remarks suggested that the Minister for
Labour should do his utmost in order to
create more employment for the unemployed
and to use his influence with the Board of
Guardians with a view to getting relief
granted to these workless men who had exhausted trade union funds and possibly had
exhausted the little store of money at their
disposal to keep them on a rainy day.
I should like to inform the Member for
North Belfast (Mr. M'Guffin) that the Board
of Guardians appeared before the City Council yesterday, to confer with them with re
gard to the unemployment and distress that
exist in the city of Belfast. Several deputations representing the Trade Union world.
appeared before the Minister of Labour and
the Minister suggested what course they
should adopt and expressed his absolute
sympathy with the many who found themselves in a condition of destitution. My hon.
Friend the Member for North Belfast (Mr.
M'Guffin) stated that he and the Member for
East Belfast (Mr. Donald) and the Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Burn) appeared before
the Board of Guardians to emphasise the
necessity of giving greater relief to those
destitute men and women who are out of
work through no fault of their own. The
Board of Guardians, led by their chairman,
appeared before the City Council yesterday
and what was the statement the chairman
made? He stated that there was no more
destitution in the city to-day than there has
been for several years and until the Workhouse was full they would not be in a
position to do any more than they are doing
at the present moment. Therefore, according
to his statement, it will be necessary for the
destitute people referred to to become
inmates of this institution and to crowd it
out before anything tangible can be done to
alleviate the great distress amongst workless
people to-day. What has our Department
done up to the present? I would like to
say to the hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. M'Guffin) that as well as paying this
unemployment benefit we have endeavoured
with the help of the Local Authorities, the
Water Board, the Poor Law Board, and the
City Council, to create as much work as
possible, to take as many men as possible
off this fund, and consequently off the streets
of the city. Up to the moment in Belfast
and district, 61 schemes have been approved
of by the Committee which is presided over
by my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Labour. Grants have been given by that
Committee to the extent of £179,317 but the
total cost of the schemes will be £836,713.
When these schemes are properly started,
they will employ 3,683 men. To-day there is
at work on these schemes 1,036 men so that
the Minister of Labour or the Committee
that has been set up by the Ministry of
Labour is doing some real work by endeavouring to provide and find employment for
men who have none.
Some reference was made to the other
Counties, leaving aside Belfast, and I deduced from the observation made that
nothing was being done for those other
Countios. 64 schemes have been approved by
the Minister of Labour for the other Counties.
outside Belfast. The total amount of grants
sanctioned by the Minister of Labour is
£29,270. The total cost of the schemes will
be £104,267, and the maximum number of
men we hope will be employed upon these
schemes will be 1,410. To-day there are employed 300 men. I should like to say that
these works or these schemes that we have
in operation are schemes of real and permanent value to the community. What do they
consist of? They consist of dwelling-houses
for the working classes. I think that no
scheme could be introduced by the Minister
of Labour that would have greater approval
amongst working class people than this proposed construction of houses for the working
classes. There are also street and road improvements, prevention of flooding works, and
the reconstruction of water supply and tramway system. I have given these figures for
the purpose of showing that the Minister
of Labour is alive to the great need of providing work for the unemployed, and also
for the purpose of showing that our Public
Boards are also alive to the situation and
are anxious to co-operate with the Minister
of Labour in order to provide work for those
most in need of it.
I do not know what my hon. Friend the
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald) meant
when he said that we were paying out millions
of money. Did he mean millions in unemployment benefit? Does the hon. Member for
East Belfast suggest we should stop paying
unemployment benefit? He went on to state
that there are no unemployed in Germany.
There people are being kept fully employed,
and I would like to say to the hon. Member

1. Dr. CAMPBELL asked the Prime
Minister if, in view of the postponement of
the introduction of an Education Bill based
on the recommendations of the Lynn Committee, the Government can give any assurance that the financial position of properly
qualified Secondary teachers shall be no worse
for the current scholastic year than it would
have been if the recommendations of the
Interim Report had been adopted by Parlia
ment during the current Session.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
M'Keown): I have been asked to answer the
hon. Member's question. I can assure him
that the recommendations of the Lynn Committee are being considered by the Minister
in framing the Education Bill, which he proposes to bring before the House at the earliest
possible moment of the Session in the new
year. My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Education, has already given an assurance
that he will use every effort, having in view
general financial considerations and the equitable circumstances of each claim of this
nature, to secure that any benefits which may
accrue to the teaching profession from the
passage of this Education Bill shall be retrospective so far as the current school year 1922-
23 is concerned. But this is a matter which
will necessarily be left to the decision of this
House, and I am, therefore, unable to give
the pledge implied in the hon. Member's question.
Mr. MARK: I would like, if possible, to
elicit a little more information on this subject. On page 53 of the Interim Report of the
Education Committee there is a recommendation which reads as follows:-
"We consider that the scales of salaries
and grants now recommended should become
operative at the beginning of the school
year 1922-23, and that Parliament should
provide such sums as may be sufficient to
raise the salaries of Intermediate teachers
to approximately similar rates for the
period of the school year that has elapsed
since 1st February, 1922, when the Minister
took over the control of education in Northern Ireland."
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member can only
ask a definite question now. If he wishes to
make a speech he must wait for the motion
for the adjournment, but if he can put it in
the form of a question he is in order.
Mr. MARK: It was necessary that I should
read that extract from the Interim Report
in order to put my question. Is it the intention of the Government to carry out that
recommendation, and if it is, will they consider the propriety of making an immediate
payment on account of the salaries so earned
as from 1st February last to alleviate the
great distress that is existing at present
amongst Secondary teachers?
Mr. DUFF: Arising out of the answer of
the right hon. Gentleman, will he undertake
before he commits the Government to the
sums recommended in the Interim Report, to
make enquiries with the object of finding out
whether those sums are greater than those
given in similar circumstances to the Secondary teachers under the Scottish Educational
Authorities?
Mr. M'KEOWN: I can only refer both hon.
Members to the first part of my previous
answer.

SUPPLY.
SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES, 1922-1923.
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
CLASS 2. No. 7.
SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £313,348 be
granted to his Majesty to complete the
sum necessary for the services of the period
ending on the 31st of March, 1923, to defray
the expenses of the Special Constabulary."
The PRIME MINISTER: It will be within
the recollection of the House that when the
Estimates were introduced in the early
part of the year I asked hon. Members to be
kind enough to defer criticism until the
autumn for many weighty reasons.
The Vote itself ought, strictly speaking,
of course, to be introduced by my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Home
Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), but when I tell
the House that the sum of money involved
here, amounting to £2,875,000 odd, is borne
entirely by the British Exchequer, and that
the cost of the whole of our Constabulary for
this year does not fall upon Ulster money or
Ulster funds in any respect, it will be realised
that, as I was instrumental in persuading the
British Treasury to grant us this sum of
money, it is more fitting that I should explain to the House exactly how matters
stand. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It does
not do to be ungracious in matters involving
such large principles and such a vast sum
of money as we are dealing with in these
Estimates, and I would like to pay tribute
to Mr. Winston Churchill especially for the
manner in which he has helped me and
helped Ulster in those matters which
materially affected our welfare. (Hon. Members: Hear hear.) I am only too sorry to
see that he has been laid aside by serious
illness just at a very critical moment in the
affairs of Great Britain. His judgment, his
tact, his patience during very long and try
ing conferences, at which I and some of my
colleagues were present, won the admiration
of all of us. I can only say that from my
heart, and give honour where I think honour
is due. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Some
may take exception to those words, but I will
say that I got more assistance from Mr.
Churchill than from some of our own
Unionist colleagues-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear)-and that, strange as it may seem, he
against whom Ulster bore so heavy a grudge
at one time, has reverted to the real heart
within the man, the heart of his father-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and I have told
him that after all there is some little benefit
in heredity. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
This sum of money, therefore, which we
discuss to-day is a sum of money which is
not only promised to us, but a sum of money
which has already been voted by the British
House of Commons, and which is to all intents
and purposes in the Treasury of my right hon.
Friend beside me (Mr. Pollock); so that there
can be no doubt, no question as to its availability for this particular purpose without
costing the Ulster people one single shilling
above what appears here on the Estimates.
I would like to clear away some of those
misapprehensions which still exist regarding
a portion of this Vote. May I ask hon.
Members not to pay very much attention
to Page 2, which classifies the Vote in a
different manner to the way in which it is
laid out on the subsequent pages and summarised more readily for us to be able to
discuss it. With regard to the first item-the
Military Adviser's staff, consisting to a large
extent of persons who came over here, and
not of what are called pure Ulstermen-I
would like to make only a very short comment.
There should be no antipathy towards those
gentlemen and officers-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear)-none, because they came over here
at my invitation. They did not thrust themselves upon us, but they came at my invitation
specially to assist Ulster during one of her
gravest crises, and it was only natural that
the people of Ulster at that time were in a
better position to judge of the value of their
services than perhaps to-day when, the crisis
having passed, we have drifted into more
quiet, peaceful times, But is anyone prepared
to tell me that the risk is all over? Will
anyone say to me that you can scrap your
machinery, that you can take the mainspring
out of your watch and it will still go on?
That is a risk which I as Prime Minister
and Leader of the people of Ulster will not
take at the present time. There are still
looming before us several very difficult and
complicated matters. There are still looming
before us the questions of the boundary and
of the relations between the North and South
as regards the Council of Ireland; and besides
all that there is a considerable amount of
what I may call inflammable matter in our
midst, to which if any ill-advised person set
a match at any moment no one could foresee
how far-reaching might be the consequences.
I like to be prudent. I like to be very prudent where there is any danger on the
horizon. Therefore, I am asking the Committee to-day to pass these Estimates on the
broad grounds that they are the very mini-

Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
mum on which we could work this year,
and also that they did afford to Ulster in
my opinion the system of Constabulary which
was most fitted to her peculiar needs, and
to bear in mind that while I am asking for
this Vote in the ordinary way in order that
the House may have full cognisance of what
is going on, I have also to cast my eyes to the
financial year 1923-24, for we are living still
in a state of uncertainty. The attitude I take
to the British Government is this: You have
handed us over an imperfect machine; you
handed us over a country which was seething,
and which was in such a turbulent condition
that your own military forces were unable
to control it, and, therefore, it is really your
duty to supply Ulster with some substitute
for those forces by allowing her to raise her
Special Constabulary to protect the lives and
property of the people inside our area. I
have always held that that is the proper
way to approach the British Government,
and I still tell the British Government that we
do not consider that we are fully out of the
wood, and it is on those grounds I can
approach them with respect to meeting us in
some way as regards the cost of the Special
Constabulary for next year. I have, then,
dealt with the first item, namely the Military
Adviser's staff, except as regards the point
that the Military Adviser and those officers
were instrumental in securing for the benefit
of Ulster equipment to the value of at least
£850,000, which does not appear on these
Estimates at all. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It may be that some people will say
Why have twenty or thirty thousand pounds
spent upon a headquarters staff?" It is a
mere fraction of the stores and equipment
which came into Ulster here, and besides
which it is a mere fraction in connection
with the grave responsibility they had to
share with me in making such plans as would
ensure the safety of the people.
I pass over the Criminal Investigation
Department altogether. It is being reorganised, and in the coming financial year I hope
my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
will be able to give an account of that reorganisation, and how the Department stands
in relation to his office. I come, then, to the
three classes of Constabulary on which we
rely for our safety and security over and
above the splendid new force the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. The Royal Ulster Constabulary
as a Force is not involved in these Votes
to-day, but the four classes of Special Constabulary-A, B, C and C1-are involved.
May I take Class "A," and may I try to
meet some of the criticism that reaches me
from various quarters throughout the Six
Counties? You are all aware that about
the middle of the financial year the British
Government rationed us-I think that is
perhaps as good a word as I can use with
regard to the amount of money they would
allow us to spend on these particular Services
-they rationed us by first of all voting
£850,000 and then £2,000,000. They wrote to
our Government, they wrote to me, and they
finally decided that we must arrange our
forces in such a way that the cost would
not fall beyond £2,850,000. I had then, of
course, to face a very great difficulty, and
whatever may be said with regard to the arrangements that are shown in this paper
here the critics must criticise me and my
Cabinet, and must not think that orders
are given by either the Military Adviser or
the Inspector-General, or County Commandants or anyone else prejudicing the position
of those Specials who are within their area.
I take the full responsibility on my own
shoulders for the arrangements that are
made here, and when I take that responsibility I take it for this reason, that I was
the originator of the Special Constabulary
myself. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I had
nursed that Force and tried to protect that
Force, and to see fair play granted to each
of the categories "A" and "B" and "C."
Further than that, I have fought like a
tiger on the other side of the water to get
all this for the Special Constabulary and to
build it up into the splendid Force it is
to-day. Oh, how I fought and fought for
those men who are protecting our homes
and who are acting as Ulstermen in the
very best sense of the term! I fought for
them, and fought successfully, and I ask
any of the critics throughout the Six
Counties not to criticise those who really
had nothing to do with the scheme, to let
them criticise me, and let them send me
any possible modifications or improvements
in the scheme which, after consultation with
those very highly efficient officers, we had
been able to devise. Let me take a few
of those criticisms that have come to my
ears. One is that we should never have
reduced the pay-you will observe it on
Page 4 at the bottom-from 70/- to 49/- a
week. Well, to meet that criticism, let me
put it this way: I was faced first of all with
the problem confronting all of us of serious
unemployment in the Six Counties. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I was faced with the
problem that we had to have men, armed
men, trained men, those who were prepared
to take on the work of protecting where other
people were unable to do it. If we had
continued at the full rate of pay to the end
of this financial year, it is obvious that I
would have been forced into the awkward

we might have done what is customary in

day we might have gone in stages covering

been arrived at more gradually and not
in such precipitous

argument there again was
that
was threshed out by my colleagues and myself
till we came to the conclusion that if we
were to take that step once more we would
have to discharge men in order to make up
for the pay that would be paid in that period,
and it struck us that on the whole it was
fairer to make this cut which was necessary
to keep us within the £2,850,000, to make the
cut at once, to face the consequence, and at
all events be able to say, "We have got
the most of you employed, we have got most
of the benefits for all of you," rather than
having to cut down still further a Force
which we are all most anxious to maintain
both in efficiency and numbers. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That is the answer to
those who say we might have done something
to ease the situation instead of precipitously
cutting off the full number of men in one
fell blow. Then another criticism is directed
against us because they say, "Your 'A'
Special Constabulary are performing the
same work in many instances as the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, which is still at the
Desborough rates of pay." Well, first of all,
there is really this distinction, the Royal
Ulster Constabulary is to be a permanent
Force, and it is desired to attract into that
Force the very best men from any other
occupation they may be in in Ulster at the
present moment. We want the very best
men who are fit to be police constables in
the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and we do
not hesitate for a moment to take a man
who is fit for the post, even if he is one of
the best men in the yards, because we know
it is a permanent position for him for which
he is suitable, and serving in the Force he is
serving the best interests of Ulster without
doing any harm to the yards because he
makes a vacancy which can be filled by someone who possibly is not of the standard
necessary for the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
But with regard to the "A" Specials, it is
an entirely different pair of shoes. If you
have the wage with the allowances, to which
I am going to refer later, up to such a high
standard you may take men from permanent
positions in trade into the "A" Specials,
which is a blind alley-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)—and which causes such disappointment to them later on when they may
have lost their job in the yard and may have
lost their job as a Special. Therefore, it is
the height of wisdom to differentiate in that
way in order to hold up some little warning
to men who are short-sighted, and because of
the pay and conditions of the Specials they
would be wise not to give up a permanency
in order to get into the Force, which we all
know is bound sooner or later gradually to
disappear, and, I hope, to disappear with the
same honour and glory with which it has
covered itself up to the present day. This is
another very important reason why the
differentiation has been found necessary.
Again, I say that those who clamour for
bringing the pay up to the same level as the
Royal Ulster Constabulary are only doing a
disservice to some of their colleagues by
having them cut off and turned out into the
world at the present moment. Then I would
ask those critics to bear in mind that with
regard to the "A" Special Constabulary you
will observe an item of £1,052,103. If hon.
Members will turn to page 6 they will see
there the allowances that are also granted to
the "A" class. I do not desire to go through
item by item, it is very plain for anyone to
read; so that when one talks about the wages
or pay of the men being 49s a week it will
readily be seen that that is supplemented in
very many instances by those various items
here. Motor transport drivers get 2s 6d per
day up to 30th September and then 2s; motor
transport fitters, 5s per day extra, after 30th
September 4s per day; wireless operators,
2s 6d per day to 30th September, 2s from that
date onward. There are rent allowances
to the constables coming to £32,000; medical
allowances, £8,066; boot allowances, £25,252;
and there are subsistence allowances which
will be found on page 7 under a special
heading, the allowances for officers and men

Special Constabulary
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
amounting to £80,000. The rents of barracks
and compensation in respect of commandeered premises come to very nearly
£100,000; barrack furniture, £12,000; fuel,
light and water, £7,000, and so on. I do not
say for a moment that in all instances these
men have had a bed of roses, but I do say
that we have, after anxious thought and
consideration, done our very best for this
splendid Force, and I hope the critics will
take into consideration all I have said, and
they will find there are very few cases where
emergency has raised a Force of the kind
where it has been possible for a Government
to deal with them so well.
Another point I would like to make is
this: In persuading Great Britain, through
its House of Commons, where the Votes have
to be passed and Ministers sit round the
Cabinet table as we do here-in persuading
them of the necessity and justice of this
Force I have always been able to point out
the marvellous accomplishments. I do not
believe there is any part of our Empire
where you could suddenly transform such a
vast percentage of the people into armed
men, and at the end of eighteen months or
two years have such a magnificent record as
we have in the case of our Special Constabulary. Therefore, in fighting their
battles, as I shall do before the Cabinet for
the coming year, I trust I shall be able to
approach them with the same clean record
that I have been able to do on every previous
occasion, and I have no fear on the subject.
I now come to Class B. Everybody knows
the B's. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Everybody praises the B's. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I have not heard in our broad
acres a complaint against the B's since they
were first formed. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). They have been simply magnificent,
and everyone knows how well they have
adapted themselves to a very peculiar
situation. They are the holders of our outposts. They are always on the spot. They
know everything that is going on in their
locality. They are ready at a moment's
notice to take up any duty which they are
called upon to do in order to protect what,
after all, is the heart of Ulster, and that is
the boundaries of Ulster. No praise is too
high for them, and therefore when one looks
at the Estimate that is here, a modest Estimate-it has to be looked for on
two pages, on page 5 and on page 6-the
item that is really worth considering is the
£220,000 for the year's Service.
Page 5 is for those who are fully mobilised
and become members of the R.U.C., with
full responsibility for the time, but we have
actually got for the sum of £220,000 the men
upon the borderland and in our interior who
are best fitted to deal with a certain class of
disturbance in our midst. They have performed their duty at what I call the minimum compensation, and I believe I am right
in saying here that with that spirit that
animates them, if they were asked to do the
same duty for nothing at all they would only
be too delighted to do it for the honour of
Ulster. I believe in my heart if there were
no money forthcoming they would be delighted to do the work they have done without any compensation or reward. I trust,
however, that the same remarks regarding the
A's are applicable to the B's, and that I will
be able to convince His Majesty's Government of the wisdom, not altogether for the
sake of Ulster but for the sake of the Empire,
that there should be no more stirring up of
trouble which only spreads elsewhere, which
only causes a conflict in other parts of
the Empire and in other parts of the world,
that there is really no protection against that
except having a firm, strong, well-disciplined
force such as comprised in these three catagories.
With regard to Class C, I need not touch
upon that Class, which is well known to
everyone as merely the old men, if I may
say, of the Force, or the specially circumstanced men who require protection and are
not physically or otherwise able to go out
to assist in the common danger. I come to
Class C1. Now, C1 is, in my opinion, very
necessary to complete the picture. You have
your mobile A's, the A's who are SO
staunchly helping their brothers of the
R.U.C., to maintain our barracks at full
strength, and you have our B's always on
duty and engaged in civil work. The C's
have a more-shall I call it-military formation, although under the same jurisdiction
as the rest of the Constabulary, and under
my right hon. Friend the Minister of Home
Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates).
The C's have been conceived because there
is always a feeling in my mind that perhaps
our military would be taken away, and that
having no military we have no military
formation to take their place; and the C's
are ready and willing, most of them ex-
Service men, to undergo the fortnight's
training and the drills which take place from
time to time in order to perfect themselves
in case there is a withdrawal of troops from
our area. Just picture the anxiety quite recently with regard to the Near East. You
can imagine the Commander-in-Chief in that
theatre of war calling out urgently for more
troops and more troops if it had been necessary to have gone to war? The people of

Special Constabulary.
19 OCTOBER 1922

Ulster, knowing them as I do, would have
said, Well, we will look after ourselves on
behalf of the Empire, and if the British Government requires the troops here they shall
have them." Then we were bound to picture
the gap that would be left by the depletion
from our shores of those fine regiments that
have done so much for us during the past
18 months.
The C's fit into that picture most accurately. They are, of course, more readily got
together and controlled in the largest
centres than in the scattered country areas,
but wherever they have been organised I can
only say that the same good name and reputation have followed them as the other catagories of the Specials, and I am most hopeful
that this scheme, which up to the present
has been so fitting for our needs, may be perpetuated sufficiently long to see us over every
danger. I will, as long as I am needed, not
allow any man to say when that danger is
over except myself. I am the only judge.
I am splendidly advised by my right hon.
Friends here, but, as you know, the final
decision with regard to a matter of such
supreme importance must rest upon the
Prime Minister for the time being.
Until I am perfectly satisfied that the South
of Ireland means business, besides all the
talk that is going on, and proposes to deal
with the miscreants in the way we have dealt
with them here, and brings them before the
bar of justice; until it has secured stable
conditions so that we are able to talk to them
on the same plane as we are happy to find
ourselves here to-day; until they have settled
those crucial points that affect not only
Southern Ireland but Northern Ireland;
until they have thoroughly satisfied the
British Government that they mean to remain loyal and true inside the ambit of the
Empire; and until we can really see all these
things, not only spoken about and hoped for,
but actually accomplished, I certainly will
never say that Ulster is in a sufficiently
satisfactory position to do away with the
magnificent Force which I ask this Committee to support by passing the Estimates
to-day. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. DONALD: Dealing with this Vote,
may I take my mind back to this sum of
money when it was before the House in
another place, due to a request that the right
hon. Gentleman the Prime Minister made
to the Imperial Government. When I take
my mind back to that Supplementary Vote
in the Imperial House, and think of the
opposition set up by the hon. Member for
Central Hull and his friends, I think it is
sufficient justification for me to give my
sanction to this Vote. In looking over the
whole situation I have come to this conclusion, that even if it was an experiment it was,
in my judgment, a very cheap experiment,
when we take into consideration the state of
the country outside the Six Counties. The
plan adopted by the Prime Minister and our
Government has turned out to be very economical. What is the state on the other side
of the Six Counties? Why, I read the other
day that the Criminal Injury Bill is going
to be 25 or 30 millions.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: It is far more.
Mr. DONALD: I am putting it very
moderately. I have an idea of what it will be
when it comes to the Imperial House for
their sanction, and what will be said. What
I want to make out is this, that if our
Government, for the sake of a few millions,
have, by this method of setting up a voluntary
Force, put the Six Counties into such a position that people can go about their daily
avocations, then I say they have done a great
service not only to the Six Counties but to
the Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
May I say that I think this sum is not
enough, and for this reason? My right hon.
Friend should have kept on all the "A"
Specials, and made the Imperial Parliament
pay for it, in view of the fact that here in
our midst we have law and order. I hope
he will put that argument up to them again.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps my hon.
Friend will not object to me intervening at
this stage. After all I am not a Member of
the Imperial Parliament. My hon. Friend
(Mr. Donald) and several other hon. Members

I have got £2,850,000 single-handed out of the

I would ask my hon Friend just to put on

but I know, as Prime Minister, a little

Mr. DONALD: If I was not able to get
these millions the Prime Minister referred
to at any rate I have drawn from him a
very important statement. I do not wish in
any way to cause any alarm or misconception.
I will proceed further to develop my argument by asking the Prime Minister if he
could not strike a further reduction in the
pay of the Special Constabulary and thus
retain more men in the Force. That was
the suggestion I was going to make to the
Prime Minister. The Prime Minister said
before that the pay was reduced from 70/-
to 49/- a week. The right hon. Gentleman
knows that from the very beginning I have
always said that the pay was too high. I
maintain still that these men should never
have had 70/- a week. The reply of the
Government was that it was laid down for
them and they did not fix the figure. We
have now arrived at the time when we can
fix the figure. Even 49- will practically be
the wages of a skilled worker in the near
future, and I do not think the Special
Constabulary would have any grievance if
you struck another reduction and thus tried
to keep a few more men on for a further
period. That is my suggestion. They now
have 49 a week, plus an allowance, which
is a considerable amount. A skilled worker
has no "plus" on his 49/-. I say quite
frankly that the Government is justified in
asking for this sum. I know the Prime
Minister is a very good beggar, and if he
will go back again and ask for a further
sum I hope to be in my place to help to
fight for the money he asks for. I know
quite well what is at the back of the Prime
Minister's mind. It is also at the back of
my mind, and that is that we have not yet
passed through the danger zone. I know
that perfectly well. This country, as well
as Great Britain, is passing through a very
trying period. We do not know what the
composition of the next Government is going
to be, and we should hold on until we see
what it is going to be and not make any
reduction in our forces in the meantime. I
do not think there is any room for criticism.
I could criticize some of these salaries but
the Prime Minister has stated clearly that
the money is coming from the Imperial
Government, although I must point out that
it is coming from the taxpayers both in
Great Britain and the Six Counties. They
have all got to pay into the same till. However, in view of the condition of things I
am prepared to give my vote in favour of
these Estimates, and I do not wish further
to criticise anything they contain. It is an
economical proposition that if we are able to
keep our country in a peaceful condition by
the expenditure of this sum we should not
hesitate to sanction it, but when it comes to
the question of asking for four or five times
this amount I shall probably vote against it.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I do not rise for the
purpose of offering any criticism, because
I do not think I am in a position to criticize
the admirable statement made by the Prime
Minister. I think it was a compliment to
the House, and one that the House appreciates, that the Minister of Home Affairs
saw fit to ask the Prime Minister to present
this Vote. It is a very formidable Estimate,
and it is not possible for us to criticize it
in detail. We can only rely on the wisdom
of the Cabinet when they say they endorse
it because it is indispensable and necessary
for the establishment of peace and of law
and order in our midst. We are quite entitled to criticize the Vote if we feel inclined
to do so, and we are not justified in refraining from offering observations upon it on
the ground that we have not got to meet
the bill. I am very much afraid lest it may
become necessary to establish such a system
as this for the permanent protection of our
own area. I would not like it to have to
be done on so large a scale, but if it is
necessary the House has already subscribed
to the statement of the Prime Minister that
he would vote to the very last penny in

to know that the Vote will be modified in

We are not going to look upon this as a

recognise that peace and order have been
established, and we hope that will be permanent, but if fresh measures are necessary I
think you may rely on this House to vote
any expenditure that is necessary.
is nothing so important to us as the maintenance of peace, and if peace and order

19 OCTOBER 1922
I do not think this Government is in any
way responsible for the condition of affairs
that makes this Vote necessary. It is a
legacy that has been handed down to us and
a burden that has been imposed on the
Government by the condition of affairs that
existed when the Government came
into
power. For that we have no responsibility
whatever. I am very much of the opinion
that what is put down to religious, and even
political differences is not after all attributable to that cause. I think we are still
suffering in a moral sense from the aftermath
of the War, and I think the prodigality that
took place during the War has been imitated
on a smaller scale in other places throughout
the world, and even in our own country. I
have the idea that if those who are in spiritual
authority would administer an admonition to
those who are under their care and raise
them to a higher ideal of moral duty something could be accomplished which even the
power of the law or military force would
never be able to effect. Scientists tell us we
have been evolved from a lower to a higher
existence. I suppose it is true in the moral
sense, and I am afraid that the sad spectacle
of murder and outrage that we are looking
on to-day is, as it were, a reversion to type.
I hope it is not so, but very much depends
on those people who are in a position of
most influence to see that such wrong ideas
as obtain at the moment in society shall
quickly disappear. I do not think there
is anything in connection with this Vote
that we are in a position to criticize, and
I can only say that it is with the greatest
possible pleasure that I accord my assent to
the Vote on the ground that the object for
which it was created has been abundantly
realized.

PAPER PRESENTED TO PARLIAMENT.
Ministry of Finance-Regulations made by

Issue, and Cancellation of Northern Ireland
Treasury Bills under Sundry Acts. (By
Act.) To be printed.
Oral Answers to Questions.
R.I.C. AND R.U.C.
1. Mr. GRANT (for Mr. M'Guffin) asked the
Minister for Home Affairs if he can state
the number of men of the late R.I.C. who,
having refused transfer to the R.U.C., have
since their disbandment been admitted to
the latter Force, also the reason of their
admission?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): 28 Members of the
R.I.C. who withdrew their applications for
the R.U.C. have since their disbandment
been admitted to the latter Force. Each
application was thoroughly investigated, and
in no case was any applicant accepted unless
some special and exceptional grounds for his
withdrawal were disclosed, and that his
former Officers recommended his readmission.
SUPERVISOR OF TYPISTS.
2. Mr. GRANT (for Mr. M'Guffin) asked
the Minister of Finance if an appointment
as Supervisor of Typists in the Northern
Government has recently been made, and, if
so, can he state the name of the person
appointed, the salary attached to the
position, and the nature of the duties to be
discharged?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer to the first part of the
question is in the negative. There is no
such position as Supervisor of Typists in the
Northern Government.
The second part of the question does not,
therefore, arise.
GOVERNMENT STAFF LIST.
3. Mr. GRANT (for Mr. M'Guffin) asked the
Minister of Finance if he will present the
House with the Government Staff List, giving the name, position, and salary of each
Member.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have considered the request of the hon. Member, and am of opinion
that I would not be justified in authorising
the expenditure involved by the compilation
and printing of the List in question. I am
influenced in this decision by the fact that
a full List of posts and salaries attached
thereto is included in the Estimates already
presented to the House.
Facilities will, however, be given to any
hon. Member to inspect the Records kept in
the Establishment Branches of the various
Ministries, and I hope that any hon. Members interested will avail themselves of these
facilities rather than press the Government
to incur expenditure which scarcely appears
warranted.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Uniformity of Laws Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed, "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
This Bill, as its title shows, is intended to
apply to Northern Ireland certain Acts already passed by the Parliament of the United
Kingdom. I am sure that so far as general
legislation is concerned we desire to keep
abreast, as it were, with the Imperial Parliament, and accordingly we thought it was
proper that where certain Acts had passed
which but for the separation of Ireland from
Great Britain and the separation of North
from South would probably have been made
applicable to Ireland, these Acts, or some of
them at least, should be applied to Northern
Ireland. Accordingly the Bill before this
House provides that certain Acts which appear in the Schedule, and which are already the law of the land so far as Great
Britain is concerned, should be applied to
Northern Ireland. I do not suggest for a
moment that we should slavishly follow
Great Britain in everything in the way of
legislation, but at the same time where we
find an Act which probably would have been
applied to this country had it not been for
the changes consequent on the Government of
Ireland Act, I think we should as far as
possible try to adopt that legislation, and the
Bill before the House is intended to carry
out that object in so far as it goes.
I know that there are other Acts which hon.
Members perhaps think ought to have been
included in this Bill. We have considered a
XXX

Acts shall have effect as Acts passed by the

of this Act. The first Schedule deals with a
matter connected with the prosecution of
women who had unlawfully caused the death

The Second Schedule deals with the Gaming

up
transactions, but I think I may sum

of 1835 and under certain decisions which

and after the cheque had been paid out of

It was held that if
Sutter against Lewis.
I, a person who had made a bet and lost,
paid a cheque over to a bookmaker, and
even though the cheque may have passed
through the Banks and through a number
of hands, still if it can be proved that the
bookmaker ultimately got the money placed
to his credit I should be allowed to turn
round and sue the bookmaker to get back the

to be put an end to. Once the money passes,
whether it is money or whether it passes by

other words, you may agree with the thing
in principle or you may disagree, but when
a man has paid money for betting transactions he must stand or fall by them. Consequential upon that, suppose, in a case 1
put, I had not been a thrifty young man and
I was, shall I say, scattering my patrimony,
and that I had trustees who were looking

Britain abolishes that state of affairs, and,
therefore, relieves trustees from the perilous

The Third Schedule is "An Act to amend

regulations for the making and sale of bread.
and for preventing the adulteration of meal,
flour, and bread." This Act was passed in
July last by the Imperial Parliament.
was passed as an agreed Measure, and its

tration of the law. By the Bread Act of

Second Reading.
1838 it was unlawful to use for bakery
purposes that which we are all now very
well acquainted with, namely self-raising
flour. The Act was frequently broken and
the breach of it was very frequently winked
at. The object, as I say, of that Bread
Act was to prevent certain adulterations of
wheat flour, to prevent wheat flour from being
adulterated by certain other cereals to the
prejudice and danger of persons who deal
in it. That position altered when selfraising flour was invented. We know selfraising flour is used in practically every
household and every baker's shop. Under
the Bread Act of 1838 it was adulteration
and the use of it was illegal. The idea is
to wipe away that anomaly. The practice
has been in existence for a number of years,
which the law says is illegal, but which in
reality is not treated as being illegal, and
accordingly the Bill before the House will
remove this illegality. At the same time it
safeguards the public against adulteration,
because it empowers the Ministry of Home
Affairs to prescribe regulations under the
Public Health Regulations (Food) Act, 1907,
preventing or restricting the use of ingredients which might be deleterious to the
public. Similarly, powers were vested by the
Act and Schedule in the Ministry of Health
in Great Britain, and the Ministry of Home
Affairs will keep in close touch with the
Ministry of Health in Great Britain.
A
The next Schedule is "An Act to provide
for the better protection of the public in
relation to the sale of tea." I do not think
this requires very many observations.
Select Committee sat in Great Britain in
the year 1914, and this Sale of Tea Act was
carried in the Imperial Parliament as an
agreed Measure. Tea used to be sold in very
heavy paper packets, the net weight of the
tea being less than what was paid for. It
was held in numerous places where attempts
were made to convict the seller of the toa
for obtaining money by false pretences that
the only remedy open to the buyer was by
civil action. That was a very unsatisfactory
state of affairs, because it was not worth
any particular person's while to bring an
action to recover, say, the value of onesixteenth or one-quarter of an ounce of tea.
Accordingly the Tea Act, which was passed
as an agreed Measure, deals with this state
of affairs and makes certain consequential
regulations which, I believe, will be of great
benefit to the public.
The next one is the Fifth Schedule. This
is "An Act to make better provision for
the prevention of fire in premises where raw
celluloid or cinematograph film is stored or
used." The object of this Act was to give
effect to the recommendations of a Special
Committee which sat in the year 1913 regarding the question of the public safety
in shops and other places in which celluloid
films were used or kept. The effect of that
Act passed in Great Britain was to apply
permanently certain Regulations which were
made under the Defence of the Realm Act
for securing safety in connection with cellu
loid. The Act which is now before the House
is identical with the Imperial Act, subject,
of course, to the necessary modifications to
make it applicable to Northern Ireland. It
provides for the registration of premises in
which raw celluloid or cinematograph films
are stored and for the inspection of those
premises by the Local Authorities. It empowers the Local Authorities to require
reasonable means of escape in case of fire
from such premises, and also prescribes certain conditions of construction and situation
so as to obviate the danger of fire to adjoining premises. The Act also prescribes certain
precautions which must be observed in the
workrooms and store-places. The Bill does
not relate to cinemas. The reason of that is
that they are already dealt with under the
Act of 1909. The expenses of the Local
Authorities are provided for by the payment
of fees. Those are to be prescribed by the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and they are to
be payable by the occupiers of the premises
involved. These fees have already been fixed
in England and Scotland at two guineas a
year by Order of the Ministry of Health
and of the Secretary for Scotland.
Now, I hope I have not detained the House
too long. I just wanted to give in the
shortest possible compass an idea of what
these various Measures are, but I would
point out to hon. Members that if we are
to have a particular Schedule we must have
the Schedule, the whole Schedule, and
nothing but the Schedule. In other words,
if we
are to have a Uniformity of Laws

corresponding Act will be no longer uniform
with the Act passed in Great Britain. 1
hope hon. Members, therefore, will, shall
I say, let me down as lightly as possible in

I would like to announce beforehand that
I am not in a position to accept any amendment. I beg to move.

The unfairness of the whole thing appeals
to everyone, and any man who is actuated
by, or has any sense of, justice at all revolts
against the thought of having the poor
woman in the dock, having her as a prisoner
when she is only the victim, while the real

It is obviously of practically no benefit to
reduce a woman's alleged crime from murder
to infanticide and allowing her practically to
go free if at the same time you allow the
real criminal to walk about with his hands
in his pockets sneering and laughing at the
poor woman he has landed in this plight.
I would suggest to the Attorney-General if

the English Bastardy Act which has been
in force for fifty years be simply extended
to this country. I make that appeal to the

and extended Act was being discussed in
the English House of Parliament on a comparatively recent occasion the Second reading
was carried by a huge majority, and in that
discussion the sturdiest supporters of that

this beneficial legislation which had existed

got beyond the Second reading in England,
will be carried to perfection at the next
Sitting of Parliament. I have a pledge from
the Minister of Home Affairs here on behalf
of the many social reformers who are interested in this question that if this Bill does
not mature he will bring in in our next
Session a short Bill extending the English
Bastardy Act to Northern Ireland. There
is a simple remedy. I do not know what is
in the lap of the gods with regard to English
legislation in the next Session. I do not
know who will be in office, but I know whom
I would like to see in office, and I know the
men I would like to see out of office, but
nobody can tell what may come forth as
the result of this upheaval in England.
I want the Attorney-General to take advantage of this opportunity and consent to an
extension of this Act. We have 3,000 illegitinate births in Ireland every year, and
fear that 600 or 800 of those take place in our
Six County area. I speak from practical
experience, and you may take my word for
it that the mothers have to bear the entire
support of the children. The mothers go
out to service, the children are placed with
foster-mothers, and are very often neglected,
with very serious results to their health. I
need not discuss the advantages of an extension of this measure on the lines I have
indicated. I simply appeal to the House and
to the Attorney-General to take advantage
of this Act and to extend it to Northern
Ireland. If it gives us the power to inflict
a penalty of 5s a week on the fathers of
these illegitimate children, I pledge my word
that it will reduce the number of illegitimate
births in the Six County area by a half. I
hope the House will consider this question
very favourably. I think this is a rare
opportunity of doing a good and beneficial
piece of legislation without the trouble of
introducing a Bill.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I would like to say in

My intention in rising was to draw attention to the second Schedule in the Bill. I
think it would be a great pity if the power

made whereby young fellows in their 'teens

I think the trustees should not be deprived

of discretion from forming habits of gaming.
I hope that in some way the Attorney-General will try and protect these young people
from the hands of gamesters.

that have been made by the two Gentlemen

However, this is not a Bill that is primarily
connected with illegitimacy. I think that
both the Gentlemen who have criticised the
Bill have gone on the assumption that this
abolition of the punishment of murder for
infanticide is solely confined to single women.
As a matter of fact it has a general application: it applies not only to single women but
to married women in cases of murder that
has taken place in the circumstances that
were mentioned. But the Government have
thought it better that they should await the
legislation of the Imperial Parliament with
regard to illegitimacy. The whole matter has
been very carefully considered, and we thought
it better that we should have the advantage of
the investigations that have been made on the
other side, and that we should take advantage of the Act in its final form, just as we
are doing with these Acts that have already
been passed by the Imperial Parliament.
Regarding the observations that were made
by my Friend and Colleague, the Member for
County Antrim (Mr. Crawford), on the
Gaming Act, I fear that he is under a misconception, because boys in their 'teens or

They are prevented by the Infancy Act,
which prevents anyone under the age of 21
from entering into a valid contract, of

respect of other people who have engaged in
these betting transactions during their lifetime. They have paid over money by cheque
and then, after the death of such a person,
the unfortunate executor is compelled by the
persons who are entitled to the estate in re-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 24th October, 1922.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Agriculture if he will state what are the
details of the facilities to be provided in the
City of Belfast for the convenience of those
who have business to transact with the Ministry of Agriculture, under the proposed
arrangement of offices in connection with the
various Ministries? In addition to the Conference or Committee room which, it has
been stated, will be at the disposal of the
Minister of Agriculture in Belfast, what
portion of the technical and administrative
staff of the Ministry will have permanent
offices in the City? Having regard to the
fact that the Minister of Agriculture and
Commerce will have his entire staff in connection with the Ministry of Commerce in
the City, is it not most desirable that his
entire staff in connection with the Ministry
of Agriculture should also be located in the
City?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): It is the decision of the Govern
ment that the Administrative Headquarters
of all the Ministries with the exception of
that of the Ministry of Commerce shall be
located at Stormont. In order that the convenience of the public might be met as far
as possible, it was provided that, subject to
the general decision, each Ministry was free
to establish a branch othee in the city. I
went into this aspect of the matter very
carefully and arrived at the conclusion that
in practice, a small branch office of the
Ministry of Agriculture would prove to be
merely a local telephone exchange, and that,
consequently, so far as it was intended to
meet the needs of Members of the farming
community having business to transact with
the Ministry, such an office would be of no
real convenience.
I next considered the question of having a
city office which would be fairly representative of the various departments of the
Ministry's activities, and I now give you the
factors which determined me to have no accommodation in the city other than a Conference or Committee rooms.
The varied work of the Ministry of Agriculture falls into several more or less distinct
sub-departments. Any representative office
situated in the centre of the city, to be satisfactory, must reproduce these sub-departments. This reproduction means that to a
certain extent the staff of the Ministry,
together with the files, documents, etc., must
be duplicated. Such duplication is opposed
to the interests both of efficiency and
economy.
Mr. CRAWFORD: The answer is so unsatisfactory that I would like to give notice that
I will raise this matter on the motion for
the adjournment.

Motion made and Question proposed: "That

Bill."
Mr. GRANT: I would like some information in connection with this Fourth Schedule.
Section 1, sub-section 4, says-
This section shall not apply to any sale
of less than two ounces of tea, which does
not purport to be a sale of two ounces or
more, or to any package which contains
less than two ounces of tea, and which does
not purport to contain two ounces or more.
I take it that the idea of this Bill is to
protect the poorer class of people, and there
is no provision in this Schedule whereby a
package containing two ounces or more will
be weighed in the presence of the customer.
I should like to see it laid down that the
package must be weighed in the presence of
the customer. Then Section 3 provides for
the execution of the Act by local authorities.
I want to know who will be the local authority. Will it be the Belfast Corporation
who will administer this Act? I would like
some information on that point.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
Regarding the question which the hon. Member (Mr. Grant) has raised on Section 1, subsection 4, I do not know whether he was
present yesterday when I made a statement
to the House on the Second reading of this
Bill, but I intimated that it would be absolutely impossible for us in a Bill of this
character, where we go out to assimilate the
law in Northern Ireland to the law in Great
Britain, to accept any Amendment. If in
practice it is found that provision of this
kind creates hardship then we can introduce
subsequent legislation of our own, but the
very frame of this Bill is that we wish to
adopt in Northern Ireland specific Acts which
have been passed in the Parliament of Great
Britain. Accordingly, it would be altogether
foreign to our ideas that we should first start
out by adopting these Acts and then permit
Amendments. We must either take the Act
as a whole or leave it. If there is any great
objection to any particular Act it can be left
out of the Schedule, but if it is to be left
in the Schedule it must be left in as a whole.
I think the hon. Member (Mr. Grant) may
take it from me that if when we have had
experience of the Act, it turns out that the
law needs amendment we can amend the law
as it then is by a substantive Act of our own.
As regards the second question, the local authorities would be the County and Urban
Councils. In Belfast the local authority
would be the Corporation, and in the same
way the local authorities would be the local
authorities in the ordinary sense through
the country. I do not know whether my hon.
Friend (Mr. Grant) is satisfied or not, but we
cannot, as I say, accept any amendment, the
idea underlying it being that we adopt the
legislation as passed by the Imperial Parliament in its entirety.
Mr. GRANT: I was present in the House
when the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Best)
made his statement yesterday. I have not
even suggested yet that there should be any
amendment, but the whole principle of the
Act is that down to two ounces of tea is to
bear a label showing the net weight, but
below two ounces there is no guarantee that
people are receiving the proper amount of tea,
and in a good many cases it is not weighed
up in the presence of the purchaser. I do
not think it is an argument that, because
they have omitted this in the Imperial Parliament, we should allow it to go forward
without taking notice of it. As far as the
second part of the question is concerned, I
am satisfied with the reply of my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Best).
The CHAIRMAN: I take it that the hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Grant) does not wish to
move any amendment.
Mr. GRANT: No.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw): In moving the Second Reading of
Expiring Laws Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Megaw.]
this Bill, which has already passed through
all its stages in the Senate, I wish to give a
few words of explanation to the House as to
the necessity of a Measure of this kind. It is
a procedure that is quite familiar to the
British Legislature, and an Expiring Laws
Continuance Bill passes there every year
without comment of any kind. Last year
we had no such Measure here, because we
were not functioning at the time when an
Continuance
Expiring Laws
Bill would
naturally need to be brought forward, but
the British Parliament, by arrangement
with this Government, passed a Bill that
applied their Expiring Laws Continuance
Bill to Irish measures. The practice of
having an Expiring Laws Continuance Bill
arises in this way: The Legislature, for
various reasons, comes to the conclusion that
it is unwise to give the Government full control, perhaps, over some matter of policy,
and wishes to retain that control from year
to year in its own hands; or it often is not
quite satisfied with regard to the wisdom of
any particular measure, and thinks it would
be as well to pass it through an experimental
stage before putting it upon the Statute
Book. For that reason legislation is often
passed for one year, even in the case of
measures that are intended to have a permanent character. Very often this arises by
way of compromise, but, at any rate, it is
quite a familiar method of legislation to have
certain measures passed for one year. Perhaps the best example of annual legislation
arises in respect of the Army Act in England.
The people of England, for some reason, have
a great distrust of giving the Government
permanent power over the Army, and the
result of that is that the Executive is not
entrusted with the management of the Army
for more than one year at a time. However,
the Army Act does not come within the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill, because it is
usual each year that there should be some
modification of the Act that has been passed
the year before; but in the case of a great
many of the other measures, even where the
working of the Acts has proved quite
efficient, it has been the custom to put a
number of these measures together and to
pass them without change in the form of the
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill. A great
number of those Bills arise in regard to
emergency measures. There are times when
the necessity arises for special legislation
which it is not convenient or proper to make
permanent. A good example of that is to
be found in the legislation during the war,
when 80 many emergency measures were
passed. Some of these still exist, and, indeed,
some of them are included in the Bill of
which I am now moving the Second reading.
To come to the provisions of this Bill, and
to examine them seriatim, the first Clause
refers to certain measures that have already
been passed for a year, some of them of the
nature I have already mentioned as being
originally intended to be permanent, but
where the Legislature was not quite satisfied
as to the wisdom of the measure, and so they
passed them as expiring laws year by year.
The first Clause is intended here to make a
few of those measures permanent, including
the Employers Liability Act, which
passed as far back as 1880, and which has
been included in the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill from 1880, till the present
day. Another one is the Motor Car Act,
which enables Local Authorities generally to
control the registration of motor cars and
to make regulations with regard to it. It is
now proposed by Clause 1 to make those Acts
permanent so far as Northern Ireland is
concerned.

Mr. CRAWFORD: I would like to assure
the House that in attempting this afternoon
to voice the feelings of about three quarters
of a million of people who I believe are
suffering under an injustice I am not endeavouring in any way to embarrass the Ministry
in their attempt to make such arrangements
as they think fit for carrying out the business
of this portion of the Empire. I would like
to remind the House that the farming industry is the greatest industry in Northern
Ireland. Without in any way attempting to
minimise the importance of such a thing as
the great shipbuilding concerns that reflect
so much credit on Northern Ireland, I would
like to point out that poultry and eggs alone,
which would be a very small proportion of
what is produced by the farming industry,
amount to more money than the great ship-

building industry of the City of Belfast.
would like to remind hon. Members away deep
down at the very heart of things we have
inspired authority for saying that the King
is served by the people, and it was with
great astonishment that the farming people
throughout the whole of the North read on
the 5th ult. in the public Press that for the
convenience of the public a portion of the
staffs of the Ministers of Finance, Home
Affairs, Education, Labour, and the whole of
the staff of the Ministry of Commerce would
be in the centre of the City. Notwithstanding
the fact that the farming population constituted three-quarters of the whole population of Northern Ireland there was
absolutely no mention of any convenience
being made for agriculture.
On the 6th ult., the day after that appeared,
it was intimated that the Ministry of Agriculture would have a large room in the City
for the purpose of holding conferences. Such
a thing exists already in the City, and if
the Minister of Agriculture had been trying
to manage things in as economical a way as
possible he would have known that in the
future as in the past a room occupied by the
farmers a large room for the purpose-would
be placed free and without expense at his
disposal. If they were only wanting to have
a conference room where they could meet
deputations of farmers that room could have
been had easily and without any expense at
all. It is really of great advantage to farmers
to have a room of this description. The
inference in the answer given by the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Archdale) is that it is
convenient that all papers and statistics, and
the whole of the staff, should be at Stormont.
Just think of the inconvenience that means.
The head office of the Farmers' Union is in
the City of Belfast. Any important branch
of business that they want to bring forward
before the Minister of Agriculture can only
be discussed in a conference room with the
Minister, but they would have to go to Stormont to get any information or statistics or
YYy
