Facilities for Farmers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Crawford.]
anything of that description.
Bad as that
would be for representatives of the Farmers'
Union it would be a great deal worse for any
farmer coming into the City. We must remember that the work of the Ministry of
Agriculture is not only an administrative
work but an educational work as well, and
farmers coming into the City require not only
to get a leaflet put into their hands but to
get much more valuable information in the
matter of conversation.
as
Supposing a farmer wants to import an
animal from Scotland for the purpose of improving the breed of his cattle it is necessary
under the present Orders to get a permit to
do it. Is the farmer to be expected to come
into Belfast, and, having transacted his ordinary business, find his way out to Stormont?
It would take more than half an hour in a
taxi to get to Stormont. Is it fair to the
farmer who is introducing an animal to
improve his breed to be compelled to go from
the centre of the City to Stormont to get that
permit? It may be right, but I say it is not
fair to put him to this inconvenience. Supposing he wants to get information
to the value of manures, a most important thing, or he wants to get information as to the value of seeds, is it
right that he should have to go to Stormont to get the information there from clerks
in that place? Supposing a farmer has got
an idea-and farmers are not destitute of
ideas and are reading rather more now than
in times past-into his head that it would
pay him to produce some other crop than
he was in the habit of producing, and he
wanted to get the statistics of prices as to
how much was paid to produce it in other
places, and wanted to get first hand advice,
is he to go to Stormont? Surely it would be
advisable to get it inside the City.
I am not making any complaint on behalf
of farmers as to the facilities given to other
branches. It is quite right to have the Ministry of Finance in the city. There is no
question in the world about that. In the
matter of income tax we would have no complaint if they removed that a great deal
further away than Stormont. The Home
Affairs are perfectly right. Finance
is largely administrative and attractive and
the Home Office is punitive. Education is
right to have some office in the city, and the
people most interested in it are the trained
teachers who are able to fight their own case
and the result is they have an office in the
city. Commerce is quite right. It is right
that commercial men should have an office in
the city where they can get information
quickly that would help them in their business. None of us complain of that. With
regard to these things we say to the Government what ought to be done ought not to be
left undone, and why agriculture should be
the only one left out is a thing I cannot
understand. Farmers have few people to advocate their claims. Labour is well organised
and can make its voice heard and is always
listened to. No one complains of that. Business men can make their voice heard through
their Chambers of Commerce, but the farmers
are scattered through the country-225,000 of
them, and of that number 115,000 are farmers
under 50 acres. They have not the time to
organise and cannot make their voice felt the
same as other people. The matter is an exceedingly important one, and my mission this
afternoon is to ask the Cabinet of Northern
Ireland to make things easy for these people.
It is said by a great man that the person who
can make two blades of grass grow where only
one blade grew is a public benefactor. Help
these men; help them to produce as much as
it is possible, and make it as easy for them to
help themselves as it is possible to do.
I know that the Ministries can divide their
departments into watertight compartments.
It is comparatively easy to sectionalise these
things, and have one office here and another
there. The Ministry of Agriculture is a
comparatively small department. I would
remind the House that the Minster of Agriculture and the Minister of Commerce are
one and the same person, and much as the
right hon. Gentleman is esteemed throughout
the country-he is a great favourite with the
people, who are on better terms with the
Ministry of Agriculture than at any time in
my memory-clever as the right hon. Gentleman is, he has not any of the qualities
associated with Sir Boyle Roche's bird-he
cannot be in two places at once.
In mercy to the right hon. Gentleman I
ask you to see that the Ministry of Commerce
is in the same place in the city as the
Ministry of Agriculture, and make it easier
for the right hon. Gentleman to continue on
a greater scale in the future the noble work
he has been doing in the past. You may say
it will cost something, and that I have not

this programme which I have mentioned was

Friends who have taken such an interest in

central building should be erected in the city

that the Ministry of Commerce, which

with the other Ministries, should be

that, in addition, the various departments
of the Ministry of Finance-the Stamp Office,

was desired when they reached the city,

POLICE RAID IN FALLS AREA.
1. Mr. DONALD: I thank you, Mr.
Speaker. I beg to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs a question of which I have given
private notice: Whether he is in a position
to give any information regarding a police
raid which is stated to have taken place in
the Falls Road area this morning.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): A party of police this
morning raided a house, No. 14 Dunmore
Street, in the Falls Road area, and discovered, concealed under the floor of the
house and buried in the yard, the following:
37 Rifles.
40 Bayonets.
30 Bombs (most of them detonated).
4 18-lb. Shells.
5,000 rounds mixed rifle ammunition.
1,000 rounds of small arm ammunition.
1 Aerial torpedo.
3 Verey pistols.
10 Revolvers and pistols.
Bag of bomb parts.
st. Gelignite.
Large bag of detonators.
3 doz. Fuses for land mines.
5 Thompson machine gun drums.
Various parts of machine guns.
13 Bandoliers.
6 Water bottles.
9 Revolver holsters.
Large quantity of mixed shot.
Various parts of small arms.
1 Electric battery.
1 Electric torch.
Three men were found on the premises and
were arrested.
CENSORING OF LETTERS.
2. Mr. DONALD (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether it is
by instructions of the Northern Government
that letters are being censored in Northern
Ireland, and if so, for what reasons.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Letters have been
censored for some time back in Northern
Ireland on the instructions of the Northern
Government in order to assist them in dealing
with the exceptional situation.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
while I agree that it is necessary to take these
steps, may I ask my right hon. Friend if he
is aware that only this week grave anxiety
has been caused to Loyalists through their
letters having been censored, and will he in
future be more careful in censoring the letters
of loyal subjects?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I shall be very glad
indeed if the hon. Member will bring to my
notice any particular case of this kind, but
he may be perfectly satisfied that the Censor
takes great care in carrying out his duties.

Message from Lord Lieutenant.
The PRIME MINISTER, at the Bar,
reported the following Message from His
Excellency the Lieutenant-General and General Governor of Ireland :-
"I cannot leave Northern Ireland without
saying how thoroughly I have enjoyed my
visit and how deeply grateful I am for the
welcome that has been given to myself and
Lady FitzAlan. Both of us have been
greatly struck by the efficient arrangements
made for our visit throughout the Six
Counties, by the authorities both Civil and
Military.
I was honoured on the occasion of my
visit, for I was proud to be invited to
unveil at Enniskillen a Memorial to the
Fermanagh men who fell in the late war;
and I have received during these last three
days a vivid impression of the loyalty and
the active determination, which have meant
so much in the history of the Six Counties.
I have been profoundly encouraged by all
that I have heard and seen of the work
which the Government and Parliament of
Northern Ireland have done for the happiness and welfare of their people, and I see
in the peace and order now prevailing a
notable contribution towards that general
return of prosperity to all Ireland for which
I earnestly pray, and to which I confidently
look."

Written Answer to Question.
LICENCES FOR WIRELESS APPARATUS.
Mr. ROBB asked the Minister of Commerce
whether the issue of Licences to use apparatus in Northern Ireland for the reception
and transmission of wireless signals has now
been sanctioned by the General Post Office,
and, if so, what arrangements he has made
with the General Post Office in regard to the
procedure to be adopted, and what steps he
has taken to ensure that the wireless interests
of Northern Ireland are safeguarded.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): I am glad to be able to inform
the House in reply to the honourable Member's question that while the Ministry of
Commerce has no statutory or other powers
in connection with wireless matters it has
come to a satisfactory arrangement with the
Postmaster-General, under which an undertaking has been obtained that Northern Ireland will participate to the same extent as
any other part of Great Britain in all facilities granted by the Postmaster-General.

Moreover the Ministry of Home Affairs is
now able, in approved cases, to agree to the
granting of licences, for the reception of
wireless signals, by the Postmaster-General
to persons interested in wireless telegraphy
from the scientific standpoint and possessing
some practical knowledge of the use of wireless apparatus. Applicants for such licences
should apply to the Ministry of Commerce.
In regard to broadcasting no arrangements
have yet been made either here or in the
rest of Great Britain for the issuing of
licences for broadcasting receiving sets,
which are used merely for purposes of
entertainment. The Ministry of Commerce
is, however, making arrangements with the
Postmaster-General in connection with this
matter, in order that as soon as the machinery for the issue of these licences is set up
in Great Britain, similar facilities, adapted
to special local conditions, may be made
available simultaneously in.Northern Ireland.

Adjournment of the House.
Statement by the Prime Minister.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn."-(Capt. Dixon.)
The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend
opposite (Mr. M'Guffin) anticipated me in
suggesting that something might be said
before we adjourn. I had intended to refer
to one or two matters which I consider of
such importance that it would be a pity if
we broke up as a House without my being
able to say a word or two in explanation.
In the first instance I think the House will
consider it only courteous on my part to
refer with the deepest sense of gratitude to
His Excellency the Lord Lieutenant for
having honoured us with a visit-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and not confined himself
alone to the unveiling of the War Memorial
at Enniskillen, but for having visited other
parts of our Province and laid himself out
to get to know as many of the citizens as it
was possible in the time at his disposal. I
feel sure that all of us are deeply grateful
for the manner in which he made himself
acquainted with our local needs and requirements, and also associated himself with all
those with whom he came in contact. I have
had a wire from His Excellency this morning
announcing his safe return to London, and
I can inform the House that he left here with
the best wishes of all classes and denominations. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I think I may also crave the indulgence of
the House to pay a tribute to Lord Londonderry for the loyal manner in which he has
stuck to us during these trying times. This
is the first time the House has met since he
came to a decision of no ordinary importance
in the life of a man who has devoted himself
to politics, and the House is well aware that
there is no higher ambition that can be felt
by a politician than a seat in the British Government. It was offered to him freely, and
he would have filled with distinction the post
that was allocated to his talents. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We who are in
closest touch with him know of the intense
interest he has taken in the Flying Service,
which, I have no doubt, will become more
and more important as time goes on. His
ideas have been far-reaching and very broad
regarding that branch of the Service for the
defence of our country, and, therefore, it is
something at all events to know that he has
been able of his own initiative to refuse that
high honour on the ground simply and solely
that he felt his duty lay in Ulster and that
Ulster required him and wanted him. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) In interpreting the
feelings of the people he certainly interpreted
my desire, my earnest wish. Therefore, we
as a House tender to him our heart-felt gratitude for having taken the decision that he
did at this time, and we only trust he will
live to remember that in our defence he
thought of us first and himself afterwards.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The next point that I desire to touch upon
is one that I would not have brought into
the House had it not reflected upon the
honour of my colleagues in the Cabinet and
practically upon every Member of this House.
There was a meeting against Prohibition yesterday where the chairman "charged the
Government "-I quote from the paper-
"with a complete breach of faith and with
weakness in going back on their first idea
of a Royal Commission on the subject at the
clamour of teetotallers." I only wish to
make this remark that there is only one thing,
practically only one thing, that I resent and
deeply resent, and that is the charge of a
breach of faith-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-and I felt so deeply my colleagues and I
were involved in this that I take the earliest
possible opportunity to refute such a charge.
I have in my hand my own election address,
and embodied in it is a manifesto that I issued
to the people of Ulster just before the last
paragraph?
"The first Parliament will be faced with
problems gravely affecting the future. The
best way to extend our resources, expand
trade, stabilise agriculture and other industries, re-model education, amend the
Licensing Laws-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and to ensure a brighter future for
the great masses of workers in our midst
is to begin by concentrating on the supreme
issue of securing a strong working majority.
without which government could not be
carried on, and without which society must
inevitably fail."
I stand on these words at the election. It
was forecasted there quite clearly that the
first Parliament would be faced with the problem of amending the Licensing Laws, and I
repudiate in the strongest language that there
has been any breach of faith by the Government; and I would also like to say that from
that date to this the Temperance Party,
either inside this House or outside this House,
have never approached me on one single
occasion to fulfil that pledge in our election
address (hon. Members: Hear, hear)-because I believe the people of Ulster trusted
that what we put into that was sincerely
meant by those of us who signed it. And,
therefore, I must pay a tribute to those who
so keenly feel on this subject that they have
never by word or sign indicated that they
thought the time had come to deal with this.
When as a Cabinet some short time ago we
reviewed the situation and when we, I think
quite rightly, diagnosed the fact that we had
reached somewhat calmer waters and that
there was no risk of the disturbances which
we had in the past, we thought we ought
Prime Minister's Statement. 1144
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Prime Minister]
loyally to carry out what each of us subscribed to in our election address, and we
intend to do it. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I am only sorry that the words I used when
I first mentioned this in the House have not
carried more weight. It is our desire, and
I am sure it is the desire of all hon. Members
of this House, to be fair and just in the
matter, to be moderate to a degree, in order
that there should not be started throughout
Ulster any division of opinion amongst those
Loyalists who have carried us so far on the
path of peace and prosperity. Even at the
eleventh hour I appeal to all to be moderate
in their language, to study these questions
purely from the point of view of advantage
to the people as a whole, and not allow to
creep in any acrimony such as was apparent
in the report of the meeting that was held
yesterday.
I now come to the fourth point I would
like to touch upon, that is with regard to the
The
calling of the House together again.
House is fully acquainted with the situation
across the Channel, and hon. Members acquiesce in the view that this House should rise
as early as possible in order to release hon.
Members of this House who have to seek reelection, and who otherwise have to take part
in a campaign which may have a very vital
effect upon the future of our province.
Therefore, in deciding to adjourn with the
power of calling the House together again, it
will be within the recollection of everyone
that when the 6th of December is passed the
month begins in which we will have to make
the choice either to vote out dr remain
within the Free State. There has never been
any doubt in the mind of any hon. Member
of this House on that point. At the same
time we have to go through the formula of
doing it, and, therefore, we are very anxious
to sit as soon as possible in the early stages
of that month in order that it may not go
forth to the world that we had the slightest
hesitation about the act we propose to take.
If there was any delay people would wonder,
whereas if we take the first moment available
for us to call the House together and to lay
before it a motion which the Government will
propose, then I think there can be no misunderstanding in any part of the globe about
our continued anxiety to remain with Great
Britain in the closest possible alliance, and
at the moment, at all events, to stay quite
clear of a Dublin Parliament. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
That will be the important business, but by
then it may be possible to consider any other
matters that have arisen in the meantime. I
hope and trust that the anxious questions
which will be engaging my attention between
now and that date will eventuate with success
to our province. I need hardly emphasise to
the House the gravity of the questions that
still remain outstanding-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-but I know that in my absence,
as I must be a great deal in London in
connection with this ticklish business, not
only will Members of this House but the
people of the whole Six Counties will stand
firm and true together, so as to get over
what I sincerely trust will be the last fence
leading to the land of promise, peace and
happiness to our people. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

We are not out to sacrifice the interests of
the trade. We are not out for confiscation.
I am pledged to that extent-I am not out
for that. I am out for reform, and that is
what is demanded by the Prime Minister
himself nothing more than reform, such reform as will be beneficial to the community,
and such reform as the Temperance Party
will insist on having. I am glad to know
that the Prime Minister is fully alive to the
dangers and difficulties of the situation, and
the House is prepared to support him in any
action he may take to have the rights and
privileges of our House established by such
a measure as may be necessary. That is all
I wish to say with respect to the matter. 1

We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland
in Parliament assembled, having learnt of

for the ratification of the Articles of Agreement for a Treaty between Great Britain

Address to His Majesty. 1148
Constitution Act-
7 DECEMBER 1922.
The PRIME MINISTER: I think it will be
for the convenience of the House if I read the
terms of the humble Address to his Majesty
in the first instance, make a few remarks on
the subject afterwards, and that, unless some
very important point arises that hon. Members would care to discuss, we should allow
this very important and serious Address to
go through without unnecessary discussion.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There are
several reasons for such a course. We desire
that it should get to the Senate at the earliest
possible moment in order that they may likewise take their part in opting out of the Free
State, and that there should be no risk run
of the Addresses not both crossing over to be
in the hands of His Majesty to-morrow. My
suggestion, therefore, is that, as there are
other matters on which I myself would like
to make a few comments, we should confine
ourselves really to debate when the Motion
for Adjournment is put, when we can cover
all the ground and express our opinions quite
freely as to matters that have recently happened. The Address which I beg to move is
as follows:
MOST GRACIOUS SOVEREIGN,
We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland
in Parliament assembled, having learnt of
the passing of the Irish Free State Constitution Act, 1922, being the Act of Parliament
for the ratification of the Articles of Agreement for a Treaty between Great Britain
and Ireland, do, by this humble Address,
pray your Majesty that the powers of the
Parliament and Government of the Irish
Free State shall no longer extend to
Northern Ireland.
In moving this humble Address I desire
first of all to say that no one could take exception to the fact that we assemble at tha
earliest possible moment in order to make
perfectly clear not only to Southern Ireland
but to the world that, so far as we in Ulster
are concerned, we have no desire to do more
than co-operate with our separate institutions here for the prosperity and peace of the
whole of Ireland. No one in this Assembly,
and certainly none of the Loyalists in Ulster
have expected any other action on our part.
for a very long time past, and I am sure hon.
Members will acquit me of any ambiguity on
this subject since I have had the honour to
lead them in this House. The Provisional
Government in their debates yesterday
touched upon the question of Ulster at some
time, either sooner or later, desiring to join
up with them in some form, or other in order
to secure what they call the co-operation and
unity of Ireland. I have to say with regard
to that that the only possible way of securing
co-operation and happiness is for the South to
settle its own affairs, and for the North to
carry on as it is at present under its own
Parliament, its own Executive, and its own
other authorities. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) There is no use our holding out at the
moment any hopes whatever of a desire on the
part of the Ulster people to go in under a
Dublin Parliament. To reiterate this over
and over again becomes necessary, because
some people seem to take fright at an action
here or an action there which ought not in
any way to cause alarm. I would like to
point out that so long as I stand at this Table
there is no thought in my mind, and certainly never any desire in my heart, to do
other than carry on the Northern Government with its own Parliament and its own
affairs, so that there is at all events a very
good barometer for the people to judge by in
finding me still at this Table. The moment
there is any question of going under a
Dublin Parliament I refuse to stand here.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I cannot conceive that it is for the good of the people
or for the good of Ireland as a whole to
attempt anything of the kind, and therefore
we may go ahead in our own way for the
betterment and well-being of our own people
here, trusting that the South may settle its
affairs and get settled down to good government.

The PRIME MINISTER: I wish to thank
the House for the very cordial way in which
they have supported me in the suggestion that
we should discuss any matters of importance
when we are out of the Free State instead of
when we are in it, although that is a mere
technicality. I observed with astonishment
some remarks made yesterday in the Southern
House, and it is because I fear that certain
persons may take alarm at the views expressed
regarding the Boundary Commission that I
desire to say something of serious importance
to this House to-day. We are all aware of the
various criticisms made from time to time
regarding the Boundary Commission, and the
House has still in recollection my statement
on behalf of the Government that we would
take no part in that Commission. (Hon Members: Hear, hear.) The House still bears that
statement well in mind. I had the pleasure

This bargain was entered into by the wrong

protect themselves." And right nobly did

Hear, hear.) But just as they rose to that

the heather, it is still almost at the cottage

about this Commission merely bringing into

To tell the truth I was rather glad that
was the attitude taken by those in Dublin
who were so anxious to get the Treaty, and
for this reason: I held from the very beginning that the portion of the Treaty which
deals with the Commission is ultra vires.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I have held
that opinion straight through without any
hesitation whatever. I believe it is common
law that if an arbitration is suggested, and
one party to that arbitration refuses to function, the arbitration cannot take place. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). It is my deliberate
opinion, and I am fortified by the opinion
of counsel of the highest eminence, which I
have in my pocket at the moment, that if
the two who entered into this bargain behind
our backs agree together and say that there
is to be a Boundary Commission, they will
find that it is impossible for them to have
such a Commission. And they dare not
bring an Amending Bill through the House
of Commons-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)--
because, thanks to the indefatigable energies
of our delegation recently in going through
the whole of the constituencies, we have
secured a majority for Ulster in the British
House of Commons that would not pass a
Bill which would impose on us some persoa
to act for us as a member of that Commission.
Therefore I feel perfectly clear in my mind
that if one party to the arbitration is
sufficiently stubborn-and I have already
said that I am very stubborn in a matter of
this kind-then the Commission cannot get to
work, and therefore the drafters, those who
put their heads together and drafted the
Constitution of the Free State have made a
drafting error, and the consequences can rest
upon them, and them alone. I was never consulted, and this House and the country were
no party to it. The House may suggest that,
therefore, a deadlock has been reached. May

I do not believe for one moment that such

the Imperial House has been fighting and
lobbying against it night and day, with the
result that the Government had to put off the
Second Reading. I do hope and trust that
before this matter is finished the agriculturists of England will see that this is a
matter of life and death to us, and that it
must re-act on themselves if they turn their
backs on their brother farmers at the present
moment. I hope I have made this point clear.
I do not think there is any need for me to
assure the House that the Government is behind the farmers in the points raised by the
hon. Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr.
Coote). We are out to do everything we can
for Ulster, and we are only too happy to get
up in this House and to answer any question
that is asked in regard to these subjects. I
can assure my hon. Friend that so long as
our own Prime Minister is at the head of
this Government no one need have any suspicion that he is not doing his best for the
people he represents.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: There are just
one or two observations that I wish to make
on the various points that have been mentioned here during the last few minutes.
First of all, I think this House will be impressed with one thing, and that is the wisdom of the course that this Parliament and
the people of Ulster adopted in having their
representatives in the Imperial Parliament.
We see that questions vitally affecting Ulster
as a whole will be dealt with there from time
to time, and we have all noticed the very
forceful and effective way that the representatives from Ulster in the Imperial Parliament have dealt not only with this question
of the restriction upon cattle, but with other
matters that are vital to the prosperity and
happiness of our people in Ulster as a whole.
A good many things have happened since we
last met here as a House. I think we were
all extremely delighted to hear the very forceful and powerful speech made by the Prime
Minister here this afternoon. He dealt with
one question that everybody in Ulster is interested in-that is the question of the boundaries and after that speech I do not think
that this House or the people we represent
need have any anxiety whatever in regard to
the attitude of the Prime Minister, of the
Government, or of this Parliament as
whole. The only observation that I would
make in regard to the question of the boundaries is this: this House, I believe, has the
a
.
fullest confidence in the Prime Minister and
in the Government in regard to any action or
steps they may take in regard to the boundaries, and I believe that our people as a
whole ought to rest satisfied, and ought not
to feel in the slightest degree nervous, about
this whole matter. I believe the best will be
done that can be done by the Prime Minister
and those associated with him in regard to
this whole question.
I wish to refer to some other matters that
bave been raised by my hon. Friend, the
Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr.
Coote). When the Free State Constitution
Bill was going through the House of Commons, along with it was another measure
called the Consequential Bill, and I desire
to refer now to some things in that Bill. We
are all well aware of the very peculiar position of our State in regard to the Council of
Ireland. Originally there was to be equal
representation from the North and South,
but, owing to the Treaty and to the Free State
Bill, the South of Ireland under the Act of
1920, had there been no alteration whatever,
would still have had the right to interfere
with our affairs, and we would have had no
right to interfere with them. I think on the
face of it any Government, or any fairminded person, would say that that was not a
right and a proper position in which to place
one of the parties. We are not satisfied fully
in regard to what has taken place, but what
has been secured is a vast improvement upon
what existed. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
If we have not got control of those reserved
services, then I take leave to say the other
choice was the choice that now remains in
the Bill, that if we could not get control of
the reserved services, then the other people
who ought to have control of them are the
Imperial authorities. I think that is a considerable improvement upon what existed
previously, and I hope that before the five
years have expired a better arrangement will
be arrived at. If not, then I am sure that the
Ulster Parliament and its people will see that
the time has arrived for them to say that
these are matters which the Ulster people
have the right to deal with themselves.
I think the question of the ex-Servicemen's
cottages has been disposed of by the hon.
Member for Belfast (Captain Dixon), as well
as by the Prime Minister, and there is nothing there that need give us undue worry
or alarm. If the South of Ireland will not
pass measures dealing with it, then we have
the assurance that it will be dealt with in
another way. SO that the ex-Servicemen
throughout Ulster will have no grievance and
that their rights will be secured to them in a
just and proper manner.
There are several other matters that have
not been referred to here on which I think
we have the right to congratulate the Government. I think a very big advance has been

made when we have secured a Governor-
General for ourselves. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) The hon. Member for Fermanagh
and Tyrone has told us that we have had to

not to go to Dublin Castle now on any matter, and Ulster's position as a separate governing entity has been emphasised by the fact
that we are going to have a Governor-General
for Ulster itself. That is a very big advance
on anything that existed previously.
There is another matter in which a considerable improvement has been made by this
Consequential Bill. The hon. Member for
Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr. Coote) elicited
the fact that the probability is that we might

Office, but that we might be dealing with the

at the Home Office at the moment an Ander.
son who was formerly at Dublin Castle, but

some very valuable improvements. On the

arrived at are, I think, very much more

think we have a right to congratulate ourselves upon the successful efforts made by
the Government in effecting various and considerable improvements by the Consequential
Bill. I sincerely hope that we are now settled
as a Government upon strong and firm foundations, that this House and the people as a
whole will work loyally together, and that

Government in all that they may do to estab
lish law and order and to have a peaceful
community. I believe, notwithstanding all

history as a Government here in Ulster that
is so full of promise as it is to-day. I believe
all the difficulties will be surmounted, and
that through the goodwill of the people and
through the energy and ability of the Government as a whole, in the coming days we will
see an Ulster not only loyal to the British
connection, but anxious to do everything
that they can to help Great Britain and to
help the Empire, and in that way they will
be true to their best traditions. I hope further that in our efforts in the coming days
we will be able so to legislate that we will
help our people as a whole, and thus make
Ulster a happier and a more prosperous place
to live in. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

land? It was put in specifically, I believe,

from time to time thrown up-the one

It is in contemplation by the British

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
NEWTOWNSTEWART POSTAL
SERVICES.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of Commerce if he is aware that farmers and others
living within a mile of Newtownstewart are
handicapped by the fact that their letters
and newspapers, which are received in the
Newtownstewart Post Office about eleven
o'clock a.m., are kept over until the next
morning, and whether, in the interest of the
trade of the district, he will use his influence
with the Post Office authorities to revert to
the arrangement of some months ago, when
the departure of the postmen was delayed
until the day's mail came in?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): This matter was taken up by
the Ministry of Commerce with the Postal
Authorities in October last. The system of
delaying the departure of the postmen to
which the hon. Member refers and which
was in operation during the summer months
not only dislocated the system of collection
for the evening outward mail, but frequently
kept the postmen on duty till a very late
hour, and accordingly the Postal Authorities
cancelled this temporary arrangement.
The matter is still the subject of discussion with a view to discovering some
method of meeting the difficulty mentioned
by the hon. Member, but as he will appreciate, the matter can be more satisfactorily
dealt with in the general reorganisation of
the postal service in Northern Ireland.
Mr. MILLER: Arising out of that answer,
this matter is a great inconvenience to the
public, and the sooner it is settled the better
for the good of the community and for the
good of the greatest number of inhabitants
in the community. I understand that the
right hon. Gentleman-

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Loans Guarantee Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This small Measure known as the
Loans Guarantee Bill, of which it is now
my duty to move the Second Reading, is an
adaptation of much more pretentious
measure called the Trade Facilities Act,
which has been passed recently by the Ima
1179 Loans Guarantee Bill-

12 DECEMBER 1922.
Second Reading.
perial House. The British measure consists
of three separate sections devoted to three
separate and distinct subjects. This measure
of ours, on the other hand, concerns itself
with only one single matter, and is designed
to achieve only one single object, and that
is to assist industry and at the same time
to create employment in our own area. As
the House will observe it contains practically
only one Clause with six sub-sections, and it
is so comparatively simple in its character
that its import will be readily grasped by
hon. Members. As its name implies it is a
guaranteeing measure, that is to say it is a
measure intended to authorise the Government to guarantee loans to public bodies, to
Corporations, and to other persons, provided
that there is sufficient security behind the
borrowers to warrant the Government in
undertaking the liability of guaranteeing the
lenders against any possible loss. It is a
fact, of course, that there is a clear differentiation between lending and guaranteeing.
The duty of the Government under this Bill
is simply to guarantee and not to lend.
Towards the end of the year 1921, it will be
remembered, a Bill of a similar character,
authorising the Government to guarantee
manufacturers and others, passed the Imperial Parliament with a maximum of
£25,000,000. This was largely taken advantage
of on all hands, and the results from the
point of view of the employment of labour
were of such a satisfactory character that
the Government considered it wise to pass a
similar measure-the one to which I have
referred earlier guaranteeing a maximum of
a second £25,000,000 for exactly similar pur
case it is proposed
In
our
poses.
to follow the precedent of the Imperial
Government in respect of the procedure
under this Bill, that is to say we propose to
establish a small Advisory Committee composed of three persons of financial experience, intelligence and independence, whose
duty it will be to determine on the evidence
which is submitted to them whether the
conditions or circumstances of the applicants
conform to the intentions of this Act. The
two primary considerations involved are,
first, that the security offered is sufficient
to warrant the Government in undertaking
the liability, and, second, that the amount
of employment provided under the scheme is
commensurate with the Government guarantee. These two important considerations
will be determined by the Investigating
Committee to which I have just referred.
This Committee will have the assistance of
experienced technical persons, such as trained accountants of knowledge and experience,
to advise them on this matter, while the veto
of the Ministry of Finance is, of course,
constantly maintained.
:
The principal advantage of this measure
arising from a Government guarantee to
individual firms is that a low rate of interest
can possibly be secured by having the Government guarantee behind the transaction.
This guarantee will be offered to banks,
large insurance companies, and institutions
of that class which are in the habit of advancing money under certain measures of
security, while at the same time it will,
I am sure, be agreed that it will enable
individual firms to use their own capital to
a larger extent in developing industrial
works in fact, the facilities which will be
offered them in this measure will assist in
providing them with liquid capital with
which to carry on their own undertakings
with greater energy than perhaps they
would otherwise do. Again, the main concern of our Government, naturally, in prosecuting this Bill is that work may be
provided for the unemployed, and I can
hardly think that any sacrifice we would
make, or could make, would be too great to
accomplish such a desirable result. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Unlike Great
Britain, our industries are not sufficiently
distributed or widespread, and we are peculiarly unfortunate in this respect, that
our two staple industries here shipbuilding
and linen-are just the two industries which
have been most severely stricken by the
unexampled depression of trade with which
we are all familiar.
The author of the Excess Profits Tax, the
present British Prime Minister, has, I
believe, admitted that the extraction of such
vast sums of money from industry has had
its repercussion in the present conditions of
trade, whilst I think it is generally agreed
that the heavy burden both on national and
local taxation is probably the greatest of the
contributory causes of the deplorable conditions of unemployment at the present time.
It is useless, I suggest, to moralise upon the
causes unless by an analysis of the causes
we could discover and administer some
remedy, but I am sure of this, that we
cannot make any mistake if we use Our
utmost endeavours to provide facilities for
encouraging those of our people who can
and who are willing to prosecute schemes
for encouraging the employment of labour
which would, I have no doubt, ameliorate
the conditions under which we are unfortunately labouring at the present time. The
employment of men is in one sense more
important than that of women, because it
is obvious that the man, who is generally
the head of the house, makes provision for
an average of from four to five in his household. Therefore, if any additional employment in our shipbuilding yards can be
secured it will undoubtedly be very helpful
to us in the present conditions. We know,
as a matter of fact, that there are a number
Appropriation Bill. 1182
Loans Guarantee Bill.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
of orders upon the books of our local shipbuilders, but they are not permitted to execute these orders or proceed wih the work
because of the condition of trade. The shipowners who have given the orders are not
prepared for reasons which, I have no doubt,
are perfectly adequate, to themselves at any
rate, to proceed with the work when the
conditions of shipowning and shipworking
are so depressed as those that exist at the
present time. In addition to these orders
there are also, as we know, several ships
upon our stocks that are partially completed
and I have no doubt that these are held up
also for economic reasons by the shipowners
who do not desire delivery and have postponed operations upon them. We have
opened negotiations with a view to discovering whether it would not be possible to
expedite some of the work upon several of
these ships, and I have good hopes that we
may succeed, in some instances at least, in
getting a start made. If we do it will
provide occupation for some of the very best
type of men, men who, for a very considerable time, as we know, have been walking
unemployed, and to whom it is a great
humiliation indeed to have to accept what
is known as the unemployment dole from the
Bureau. These men are generally selfrespecting men-I am speaking now of the
high-class artisans employed in the shipbuilding works-and to afford them an opportunity of getting work will, I am sure,
commend itself to this House as it does to
the Government. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I think if we can tide over the next
twelve months so far as our shipbuilding
trade is concerned-I am referring to that
now that we shall see a revival of conditions in the trade, and for this reason,
that so many of the older ships are now becoming obsolete and, as it is fully appreciated by shipowners that steamers equipped
with modern types of engines are so much
more economical than those already in existence, there will be a great temptation to
shipowners to undertake new work and to
provide themselves with fresh tonnage of the
improved type if the necessary capital is
forthcoming to enable them to undertake
investments. Of that I am satisfied, but
I believe it will take some time before these
conditions ensue.
The First Sub-section of the Measure empowers the Government, as will be seen,
through the Ministry of Finance, to guarantee certain loans, the limit of such guarantee being £2,000,000. The Second Subsection limits the operation of this Measure
to twelve months. We think this is desirable under the circumstances, as it is unwise
to allow measures of this kind, where Government pledges may be given, to remain
unlimited. Sub-sections 3 and 4, as will be
seen, are purely formal and are not likely to
become operative. Sub-section 5 makes provision for the submission to Parliament
every three months of the transactions which
have been undertaken by the Ministry, and
at the expiration of the year a full statement
will be laid before Parliament of the operations of the Measure as it has been carried
out. I think with these explanations the
House will be able to understand the importance of this small Bill, and I now move
the Second Reading in the hope that it may
carry out the beneficent ends which at any
rate the Government have in view in submitting it to the House.

Standing Orders (Locai Bilis).
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS
(Mr. Moles): I beg to move the first of the
Amendments to the Standing Orders relative
to Local Bills which appears on the Paper
in my
name. A year's experience of the
Standing Orders, which we drew up with so
much care and attention, has suggested to
us little more than verbal changes and some
little detail which make at once for public
utility, the convenience of the House, and
the cheapening of expense. The first amendment on the Order Paper, which I now beg
to move, is to leave out No. 38, in order to
insert the following:-
On or before the twenty-first day of
December a printed copy shall be deposited-
(1) Of every Local Bill at the Ministries
of Finance, Home Affairs, Labour, Education, Agriculture, and Commerce in Belfast.
(2) Of every Local Bill at the Office of
His Majesty's Treasury, at the General
Post Office, at the Irish Office, and at the
Office of Woods in London.
(3) Of every Local Bill affecting any dock,
harbour navigation, pier or port, at the
Board of Trade in London.
If hon. Members will look at the original
Standing Order they will find that the Ministries of Finance, Home Affairs, Labour, and
Agriculture were included. It is proposed
now to add to that Standing Order the additional Ministries of Education and Commerce
in Belfast which have been set up. The purport of that is so obvious that I need not
explain it. It is simply to keep in conformity
with the original Order that all Ministries
should be kept in touch with the provisions
of these Private Bills. The second has been
arranged in consultation with the authorities
upon the other side, at Westminster, and
there again the object is, of course, to safeguard and protect the public interests that
may be involved. The third is so palpable
that I do not propose to take up time in
explaining it. I beg to move.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
My hon. Friend, the Chairman of Ways and
Means, has explained this matter very carefully, but I would like to call attention to
the question of the abolition of the Irish
Office. I have been in consultation-I think
it is only four days ago with the Colonial
Office and the Home Office regarding the
future arrangements between ourselves and
the British Government. It has been decided
that Southern Ireland-the Free State-shall
use the Colonial Office as its general channel
of communicating with the British Government, and that on the other hand the Home
Office will be the natural channel for the
Government of Northern Ireland to communicate with the British Government.
Members: Hear, hear.) I understand that
the Irish Office has already been, or is in
process of being, practically obliterated. Consequently, if my hon. Friend (Mr. Moles) does
not object in any way I would suggest to him
that he should add after "the General Post
Office" the words "the Home Office," as that
would be our channel of communicating with
the British Government in future. I do not
suggest that he should omit the Irish Office
from his list, but the adoption of my suggestion would prevent him having to come to
this House later on to insert the Home Office
in the Standing Order.
(Hon.
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS:

The technical difficulty was that there was,

Prime Minister.

We do not trust in this juggling of offices

Oral Answers to Questions.
SUNDAY INSPECTIONS OF SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
1. Mr. COOTE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs if he will state what are the special
reasons for selecting the Christian Sabbath
as a day on which to hold official Government
inspections of the Constabulary Forces in
Ulster by His Majesty's Ulster Government?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I presume the hon. Member
refers to the inspections of the Forces when
attending Church Parades. It has always
been regarded as part of the duty of Crown
Forces to attend Divine Service, and I should
be sorry if this salutary practice was neglected in the Special Constabulary Force.
Mr. COOTE: In consequence of the unsatisfactory nature of the answer of the right
hon. Gentleman I beg to give notice that I
shall raise this question on the adjournment
this evening.
Land Purchase.
Land Purchase.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
LAND PURCHASE.
2. Mr. COOTE asked the Prime Minister
whether he is able to give any information
with regard to the steps to be taken by the
British Government in fulfilment of their
pledge to transfer the remaining property
of the owners of lands in Northern Ireland
subject to the Land Acts to the occupiers
on terms fair to both parties, and on the
basis agreed to by the Land Committee of
the Irish Convention of 1917-1918.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): As the administration of land
purchase is a matter which is reserved to
the Imperial Government under the Government of Ireland Act, the question cannot
be answered with authority in this House.
Assurances have from time to time been
given by Imperial Ministers that legislation
would be forthcoming for the purpose of
completing land purchase in Ireland, and I
have no reason to believe that these promises
will not be carried out so far as Northern
Ireland is concerned at an early date. I
have no information as to the provisions
which will be contained in any such legislation, but possibly it may follow the lines
of the abortive Irish Land Bill presented
to the Imperial House of Commons on 11th
November, 1920.
Mr. COOTE: Arising out of that answer
may I ask the right hon. Gentleman whether
his Government is taking any steps, or has
taken any steps, to press upon the British
Government the necessity of performing the
obligations which they solemnly entered into
in respect to many questions put to them
principally by the Speaker of the present
House. Has anything been done to fulfil
the specific promises entered into that they
would bring in simultaneously with the Act
of 1920 an Act for the liberation of landlord
and tenant in Ireland?
Mr. POLLOCK: No formal pressure has
been brought by this Government on the
Imperial Government to implement their
promises in regard to land purchase, but I
may remind my hon. Friend (Mr. Coote) that
Mr. Ormsby Gore, the Minister concerned
with this matter, stated in the House on the
27th November last, that a Conference of
Irish Ministers would be held in Dublin
to arrive at a scheme of land purchase, and
he anticipated they would then consult the
United Kingdom. The conditions, of course,
were materially changed by the rebellion in
Southern Ireland, and by the new Constitution that was agreed to with Southern
Ireland, so that I apprehend whatever delay
has taken place is largely the result of the
political conditions rather than a disinclination of the Imperial Government to
implement their promises.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that reply,
will our Government be represented at that
Conference?
Mr. POLLOCK: In Dublin?
Mr. DONALD: Yes.
Mr. POLLOCK: This is the matter that
Mr. Ormsby Gore referred to touching upon
the relations of the British authority with
the Free State in regard to whatever
obligations exist between Britain and
the Free State in respect of land purchase.
The position of the British Government in
Northern Ireland is, of course, very different,
because I understand that so far as any
financial obligations are concerned the
British Government has repudiated them in
respect of Southern Ireland. Of course,
such repudiation would not apply to Northern
Ireland, and, therefore, it may be that the
Imperial Government is anxious to settle or
to define an arrangement for the whole of
Ireland before undertaking their legislation.
Mr. COOTE: May I intervene for a moment.
Our point is that the Government of Northern
Ireland is taking no steps in regard to land
purchase to impress upon the British
Government the necessity of carrying out
their pledges. Would the Government not
be better employed on this matter than on
some of the smaller things which are engaging
their attention? Is this not a matter that
has to do with the settlement of the country
generally?
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I might
be allowed to reply to that. The question
of land purchase is one which is always
before my colleagues and myself. My hon.
Friend (Mr. Coote) is in a great hurry in
regard to this matter, but until we voted
ourselves out of the Free State it was impossible for the British Government to
decide a matter of the kind. Now that we
have done so I am just as anxious as my
hon. Friend to see the whole of the land
purchase scheme carried out for Northern
Ireland, and he can rest assured that I will
prosecute the matter with the same vigour
as I have always done.

ANSWER TO ADDRESS.
The PRIME MINISTER (at the Bar of
the House) reported that His Majesty,
having been attended with the Address of
the 7th day of December, was pleased to
receive the same very graciously and to give
the following answer:-
I have received the Address presented to
me by both Houses of the Parliament of
Northern Ireland in pursuance of Article
12 of the Articles of Agreement set forth
in the Schedule to the Irish Free State
(Agreement) Act, 1922, and of Section 5 of
the Irish Free State Constitution Act, 1922,
and I have caused my Ministers and the
Irish Free State Government to be so informed.

political economists will tell you that it

find that supply and demand sometimes do
not control the situation, and we will have
to get at something else. I think it was
John Ruskin who made a direct improvement
upon the political economy of his day. He
woke the nation to the fact that you must
deal with men not as hands but as souls.
He went a little further, and he saw that
the chief element which underlay our
industrial difficulties was the lack of sympathy with which the unemployed have to
contend. I am not finding fault with this
Government in the matter. Far be it from

Committee.
When shipbuilding was considered it was
only because it presented itself in Belfast as
an industry that was primarily in need of
some sympathy and some support, and not
in the interests of shipbuilders as such, because the shipbuilders were ready to proceed
with the work that they have in hands, and
with the orders they have received, but for
the fact that the owners were not prepared to
permit the shipbuilders to continue the work
owing to the depressed condition of the trade
of the world. The Government, then, considered it was their duty to investigate these
circumstances, and, as I mentioned yesterday,
we have begun some negotiations in which
the owners are introduced, in order to induce
them to permit the shipbuilders to proceed
with the work in Belfast. Can my hon.
Friend suggest that the building or the finishing of half-a-dozen ships will not promote
employment? Is it not a fact that in every
ship there will possibly be 500, 600, or 700 men
employed? Surely if 6,000 or 7,000 men-even
if you limit your survey to the shipyards-are
taken from the street and employed in the
shipyards, that is a vindication of our policy
-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-more
especially as the Government, although
giving these guarantees, will not, I apprehend, run the slightest modicum of risk.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Has the right hon. Gentleman any assurance from any reputable firm
that the saving in respect of interest will lead
to all these sanguine results that are being
outlined at the moment with regard to unemployment?
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not apprehend that
the saving in interest is the main consideration. The main consideration presumably
with large companies who have ships partially paid for, or partially constructed, is
that the necessary money is provided to
finish the ships and turn them out ready
for work until they are ready to pay for the
ships. That, in fact, as I judge it, is the
principal inducement that will be offered to
those who will take advantage of this scheme
which I am now outlining. This schememay I say?-is not limited to shipbuilders.
I only mentioned shipbuilders yesterday because the shipbuilding industry is so visible,
if I may say so, is before us so much, and
because it is one of the great staple industries whose workers are unemployed. It was
only because of that that I indicated shipbuilding as an example, but there are many
other cases in which constructive work can
be undertaken in Northern Ireland, and in
which advantage might be taken of credit
of this kind, and in which the saving of
interest might be a great inducement to
people to enter into such work. These are
matters that are easily understandable, I
think, by hon. Members who will take some
time to think over them.
In regard to the great measure which was
passed a year ago by Great Britain, I find
that shipowners did take advantage of it.
I see here pefore me that Beardmore, of
Glasgow, one of the largest shipbuilding
firms in the world, completed a ship belonging to the Italian Government, and that
the Palmer Shipbuilding Company also
availed themselves of it, so that in following
this precedent we have a direct example and
a perfect justification for our action, which,
as I repeat, is only dictated by the one
object, and that is to develop employment
in Northern Ireland in the distressing conditions with which we are faced. There
were applications from Ulster, let me say,
to the Imperial authority in respect of advances under the British Act, but for various
reasons these were not prosecuted. I suppose there were greater difficulties on this
side because of the non-existence here of the
necessary examining factors to enable them
to judge as to the character of the security
and so on, but, as a matter of fact, I know
these schemes were not prosecuted.
In regard to road grants and such like
improvements as my hon. Friend (Mr. Coote)
touched upon, it is not conceivable, I think,
in the interests of the taxpayers of Northern
Ireland, that grants of any kind, or even
guarantees of any kind, should be made to
county councils in such circumstances, in
view of the fact that they are getting very
substantial amounts indeed from the taxation
that accrues from mechanically propelled
vehicles. I judge that that will not exactly
come under the purview of this measure.
Agriculture also must be ruled out, because
there is no substantial asset there in the
form of security, and one of the very first
things that must be required by this Government and by the Committee is that the
character of the security behind any guarantee must be of such a substantial character
that the taxpayers of the country will not
be subjected to any risk. I think I have
made the matter sufficiently clear that my
hon. Friends will understand that this is
a matter of vital interest in regard to the
question of unemployment.

The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps my hon.
Friend will excuse me, before he enters on
the specific matter about which he has given
notice, when I suggest that it would be to
the advantage of Members if I say a word
or two in which I am sure he will acquiesce.
It is with regard to the appointment of our
new Governor. I do not think it would be
fitting for this House to allow such an occasion to pass without my being able to
assure him of the appreciation that we all
feel of the gracious act of His Majesty in
allocating to Northern Ireland a man who
has lived his whole life in our midst, who
is our premier Duke, who is interested in
the welfare of the whole province, and whose
family, for as long as any of us can remember, served not only the interests of Ulster,
but of Great Britain and the Empire. I
may say that I think there is not a man in
Ulster who is so well-known personally to
Members of the Senate and the House of
Commons as the Duke of Abercorn-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)- and I think there
is not a man who stands higher in their
esteem and whom they would welcome more
as their first Governor. Therefore, I take
the opportunity of saying that it is the
feeling of this House that I should convey
to him our respects and our hearty congratulations on the high honour that has been
conferred
upon him, as well as the high
honour that has been conferred upon Ulster.

FORTHCOMING VISIT OF LORD DERBY.
another
Then I would like to make
statement to the House that may be of interest, and that is, that when I was last in
London I asked Lord Derby, the Secretary
of State for War, if he would be kind enough
to pay us a visit here, in order to inspect
our great Force of Special Constabulary as
well as our Royal Ulster Constabulary.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am glad to
say that, with his usual geniality and kindness, he acquiesced in my suggestion, and
has promised to come over here to witness
a review, or if necessary to go round the
country to inspect the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the Special Constabulary at
their work. I can only say that I welcomed
his consent on behalf of Ulster, and on behalf of this House, and I said I knew that
when he came he would meet with a right
royal welcome, and would see a Force which
he, as Secretary of State for War, would feel
proud existed inside the United Kingdom,
because that Force is one which he knows,
and we all know, is for the purpose of resisting the King's enemies and preserving
peace, law and order in our midst. Therefore, I thought I would take the opportunity
to-day of letting it be known throughout all
ranks of the Force that, when the Secretary
of State does come here, I will look to them
to have a brave show, if I may say so, in
order that he may be deeply impressed with
the steps that we have taken here to safeguard our interests and to preserve law and
order.

Mr. COOTE: Pursuant to the notice which
I gave, I wish to develop my argument in
connection with the reply of the Minister
of Home Affairs to Question No. 1 upon the
Paper. I do not approach this question in
any captious mood whatever. With hundreds of thousands of others I was deeply
pained when I saw by reports in the Press
that on two occasions official Government
inspections were held of members of the "B"
Force before they entered upon their Church
parade. I should not have taken up the
time of the House to develop my argument
on this question were it not for the reply
that the Minister himself gave on the floor
of this House. To my mind it was petty and
captious, and it was unworthy of any Minister to stand up there under the protection
of a reply which could not be the subject of
comment, and to answer with a sneer and an
innuendo which were entirely, I think, out
of place. If I may say so, it was very small
indeed.
He said, I think, that it would be a sorry day,
or something to that effect, when loyal men
could not take part in a Church parade. This
question does not condemn ordinary Church
parades by military forces. We have all
taken part in these. We have nothing
to prick our consciences with on that. What
we object to is that prior to or after the
Church parade there is an inspection-a
military inspection to which the Government
lends its aid, to which the head of the force
goes down and gives his official sanction.
This is very aggravating, and is causing very
great pain to the people of Ulster. We know
also that prior to these parades there were
people going through many sections of
Ulster trying to institute parades on Sunday.
I suppose the idea is that it is an ideal day,
and because the people are not doing manual
work on Sundays they will go to these
parades. The man who gives such a reply
does not deserve the name of Ulsterman. He
does not understand the spirit of Ulster. He
does not realise the deep convictions which
are held on this matter. Remember, a man
will not rob God in order to save himself.
That is not the way in which Ulster has been
built up and held. That is not the way it is
going to be held. In breaking the Decalogue,
and in working for material considerations.
you are not going to have the blessing of

been very good to us in taking care of Ulster.
It has not been through the brilliancy of our

the mercy of God that saved us. It was His

Mr. M'GUFFIN: In one sense I much regret that this matter has obtruded itself on
the House. It has created a very big
impression, and one must speak with respect.
I was as rigidly brought up as any Member
of this House in Sabbath observance. I had
to attend my Church, and undergo a sort of
Church parade, too. We were paraded to see

cleaned to go to church, and what is that
but a parade before church? I am rather
surprised that this matter takes hold of the
hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh
(Mr. Coote) in such a way, because more
serious happenings have been taking place
throughout the Kingdom, happenings that
have stirred me a great deal more than a
mere parade of the police forces. Those who
have been living in London, like Members of
this House who represent constituencies at
Westminster, must be aware of the fact that
the County Council has issued a notification that all sorts of sports can take place in
the public parks. You can have tennis,
cricket, and football and any other sort of
game in the public parks in London, and there
has been no serious protest from the nation.
In fact, you have hardly heard any dissent.
Some persons tried to raise a furore over it
in the Press, and absolutely failed, because
the people have altered their attitude absolutely with respect to this matter. If there is
anything upon which we as a people have been
misled more than another it is the idea that
we were made for the Sabbath rather than
the Sabbath for us. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) He who made the Day
is greater than the Day. It is not
the day, but the way we comport ourselves and conduct ourselves during the

To raise this question in this House in my
opinion is like straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel. It is one of those punctilios

in the Supreme Being not because of the institution of the Sabbath, but because of the

which appeals to me more-aye, even morethan the Decalogue. If my hon. Friend (Mr.

through the corn fields and He rubbed the
ears of corn and fed Himself from them to
show that there were considerations that must
be taken into thought when man proposes to
interpret what is called the Law of God. These
strictures with regard to these things are
doing harm. The whole position has been

MINUTES OF INSPECTORS' AND
TEACHERS' MERIT MARKS.
1. Mr. M'BRIDE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Minister of Education if it
is a fact that copies of Minutes of Inspectors'
EEee
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. M'Bride].
and Teachers' Merit Marks in National
Schools have been forwarded to Larne Urban
Council, and, if so, why it has been done; if
these Reports are sent out to all Councils for
Schools in their area; how long this Rule
has been in force; and whether these Reports are not confidential and for the information of Manager, Teachers, and
Ministry's officers.
The MINISTER OF
FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In the absence of my hon. Friend,
the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry
of Education, I have been deputed to reply
to the question of the hon. Member.
The Larne Urban Council, as successors to
the Town Commissioners, are the Trustees of
the Kirkpatrick Endowments under Endowment Scheme No. 204, framed under the
Educational Endowments (Ireland) Act, 1885.
Under the terms of that Act and the Endowment Scheme framed thereunder the Trustees
or Governors of the Schemes are entitled to
receive the Inspector's Report on the schools
included in their respective Schemes.
The Reports so furnished to the Secretaries
of the Schemes include the Inspector's
Minute on the General Inspection and a copy
of the Table showing the efficiency of instruction by each teacher in each subject
taught by him.
These documents are confidential and are
for the information of the Managers,
Teachers, Ministry's officers, and Governors
or Trustees of the Endowment, and are not
sent to any Councils not entitled to them.
ESTATE DUTY.
Mr. MARK (by Private Notice) asked the
Minister of Finance whether in case of a
person dying domiciled in Northern Ireland
leaving assets in England and Scotland as
well as in Northern Ireland, Estate Duty on
the assets in England and Scotland as well as
on those in Northern Ireland has to be paid
before any Grant of representation will be
issued; whether before such assets in England and Scotland can be dealt with Estate
Duty in England and Scotland respectively
has to be again paid; whether in order to
relieve such hardship and loss by such double
payment and unnecessary realisation of
capital to pay such duties some arrangement
cannot be male to get over the expense of
obtaining a refund of such double duty.
Mr. POLLOCK: The points raised by the
hon. Member have already been under consideration and were very fully discussed between officials of my Ministry and members
of the Northern Law Society shortly after the
date when the powers of assessing and collecting Estate Duty were transferred to the
Northern Government. The position is that
in the case of a person dying domiciled in
Northern Ireland, Estate Duty must be paid
in Northern Ireland on all his movable
assets wherever situate, but under Section 28
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, the
Ministry of Finance, on being satisfied that
Estate Duty is payable in Great Britain in
respect of any property situate in Great
Britain and passing on such death, shall
allow a sum equal to the amount of that Duty
to be deducted from the Estate Duty payable
in Northern Ireland in respect of that property. Before the grant issued in Northern
Ireland can be resealed in Great Britain,
Estate Duty must be paid in Great Britain
on the personal estate situate there. It follows, therefore, that if the accountable
parties elect to obtain the grant in Northern
Ireland before they have passed in Great
Britain the Schedules relating to the assets
situate in England or Scotland, a double payment of Estate Duty must be made in respect
of the assets in Great Britain.
Now, as to the remedy. This difficulty can,
however, be avoided by paying the Duty in
respect of assets situate in Great Britain
first, and thereafter having the grant of such
Duty deducted from the assessment of Estate
Duty made in Northern Ireland. This is the
course which has been recommended to the
Northern Law Society, and which, in most
cases, is in practice adopted. It will be observed that the adoption of this course
obviates the necessity for the payment of any
of the Duty twice.

PAYMENT OF MALICIOUS INJURY
CLAIMS.
Mr. M'GUFFIN (by private notice) asked
the Prime Minister whether in a statement
recently made by him he mentioned the fact
that £750,000 had been obtained in alleviation
of rates in Beifast, and if this sum is restricted to Belfast, or does it include other
local bodies?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I am glad to have the opportunity of correcting an error, which I rather imagine was
occasioned by the fact that my voice was not
very well heard at the reporters' table at the
meeting at which I made the statement.
What I intended to say, at all events, was
that Belfast would receive its proportion of
the £750,000 in alleviation of rates. I did not
intend at that time to make a full statement
with regard to the matter, but the £750,000
is the second moiety of the £1,500,000 that has
been granted by the British Government to
this Government to disburse to the authorities where the cases have been approved for
meeting charges for malicious injuries, and,
of course, the counties as well as the city of
Belfast come into that arrangement, just in
exactly the same position as they came under
the arrangement whereby £750,000 was paid
in June of the current year to meet the half
of the damage done up to the 14th of January
of this year. I am very glad to have this
opportunity of fully explaining the matter.
I intended to use the words their proportion of the £750,000."

Mr. M'GUFFIN: Im very much obliged.
Mr. DONALD: I want to be clear on that
answer. Do I understand that the Prime
Minister made it perfectly clear that this
£750,000 is the second sum, or half of the
£1,500,000 that was granted to the local authorities to meet fifty per cent. of the cost of
malicious injuries?
The PRIME MINISTER: I thought I had
made myself perfectly clear. The £1,500,000
was promised by the Government.
Mr. DONALD: In two instalments?
The PRIME MINISTER: It was promised
in two instalments, but my hon. Friend (Mr.
Donald), who is acquainted with the proce
dure in the Parliament at Westminster, will
recognise that only £750,000, or the first
moiety of that amount, was granted in this
year's Estimates, and therefore this £750,000
had to be confirmed by the present Government to be voted for next year. That has
been done, and I have received an assurance
from the Government that that will be met
as an honourable obligation, and the £750,000
will be paid on the 1st June of the coming
year, and applications will be received on
the 1st July of the coming year for the disbursement of the money.

Standing Order 97.-(Time for Presenting

No petition praying to be heard upon the
merits against any Local Bill or Provisional Order Confirmation Bill shall be received unless the same is presented by being
deposited in the Office of the Clerk of the
Parliaments before three o'clock in the
afternoon, in the case of Local Bills on or
before the twelfth day of February, and in
the case of Provisional Order Confirmation
Bills or of Local Bills not presented within
the required time on or before the tenth
day after the day on which such Bill has
been read a first time in the House of Commons.

The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS
(Mr. Moles): I beg to move the amendment
standing in my name. The object of the
amendment is to correct what was clearly a
disadvantage. Suppose Parliament should
meet in January, and all the parties to a Bill
be ready to go on, and desirous of going on,
as the Standing Order now reads they cannot
proceed until the day mentioned in the
Standing Order. It is obvious that that prejudices their position, and it is desirable to
remove that obstacle out of their way. That
is the object of the amendment. I beg to
move.
Amendment agreed to.
