PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A Message was delivered by the Gentleman
Usher of the Black Rod, as followeth :-
I am commanded by the Senate to inform this Honourable House that the
Speech of His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland, proroguing this present Parliament, is to be communicated
in the Senate forthwith, and, further, I
am commanded to invite this Honourable House to attend in the Senate in
order to hear the said Speech.
The House went, and having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the Clark's
place at the Table): I have to inform the
House that the House has been to the Senate,
where the Speaker of the Senate communicated His Grace's Speech to both Houses of
Parliament, as follows:-
HIS GRACE'S SPEECH.
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons:
The Second Session of your Parliament,
which closes to-day, will be memorable in
the history of Northern Ireland; for during
that Session you have exercised, in accordance with the powers conferred upon you
by the Imperial Parliament, the right to
remain outside the Irish Free State.
By taking this step you have retained
the representation of Northern Ireland in
the Imperial Parliament, which, therefore,
remains responsible for safeguarding your
interests in regard to all Imperial questions.
Consequent upon the severance of the
Irish Free State from the United Kingdom
the office of Lord Lieutenant for Ireland
has ceased to exist, and a separate
Governor has had to be appointed for Northern Ireland. His Majesty has conferred
upon me the honour of being your first
Governor, a position which I highly appreciate as an Ulsterman and as one who has
been closely associated with you all my life.
I am gratified that the measures adopted
for restoring law and order in the Province
have been crowned with success, in achieving which both the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the Special Constabulary have to
be congratulated; they have won the confidence of all classes of the community.
I am pleased to learn that unemployment
in Northern Ireland, although still serious,
is gradually becoming somewhat less acute.
Its full effects have been mitigated by the
legislation which you have passed, in common with the Imperial Parliament, enabling you to provide, in co-operation with
public bodies in Belfast and Northern Ireland, relief schemes for a considerable
number of ex-servicemen as well as others.
Further, the Government, by providing
credit facilities, hope to encourage com-
His Grace's Speech. 1224
Prorogation.
14 DECEMBER 1922.
mercial undertakings with a view to
unemployed persons being absorbed in
industries as quickly as possible.
Happily there are indications of a steady
though slow improvement in trade which,
beginning in the shipyards, is extending to
other staple industries. Not only have
active steps been taken by the Government
to assist this revival in trade, but it is
satisfactory to observe that many misconceptions in Great Britain and abroad regarding the high commercial standing of
Northern Ireland have been removed.
I trust that the great operations in
connection with the provision of the Parliamentary and other buildings for the
Province, which have just been started,
will make rapid progress.
Northern Ireland has been faced with
exceptional difficulties in regard to the
agricultural industry, difficulties which
affect a very large proportion of the community. The Act which has been passed
to endeavour to preserve a high standard
in cattle-breeding will, I have no doubt,
prove beneficial to your farmers by maintaining the prestige which Ulster has
acquired in Great Britain by the excellence
of her live stock, and of her other agricultural produce.
During the past Session you have passed
24 Acts of Parliament, some designed to
bring your laws into conformity with those
prevailing in Great Britain, from which
they formerly differed, and all of importance in making effective the administration of Government in Northern Ireland.
Members of the House of Commons:
I thank you for the provision of supplies
for the public services, and I congratulate
you on the fact that your financial position
is so sound, in spite of many adverse
factors.
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons:
I am glad to learn that the necessary
preliminary investigations in regard to
education and licensing reform are now so
far advanced that it is hoped it may be
possible to introduce legislation on these
subjects during the next Session.
I desire to express the earnest hope that
the time may not be far distant when the
Executive of the Irish Free State and the
Executive of Northern Ireland may meet
to settle in amicable conference those outstanding questions which affect the welfare
of both areas.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty God
may rest upon your labours.
After which the Proclamation for the
Proroguing of Parliament was read as followeth :-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
Proroguing the present Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided in effect by the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, as modified
by and in pursuance of the Irish Free State
(Consequential Provisions) Act, 1922, as from
the date of the presentation of such Address
as is referred to in the last-mentioned Act,
that the Governor of Northern Ireland shall
in His Majesty's name summon, prorogue,
and dissolve the Parliament of Northern
Ireland:
And whereas it is desirable that this present
Parliament of Northern Ireland should be
prorogued to the Twenty-seventh day of
February, One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty-three:
Now I, James Albert Edward, Duke of
Abercorn, Governor of Northern Ireland, by
this Proclamation do publish and declare His
Majesty's pleasure that the said Parliament
be, as from the reading of this Proclamation
in the Parliament of Northern Ireland,
prorogued to Tuesday, the Twenty-seventh
day of February, One Thousand Nine
Hundred and Twenty-three.
And I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal will and pleasure to be that
the said Parliament shall, on the said
Twenty-seventh day of February, One
Thousand Nine Hundred and Twenty-three,
assemble and be holden for the despatch of
divers urgent and important matters, and the
Senators and Members of the House of
Prorogation.

End of Session.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Commons of Northern Ireland are hereby
required to give their attendance accordingly.
Given at Belfast this Twelfth day of
December, 1922.
(Signed),
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
[End of the Second Session (opened

Tuesday, 14th March, 1922) of the First
Parliament of Northern Ireland, in the
thirteenth year of the Reign of His Majesty King George the Fifth.]
